en: Preface to the Re-engraved Record of the Words of Ancient Venerable Masters:
The past was thus and so; the present is thus and so; the future will be thus and so. Alas for these poor fellows!
Without cause, the Yellow-faced Old Man [Śākyamuni] plucked a flower and winked his eye, and the Golden-haired Ascetic [Kāśyapa] could not restrain himself and broke into laughter.
Yi (The Trigram for Nourishment). Unconsciously, there is leakage. When one person transmits what is empty, ten thousand people transmit it as real.

When will this ever end? Human faculties have their sharpness and dullness; thus, the responsive words have their opening and closing. Like acupuncture, moxibustion, medicine, and tonics, those with chronic ailments are suddenly revived.
Expanding and unfolding freely, the Great Void leaves no trace. Although used by the ancients, time knows neither past nor present. Walking alive upon a dead road; a dead game brought back to life.

Living, one contemplates and gives rise to awakening, like a dragon finding water; thus it is said that language is the vessel for carrying the Way, which even Buddhas and Patriarchs could not discard.
From the verses of the Seven Buddhas to the thirty-three transmissions in India and this land, their branches and lineages have proliferated beyond measure.
As for the evidence of their transmission and reception, as well as the expositions and instructions revealed in the *Lamp of the Lineage*, they are all clearly recorded.

However, many records remained incomplete and were often scattered. Later, the Abbot Yizang extensively searched for and collected materials, eventually securing the instructional sermons of twenty-two masters beginning with Nanquan.
Subsequently, he further obtained those of several other houses, including Yunmen, Zhenjing, Foyan, and Fozhao.
These were collectively titled *The Sayings of Ancient Honored Elders*, rather than being limited to [the original core].
This is so. My remarks are based merely on what I have searched out and gathered. Now, the ancients used intimacy because they had attained intimacy;
they spoke of practice because they had reached its realization. What they spoke of was like the weapons of a state, employed only when there is no other choice.

From the highest antiquity down to the present, those who act for others value nothing more than having "correct eyes. How could this be like the petty, derivative practice of carving wood to draw flowers, or engraving shells to carve clams—blindly imitating the forms while missing the essence?
This is something that can only be spoken of in the same breath as the Eye [of the Dharma]. Layman Juexin emerged from among the ranks of virtuous women;
he maintained the resolute will and integrity of a heroic man, remaining unobstructed by wealth and status and untethered by worldly appearances.

Clad in the robes of Vimalakīrti and seated in the chamber of Vimalakīrti’s son, he dwelt in right samādhi, maintaining mindfulness whether moving or still. Who was it that caused him to be thus? It is said that this was the work of the ancient masters compiled by Yi.

The text was originally printed in Minzhong, but the woodblocks have long since worn away. As it is difficult for monasteries throughout the two provinces of Zhejiang to obtain it, [the donor] courageously contributed his own funds to carve new blocks for its circulation.
He commissioned Zen monks to perform a meticulous collation and re-carving, and did not disdain my request for a preface. Alas! How extraordinary this is.
In the past, the Maiden Candrottarā challenged Śāriputra and brought forth the illumination of the Great Nirvāṇa; Ātreyī confronted Mañjuśrī...

Śrī. Regarding the meaning of "neither born through birth nor dying through death," since the Dharma arrived in China, there have been many among the virtuous women and the various great elders of spontaneous capacity who have revealed the Ultimate.
In recent times, Lady Ji of the Qin state and the Daoist Master of the Empty Chamber both belonged to families of noble lineage yet became kin to Prajñāpāramitā. Now, Jue...
The Master Xin then expounded upon the pivotal words of the ancient masters to perpetuate the seed of the Buddha. "There is no duality, nor is there any division;
there is no distinction, nor is there any interruption. Juexin Wei was the granddaughter of the late Prime Minister Wenjie of the Xiangshou era and the wife of Yu Wenchang.
As the abbot’s seat at the Xiuying Zhulin Hermitage remained vacant, she appointed Jielin Jie Wuyan to oversee the transition and formally invite the master to preside over the hermitage.
Jue Xin remarked, "The abbot is right there in the hermitage; why can he not be seen? To say he exists is to deny him;

to say he does not exist is to find him nonetheless. He is neither near nor far. When you lift your head, the hawk has already flown to Silla. If you can penetrate this, you have attained realization.
While eating a bowl of noodles, many verses were produced; all were attained without deliberate calculation.
Thus, throughout daily life, there is nothing that is not the joy of dhyāna-pleasure and the delight of the Dharma. All are presented here together.
Written on the Qingming Festival in the spring of the Dingmao year of the Sacred Song Xianchun era, at Ayuwang Monastery in Mingzhou Prefecture, Jiangzhe and other regions.
Preface by the Śramaṇa Wuchu Daguan, Abbot of Guangli Chan Temple on Mount Shan. The eminent masters of the Tang and Song dynasties transmitted the Buddha-mind lineage;

their Way was vast and their virtue complete. Within their quarters, they bestowed instructions and interrogated scholars. Their citations, selections, and responses were all endowed with "opportune words" (yijuyu). These have long been disseminated throughout the world.
Only the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) has ever been granted entry into the Imperial Canon. As for these various masters...

Regarding these records, those that could not be fully included in the *Chuanteng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) were compiled by the Abbot Cezhi into a separate collection comprising more than twenty houses,
including Nanquan, Zhaozhou, Huangbo, Linji, Yunmen, Zhenjing, Foyan, and Dongshan, totaling several volumes.
It is titled *The Sayings of Ancient Honored Elders*. This truly provides great benefit to the School of the Lineage.
*Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Elders*, Volume One;
First Generation under the Great Mirror (Dajian).
The Chan Master Da Hui of Nanyue, whose name was Huairang, was a native of Jinzhou. His secular surname was Du.
He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yifeng era. A white vapor manifested as an auspicious sign in the celestial phenomena over the region of Ankang;

the Grand Astrologer observed this and subsequently reported it to Emperor Gaozong. The Emperor then asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Grand Astrologer replied: [...the remainder of the text...]

A vessel of the state’s Dharma who remained unstained by worldly glory, Emperor Dezong issued an imperial edict for Han Jie, the Governor of Jinzhou, to personally go and offer condolences to his family.
The family had three sons, of whom the Master was the youngest; he was already three years old and possessed a brilliant and extraordinary nature, characterized by kindness and deference.
His father accordingly named him Huairang. By the time he reached the age of ten, he took sole delight in Buddhist scriptures. At that time, there were three...

Zang Xuanjing passed by his house and, seeing him, marveled at his extraordinary appearance. He told the boy’s parents, "If this child leaves the household life, he will surely attain the Supreme Vehicle and extensively deliver sentient beings.
In the third year of the Chuigong era, when the boy was fifteen years old, he took leave of his parents and went to Yuyuan Temple in Jingzhou.
There, he relied upon Vinaya Master Hongjing to receive ordination. In the second year of the Tongtian era, he received the full precepts. Subsequently, he studied the *Vibhāṣā*.
One day, Nizang sighed to himself, saying, "As for those who have left the household life, they seek the unconditioned Dharma; there is nothing superior to this, whether in the heavens or among men.
At that time, his fellow student Tanran, knowing that his teacher’s aspirations were lofty and far-reaching, urged him to go together to pay respects to Chan Master An of Mount Song.
After An had inspired and awakened him, Nizang proceeded directly to Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch asked, "What [is it]?"
"Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come from the place of Venerable An of Songshan. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? The Master was speechless.
He remained there for eight years until, suddenly, he attained realization. He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached a point of understanding."
The Patriarch asked, “How is it? The Master said, “To describe it as a single thing is not correct. The Patriarch asked, “Is there still anything to be cultivated or realized?
The Master said, “There is nothing that is not to be cultivated and realized; however, one must not be defiled.
The Patriarch said, “This very state of being undefiled is the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. Since you are thus, I am also thus. (The twenty-seventh patriarch of India.)
The Patriarch Prajñātāra prophesied of you, saying: "Though China is vast, there is no other path; it must be traversed by the feet of your descendants.

When the golden cock understands how to hold a single grain of millet in its beak, he shall offer it to the Arhat-monks of Shifang. (Furthermore, the prophecy concerning the transmission to Dàoyī says:

"If one can conceal matters within the heart, speak them by the banks of the Han River. Plunging into the lake waves to seek the moon in the water, one shall illuminate two or three people."—The Patriarch.
He said: "The former Master has spoken thus: 'From this day forward, do not transmit this robe; transmit only the Dharma.

If you transmit this robe, your life will be like a thread hanging from a string; show only the transformation of the Way. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout.
Once the essence of the flower is suddenly realized, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously attained. After you, there shall emerge a colt."
"Treading upon and killing all people under heaven must reside within your own mind; there is no need to speak of it hastily. The Master served him for fifteen years.

In the second year of the Xuān-tiàn era of the Táng dynasty, he first departed for Nányuè Mountain, where he resided at Bānrùo Monastery. He instructed his disciples, saying: "All myriad dharmas arise from the mind.
The mind has nothing from which it arises, and dharmas have nothing in which they abide. If one penetrates the ground of the mind, whatever one does will be without obstruction."
This is not for those of superior faculties; one must be careful with one’s words! A monk asked, "When a mirror is used to cast an image, once the image has been formed, where does the light go?
The Master said, "When you, Venerable Sir, had not yet left the household life, where did the appearance of the temple go?
The monk asked, "After it was formed, why does it no longer reflect? The Master said, "Although it does not reflect, it cannot deceive him by even a single point."
Mazu resided at the Chuanfa Monastery on Mount Nanyue. He lived alone in a single hermitage, practicing nothing but seated meditation.

He would not acknowledge anyone who came to visit him, nor did he acknowledge the Master when the latter went to see him. Observing that Mazu’s countenance and bearing were extraordinary, the Master recalled the prophecy of the Sixth Patriarch and began to guide him through various means.
One day, while the Master was grinding a brick in front of the hermitage, Mazu also [began to grind one].
He paid no heed. After a long time had passed, Mazu asked, "What are you doing? The Master said, "I am grinding it to make a mirror.
Mazu said, "How can grinding a tile produce a mirror? The Master said, "If grinding a tile cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation bring about Buddhahood?
Mazu then left his seat and asked, "What then is the way? The Master said, "It is like a cow pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, one beats the cow."
This is it. To strike the cart is precisely it. Furthermore, he said: "When you practice seated meditation, are you practicing to become a Buddha through sitting?

If you are practicing seated meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you are practicing to become a Buddha through sitting, a Buddha is not a fixed form. Regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject."
"If you sit as the Buddha, that is to kill the Buddha; if you grasp at the form of sitting, you have not realized its principle.
Upon hearing this instruction, Mazu was suddenly enlightened. He prostrated himself and asked, "How should I apply my mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi?"
The Master said, “You study the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, which is like a seed sown below. I preach the essentials of the Dharma, which is like the moisture from heaven.
Because your conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way. Mazu asked, “The Way has no form or appearance; how can it be perceived?
The Master said, “The Dharma-eye of the Mind-Ground can perceive the Way; the same is true for the formless samādhi. Mazu said, “There is...”
“Is there formation and destruction? The Master said, “If one perceives the Way through formation and destruction, gathering and dispersing, that is incorrect.
Listen to my verse: ‘The ground of mind contains all seeds; When meeting moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless; What is destroyed, and what is formed?
Once Mazu had received this awakening, his mind was transcendent. He attended the Master for ten years, becoming increasingly profound day by day. The Master—
There were six入室 (入室) disciples. Each was certified with the words: "You six have collectively realized my person;
each of you has attained one aspect. One attained my eyebrows—excellent in dignified demeanor (Chang Hao). One attained my eyes—excellent in his glances (Ji Da).
One person obtained my ears; he was skilled at listening to principles (serene and open). One person obtained my nose; he was skilled at knowing the vital breath (spiritually illuminating).
One person obtained my tongue; he was skilled at discourse (dignified and stern). One person obtained my mind; he was skilled in the ancient and modern (the oneness of the Way).
Later, when Mazu was propagating his teachings at Kaiyuan Temple in Jiangxi, the Master asked the assembly, "Does Daoyi preach the Dharma for the community? The assembly replied: [He does].
[The Master] had already preached the Dharma for the assembly. The Teacher said, "I have not yet seen a single message of realization come through. He then dispatched a monk, instructing him:
"When he ascends the hall, simply ask him, 'What is it? and remember his answer when you return. The monk followed these instructions and returned.
He reported this to his teacher, Mazu, who said, "Since the time of chaos, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce. The Master approved of this.

On the eleventh day of the eighth month in the third year of the Tianbao era, the Master passed away at Mount Nanyue. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dahui, and his stupa was named Zuishenglun.
Gui Deng, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, composed the inscription for the stupa.
The Second Generation under Dajian [Huineng] was Chan Master Mazu Daichi. The Master’s name was Daoyi; he was a native of Shifang in Hanzhou. His secular surname was Ma.
His dharma lineage spread throughout the world in Jiangxi, and thus he was known at the time as Mazu. A question was asked: "What is the cultivation of the Way? The Master said:
He said: "The Way does not belong to cultivation. If one says it is attained through cultivation, then once cultivated, it will again perish;

this is the same as the Śrāvakas. If one says it is not cultivated, then one is the same as an ordinary person. [The questioner] asked: "What kind of insight must one have to attain the Way? He replied: "The self-nature is originally complete.
One is called a practitioner of the Way simply by not being obstructed by matters of good and evil. To grasp at the good and reject the evil, or to contemplate emptiness, [is not the Way]."
Entering meditative absorption already belongs to the realm of conditioned activity; if one further pursues it outwardly, one becomes increasingly estranged and distant from the truth.
Simply exhaust the mental constructs (*cittamātra*) of the triple world: a single moment of deluded thought is the very root of birth and death within the triple world.

If one is free from even a single moment of such thought, the root of birth and death is eliminated, and one attains the unsurpassed, precious jewel of the Dharma King. For immeasurable eons, ordinary beings have been bound by deluded thoughts.
Flattery, crookedness, depravity, falsehood, self-conceit, and arrogance combine to form a single entity. Therefore, a sutra says: "This body is merely composed of various dharmas;
when it arises, only dharmas arise; when it ceases, only dharmas cease. When these dharmas arise, they do not say 'I arise'; when they cease, they do not say 'I cease.
The preceding thought, the succeeding thought, and the intermediate thought—moment by moment, they do not wait for one another. Moment by moment...

This quiescence is called the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). It encompasses all phenomena, just as hundreds of thousands of diverse streams all return to the great ocean and are collectively termed "ocean water.
Abiding in this single flavor, it subsumes all flavors; abiding in the great ocean, it blends all currents.
It is like a person bathing in the great ocean who makes use of all its waters. Thus, the delusions and awakenings of the śrāvakas... [the ordinary beings...]
Now, regarding delusion and enlightenment: the Śrāvakas do not know that the Sage’s mind is fundamentally devoid of stages, cause and effect, or gradations.

They cultivate causes and realize fruits through the conceptual imaginings of their own mental scope (*cittamātra*). Though they may dwell in empty concentration for eighty thousand or twenty thousand kalpas, even if they have attained awakening, they subsequently fall back into delusion.
To the various Bodhisattvas, such states appear as painful as hell; they sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence, failing to perceive the Buddha-nature. If one is of the highest...

Sentient beings with dull faculties may suddenly encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who provides instruction; they then attain realization in a single stroke of speech, bypassing all successive stages and positions.
They thus achieve sudden awakening to their original nature. Therefore, a sutra states: "Ordinary worldlings possess a regressive mind, whereas śrāvakas do not."
To speak of awakening for those who are deluded: since there is fundamentally no delusion, awakening itself cannot be established.
All sentient beings, from immeasurable kalpas past, have not emerged from the samādhi of dharmatā; they have long remained within this samādhi of dharmatā.

Whether putting on clothes or eating food, speaking or responding to others, employing the six sense faculties, or performing any activity whatsoever—all are entirely dharmatā. Failing to understand how to return to the source, they follow after names.

Chasing after appearances, deluded emotions falsely arise, creating all manner of karmic deeds. If you can, for even a single thought-moment, reflect back upon yourself, your entire being will be the sacred mind.
All of you, each realize your own mind; do not merely memorize my words. Even if you were to explain as many principles as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would be of no avail.
That mind neither increases; it cannot be said to be attained. That mind neither decreases; it can be said to be attained, and it can also be said not to be attained.
Even manifesting divided bodies, emitting light, and displaying the eighteen transformations, it is not as good as returning me my dead ashes.
Dead ashes that have already been soaked are powerless; this is a metaphor for the śrāvakas who falsely cultivate causes and realize fruits—those who have not yet been soaked.
The power of extinguished ashes remains; this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s path and practice having reached full maturity, such that no evils can defile them.

If one were to explain the Tathāgata’s provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka, they could not be exhausted even after explaining for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; they are like hooks and chains, never severed.
Yet, if one awakens to the Sage’s mind, there is ultimately nothing else remaining. I shall take my leave now; farewell.
Ascending the hall, Layman Pang asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
The Master said, "Wait until you can gulp down all the waters of the West River in a single draught, and then I will tell you. He asked again, "The original body is not obscured;
I pray the Master will cast his eyes high. The Master looked straight down. The Layman said, "Of all the stringless lutes, only the Master can play them with such wondrous skill."
The Master went straight up to look at him. The Layman bowed. The Master returned to his quarters. The Layman followed after him and said, "Just now, my cleverness turned into clumsiness.
[The Layman] asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "This very mind is the Buddha. [The Layman] asked: "Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations..."
The monk requested, "I pray that the Master will directly point out the meaning of the West. The Master said, "I have no mind for this today.
Go and ask Zhizang at Xitang. The monk went to Xitang and asked him. Xitang pointed to his head and said, "I have a headache today."
"I cannot explain it for you. Go and ask your elder brother Hai. The monk went and asked Elder Brother Hai.
Elder Brother Hai said, "When I arrived here, I did not understand. The monk returned and reported this to the Master. The Master said, "Zangtou’s head is white; Hai’s head is black.
While the Master was gathering vines, he saw Daluo approaching and made a gesture of letting go. Daluo stepped forward to receive him, whereupon the Master immediately kicked him down.
When the floodwaters receded, he let out a great laugh and said, "Countless wondrous meanings and hundreds of thousands of samādhis are all contained within the tip of a single hair.
Once you recognize this source, you are free. The Master then ordered a monk to deliver a letter to Venerable Qian of Mount Jing.
In the letter, he drew a perfect circle. As soon as Venerable Qian opened it and saw it, he asked for a brush and placed a single dot inside the circle. Later, there was a monk who...
He related this to National Teacher Zhong, who said, "Master Qin is still being deluded by Master Ma.

[The Master] asked, "Why did you say, 'This very mind is Buddha'? The Master replied, "To stop a small child from crying. [The Master] asked, "What about when the crying has stopped? The Master replied, "'Neither mind nor Buddha.
[The Master] asked, "When someone comes who is neither of these two types, how do you instruct them? The Master replied, "I point it out to them..."
"The Way is not a thing. [The monk] asked, "If one suddenly encounters someone who has realized it, what then? The Master said, "First, let him experience the Great Way for himself.
[The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "Right now, what is this meaning?
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Hunan. The Master said, "Is the water in Donghu Lake full yet? He replied, "Not yet. The Master [said, "... (text fragment ends).
Yun said, "After all this time, the rainwater has not yet filled it. Daowu said, "It is full. Yunyan said, "It is profoundly still. Dongshan said, "In what kalpa has it ever been lacking?"
Again, he asked: "Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a boat of ten thousand *hu*. How is this principle to be understood? The Master said:

"In this place there is neither water nor boat; what talk can there be of sinews and bones? One evening, while Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan were attending him as they gazed at the moon, the Master asked:
"At this very moment, how is it? Xitang said: "It is precisely the time for making offerings. Baizhang said: "Precisely..."
"Excellent practice. Quan shook his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "The Sutras return to the Canon; Zen returns to the sea. Only Puyan alone transcends the mundane world.
The Master asked Baizhang, "By what Dharma do you instruct people? Baizhang held up his whisk. The Master said, "Is it only this, or is there something else?
Baizhang threw down the whisk. A monk asked, "How can one attain accord with the Way?"
The Master said, "I should not have spoken at all. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The Master struck him and said, "If I had not struck you, people everywhere would laugh at me. A junior disciple, Danyuan, returned from his travels and drew a circle before the Master.
He then prostrated himself upon it and stood up. The Master said, "Do you wish to become a Buddha? He replied, "I do not."
He pinched the monk’s eye. The Master said, “I am not your equal. The junior monk did not respond.
A lecturing monk arrived and asked, “I wonder, what Dharma does the Chan school transmit and uphold? The Master instead asked, “What Dharma do you, O Seat-Master, transmit and uphold?
The lecturer replied, “I am fortunate enough to have lectured on more than twenty treatises and sutras. The Master said, “Are you not a lion cub? The lecturer replied, “I dare not say so.”
The Master made a sound like a sighing breath. The Host said, "This is the Dharma. The Master asked, "What Dharma is this?
The Host said, "The Dharma of the lion emerging from its cave. The Master remained silent. The Host said, "This too is the Dharma.

The Master asked, "What Dharma is this? The Host said, "The Dharma of the lion remaining in its cave. The Master asked, "Neither emerging nor entering—what Dharma is this? The Host had no reply. (Bai Zhang)
[The Master] said, "Do you see? The Dharma Master then took his leave and stepped out the door. The Master called out, "Dharma Master! The Master turned his head. The Master asked, "What is it?
The Dharma Master had no reply. The Master said, "This dull-witted monk. The Inspector of Hengzhou asked, "Is it right to eat meat and drink wine, or is it not?
The Master replied, "If you eat, it is the official’s emolument; if you do not eat, it is the official’s merit. The Master [continued].
He had one hundred and thirty-nine入室 (入室) disciples, each of whom became a patriarch in their own region, transforming beings without end.
In the first month of the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, the Master ascended Mount Shimen in Jianchang and was walking in meditation within the forest.
Seeing that the caves and ravines were level and smooth, he said to his attendant, "This withered body of mine shall return to this place next month.
Having finished speaking, he turned back. Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness. The head of the monastery asked, "How is the Master’s health these days?"
The Master said: "Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha. On the first day of the second month, he bathed, sat in the lotus posture, and entered nirvana.
During the Yuanhe era, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Daji, and his stupa was named Great Adornment (Dazhuangyan).
The third generation descendant of Dajian was Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai. He was a native of Changle, Fuzhou.

When Master [Baizhang] served as an attendant to the Great Master Ma, whenever a donor sent offerings of rice for the midday meal, as soon as the Master lifted the lid of the tray, the Great Master Ma would pick up a piece.
Huibian showed the assembly a *hubing* (a type of flatbread) and asked, "What is this? He did this every day for three years.
One day, while traveling as an attendant with Mazu along a road, they heard the cry of wild ducks. Mazu asked, "What sound is that? Huibian replied, "The cry of wild ducks."
After a long silence, Mazu asked, "Where did that sound just now go? The Master replied, "It flew away.
Mazu turned his head and seized the Master by the nose, causing him to cry out in pain. Mazu said, "And yet you say it flew away. At these words, the Master attained realization.
He returned to the attendant’s quarters and wept bitterly. His colleagues asked him, "Are you grieving for someone?"
"Are you ill? the Master asked. "No," the attendant replied. "Have you been scolded by someone? the Master asked. "No," the attendant replied. "Why are you crying? the Master asked.
"My nostrils were pinched so hard by the Great Master that the pain has not yet subsided," the attendant said. A colleague asked, "What was the cause for such a lack of harmony?
The attendant said, "You should ask the Master yourself. The colleague then asked the Master, "What did Attendant Hai do?"
Because the conditions were not harmonious, he wept in the quarters and said to the Abbot, "Please explain this for me.

The Master said, "He understands it; you should ask him yourself. When his companion returned to the quarters, he said, "The Abbot told me that you understand it, so he instructed me to ask you myself.
The Master then laughed heartily. The companion asked, "Just now you were weeping; why are you laughing now?"

He laughed. The Master said, "Just now you were weeping; now you are laughing. His fellow practitioners were bewildered. The next day, as soon as Mazu ascended the hall and sat down, the Master came forward and rolled up the bamboo mat.
Mazu immediately descended from his seat. The Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters, where Mazu said:
"Previously, I intended to cite this causal occasion for you to turn [the mind], yet why have you rolled up your mat?
The Master said, "Because my nose was aching. Mazu asked, "Where have you been coming from? The Master said, "Yesterday I happened to go out;
I did not manage to attend your teachings. Mazu gave a shout, and the Master then went out. One day Mazu asked the Master, "What..."
"Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come from behind the mountain. The Patriarch said, "Did you encounter anyone there? The Master said, "I did not encounter anyone."
The Patriarch said, “Why did you not encounter it? The Master said, “If I had encountered it, I would have presented it to the Abbot.
The Patriarch said, “From where did you get this news? The Master said, “It is my fault. The Patriarch said, “Rather, it is my own fault.
The Master went to visit Mazu again. Mazu held up his whisk. The Master said, “This very function—apart from this...”

[The Master] used it. The Patriarch hung the whisk back in its original place. After a long silence, the Patriarch said, "In the future, when you open your two flaps of skin [your mouth], with what will you provide for people?
The Master then took up the whisk and held it upright. The Patriarch said, "Is this the function? Is it apart from this function?
The Master then hung the whisk back in its original place. The Patriarch then gave a shout, which left the Master deaf for three days. Later, he resided at Hongzhou.
Mount Daxiong was so named because its rocky peaks and ridges rose to such extreme heights that it was called "Hundred Fathoms" (Bai Zhang).
Once he had settled there, before even a month had passed, guests seeking the profound mystery arrived from all directions like deer, with Guishan and Huangbo at their head.
One day, the Master said to the assembly, "The Buddha-dharma is no small matter. In the past, when I was struck by Mazu’s single shout, I was rendered speechless for three full days."

Extensive Record. Now, in speech one must distinguish between the monastic and the lay; one must recognize the terminology of the general and the specific; and one must recognize the terminology of the definitive and non-definitive teachings.

The definitive teachings clarify purity, while the non-definitive teachings clarify turbidity. By speaking of the defiled dharmas, their peripheral impurities, and by making such distinctions, one excludes the ordinary person.

The Dharma for declaring purity (*śuddhi-vyākaraṇa*) excludes the noble ones (*ārya*) and is taught according to the ninefold division of the scriptures (*navāṅga-śāsana*). For sentient beings who previously lacked the eye of wisdom, they must rely on a person to polish them.
If one were to speak before ordinary people who are like the deaf, one must simply instruct them to leave the household life, uphold the precepts, cultivate meditation, and study wisdom.
Even if the layperson is of superior capacity, one still must not speak to them in such a manner, as was the case with Vimalakīrti.

Regarding those such as Master Fu Dashi: if, in the presence of a śramaṇa, one says of another śramaṇa that he has already completed the *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal rite of four proclamations) and is fully endowed with the powers of morality, concentration, and wisdom, yet speaks further to him in such a manner, it is called "untimely speech" (*akālavāda*).

Speaking when it is not the proper time is also called "frivolous speech" (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). If one is a śramaṇa, one must speak concerning the boundaries of pure dharma; one must speak of detachment.
Phenomena such as existence and non-existence are free from all cultivation and realization, and are also free from detachment itself.

If one among the śramaṇas strips away habitual defilements yet the diseases of greed and hatred are not removed, they are called "deaf laypeople"; such individuals must also be taught to cultivate dhyāna and study wisdom.
If it is a member of the Two Vehicles whose diseases of greed and hatred have been exhausted and eliminated, they abide relying upon non-greed.
It is for this reason that it is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It obstructs the light of the Buddha and constitutes the shedding of the Buddha’s blood.

One must also instruct them to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and study wisdom (*prajñā*), and one must distinguish between pure and turbid speech. "Turbid dharmas" refers to various names such as greed, anger, craving, and grasping.
"Pure phenomena" refers to various names such as bodhi, nirvāṇa, and liberation. It is simply the present mirror-like awareness.

However, regarding the two currents of purity and turbidity, all dharmas of ordinary beings and sages, the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, and all mundane and supramundane dharmas—[it is this very awareness].
One must not have even the slightest trace of attachment or grasping. Since there is no attachment or grasping, one relies upon and abides in non-attachment, taking this to be the truth;
this is the "goodness of the beginning. This is the state of a mind established in discipline; this is the person of the Śrāvaka; this is the person who clings to the raft and refuses to abandon it;

this is the path of the Two Vehicles; this is the fruit of *dhyāna*. Since there is neither attachment nor grasping, nor does one rely upon and abide in non-attachment, this is the "goodness of the middle."

This is the teaching of half-syllables; it is still like the formless realm. One may avoid falling into the path of the two vehicles, yet one avoids falling into the path of the demonic hordes only because this remains a sickness of *dhyāna*—a bondage for Bodhisattvas.
When one neither relies on nor clings to anything, and furthermore does not even form a conceptual understanding of such non-reliance, this is the "goodness at the end.
This is the teaching of full-syllables; it avoids falling into the formless realm and avoids falling into the sickness of *dhyāna*.

One avoids falling into the vehicle of the bodhisattvas and avoids falling into the station of the Māra kings, because of the obstacles of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the stages (*bhūmyāvaraṇa*), and the practices (*caryāvaraṇa*).

One perceives one's own buddha-nature as clearly as seeing forms at night. As it is said regarding the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), two delusions are severed: first, the subtle delusion regarding the knowable (*sūkṣmajñeya-ajñāna-moha*).

2. The ignorance regarding the extremely subtle objects of knowledge (*paramāṇu-sūkṣma-jñeya-ajñāna*). Therefore, it is said that there is a person of great wisdom who tears open the dust to reveal the sutra scrolls.

If one can pass beyond these three phrases, one will not be governed by these three sections. The teachings provide an analogy: like a deer leaping through the net three times, such a person is called a Buddha outside the entanglements;
nothing can bind him. This belongs to the Buddhas subsequent to Dīpaṃkara; this is the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*).
This is the supreme wisdom. This stands upon the path of the Buddha. This person is a Buddha; they possess the Buddha-nature. They are the Teacher.
They are the one who brings about the wind of non-obstruction. They are unimpeded wisdom. Hereafter, they will be able to attain mastery over the merit and wisdom of cause and effect.
They act as a vehicle to transport cause and effect. Abiding in birth, they are not detained by birth; abiding in death, [they are not detained by death].
One is not obstructed by death. While abiding within the five aggregates, one is like a door that has been opened and is not hindered by the five aggregates;
going and staying are free, and entering and exiting are without difficulty.

If one can be thus, regardless of the high or low status of their station—even a body as small as an ant’s—so long as one can be thus, it is entirely a pure and wondrous land, inconceivable. This is still merely an intellectual understanding.

This is the language of binding. He himself has no sores; do not wound him. The sores of the Buddha and the sores of the Bodhisattvas consist solely in speaking of dharmas such as existence and non-existence—all of this is wounding.
Existence and non-existence govern all dharmas. The Ten Stages (daśabhūmi) are a river of turbid flow; the assembly makes it a clear stream.

To speak of the characteristics of vertical clarity and to speak of the faults and afflictions of turbidity—[this was directed] toward the ten great disciples of former times: Śāriputra, Pūrṇa... [and so forth].
Rāhula, Ānanda of right faith, and Sunakṣatra of wrong faith—each has their own standard and each has their own measure.
One by one, they were exposed by the Teacher. They are not like the Arhats of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis who dwell in concentration for eighty thousand kalpas;
they merely rely upon and cling to their own practices and are intoxicated by the wine of pure dharmas. Therefore, when the śrāvakas hear the Buddha...
Such a person cannot give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that those who have severed their roots of goodness lack Buddha-nature;
the Teaching describes them as being in a terrifying, deep pit of liberation. If the mind retreats for even a single thought-moment, one falls into hell as swiftly as an arrow shot.
Furthermore, one cannot categorically say they fall back, nor can one categorically say they do not fall back. Take for instance Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Śākyamuni;
when they returned to the stage of a *srotāpanna* to lead others of their own kind, one could not say they had fallen back.
At such a time, they were simply called "people of the *srotāpanna* stage. It is just like present-time discernment and awareness, provided that one is not affected by anything.
There is a conduit for all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, that penetrates the three phrases and transcends all conditions of favorability or adversity.
Even if one hears of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas appearing in the world, it is as if one has not heard them;

yet this is not a state of dwelling in non-hearing, nor does one form a conceptual understanding of such non-dwelling. To say that such a person "retreats" is impossible to calculate or measure, for one cannot grasp them. This is a Buddha.

To say that the Buddha dwells eternally in the world yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas, while claiming that he turns the wheel of the Dharma and then regresses, is likewise to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
To say that the Buddha does not turn the wheel of the Dharma and does not regress is likewise to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

Zhaò said: "The Way of Bodhi cannot be schemed or measured. It is so lofty that there is nothing above it; so vast that it has no limit. It is so profound that there is nothing below it; so deep that it cannot be fathomed."

"Measuring" is a verbal expression; it is like setting up a target only to draw an arrow upon it. To say that present awareness (*jianjue*) is still not [the truth] and to attempt to distinguish the clear from the turbid is entirely the teaching of demons.
To claim that there exists something other than this present awareness apart from what is perceived is also the teaching of demons.

To cling to this present awareness as being fixed is likewise the teaching of demons; it is called the doctrine of the Natural Heretics (*svabhāva-tīrthika*). This present awareness is itself the Buddha.
These are words of measurement; these are words of calculation. They are like the howling of a jackal and still belong to the realm of sticky glue.
Originally, one does not recognize that self-knowing and self-awakening are one's own Buddha, but instead runs outward in pursuit of a Buddha.

Using the teachings of a spiritual friend as medicine—namely, self-knowing and self-awakening—one treats the illness of running outward in pursuit. Once one no longer runs outward in pursuit, [the medicine is no longer needed].
When an illness has been cured, the medicine must be discarded. If one clings to self-knowledge and self-awakening, this is the sickness of *dhyāna*.

This is the ultimate *śrāvaka*, like water that has turned to ice; though the ice is entirely water, it is difficult to hope for it to quench thirst. It is also called a terminal illness, for which worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness.

From beginningless time, one has never not been a Buddha; do not, however, form a conceptual understanding of "Buddha. The Buddha is a medicine for the side of sentient beings; when there is no illness, there is no need for medicine.

Do not eat it. When both the medicine and the illness have vanished, it is like clear water. The Buddha is like licorice mixed with water, or like honey mixed with water; it is exceedingly sweet and delicious.
If one were to count it alongside clear water, it would not be attached [to that category]. It is not that this is non-existent; rather, it is what is inherently possessed.
It is also said that this principle is what all people inherently possess. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas call such a person "one who shows the pearl. From...
This "coming" is not a thing. There is no need to know it or understand it; there is no need to affirm it as being you or deny it as not being you.
Simply cut off the phrases of duality. Cut off the phrase of existence and the phrase of non-existence. Cut off the phrase of non-existence and the phrase of not-non-existence.
When the traces of duality do not appear, and when the two ends do not grasp at you, no measure or calculation can govern you. It is not a matter of deficiency. It is not...
It is complete. It is neither ordinary nor holy; neither luminous nor dark. It is not possessing knowledge, nor is it lacking knowledge.
It is neither bound nor liberated. It is none of the various names and designations. Why is it not true speech?
For how could one carve out the characteristics of a Buddha from empty space? Or how could one say that empty space is blue, yellow, red, or white?

It can be so accomplished. As it is said: "The Dharma has no peer, for there is nothing with which it may be compared. The Dharmakāya is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories;
therefore, it is said that the holy body is nameless. The principle of reality as it truly is cannot be expressed in words, and the gate of emptiness is difficult to enter.
It is like the *tāmra-kīṭa* (lac-insect) which can settle anywhere except upon a flame. Sentient beings are likewise; they can dwell everywhere...
It is able to take objects as its conditions, yet it alone cannot take Prajñā as its object.
To seek out a single point of knowledge or understanding by associating with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) is the "demon of the spiritual friend," for it gives rise to views based on words.

If one generates the Four Great Vows, vowing that one will first attain Buddhahood only after all sentient beings have been fully delivered, this is the "demon of the Bodhisattva’s dharma-wisdom"; such vows do not allow for abandonment.
Therefore, if one observes the precepts of fasting, cultivates dhyāna, and studies wisdom—these are tainted roots of goodness.

Even if one sits at the site of enlightenment, manifests the attainment of perfect awakening, and leads as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges to all realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, these are the roots of goodness of Māra.

Because of giving rise to attachment. If one is entirely free from defiled craving toward all phenomena, such that the divine principle remains alone and one dwells in profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without further ascending, this is the demon of *samādhi*.
Because of long indulgence in it, one fails to reach supreme *nirvāṇa*, which is the tranquility of detachment;
this is the work of Māra. If one does not depart from various nets of Māra through wisdom, even if one can explain a hundred volumes of the Vedas, [it is still bondage].
The sutras state: "All these are the dregs of hell. To seek anything resembling the Buddha among them is impossible.

Now, when one hears it said that one should not cling to any phenomena—whether good or evil, existent or non-existent—one immediately falls into emptiness, failing to realize that this is abandoning the root while pursuing the branches.
This, however, is falling into emptiness. To seek a Buddha, to seek Bodhi, or to seek all dharmas of existence and non-existence, is to abandon the root and pursue the branches.
At present, one merely uses coarse food to sustain life, mends tattered clothes to ward off the cold, and scoops up water to drink when thirsty;
beyond this, one has not the slightest attachment to any dharma of existence or non-existence. Such a person gradually attains lightness and clarity.

[This is] the division. A true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) does not cling to existence, nor does he cling to non-existence. He is liberated from the ten types of demonic speech; his words do not bind others.

In all his discourse, he does not claim to be a teacher; his speech is like an echo in a valley. His words fill the world, yet there is no fault in his mouth. Such a one is worthy of being relied upon.
If, however, someone says, "I can speak and I can explain," and claims, "I am the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), and you are the disciple"—
This is identical to the teachings of Mara. Without cause, they speak of "the Way existing through direct perception," or whether it is Buddha or not-Buddha, or Bodhi, Nirvana, or Liberation.
Without cause, they speak of "one knowledge" and "one understanding. When someone raises a hand or points a finger, they claim it is Zen or the Way.
These words bind people; before they have even found a moment of stillness, they only serve to further increase their delusion.
The monk’s cord: even if one does not speak, there are still faults of speech. It is better to take the mind as one's teacher than to let the mind be one's teacher.

Within the teachings of provisional meaning, there are teachers of humans and devas, and there are guides; however, within the teachings of definitive meaning, one does not act as a teacher of humans and devas.

Do not take the teachings as your teacher. You have not yet attained the profound mirror [of realization] by relying upon them; for now, you may rely upon the definitive (nītārtha) teachings, as they still possess a degree of affinity with reality.
As for the non-definitive (neyārtha) teachings, they are only fit to be spoken before the ears of worldly fools.
At present, simply do not abide in any phenomena of existence or non-existence, nor abide in a state of non-abiding, nor even form the cognition of "non-abiding."
[The Master] explained: "This is called a Great Good Spiritual Friend (mahākalyāṇamitra). It is also said that the Buddha alone is the Great Good Spiritual Friend, for there is no second person.
All others are entirely termed 'outsiders' (tīrthika) and are also termed 'the teachings of Māra.

Now, this is simply to break through the dualistic phrases regarding all phenomena of existence and non-existence; one must merely avoid the matters of greed, defilement, liberation, and bondage. There are no other words or phrases."

Regarding the teaching of others: if one claims that there are separate words and phrases for teaching others, or that there is a separate dharma to bestow upon others, this is called a heterodox path and is also termed the teaching of Māra.
One must recognize the language of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and the language of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*). One must recognize prohibitive language and non-prohibitive language.

One must recognize the language of saṃsāra. One must recognize the language of medicine and disease. One must recognize analogies of contrariety and conformity. One must recognize the comprehensive...

A separate statement: To say that one attains Buddhahood through the practice of the Way, that there is cultivation and realization, that "this mind is Buddha" or "this very mind is Buddha"—these are the words of the Buddha as provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), non-exclusive statements, general statements, statements that merely combine and load [the burden], statements that select from the side of defiled phenomena, analogical statements, dead words, and words spoken before ordinary people. They are not—
It is permitted that through cultivation one attains Buddhahood; yet there is neither cultivation nor realization, neither mind nor Buddha. That "Buddha" is also a term spoken by the Buddha;
it is a definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), a negating expression, a distinct expression, an expression like a hundred-peck load, and an expression outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
This is an inverse analogy. This is a statement that distinguishes the limit of pure dharmas. This is a statement of arising.

This is a statement for those on the stages of realization, from the stage of Srotāpanna upward through the ten bhūmis. All mere words and phrases belong to the defilement of dharma-objects (dharmaviṣaya).

All mere words and phrases are subsumed under the side of afflictions (kleśapakṣa). All mere words and phrases belong to the teachings of provisional meaning (neyārtha); [only] the definitive meaning (nītārtha) [is otherwise].

The provisional teaching is upholding; the non-definitive teaching is transgression. In the Buddha-ground, there is neither upholding nor transgression; both definitive and non-definitive teachings are ultimately not permitted.
One discerns the ground from its sprouts; one discerns clarity from its turbidity. It is simply the present mirror-like awareness (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
If one counts from the side of clarity, mirror-like awareness is not clarity; non-mirror-like awareness is not clarity; nor is it non-clarity.
It is neither holy, nor is it unholy; it is neither seeing. When water is turbid, one speaks of the faults of the turbid water;
if the water were clear, there would be nothing at all to say—speaking would only make that water turbid.

If there is a question that asks neither "is" nor "is not," and a teaching that says neither "is" nor "is not," the Buddha does not preach the Dharma for the sake of a Buddha. In the equal and true *dharmadhātu*, there is no Buddha, and there is no saving.
Sentient beings—when a Buddha does not dwell in the state of being a Buddha, he is called the True Field of Merit. One must distinguish between the host and the guest:

when one greedily becomes defiled by all phenomena of existence and non-existence, and is deluded by all phenomena of existence and non-existence, one's own mind is the Demon King, and its illuminating functions belong to the subjects of the Demon.
It is simply this present mirror-like awareness; it merely does not rely upon or dwell in any phenomena of existence or non-existence, whether worldly or supramundane.
Regarding the dharmas of the intervals: do not form a conceptual understanding of non-arising and non-abiding, nor rely upon or dwell in the absence of such understanding.
One’s own mind is the Buddha; its illumination and function belong to the Bodhisattvas. Each thought-moment is the sovereign master; illumination and function belong to adventitious dust.

It is like describing water by means of its waves: in illuminating the myriad phenomena, there is no deliberate effort. If one can achieve tranquil illumination, it does not depend on some profound esoteric principle; it will naturally penetrate through all time, past and present.
It is like the spirit within the clouds: though it has no conscious effort of illumination, its ultimate function ever abides, enabling it to act as a guide in all places.

As for the nature and consciousness of sentient beings, they have never before trodden the steps of the Buddha; this is the nature of sticky glue, which for a long time has adhered to all phenomena of existence and non-existence.
They cannot suddenly ingest the medicine of the profound principle, and when they hear words that transcend the conventional, they do not believe them. For this reason, Bodhi... [text continues].
Under the *tī* tree, he remained in silent contemplation for forty-nine days. His wisdom was so profound and obscure that it is difficult to explain; it is beyond all analogy.
To say that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; to say that sentient beings lack Buddha-nature is likewise to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
If one says there is Buddha-nature, it is called the slander of attachment; if one says there is no Buddha-nature, it is called the slander of falsehood.

This is slander. For instance, to say that the Buddha-nature exists is the slander of exaggeration (*samāropa*). To say that the Buddha-nature does not exist is the slander of deprecation (*apavāda*).

To say that the Buddha-nature both exists and does not exist is the slander of contradiction. To say that the Buddha-nature neither exists nor does not exist is the slander of frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one initially refrains from speaking, sentient beings will have no opportunity for liberation. If one initially desires to speak, sentient beings will again follow [after it].
Speech gives rise to understanding; the benefit is slight while the loss is great. Therefore, it is said: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana.
Looking back later, one finds that all Buddhas of the past preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

What was previously provisionally spoken and provisionally established as names was originally not the Buddha, yet they spoke of it to others as being the Buddha; it was originally not Bodhi, yet they spoke of it to others as being Bodhi.

Regarding [terms such as] *tīrṇa* (crossed over), *nirvāṇa*, and *vimukti* (liberation): knowing that he would be unable to carry a burden of a hundred *shi*, one first gives him a burden of one *sheng* or one *he*.
Knowing that he finds it difficult to believe the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*), one first speaks to him of the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*).

Thus, even if only wholesome dharmas circulate, they are superior to unwholesome dharmas. When the limit of the wholesome fruit is fulfilled, the unwholesome fruit then arrives; having attained Buddhahood, there is...
When sentient beings reach nirvana, there is the reaching of birth and death; when they attain illumination, there is the reaching of darkness.

These are merely the reciprocal reversals of the causes and effects of the outflows (āsrava), and there is nothing that does not involve a response and offering. If one wishes to avoid witnessing such reciprocal reversals, [one must cultivate the Way].

Simply sever the two ends; then measure and calculation will have no jurisdiction. There is neither Buddha nor sentient being, neither intimacy nor estrangement, neither high nor low, neither even nor uneven, neither going nor coming.
It is simply not clinging to words and letters, blocking off both ends so that you cannot seize them.
Thus one is freed from the mutual conditioning of suffering and pleasure, and freed from the reciprocal response between light and darkness. This is the true principle, the ultimate reality.
It is not real; it is neither false nor non-false. It is not a measurable entity, like empty space which cannot be cultivated or altered.
If the mind forms even the slightest conceptualization, it is immediately caught within the confines of measurement and enumeration.
It is like a divination omen, governed by metal, wood, water, fire, and earth; or like sticky glue, adhering in all five places, so that the Demon King seizes it and gains mastery over it.

Returning home, the teachings and instructions all consist of three successive phrases that are good in the beginning, middle, and end. First, one must directly cause them to give rise to a wholesome mind.
Second, one breaks through that wholesome mind. Third, only then is it called "truly good. A bodhisattva is not a bodhisattva; this is what is called a bodhisattva.
Dharma is not dharma, yet not non-dharma—it is entirely like this. If one were to speak only a single phrase, it would merely cause sentient beings to enter [a partial state].
As for hell: if one speaks of these three phrases simultaneously, one enters hell oneself; it does not concern the Master’s responsibility.
To realize that the present awareness is one's own Buddha is the "goodness in the beginning. Not remaining fixed in this present awareness is the "goodness in the middle.

Furthermore, not forming a conceptual understanding of "not remaining fixed" is the "goodness in the end. This is just as previously mentioned regarding the succession from Dīpaṃkara to the subsequent Buddhas. Only...

This is neither ordinary nor holy. Do not mistakenly say that the Buddha is neither ordinary nor holy. The First Patriarch of this land said: "To be without capacity and without holiness is to be a holy Buddha.
If one speaks of the Buddha as being holy, he is not merely a spirit of the nine grades, nor a class such as dragons or animals, nor anyone from Śakra or Brahmā downward;
all these are capable of transformation. Even spirits of the highest grade know the past and present across hundreds of kalpas.

These are merely matters of the current age; how could they possibly be the Buddha? For instance, when the body of an Asura King was exceedingly large—equaling twice the size of Mount Sumeru—and he realized his strength was insufficient during battle with Śakra, he led a host of a million soldiers into the hollow of a lotus fiber to hide himself.
His transformative powers and eloquence were by no means meager. Furthermore, these are not Buddhist terms; their phrasing is leisurely and relaxed, and their progression is erratic.

They are not the same. When one has not yet awakened or attained understanding, it is called greed and anger; once awakened, it is called the Buddha’s wisdom. Therefore it is said: "It is not a different person from before;
it is only different in the sphere of one's conduct. Question: "When cutting grass, felling trees, digging the earth, or tilling the soil, is there the mark of karmic retribution?
The Master said: "One must not definitively say there is retribution, nor must one definitively say there is no retribution."

Whether there is guilt or innocence depends on the person concerned. If one is stained by craving for all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—and possesses a mind of grasping and rejecting, failing to pass beyond the three phrases, this person is certainly said to be guilty.

If one passes beyond the three phrases, the mind is like space, yet one must not even form the thought that it is space; this person is certainly said to be innocent. It is further said: "If guilt has been committed..."
It is impossible that the Way should see sin. It is also impossible that the Way should have sin if one has not committed it.
As stated in the Vinaya, even those who originally intended to kill or who killed in a chain of succession do not incur the karmic offense of killing;

how much more so for those in the Chan lineage who inherit the tradition with a mind like empty space, which does not retain a single thing and lacks even the characteristic of emptiness—how could they take up sin?
Where should one settle? It is also said that the Way of Chan requires no cultivation; simply do not defile it.
It is also said that by merely melting away the internal and external, once the mind is exhausted, one attains it. It is also said that one should simply rely on the illumination of objects;

right now, when illuminating all phenomena such as existence and non-existence, there is absolutely no grasping, nor should one take up attachment. It is also said that one should study in this manner: studying like washing away stains.

Regarding clothing: the clothing is what is inherently present, while the grime is adventitious. Upon hearing it said that all existence consists of sounds and forms, which are like greasy filth, do not allow the mind to settle upon them at all.
Under the Bodhi tree, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics belong to the realm of form.

The twelve divisions of the teachings belong to sound. Now, if you can cut off the flow of all existence and non-existence, sounds and forms, so that the mind is like empty space, then you should study in this manner.
It is only when you act as if your head were on fire that you will succeed.

When the time of death arrives, even if you follow the old familiar path, you will not reach the end. At such a time, if you are newly adjusted and just beginning to learn, there will be no time for attainment. At the moment of death—
At the time of death, only supreme realms will manifest before you. You will experience first those things for which you have the strongest attachment according to your own inclinations.
Just as you do not commit evil deeds now, at that time there will likewise be no evil realms; even if there were, they would transform into auspicious realms.
If you fear that at the moment of death you will become panicked and lose your self-mastery, you must achieve mastery right now.

Only then can you attain it. If, right now, you have no attachment or defilement toward any single object or phenomenon, and you do not rely upon or dwell in intellectual understanding, you are a free person.
The present moment is the cause; the time of death is the fruit. Since the karmic fruit is already manifest, why should you fear it?

What is feared is the distinction between "ancient" and "present. If there were an ancient time, there would also be a present time. If there were Buddhas in the ancient past, there are also Buddhas in the present.
The Buddha. If one attains it now, one will attain it until the very end of the future.

At this very moment, in every single thought-moment, one is not governed by any phenomena of existence or non-existence. From antiquity to the present, the Buddha is simply a person, and the person is simply the Buddha.
This is also samādhi; there is no need to bring concentration into concentration, no need to cultivate dhyāna through conceptualization, and no need to seek the Buddha.

Seeking the Buddha is like seeking the Dharma through the Dharma: the Dharma does not seek the Dharma; the Dharma does not obtain the Dharma; the Dharma does not practice the Dharma; the Dharma does not see the Dharma.
One naturally attains the Dharma, not by means of attainment. Therefore, a bodhisattva should maintain right mindfulness of the Dharma in this way.
It remains utterly alone; yet there is no dharma that knows this solitary remaining. The nature of wisdom is suchness (*tathatā*); it is not something established by causes.

It is also called the "knot of essence" (*tattva-grantha*) and the "accumulation of essence" (*tattva-samudaya*). It is not known by wisdom (*jñāna*), nor is it cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is beyond the reach of thought and deliberation.
The essence of stillness and silence is exhausted; all calculation and deliberation are forever extinguished. It is like the great currents of the ocean being spent, so that waves no longer arise.
It is also said to be like the waters of the great ocean when there is no wind and no rippling waves. If one suddenly perceives these ripples, this is the coarse within the subtle.
To extinguish the perception within perception is like the subtle within the subtle; this is the realm of the Buddha. From this initial knowing, [the path begins].
It is called the Summit of Samādhi; it is also called the King of Samādhis; it is also called the Wisdom of Suchness.

It gives birth to all samādhis and consecrates the crowns of all Dharma-princes. Regarding all forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, mental objects, and buddha-fields, it attains perfect enlightenment.
It penetrates both the internal and external without any obstruction. Whether it be a single form, a single atom, a single Buddha, or a single...
Form: all Buddhas are all forms; all atoms are all Buddhas. All forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena are likewise so.
Each one pervades all lands. This is the coarse within the subtle. It is a virtuous realm.
It is that which is known, perceived, heard, and seen by all those who flow upward; it is also the birthplace of all those who flow upward.
Entering into death, it transcends all existence, non-existence, and their like; this is what is taught regarding the *ūrdhvasrotas* (one who flows upward).
It is also the *nirvāṇa* of the *ūrdhvasrotas*. This is the unsurpassed path, the mantra of the unequaled, and the foremost teaching.
Among all teachings, it is the most profound; no one can reach its limit. The Buddhas protect and keep it in mind. It is like clear waves that can discern whether all waters are pure or turbid.

With a profound current and vast function, protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—if you can act thus, I shall at that time manifest to you a body of pure radiance.
It is further said: "Just as your own [nature] is equal and your speech is equal, so too am I.

The sound of a single Buddha-field, the fragrance of a single Buddha-field, the taste of a single Buddha-field, the touch of a single Buddha-field, and the phenomena of a single Buddha-field—all are likewise."
It is thus for all of them. From here upward to the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), the vertical and horizontal dimensions are all likewise.

If one clings to this initial cognition as being liberation, it is called the "summit-knot" (*mūrdhā-bandhana*) and is also called the "falling summit-knot. This is the very root of all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).
One gives rise to self-originated knowledge and views; though there is no rope, one binds oneself. Because of what is known, one is bound to the twenty-five worldly existences.

Furthermore, one scatters all doors of affliction and becomes fettered to others. This is the first stage of knowledge, which the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive and name the *īṣan-manas* (the "slightly flickering" consciousness);
it is also called the "subtle affliction. Upon its immediate severance, having been eliminated, it is termed the "abiding of the returned spirit."
The empty cave is also called being intoxicated by the wine of samādhi; it is also called being bound by the māra of liberation.

While the world undergoes formation and destruction, one is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*) and remains entirely unaware of the outflows (*āsrava*) as they migrate toward other lands.

It is also called the terrifying abyss of liberation from which one cannot escape. Bodhisattvas distance themselves from all such states. It is also said that, having lost one’s footing, one becomes a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) over the four continents.
If an ordinary person practices the ten wholesome deeds for a single day, the merit and wisdom thereof cannot even be calculated. To possess self-reflexive awareness is called a "King" (Cakravartin).
To contemplate and become attached to all phenomena as being existent or non-existent is called a "Wheel-Turning King.

However, when one now, within the inner depths of one's being, does not admit any phenomena such as existence or non-existence, and remains beyond the four conceptual extremes, this is called "Emptiness. Emptiness is called the "Medicine of Immortality. This is what is meant by "invoking."
The former king was named Amṛta (Immortal Medicine). Although it was called "Immortal Medicine," when taken together with the king, it was neither two distinct things nor one single thing.
If one were to interpret it as being either one or two, he would also be called a Cakravartin King.

Just as if someone today were to provide offerings of the four requisites of merit and wisdom to beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth across four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, according to their...
When eighty years had passed since his desire was fulfilled, he later thought: "Now these sentient beings have all grown old;
I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma, causing them to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, up to the path of arhatship."
If such a donor bestows all manner of articles of pleasure upon sentient beings, their merit is already immeasurable;
how much more so when they cause them to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to and including the path of an *arhat*—the merit of which is infinite and boundless.
Yet even this does not equal the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the sutra and rejoices. The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) says: "Queen Māyā gave birth to..."
The five hundred princes all attained the fruit of *pratyekabuddha* and entered parinirvāṇa. Each had a stūpa erected for their veneration, and they paid homage to each one, exclaiming:
"It would have been better to have given birth to but a single son who attains unsurpassed *bodhi*.

To consider the expenditure of my mental and physical strength—it is as if, among hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of people, only one person should attain it; its value is equal to three thousand great [worlds]."

Throughout the thousandfold world-system, I have therefore constantly exhorted all people that they must profoundly understand their own fundamental nature (*svadharma*). If this fundamental nature is profoundly understood, one will thereby attain merit and wisdom;
it is like a nobleman employing the lowly, or like a carriage that does not remain stationary. If one maintains this understanding, it is called the jewel within the topknot.
It is also called a "valuable jewel," and it is also called "carrying excrement in. If one does not maintain this as liberation, it is like giving him the bright pearl from the King’s topknot;
it is also called a "priceless great treasure," and it is also called "carrying excrement out.

The Buddha is originally a person outside the entanglements, yet he comes within the entanglements to act as a Buddha in this way. He is truly a person on the other side of birth and death; he is truly profound.
To cut off those on the other shore and come back toward this shore—such is the way of becoming a Buddha. Neither humans nor monkeys can traverse it.

Humans represent the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages; monkeys represent ordinary beings. Reading the sutras and examining the teachings to seek all-encompassing knowledge and understanding is not categorically forbidden.
One may understand the teachings of the Three Vehicles and skillfully obtain the ornaments of the *ratna-keśara* (jeweled necklace).
The thirty-two marks are their dwelling place; though one seeks the Buddha there, he is not to be found.
The teaching states that even those who study the Tripitaka of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) are not permitted to be approached, let alone those who practice it themselves.

Such individuals are precept-breaking bhikṣus, "Arhats in name only," who, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, are categorized among the sixteen types of evil practitioners (duḥśīla). They are equal to hunters and fishermen, acting for the sake of profit.
Because of nurturing [the body], one kills and harms. The Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras are like ambrosia (*amṛta*), yet they are also like poison.

If they can be digested, they are like ambrosia; if they cannot be digested, they are like poison. When reading the scriptures and examining the teachings, if you do not understand the discourse on birth and death, you will certainly fail to penetrate their meaning and phrasing.
Do not read them as if they were the most supreme; however, it is also said that one must examine the teachings and must also engage in investigation (*vicaya*).
Good friends, first you must have eyes of your own; you must be able to discern the discourse on the birth and death of others before you can succeed.
If you cannot discern this clearly, you will certainly fail to penetrate through it; it would merely serve to further increase the bonds of the bhikṣu.

This is why those who teach the profound essence do not send students to read written texts. As it is said: "Speak of the substance, do not speak of its characteristics; speak of the meaning, do not speak of the words."
This kind of discourse is called true discourse. If one speaks merely of words and letters, all such speech is slander; this is called false discourse.

When a Bodhisattva speaks, they should speak in accordance with the Dharma, which is also called true discourse. They should cause sentient beings to grasp the mind and not the phenomena; to grasp practice and not the [mere] teachings;
to speak of the person and not the characters; to speak of the meaning and not the text; and to speak of the Path while asserting that there is no dhyāna in the desire realm.
This is also the speech of one who possesses but a single eye. Since it is said that there is no dhyāna in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), by what means can one reach the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?

First, by practicing two kinds of concentration on the ground, one subsequently attains the first dhyāna, including the attainment of cessation with perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation without perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

There is the meditative absorption of cessation (saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti), by which one is born into the heavens of the four dhyānas of the form realm (rūpa-dhātu) and so forth. There is the meditative absorption of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), by which one is born into the heavens of the four emptinesses of the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu) and so forth.
The desire realm (kāma-dhātu) clearly possesses no dhyāna; dhyāna belongs to the form realm. Question: As it is now said that there is dhyāna in this land [Jambudvīpa], how is this so?
Master: Non-movement and non-dhyāna is the Tathāgata-dhyāna; it is free from the conceptualization of birth and dhyāna. Question: What is meant by "having" [dhyāna]?
"Sentient beings have no Buddha-nature; insentient things have Buddha-nature. The Master said: "From humans to Buddhas is the attachment of sacred emotion;

from humans to the hells is the attachment of ordinary emotion. If, at this very moment, you harbor a stained and affectionate mind toward the two realms of the ordinary and the sacred, this is called 'sentient beings having no Buddha-nature.
If, at this very moment, [you are free of such attachment] toward the two realms of the ordinary and the sacred, as well as all..."
Regarding all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, there is absolutely no mind of grasping or rejecting, nor is there even the cognition or understanding of such grasping or rejecting;
this is called "insentient things possessing Buddha-nature. It is simply because they lack emotional entanglements that they are termed "insentient.

This is not the same as the insentience of wood, stone, empty space, chrysanthemums, or green bamboo, which are taken to possess Buddha-nature. If one were to say they do possess it, why does the Sūtra not [state so]?
To see those who have received the prediction of enlightenment and attained Buddhahood is simply to reflect upon one's own present awakening;

it is merely that one is not altered by sentient beings. This is like the green bamboo: there is nothing that does not respond to conditions, and there is nothing that does not know the proper time. This is like the yellow chrysanthemum. It is further said:
"If one has ascended the steps of the Buddha, even insentient things possess Buddha-nature. If one has not yet ascended the steps of the Buddha, sentient beings lack Buddha-nature."
Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Masters, Volume One;
Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Masters, Volume Two:
The Third Generation under Dajian (Continuation of the Sayings).

The Chan Master Baizhang Dazhi was asked by a monk: "Regarding the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood—how is this so?
The Master said: "Kalpa (劫) means stagnation; it is also called dwelling."
Abiding in one good, one is stalled at the ten goods. In the Western Land [India] this is called "Buddha" (buddha), and in this land it is called "Awakening" (jue).

When one’s own self-reflexive awakening becomes stalled and attached to goodness, such people of good roots lack Buddha-nature; therefore, it is said that the Buddha-dharma does not manifest before them, and they cannot attain the Way of Buddhahood.
