To encounter evil and abide in evil is called the awakening of sentient beings; to encounter good and abide in good is called the awakening of śrāvakas. Not abiding in good—[is the awakening of the Bodhisattvas].
Not relying on or dwelling upon the two extremes of evil, yet taking this as being correct, is called the awakening of the Two Vehicles; it is also called the awakening of the Pratyekabuddhas.

Since one neither relies on nor dwells within the two extremes of good and evil, and furthermore does not form a conceptual understanding of such non-reliance, this is called the awakening of the Bodhisattvas.
Neither abiding in anything, nor forming a conceptual understanding of non-abiding—only then can it be called the awakening of a Buddha. As it is said:
"A Buddha does not abide in Buddhahood; this is called the true field of merit. If, among ten million people, there should suddenly be one who attains this, [they are truly rare].
It is called the Priceless Jewel. It can act as a guide in all places: where there is no Buddha, it declares itself to be the Buddha;

where there is no Dharma, it declares itself to be the Dharma; where there is no Sangha, it declares itself to be the Sangha. This is called turning the Great Wheel of the Dharma. Question: From the ancestral patriarchs of old...
"All possess esoteric instructions that are transmitted from one to another. How is this so? The Master said: "There are no esoteric instructions.

The Tathāgata has no secret treasury. It is simply the present mirror-like awareness; speech is clear and distinct. If you seek its form or characteristics, they are utterly unobtainable—this is the 'esoteric instruction.
From the stage of Srotāpanna upward, even through to the tenth bhūmi, whatever words or phrases exist all belong to the Dharma."

Dust and defilement. Any mere words and phrases are entirely subsumed under the side of affliction (*kleśa*). Any mere words and phrases belong entirely to the teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Any mere words and phrases are all disallowed; they are all contrary to the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). What further "esoteric language" could there be to seek? Question:
"When emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, it is like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. How is this so? The Master said: "Emptiness is a metaphor for..."
"A bubble. The ocean is a metaphor for the nature (nature of reality). One’s own numinous, awakened nature exceeds even empty space;

thus it is said, "Emptiness arises within great awakening," like a single bubble emerging from the sea. Question: "When clearing a forest, do not cut down the trees. What does this mean? The Master said: "The 'forest' is a metaphor for the mind;
the 'trees' are a metaphor for the body. Because one speaks of the forest, fear arises; therefore it is said, 'When clearing a forest, do not cut down the trees.'"

Question: "Speech is like shooting an arrow at a target; once the words have hit the mark, one cannot avoid suffering. Since the burden of suffering is the same for both, how can one distinguish between the monastic and the lay?
The Master said: "But it is simply that the arrow was fired and met its counterpart midway. Had there been a discrepancy, there would surely have been injury.
Seeking an echo in a valley, the form remains absent for kalpas; yet the echo is right at the edge of the mouth. Gain and loss depend on the question that comes. He then turned [the question back].
Questioning that which one takes refuge in, one is struck back by an arrow. It is like knowing an illusion to be no different from non-illusion. The Third Patriarch said:
"Not recognizing the profound principle, one’s efforts at contemplating stillness are in vain. He also said: "To take an object as one's vision is like holding up a piece of rubble;

what can it possibly accomplish? If one says one does not see, how is this different from wood or stone? Therefore, both seeing and not seeing involve error. To provide an illustration: [as in the case of the arrow].

[The Master] said, "All. Question: "If there were originally no afflictions (*kleśa*), how could there be the thirty-two marks [of a Buddha]? The Master said: "That belongs to the realm of the Buddhas.
Originally there were afflictions; now there are the thirty-two marks. It is simply this ordinary mind of the present. Question:
"How is it that the Bodhisattva Anantagātra did not see the crown of the Tathāgata’s head? The Master said: "It was because he formed views of finitude and views of infinitude."
One does not see the Tathāgata’s uṣṇīṣa. It is simply that, right now, there is no perception whatsoever of existence, non-existence, and so forth, nor is there even the perception of non-perception.
This is called the manifestation of the uṣṇīṣa. Question: Nowadays, all śramaṇas claim, "I rely on the Buddha's teachings;

I study one sūtra, one śāstra, one dhyāna, one vinaya, and possess one bit of knowledge and understanding. Thus, they ought to receive the fourfold offerings of the *dānapati* (donors) to consume them. Is this so?
"Is it possible? The Master said: "It simply concerns the present functioning of illumination and application.

Whether it be a single sound, a single form, a single fragrance, or a single flavor—regarding all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent—at every single object, there is not even a speck of dust of grasping or defilement.
Nor does one dwell upon the absence of grasping or defilement, nor is there any conceptual understanding of 'not dwelling. Such a person could even consume ten thousand taels of gold daily."
It can be eliminated. It is simply that when one now illuminates all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, at the gateway of the six sense organs, one must scrub and pare them away completely.
If there is even a hair’s breadth of craving that cannot be removed—even down to begging from a donor for a single grain of rice or a single thread of silk—[it remains].
Each and every one of them wears fur and horns; they pull plows and carry heavy loads. One must repay these debts before one can attain [liberation].

Because you do not rely on the Buddha—whereas the Buddha is one who is unattached, one who seeks nothing, and one who relies on nothing—yet now you are busily and greedily searching for the Buddha, you have missed him entirely.
Therefore it is said: "Though long in close proximity to the Buddha, one does not recognize the Buddha-nature; one merely observes the Savior of the World."
Within the cycle of rebirth among the six realms, those who see a Buddha only after a long time are told that a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
Mañjuśrī is the ancestral teacher of the seven Buddhas and is also called the foremost Bodhisattva in this Sahā world.

That he suddenly conceived the thought of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma was due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; it was as if two Iron Ring Mountains were brought down. It was not that he lacked understanding.
I specifically establish this as a standard for all students, so that future learners do not harbor such views or hearsay.
Simply let there be no dharmas such as existence or non-existence, nor any views such as existence or non-existence; let each and every one of you pass beyond the three propositions.
This is called the wish-fulfilling jewel; this is called the precious flower that supports the feet.

If one forms views of a Buddha or views of the Dharma, these are merely views of existence, non-existence, and so forth, which are termed "cataracts of the eye" because they perceive what is seen. They are also termed "entanglements of view" and "obstructions of view."

It is also called the "thicket of views. Just as in the present moment, every thought-moment and all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, as well as all defilements and impurities, can be completely cleared away.
Yet, every single speck of dust and every single color is entirely one Buddha; the arising of a single thought is entirely one Buddha.

As for the five aggregates (*skandha*) throughout the three periods of time, who could know their number in every thought-moment? This is what is called the Buddhas filling and obstructing the void of space. This is...
He is named a Buddha of Emanation; this is what is called a jeweled stūpa. For this reason, he constantly sighed, saying: "Alas!
Behold the life upon which I now depend—relying on a single grain of rice or a stalk of vegetable. At mealtime, I may not eat and die of hunger; I may not obtain water and die of thirst."

One cannot die of cold or fire; lacking even one day, one does not come into being, and lacking even one day, one does not pass away. Held fast by the four great elements, one is no better than those who have already attained:
they enter fire unburnt and enter water unsunken; if they wish to burn, they burn; if they wish to drown, they drown;
if they wish to live, they live; if they wish to die, they die. They go and stay with freedom—such a person possesses true autonomy.
Section. If the mind is not distracted, there is no need to seek the Buddha, nor to seek Bodhi or Nirvana. If one clings to seeking the Buddha, one belongs to greed; greed turns into a disease.
Therefore it is said that "the Buddha-disease is the most difficult to cure. One may take food only if one slanders the Buddha and destroys the Dharma.

As for "food," this refers to the food of the untainted (anāsrava) and the food of liberation—the nature of one's own numinous awareness. These words are intended to treat the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages.

"Sickness" refers to the stages from the first bhūmi up to the tenth. At present, as long as one possesses any mind of seeking, one is entirely termed a "precept-breaking bhikṣu," a "bhikṣu in name only," or a "jackal.
It is evident that such a person cannot digest the offerings of others.
At present, hearing sounds is like an echo; smelling fragrances is like the wind; and one is detached from all dharmas of existence and non-existence. Furthermore—
They do not abide in detachment, nor is there any understanding of non-abiding. Such a person cannot be burdened by any defilements of sin.
Because they seek unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa, they are called "those who have left home. Yet even this is a perverse aspiration;

how much more so when one engages in worldly disputes seeking victory and defeat, saying "I am capable" and "I understand," coveting a single group of followers, cherishing a single disciple, or longing for a single [disciple].
Regarding one's dwelling, one should establish a single patron; one should accept only one robe and one meal, and seek only one name and one benefit.
Furthermore, to say, "I have attained all unimpeded [knowledge]," is merely self-deception.

If, even now, you cannot act as the master over your own five aggregates (*skandhas*), such that when others cut and dismember you limb by limb, you remain entirely free from resentment or stinginess and do not experience affliction—even to this extent...
If one's own disciple is beaten by others from head to foot, regarding such matters as these, one must not give rise to even a single thought of "self" or "other.
Even while abiding in this state, if one does not consider it to be so [as mere phenomena], this is called the defilement of dharmas.
Even those at the tenth stage cannot shed this; they flow into the river of birth and death. For this reason, I constantly exhort all people: you must fear the Dharma.
If one regards the dust-like afflictions with fear as if facing the three miserable realms, then there is a portion of independent liberation.

Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvana, one would not harbor even the slightest thought of cherishing it. Such a person is a Buddha at every step, without needing to tread upon lotus flowers, manifesting ten billion bodies.
Yet, if right now, toward all dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—one still possesses even a hair’s breadth of attachment...
A defiled mind—even if one treads upon lotus flowers—is likewise the work of Māra.

If one clings to the notion that one is inherently pure, inherently liberated, and that one is oneself the Buddha or oneself the realization of Chan, one belongs to the naturalist heretics (*svabhāvavāda*).

If one clings to the notion that [enlightenment] is accomplished through causes and conditions and realized through cultivation, one belongs to the causal heretics (*hetuvāda*). To cling to existence is to belong to the eternalist heretics; to cling to non-existence...
To cling to "neither existence nor non-existence" is to belong to the heretics of the view of emptiness;
they are also called the deluded heretics. Simply now, do not form views such as that of a Buddha or Nirvana;
when there are no views whatsoever regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth, and even no view of "non-existence," this is called the Right [View].
Seeing, yet there is no hearing of anything, nor is there non-hearing; this is called "right hearing. This is what is meant by "subduing the heterodox.
There is no arrival of the demons of ordinary beings; it is the Great Divine Mantra. There is no arrival of the demons of the Two Vehicles; it is the Great Luminous Mantra.

There is no arrival of the demons of Bodhisattvas; it is the Unsurpassed Mantra. Furthermore, there is no arrival even of the demons of the Buddhas; it is the Peerless Mantra. It transforms all in a single instant.

First, transforming the *asura* of flattery and crookedness born of birth; second, transforming the *asura* of flattery and crookedness of the two vehicles; third, transforming the *asura* of flattery and crookedness of bodhisattvas.
These three transformations constitute the pure land. However, all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent, mundane or sagely—are like gold ore.
One’s own nature is as it truly is, like gold. Just as when gold and its ore are separated from one another, the pure gold is revealed;

yet if someone seeking coins or treasure were to transform that gold into coins and give them to others—just as with the substance of flour, which is truly pure and free of grit or salt, and someone begging for *tsampa* (roasted barley flour) might transform that flour into *tsampa* and give it to them—it is also like a wise minister who well understands the King’s intent.

When the King traveled, he would ask for *sindhuva* [salt], and [the attendant] would immediately offer him a horse. When he ate, he would ask for *sindhuva*, and [the attendant] would immediately offer him salt.
These are metaphors for those who study the profound principle (*xuanzhi*): they are skillfully able to penetrate it and respond to circumstances without fail.

They are also called the "Six Extraordinary Lions. Master Zhigong said: "They manifest a hundred transformations according to the needs of beings. A Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds neither suffers from hunger nor from satiety."
Entering water, one does not drown; entering fire, one is not burned. Even if one wishes to be burned, one cannot be burned. This is because he is constrained by measure and number.
The Buddha is not like this: entering fire, he is not burned; yet if he wishes to be burned, he burns; if he wishes to drown, he drowns.
He brings the four great elements and the winds and waters into freedom. All forms are the Buddha’s form; all sounds are the Buddha’s sound.
One’s own turbid, deceitful, and crooked mind is entirely transcended beyond the three phrases. Only then can one speak these words. The Bodhisattva is pure.
Disciple, understand that all speech neither clings to existence nor clings to non-existence. All manifestations and functions are unrestricted.

Regarding clarity and turbidity: to not take medicine when ill is the mark of a fool; to take medicine when not ill is the mark of a Śrāvaka. One who dogmatically clings to a single dharma is called a Śrāvaka of fixed nature.
One who is exclusively devoted to extensive learning is called a Śrāvaka of overweening pride. One who knows others is called a Śrāvaka in training (*śaikṣa*).
One who is submerged in emptiness, stalled in quiescence, and possesses self-knowledge is called a Śrāvaka beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). [This applies to] greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth.

This is poison; the twelvefold teaching is the medicine. If the poison has not been digested, the medicine cannot be eliminated. To take medicine when one is not ill causes the medicine to turn into illness;
once the illness has departed, the medicine does not vanish. "Neither arising nor ceasing" is the meaning of impermanence. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
There are three evil desires: first, the desire to be surrounded by the fourfold assembly; second, the desire for all people to become one's disciples;
third, the desire for all people to know that one is a holy man and an arhat. The *Kāśyapa Sūtra* says:
1. Desiring to see future Buddhas; 2. Desiring to become a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*); 3. Desiring to belong to the great Kṣatriya caste; 4.
Desiring to obtain birth in the great Brahmin caste; and even up to: wearying of birth and death and seeking *nirvāṇa*. Such are evil desires.
First, you must sever it. At present, any grasping, defilement, or stirring thought is entirely termed "evil desire" and belongs entirely to the six heavens;
it is all governed by Pāpīyān. Question: What about the statement that for twenty years he was constantly made to remove excrement?
The Master said: Simply cease all knowledge and views of existence and non-existence; simply cease all greedy seeking. Each and every one must pass beyond the three propositions.
This is called removing filth. However, seeking the Buddha now, seeking bodhi, and seeking all dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—is called bringing filth in; it is not called taking filth out.

All current views of Buddhahood, understandings of Buddhahood, and whatever is seen, sought, or clung to, are entirely called the filth of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). They are also called coarse speech and dead words.

Just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses, casual speech is not called frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). It is when a speaker distinguishes between the clear and the turbid that it is termed frivolous proliferation.
The scriptural texts, in their entirety, contain twenty-one kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which sift and purify the defilements and burdens of sentient beings.

For a śramaṇa to observe the fasts and precepts, to practice patience and gentleness, and to cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity—these are the ordinary rules of the monastic community.
To understand it thus is precisely to follow the Buddha’s teaching; it is simply that one must not allow for greed, attachment, or clinging.
If one hopes to attain Buddhahood, Bodhi, or other such dharmas, it is like reaching out one's hand to touch fire. Mañjuśrī said: "If one gives rise to the view of a Buddha..."
To hold views regarding the Dharma is to bring harm upon oneself. This is why Mañjuśrī brandished a sword against Gautama and Aṅgulimāla wielded a blade against the Śākyas;

as it is said, "A Bodhisattva may commit the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) yet does not enter the Avīci Hell," for his is the "perfectly penetrating" immediacy, unlike the five heinous crimes of ordinary beings that lead to immediacy. From Pāpīyān down to the Buddha, all are but defilements.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of attachment. To rely on and cling to such [distinctions] as these is the path of the Two Vehicles;

how much more so when one engages in contentious debate to seek victory and defeat, saying "I am able" and "I understand"? Such are merely called monks of contentious debate, not monks of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Right now, simply not being greedily stained by any phenomena of existence or non-existence is called "non-arising" and is called "right faith. This is to have faith in all things.
Dharma is called "incomplete faith," and it is also called "incomplete perfection of faith. It is also called "partial faith that is incomplete"; for this reason, one is termed an icchantika.
If you now wish to attain direct awakening and understanding, you must simply cause both person and dharma to subside, both person and dharma to be severed, and both person and dharma to be empty.
To penetrate beyond these three phrases is called "not falling into any categories. Here, "person" refers to faith, and "dharma" refers to precepts.

Regarding the giving of the wisdom of hearing and so forth: the bodhisattva’s patience does not constitute Buddhahood; patience does not create sentient beings; patience does not consist in upholding the precepts;

patience does not consist in breaking the precepts. Therefore, it is said that there is neither upholding nor violating. Wisdom is turbid while its illumination is clear; insight is clear while its cognition is turbid.

When present in a Buddha, it is called "illuminating insight" (*jñāna*); in a bodhisattva, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*); in the context of the two vehicles and ordinary beings, it is called "cognition" (*vijñāna*), and is also termed "affliction."

Regarding affliction (*kleśa*): in the context of the Buddha, it is spoken of as the fruit; in the context of sentient beings, it is spoken of as the cause. In the context of the Buddha, it is called "turning the wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra-pravartana*);
in the context of sentient beings, it is called "the turning of the wheel of Dharma. In the context of Bodhisattvas, it is called "ornaments of necklaces";

in the context of sentient beings, it is called "the forest of the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*). In the context of the Buddha, it is called "fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*). Because this ignorance is itself luminous, it is called "non-ignorance" (*an-avidyā*). Thus, it is said: "Non-ignorance."
Luminosity is the essence of the Way; it is not like the ignorance that obscures sentient beings. That [ignorance] is the object; this [luminosity] is the subject.
That is what is heard; this is the hearing. They are neither identical nor different, neither discontinuous nor eternal, neither coming nor going.
These are words that transcend birth; these are words that go beyond the tracks. It is neither luminous nor dark, neither Buddha nor sentient being. In short, it is just so.

Coming and going, annihilation and permanence—these are the "dead words" regarding the Buddha and sentient beings. Concepts such as pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness, identity and difference, or annihilation and permanence, belong to the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Prajñāpāramitā is one's own Buddha-nature; it is also called Mahāyāna. *Mahā* has the meaning of "great," and *yāna* has the meaning of "vehicle.
If one merely clings to one's own cognitive awareness, one again becomes a naturalist non-Buddhist.

There is no need for guarding. To be thus awakened in the present moment is it; there is no need to seek Buddha elsewhere. If you were to seek elsewhere, you would again belong to the causal external paths.

The First Patriarch of this land said: "If the mind has something it considers right, there will necessarily be something it considers wrong. If you prize one thing, you will be deluded by that one thing;
if you value one thing, you will be deluded by that one thing. Faith is deluded by faith, and lack of faith is likewise."
This constitutes slander. [The Buddha] is neither esteemed nor unesteemed; neither believed nor disbelieved. The Buddha is likewise not non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
Although he is not non-action, he is also not a dark void like empty space. The Buddha is a being of great mind who possesses abundant discerning awareness (*pratyavekṣā-jñāna*).
Although his discerning awareness is abundant, that discerning awareness is pure and clear. The demons of greed and hatred cannot seize him. The Buddha is one who is bound...

The outsider has not the slightest bit of craving or grasping, nor does he have the conceptual understanding of "non-craving" or "non-grasping. This is called being fully endowed with the six perfections and the myriad practices.
If one requires ornaments, all varieties are present; yet if they are not required, others do not use them, and they are not lost.
He brings about the freedom of cause and effect, merit and wisdom; this is true cultivation. It is not the case that one merely calls laboring under heavy burdens "cultivation," for it is not so.
The three bodies are one essence; the one essence is the three bodies. First, the Dharmakāya Buddha of the true mark (*dharmatā*). The Dharmakāya Buddha is neither bright nor dark;
brightness and darkness belong to illusory transformations. The true mark derives its name from being in contrast to the void.
Fundamentally, there are no names or categories whatsoever. As it is said, "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any numerical reckoning.

Such expressions as "attaining Buddhahood" or "offering a canopy" are merely conventional terms for measuring and weighing; they derive their names by distinguishing the pure from the turbid. Therefore, it is said: "The Dharma-body Buddha is the true reality (*dharmatā*)."
This is called the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha. It is also called the Space-like Dharmakāya Buddha. It is also called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
It is also called the Eighth Consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). It is also called the Nature School (*Xing-zong*). It is also called the Emptiness School (*Kong-zong*).
It is also called the Buddha dwelling in a land that is neither impure nor defiled. It is also called the Lion in the Cave. It is also called the Subsequent Wisdom of the Vajra. It is also...
It is called the stainless dāna; it is also called the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); it is also called the profound principle. The Third Patriarch said:
"If one does not recognize the profound principle, one's efforts at contemplating stillness are in vain. 2. The Sambhogakāya Buddha. This is the Buddha beneath the Bodhi tree;

it is also called the illusory-transformation Buddha, the Buddha of marks and signs, and the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. This is named the Vairocana Buddha of the Perfectly Complete Sambhogakāya. It is also...
It is named the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). It is also called the seventh consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and it is also called the Buddha who recompenses causes and responds to fruits.
It is identical with the fifty-two stages of *dhyāna*; it is identical with Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; it is identical with all Bodhisattvas and others;
and it equally undergoes the suffering of birth and death, yet it does not share the suffering of sentient beings bound by karma. 3. The Nirmāṇakāya Buddha is simply as it is now, within one...
All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, are entirely free from attachment and likewise free from non-attachment.
Beyond the four extremes, all speech and eloquence are called the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. This is named the Śākyamuni Buddha of a thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred million emanations;
he is also named the Great Miraculous Transformation, the Playful Supernatural Power, the Wondrous Discerning Wisdom, and the Sixth [Consciousness].
Consciousness. As for the one who makes offerings: they purify the three karmas. In the past limit, there are no afflictions to be severed;

in the middle limit, there is no self-nature to be maintained; in the future limit, there is no Buddha to be realized. These are the severances of the three limits. These are the purities of the three karmas. These are the emptinesses of the three wheels.
These three kinds of giving are empty. How does a bhikṣu serve the Buddha? It is said that one who does not leak from the six sense faculties is also called "adorned.
Being empty and free of all outflows is the adornment of the forest trees; being empty and free of all defilements is the adornment of the flowers and fruits.

Being empty and free of the Buddha-eye, yet employing the Dharma-eye to discern the clear and the turbid for the sake of practitioners, while also not forming any conceptual understanding of such discernment between the clear and the turbid—this is [the true service].
This is called "even unto the absence of eyes. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: "The Dharma-body cannot be sought through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
It is not seen by the fleshly eye, because it is formless. It is not seen by the divine eye, because it is without delusion.
It is not seen by the wisdom-eye, because it is free from marks. It is not seen by the Dharma-eye, because it is free from all conditioned activities. It is not [seen by] the Buddha-eye..."
What is seen is so because it is free from all consciousnesses. If one does not form such a view, this is called the Buddha-view.

Being identical to color yet not a shape, it is called true color. Being identical to space yet not a vast void, it is called true emptiness. Color and emptiness are also expressions of the mutual treatment of medicine and disease.
The *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* says: "One cannot say that it is identical to color nor that it is not identical to color; nor can one say that it is identical to emptiness."
It is not identical with emptiness. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not admit any phenomena of existence or non-existence;

this is called entering the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). A Bodhisattva in the seventh stage does not regress. From the seventh stage upward through the three higher stages, the Bodhisattva’s mental ground is clear and easily influenced:
to speak of fire is to burn. Moving upward from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), giving is a sickness and stinginess is the medicine.
From the realm of form downward, stinginess and greed are the disease; giving is the medicine. There is that which is called "unmanifest precept" (*avijñapti-śīla*): it severs worldly dharmas;
however, as long as one does not physically or manually perform [an act], there is no transgression—this is called the unmanifest precept. It is also called the non-outflow precept (*anāsrava-śīla*).
If one merely raises a thought or stirs a single notion, it is entirely termed breaking the precepts. Simply now, do not be affected by even one...
All objects of existence and non-existence are delusive distractions; one neither dwells upon nor relies on them, nor is there any cognition or understanding that does not so dwell or rely.

This is called universal learning. This is called diligent mindfulness. This is called widespread dissemination. When one has not yet awakened or understood, it is called the mother; when one has awakened and realized, it is called the child.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as the absence of awakening, understanding, or cognition—this is called the simultaneous loss of both mother and child. There is nothing [to be lost].
There are no fetters of goodness, no fetters of evil, no fetters of Buddha, and no fetters of sentient beings; their measure and number are likewise so.

Even unto the point where there are absolutely no fetters of any measure or number, it is said that the Buddha is a person who has transcended all fetters and surpassed all measures. He knows the meaning and phrasing of craving and attachment.
It is like a mother who loves her child and gives the child only butter to eat, remaining entirely unaware of whether it is digested or not.

This analogy refers to the afflictions of those in the ten stages who receive the honor and nobility of humans and devas; the afflictions of the meditative bliss and merit of the form and formless realms;
and the lack of mastery over supernatural powers such as flying, ascending, becoming invisible, or appearing at will to reach the pure lands of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

The afflictions of listening to the Dharma; the afflictions of learning the causes and conditions of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the afflictions of learning emptiness, equality, and the Middle Way;
the afflictions of learning the three clarities, the six supernormal powers, and the four unhindered knowledges; the afflictions of learning the Mahāyāna mind and giving rise to the four great vows;
and the afflictions of clear understanding regarding the first, second, third, and fourth stages. [The afflictions of] the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages...
On the various stages, there are afflictions of knowledge and vision; for Bodhisattvas of the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, there are afflictions of dualistically illuminating the two truths;

and up until the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, there are afflictions of the millions of asaṃkhyeya practices—namely, the attachment to the meaning and phrasing of what is known and understood.
Not realizing that it was actually the fetters of affliction, it is said: "The river of views can sweep away even the fragrant elephant.
Question: "Do you see? Answer: "I see. Question: "What is it like after seeing? Answer: "Seeing is non-dual. Since it is said that seeing is non-dual, one does not use seeing to see seeing.
If there were a further seeing of seeing, would the former seeing be correct, or the latter seeing? It is as the saying goes: "the seeing of seeing."

At that time, seeing is not seeing; even seeing is already free from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. Therefore, one does not practice the dharma of seeing, does not practice the dharma of hearing, and does not practice the dharma of awakening.
The Buddhas swiftly bestow upon such a person a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). An objection is raised:

"Since 'seeing' is not a term used for bestowing a prediction, what further use is there for a prediction? The Master said: "One who first awakens to the fundamental principle (the *zong*) is not hindered by any [concepts of] existence or non-existence."

One is constrained by the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). It is like washing a soiled garment; therefore, it is said that being free from characteristics is called Buddhahood. When both the void and the real are entirely non-existent, the central purport alone is profound and mysterious.
One who attains this single path shares in the Way; those of later generations who accord with its stages are thus said to receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the father, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the mother; the self is the illness, and treating the self is the medicine. The self is the sword.
It means to kill one's own parents of ignorance and craving; thus it is said, "to kill the father and harm the mother.
A single phrase such as this destroys all dharmas. It is the same with eating food at improper times:
right now, all dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—are entirely instances of eating at improper times. This is also called "evil food" or "filthy food placed within a precious vessel."
This is breaking the precepts; this is false speech; this is eating impure food. The Buddha is one who seeks nothing;
yet now you greedily seek all dharmas, whether existent or non-existent. All that you do is contrary [to his teaching] and is, in fact, slandering the Buddha.
Wherever there is greedy attachment, it is entirely called "reaching out the hand. Now, simply do not be greedily attached, nor dwell upon that non-attachment, nor even rely upon that non-attachment.
There is no understanding that does not rely upon abiding; this is called the fire of prajñā. This is burning one’s fingers; this is not sparing one’s body or life;
this is being dismembered limb by limb. This is the supramundane; this is holding worlds in the palm of one’s hand and transferring them to other realms.

Right now, if within the twelve divisions of the teachings and all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—there were even a hair’s breadth remaining within the internal organs, [it would not be so].
To linger is to remain within the net. Whatever is sought or obtained, whatever thoughts arise or mental stirrings occur—all these are termed jackals.
If, right now, within one's very bowels there is nothing sought and nothing obtained, such a person is a great donor and a lion’s roar.
Furthermore, they do not abide in non-attainment, nor do they have the conceptual understanding of not abiding.
This is called the sixth lion-like excellence: the non-arising of the notion of self and the non-occurrence of any evils. This is to contain Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed;
it is to remain unmoved by all greed, anger, the eight winds, and so forth. It is to be able to swallow the waters of the four great oceans into one’s mouth;
it is to not accept any false speech, such that it does not enter the ears and does not cause the body to give rise to even a single [affliction].
To harbor malice toward others is to take all fire into one’s own belly.

If, right now, you are neither deluded nor distracted by each and every object, neither angry nor delighted, and if you scrub and scrape away at the gates of your own six sense-faculties until they are pure and clean, you are a person of no affairs.
This surpasses all intellectual understanding; it is the asceticism (*dhūta*) of diligence. This is called the "heavenly eye" (*divyacakṣus*), and it is also called...
Clear illumination is the eye; this is called the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This constitutes the carriage that carries cause and effect.

When a Buddha appears in the world to deliver sentient beings, the preceding thought does not arise and the succeeding thought does not continue. The cessation of the karma of the preceding thought is called "delivering sentient beings.

If the preceding thought is one of anger, one immediately treats it with the medicine of joy; this is precisely what is meant by "a Buddha exists to deliver sentient beings. However, all of this is...
Regarding verbal teachings: it is just like treating illness. Because illnesses differ, the medicines also differ.

Therefore, at times one speaks of the existence of a Buddha, and at times one speaks of the non-existence of a Buddha. These are true words used to treat illness. If the illness is cured, every word is a true word;
if the illness is not cured, every word is a false word. That which is a true word becomes a false word because it gives rise to views. Falsehood...
Delusion is true speech, for it cuts off the inversions of sentient beings. Being ill is false; there is only the appearance of false medicine to counteract it.
When the Buddha appears in the world to deliver sentient beings, these are the words of the ninefold teaching and the words of the provisional teachings.
Hatred and joy, illness and medicine, are all one's own self; there are no two people. Where, then, is there a Buddha appearing in the world? Where...
There are sentient beings in this world who may be delivered. As the Sūtra says: "In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain *parinirvāṇa*. It also says:
"Not craving the Buddha’s *bodhi*, and not being stained by attachment to the existence or non-existence of all phenomena, is called 'delivering others.
Not remaining attached to one's own self is called 'delivering oneself. Since illnesses differ, so do the medicines; since prescriptions differ, they cannot be treated as one.
To adhere rigidly to the Buddha, to Bodhi, or to other such dharmas is entirely to rely on a fixed direction;

therefore, it is said that when one reaches a wise person, one may not maintain a single-sided view. What is expounded in the teachings is likened to yellow leaves, and is also like an empty fist used to deceive small children.
If a person does not understand this principle, they are said to be identical to ignorance. As it is said: "A bodhisattva practicing Prajñāpāramitā must not grasp at a self."

Regarding speech and following instructions: hatred is like a stone, while attachment is like a river. Right now, simply being without hatred and without attachment is to penetrate mountains, rivers, and stone walls.
This is directly for treating the "deafness" of worldly illness; extensive learning and eloquent discourse treat the "blindness" of worldly illness.
From the human realm up to Buddhahood is gain; from the human realm down to hell is loss. It is the same with right and wrong. The Third Patriarch said:
"Gain and loss, right and wrong—let them all go at once. Not grasping or dwelling upon any phenomena of existence or non-existence is called "not dwelling on conditioned objects.
Furthermore, not relying on or dwelling in non-reliance is called "not dwelling in the patience of emptiness. To grasp at oneself as... [is the error].

The Buddha himself is one who has realized the path of dhyāna; this is called "internal vision. To cling to that which is accomplished through the cultivation and realization of causes and conditions is called "external vision.
Master Zhì said: "Internal vision and external vision are both errors.

When the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue each do not greedily become defiled by any phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—this is called "upholding the four-line gāthā," and it is also called the "four fruits. Within the six sense bases, there is nothing [to be grasped].

This is the trace; it is also called the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). It is simply that, right now, one is not obstructed by any phenomena of existence or non-existence, nor does one dwell in dependence upon being unobstructed, nor is there any conceptual understanding of "not dwelling in dependence.
This is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*). One does not cling to this supernormal power.
This is called "no supernatural power" (aśrāvaka). It is as the saying goes: "The tracks of a bodhisattva who possesses no supernatural powers cannot be sought.
This Buddha is a person of the highest caliber, most inconceivable. "Human" refers to oneself; "heaven" refers to the illumination of wisdom.

To praise is to rejoice. Rejoicing belongs to the object; the object is heaven, and the praise is human. When human and heaven intersect, both are able to see one another. This is also called "pure wisdom."
To be a celestial being is to be a person of right wisdom. Originally one is not a Buddha; to point toward another and say "this is a Buddha" is called the "knot of essence.
Right now, simply do not form the conceptual understanding of a Buddha, nor dwell in the conceptual understanding of non-existence.

This is called the "extinction of knots," and it is also called True Suchness (*tathatā*), or Essential Suchness. To seek a Buddha or seek Bodhi is called manifesting the body and mind. Right now, simply...

All states of seeking mind are collectively termed the manifestation of body and mind. For example, when one seeks Bodhi, although it is a supreme seeking, it further increases the accumulation of dust and afflictions.
Seeking the Buddha belongs to the assembly of Buddhas; seeking all dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, belongs to the assembly of sentient beings.

It is simply a matter of present discernment and awareness: if one merely does not rely on or dwell in any dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, one does not enter into the ranks of these assemblies. It is simply...
Now, regarding each individual sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, mental object (*dharma*), and so forth, one does not find them unlovely; regarding each individual object, one does not harbor greed.

Merely being free from the ten states of a turbid mind constitutes attaining Buddhahood through the "cause of realization" (*vibodhana-hetu*). Those who study words and phrases to seek understanding are said to attain Buddhahood through the "conditional cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*).
To see the Buddha and know the Buddha is what is called "speaking of the Buddha. Yet, to have [a conceptual] knowledge or vision is, in fact, to slander the Buddha. If one says "Buddha"...

One who knows the Buddha, sees the Buddha, hears the Buddha, or speaks of the Buddha attains [realization] immediately. One who sees fire attains it immediately; one who sees oneself as fire does not attain it. It is like a knife cutting an object:
the knife attains it, but the object does not cut the knife. Those people who know the Buddha, see the Buddha, hear the Buddha, or speak of the Buddha are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These are what the Buddha knows; these are what the Buddha sees; these are what the Buddha hears; these are what the Buddha speaks. Among ten thousand, there may be one.
There is not one. It is simply because you yourself lack eyes that you rely on others to act as your eyes; in the teachings, this is called *anumāna-jñāna* (inferential knowledge).
Even your current craving for the Buddha’s intellectual understanding is itself inferential knowledge. Worldly metaphors are "conformable metaphors" (*anuloma-upamā*);

teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) are conformable metaphors, while teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) are "counter-metaphors" (*pratiloma-upamā*). Sacrificing one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain is a counter-metaphor. As it is now...
Not loving the Buddha’s bodhi and other such dharmas is an inverse analogy. It is difficult to relinquish what is likened to the head, eyes, marrow, and brain.

That which reflects all objective phenomena of existence and non-existence is called the "head. Being disturbed by the marks of all objective phenomena of existence and non-existence is called the "hands.
When there is no reflection of any prior objects at all, it is called the "marrow and brain. The noble stages practice the causes of the mundane; the Buddha enters among sentient beings.

They attract and guide [beings] through those of their own kind. When hungry ghosts have their limbs and joints ablaze with fire, they preach the *prajñāpāramitā* to them, causing them to resolve their minds [upon awakening].
If [the bodhisattva] were exclusively situated in the stage of the noble ones (*āryabhūmi*), by what means could they reach that place and converse with them?
The Buddha enters among all classes of beings and acts as a boat or raft for sentient beings, sharing in their suffering through boundless toil and exhaustion.

When the Buddha enters places of suffering, he likewise undergoes suffering together with sentient beings; yet the Buddha alone possesses the freedom of coming and going, which is unlike that of sentient beings.
The Buddha is not empty space. How could he not suffer when undergoing suffering? If one says he does not suffer, these words are contradictory and false. It is no ordinary matter.
Do not speak. Do not mistakenly say that the Buddha’s supernormal powers are either autonomous or non-autonomous; rather, be a person of shame and modesty.
Do not dare to say that the Buddha is conditioned or unconditioned, nor do you dare to say that the Buddha is free or not free, except when praising medicinal prescriptions.

One does not wish to expose the ugliness of both ends. The Teaching says: "If a person establishes the Buddha’s Bodhi and places it within the realm of 'that which exists' or 'this side,' that person incurs great sin.
It also says: "It is no fault to speak in such a manner before one who does not recognize the Buddha.
Just as stainless cow's milk can cure diseases of the tainted, that cow does not dwell on high plateaus, nor..."
He dwells in the low-lying marshes; this cow's milk is fit to serve as medicine. The high plateau is a metaphor for the Buddha, and the low-lying marshes are a metaphor for sentient beings.
As it is said, the Tathāgata’s true wisdom and *dharmakāya* likewise have no such illness; his eloquence is unimpeded, and he ascends with sovereign mastery.
Neither arising nor ceasing—this is what is called birth, old age, sickness, and death. Suffering from chronic illness, he consumed a mushroom broth in the dark and died of dysentery;
this was the dark act of concealing the traces of his enlightened head. When both light and darkness are dispelled, there is nothing to grasp, yet even "non-grasping" does not exist.
He is neither bright nor dark; born in the royal palace, he took Yaśodharā as his wife and attained the Way through the eight signs.
The Śrāvakas and non-Buddhists are bound by their deluded conceptualizations, such as claiming that the body does not consume mixed food.
Cunda said, "I know that the Tathāgata will certainly not accept or eat [the offering]. One must first possess two eyes to illuminate both sides;
do not merely carry one eye toward a single direction, for how then could you reach either side? It is like the goddess Puṇyā (Merit) and Andhakāra (Darkness).
The two women followed him, but the wise host accepted neither. Now, the mind is like empty space; only through study does it begin to achieve realization.
The High Patriarch of the Western Land said, "The Snowy Mountains are a metaphor for Great Nirvāṇa.
The First Patriarch of this land said, "The mind is like wood or stone. The Third Patriarch said, "Utterly forget all conditions. Caoqi said, "Do not entertain either good or evil at all."
Reflecting on this, my former teacher said: "It is like a person who is lost and cannot distinguish directions. Master Zhaolun said:

"Closing off wisdom and blocking the ears, one awakens alone in the profound darkness. Mañjuśrī said: "Because the mind is identical to empty space, I pay homage to that which has no object of observation.
Regarding these most profound sūtras, they are neither heard nor upheld; it is simply that, at this very moment, all dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—are entirely...
Neither seeing nor hearing; the six sense faculties are sealed shut. If one can study in this manner and uphold the sutra in this manner, only then does one have the capacity for cultivation.

These words are harsh to the ear and bitter to the mouth, yet if one can act accordingly, then in the second or third lifetime, one will be able to sit upon the Great Path-Assembly in a place where there is no Buddha, manifest the attainment of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, and transform evil into good.

It transforms the wholesome into the unwholesome; it causes unwholesome dharmas to teach and transform Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and causes wholesome dharmas to teach and transform those in the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts.
It can lead toward the realm of light to untie the bonds of light, and lead toward the realm of darkness to untie the bonds of darkness. It can take gold and turn it into dust.
One can turn a handful of dust into gold; one can accomplish all manner of things with complete freedom of transformation.

Should there be anyone seeking refuge beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Bhagavān immediately manifests his thirty-two marks before that person, speaking in their own voice and preaching the Dharma to them, transforming them according to their individual capacities.
Adapting to objects through diverse forms, he manifests in all realms of existence, yet remains free from the notions of "I" and "mine. Just so...
These belong to the affairs of that [limited] realm; they are still but minor applications, yet they are likewise subsumed within the gateway of Buddha-activity. As for the great application:
the great body is hidden within the formless, and the great sound is concealed within the faint resonance. It is like fire within wood, or like the sound of bells and drums.
When the causes and conditions are not yet complete, one cannot speak of existence or non-existence. Rebirth in the heavens as a lateral reward is cast aside like mucus or spittle.
The Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices are like riding a corpse across to the other shore, or like escaping from a prison through a latrine hole.
The Buddha is adorned with the thirty-two marks; these marks are called "soiled garments. It is also said:
"To say that the Buddha never at any time receives the five aggregates is impossible. The Buddha is not empty space; how could he never receive them?
The Buddha simply possesses the freedom to come and go, unlike sentient beings, who [migrate] from one celestial realm to another, from one..."
From one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field—this is the constant law of all Buddhas. Furthermore, it is said:

according to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, when receiving the offerings and alms of others, even if those others are in the midst of hell, the Bodhisattva practices compassion and transforms them through their own kind;

thus, they repay the kindness of others and cannot remain forever in nirvana. It is further said: it is like fire seeing fire—one must simply not touch it with the hand, and the fire will not burn the person. Only...

Now, simply be free from the ten kinds of turbid minds: the greedy mind, the loving mind, the defiled mind, the hateful mind, the grasping mind, the dwelling mind, the dependent mind, the attached mind, the seizing mind, and the longing mind.
Each of these consists of three phrases, yet each and every one must pass beyond these three phrases.
This is entirely a matter of illumination and function; let it be as you wish, whether horizontal or vertical. It is simply all movement and activity.
Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether weeping or laughing—all are the Buddha’s wisdom.
Under the Fourth Generation of Dajian (Mazu), there was Chan Master Huangbo Duanjie of Yungzhou; his name was Xiyun, and he was a native of Fuzhou. When the Master first arrived in Luoyang...
The Master was walking for alms in the capital when he heard the sound of a bowl being struck. A woman appeared from between the forest doors and said, "You are truly insatiable.
The Master replied, "You have not yet given anything, yet you reproach me for being insatiable. Why is that? The woman smiled and closed her door. The Master marveled at this;
he approached and spoke with her, and she revealed much to him. After a short while, Ba (Huangbo) took his leave. The woman told him, "You should go to Nanchang to see [Dongshan Liangjie]."
As for Master Mazu: when the Master arrived at Nanchang, the Great Master had already passed away. Hearing that his stupa was at Shimen, he went there to pay his respects.
At that time, Chan Master Baizhang Dazhi was dwelling by the side of the stupa.

The Master explained the purpose of his long journey, wishing to hear the words upon which the Master had relied during his lifetime. Baizhang then asked, "Majestic and dignified, from where have you come? The Master replied:
"Sublime and majestic, he comes from Lingnan. The Master said, "Being so sublime and majestic, what should you be doing?
The Teacher replied, "Being so sublime and majestic, I am not doing anything else," and then prostrated himself. He further related: "I went to attend upon Master Ma once more.
While standing in attendance, the Master looked at a whisk in the corner of his rope bed. I asked him, 'Is it used as this very thing, or is it apart from this thing? The Master..."
Xuefeng said, "In the future, when you open up these two flaps of skin, with what will you act as a person? I took up my whisk and held it upright.
The Master said, "Is this the function? Is it apart from the function? I hung the whisk back in its original place, whereupon the Master let out a thunderous shout.
"I have actually been deaf for three days. Upon hearing these words, the Master involuntarily stuck out his tongue.

Baizhang said, "In the future, will you not take up the lineage of Master Ma? The Master replied, "Not so. Today, because of what you have raised, I have come to see the great capacity and great function of Mazu.
Yet, I do not yet know Mazu. If I were to succeed Mazu, my descendants would lose themselves in the future."
Baizhang said, "When one's insight matches that of the master, one has diminished the master’s virtue by half. You have truly achieved a level of realization that surpasses your teacher.
One day Baizhang asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from gathering mushrooms at Mount Daxiong.
Baizhang asked, "Did you see any tigers? The Master let out a tiger's roar. Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to strike him. The Master gave Baizhang a slap. Baizhang [laughed].
Laughing heartily, he returned. Entering the hall, he said: "Under Mount Daxiong there is a great beast; you all must watch out for it.
Today, the old fellow Baizhang has been personally caught by its mouth.

While the Master was at Baizhang, during a communal work session to clear a field, Baizhang asked, "Venerable Yun, clearing this field is no easy task. The Master replied, "I am simply performing my duties along with the assembly. Baizhang [continued]: "... (The text ends here).
Baizhang said, "I fear it will trouble you. The Master said, "How would I dare decline such toil? Baizhang asked, "How many fields have you been able to open?
The Master struck the ground three times with his mattock. Baizhang then gave a shout. The Master covered his ears and departed.

Later, the Master asked Baizhang, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle (zongcheng), how do you instruct people? Baizhang remained seated as he was. The Master said, "What will future descendants transmit and receive?"
Baizhang said, "I took you for someone," and he immediately rose and left.
Nanquan asked the Master, "Who dwells in a place where the city is made of gold and the walls are made of silver? The Master replied, "The dwelling place of the sages. Nanquan said:
"Furthermore, there is another person; in what land does he dwell? The Master stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there. Baizhang said, "You cannot say it.
Why do you not ask Old Master Wang to speak? The Master said, "Furthermore, there is another person; in what land does he dwell? Baizhang said, "What a pity!"
The Master ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, he took up his staff and struck them all at once to disperse them. He then called out to the assembly;
when they turned their heads, the Master said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; there is little rain and much wind. One day, the Master clenched his fist and said to the assembly:
"The old monks of the world are all here. If I let slip a single thread of opportunity, you may run wild in every direction;
if I do not let it pass, you will not survive even a single squeeze. At that time, a monk asked, "What is it like when you let slip a single thread?"
The Master said, "Seven releases, eight crossings. [Pei asked: "What about when there is no letting pass? The Master said, "Pǔ (Universal).

One day, Prime Minister Pei invited the Master to his prefecture and presented him with a volume of his own writings. The Master received it and placed it upon the seat, not glancing at it even slightly.
After a long while, he asked, "Do you understand? Pei said, "I have not fathomed it. The Master said, "If you were to understand it in this way, you would still be close enough."
"A mere trifle. If it were to be expressed through paper and ink, what would remain of our school? Pei then presented him with a poem in one chapter, which said:
"Since the Great Being transmitted the Mind-Seal, A seven-foot body with a pearl upon his brow. Hanging his staff for ten years, he has dwelt by the waters of Shu."
"Today, Floating Cup crosses the banks of the Zhang River. A thousand dragon-elephants follow his lofty steps. Ten thousand miles away, fragrant flowers form a cause for excellence.
I wish to serve you as a disciple, Master, yet I do not know to whom you will entrust the Dharma. The Master showed no sign of joy.
From that time on, the teaching style of Huangbo flourished throughout the region south of the Yangtze River. A question was asked: "What is the Way? How does one practice? The Master said:

"What thing is the Way? You wish to practice. Another question was asked: "Regarding the succession of the patriarchal masters in all quarters, how should one engage in Chan meditation and study the Way?
The Master said: "Those are words for guiding those of dull faculties; they should not be relied upon as ultimate truth. [The questioner] said: "Since these are for guidance..."
[The questioner] said: "This was spoken to address those of dull faculties; I do not yet understand what further Dharma is taught for those of superior faculties.
The Master said: "If one is of superior faculties, where else would one go to seek it? Even one's own self cannot be found; how much less could there be another dharma to be grasped by the mind?
Have you not seen it said in the teachings: 'What is the form of each and every dharma? [The questioner] said: 'If this is so, then we need not concern ourselves with anything at all.'"
[The student] said, "I am seeking him. The Master said, "If it is so, then you will save your mental effort. [The student] said, "If that is the case, then he is completely cut off;
it cannot be that he does not exist. The Master said, "Who taught him to be non-existent? Who is he? You intend to seek him."
[The student] asked, "Since you do not permit seeking, why did you also say, 'Do not cut off others'?
The Master said, "If one does not seek, then it simply ceases. Who taught you to cut off? When you look at the empty space before your eyes, how would you go about cutting it off?
[The student] asked, "Can this Dharma be considered the same as empty space? The Master said, "I have never told you whether empty space is the same or different. I am merely—"

[The Master] spoke thus: "If you were to produce an intellectual understanding here, it would be as follows. [The student] asked: "Does this mean that one should not produce an intellectual understanding with people?
The Master said: "I have never obstructed you. However, understanding belongs to the realm of emotion (*qing*). When emotion arises, wisdom is blocked. [The student] asked:

"In this matter, should one not give rise to emotion? Is that so? The Master said: "If you do not give rise to emotion, who is there to say 'this'? [The student] asked: "As soon as one [speaks] toward the Harmony..."
The student continued speaking. "Why do you say that your words have fallen? The Master said, "You yourself are one who does not understand speech.
What 'falling' or defeat could there be? The student asked, "All the many words spoken until now were merely words of resistance;
not once has there been a real dharma pointed out to people. The Master said, "Real dharma is without inversion. It is in the very place where you now ask that it arises."
"Inverted! What real dharma are you seeking? [The student] asked, "Since the source of the question itself gives rise to inversion, how would you answer it, Master?
The Master said, "Just take an object and look at your own face; do not concern yourself with others.
He added, "You are just like a foolish dog that barks whenever it sees something move, unable to distinguish whether it is the wind blowing through the grass or anything else. He further said, "I..."
Since the time this Chan school was transmitted from master to disciple, it has never taught people to seek knowledge or seek understanding;

it speaks only of "studying the Way. Yet even this is merely a term used for guidance. Furthermore, the Way cannot be studied. If one harbors the intention of being a student, one instead becomes deluded regarding the Way.
The Way has no location or direction; it is called the Mahayana mind. This mind does not exist within, without, or in between; in truth, it has no location.
First, you must not form a conceptual understanding. This is merely saying that you currently take the sphere of your emotional and intellectual capacity (*qingliang*) to be the Way.
If this emotional and intellectual capacity is exhausted, the mind has no location or direction. This Way is celestial and natural, fundamentally devoid of names.
It is only because worldly people do not recognize it and remain deluded within their emotions that the Buddhas appear in the world to explain this matter, fearing that you all might...

This is clear. One provisionally establishes the name "the Way," yet one must not cling to the name to give rise to understanding; thus it is said, "having caught the fish, one forgets the trap. When body and mind are spontaneous, one attains the Way.

By realizing the mind, one reaches the source; therefore, one is called a śramaṇa. As for the fruit of the śramaṇa, it is accomplished through the cessation of discursive thought (*śamatha*), not through learning.
If you now seek the mind with the mind, you are merely looking toward another's house. Intending only...
To study and grasp—when can one ever find such a time? The minds of the ancients were sharp; upon hearing a single word, they immediately ceased their learning.
Therefore, they were called "idle men of the Way who have ceased learning and attained non-action. People of the present day, however, only desire to acquire much knowledge and many interpretations.
To extensively seek out the words and their meanings while calling this "cultivation" is to remain ignorant; such vast knowledge and understanding, on the contrary, result in obstruction.

It is like knowing only how to give much butter and milk to a child to drink, yet being entirely unaware of whether it has been digested or not. Those who study the path of the Three Vehicles are all of this same nature;
they are all called those for whom food is undigested—meaning that their intellectual understanding remains undigested and acts as a poisonous drug. All [of them] are thus.
This is grasped within the midst of arising and ceasing; within True Suchness (tathatā), none of this exists at all. Therefore it is said: "Within the treasury of my King, there is no such sword.
All previous points of understanding must be entirely set aside and rendered empty;
this is the Empty Tathāgatagarbha. As for the Tathāgatagarbha, not even a speck of dust can exist therein; this is the emergence of the Dharma King who destroys existence.
It appears in the world. It is also said: "At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was not the slightest dharma that I could obtain.

These words are simply for the sake of emptiness. You must merely dissolve the limits of your intellectual understanding; when the sentiments of both the internal and external are exhausted, you will be entirely without reliance or attachment, becoming a person of no affairs.
The teaching-nets of the Three Vehicles are merely medicines applied according to capacity; they are spoken as appropriate to the occasion and established according to the time. Each...

Each is different. However, if one can understand this, one will not be deluded. First, one must not cling to the literal meaning or form interpretations based on a single capacity or a single teaching.
Why is this so? Because, in reality, there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach.
In our school, we do not discuss such matters; we simply know that when the mind is stilled, it is enough. There is no further need for retrospective thought or prospective deliberation. Question:
"From antiquity until now, it has always been said that 'this very mind is Buddha. I do not yet understand which mind is this that is Buddha. The Master said, "How many minds do you have?
[The student] said, "Is it that the ordinary mind is Buddha, or is it that the holy mind is Buddha? The Master said, "Where is there such a thing as an ordinary or a holy mind?
[The student] said, "In the teachings of the Three Vehicles, it is currently stated that there are ordinary and holy beings. How can you, Reverend, say [there are none]?"
[The student] said, "No. The Master said, "Within the Three Vehicles, I have clearly told you that the minds of ordinary beings and sages are illusory. Yet now, you do not understand;

instead, you cling to them as being existent and take what is empty to be real—is this not itself an illusion? Because of this illusion, the mind is deluded. You need only eliminate ordinary sentiments and holy states;
outside of the mind, there is no other Buddha. The Patriarch came from the West to point directly to all people that they are [complete]."
The essence is the Buddha; you do not recognize this now, clinging to the ordinary and clinging to the holy, racing outward and thereby deluding your own mind.
This is why I tell you: "The very mind is the Buddha. When a single thought of emotion arises, one immediately falls into the various realms of existence.

From time immemorial until this day, it has not been different; there is no separate dharma. Therefore, it is called the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment. [The student] said: "Regarding what the Master has said, 'the very mind...'"
"What kind of principle is this? The Master said, "What principle are you looking for? As soon as there is a principle, the mind immediately becomes dualistic.

[The student] asked, "Your previous statement was that from time immemorial it has not been different from today. How is this so? The Master said, "It is precisely because you are looking for it that you yourself create the difference.
If you did not look for it, where would there be any difference? [The student] said, "Since it is not different, why [is there still seeking]?"
Regarding the statement "it is immediate": the Master said, "If you do not recognize the ordinary and the sage, who is it that tells you 'it is immediate'?
Whether it be immediate or not immediate, the mind is no longer mind. Within this state, both the mind and the immediate are forgotten; where else would you seek it further?"

Question: Delusion is able to obstruct one’s own mind; I do not yet understand by what means delusion is now to be dispelled. The Master said: To give rise to delusion and then attempt to dispel it also constitutes delusion.

Delusion originally has no root; it exists only because of discrimination. You need only refrain from calculating or dwelling on thoughts regarding the two categories of ordinary person and sage, and delusion will naturally vanish.
If you further intend to devise some means to dispel it, you will not achieve even a fraction of success.

[The student] said: "If one relies on grasping, it is called 'self. [But you say] one must cast off both arms to surely attain Buddhahood. Since there is no reliance or grasping, how can there be any transmission?
The Master said: "It is transmitted mind-to-mind. [The student] asked: "If it is the mind that is transmitted, why do you say that the mind, too, does not exist? The Master said: "..."
"Not attaining a single dharma" is what is called "transmitting the mind. If one realizes this mind, it is precisely no-mind and no-dharma. [The student] asked:
"If there is no mind and no dharma, how can it be called 'transmission'? The Master said: "When you heard of the 'transmission of the mind,' you assumed there was something to be obtained.
Therefore, the Patriarch said: 'When the nature of mind is recognized, it may be called inconceivable; when fully realized, there is nothing [to be grasped].'"

[The Master] said: "It is attained. At the time of attainment, one does not speak of 'knowing. If this matter were taught through the intellect, how could it possibly suffice? Question: "As for the empty space right before one's eyes, is that not an object?
Is there not a way to point to that object to reveal the mind? The Master said: "What kind of mind would you have me teach you to see within an object?
Even if you were able to see it, it would merely be a mind that reflects an object—just like a person using a mirror to look at their own face."
"Even if you were to see his features clearly, it would still be nothing more than a reflection; how could it have anything to do with you?
The student said, "If it were not for this reflection, when could I ever see him? The Master said, "If you involve yourself in causes and conditions, you will always have to rely on external things.
When will there ever be an end to that? Have you not seen him say to you: 'I let go my hand to you—there is not a single thing'? It is all in vain to speak thus."

[The student] said, "There are thousands of kinds [of things]. If he has recognized them, is there then nothing left to be illuminated? The Master said, "If it were nothing, what further need would there be for illumination?
Do not go on talking in your sleep with your eyes open."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A hundred kinds of extensive knowledge are not equal to the fact that having no seeking is foremost.
A man of the Way is a person of no affairs; truly, he has no such manifold thoughts. Even 'no affairs' does not exist—disperse! A monk asked: "What is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)?
The Master said: "Why do you engage in such entanglements? It is fundamentally pure; why rely on words, speech, questions, or answers? Simply let there not be one."

A completely focused mind is precisely what is called untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Whether you are walking, standing, sitting, or lying down each day, and in all your speech, simply do not become attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Every word you utter and every blink of your eye will then be identical to the untainted.

In this current age of the Dharma’s decline, those who go forward to study the Way of Chan are mostly attached to all sounds and forms. Why not make your mind accord with my mind, which is like empty space?
Only when you depart like a withered tree or a stone, or like cold ashes and extinguished fire, will there be a slight degree of correspondence.
If it is not thus, one day you will be interrogated by Old Man Yama. You need only distance yourself from all phenomena of existence and non-existence.
The mind is like the orb of the sun, ever present in the void; its radiance is spontaneous, illuminating without the act of illuminating.
This is not a matter of seeking ease. When one reaches this state, there is no place of rest;
this is precisely walking the path of all Buddhas, which is to give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. This is your pure *dharmakāya*, named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. If...

If you do not understand this meaning, then even if you study extensively, practice with diligent hardship, and subsist on grass clothing and wooden food, if you do not recognize your own mind, all such efforts are termed "deviant practices.
You will certainly become an attendant of the celestial Māras. What benefit can there be in practicing in such a manner?
Therefore, Master Zhigong said: "The Buddha is originally made by one's own mind; how can you seek him within words?
Even if you were to study until you have perfected the Three Worthies, the Four Fruits, and the Ten Stages, you would still merely be sitting among ordinary beings and sages.
Have you not heard it said: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of birth and death. When their momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, bringing about the next life'?"
It is as you wish. But how can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark (*dharmatā*), which transcends all in a single leap and enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata?
Since you are not such a person, you must extensively study intellectual understanding within the gates of transformation and edification established by the ancients. Master Zhìgōng said:
"If one does not meet a world-transcending enlightened teacher, it is in vain that one takes the Dharma-medicine of the Mahāyāna. You must now, at all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or...
Lie down. Simply practice being without-mind (*amanasikāra*). Though this may become real after a long time, because your strength is small, you cannot transcend suddenly.
You must obtain a point of entry for three years, five years, or perhaps ten; then you will naturally understand.
Since you are unable to do so, you insist on using the mind to study Chan and study the Way. What connection does this have with the Buddha-dharma? Therefore it is said: "It is like..."
All that has been spoken thus far is for the purpose of transforming people, like using yellow leaves as gold to stop a small child’s crying;
it is certainly not the reality. If there were actual attainment, you would not be a guest under my school’s gate. Furthermore, what connection does this have with your own fundamental nature?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "In reality, there is not the slightest dharma that can be named 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'.

If one can truly grasp this meaning, only then will one know that both the Buddha-way and the Mara-way are equally mistaken. Originally pure and luminous, it has no squareness or roundness, no largeness or smallness, and no characteristics such as length or shortness.
It is without outflows and unconditioned; it is without delusion and without awakening. To see it clearly, there is not a single thing.
There are no phenomena, no persons, and no Buddhas. The great trichiliocosm and its myriad worlds are but bubbles upon the ocean;
all sages and worthies are like lightning flashes. Nothing is as real as the mind. The Dharmakāya, from antiquity until now, is identical to that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
where is there even a hair’s breadth lacking? Having realized this meaning, you must exert yourself with great diligence throughout this life to transcend it.
"Breath does not preserve the inhalation. Question: "The Sixth Patriarch was unlearned in the scriptures; how did he come to receive the robe and become the Patriarch?
The Venerable Xiu was the head of five hundred monks and served as a teaching master, having lectured on thirty-two volumes of sutras and treatises.

Why was the robe not transmitted to him? The Master said: "It was because he had a mind. That is a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Whatever he cultivated and whatever he realized, he took it to be..."
It is so. This is why the Fifth Patriarch transmitted [the Dharma] to the Sixth Patriarch. At that time, the Sixth Patriarch simply attained a silent resonance;
he received the profound, secret intent of the Tathāgata, which is why the Dharma was entrusted to him. Have you not seen it said: "The Dharma, by its very nature, is no-dharma"?
Non-dharmas are also dharmas. Now, at this time when I entrust non-dharma, how has dharma ever been a dharma?

If you understand this meaning, only then can you be called a child of the renunciant life; only then is it fit for cultivation. If you do not believe this, why did the Venerable Ming run all the way to the summit of Mount Dayu to seek out the Sixth Patriarch?
The Sixth Patriarch then asked him: "What have you come to seek? Do you seek the robe, or do you seek the Dharma?"
The Venerable Ming said, "I have not come for the sake of robes, but have come for the sake of the Dharma.
The Sixth Patriarch said, "For a moment, collect your thoughts; do not deliberate on anything good or evil. The Venerable Ming then submitted his reply.
The Sixth Patriarch said, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—at this very moment—bring me back the face of the Venerable Ming before your parents were born."

Upon these words, Ming the Elder suddenly attained realization through silent resonance. He then prostrated and said, "It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
