While I was in the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch, I wasted thirty years of effort. Only today do I realize it was not right. The Sixth Patriarch said, "So it is.
It is only at this moment that you truly know the reason the Patriarch came from the West: to point directly to the human mind."
The mind sees its nature and becomes Buddha; it does not depend on words and explanations.

Have you not seen how Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe, what other Dharma did the World-Honored One transmit? Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes. Kāśyapa said:
"Throw down the banner pole in front of the gate! This is the very signpost of the Patriarchs.
Ānanda served as an attendant for thirty years, yet because he relied too much on his erudition and wisdom, the Buddha rebuked him, saying:

"Your thousand days of studying wisdom are not equal to one day of studying the Way. If you do not study the Way, even a drop of water will be difficult to digest. Now, for those who have left the household life—
One must know that only by having a portion of the matter transmitted from above can one truly succeed.

For instance, although Niu-t’ou under the Fourth Patriarch spoke both horizontally and vertically, he still did not yet know the pivot of the "upward" direction. Only with such an eye can one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox schools.
Furthermore, as for human affairs, you ought not to be able to comprehend them; you merely know how to learn words and keep them tucked away inside your bag.
Everywhere you go, you claim, "I understand Chan. But can this actually take the place of your own birth and death?
To treat an elder with such contempt—you will enter hell as fast as an arrow. As soon as I saw you step through the gate, I recognized you immediately. Do you know it yet? Hurry!
"You must exert effort. Do not treat this lightly. Wearing but a single robe and subsisting on mouthfuls of food, do not let this one life pass in vain.
Those with clear eyes will laugh at you; in the end, you will be reckoned as nothing more than a common worldly man. You should examine for yourself how far you have come.
For whose sake is this matter? If you understand, then understand; if you do not understand, then disperse. Be careful. Question: "What is the West?"

When asked about his intention [in coming], the Master struck him. All other skillful means employed by him were intended for those of superior capacity; those of middling or inferior faculties could not fathom their depths.
He passed away at his native mountain during the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Duanjì, and his stupa was named Guangye.
Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Masters, Volume Two;
Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Masters, Volume Three;
The Wanling Record of Chan Master Huangbo Duanji.
Prime Minister Pei asked, "Among the four or five hundred people in the mountains, how many have attained the Master’s Dharma?
The Master said, "Those who have attained it cannot be measured by number. Why? Because the Way is realized within the mind; how could it reside in words and speech?
Words and speech are merely for the purpose of instructing the ignorant. He asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The very mind is the Buddha; no-mind is the Way. Simply—"

The unborn mind does not stir thoughts of existence or non-existence, long or short, nor of self, other, subject, or object. The mind is fundamentally the Buddha; the Buddha is fundamentally the mind.
The mind is like empty space. Thus it is said: "The true Dharma-body of the Buddha is like empty space;

do not seek it elsewhere. All seeking is suffering. Even if one were to practice the six perfections and myriad deeds for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one would [only attain] Buddhahood and Bodhi [through this realization]."
This too is not ultimate. Why? Because it belongs to the conditioned activity of causes and conditions; when causes and conditions are exhausted, it returns to impermanence. Therefore it is said:
"The retribution-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the preachers of the Dharma. One should simply recognize one's own mind."

"There is no self and no person; from the very beginning, one is a Buddha. A question was asked: "If the sage being without mind is the Buddha, then when an ordinary person is without mind, does he not sink into emptiness and stillness?

The Master said: "In the Dharma, there are neither ordinary persons nor sages, nor is there sinking into stillness. The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent; do not form the view of it being a Buddha.
The Dharma is fundamentally non-nonexistent; do not form the view of its existence. Existence and non-existence are both merely views born of emotional attachment. It is like..."
It is like a phantom or a cataract. Thus it is said: "Seeing and hearing are like phantoms and cataracts; cognition and awareness are but sentient beings.

Within the ancestral gate, one discusses only the cessation of mental activity and the forgetting of views. Therefore, when mental activity ceases, the Buddha-way flourishes; when there is discrimination, the demonic armies blaze.
Question: Since the mind is fundamentally the Buddha, does one still cultivate the six perfections and the myriad practices? The Master said: Enlightenment resides in the mind;

it has no relation to the six perfections or the myriad practices. The six perfections and myriad practices are entirely gates of transformation—mere peripheral matters for engaging with sentient beings and delivering them.

Even if one were to reach the stages from Bodhi, True Suchness, the Ultimate Reality, and Liberation up to the Dharma-body, and even through all the way-stations of the ten bhūmis and four fruits of sagehood—these are all merely gates of deliverance and do not pertain to the Buddha-mind.
The mind itself is the Buddha; therefore, among all the various gates of deliverance, [the Buddha-mind is the essential core].
The Buddha-mind is supreme; it is simply a mind devoid of birth-and-death, afflictions, and the like, and thus it does not employ dharmas such as bodhi.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddha taught all dharmas to deliver my manifold minds; since I have no manifold minds, what use have I for all dharmas?
From the Buddhas down to the Patriarchs, there has never been a discussion of separate matters; they have discussed only the One Mind, which is also called the One Vehicle.
Seeking throughout the ten directions with earnest scrutiny, one finds no other vehicle; this assembly has no branches or leaves, but consists only of the truly real.
For this reason, this meaning is difficult to believe. When Bodhidharma came to this land, during the Liang and Wei dynasties, there was only Master Ke who secretly believed in his own mind.
Upon hearing the words, he immediately realized that the mind is Buddha; body and mind are both non-existent—this is called the Great [Vehicle].
The Way. The Great Way is fundamentally equal. Therefore, one deeply believes that all living beings share the same true nature (*dharmatā*). The mind-nature is not different;
nature is itself the mind, and the mind is not different from nature—this is called the Patriarch. Thus it is said: "When you recognize the mind-nature, it can be described as inconceivable.
Question: Does the Buddha save sentient beings? The Master said: "In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata saves."
[The interlocutor said: "As for 'one who has crossed over,' since even a self cannot be found, how could there be anything that is not-self?

Since both the Buddha and sentient beings cannot be found, why do you say that the thirty-two marks currently manifest and that one delivers sentient beings? How can you say they do not exist? The Master said: "All marks whatsoever are empty and false.
If one perceives all marks as being no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. As for the Buddha and sentient beings, they are entirely..."
This is your fabrication of false views. It arises solely because you do not recognize your original mind and instead indulge in arbitrary interpretations.

As soon as you form a view of Buddhahood, you are obstructed by the Buddha; as soon as you form a view of sentient beings, you are obstructed by sentient beings. Forming views of ordinary or holy, pure or defiled, and so forth—all become obstructions.
Because these obstructions cloud your mind, they collectively result in the cycle of birth and death, just like a released monkey.
One catches one; there is no end to this. This is all study, yet you must simply attain non-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

There is neither ordinary person nor sage, neither purity nor defilement, neither great nor small, neither outflow (*āsrava*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Within such a single mind, apply skillful means (*upāya*) with diligent adornment.
You, Virtue, have studied and mastered the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures; you must completely cast aside all views and understandings.
Therefore, having removed all else, only a single bed was left; he lay there ill, simply not giving rise to any views.

Since not a single dharma can be apprehended, he is not obstructed by dharmas. Having transcended the realms of both ordinary beings and sages within the three worlds, he may for the first time be named a world-transcending Buddha.
Thus it is said: "I bow my head to him who is like space; space has nothing upon which it relies, surpassing even the heterodox paths."
Since the mind is not different, phenomena are also not different. Since the mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), phenomena are also unconditioned.

All phenomena arise entirely through the transformations of the mind; therefore, because my mind is empty, all phenomena are empty. The thousands of grades and myriad categories are entirely identical. Throughout the entirety of the empty realm of the ten directions, there is but the single substance of the mind.
The mind is fundamentally not different, and phenomena are also not different—it is only due to your own views and understanding.
They are not the same. For example, it is like the gods who eat from identical precious vessels; according to their respective merits, the color of the rice differs.

In truth, the Buddhas of the ten directions have not the slightest dharma that can be called "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. It is simply the One Mind. In reality, there are no marks of difference, no radiance, and no victory or defeat.
Because there is no victory, there is no mark of a Buddha; because there is no defeat, there is no [mark of a non-Buddha].
[The questioner] said: "If the mind has no marks, how can it be entirely devoid of the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary characteristics used to transform and deliver sentient beings?
The Master said: "The thirty-two primary marks belong to the realm of marks; all marks whatsoever are empty and false.
The eighty secondary characteristics belong to the realm of form; if one perceives me by means of form, such a person walks upon a deviant path and cannot see [me]."
The Tathāgata was asked: "Are the Buddha-nature and the sentient-being-nature the same or different? The Master said: "In essence, there is neither sameness nor difference.

However, if one relies on the teachings of the Three Vehicles, one speaks of there being a Buddha-nature and a sentient-being-nature; thus, there are the causes and effects of the Three Vehicles, and therein exists sameness and difference.
But if one relies on the Buddha Vehicle and the transmission of the Patriarchs, such matters are not spoken of; rather, it points directly to..."
The One Mind is neither identical nor different; it is neither cause nor effect. Therefore it is said: "There is only this One Vehicle path;
there is no second, nor is there a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means. Question: Why did the Bodhisattva Anantagātra not see the mark of the Tathāgata’s crown?
The Master said: "In truth, there was nothing to be seen. Why? Because the Bodhisattva Anantagātra is himself the Tathāgata."
Come. You should not see anything further. I merely teach you not to form the view of a Buddha, so as not to fall into the extreme of Buddhahood;

not to form the view of a sentient being, so as not to fall into the extreme of sentient beings; not to form the view of existence, so as not to fall into the extreme of existence; not to form the view of non-existence, so as not to fall into the extreme of non-existence;
not to form the view of the ordinary, so as not to fall into the extreme of the ordinary; and not to form the view of the holy, so as not to fall into the extreme of the holy. Simply be without...
All views are themselves the body of boundlessness. If there is a locus for views, one is termed a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
Non-Buddhists delight in various views, whereas a bodhisattva remains unmoved amidst all views. The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas;
therefore it is said: "Maitreya is also suchness; the multitude of sages and worthies are also suchness. Suchness is non-arising; suchness is non-ceasing.
As it is, there is no seeing. As it is, there is no hearing. The crown of the Tathāgata’s head is perfectly round, yet there is neither roundness nor the perception of roundness;
therefore, it does not fall into the extreme of roundness. Thus, the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories.

It is provisionally likened to empty space: as perfect as the great void, without deficiency and without excess, indifferent and without affairs. Do not force yourself to debate other realms; such debating leads to attachment.
This immediately becomes consciousness. Therefore it is said: "The perfect realization sinks into the ocean of consciousness; its流转 (transmigration) is like a drifting tumbleweed.
One merely says, "I know," "I have learned it," "I have attained awakening," or "I am liberated.
Or one thinks, "I possess the principle. When things go well, one is joyful; when they go poorly, anger arises. What use is such a view? I tell you: it is all in vain and without purpose.

Do not waste your efforts in vain; do not seek the Truth. You must simply cease all views. Therefore, both internal and external views are erroneous, and both the Way of the Buddha and the Way of Māra are equally flawed.
This is why Mañjuśrī was temporarily cast into the two Iron Ring Mountains for giving rise to dualistic views.

Mañjuśrī is ultimate wisdom (jñāna), while Samantabhadra is expedient wisdom (upāya). Although these two are contrasted as expedient and ultimate for the sake of mutual correction, in the final analysis, there is neither expedient nor ultimate;
it is solely the one mind. This mind is neither Buddha nor sentient being, and thus there is no divergent view. Were there even the slightest notion of "Buddha," [it would be a delusion].

One then gives rise to the view of a sentient being, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of permanence, and the view of annihilation. These then become the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
Because one is obstructed by these views, the Patriarch directly pointed out that the fundamental mind and fundamental essence of all sentient beings are originally Buddha;

they do not depend on cultivation for completion, do not belong to gradual stages, and are neither light nor darkness. Because they are not light, there is no ignorance; because they are not darkness, [there is no delusion].
Therefore, there is no darkness. For this reason, there is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance. Upon entering this gate of my school, you must pay close attention.
To perceive things in this manner is called the Dharma. Because one perceives the Dharma, it is called the Buddha. When both Buddha and Dharma are absent, it is called the Sangha;
this is termed the "unconditioned Sangha" and is also known as the "Three Jewels of One Essence. Now, as for those who seek the Dharma:
Do not seek by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek by clinging to the Sangha. One should be without seeking.

Because there is no clinging to seeking the Buddha, there is no Buddha. Because there is no clinging to seeking the Dharma, there is no Dharma. Because there is no clinging to seeking the Sangha, there is no Sangha. Question: "The Master is currently preaching the Dharma before us.
How can you say there is neither Sangha nor Dharma? The Master said: "If you perceive that there is a Dharma to be found..."

To speak thus is to seek the self through sound. If one perceives a self, that is a locus. Phenomena (*dharma*) are themselves non-phenomena; phenomena are the mind itself. Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"When this mind-dharma is transmitted, how could phenomenon after phenomenon ever be a phenomenon?

When there is no phenomenon and no fundamental mind, only then does one understand the dharma of the mind-mind. In reality, not a single dharma can be obtained; this is called sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The Way...
As for the "site," it is simply not giving rise to various views and awakening to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally empty. This is called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Originally there was not a single thing; where could there be any dust? If you grasp the meaning within this, you will roam at ease—what is there to discuss?
Question: "Originally there was not a single thing. Does "no-thing" mean "is"? The Master said: "Even 'no' is not [the truth]. In Bodhi, there is no such place as 'is'."
Nor is there an absence of knowing and understanding. Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Your own mind is the Buddha;
the Buddha is the mind. Mind and Buddha are not different; therefore it is said, 'This very mind is the Buddha. Apart from the mind, there is no other Buddha. Question:
"If one's own mind is the Buddha, how did the Patriarch come from the West to transmit [the Dharma]? The Master said: "The Patriarch came from the West solely to transmit..."
"Mind-Buddha": This directly points out that your own mind is fundamentally the Buddha; mind after mind is no different. Therefore, it is called the "Patriarch.

If you see this meaning directly, you will immediately transcend all the stages of the Three Vehicles. You are fundamentally the Buddha, not something to be accomplished through cultivation. [The student] asks:
"If this is so, for what Dharma do the Buddhas of the ten directions appear in the world and preach? The Master says: "The ten directions..."
The Buddhas appearing in the world speak only of the Dharma of the single mind. Therefore, the Buddha secretly entrusted this essence of the single-mind Dharma to Mahākāśyapa;
it pervades empty space and fills the entire dharma-realm, and is called the principle of all Buddhas.
As for this Dharma, how could you understand it through words and phrases? Nor is it to be found within a single stimulus or a single circumstance.
To see this is to realize it through silent, intuitive resonance alone. This single gate is called the Gate of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

If you wish to comprehend it, simply know that there is no mind; if you suddenly awaken to this, you have attained it. If you apply the mind with the intent to learn or grasp it, you move further away from the Dharma.
Only when there is no divergent mind and no mind of grasping or rejecting—when the mind is like wood or stone—do you first possess the capacity to study the Way.

[The student] said: "If there are currently all manner of deluded thoughts, why do you say they do not exist? The Master said: "Delusion has no inherent substance; it is simply what arises from your own mind.
If you recognize that the mind is Buddha, the mind is fundamentally without delusion. Why then would you give rise to a thought to further identify with delusion?
If you do not produce thoughts or stir your mind, naturally there will be no delusion. Therefore it is said: 'When the mind arises...'"
When various phenomena arise, and the mind ceases, then those various phenomena cease. Right now, at the very moment a deluded thought arises, where is the Buddha? The Master said:

"At this very moment, when you perceive a deluded thought arising, that perception itself is precisely the Buddha. Yet, within this state, if there were no deluded thoughts, even the Buddha would not exist.
Why is this so? It is because you give rise to the thought of becoming a Buddha, and thus claim there is a Buddha to be attained."
When sentient beings see [a Buddha], they immediately think there is a sentient being to be saved. Every stirring of thought and movement of mind is entirely your own point of view.
If there were no views at all, where would the Buddha be? For example, as soon as Mañjuśrī gave rise to the view of a Buddha, he was banished to between the two Iron Ring Mountains.
It is said: "At this very moment of awakening, where is the Buddha? The Master said: "From where does the question come? From where does the realization come?"
What arises? Speech and silence, movement and stillness—all sounds and forms are entirely the work of the Buddha. Where else would you seek the Buddha?
Do not further place a head upon a head or add a beak to a beak. Simply do not give rise to divergent views: the mountains are mountains, and the waters are waters.
The monastic is the monastic; the layperson is the layperson. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, the moon, and the stars—all do not transcend your own mind.
The entire trichiliocosm is, in its entirety, your very self. Where is there any multiplicity? There is no phenomenon outside the mind. Before one’s eyes, the green mountains fill the view;
throughout the vast expanse of space, everything is so bright and clear that there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything to serve as an object for your conceptual understanding.

All sounds and forms are the grace of the Buddha. Phenomena do not arise in isolation; they are produced only by relying upon conditions. For the sake of sentient beings, there exists manifold wisdom.
Though one speaks all day long, when has one ever spoken? Though one hears all day long, when has one ever heard?
Therefore, although Śākyamuni preached for forty-nine years, he never uttered a single word. It is said: "If this is so, where is Bodhi?"
"Ti. The Master said: "Bodhi has no such place. Even a Buddha does not attain bodhi, and sentient beings do not lose bodhi.
It cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be sought by means of the mind. All sentient beings are themselves the manifestation of bodhi. He asked: [What is it?]
"How does one give rise to the bodhicitta? The Master said: "Bodhi is unobtainable. You should now simply give rise to a mind that is without attainment.
To be certain that not a single dharma can be obtained is itself the bodhicitta. Bodhi has no place of abiding; therefore, there is no one who attains it. Thus it is said:
'In the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I did not obtain even the slightest dharma. The Buddha then conferred upon me...'"
The prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*): It is clearly known that all sentient beings are fundamentally *bodhi*; they need not further attain *bodhi*.
You have now heard the exhortation to resolve upon *bodhicitta*, yet you think you will take this single mind and study it to become a Buddha, merely intending to create a Buddha-path.

Even if you were to practice for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, you would only obtain a reward-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*) or a transformation-body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*). These are distinct from your original source, the true-nature Buddha.
What connection is there? Therefore it is said: "Seeking an external Buddha with form is not like you. Question:

Since the fundamental nature is already Buddha, how can there further be the various different forms and appearances of the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence? The Master said: "The essence of all Buddhas is perfect and complete."
There is neither increase nor decrease; it flows into the six realms, perfectly complete in every place. Among the myriad species, each and every one is a Buddha.
It is like a ball of mercury that, when scattered in various places, appears as individual spheres, each perfectly round;
yet when not scattered, it is but a single mass. This one is all, and all is this one. The various forms and appearances are like houses; [when the house is abandoned, the space remains].

The donkey’s house; entering the human house; discarding the human body to attain the celestial body; and even the houses of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—all these are places where you engage in grasping and rejecting.
It is for this reason that distinctions arise. As for the nature of the original source, how could there be any distinction? Question:
"What is diligence? The Master said: "When body and mind do not arise, this is called the foremost, steadfast diligence.
The moment one gives rise to a mind that seeks outwardly, one is said to be like King Kali going out for pleasure-hunting.

When the mind does not wander outward, one is an ascetic of patience (*kṣānti*). When both body and mind are absent, that is the Way of the Buddha. Question: "If there is no mind, how can one practice this Way?"
"Is it possible or not? The Master said, "To be without mind is precisely to practice this Way. What more need be said of 'attaining' or 'not attaining'?
For instance, the moment a single thought flickers up, that is the realm; if there is no thought, the realm is forgotten and the mind naturally ceases."

There is nothing further to be pursued. Question: What is it to transcend the three realms? The Master said: Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all; you will transcend the three realms right where you are.
The Tathāgata appeared in the world to destroy the three states of existence (*trabhava*). If there is no mind whatsoever, even the three realms do not exist.
It is like taking a single atom and breaking it into a hundred parts: ninety-nine parts are non-existent, and as for the one part— [The text ends here.]
If there were such [a thing], the Mahāyāna would not be able to surpass it; even by a hundredfold, it would not suffice for the Mahāyāna to begin to surpass it.
Entering the hall, he said: "The mind itself is Buddha. From the Buddhas above down to the wriggling insects and sentient beings below, all possess Buddha-nature;
they share the same essence of mind. Therefore, when Bodhidharma came from the Western Heaven, he transmitted only the Dharma of the One Mind, pointing directly to it."
All sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas; they do not depend upon cultivation. Simply recognize your own mind as it is now, see your own original nature, and seek nothing else.
How does one recognize one’s own mind? That which is speaking these very words right now is precisely your mind.
If you do not speak and do not engage in activity, the substance of the mind is like empty space, devoid of any marks.
Its appearance likewise has no fixed location, nor is it unilaterally non-existent; it exists but is invisible. Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"The treasury of the true nature within the mind-ground has neither head nor tail; responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom'."
When it is time to respond to conditions, one cannot say whether they exist or not; at the very moment of responding, there is likewise no trace.
Knowing this, if you now simply settle within non-existence, you are walking the path of all Buddhas. As the Sutra says:
"One should give rise to the mind without dwelling on anything. That all sentient beings wander incessantly through the cycle of birth and death is due to the mental engagement with objects.
They run about and act; the mind does not rest within the six realms of existence, thereby causing one to undergo various kinds of suffering.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The minds of those who are difficult to transform are like monkeys; therefore, one must restrain their minds with various methods before they can be tamed.
Thus, when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. Therefore, know that all dharmas are [conditioned by the mind]."
All is created by the mind. Even the six realms of existence—humans, devas, and so forth, down to the hells and asuras—are entirely created by the mind. Now, simply train in non-mindfulness;
immediately cease all conditioned activities and do not give rise to deluded thoughts or discriminations. Be without personhood, without self, and without greed or hatred.

There is neither hatred nor love; there is neither victory nor defeat. Simply eliminate these many kinds of deluded thoughts, and the nature will be inherently pure from the beginning—this is precisely the practice of the Bodhi-dharma and the Buddhas.

If you do not realize this meaning, then even if you study extensively and practice with diligent hardship, eating wood and wearing grass clothes, if you do not recognize your own mind, it all counts as deviant conduct and will result only in becoming a celestial demon or an externalist.
The Way. As for the various deities of land and water—if one practices in this manner, what further benefit would there be? Master Zhi said: "The fundamental essence is produced by one's own mind;
how can it be sought within words and letters? Now, simply recognize your own mind and cease discursive thought;
then delusive imaginings and worldly toil will naturally not arise. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "Only set out a single bed, lie down as if ill, and let the mind not stir."
It is like a person lying ill; when攀緣 (pān-yuan, the clinging of the senses) completely ceases and false conceptualizations (vikalpa) are extinguished, that itself is bodhi.

If, however, your mind is now restless and unsettled, no matter how much you study to reach the stages of the three vehicles, the four fruits, or the ten bhūmis, you will ultimately remain seated among the ordinary and the holy.
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) return to impermanence; their power has a limit and an end, just as...
An arrow shot into the air falls back down once its momentum is exhausted; such is the practitioner who returns to the cycle of birth and death.

To practice in this manner, without understanding the Buddha’s intent, is to undergo hardship in vain—is this not a great error? Master Zhi said: "If one has not yet encountered a world-transcending enlightened teacher, it is in vain that one takes the medicine of the Mahayana Dharma.
Now, at all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one should simply learn to be without-mind.
There is no discrimination, no dependence, and no attachment. All day long, one proceeds spontaneously and carefree, appearing like a simpleton.
The people of the world do not recognize you at all, yet there is no need for you to teach others to recognize you.
This unrecognizing mind is like a solid rock; it has no seams or fissures. No phenomena can penetrate into your mind. Utterly still and without clinging.
Only then does there begin to be a slight degree of correspondence. To penetrate beyond the realms of the three worlds is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Not leaking mental characteristics is called untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Not performing the karma of humans or devas, not performing the karma of the hells, and not giving rise to any mind—when all conditions cease and do not arise, this very body and mind are that of a free person. This is not a one-sided state.
It is not produced; it simply arises according to one’s will. This is what the sutra means when it says, "The Bodhisattva has a mind-born body.
If you have not yet realized this state of no-mind, then clinging to appearances constitutes demonic activity. Even performing the Buddha-work of purifying the Pure Land all becomes karma;
this is called a "Buddha-obstruction," for it obstructs your own mind. Thus, you are bound by cause and effect, and you lack the freedom to go or stay as you wish.

Therefore, dharmas such as bodhi are fundamentally non-existent. All that the Tathāgata has preached consists of transformed beings, just like yellow leaves used as gold coins to temporarily stop a child’s crying.
Thus, in reality, there is no dharma named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Now that you have understood this meaning, why exert yourself further? Simply follow conditions to exhaust past karma, and do not create new calamities.
When the mind is luminously clear, all former understandings must be relinquished.

As Vimalakīrti said, "Remove all that is possessed," and as the Lotus Sutra says, "For twenty years he was constantly made to remove filth"—this merely refers to removing the mental fabrications within the mind.
Regarding this point of view, it is further said: "To sweep away the dung of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally empty and quiescent;
it simply does not allow even a single dharma to remain. Therefore, a sutra states: "The lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty.
If one says that the Buddha-way is attained through cultivation and study, such a view has no connection whatsoever [to the truth]. Or, it may be considered a single occasion.

When two people share a single object of focus—whether it be a raised eyebrow or a flicker of the eye—and their responses correspond perfectly, one says they have attained a spiritual accord and realized the principle of Chan.
Yet, if they suddenly encounter someone who does not understand, they immediately say that person knows nothing at all.

If they can establish a logical point against another, their hearts are filled with joy; but if they are refuted by the other and find themselves inferior, they immediately feel dejected and sorrowful. Such is the state of mind.
The mind and its intentions study Chan; what connection could there be? Even if you manage to grasp a few principles, you have merely attained a mental factor (*caitta-dharma*).
This has absolutely no connection to the Way of Chan. This is why Bodhidharma sat facing a wall, not allowing people to find any point of view.
Thus it is said: "To forget the workings of the intellect is the Buddha-way; discrimination is the realm of demons. This nature remains as it is even when you are deluded.
It is not lost; even at the time of awakening, it cannot be attained. This natural, celestial self-nature is fundamentally without delusion or awakening.

Throughout the entirety of the void-realm of the ten directions, there has from the beginning been only the substance of my own one mind. Even if you exert yourself in movement and activity, how could you ever depart from this void?
This void is originally neither large nor small, neither outflowing nor conditioned, and neither deluded nor awakened. When clearly seen, there is not a single thing to be found.
There is neither person nor Buddha. Cut off even the slightest measure; this is to be without dependence and without attachment—a single stream of pure clarity. This is self-nature;

this is the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena). How could there be any room for deliberation? The true Buddha has no mouth and does not preach the Dharma;
the true listener has no ears—whom could it hear? Take care. A monk took his leave to return to Guizong. Guizong said: "Go."
"Where have you been? The monk said, "I have been to various places to study the five flavors of Chan. Zhaozhou said, "In various places there are the five flavors of Chan;
here, with me, there is only the one flavor of Chan. The monk asked, "What is the one flavor of Chan?

Zhaozhou struck him. The monk said, "I understand! I understand! Zhaozhou said, "Speak! Speak! When the monk prepared to open his mouth, Zhaozhou struck him again. Later, that monk went to the Master’s (Linji’s) place.
The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Guizong. The Master asked, "What words or phrases did Guizong say? The monk then related the previous conversation.
The Master then ascended the hall and, citing this incident, said: "Master Mazu produced eighty-four men who were true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When questioned, each of them was completely soaked through. Only Guizong was slightly better. [The Master] was [once] there.
In the assembly at Yanguan, Emperor Daizong was a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*). As the Master was prostrating before the Buddha in the Buddha Hall, the novice said:
"Do not seek by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek by clinging to the Saṅgha. Elder, when you prostrate, what is it that you seek?"
The Master said, "Do not seek it by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek it by clinging to the Dharma; do not seek it by clinging to the Sangha. Constantly pay homage to such matters.
The śrāmaṇera asked, "What is the use of paying homage? The Master then struck him with his palm. The śrāmaṇera said, "That was too coarse.
The Master said, "In what kind of place are we here to speak of coarse or fine? He struck him again, and the śrāmaṇera ran away. This occurred while the Master was traveling on pilgrimage.
Upon arriving at Nanquan, one day during the midday meal, the Master took his bowl and sat in Nanquan’s place.
When Nanquan came down and saw him, he asked, "In what year did you begin practicing the Way, Elder? The Master replied, "Before the time of Vipaśyin Buddha. Nanquan said:
"It is still the lineage of Master Wuzhuo," [Baizhang] said. The Master (Nanquan) then went down.

One day, while the Master was sitting in the tea hall, Nanquan came down and asked, "Regarding the principle that 'cultivating equanimity of concentration and wisdom leads to clearly seeing the Buddha-nature,' what do you think?
The Master replied, "In the twelve periods of the day, do not rely upon or depend on a single thing. Nanquan asked, "Is this not your own realization, Elder? The Master said, "No."
“Dare. Nanquan said, “Setting aside the payment for the gruel and water for a moment, who will repay the cost of the straw sandals? The Master then ceased speaking.
Later, Guishan raised this anecdote and asked Yangshan, “Was it not that Huangbo could not catch Nanquan?”
Yangshan said, "Not so. You must know that Huangbo possesses the mechanism for trapping tigers. Miaoshan said, "The extent of your realization has grown this much.
One day, five newly arrived monks came to visit him simultaneously. One of them did not prostrate, but instead drew a circle with his hand and stood there.
The Master said, "Do you know this is a fine hunting dog? He replied, "It seeks the chamois."
[The monk] said, “The scent of a sheep has come. The Master said, “A wild goat has no scent. Where do you seek it? [The monk] said, “I have come seeking the tracks of a wild goat.
The Master said, “A wild goat leaves no tracks. Where do you seek it? [The monk] said, “I have come seeking the footprints of a wild goat.
The Master said, “A wild goat leaves no footprints. Where do you seek it? [The monk] said, “If that is so, then it is a dead wild goat. The Master said, “It is indeed a dead wild goat.”
He then ceased speaking. The next day, he ascended the seat. After the assembly had withdrawn, he asked, "The monk who was searching for the wild sheep yesterday, come forth.
The monk immediately stepped forward. The Master said, "Yesterday, I had not yet spoken my final word. What do you say to this? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "I took you for a monk of true substance; it turns out you are merely a scholar-monk. Later, the Master dismissed his assembly.
At Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou, Prime Minister Pei once entered the temple while walking and saw a mural on the wall. He asked the temple master, "What is this painting?
The temple master replied, "It is a portrait of a high monk. The Prime Minister said, "The form and shadow are here;
where is the high monk? The temple master was speechless. The Prime Minister then said, "Is there no Zen monk here?"

[The Master] said, "Ma. The Abbot of the temple said, "There is one person [who knows]. The Official then invited the Master for an audience and recounted the previous conversation, asking the Master about it.
The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! Pei Xiu responded, "Yes. The Master asked, "Where are you? At these words, the Official attained realization.
He then requested the Master once more to open the hall for formal instruction.
Now, those who study the Way must first eliminate all miscellaneous studies and external conditions. They must be resolute in their non-seeking and resolute in their non-attachment.
When they hear the most profound Dharma, it is as if a clear breeze passes by the ear—suddenly gone and no longer pursued. This is what is meant by "profound.
Entering the Tathāgata-dhyāna, one leaves behind the conceptualizations of birth-dhyāna. From the ancestral masters of old, only the One Mind has been transmitted; there is nothing else.
Regarding the two dharmas: pointing to the mind as Buddha means to transcend suddenly both the equal and wondrous forms of awakening, decisively not flowing into a second thought;
only then can one be said to have entered the gate of our school. As for such a dharma, when you, O person of ordinary capacity, arrive here, how do you intend to study it?
Therefore it is said: "When the mind is directed toward it, one is bound by the demon of directed-mind; when the mind is not directed toward it, yet again..."
One is bound by the demon of non-conceptualization; when not in a state of non-conceptualization, one is again bound by the demon of non-non-conceptualization.
These do not come from without; they arise from your own mind. Only the tracks of a Bodhisattva who possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) can they not be traced.
If, at all times, the mind harbors the view of permanence, one is a follower of the eternalist heretics (*śāśvatavāda*). If one contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena...
Those who hold the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) are precisely the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) of the nihilistic view (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, the teaching that "the three realms are mind-only" and "all phenomena are consciousness-only" is still spoken in response to those with the false views of non-Buddhists. If one speaks of the *dharmakāya* as the ultimate fruit, this is addressed to those of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*daśārya-bhūmi*).

Thus, the Buddha eliminates two types of ignorance: first, the subtle ignorance regarding the knowable (*sūkṣma-jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha*); second, [the ignorance regarding the obstruction of the outflows].

Since the Buddha has already transcended even the most subtle ignorance regarding what is to be known (*jñeya-ajñāna*), what further need is there to speak of the two types of awakening—the ordinary and the sublime?
Therefore, all people desire only to move toward light and not toward darkness; they seek only enlightenment and do not cherish afflictions or ignorance.
Thus, they claim that the Buddha is awakened while sentient beings are deluded. If one holds such a view, for hundreds or thousands of kalpas—
They are born into the cycle of the six realms of existence without further interruption. Why is this? It is because they slander the fundamental self-nature of all Buddhas.
Though others have clearly explained it to you, the Buddha is not enlightened and sentient beings are not ignorant; for in the Dharma, there is neither enlightenment nor ignorance.
The Buddha is neither strong, nor are sentient beings weak; for in the Dharma there is neither strength nor weakness. The Buddha is neither wise, nor are sentient beings foolish;
for in the Dharma there is neither folly nor wisdom. You emerge from your seat and claim to understand Chan; yet as soon as you open your mouth, your illness breaks out.
You do not speak of the root, but only of the branches; you do not speak of delusion, but only of awakening; you do not speak of the essence, but only of its function.
There is, in total, no place for you to speak or debate. All dharmas have fundamentally never existed, yet now they are not non-existent either.

Conditioned origination does not exist; the cessation of conditions is not non-existent. Fundamentally they do not exist, because the fundamental is not fundamental. Mind is not mind, because mind is not mind.
Characteristics are not characteristics, because characteristics are not characteristics. Therefore it is said: "When there is no dharma and no fundamental mind, only then does one understand."

Mind and mental phenomena: phenomena are non-phenomena; non-phenomena are phenomena. Because there is neither phenomenon nor non-phenomenon, these minds and mental phenomena suddenly and fleetingly arise.
In a single thought-moment, one realizes they are like illusions and transformations, and thus flows into the Buddhas of the past.
Yet the Buddhas of the past do not exist, and the Buddhas of the future are not non-existent. Furthermore, they are not called "Buddhas of the future. [The present...]
In every thought-moment, there is no abiding. One does not call this the "present Buddha.
When the Buddha arises, one must not deliberate over whether it is awakening or delusion, good or evil; one must by no means cling to it or sever it.
If even a single thought flickers up, a thousandfold locks cannot restrain it, and ten-thousand-foot ropes cannot bind it. Since it is thus:
As soon as you try to extinguish it or stop it, I clearly tell you: "This is your own *vijñāna*-flame.
How do you intend to cut it off? It is like a mirage; even if you search throughout the ten directions of the world, it cannot be found. Only then do I say: "It begins."
When viewed from afar, it is right here before you. As soon as you intend to pursue it, it retreats further away;
when you begin to avoid it, it comes back to chase you. You cannot grasp it, yet you cannot let it go. Since this is so, know that the nature of all phenomena is inherently thus;
there is no need to worry about it or be anxious over it. For example, if one says the preceding thought is ordinary and the succeeding thought...
This is the Sage. It is like the turning over of a hand. This is the ultimate of the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

According to our Zen school, the preceding thought is not the ordinary person, and the succeeding thought is not the sage; the preceding thought is not the Buddha, and the succeeding thought is not the sentient being.
Therefore, all forms are the Buddha’s form, and all sounds are the Buddha’s sound. To bring this up—
One principle; all principles are likewise so. To see one thing is to see all things;
to see one mind is to see all minds; to see one path is to see all paths. There is nowhere that is not the Path.

To see one speck of dust, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth throughout the ten directions are all likewise so. To see a single drop of water is to see all within the worlds of the ten directions.
The nature is water. Furthermore, to see all phenomena (*dharmas*) is to see the universal mind. All phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet the mind is not non-existent.
That which is not non-existent is wondrous existence; that which exists is also non-existent. That which is non-existent is existence—this is true emptiness and wondrous existence.
Since this is so, the worlds of the ten directions do not transcend my single mind. All lands of subtle dust...
"It arises from my single thought. If that were so, what could be said of "internal" and "external"? It is like the nature of honey being sweet; all honey is thus.
One cannot say, "this honey is sweet, while the rest is bitter. Where could such a thing exist? Therefore it is said: "Space has no interior or exterior;
the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is naturally so. Space has no middle; the nature of phenomena is naturally so."
Therefore, sentient beings are the Buddha, and the Buddha is sentient beings. Sentient beings and the Buddha are fundamentally of one and the same essence.

Birth-and-death and nirvana, the conditioned and the unconditioned, are fundamentally of one and the same essence. The mundane and the supramundane, and even the six realms and the four modes of birth, are likewise so.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—whether possessing nature or lacking nature—are likewise of one essence. To say they are "the same" means that names and characteristics are empty;
existence is empty, and non-existence is also empty. Throughout the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the origin is fundamentally this single emptiness.
Since this is so, where is there a Buddha to deliver sentient beings? Where are there sentient beings to receive the Buddha’s deliverance? Why is it thus? Because of the myriad dharmas...
Because its nature is inherently so. If you form the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), you fall into the category of the naturalist heretics.
If you form the view of no-self and no-what-is-mine, you fall into the stages of the three worthies and ten sages.
How can you now, with a mere foot or an inch, attempt to measure empty space? He has already clearly told you that phenomena do not reach one another; phenomena are themselves...
Because it is quiescent, it abides in its own place and is inherently true in its own place. Because the body is empty, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);

because the mind is empty, it is called the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Because both body and mind are entirely empty, it is called the emptiness of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).

Even the thousandfold divergent explanations do not depart from your original mind. What is now spoken of as bodhi, nirvāṇa, *tathatā*, and buddha-nature—these are no different from the bodhi of the two vehicles.
"Sā" refers to the claim that leaves are gold when one's fist is clenched.
However, when the hand is opened, the entire assembly—whether gods or humans—sees that there is not a single thing within the palm. Therefore it is said: "Originally there was not a single thing;
where could there be dust? Since there is originally no thing, the three periods of time are fundamentally non-existent. Thus, one studies the Way.
A person must enter directly with a single blade; only when they perceive this meaning can they succeed.

Therefore, when Great Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Heaven to this land, he traveled through countless kingdoms before finding only Master Ke, to whom he secretly transmitted the Mind-Seal.
This seal stamps your own original mind: using the mind to seal the Dharma, and using the Dharma to seal the mind. Since the mind is thus, the Dharma is likewise.

This is identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Within the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, who is the person who receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa)?
Who is the person who becomes a Buddha? Who is the person who attains the Dharma? He has clearly told you: awakening (bodhi) cannot be attained by means of the body.
Because the body is without marks, it cannot be attained by means of the mind. Because the mind is without marks, it cannot be attained by means of its nature (*prakṛti*).
Since this nature is precisely the original source-nature, the true and heavenly Buddha, one cannot attain a Buddha by means of a Buddha;
one cannot attain the markless by means of the markless; one cannot attain emptiness by means of emptiness; and one cannot attain the Way by means of the Way.

Fundamentally there is nothing to be attained; even non-attainment cannot be attained. Therefore it is said: "There is not a single dharma that can be attained. This is merely to instruct you to realize your original mind.
At the moment of realization, there is no sign of realizing; neither the sign of realizing nor the sign of not realizing can be attained.
Regarding such a Dharma, if one attains it, one attains it; yet the one who attains it does not consciously know it. As for the one who does not attain it—
Nor do they even realize it themselves. As for such a Dharma, how many people have known it since ancient times? Thus it is said:
"How many people in the world have forgotten themselves? Now, regarding a single occasion and a single environment, a single scripture and a single teaching—
A single lifetime, a single moment; a single name, a single word—these are apprehended before the gates of the six sense organs.
How does this differ from a mechanical wooden man? Suppose a person were to emerge who does not form conceptual interpretations based on a single name or a single characteristic;
I say that even if one were to search throughout the worlds of the ten directions for such a person, they could not be found, because there is no second person. Thus it continues.
Regarding the ancestral seat, it is also said: "The Śākya clan is unmixed and of pure singularity.

As for the statement that when the King attains Buddhahood, the princes shall likewise follow him into the homeless life—the meaning of this is extremely difficult to understand. It simply teaches you not to seek; if you seek, you will lose it.
It is like a foolish person who shouts once on a mountain; as the echo emerges from the valley, he immediately runs down the slope to pursue it, only to find that he cannot catch it.
Again he called out once more. The mountain echoed, and the sound responded. [The man] then ran up the mountain in pursuit.
Thus for a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas, he was merely a person seeking sound and chasing echoes—a man of empty life and vain death. If you had no sound, there would have been no echo.
"Nirvāṇa is without hearing, without knowing, without sound, where tracks are cut off and footprints vanish. If one attains such a state, one dwells in the very same room as the Patriarchs.
A question was asked: "In the royal treasury, there is no such sword at all. I humbly pray for your instruction. The Master said:
"The royal treasury is the nature of empty space. It can encompass the empty worlds of the ten directions, all of them entirely."
"It does not emerge from your mind; it is also called the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja (Space-Treasury).
If you say it exists or does not exist, or that it neither exists nor does not exist, all of this results in 'ram's horns. As for 'ram's horns,' they are precisely what you are seeking.
Question: "Is there a real sword within the King’s treasury? The Master said: "This, too, is ram's horns. [The questioner] said: "If there is originally no [real sword] within the King’s treasury..."
"A real sword. Why do you say that the prince took the real sword from the royal treasury and went to another country?
How can you say it does not exist? The Master said: "As for 'taking the sword and going out,' this is a metaphor for the messengers of the Tathāgata.

If you say the prince took the real sword from the royal treasury and went out, then the treasury should have been empty when he left. The nature of the original source is void; it cannot [be grasped]."
"Carried away by another person—what kind of language is that? Even if you possess it, it is all called 'the horns of a sheep'.
Question: "Kāśyapa received the Buddha’s seal of mind; may he not be considered a messenger? The Master said: "Yes. [The questioner] said:

"If he is a messenger, he should not have been able to separate himself from the horns of the sheep. The Master said: "Kāśyapa personally realized his own original mind; therefore, he was not the horns of a sheep."
If one were to grasp the mind of the Tathāgata, perceive the intention of the Tathāgata, or perceive the physical form of the Tathāgata, one would belong to the Tathāgata’s retinue as a messenger.
This is why Ānanda served as an attendant for twenty years yet saw only the physical form of the Tathāgata;
consequently, the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "You merely observe the Savior of the World, yet you cannot even avoid the horns of a sheep. Question: [What does this mean?]
As for Mañjuśrī holding a sword before Gautama, how is this? The Master said:

"Five hundred bodhisattvas attained the knowledge of past lives and saw the karmic obstructions of their previous existences. These 'five hundred' are none other than your own five aggregates (skandhas).
Because they saw these obstructions from past lives, they sought the Buddha, sought Bodhi, and sought Nirvana; therefore, Mañjuśrī took the sword of wisdom and insight to destroy them."
"Because there is a mind that perceives the Buddha, it is said: 'You have harmed me well. [The student] asked: "What is this sword? The Master said:
"The mind of understanding is the sword. [The student] asked: "If the mind of understanding is the sword, it cuts off this mind that perceives the Buddha.

As for being able to cut off the perceiving mind, how can one eliminate it? The Master said: "Use your own non-discriminative wisdom to cut off this discriminative mind that perceives existence. [The student] asked: "..."
[The student] said: "If one has the view of existence and the aspiration for Buddhahood, one will cut them off with the sword of non-discriminative wisdom (*avikalpa-jñāna*).

But what can be done about the fact that this sword of wisdom still exists? The Master said: "If non-discriminative wisdom harms the view of existence, then even the viewless non-discriminative wisdom cannot be found.
[The student] said: "One cannot use wisdom to further sever wisdom; one cannot use a sword to further sever a sword. The Master said: "Sword."
A sword harms itself; sword meets sword and they harm one another, yet even the sword cannot be found.
Wisdom harms itself; wisdom meets wisdom and they harm one another, yet even wisdom cannot be found. It is just the same when both mother and son perish together.
Question: What is the seeing of nature? Answer: Nature is itself seeing; seeing is itself nature. One cannot use nature to further see nature. Hearing is likewise.
As for nature (*dharmatā*): one cannot, by means of nature, further hear nature. It is simply you who act as nature;
when you see that which can hear and can see, then within nature there arises the duality of oneness and difference. He spoke clearly: "That which is visible cannot be seen again.
Why do you, on top of your head, place yet another head? He spoke clearly: "It is like pearls scattered upon a tray; the large ones are large and round, and the small ones are small."
Perfectly round, each is unaware of the others and each does not obstruct the others. When arising, it does not say, "I am arising"; when ceasing, it does not say, "I am ceasing.
Therefore, among the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, there has never been anything that does not accord with its time. Furthermore, sentient beings do not see the Buddha.

The Buddha does not perceive sentient beings. Those who have attained the four fruits do not perceive those on the four paths; those on the four paths do not perceive those who have attained the four fruits.

The three levels of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood do not perceive the two types of perfect enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbuddha and Pratyekabuddha); the two types of perfect enlightenment do not perceive the three levels of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood.
Even so, water does not perceive fire, and fire does not perceive water; earth does not perceive wind, and wind does not perceive earth. Sentient beings do not enter into the Dharma.
The realm. The Buddha does not emerge from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Therefore, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no coming or going, and there is neither a seer nor that which is seen.

Since this is so, for what reason do you say, "I see" and "I hear," or claim to have attained realization in the presence of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), or that the spiritual friend preaches the Dharma to me?
The Buddhas appear in the world and preach the Dharma to sentient beings; Kātyāyana merely [speaks] in terms of arising and ceasing.
The mind-transmission of the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) was scolded by Vimalakīrti, who clearly stated: "All dharmas are fundamentally unbound; what need is there to liberate them?
They are fundamentally unstained; what need is there to purify them? Therefore it is said that the true mark is thus: how could it be something that can be spoken of?
You now merely produce a mind of right and wrong, a mind of defilement and purity, having acquired a mere single knowledge and a single understanding to revolve around heaven.
He went down. Upon seeing someone, he would immediately fix his gaze as if intending to seize them. Who possesses the discernment of mind and eye? Who is strong and who is weak?

If it were like this, heaven and earth would be as vastly different [as they are]; what more could be said about "seeing one's nature"? Question: Since you say that nature is itself seeing, and seeing is itself nature, [how can there be such a distinction?]
"If nature itself is inherently without obstruction and without limitation, why is it that one does not see when an object intervenes?
Furthermore, regarding empty space, why is it that one sees when it is near but does not see when it is far? The Master said: "This is merely you giving rise to false and divergent views.
If you say that one does not see when an object intervenes but sees when there is no object, and thereby claim that nature possesses obstructions and barriers, you are entirely mistaken."
In discourse, the nature is neither seen nor unseen; phenomena likewise are neither seen nor unseen. For one who perceives the nature, where is there that is not my own fundamental nature?
Therefore, the six realms and four modes of birth, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, are all the essence of my own pure and luminous nature.
Thus it is said: "To see form is to see the mind," for form and mind are not different. It is only because...

To grasp at signs and form views, hearings, perceptions, and cognitions, and then attempt to see [the object] only after removing the preceding thing, is to fall among those of the Two Vehicles who rely on supernatural powers for their views and understanding.
To see it clearly when near in empty space but not see it when far away is to be categorized among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
It is clearly stated: "It is neither internal nor external; neither near nor far. Though near, it cannot be..."
"The 'Seer' is the nature of all things. If it cannot be seen even when close at hand, what is the meaning of saying it cannot be seen from afar?
[The student] asked: "I, a student, do not understand. How does the Master instruct me? The Master said: "I possess nothing.
From the beginning, I have never given anything to anyone. Since time immemorial, you have simply been pointed out by others."
[The Master] said: "Seeking the seal and seeking the meeting—would this not mean that both disciple and teacher have fallen into royal peril?

You need only know that when for a single thought-moment there is no receiving, this is the body without sensation. When for a single thought-moment there is no thinking, this is the body without perception.

When there is definitively no shifting or conditioned activity, this is the body without volitional formations. Do not engage in conceptualization or calculation; when it is clearly so, this is the body without consciousness."
The Aggregate of Consciousness: Now, as soon as you give rise to a single thought, you immediately enter the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); these are both cause and effect. This continues down to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which are likewise both cause and effect.

Therefore, when the youth Sudhana sought spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) at one hundred and ten locations, he sought them solely within the context of the twelve links of dependent origination. Finally, he saw Maitreya. Maitreya...
Leqiu pointed his finger and said, "Behold Mañjuśrī! Mañjuśrī is none other than your own fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*).

If your mind and thoughts are distinct and separate, and you seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) outwardly, then as soon as a single thought arises, it perishes; as soon as it perishes, another arises.
Therefore, you bhikṣus undergo birth and old age, and likewise sickness and death. From the time you have begun to repay causes and respond to effects, you are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)."
Regarding its arising and ceasing: the "five aggregates" are the five *skandhas*. When not a single thought arises, the eighteen *dhātus* are empty.
This very body is the flower and fruit of *bodhi*; this very mind is numinous wisdom, also called the "numinous terrace.
If one dwells in or clings to anything, then this body is a corpse, and one is called a "ghost guarding a corpse. Question: Regarding Vimalakīrti’s silence, Mañjuśrī offered praise.
[The questioner] sighed and said, "This is truly entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality. How so? The Master said, "The Dharma-gate of non-duality is your own original mind.
To speak or not to speak involves arising and ceasing. When there is no verbal expression, there is nothing to be displayed; therefore, Mañjuśrī offered his praise.
[The questioner] asked, "When Vimalakīrti did not speak, was there any cessation of sound? The Master said, "Speech is silence; silence is speech."
Speech and silence are non-dual; therefore, it is said that the true nature of sound is also without cessation. Mañjuśrī’s primordial hearing is likewise without cessation.
Thus, the Tathāgata constantly speaks and has never been at a time when he does not speak. What the Tathāgata speaks is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the speaking.
Because the Dharma and its speaking are non-dual, this extends even to the two bodies of recompense and transformation, as well as to bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
The mountains, rivers, and great earth; the waterfowl and the forest trees—all preach the Dharma at once.
Therefore, speech also preaches, and silence also preaches. One preaches all day long yet never speaks. Since this is so, take silence as the fundamental basis. Question:
"Regarding those who are śrāvakas, they can conceal their forms within the triple world, but cannot conceal them within bodhi. How is this so? The Master said: "Form refers to substance."

Śrāvakas are only able to sever the afflictions of the three realms through the paths of seeing and cultivation; having already abandoned these afflictions, they are unable to conceal their bodhicitta.
Consequently, they are still captured by Māra within that bodhicitta. While sitting in meditative seclusion in the forest, they still fall back into subtle views regarding the bodhicitta.
Bodhisattvas, however, have already reached a state of certainty regarding the bodhicitta of the three realms, neither abandoning nor grasping it.
Because it is not grasped, one cannot find "other" within the seven elements. Because it is not abandoned, external Māras likewise cannot find "other.
You need only apply this to a single dharma, and the seal is already accomplished. If the seal is applied to existence, the script of the six realms and four modes of birth emerges;
if the seal is applied to emptiness, the script of signlessness appears. Now, simply know that you must resolutely refrain from sealing any object whatsoever.
This seal is empty space; it is neither one nor two. Space is fundamentally not empty, and the seal is fundamentally non-existent.
Throughout the empty worlds of the ten directions, the appearance of Buddhas in the world is like seeing a flash of lightning. Contemplate all wriggling and sentient beings in this same way.
It is like an echo. Seeing the lands of the ten directions as numerous as motes of dust is exactly like seeing a single drop of water in the ocean.
Hearing all profound teachings, they are like illusions and transformations; mind after mind is not different, and dharma after dharma is not different.
Even the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises exist solely for the sake of your one mind. If you can refrain from grasping at any signs, it is therefore said to be "like."
"This is within one mind; it is adorned through the diligent application of skillful means. Question: "As when I was previously cut and mangled in body by King Kali, how was that?
The Master said: "The immortal is precisely your own mind. King Kali represents a fondness for seeking;
failing to maintain the royal throne is called 'greed for profit. Nowadays, students do not accumulate merit or cultivate virtue, yet as soon as they see something, they intend to imitate it."
How is this different from King Kali? When he saw the form, he destroyed the seer’s eyes; when he heard the sound, he destroyed the seer’s ears;
and it was likewise even when [the seer] perceived [the touch]. This is what is called "having one's limbs severed joint by joint. It is said:
"If the seer were truly patient, there should have been no further severing of limbs joint by joint. One cannot be patient with a single mind and yet [suffer such injury]."
"It is not patient acceptance. The Master said, "Your view of non-arising, your interpretation of patience, and your pursuit of liberation—all of these are injuries.
[The student] asked, "When the Immortal was being cut, did he still know pain? The Master said, "In this state there is no experiencer; who is it that feels the pain?
[The student] asked, "If you do not feel pain, why do you come forward seeking something? [The student] asked, "Regarding the prediction of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara..."
"Is it within five hundred years, or outside of five hundred years? The Master said: "Within five hundred years, one does not receive a prediction (vyākaraṇa).
As for what is called a 'prediction,' it is that you are fundamentally determined to neither forget nor lose [the truth]. You do not seek bodhi through conditioned phenomena;

rather, you simply realize that the world is not the world. Furthermore, you do not obtain a prediction separately outside of the five hundred years, nor do you [obtain it] within the five [hundred years]."
[The student] said: "One receives the prediction [of enlightenment] within a hundred years. Have you already realized that the characteristics of the three periods of time are unattainable?

The Master said: "There is not a single dharma that can be attained. [The student] said: "For what reason do you say that one has passed through five hundred lifetimes, such that the duration before and after is extremely long? The Master said:

For five hundred lifetimes, one remains long; yet it should be known that they are still merely a *ṛṣi*. Thus, at the time of Dīpaṃkara’s bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), there was truly not even the slightest dharma to be attained.
Question: The scriptures state, "I have eliminated the inverted perceptions of billions of kalpas and attained the Dharmakāya without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
How is this to be understood? The Master said: If, by practicing for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there were something to be realized or attained, [it would be exhausted].
"Even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one may not attain it;
yet if one were to obtain the Dharma-body within a single kṣaṇa and directly perceive one's nature, this would still be the ultimate discourse of the Three Vehicles' teachings. Why?

Because it implies that the Dharma-body is something to be obtained, and thus it is all subsumed under the category of teachings of incomplete meaning (neyārtha). Question: "Does one who perceives the Dharma with sudden realization perceive the intent of the Patriarchs? The Master said:"
The Patriarch’s mind transcends the void. He asked, "Is there a limit? The Master said, "There is no limit.

These are all methods of numerical measurement and relative opposition. The Patriarch said, "It is neither limited, nor unlimited, nor is it 'neither limited nor unlimited,' because it is free from all relativity.
You students today have not yet been able to transcend the teachings of the Three Vehicles."
They all clamorously call themselves Chan masters. I have already told you clearly: since you are all studying Chan equally, do not recklessly give rise to heterodox views.

It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves. In every movement and every stillness, in a single kṣaṇa, thought after thought is no different [from the source].
If it were not thus, one would not escape saṃsāra. Question: The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories. For what reason is this so?
"The Buddha’s bodily relics amount to eight *hu* and four *dou*. The Master said, "If you hold such a view, you see only the provisional relics;

you do not see the true relics. [The student] asked, "Are these relics inherently existent, or are they the result of meritorious effort? The Master said, "They are neither inherently existent, nor are they the result of meritorious effort.
[The student] asked, "If they are neither inherently existent nor the result of meritorious effort, for what reason did the Tathāgata [leave them behind]?"

[The monk replied: "It is beneficial. Only when refined and polished does the golden bone remain forever. The Master then scolded him, saying: "If you hold such a view, how can you be called a student of Chan?
Have you ever seen bones in empty space? The minds of all Buddhas are identical to the great void;
what bones would you seek? [The monk] said: "Now we see that there are śarīras (relics). What kind of dharma is this? The Master said: "This arises from your delusion."
As the thought arose in his mind, he immediately saw the śarīra. He asked, "Does the Master have any śarīra? I beg you to bring it out so that I may see it.
The Master said, "True śarīra is difficult to see. You should simply take the entire Mount Sumeru with your ten fingers and reduce it to fine dust."
One immediately beholds the true śarīra.
Now, in practicing Chan and studying the Way, one must ensure that the mind does not arise in any situation. It is said that when deluded activity ceases, the Buddha-way flourishes;
when discrimination arises, the demonic army thrives. Ultimately, there is not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma to be obtained. Question: Regarding the transmission of the Patriarchs...

[The student asked: "To whom did you transmit the Dharma? The Master said: "I have no Dharma to give to anyone. [The student asked: "Why then did the Second Patriarch request that you set his mind at rest? The Master said:
"If you had said there was a mind, the Second Patriarch would have been able to find it. Since the mind cannot be found, [there is nothing to be set at rest]."
Therefore it is said: "I have finished settling your mind for you. If there is anything attained, it entirely falls within the realm of birth and extinction.

Question: "Does the Buddha exhaustively eliminate ignorance? The Master said: "Ignorance is precisely the place where all Buddhas attain the Way. Therefore, dependent origination is the site of enlightenment (dōjō).
Every speck of dust and every color perceived immediately accords with the boundless rational nature. Whether lifting or setting down the foot,"
"One does not leave the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). The site of enlightenment is non-attainment. I tell you:
precisely this non-attainment is called sitting at the site of enlightenment. [The student] asked: "Is ignorance (avidyā) light or darkness? The Master said: "It is neither light nor darkness.
Light and darkness are phenomena of alternation; ignorance is neither light nor dark. This 'not being light' is precisely the fundamental light."
Brightness is not darkness. This single phrase alone confuses the eyes of all people in the world. Therefore it is said:
"Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they exhausted their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.

His unimpeded wisdom transcends empty space; there is no place for your discursive arguments to reach it. Śākyamuni’s capacity is equal to that of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
Suddenly, a bodhisattva emerged, who could stride across the entire trichiliocosm without leaving a single pore of Samantabhadra.
With what capability do you now intend to emulate him? [The student] said:
"If it cannot be learned, why is it said that 'the source of returning is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means'? What should one do? The Master said:
Regarding "the source of returning is non-dual": the true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature. Regarding "there are many gates to the skillful means":
Śrāvakas perceive the arising of ignorance and perceive the cessation of ignorance;

Pratyekabuddhas see only the cessation of ignorance and do not see its arising, realizing quiescence in every thought-moment. The Buddhas, however, see sentient beings as being born throughout their entire lives yet without birth.

Throughout the day it is extinguished, yet there is no extinction; without birth and without extinction, this is the fruit of the Mahāyāna. Thus it is said: "The fruit is fulfilled and Bodhi is perfected;
the flower opens and the world arises. Raising the foot is the Buddha; lowering the foot is the sentient being.

The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, are those for whom principle is fulfilled and phenomena are fulfilled. Sentient beings are fulfilled in birth and death; all are equally fulfilled. Because they are fulfilled, they do not [cease].

Qiu, you are now studying the Buddha in every thought-moment, yet you harbor aversion toward sentient beings. If you harbor aversion toward sentient beings, this is to slander the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Therefore, since the Buddhas appeared in the world, they have carried baskets for removing filth to clear away the filth of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
This is simply to teach you to eliminate your long-standing mind of study and mind of views. If these are eliminated completely, you will not fall into frivolous proliferation.
The Treatise also says, "Carry out the excrement. This is simply to teach you not to give rise to the mind. If the mind does not arise, one naturally becomes a great sage.
One must certainly not discriminate between Buddhas and sentient beings; when there is no discrimination regarding anything at all, only then can one enter the gate of our Caoxi school.
Therefore, the ancient sages of the past said: "To practice my Dharma-gate even slightly is, for that reason, non-practice."
This Dharma-gate of mine is simply the gate of the single mind. When all people come here, none dare to enter.
It is not that there are none at all; it is simply that few attain it. Those who attain it are Buddhas. Take heed! Question: How can one avoid falling into stages? The Master said:
