"Just eat all day long, yet never chew a single grain of rice; walk all day long," [and yet never leave a footprint].
One has never trodden upon even a single patch of ground. At such a time, there is no person and no mark of self;

though one is never apart from all phenomena throughout the day, one is not deluded by external objects—only then is one called a person of mastery. Moment after moment, one does not perceive any marks.
Do not recognize the three time periods of past, present, and future. The past has no going; the present has no abiding; the future has no coming.

Sit peacefully and uprightly, allowing things to proceed spontaneously without constraint; only then can it be called liberation. Strive! Strive! Within this gate, among a thousand or ten thousand people, only three or five will attain it.
If you do not take this as your primary concern, there will come a day when you suffer calamity. Therefore, it is said: "Attachment."
One must now bring this to completion through effort; who can endure the remaining calamities for successive kalpas?

The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Linji Huizhao of Zhenzhou, compiled by his dharma-heir junior disciple Huiran.
The Provincial Governor, Attendant Wang, together with various officials, requested the Master to ascend the seat. The Master entered the hall and said: "Today, this mountain monk..."
Having no choice but to comply with human sentiment, I have now ascended this seat.
However, were I to discuss the Great Matter according to the tradition of our ancestral patriarchs, it would be truly impossible to open one's mouth; there would be no place for you to set foot.

Today, because the Attendant has made a firm request, how can I conceal the essential principles of the lineage? Are there any masters, warriors of the Way, who will immediately unfurl their banners and deploy their ranks? Step forward!
Let us look at the evidence from the assembly. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed.
The Master said, "This monk is indeed capable of engaging in debate. [The monk] asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral wind does he succeed?"
The Master said, "When I was with Huangbo, I asked three times and was beaten three times.
As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout and struck him, saying, "One must not try to drive a stake into empty space.

A presiding lecturer asked, "Are not the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings the means for clarifying Buddha-nature? The Master said, "The weeds have never been cleared away. The lecturer said, "..."
"Does the Buddha ever deceive people? The Master said, "Where is the Buddha? The host remained silent. The Master said, "In the presence of the Attendant, you intended to deceive this old monk.
Withdraw quickly! Withdraw quickly! You hinder others from seeking instruction.
He spoke again, "Today's Dharma assembly is for one great purpose. Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? Come forward quickly and ask. As soon as you open your mouth—"
Do not engage in further discussion. Why is this so? Have you not seen the Buddha Śākyamuni say: "The Dharma is apart from words;

it does not belong to causes, nor does it reside in conditions"? It is because you lack sufficient faith that there is such entanglement today. I fear that this will cause you, Attendant and all officials, to stagnate and remain ignorant of the Buddha-nature.
It would be better for you to withdraw for now. (He gives a shout and says: "People of meager roots of faith!"
"There will never be an end to this. I have stood for a long time; take care.
One day the Master arrived at Hebei Prefecture. The Prefectural Governor, Attendant Wang, invited the Master to ascend the seat.

At that time, Magu came forward and asked, "Of the Great Compassionate One’s thousand hands and eyes, which one is the True Eye? The Master said, "Of the Great Compassionate One’s thousand hands and eyes, which one..."
"This is the True Eye. Swift path! Swift path! Magu pulled the Master down from his seat and sat back down himself.
The Master stepped forward and said, "How do you do? As Magu hesitated, the Master likewise pulled Magu down from his seat and sat back down himself.
Magu then departed, and the Master descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Upon this mass of red flesh there is a true person of no rank who constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face of all of you.
Those who have not yet realized this—look, look! At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "What is the true person of no rank?
The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized the monk, and said, "Speak! Speak! As the monk hesitated, the Master pushed him away and said, "No rank."
"What a dried-up piece of excrement the True Man is! Having said this, he returned to the Abbot’s quarters.
He ascended the hall for a formal discourse. A monk came forward and bowed; as the Master began to speak, the monk said, "Old Monk, do not stick your head out.
The Master asked, "Where do you say it has fallen? The monk then gave a shout. Another monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma?"
The general meaning: The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Tell me, was that a good shout?
The monk said, "A grass-robber has been utterly defeated. The Master said, "Where does the fault lie? The monk said, "A second offense will not be tolerated. The Master then shouted.
That day, when the two head seats of the two halls met and shouted at the same time, a monk asked the Master, "Is there still a distinction between guest and host? The Master—

[The Master] said, "Host and guest are clearly distinct. The Master continued, "If you, the great assembly, wish to understand the Linji phrase regarding host and guest, go ask the two head seats in the hall," and he then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master held up his whisk. The monk then gave a shout. The Master struck him.
Another monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master likewise held up his whisk. The monk then gave a shout. The Master also shouted.
The monk hesitated. The Master struck him. The Master then said, "O assembly, those who seek the Dharma..."
"I would rather risk losing my body and life than avoid it. For twenty years I was with my late teacher Huangbo;
three times I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I received his blows from his staff, which felt to me like being brushed by a bundle of mugwort.
Now I think even more of getting one more blow; who will deliver it for me? At that time, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I, [Name], will."
"It is done. The Master picked up his staff and presented it to him. As the monk was about to receive it, the Master struck him. He ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "What is the matter on the edge of the sword? The Master said, "A disaster! A disaster! As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
The Master struck him. He asked, "As for the practitioner in the stone chamber who forgot to lift his foot while treading the pestle—where did he go?
The Master said, "He was submerged in a deep spring. The Master then said, "To anyone who comes, I do not fail them; I recognize their place of origin.
If they come in such a way, it is as if they have lost themselves. If they do not come in such a way, they bind themselves with no rope. One.
In the midst of all activities, do not allow your discernment to become confused. Whether you understand or do not understand, it is all an error. I have spoken clearly and plainly;
let the people of the world judge and criticize as they please. Long-standing, take care.
Ascending the hall, he said: "One person stands atop a solitary peak with no way to emerge;
another person stands at the crossroads with neither front nor back. Which one is ahead? Which one is behind? Do not act as Vimalakīrti;
do not act as Dharma Master Fu. Be careful!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "There is one person who remains on the road for kalpas without leaving home; there is another person who leaves home and is no longer on the road.
Which of these two is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans? He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "The seal of the three essentials opens; the vermilion dot is narrow. There is no room for hesitation;
host and guest are distinguished. The monk asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "How could subtle understanding fail to admit Wuzhuo’s question?
How could Upagupta fail to match the power of cutting through the stream? The monk asked, "What is the third phrase? The Master said, "Look!"
"The puppeteer performs the marionettes; all the pulling and manipulating depend on the person inside. The Master spoke again: "A single phrase must possess the three mysteries;
each mystery must possess the three essentials. There is the provisional and there is the functional.
How do you all understand this? He then descended from his seat.
The Master held an evening session for the assembly, saying: "Sometimes the person is taken away but the environment is not; sometimes the environment is taken away but the person is not;

sometimes both person and environment are taken away; and sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away. At that time, a monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'?
The Master said: "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade upon the earth; the infant’s hair hangs down, white as snow."
[The Master] said, "Silk. The monk asked, "What is 'seizing the environment but not seizing the person'? The Master said, "The imperial decree has already been issued and reached all under heaven;
the general is beyond the frontier, where smoke and dust have ceased. The monk asked, "What is 'seizing both the person and the environment'?

The Master said, "In Bing and Fen, all communication is cut off; one dwells alone in a single place. The monk asked, "What is 'neither seizing the person nor seizing the environment'? The Master said, "The King..."
As he ascended the jeweled hall, the village elders sang songs of praise. The Master then said: "Those who study the Buddha-dharma today must first seek a genuine insight.
If you attain genuine insight, you will be unstained by birth and death, and you will have freedom in going and staying.

You need not seek excellence; excellence will arrive of its own accord. O practitioners of the Way, it is simply that the virtuous predecessors of old all possessed a path for transcending the ordinary."
As for the way I, this mountain monk, instruct people: it simply requires that you do not allow yourself to be deluded by others. When you need to act, act; do not hesitate further.
Why is it that students today fail to attain realization? Where does their ailment lie? Their ailment lies in their lack of self-confidence.
If you cannot have confidence in yourself, you will immediately become lost and adrift, following after all external conditions and being turned around by those myriad objects.
You lack freedom. If you can bring to rest this mind that incessantly chases after things, you will be no different from the Patriarchs and Buddhas.
Do you wish to recognize the Patriarchs and Buddhas? They are simply those listening to the Dharma right before you. It is only because students do not have sufficient faith.
They then rush outward in search. Even if they should find something, it will all be the superior marks of words and letters; they will never attain the living ancestral meaning.

Do not err, O practitioners of Zen! If you do not encounter this at this time, you will wander through the three realms for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, pursuing pleasant appearances until you are cast away to be born within the bellies of donkeys and oxen.
O followers of the Way, according to my own realization, I am no different from Śākyamuni.
It is different. Today there are many ways in which it is used; what is lacking? A single ray of divine light has never ceased.
If you can see it thus, you will simply be a person of no concerns for the rest of your life. Virtuous One, the three realms offer no peace;
they are like a house on fire. This is not a place where you may stay long. The murderous ghost of impermanence makes no distinctions in a single kṣaṇa.
Whether noble or base, old or young, you are no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas. Simply do not seek outside.

That pure light within your single thought-moment is the Dharma-body Buddha within your own house. That non-discriminating light within your single thought-moment is the Sambhogakaya Buddha within your own house.
That non-distinctive light within your single thought-moment is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha within your own house.
The Buddha of the Body (*kāyabuddha*). These three bodies are the very person before you right now who is listening to the Dharma.
It is simply because one does not run outward in pursuit that such a function exists. According to the masters of the sutras and śāstras, these three bodies are taken as the ultimate limit;
however, from my own perspective, this is not so. These three bodies are merely names and also the three bases. As the ancients said:
The body is established based on its meaning; the land is discussed according to its substance. The Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are clearly known to be but light and shadow.
"Virtuous One, you should first recognize the person who plays with light and shadow as the fundamental source of all Buddhas.

Every place is the dwelling place where the followers of the Way return. It is your physical body of the four elements that cannot understand preaching or hearing the Dharma. [Your] spleen, stomach, liver..."
The gallbladder does not understand preaching or hearing the Dharma; empty space does not understand preaching or hearing the Dharma. What, then, understands preaching and hearing the Dharma?
It is this very thing, vividly present before you right now—not a single form or segment, but solitary clarity.
This is what understands preaching and hearing the Dharma. If you can see it thus, you will be no different from the patriarchs and Buddhas. Simply, at all times...

Do not allow for further interruption within this state; it is present everywhere before one’s eyes. It is only because emotions arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptual thoughts transform that the essence becomes alienated.

For this reason, one transmigrates through the three realms and undergoes all manner of suffering. According to my own perspective, there is nothing that is not profoundly deep, and nothing that is not liberation.
O practitioners of the Way, the Dharma of the mind is formless and pervades the ten directions. When it is in the eye, it is called seeing; when it is in the ear, it is called hearing.
Hearing occurs in the ear; smelling fragrance in the nose; conversing in the mouth; grasping with the hands; and running about with the feet.
Originally there was one refined spirit, which divided into six harmonious combinations. Once the single mind is no more, liberation is attained wherever one is. Thus I, this mountain monk, speak.
Where does the meaning lie? It is simply because you, followers of the Way, cannot cease your mind of constant seeking;
you merely pursue the idle realms and circumstances of the ancients. Followers of the Way, adopt my own perspective: it cuts off the heads of both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas.

One whose mind is fulfilled in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is like a hired laborer; those of the two levels of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) are men bearing shackles and chains; even Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are like...
The filth of the latrine and the states of bodhi and nirvana are like a tethering stake for a donkey. Why is this so?

It is simply because you, O practitioners of the Way, do not realize that the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas are empty; therefore, these obstacles arise. If one were a truly authentic person of the Way, they would never be like this.

One can simply follow conditions to exhaust past karma, putting on clothes as they come, walking when one wishes to walk, and sitting when one wishes to sit, without a single thought of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood. Why is this so? An ancient said:
"If you wish to act with the intent of seeking Buddhahood, that Buddha is but a great omen of birth and death. Venerable sir, time is precious; do not merely intend to dabble in worldly affairs.
Studying Chan and studying the Way, you recognize names and recognize phrases; you seek the Buddha, you seek the Patriarchs, and you seek spiritual friends.
Do not let your mental calculations go astray. O practitioner of the Way, you have but one father and mother—what more do you seek?
You must reflect upon yourself. As the ancients said: "Yajñadatta lost his head. When the seeking mind comes to rest, there is nothing more to do. Venerable Sir, you must simply maintain equanimity.
Constantly, do not act with pretension. There is a certain class of ignorant, bald slaves who immediately see gods and ghosts, pointing east and scratching west, and predicting fine weather or rain.
All such as these must pay their debts; there will come a day when they must swallow hot iron balls before King Yama.
The sons and daughters of good families are being ruined by this sort of wild fox spirit.
[The ghost] appeared, immediately acting strangely. "Blind Lüsheng," it cried, "the day will come when you must pay for the rice!

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Followers of the Way, you must earnestly seek true and correct insight so that you may walk freely throughout the world, avoiding being deluded by such malevolent spirits.
To have no affairs is to be a noble person; simply do not engage in artificial contrivances. It is nothing other than this state of equanimity."
"Constantly! You intend to seek it outside by leaning on others and looking for a foothold; you have erred. If you merely intend to seek the Buddha, know that 'Buddha' is but a name and phrase.
Do you recognize that which is the seeker? Even when the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods and ten directions appear in the world, they do so solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
The practitioners of the Way today who study the path likewise do so solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma. Only upon attaining the Dharma is there completion; as long as it is not attained,"
Based on the aforementioned five paths of saṃsāra, what is this Dharma? As for "Dharma," it is the mind-Dharma. The mind-Dharma is formless and penetrates throughout the ten directions;
it is manifest and functioning right before one's eyes, yet people fail to believe this and instead cling to names and phrases, seeking within words and conjecturing about the Buddha-Dharma.
This is worlds apart from the truth. O practitioners of the Way! When I, this mountain monk, preach the Dharma, what Dharma do I speak?
When one explains the Dharma of the Mind-Ground, one is then able to enter the mundane and the sagely, the pure and the defiled, the real and the conventional.

Yet, these are fundamentally not your own reality, conventionality, mundanity, or sageliness; rather, you are able to bestow names upon all that is real, conventional, mundane, or sagely, while reality, conventionality, mundanity, and sageliness cannot bestow names upon this person.
O followers of the Way, grasp it and use it immediately; there is nothing more to it.
They are attached to names and label this "the Profound Meaning. My teaching of the Dharma, however, differs from that of the people of the world.

Suppose, for instance, that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were to appear before me, each manifesting their own form, and ask about the Dharma; as soon as they say, "I inquire of the Master," [the matter is resolved].
"I have long since discerned it all. This old monk sits securely. Even when other seekers of the Way come to see me, I have discerned them all.
Why is this? It is simply because my vision is distinct: externally, I do not grasp at ordinary beings or sages; internally, I do not dwell in the fundamental source.
Having seen through to the bottom, I no longer harbor doubt or error."

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Followers of the Way, there is no place in the Buddha-dharma where one must laboriously apply effort; it is simply the ordinary state of being without affairs.
To defecate and urinate, to put on clothes and eat food, and to lie down when weary—fools laugh at me for this, but the wise understand.
An ancient said: 'To apply effort outwardly is to be nothing but a foolish, stubborn fellow. You should take charge wherever you are; in every place where you stand..."

Reality. The realm cannot be exchanged back and forth. Even if one possesses habitual tendencies from the past or has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution, these naturally become the great ocean of liberation.
Yet, those who study nowadays do not recognize the Dharma at all; they are like sheep that touch their own noses, immediately placing whatever they encounter into their mouths.
Failing to distinguish between master and servant, and unable to differentiate guest from host—such as these are those who enter the Way with a deviant mind, creating only turmoil.
To remain within [the mundane] is not to be called a true renunciant; such a person is precisely a true worldly householder.
One who truly renounces must discern the ordinary and the authentic insight; they must discern Buddha and Māra, discern the genuine and the counterfeit, and discern the commoner and the sage.
If one can discern in this manner, they are called a true renunciant. If one cannot distinguish between Māra and Buddha, they are merely a renunciant in name.
To enter a household and be called a "sentient being who creates karma" does not yet qualify one as a true renunciant.
Right now, there is a Buddha and a Mara that are of the same substance and inseparable, like water and milk mixed together; even a king of geese cannot separate them when drinking milk.
If you are a practitioner with clear eyes, strike both Mara and Buddha alike. If you cherish the holy and loathe the ordinary, you will drift and sink within the sea of birth and death.
Question: What is Buddha and what is Mara? The Master said: "The place where your single thought of mind harbors doubt is Buddha and Mara.

If you can realize that the myriad dharmas are unborn and that the mind is like an illusion or a transformation, such that not a single speck of dust or a single dharma remains and all places are pure—that is Buddha.
Yet, Buddha and Mara are the two realms of defilement and purity. According to my own view, there is neither Buddha nor sentient beings."
There is no past and no present. One who attains it simply attains it; it does not pass through time or seasons. There is no cultivation and no realization; there is no gain and no loss.
At all times, there is no other dharma apart from this. Should there be even a single dharma that exceeds this, I would say it is like a dream or a magical illusion.
What I, this mountain monk, have spoken is nothing other than the solitary, vivid clarity right before you, O practitioners of the Way, as you listen now.
This person is unimpeded in all places, penetrating throughout the ten directions. They attain mastery over the three realms and enter all objects of perception;
no distinctions can alter or obstruct them. In a single kṣaṇa, they penetrate the Dharma-realm. Encountering a Buddha, they speak of the Buddha; encountering an Ancestor, they speak of the Ancestor.
When encountering an arhat, he speaks of the arhat; when encountering a hungry ghost, he speaks of the hungry ghost.

He travels through all lands, teaching and transforming sentient beings without ever for a single thought-moment being apart from [this reality]. Wherever he goes, there is purity; his light penetrates the ten directions;
the myriad dharmas are one suchness. O practitioner of the Way! You great man, today you finally know that fundamentally there is nothing to do. It is only because you did not believe.
Furthermore, they gallop about from moment to moment, seeking a head while already possessing one; they cannot rest of their own accord.

This is like a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching who, upon entering the Dharma-realm, manifests his body within the Pure Land, loathing the mundane and yearning for the sacred. Such individuals have not yet forgotten grasping and rejecting; the mind of defilement and purity still persists.
According to the views of the Chan School, this is not the case at all; it is simply the present moment, with no further temporal divisions.
Wherever this mountain monk speaks, it is all a matter of medicine and disease counteracting one another for the duration of a single occasion; there is no real dharma at all.
If you can see it in this way, that is true renunciation. Such a person could digest ten thousand taels of gold a day. But you practitioners, do not act recklessly!

To be stamped by the teachers of various quarters until their seals break through your face, claiming, "I understand Chan, I understand the Way," with eloquence like a cascading river—all of these lead straight to hell.
As for karma: if one is a true seeker of the Way, one must not seek worldly excellence; rather, one must urgently seek genuine insight.
Only when one attains genuine insight will perfect clarity finally be realized.
Question: What is true and correct insight? The Master said:

"Simply, whether you enter the mundane or the sacred, enter defilement or purity, enter the lands of all Buddhas, enter Maitreya’s pavilion, or enter the Dharma-realm of Vairocana—everywhere there appear lands undergoing their formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness;
Buddhas appear in the world, turn the Great Wheel of Dharma, and then enter Nirvana."
He does not perceive any signs of coming or going; seeking its birth and death, it is utterly unattainable.

He thus enters the realm of non-arising dharmas (*anutpattika-dharmadhātu*) and wanders through lands everywhere, entering the *Avataṃsaka* world-system. He perceives that all phenomena (*dharma*) are characterized by emptiness and that none possess substantial reality.
Only the person who listens to the Dharma without dependence is the mother of all Buddhas; therefore, the Buddha [arises] from...
Birth is without support. If one awakens to this lack of support, even Buddhahood is not attained. If one attains it through such a vision, that is the true and correct understanding.

Students do not comprehend this; because they cling to names and phrases, they are obstructed by the designations of "ordinary" and "sage," which thereby blocks their Dharma-eye and prevents them from attaining a share of the harvest.
For instance, the twelve divisions of the teachings are all expressions of manifestation. As for the student...
It will not. One merely gives rise to understanding based upon the names and phrases that manifest [the teaching];

all such things rely on and depend upon [concepts], falling within the realm of cause and effect, and thus one cannot avoid birth and death within the three realms. If you wish to attain freedom in going and staying, or in being liberated from and attached to birth and death, you must right now recognize the person who hears the Dharma:
formless and signless, rootless and groundless, without a place of abiding, and vibrantly alive.

All these myriad provisional designations and applications are, in truth, merely non-places; therefore, the more you seek them, the further away they recede, and the more you pursue them, the more they diverge.
This is what is called "the secret. O practitioners of the Way, do not mistake this dream-like, illusory companion for reality;
before long, it will return to impermanence. Within this world, what thing can you find that constitutes liberation?
Seek out a mouthful of food to eat and patch together your worn-out robes until the time passes; meanwhile, you must seek out a true teacher.
Do not be negligent or pursue worldly pleasures, for time is precious. Every thought-moment is impermanent. On a gross level, one is oppressed by earth, water, fire, and wind;
on a subtle level, one is pressed by the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. O followers of the Way, at this time you must first recognize the four kinds of signless realms.
"Do not allow yourself to be tossed about by external objects.
He asked, "What are the four kinds of signless objects? The Master said, "The moment you harbor a single thought of doubt, you are obstructed by earth."
If in a single thought-moment your mind feels attachment, you will be drowned by water. If in a single thought-moment your mind feels anger, you will be burned by fire.
If in a single thought-moment your mind feels joy, you will be swept away by wind. If you can discern things in this way, you will not be turned by external conditions;

you will employ conditions everywhere, surging east and sinking west, surging south and sinking north, surging in the center and sinking at the periphery, or surging at the periphery and sinking in the center—treading upon water as if it were earth.
The ground. Treading upon the earth as if it were water. Why is this so? It is because one has realized that the four great elements are like dreams and illusions.
O practitioner of the Way, you who are listening to the Dharma right now are not these four great elements; rather, it is that which can employ them.
If you can see in this way, then you will be free to go or stay at will. According to my own view, do not disparage this teaching. If you cherish it—
"Sage. This is the name "Sage. There are some students who seek Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai;
they have already made a mistake. Mañjuśrī does not exist on Mount Wutai. Do you wish to recognize Mañjuśrī? It is simply that which you employ in the present moment.
From beginning to end it is no different; at every place there is no doubt. This is the living Mañjuśrī. When your single thought-moment is free of—
The light of differentiation: everywhere and at all times, this is the true Samantabhadra. Within a single thought-moment, you can naturally untie your own bonds;

wherever you are, you are liberated. This is the dharma of Avalokiteśvara-samādhi. They function as both principal and attendant to one another: when they emerge, they emerge simultaneously. One is three, and three is one.
Only when you understand it in this way can you truly begin to contemplate the teachings.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who study the Way today must first have self-confidence; do not seek it outwardly.

Otherwise, you will all ascend into idle sensory realms and fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox. As for the existence of patriarchs and Buddhas, these are merely matters within the traces of the teachings."
There are those who pick up a single phrase—whether it emerges from the midst of the hidden or the manifest—and doubt immediately arises.
It illuminates heaven and earth, yet when they go elsewhere to seek its meaning, they remain utterly bewildered. Great men, do not merely debate who is the master and who is the thief.
They debate what is right and what is wrong; they discuss form and wealth; they pass their days in idle chatter.

In this mountain monastery, I make no distinction between monk and layperson. Whosoever comes here, I recognize them all, regardless of where they may have emerged. Any fame, reputation, or verbal expression is nothing but a dream or an illusion.
Rather, it is the person who rides upon these conditions that is the profound essence of all Buddhas. Buddha.
The objective realm cannot claim for itself, "I am the Buddha-realm. Rather, it is this person of no-dependence who emerges riding upon the realm.
If someone comes forth and asks me for the Buddha, I immediately respond by manifesting the realm of purity.
If someone asks me about the Bodhisattva, I immediately respond by manifesting the realm of compassion. If someone asks me about Bodhi, I immediately respond by manifesting the realm of purity.
The wondrous realm emerges. When someone asks me about nirvāṇa, I respond by manifesting the realm of quiescence.

While the realms consist of myriad distinctions, the person remains undifferentiated; therefore, I manifest forms in accordance with objects, like the moon reflected in water. O practitioners of the Way!
If you wish to attain the Dharma as it truly is, you must be a true great man (*mahāsattva*) before you can succeed. If you are weak, timid, and compliant with the mundane world, then...
It cannot be so. Such a vessel as this, being cracked and leaking (the first character pronounced *xī*, the second *suòjià*), is unfit to hold clarified butter (*tíhú*).

As for one who possesses a great vessel, they simply do not allow themselves to be deluded by others; wherever they act as the master, in every place where they stand, all is true. Whenever anyone comes before them...
None of these can be received. If you harbor even a single thought of doubt, the demon immediately enters your mind. When a Bodhisattva doubts, the demons of birth and death find an opening.

You need only cease discursive thinking and seek nothing further outward. When objects appear, simply reflect upon them. You must simply believe that in the present moment there is not a single thing to be grasped.
A single thought of yours gives rise to the three realms; following conditions and being affected by external objects, it is divided into the six [consciousnesses].
Dust. What is lacking in your current application? In a single kṣaṇa, you enter the pure and the impure;
you enter Maitreya’s pavilion and the land of the Three Eyes. You travel everywhere, seeing only empty names.
Question: What is the land of the three eyes? The Master said: "I shall enter with you into the Land of Pure Subtlety, don the robes of purity, and preach the Dharma-body Buddha.
Then we shall enter the Land of Non-differentiation, don the robes of non-differentiation, and [preach the same]."
When speaking of the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*), one enters the land of liberation and wears garments of light;

when speaking of the Transformation Body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*), these three eyes and lands are all transformations based upon [the source]. According to the masters of the sutras and śāstras, they take the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) as the root and the Reward and Transformation bodies as its function.
From the perspective of this mountain monk, the Dharma Body itself does not understand how to preach the Dharma. Therefore, an ancient said:

The "body" (kāya) is established based on its meaning, while the "land" (kṣetra) is discussed according to its substance. Thus, the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are clearly known to be dharmas established through conceptual designation.
They rely upon the realm of pervasive emptiness; they are like an empty fist or yellow leaves used to deceive small children. They are [merely] placed upon thorns, brambles, and dry bones.
What juice are you seeking? Outside the mind there is no dharma; within, it is likewise unattainable. What thing are you searching for?
You all speak of cultivation and realization; do not err. Even if there were something attained through cultivation, it would all be the karma of birth and death.
You say that you cultivate the six perfections and the myriad practices together, but I see them all as the creation of karma. To seek the Buddha and seek the Dharma is itself the creation of hell.
The karma of the hells. Seeking to become a bodhisattva is also the creation of karma. Reading sutras and studying the teachings is also the creation of karma.

The Buddhas and the patriarchs are people of no affairs; therefore, whether they are with-outflows-and-conditioned (*sāsrava-saṃskṛta*) or without-outflows-and-unconditioned (*anāsrava-asamskṛta*), they perform the karma of purity.
There is a certain class of blind shavelings who, having eaten their fill, sit in meditation and practice contemplation, seizing upon thoughts and outflows and refusing to let them go.
To let go and arise, to loathe clamor and seek stillness—this is the dharma of external paths. The Patriarch said:

"If you dwell the mind to observe stillness, raise the mind to reflect outwardly, gather the mind to clarify inwardly, or concentrate the mind to enter meditative absorption—all such practices are merely contrived efforts.
How can you, who are now listening to the Dharma in this manner, intend to cultivate them, realize them, or adorn yourself with them?"
"It is certainly not something to be cultivated, nor is it something to be adorned. If one were to attempt to adorn it, everything could indeed be adorned;

do not, however, fall into error. You practitioners, do not take the words from the mouths of these various teachers to be the true Way, nor consider them the inconceivable influence of a *kalyāṇamitra*.
I am but an ordinary person, and my mind does not dare [to presume otherwise]."
"You have been measuring other venerable elders for many lifetimes, you blind fellow. For your entire life, you have held only this kind of view;
you have brought these two eyes to naught. You are shivering with cold, like a foal on a frozen ice field.

I do not dare disparage the *kalyāṇamitra*, for I fear creating the karma of speech. O seeker of the Way, it is only when one is a great *kalyāṇamitra* that one first dares to disparage the Buddhas and the Patriarchs."
It is not that the world rejects the teachings of the Tripiṭaka or insults those of lesser capacity; rather, one seeks among both the rebellious and the compliant to find someone.
Therefore, for twelve years I have sought even a single person whose karmic nature is as small as a mustard seed, yet none could be found.
If one encounters a "Chan master" like this young bridegroom, he immediately becomes terrified, is driven out of the monastery, is denied food, and finds neither peace nor joy.
Since ancient times, when the predecessors of old traveled everywhere, people did not believe them; it was only after they were driven out that people realized their worth.
If everyone everywhere were willing to accept them, what would they be worth? Therefore, when the lion lets out a single roar, the jackals’ skulls split apart. O practitioners of the Way!
Everywhere else it is said there is a Way to be cultivated and a Dharma to be realized. But tell me, what Dharma do you realize? What Way do you cultivate? What do you use right now?
"What is lacking in this place? What needs to be repaired? Later, a junior monk, failing to understand, immediately believed such a wild fox spirit-demon and granted him authority to speak.
He bound others with his words, claiming that his conduct accorded with principle.
Only by guarding and cherishing the three karmas can one first attain Buddhahood. To speak in this manner is like a fine spring rain. An ancient said:

"When you encounter a person who has attained the Way on the road, do not, for the first time, point it out to them. Therefore it is said: "If a person cultivates the Way but the Way does not proceed, ten thousand kinds of heterodox states will compete to arise.
When the sword of wisdom emerges, there is not a single thing; before the bright side is revealed, the dark side is already clear."
Therefore, as the ancients said: "The ordinary mind is the Way. O Virtuous One, what thing are you seeking?
Right now, before your very eyes, this person who hears the Dharma without dependence is vividly and clearly manifest, never lacking anything.

If you wish to be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, simply see in this way; do not entertain doubts or errors. When your mind-moment after mind-moment does not differ, it is called "alive."
The Patriarch said: "If the mind were different, then essence (nature) and form would be distinct. Because the mind is not different, essence and form are not distinct.
Question: "What is the state where mind and mind are not different? The Master said: "The moment you intend to ask, it has already become different.
Essence and form are each divided; do not err, O follower of the Way. All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, have no self-nature and no nature of arising. It is only..."
There is the name "emptiness," yet names themselves are also empty. You take these idle names as real; you have made a great mistake.

Even if they were to exist, they would all be objects of transformation based upon something else: there is the basis for bodhi, the basis for nirvāṇa, the basis for liberation, the basis for the three bodies, the basis for object and wisdom, the basis for the bodhisattva, and the basis for the Buddha. What are you seeking within this realm of dependent transformation?
All things—even the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings—are merely used-up paper for wiping away impurities.
The Buddha is an illusory transformation body; the Patriarchs are old bhikṣus. Are you still your mother’s natural child? If you seek the Buddha, you will be seized by the demon of the Buddha;
if you seek the Patriarchs, you will be bound by the demon of the Patriarchs. If you have any seeking, it is all suffering; it is better to have none.
Incident. There was a certain shaven-headed bhikṣu who said to a student of the Way: "The Buddha is ultimate;
only after three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas of practice and the fulfillment of the fruit did he finally attain the Way.
"Dàoliú (Dharma-stream), if you say the Buddha is ultimate, for what reason did he lie down on his side and pass away between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara eighty years later?"
"Where is the Buddha now? It is clearly known that he is no different from me in birth and death. You say that the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics constitute the Buddha;
then a Wheel-Turning Sage King should be a Tathāgata. It is clearly known that these are but illusory transformations. As an ancient said:

The Tathāgata’s manifested physical forms were intended to accord with the sentiments of worldly beings; fearing that people might give rise to the view of annihilation, he provisionally established empty names, falsely speaking of thirty-two or eighty marks.
This empty sound and apparent body are not the essence of awakening; formlessness is the true form.
"You say that the Buddha possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and is thus inconceivable.
Yet all the devas, immortals (*ṛṣi*), asuras, and powerful spirits also possess supernormal powers; should they therefore be considered Buddhas? Practitioner, do not err! Consider this:
when the asuras fought with Śakra, Lord of Devas, and were defeated, they led their eighty-four thousand followers into the hollow of a lotus fiber to hide."

"Is this not the holy one? As for what this mountain monk has raised, all of it pertains to the supernormal power of karma (*karmarddhi*) and the supernormal power based on meditative concentration (*samādhirddhi*). Now, the six supernormal powers of a Buddha are not like this.
Entering the realm of form, he is not deluded by form; entering the realm of sound, he is not deluded by sound; entering the realm of fragrance...

They are not deluded by fragrance and enter the realm of taste; they are not deluded by taste and enter the realm of touch; they are not deluded by touch and enter the realm of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
They are not deluded by mental objects. Thus, they realize that the six kinds—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects—are all characterized by emptiness.

They cannot bind this person of the Way who relies on nothing. Although such a one possesses the substance of the five aggregates and outflows, they possess the spiritual powers that move through the earth.
O practitioners of the Way! The true Buddha has no form; the true Dharma has no marks. You merely fashion patterns and models upon these illusory transformations.
Even if you were to seek and obtain something, it would all be the spirit-demons of wild foxes—it is certainly not the true Buddha; it is a heterodox path.
Regarding this view: A true student of the Way does not grasp for Buddhas, nor for Bodhisattvas or Arhats, nor for the excellence of the triple world.
They are utterly detached and liberated, unconfined by external things. Even if heaven and earth were overturned, they would harbor no further doubt.
The Buddhas of the ten directions appear before me, yet not a single thought of joy arises. The three miserable realms and the hells manifest all at once, yet not a single thought of fear arises.
Why is this so? Because I perceive the empty nature of all phenomena: they exist when transformed, and do not exist when untransformed.
The triple world is but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Therefore, as for dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky, what need is there to grasp them? There is only the Way.

Those who listen to the Dharma right now before my eyes—should they enter fire, they are not burned; should they enter water, they do not drown; they enter the three miserable realms of hell as if visiting a garden;
they enter the realms of hungry ghosts and animals yet do not suffer their retributions.
Why is this so? Because it is a Dharma free from aversion. If you love the holy and hate the ordinary, you will sink and float within the sea of birth and death; for afflictions arise from the mind.
"There is existence; there is non-existence. What can afflictions constrain? There is no need for the toil of discriminating and grasping at signs; one will naturally attain the Way in an instant.
If you intend to follow others and learn through such restless wandering, you will ultimately remain within birth and death throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
It would be better to do nothing and sit cross-legged at the corner of a bed in the forest. O practitioners of the Way! If students come from various quarters,"
When master and guest have met, there is immediately a single phrase that precedes all verbal expression.
When a student brings forth a word of expedient means from a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), it is cast across the corners of the friend’s mouth; see whether you can recognize it or not.
If you recognize it as an objective condition (*viṣaya*), seize it and throw it straight into a pit. Then the student shall immediately seek it.

After [the teacher] had thus acted, he then sought out the words of a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) and, relying on the previous method, seized [the student] again. The student said, "What superior wisdom!
The great good spiritual friend then said, "You truly do not know how to distinguish between good and evil.

Suppose a good spiritual friend were to take out a piece of 'objective matter' (jing-kuaizi) and dangle it before you; if you can discern it and do not act as its master, you will not be deluded by that object."

The spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) immediately manifested half his body. The student shouted. The spiritual friend again entered into all paths of differentiated speech and engaged him in a vigorous struggle.
The student said, "I do not recognize good or evil, you old shaven-headed slave! The spiritual friend sighed and said, "A true practitioner of the Way.
If spiritual friends in various quarters cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, when a student comes to inquire about Bodhi—
"Explaining Nirvana and the objective wisdom of the three bodies—the blind old teacher then proceeded to explain them for him.
Being reviled by that student, he took up his staff and struck him, saying, 'You lack decorum! But it is simply because you, as a *kalyāṇamitra*, have no eyes;
you must not be angry with him. There are a certain kind of ignorant, bald slaves who point east and mark west, talking of fine weather and rain."
"Fine lanterns and lamp-posts! Look at how many hairs there are on your eyebrows! This matter possesses its own karmic conditions;
if a student does not understand it, their mind immediately goes mad. Those of such a sort are all nothing but wild fox spirits, demons, and goblins.
When a fine student encounters them, they let out a loud, mocking laugh and say, "Blind old shaveling! You delude and confuse the people of the world. "Followers of the Way," he said, "come forth!"

"Young man, you must also study the Way. Just as I myself in the past once applied my mind to the *vinaya*, and also sought out and investigated the sutras and śāstras, I later realized they were merely medicines for saving the world—merely expository teachings.

Consequently, I cast them all aside at once and went to seek the Way and practice Zen. It was only after meeting a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) that my eye of the Way finally became clear."
Only then did I first recognize the Old Monk of the World and come to know what is heterodox and what is orthodox.

This was not something I knew from birth; rather, it was attained through investigation and refinement. One day, I realized this for myself. "Followers of the Way! If you wish to attain a realization that accords with the Dharma, simply do not allow yourself to be deluded by others.
Whether facing inward or outward, kill whatever you encounter. Kill the Buddha when you meet the Buddha; kill the Patriarchs when you meet the Patriarchs."

Only by killing an arhat does one kill an arhat; only by encountering and killing one’s parents does one kill one’s parents; only by encountering and killing one’s kinsmen does one kill one’s kinsmen.

Only then does one attain liberation, no longer constrained by things, but penetrating through them with sovereign freedom. As for those seekers of the Way from all quarters, there is none who has emerged without relying on something.
Here, I strike them from the very beginning: if they emerge from my hand, I strike them with my hand; if they emerge from my mouth...
If you come forth, I strike you in the mouth; if you come forth from the eyes, I strike you in the eyes. Not a single one has emerged in solitary independence;
they have all merely followed the idle devices and realms of those ancients. This mountain monk possesses not a single dharma to give to others;
I do nothing but treat illnesses and untie bonds. You practitioners from all quarters, try to emerge without relying on external things, and I will consult with you.
For ten years and five years, not a single person has appeared; they are all merely spirits of grass, leaves, bamboo, and wood, or wild foxes and demons.

These creatures gnaw recklessly upon heaps of dung and deceive the blind. They pointlessly consume the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions, claiming, "I am an ordained monk," yet holding such views as these:
they tell you there is no Buddha and no Dharma, and that there is neither cultivation nor realization.
Realization. What object do you seek by looking elsewhere in this very way? You blind fellow! To put a head on top of your own head—what is it that you lack?
Dharma-heir, what you employ right before your eyes is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; yet you simply do not believe it.
Do not mistakenly seek it outwardly. There is no dharma outside; it cannot be found within either.
You would do better to take my words and simply rest in non-action. Do not continue what has already arisen; do not allow what has not yet arisen to arise.
This would surpass ten years of your traveling as a mendicant. According to my own view, there are not so many varieties; it is simply this:
Ordinarily, you wear clothes and eat food, passing the time with nothing to do.

You who have come from all quarters are all those with a mind seeking the Buddha, seeking the Dharma, seeking liberation, and seeking transcendence. You deluded people of the triple world—where would you go to leave the triple world?
Buddhas and patriarchs are merely names and phrases used for designation. Do you wish to recognize the triple world? It is not separate from this very moment.

The ground of mind for one who listens to the Dharma: when a single thought of yours is characterized by greed, it is the realm of desire; when a single thought of yours is characterized by anger, it is the realm of form;
when a single thought of yours is characterized by delusion, it is the formless realm. These are the furnishings within your own house. The three realms do not themselves say, "I am the three realms.
Rather, O followers of the Way, it is this very spirit that shines vividly before your eyes, illuminating all manner of things.
One who has crossed to the other shore of the world bestows names of peace upon the three realms.

Venerable sir, the physical body composed of the four great elements—from the spleen, stomach, liver, and gallbladder, down to the hair, fur, nails, and teeth—is impermanent. One perceives only the empty marks of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
That place where your mind ceases to think is called the Bodhi tree; that place where your single thought-moment cannot cease is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
The Tree. Ignorance has no place of abiding; ignorance has no beginning or end.
If you cannot bring your mind to rest moment after moment, you will ascend that tree of ignorance and enter the six paths and four modes of birth, donning fur and wearing horns.
If you can bring it to rest, this is the pure realm of body and world. When not a single thought arises, you have ascended the Bodhi tree and attained the supernormal powers of the three realms.

Transformation: the transformation body born of the mind; the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna; the body’s own radiance illuminating itself. When one thinks of clothing, there are a thousand layers of fine silks;
when one thinks of food, a hundred flavors are fully provided. Furthermore, there are no accidental illnesses. Since Bodhi has no place of abiding, therefore there is no one who attains it.
O practitioners of the Way! What more is there for a great man to doubt? As for that which is employed before one’s eyes—who else could it be?
Seize it and employ it immediately; do not become attached to names. This is called the "Mysterious Principle. Seeing it thus, do not disdain this Dharma. As the ancients said:
"The mind turns following the myriad objects; in the turning, it is truly profound. Following the flow, recognize the nature; then there is neither joy nor sorrow."
Wu-yü said: "O practitioner of the Way! According to the insights of the Chan school, life and death follow their natural course.
Those who study must be extremely meticulous. It is like the meeting of host and guest, where there is an exchange of discourse;

sometimes manifesting form in response to objects, sometimes functioning as the whole body, sometimes employing skillful means through expressions of joy or anger, sometimes appearing as half the body, and sometimes riding upon lions or elephant kings."
Suppose there is a genuine student who lets out a shout. First, he presents a lacquer basin.

The master (the "good knowledge") fails to recognize it as an objective condition and, entering that condition, puts on airs and affects a certain manner. The student then shouts again. The former person refuses to let go.
This is a terminal illness; it cannot be cured. This is called "the guest looking at the host," whether it be the student or the master.
He does not bring forth any object; rather, wherever the student asks, he immediately seizes it from the student.

Once seized, the student will not let go even at the cost of his life. This is the host looking after the guest. Or, there may be a student who encounters a single pure state before a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When the spiritual friend discerns that this is such a state, he seizes it and hurls it into a pit. The student says, "Excellent! Spiritual friend!"
He then said, "Alas! You do not recognize good from evil. The student immediately prostrated. This is called "the host looking at the host.
Or, there may be a student who comes before a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) wearing a cangue and shackles, and the spiritual friend further places another layer of cangue and shackles upon him;
the student rejoices, and neither can distinguish between them. This is called "the guest looking at the guest. Venerable Sir, I am like this.
What has been raised here is entirely for the purpose of discerning demons, distinguishing [the true from the false], and knowing what is deviant and what is correct.

O practitioners of the Way, the reality of things is truly difficult; the Buddha-dharma is profound and mysterious. Even when one understands it to some extent, this mountain monk spends the entire day explaining it to them, yet the students pay no heed.
Though they have trodden over it ten thousand times underfoot, it remains pitch black and void, without a single trace or form to be found. It passes by...
Passing through solitary clarity, students lack sufficient faith and instead give rise to intellectual interpretations based on names and phrases.
Reaching fifty years of age, they do nothing but carry the corpses of others along, lugging their burdens as they wander the world. The day will come when you must pay for your straw sandals.
"Virtuous One," the mountain monk says there is no dharma outside; yet when students do not understand this, they immediately form interpretations within.
He then sat leaning against the wall, his tongue pressed against the upper palate, remaining perfectly still.
To take this as the Buddha-dharma of our ancestral school is a great error. If you take such an unmoving, pure state as being correct, you are identifying ignorance as your master.
An ancient said: "A deep pit of profound darkness—this is truly terrifying. This is precisely what that refers to.
Furthermore, if you identify with that which moves, then all grasses and trees move; they too should be the Way.
Thus, that which moves is the element of wind, and that which does not move is the element of earth. Both movement and non-movement are devoid of self-nature.
If you try to grasp it where there is movement, it stands where there is no movement. If you try to grasp it where there is no movement...
"I seize him. He stands facing the place of movement, like a fish hidden in a spring that stirs the waves and leaps forth of its own accord.
Venerable Sir, movement and non-movement are two kinds of objects. Does the person who walks without reliance employ movement or non-movement?
For instance, when students from various quarters come here, I, this mountain monk, sever them according to their three types of faculties. If those of middling or inferior faculties come..."
I then seize their realm but do not eliminate their dharma. Or, if those of middling or superior faculties come, I then seize both their realm and their dharma.
If those of the highest superior faculties come, I do not seize either their realm, their dharma, or their person.
If a person of extraordinary insight comes, I, this mountain monk, manifest my total functioning here, bypassing all levels of faculty. Venerable Sir, you have arrived.
In this place, where the student exerts effort, there is no passage for the wind. Even a spark of stone-fire or a flash of lightning has already passed.
If the student’s eye wavers, there is no connection. To conceive a thought is already an error; to stir a single念 (nian) is already to deviate. There may be those who understand this.
It is not apart from what is before your eyes. Great Virtue, you carry your alms-bag and your staff as you run about the neighborhood;
seeking the Buddha, seeking the Dharma—do you recognize this very one who is thus rushing about right now? It is lively and active, having no roots or trunk;
it cannot be gathered by piling up, nor can it be dispersed by pushing away. If you seek it, it moves further away; if you do not seek it, it is already before your eyes. This is the numinous sound.
Listen closely. If a person does not believe, they will labor in vain for a hundred years. O practitioners of the Way! In a single kṣaṇa, one enters the Flower Treasury World (Avataṃsaka-lokadhātu).
One enters the land of Vairocana; one enters the land of liberation; one enters the land of supernormal powers; one enters the land of purity. One enters the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);
one enters the defiled and the pure; one enters the mundane and the sagely; one enters the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.
Search for it everywhere; nowhere can one find birth or death. There is only an empty name—a phantom, a flower in the sky.
Do not trouble yourself to grasp it. Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once. O practitioners of the Way!
This mountain monk’s Buddha-dharma has been transmitted directly and authentically from Master Magu, Master Danxia, Master Daoyi, and the one who dragged the stone on Mount Lu.
"O Upādhyāya, you have traveled throughout the world on this journey, yet no one has been able to believe you; all have raised slander against you.
As for the way Upādhyāya Daoyi functions—pure and unadulterated—his three hundred to five hundred disciples are entirely unable to perceive his intent.

Likewise, as for the way Upādhyāya of Mount Lu functions with spontaneous, true, and authentic mastery in both favorable and adverse circumstances, the students cannot fathom its limits. All were thus [enlightened].
Utterly bewildering. Like Master Danxia playing with a pearl, whether it was hidden or manifest; whenever students came, they were all scolded.
Like Magu’s way of acting, as bitter as Huangbo’s, one could not draw near. Like Shigong’s way of acting, seeking the person upon the tip of the arrow;
those who came were all struck with fear. As for this mountain monk’s way of acting today, it is the true process of formation and destruction—playing with it.
Spiritual transformations! Entering all realms, remaining uninvolved wherever one is, the realm cannot change him.
Whenever there is someone who comes seeking him, he immediately goes out to look at them; they do not recognize him, so he puts on various kinds of clothes to cause people to develop understanding.
They follow his words and phrases exclusively. Alas! These blind shavelings, these sightless men, take the clothes he wears and mistake them for blue.
"Yellow, red, and white—I have cast them off and entered the realm of purity. Upon seeing this, the student immediately gave rise to longing and desire.

I then cast them off once more, whereupon the student lost his mind and wandered about in a daze, crying out, "I have no clothes! I then said to him: [Note: The original text contains a phonetic transcription of a dialectal expression (likely Cantonese) used by the master to address the student.]
"Do you recognize the person who is wearing these clothes? Suddenly he turns his head; now he has recognized me.
"Virtuous One, do not mistake the clothes for me. Clothes cannot move; it is the person who wears the clothes.

There is the garment of purity, the garment of non-arising, the garment of bodhi, the garment of nirvana, the garment of the patriarchs, and the garment of the Buddhas. Virtuous One, all that exists consists of names, sounds, phrases, and sentences."
All of these are transformations of clothing. Stirred up from the ocean of vital energy at the navel wheel, they are formed into phrases and meanings by the clashing of teeth.
Clearly understand that these are illusory manifestations. Venerable One, external vocal karma and internal mental factors arise through volition and mindfulness—all of them are merely clothing.
You simply take that clothing which you wear as being real understanding; even if it passes through the dust of ages...
The kalpa is merely the circulation of clothing; one wanders through the three realms and revolves in birth and death.

It is not as good as being without affairs—meeting others without recognizing them, speaking together without knowing their names. That students of the present day do not attain this is because they take names and words to be understanding.

The Great Strategist has transcribed the words of this dying old man, wrapping them in three layers and five folds, not allowing others to see them, claiming they are the profound essence (*xuanzhi*) and treating them as something precious.
This is a great error. You blind fellow, what kind of juice do you seek from a withered bone?
There is a certain class of people who do not recognize good from evil; they take the meaning from the teachings and speculate upon it, forming mere phrases.
This principle is like taking a lump of excrement in one's hand, putting it in one's mouth, and then spitting it out to give to another; it is just like commoners playing the "whispering game.
One’s entire life is spent in vain. One claims to have left the household life, yet when questioned about the Buddha-dharma, one immediately closes one's mouth and has no words.
The eyes are like pitch-black pits, and the mouth is like a wooden beam. Those of such a kind, upon encountering...
When Maitreya appears in the world, you shall be transported to another world and made to dwell in hell to undergo suffering.
Venerable sir, why do you go from place to place seeking some external thing? Tread upon your own soles: there is no Buddha to be sought, no Way to be realized, and no Dharma to be attained.
To seek outside for a Buddha with form is not to resemble your own nature. If you wish to recognize your original mind—
Neither conjoined nor separated, O follower of the Way: the true Buddha has no form, the true Way has no substance, and the true Dharma has no marks.
These three dharmas are interpenetrating and unified in one place; since they cannot be distinguished, such people are called sentient beings of the vast, indistinct karmic consciousness.
Question: What are the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way? We beg for your instruction. The Master said: "The Buddha is the purity of the mind.
The Dharma is the radiance of the mind. The Way is the pure light that is unimpeded everywhere. These three are one."
All are merely empty names and lack substantial reality. For one who is a true student of the Way, the mind remains uninterrupted from moment to moment.
Since the Great Master Bodhidharma came from the Western lands, he sought only a person who would not be deluded by others.
Later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he was enlightened in a single word; only then did he realize that all his previous efforts had been in vain. Today, I, this mountain monk, see it thus.
The state [of realization] is no different from that of the patriarchs and Buddhas. If one attains it within the first phrase, one becomes a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas.
If one attains it within the second phrase, one becomes a teacher to humans and devas. If one attains it within the third phrase, one is unable to save even oneself.
Question: "What is the meaning of [the Master’s] coming from the West? The Master said: "If there were a meaning, you would not even be able to save yourself. [The questioner] asked:
"Since there is no meaning, how did the Second Patriarch obtain the Dharma? The Master said: "To 'obtain' it is precisely not to obtain it. [The questioner] asked:
"If it is not obtained, what is the meaning of this 'not obtaining'? The Master said: "It is because you run about everywhere in pursuit, and your mind cannot come to rest."
According to the words of the Patriarch: "Alas, O man! You are seeking your head with your head.

If you could immediately turn the light back upon yourself and reflect within these words, seeking nothing else, and realize that your own body and mind are no different from those of the Patriarchs and Buddhas—being thus free from affairs at that very moment—only then can it be called "attaining the Dharma.
Venerable Sir, in these present times, this mountain monk has no choice but to speak; I have exhausted my meager talent to utter these words.
Do not err. According to my own realization, there are truly not so many varieties of principles. When you need to use them, you use them; when you do not need them, you simply let them rest.

As for what is preached everywhere—that the six perfections and ten thousand practices constitute the Buddha-dharma—I say they are merely the gate of adornment and the gate of Buddhist activity, not the Buddha-dharma itself.
This extends even to observing fasts and precepts, or carrying oil without spilling a drop. I say...
If your eyesight is not clear, you must pay it all back as a debt; the day will come when you must be paid for the food. Why is this so?
Because you have entered the Way without penetrating its principle, and you must return the offerings of the faithful with your own body. At eighty-one years of age, the tree will simply not grow.

Even such practices as sleeping alone on a solitary peak, eating only one meal at dawn, sitting long without lying down, and practicing the Way during the six periods—all these are merely the creation of karma.
People—even down to their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains, their kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, and their elephants, horses, and seven treasures—give all these away as alms.
Such views are all rooted in the suffering of body and mind, and thus they still invite bitter fruits. It is better to remain in non-action, pure and unmixed.
Even Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Grounds who have reached the fullness of their hearts all seek this; yet, O Stream of the Way, its traces are utterly unfindable.
For this reason, the devas rejoice and the earth deities support his feet, and there are no Buddhas of the ten directions who do not offer praise. Why is this so?
It is because the practitioner of the Way who now listens to the Dharma leaves no trace behind.
Question: “The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
I do not yet understand the meaning of this; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said:

“Mahābhijñā (Great Penetration) means that one personally penetrates everywhere that the myriad dharmas are without nature and without marks; thus it is called Great Penetration. Jñānābhibhū (Victorious Wisdom) refers to [the realization] regarding all things...”
Abiding without doubt and not grasping a single dharma is called "supreme wisdom. As for the Buddha, it is the purity and radiance of the mind that penetrates the entire Dharma-realm;
thus he is named Buddha. Regarding "sitting at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas," this refers to the ten pāramitās.

As for "the Buddha-dharma not appearing before one," since the Buddha is fundamentally unborn and the Dharma is fundamentally unceasing, how could there be anything further to appear? One cannot achieve [realization] through such means.
As for the Buddha-way: a Buddha need not become a Buddha again. An ancient said, "The Buddha is always in the world, yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
O practitioner of the Way: if you wish to become a Buddha, do not follow after the myriad things. When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise.
When the mind ceases, the manifold phenomena cease; when the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Whether mundane or supramundane, there is neither Buddha nor dharma; they do not manifest before one, yet they have never been lost.

Should anything appear to exist, it is all but names and phrases used to guide the young, established as medicine for the disease, and expressed through words and sentences. Yet these names and sentences do not themselves constitute names and sentences; rather, they are...
"O Great Virtue, that which you currently possess—this clear, lucid, discerning, perceiving, hearing, knowing, and illuminating awareness—is itself all names and phrases.
Only by committing the five deeds of immediate retribution can you attain liberation."

Question: What are the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*)? The Master said: Killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and burning sutras and images—these are the five deeds of immediate retribution. Question: What is the father? The Master said:

Ignorance is the father. If, in a single thought-moment, you seek the place where it arises and ceases and cannot find it—like an echo in space, remaining without affairs wherever you go—this is called "killing the father.
[The student] asked: "What is the mother? The Master said: "Craving is the mother.

If, in a single thought-moment, you enter into the realm of desire and seek that craving, you see only the empty nature of all phenomena; being without attachment in every place, this is called [killing the mother]."

[The monk] asked, "What is meant by 'harming one's mother'? The Master said, "If you do not give rise to a single thought of conceptual understanding within the pure *dharmadhātu*, you will be in darkness everywhere;
this is what is meant by 'shedding the blood of the Buddha. [The monk] asked, "What is meant by 'breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha'?
The Master said, "When your single thought-moment directly penetrates the afflictions and fetters, such that they are like space—having no substance—this is it."
"Relying on this is what constitutes breaking the harmony of the Sangha. [The student] asked: "What is meant by 'burning the scriptures and images'? The Master said:

"To see that causes and conditions are empty, the mind is empty, and dharmas are empty—to decisively sever [all attachments] in a single thought-moment and be utterly free from affairs—this is what it means to burn the scriptures and images, O Virtuous One.
If you can realize it in this way, you will avoid being obstructed by the names of 'ordinary' or 'sage. Your single thought-moment simply turns toward emptiness."

To grasp at the fingers while seeking the fist is a superficial understanding. Amidst the dharmas of roots and objects, you vainly concoct strange delusions; you disparage yourself and retreat in submission, saying, "I am an ordinary person, while others are sages.
You have been born as a bald-headed monk many times—what such haste is there to die? Having donned the skin of a lion, you instead let out the howl of a jackal.
A true man does not lack the breath of a man; do not fail to recognize the things within your own house.

If you are willing to believe this, yet you still seek it only outwardly, relying on the idle phrases of the ancients, leaning on the "negative" to seek the "positive," and failing to achieve independent penetration;

then whenever you encounter an object you will follow its conditions, and whenever you encounter a sensory dust you will grasp at it, so that delusion arises at every touch and you have no standard of your own. O practitioners of the Way!
Do not grasp at what this mountain monk says. Why? Because these words have no foundation; they are like painting the void for a brief moment, comparable to the metaphor of a painted image.
O practitioners of the Way, do not take the Buddha as your ultimate goal; in my view, he is like a latrine hole.
Bodhisattvas and Arhats are all merely shackles and fetters used to bind people. This is why Mañjuśrī took up his sword and slew Gopāla.
"Oṅgula took up a blade and harmed the Śākyas. O practitioner of the Way, there is no Buddha to be attained—not even the three vehicles or the five natures.
The traces of the Perfect and Sudden Teachings are all merely medicinal prescriptions for treating specific ailments at a particular time; none possess any real dharma.

Even if such things were to exist, they are all merely conventional expressions, manifesting through the arrangement of written characters. To speak of them as such is simply a matter of provisional classification. O practitioner of the Way, there is a certain class..."
The bald-headed one then applied his efforts toward the interior [of the mind], intending to seek the Dharma that transcends the world;
he was mistaken. If a person seeks the Buddha, that person loses the Buddha. If a person seeks the Way, that person loses the Way. If a person seeks the Patriarch, that person loses the Patriarch.
Venerable Sir, do not be mistaken! For now, I shall not accept your interpretation of the sutras and treatises, nor will I accept your status as a king.
"Great Minister, I do not take your eloquence that flows like a rushing torrent; nor do I take your cleverness and wisdom.
I seek only your genuine insight. O practitioner of the Way: even if you could explain a hundred volumes of sutras and treatises, it would not equal a single master who has nothing to do.
If you understand [the teachings], you will look down upon others; such victory and defeat belong to the asuras. Therein lies no distinction between self and other."
This clarifies that it increases the karma for the long-lasting hells. For example, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, despite his understanding of the twelvefold teachings, was reborn in hell in his very body;
the great earth could not contain him. It would be better to rest in non-action: when hunger comes, eat; when sleep comes, close your eyes.
Fools may laugh at me, but the wise alone understand. O followers of the Way, do not seek within words and letters; the mind becomes weary and exhausted. Inhale...
Air-conditioning is of no benefit. It is better to contemplate for a single thought-moment that dependent origination is birthless, thereby transcending the Three Vehicles.

You provisional practitioners and Bodhisattvas of great virtue, do not let the days pass by in negligence. In the past, when this mountain monk had not yet attained a place of insight, it was all pitch black.
Time cannot be spent in vain. With burning urgency in the belly and a restless mind, one must run and travel to seek the Way; only then will one gain strength.

It is only now that we, fellow seekers of the Way, have come together to engage in such discourse. I exhort all you practitioners: do not concern yourselves with food and clothing. Observe how easily the world passes away;
a true spiritual friend is difficult to encounter, appearing only once in a long time like the *udumbara* flower. You have heard this said everywhere.
Suppose an old fellow Linji were to come forth and attempt to pose difficult questions; he would be rendered speechless.
The mountain monk would employ his entire being in action, so that the student’s eyes would open in vain while his mouth could not move at all.

Utterly bewildered, he would not know how to answer me. I would say to him: "The treading of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure. You all merely point to your chests wherever you go.
Dianri said, "I understand Chan; I understand the Way. Yet when three or two of you arrive here, there is nothing to be done. He gave a shout and said, "Alas!
You take this body and mind and wander everywhere, flapping those two pieces of skin to deceive the common folk. The day will come when you eat iron rods;
