Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Masters, Volume Eleven:
The Record of Chan Master Ciming (Tenth Generation Descendant of Nanyue, Successor of Fenyang).
The Master’s name was Chuyuan. He was of the Li clan of Qingxiang in Quanzhou. In his youth, he was a scholar.
At the age of twenty-two, he received full ordination at Yinjing Temple on Mount Xiang, south of the city. His mother was a woman of virtuous conduct and sent him away to travel for study.
The Master had joined eyebrows and prominent eyes; he was tall and robust, yet he disregarded formal discipline, such that wherever he went, he was rebuked by senior masters. Because...
He was a man of few words. The Master smiled and said, "The trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure.
He once carried a chest of antiques on a bamboo staff and traveled through the regions of Xiang and Mian. Together with Shouzhi and Guquan, he formed a traveling party and entered Luoyang.
Having heard that the reputation of Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao was preeminent in the world, he resolved to personally attend upon him.
At that time, the imperial court was launching a punitive expedition against Hedong, and heavy troops were stationed throughout Ze and Lu; many urged him not to go. The Master paid them no heed.

He crossed the Great River, ascended Mount Taihang, changed his clothes to resemble those of a servant, and concealed his identity among the ranks of the fire-corps. Sleeping in the open and lodging in the grass, he arrived at—
Longzhou then proceeded to Fenyang. Previously, Fenyang had told the head seat, "Before long, an extraordinary monk will arrive to uphold our Way.
One day, he suddenly led the head seat on a mountain excursion. The head seat asked, "Where are we going? Fenzhou replied: [The text ends here.]
He sent an attendant away. The Head Seat said, "Why does the Master act so perversely? Fenzhou said, "Just go.
When the Master eventually encountered the teacher, he returned with him. For two years, he was not permitted to enter the inner quarters for private instruction.

Whenever the Master went to the abbot’s quarters, Fenzhou would gauge his intent by either berating and scolding the attendants or disparaging the various other teachers; yet whenever he offered instruction, it was always...
One night, a man of vulgar and low character came to the Dharma assembly and complained, saying, "Since arriving at this seat of the Dharma, I have received no instruction.

As the years and months slip by, I have not clarified my own matter; thus I have lost the benefit of having left the household life. Before he had finished speaking, Fengyang scolded him, "You are a wicked teacher!
How dare you deceive and sell me out? He raised his staff to drive him away. As the man prepared to plead for mercy, Fengyang suddenly covered his mouth.
He then attained great enlightenment and said, "Thus I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary sentiment.
He served [Linji] for seven years, after which he went to visit Tangming Song, Shending Yin, and Dongshan Cong. Subsequently, he entered the gates of Yang Dainian and Li Duye;
their spiritual dialogues were in perfect accord. Thereupon, his Dharma path flourished greatly. Huang Gong Zongdan, the Magistrate of Yichun, invited him to open a Dharma center at Nanyuan.
He subsequently moved to Daowu, Shishuang, Foyan, and Xinghua. Duke Li Zunxu submitted a memorial requesting that he be granted ceremonial robes and an honorary title.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? He replied, "Do not become angry when you step upon it. The monk asked, "What is one who is on the Way?"

[The Master] said: "Carrying on the chest and bearing on the back. A question was asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He replied: "The whole family has been sent off to the ferry crossing.
A question was asked: "What is one among those of different species? He replied: "Long head and short legs. [The questioner] said: "Thank you for the teacher’s instruction."
[The Master] said, "Half-folded and fully sealed. The monk said, "Is it just like this? [The Master] said, "Jie!
As the monk was speechless, the Master struck him. A monk asked, "What is it like when the lotus flower has not yet emerged from the water? [The Master] said, "Jie!"

[The Master] said, "The water is deep; it cannot be covered. [The student] asked, "What is it like after it has emerged from the water? [The Master] replied, "It does not obstruct people coming and going. [The student] asked, "What is it like after the flowers have bloomed?

[The Master] replied, "Its fragrance pervades north and south. [The student] asked, "What is it like after the fruit has formed? [The Master] replied, "To feed the fish and nourish the turtles. [The student] asked.
"What is Chan? [The master] replied, "The nostrils enter the earth. The Master, along with Da-yu and several others, took leave of Fen-yang;
they vied with one another to refuse the role of lead participant. Fen-yang said, "This journey cannot be deferred based on seniority in precepts. Listen to my verse:"

"The heavens have no head. Outside the city walls of Jizhou, spears and halberds rise up. A general passes beneath the trees on a single horse. Inside the city walls of Yuanzhou, there is a clamor and hubbub.
The Master (Chuyuan) suddenly stepped forward from the ranks and said, "Who is Chu-yuan that he would dare receive such a prediction from the Abbot?
He then led the assembly in paying their respects. Fen-yang further blessed him, saying, "I personally realized samādhi in the presence of my former teacher."
"You have now attained it; you should go to the south and greatly propagate my Way. He then went to the seat of Chan Master Dongshan Bao, where he faced the wall all day long.
Bao asked, "What was the intent behind Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall? The Master replied, "An empty stomach and a haughty mind.
The following day, when Bao ascended the hall, he invited the Master to serve as the First Seat. When the Master resided at Nanyuan, on the day he opened the hall for formal teaching:
He struck the mallet and said: "O assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary meaning.

The Master then said: "Does the great assembly understand? It is like the clear waters of Yi-yang or the stone bridge of Nan-yue. If you do not understand, it is merely deceiving you all. Therefore it is said:
'When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted a phrase outside the teachings. Now tell me, what was it that he transmitted outside the teachings? He pointed directly..."
The human mind: seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha. Now, all of you here are people pointed out by the Patriarchs; do you believe it?
If you can believe it, you will study alongside the Patriarchs and Buddhas. If you cannot believe it, you may be said to have brought about your own discouragement.
This assembly today is no small matter; I offer this single incense burner for my Master Wude.
Now tell me, do you all recognize Chan Master Wude? If you do not, ask your questions if you have doubts.

A monk asked, "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, Brahma led the way before him and Indra followed behind. Today, as the Master appears in the world, we pray that you will preach the Dharma.
The Master said, "Very well. The monk said, "In that case, I shall go about with my bones ground to powder and my body shattered to pieces. The Master said, "Three..."
Moonlight and wild flowers carpet the ground like brocade; the yellow leaves of the ninth month provide the shade. A question was asked:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said: "Three snakes and nine rats on a mu of land."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, it is utterly beyond the reach of words and explanations. For the attendant to offer incense already constitutes excessive activity.
Thus, when Śākyamuni closed his room, he had already fallen into prolixity; when the layman remained silent, he instead produced much speech.
Why is this? Each has left the home-life, each has traveled on pilgrimage. Now I ask you all: what is the essence of leaving the home-life and traveling on pilgrimage?"
Is it not this very matter: wearing clothes, eating food, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; extensively studying and hearing much; being without words and without speech?
If you understand it in this way, it is much like swinging a club to strike at the moon. Since such an understanding is not permitted, how then should one understand it?
Is there anyone among the assembly who can discern right from wrong? If there is, please come forward and testify before the assembly. If...
"I have not yet been able to do so. I have a doubt and ask for instruction. A monk asked, "The drum has just finished its roll and the great assembly has gathered like clouds.

The Patriarchal intent came from the West; please, Master, proclaim it for us. The Master said, "From where have you come? The monk said, "Fenyang’s single phrase was personally proclaimed by the Master;
what is the matter at Nanyuan today? The Master said, "Have you seen Nanyuan? The monk asked, "There is speaking and there is saying."
"All these are merely discourses of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). To be without words and without speech is not yet the place for a monk’s practice.

Fortunately, we are here before this assembly of humans and devas; I pray that the Master will grant us his instruction. The Master said, "Grant this mountain monk a single thread of discourse, and I shall entangle you in a web of words (*gēténg*). The monk said, "..."
"If that is so, then it is solely for the sake of circulation. The Master said: "A single mass of white clouds stretches across the world;
who among you can emerge from within it?
The Master entered the prefecture. Monk Chongsheng invited him to ascend the hall and say the Dharma, saying: "In this Dharma Hall of Chongsheng, one must not..."
In this place, the Buddha speaks and the Dharma is preached. Even so, though it may be thus, "officially a needle is not permitted, yet privately carts and horses pass through.
This is very much like carrying water to the riverhead and selling it there. Is there anyone among the assembly who can examine this?
Come forth and examine it; is there anyone? Is there anyone? At that time, a monk asked: "I have already heard the various dharmas; today I hear their resonance. I request—"
The Master skillfully expounded the True Vehicle, saying: "Heaven is not high; earth is not distant. The monk said: "A solitary peak rises above the myriad mountains;
ten thousand miles away, a hundred flowers bloom anew. The Master said: "If you are not a guest with a straight hook, your toil reaching the coastal shores is in vain.

A question was asked: "In days of yore at Vulture Peak, the half-seat was shared. What was the meaning of the two masters meeting? The Master said: "The wind from which it comes can be discerned. [The monk] stepped forward.
[The student] said, "If that is so, then the assembly listens intently; I, a student, prostrate. The Master said, "Wise people are hard to find.
[The student] asked, "What is the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas? The Master said, "When the golden moon first emerges from the sea, where is it not clearly revealed?
[The student] further asked, "May I request your instruction, Master? The Master said, "The great ocean has no bounds; it does not harbor those who dwell in the clouds and water."

He then said: "If you seek the principle within words, you bury the ancestral style. Even if one is thoroughly proficient in the meaning of a single phrase, I dare say that such a person has not yet awakened.
Therefore it is said: 'The mountains are green and the waters are blue; the sparrows chirp and the crows caw. Ten thousand streams share the same source, yet the clouds over the sea differ.
The Buddhas of the future have mouths like lanterns; the Buddhas of the past prescribe remedies according to the illness. Present...
"Amidst all Buddhas, one falls into a pit or a ditch. How do you speak that single phrase regarding not falling among the ordinary or the sagely?
After a long silence, he said, "To add a point to an arrowhead," and then descended from his seat.
The Master arrived at Yangshan and was requested to ascend the hall. He said: "When the precious mirror is set upon its stand, the myriad phenomena naturally manifest.

When the Great Sword is held in hand, killing or giving life is decided in the moment. Now tell me, is there anything that is not encompassed by this? If there is, bring forth a single phrase immediately.
If there is none, then those of you who are beginners and students, if you have doubts, please ask. At that time, a monk asked: "I know that the Master has long lain deep..."
"In the pond. "What about the matter of Dayang ascending the hall? The Master said: "When rain comes, the mountains grow dark;
when clouds emerge, the caves become bright. The student said: "I do not understand. I beg for further instruction. The Master said: "Take up the flagpole and go pound rice elsewhere."
The monk remained silent. The Master said, "To play with the tide, one must be a man who plays with the tide. A question was asked:

"Regarding the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Dharma did not manifest before him and he could not attain the path of Buddhahood—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "A total embarrassment. The monk pressed further: "As for that Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū himself, what then? The Master said, "Eight."
"Ten old men acting like youths. The student asked, "I am at the age of sixty (er-shun). I beg the Master to grant me further expedient means.
The Master said, "Everyone bows and serves him. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Lotus flowers cradle his feet."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is it like when the oil is exhausted and the lamp goes out? The Master said, "Raising a son who does not equal his father.
A monk asked, "What is it like when traveling as a cloud over the sea? The Master said, "Suffering. A monk asked, "What is the place where you, the Master, find enjoyment? The Master said, [silence].
Stumped. As the monk was about to offer a word, the Master struck him. A monk asked, "What is it like when one loses what is before and forgets what is after? The Master said, "No.
He ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said, "All the Buddhas of the past, present, and future;
the twenty-eight patriarchs of India; the six patriarchs of the Tang land; and all the old monks throughout the world—these have all been transformed into Nan-yuan’s staff."
"The staff is departing. Where, you all, shall you find a place to settle your bodies and establish your lives?
Look, look! The staff is piercing through the skulls of you all. Is there anyone who recognizes this pain and itch?
If there is, come forth and leap before the assembly! If there is none, Nan-yuan has lost face today. He let out a shout and struck the ground once with his staff.
[The Master] descended from his seat.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
O virtuous ones, if you can believe this, it will not fail to save you effort. It may be called 'Good Wealth entering Maitreya’s pavilion,' where there is no limit."

The Dharma gates are entirely pervasive; one attains great non-obstruction and awakens to the non-arising of dharmas—this is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Boundless lands and realms, self and others, are not separated by even the tip of a hair. Ten eons of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from this very moment of thought.
Now I ask you all: what is this "moment of thought"? It is simply the nature of your own ignorance.

This is precisely your own nature of fundamental enlightenment, wondrous and luminous. It is because you fail to understand the root source of birth and death that you cling to the false as real and are driven by delusion, thereby falling into saṃsāra and undergoing all manner of suffering.
If you can turn the light back upon yourself and reflect inwardly, you will spontaneously awaken to your original true nature, which is neither born nor extinguished.
Therefore, the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; it is a phantom body of empty transformation.
This is precisely the Dharma-body. As for this impure body composed of the four elements and five aggregates, it possesses no substantial reality;

it is like a dream, like an illusion, like a shadow, and like an echo. Since immeasurable kalpas past, one has wandered through birth and death, driven by craving and attachment, without a moment’s rest.
Emerging from here and entering there, the bones accumulated would equal Mount Vipula, and the milk drunk would equal the waters of the four great oceans.
Why is this? It is because of a lack of wisdom; one is unable to realize that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty and entirely devoid of substantial reality.
Driven by delusion and constrained by craving, one lacks sovereignty. Therefore, the World-Honored One said: "The cause of all suffering is rooted in craving.
If craving is extinguished, there is nothing upon which to rely. If you can understand that this illusory body is empty...
It is provisional. Originally empty and quiescent, no views arise; there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span. All phenomena are as they truly are.

This illusory, transformed empty body is itself the Dharma-body. When the Dharma-body is fully realized, not a single thing exists; there is only the hearing of the Dharma and the preaching of the Dharma.
The Great Way is void and profound; the True Teaching is free from attachment. Thus it is said: "The fundamental source and original nature are the natural Buddha. It is further said:
"The five aggregates are floating clouds, coming and going in emptiness; the three poisons are bubbles on water, vainly appearing and disappearing.

If one acts in this manner, for the sake of delivering all from suffering and calamity, even the immeasurable and boundless afflictions and conceptual understandings will all become utterly pure. This is called purity.
The pure Dharma-body. If one reaches this stage, one is able to emerge from here and enter there, casting off this body and assuming another, whether in hell or heaven, in this realm or another.
One moves with sovereign ease in all directions, floating or sinking at will, radiating light in response to things and providing instruction according to the capacity of beings.
To call this "the manifestation of a thousand billion transformation bodies" is, as such talk goes, nothing less than speaking of a dream while dreaming.
Mixing mud with water, spitting out excrement and urine, and failing to distinguish between good and evil, he then laughs loudly, saying:
"If you were to approach the gate of a patch-robed monk, you would not have even dreamed of the stench of his sweat, let alone the distance of eighty thousand miles! Nevertheless, even so..."
Matters are not univocal; they are merely provisional names used to guide sentient beings. [The Master] gave a shout and addressed the assembly, saying:
"When Mazu Daoshi said 'the mind is Buddha,' it was for those who had not yet attained awakening. When Panshan said 'neither mind nor Buddha,' [it was for those at a later stage]."
These are merely idle speculations. Xuefeng’s “rolling the ball” is a trick to deceive small children; Yunmen’s “looking in the mirror” makes the bystanders laugh;
Xiaoshi’s “self-pity in the small room” is a great blunder; Deshan’s “staff upon entering the gate” was before he met a truly extraordinary person;
Linji’s “shout upon entering the gate” is far too frivolous; and Huangmei’s presentation of a verse shows that he had not yet forgotten self and others.
Furthermore, they speak of patriarchs transmitting to patriarchs, yet they slander one another in turn. To reach this point, one must truly be a person of substance;
thus it is said: "The hawk begets a hawk chick; the falcon begets a falcon chick. Even so, it is still just a tea pitcher from Gong County.
He then snapped his fingers once and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Coming up, step by step one ascends higher; going down, the entire body is unimpeded. Therefore it is said:"

Sometimes one strikes first and then sings; sometimes one sings first and then strikes; sometimes striking and singing occur simultaneously; sometimes striking and singing do not occur at the same time.
Thus, when the King ascends the jeweled throne, the rustic old man breaks into song.
Is there anyone here now who can sing such a song? After a long silence, he said: "Though the wooden man raises his hand, the stone woman does not lift her head. He let out a shout.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind; the sands-of-the-Ganges of wondrous meanings are all contained within the source of the heart.
There are no three realms from which to escape, and there is no Bodhi to be sought. Humans and non-humans are equal in their fundamental nature and characteristics.
Since this is so, why did Nanda strike the Imperial Bell? After a long silence, he said: "The Persian's nostrils are long and long indeed."

Addressing the assembly: When speaking of Buddhas and Patriarchs, it is all just mixing mud with water. Whether moving upward or downward, the patch-robed monks’ worn-out straw sandals do not function in such a way.
To bind oneself when there is no rope—how can one speak that single phrase of solitary liberation?
Is there anyone who can say it? Try bringing forth a phrase for this assembly in reverse; is there anyone? Is there anyone? After a long silence, he said: "Upon the tomb."
He added more mud. He let out a shout. The Master asked a monk, "What is your name? The monk said, "Haiman. The Master said, "The ocean has neither increase nor decrease;
why then is it full? The monk said, "Master, do not deceive Haiman. The Master said, "Nanyuan’s fault."
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Clouds pass over a thousand mountains, all green.
The Master said, "Why are you in such a hurry? The monk said, "The wild geese depart; the sound of the water is mournful. The Master gave a shout. The monk also shouted. The Master struck him.
The monk also struck him. The Master said, "You blind fellow! By your right, you should have been driven out through the main gate. But considering that you are a newcomer, sit here and eat."
Tea. The Master asked a monk, "A traveler on the path must know there is a matter of traveling. What is this matter of traveling? The monk said, "I know it.
The Master said, "What is the matter that you know? The monk said, "The mountains are high and the waters are deep.

The Master said, "Since you have come from afar, sit for a while and drink some tea. The monk said, "Yes, yes. The Master asked Chief Seat Xianying, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, [blank].
"Jinluan. The Master said, "Where did you spend the summer retreat? He replied, "Jinluan. The Master said, "Where did you spend the previous and subsequent summers?
He replied, "Jinluan. The Master said, "Where did you spend the very first summer? He replied, "Master, why do you not understand my words? The Master said, "I am unable to examine you;
I shall have the attendant from the storehouse brought here to examine you. For now, let me have a bowl of tea prepared for you."
Wetting his mouth. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk made a horizontal stroke in front of him with his hand. The Master said, "What words are these?
The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "What are you doing? The monk clapped his hands once, and the Master struck him. The Master said, "Blind fellow! Why do you act so recklessly?
He took up his sitting cloth and drove him straight out of the Dharma Hall. The Master said, "After passing through Langya, at that time Jue..."
The Zen Master resided there. Previously, when the practitioner Jue arrived at Langye and entered the abbot’s quarters, Jue asked him, "Where have you recently come from?
He replied, "From the Two Zhe regions. Jue asked, "Did you come by boat or by land? He replied, "By boat. Jue asked, "Where is the boat now? He replied, "..."
As he was descending the steps, Xuedou asked, "How do you express the phrase that does not involve the journey? Jue raised his sitting mat, gave it a thump, and said, "Fabricated old man!
You are as numerous as hemp and millet. He then shook out his sleeves and departed. Xuedou asked an attendant, "Who was that?
The attendant replied, "It was Zen Master Jue. Xuedou then went in person to the guest quarters and asked, "Could that have been Zen Master Jue?"
"Do not be surprised that I have just now offended you. He raised his staff and shouted, "I have long heard of your reputation in Zhejiang;
it turns out your understanding is merely like this. How can you claim your fame spreads throughout the world? Juexian then prostrated and said, "Huijue has committed a transgression.
When the Master arrived at Langye, Juexian invited him to stay; the Master lingered there for several days, and the matter was brought up during their night conversation.
The Master smiled and said, "Jujian has just been able to understand for himself. Jue remained silent. The Master then sang the Song of the Cowherd Boy for him:
"The cowherd boy is truly happy; Barefoot and wearing a straw hat, he holds the two horns. He lies across the ox and sings toward the heavens."
Someone asked, "How is it that the ox has not yet thirsted? He turned his head and looked; the level field was vast. Let it roam in all four directions without restraint;
on all eight sides, it wanders at will without confinement. To bring it back, one need only pull at the end of the rope. Little calf, stroke its coat with the grain.

His strength is not yet sufficient to lift him up; for now, let him rest on this small, level slope. Fearing he might lose his four hooves upon the high peak, the sun has already risen high—cease grazing!
Holding fast by the tip of his nose, young and old alike, they lead him all at once into the pen to sleep.
Muddying the ground, they watch as he tumbles east and west. "Ha ha ha! Is it well? Is it not well? Then they take up their transverse flutes and play them with the wind.
He blows. He causes the five lakes, mountains, and islands to tremble. Riding backward upon an ox, he sheds his coarse cotton robe. Those who know the sound need not seek it along the road.
If you ask where the cowherd dwells, he points east and west with his whip; there is not a single treasure to be found. Jue Mo attained the samādhi of playful mastery.
A monk asked, "What is the guest within the guest? The Master said, "His prostrations are even more earnest. How?
"This is the guest within the host. The Master said, "The staff is always in my hand. "What is the host within the guest?
The Master said, "The staff sweeps across heaven and earth. "What is the host within the host? The Master said, "A sword held in the hand of one who carries a steamer.
Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A bamboo staff from Xiao and Xiang. Question: "When neither patriarchs nor Buddhas are established, what then? The Master said, "The mouth."
[The Master] produced a tuft of reeds from above. The questioner asked, "What is it like when one turns back as soon as one sees [the truth]? The Master said, "The Provincial Governor of Hunan.

The questioner pressed further, "Please speak, Master, regarding the final earnestness. The Master said, "How very clear! The questioner said, "The assembly is listening intently. The Master said, [silence].

[The Master] did not yet dare to grant his consent. A question was asked: "When one cannot advance further, what then? The Master said: "It cuts off all doubts. Question: "What is it like when one ascends higher step by step?
The Master said: "Clouds arise beneath one's feet. Question: "What is the Southern Spring Dog? The Master said: "Its snout. Question:
"What is Chan? The Master said: "The nostrils enter the earth. Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: [Silence].
"Stone cannot penetrate it.
He ascended the hall and said, "The Buddhas emit radiance to assist in the manifestation of the meaning of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
He then held up his staff and said, "This is Nan-yuan’s staff; which one is the meaning of the true mark? If you see it as such, you are caught by it."
This is what is turned by seeing and hearing. If you do not see, where are your traveling eyes? (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat. Entering the hall, he says:
"As soon as a single speck of dust is raised, the entire earth is fully contained within it. Within the tip of a single hair is a lion; within the tips of ten billion hairs [is the same]."
He manifests ten billion lion heads from a single hair-tip; within one hair-tip appear thousands and tens of thousands of heads. Simply recognize one head.
Then he raises his staff and says: "This is Nan-yuan’s staff. Which one is that one head?"
[The Master] let out a shout. He struck his staff once and descended from the seat. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "An old man develops an illness.
A monk asked, "What is the phrase for receiving a beginner? The Master said, "One stroke, two pieces.

A monk asked, "What is the phrase for testing a patch-robed monk? The Master said, "Hanshan and Shide. A monk asked, "What is the phrase for when the true command is being exercised? The Master said, [He remained silent.]
The Master said: "A thousand come, ten thousand go. Question: "What is the phrase that establishes heaven and earth? The Master said: "The heavens are high; the seas are vast. Question:
"How is it when sitting side by side with the Master? The Master said: "A thread passes through yellow leaves."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad dharmas are one body with me.
He then held up his staff and said, "This is Nan-yuan’s staff; which one is the 'body'? After a long silence, he said, "To cross the river, one must use a raft;
once on the shore, the boat is no longer needed. He let out a shout, struck the ground once with his staff, and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—these are all swallowed in a single gulp by Nanyuan’s staff.
The sentient beings therein do not perceive it, nor are they aware of it. Where, then, are the nostrils of you monks?
If you know where they are, you may carry this staff slung across your shoulder and gaze at the clouds and sky. If you do not know, [it remains] long."
[The Master] sat down on the bed. [There was] porridge and rice. He gave a shout and descended from his seat. A lay official asked, "What is the realm of Nan-yuan?

The Master said, "Digging a pond to await the moon in autumn; planting bamboo to shade the sun in summer. "What is the person within the realm? The Master said, "In the city, the young gentlemen are noble in every way;
beneath the forest trees, the practitioners of the Way are poor in every matter. A questioner asked, "For a long time I have been ignorant of the pearl in my garment."

"Please, Master, give me instruction. The Master said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. The monk said, "There is no way to escape. The Master said, "Your feet are planted and cannot move.
A Dharma Seat Master asked, "I do not ask about the teaching that speaks of 'causes and conditions' versus 'spontaneity. What are causes and conditions?
The Master said, "How long has it been since you first began studying? The Master further asked, "What is spontaneity? The Master said, "Withdraw quickly!"
[The monk] quickly withdrew. He obstructed another person from questioning.
The Master was staying at Daowu. He ascended the hall. A monk asked: "Bodhidharma came from the West specifically for the sake of the present age; he did not bend the fundamental lineage."
"Please, Master, utter a verse. The Master said: "Clouds and rain sprinkle the vast sky; flowers bloom everywhere in spring. The student replied: "The mountain pines are cool and serene;
the morning moon shines upon the long river. The Master said: "Once a single word has been set in motion, who would say it differs between ancient and modern?"
The student said, "Clouds arise upon the peaks; flowers bloom before the crags. The Master said, "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office;
yet where has one ever seen a single person beneath the forest trees? The student said, "Today I have met the Master. The Master then gave a shout.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.

Now tell me, how would you express this in a single phrase: 'Walking by day and sleeping at night'? After a long silence, he struck the ground once with his staff and said, "Deshan bears witness. He then descended from the seat.
A monk asked, "When the *xièzhài* (unicorn) stands before the carriage, if a student hesitates, how can they enter? The Master said, "Return [to your original state]."
"Do you feel a headache? He ascended the hall and said:
"The mind turns according to the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound. If one recognizes one's nature while following the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
He raised his staff and said: "This is Daowu’s staff. Which one is..."

All of you, people of the world: the sands of buddha-lands, the sands of buddhas of the Western Heaven, the twenty-eight patriarchs of India, and the six patriarchs of the Tang land—all turn the Great Dharma Wheel upon the staff of Daowu. Do you all see it? If you see it...
Wandering to the Western Heaven in the morning, returning to the Eastern Land in the evening. If you do not see it, there is congee at dawn and rice at the time of the midday meal.
(He strikes his staff once and descends from the seat.)
Ascending the hall, he said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally still and vast.
It can act as the lord of all phenomena, yet it does not wither along with the four seasons. He held up his staff and said: "This here is Daowu’s staff; which one is the lord of all phenomena?"
After a long silence, he said, "If you see that all marks are no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata. He gave a shout, struck his staff once on the ground, and descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Sometimes illumination comes first and function follows; sometimes function comes first and illumination follows; sometimes illumination and function occur simultaneously;
and sometimes illumination and function do not occur simultaneously. Therefore it is said: 'There is light and there is darkness;

there is arising and there is falling. [He let out a shout] and said: 'Now tell me, was that illumination or was it function? Can the monastics and the laity distinguish this? Come forward and show your wares.'"
[The Master] looked at him with a look of disapproval. "If you do not have it," he said, "I have lost today.

He gave a shout and descended from his seat. He ascended the hall. A monk came forward and bowed; as soon as he rose, he gave a shout. The Master asked, "What is this? The monk shouted again. The Master said, "Blind!"
The monks prostrated. The Master said, "Thirty blows—wait until another time to come and receive them. A monk asked, "What was the meaning of the ancients facing the wall?
The Master said, "He had years of age but no virtue."
The Master was residing at Shishuang. On the day he ascended the hall, a monk asked: "Vimalakīrti’s single silence did not yet accord with the ancestral school;

the simultaneous application of staff and shout leaves those of middling capacity at a loss. For this assembly today, we pray the Master will provide a skillful means. The Master said: "The stone sprout grows when it meets spring."
"Frost flowers bloom facing the sun. The monk said, "In that case, the sunbirds chatter away; after the rain, the hundred flowers are new.

The Master said, "Were it not for the fisherman’s guidance, how would one know the depth of the water? The monk said, "Steep waters follow the swift current; the clouds part to reveal the azure sky. The Master said, "I walk amidst the wild weeds; you, too, have entered the deep village. The monk responded with an assent and said: Frost flowers bloom facing the sun. The monk said, "In that case, the sunbirds chatter away; after the rain, the hundred flowers are new. The Master said, "Were it not for the fisherman’s guidance, how would one know the depth of the water?

The monk said, "Steep waters follow the swift current; the clouds part to reveal the azure sky. The Master said, "I walk amidst the wild weeds; you, too, have entered the deep village. The monk responded with an assent and said:
"The official will not allow even a needle. [The monk] asked further, "May I ask one more question? What is your meaning, Master? The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows;
it will be only after thirty years that you will begin to know the pain and the itch. The monk flourished his sleeves and withdrew. The Master said, "A dream.

[Another] asked, "When tuning the strings on a square wooden board, how is it? The Master said, "The flagpole is one chi and two cun long. [The monk] stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then it is in the hands of the Master."
[This occurred] at the present time. The Master said, "His feet kick, yet he does not move. The monk said, "Do not say that you do not recognize his voice.
The Master said, "It is uncertain whether he will awaken after thirty years. A monk asked, "How is it when the ancient mirror has not yet been polished?
The Master said, "Beating a drum in Silla. The monk pressed further, "How is it after it has been polished? The Master said, "Dancing in India."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The blue lotus has already blinked many times; Kāśyapa’s faint smile was but self-deception. Sitting at Shaoshi, he was ashamed of his folly and cut off his arm;
at Huangmei, he presented various verses of understanding. Entering the gate with blows and shouts—layer upon layer of error;

the ancestral vehicle of the Ultimate—here one carves out one's own flesh. The public case is already manifest; who would feel shame? To discern the 'Aha! and the 'pecking'—to laugh at the bystander. (1)
Sujue came to know this was an error; it was not that his teacher lacked further causeless [teachings]. Every man possesses the ambition to pierce the heavens;
look at the Big Dipper and the Southern Star from opposite sides.
Verse on the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials in Response to the Sangha’s Request for Instruction. First Mystery:
What could the Buddhas of the three periods of time possibly proclaim? Out of compassion, they appear in dreams, yet people treat them with levity; sitting upright, they [return to their true state].
This constitutes falling into the extreme of nihilism.
The second mystery: even for a sharp-witted monk whose eyes are not yet clear, the spark of a flint or a flash of lightning is known to be dull.
Raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye is already traversing mountains and passes.
The third mystery: Myriad phenomena are arrayed as the universe expands; clouds disperse into the cavernous void and the mountains and peaks are still;
fallen flowers and flowing water fill the long river. The first essential:
How can one speak of the wondrous nature of the holy and the common? To deliberate upon it is to traverse a long road; to lift one’s eyes is to fall into the seven perversions.
The second essential: Striking the *ghanṭā* on the mountain peak, those with sovereign spiritual powers come; at the gate of much learning, one cries out. The third essential:
Rising up and falling over causes others to laugh; within the palm, one grasps heaven and earth; a thousand differences are all illuminated as one.

I report this to you, O Master of Profound Penetration: the staff and the shout must be applied according to the moment. If you clearly understand the intimate intent, the great sun will shine even at midnight.
Because a monk requested instruction, Linji’s two hall heads both let out shouts;

the verse describes the mechanism of "pecking and hatching," where arrow meets blade. In that fleeting instant, host and guest were distinguished. The Patriarchal Master, out of compassion for sentient beings, bestowed this upon the monastic community.
Sū: "The waters of the Yellow River in Beidi are thoroughly turbid.
Because someone requested instruction on the Buddha-talk of Huichao, there was a verse.
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "You are Huichao. [Huichao] prostrated, stepped forward, joined his palms, and pondered.
A hundred thousand miles away.
Because a monk requested further instruction on Yunmen’s talk of "surpassing Buddhas and patriarchs," [the Master] declared:

"How does one surpass Buddhas and patriarchs? Serve the monks with rice cakes at the midday meal; eat as much as you desire. In Hunan, he unfurled his alms bowl; in Silla, he displayed his begging bowl.
Bite. A Persian from Daishi requested a ferry crossing;
because a monk asked for further instruction, he [the Master] recounted the first verse of the Three Verses on the Secret Instructions:
"The great earth, mountains, and rivers leak away; Vimalakīrti has just become silent, and Mañjuśrī immediately becomes loquacious."
The Second Secret: When observing the unfolding of time and occasion, speech and silence—how could they possibly interfere? It is like the autumn moon at midnight. The Third Secret:
A distant road is difficult to traverse; it is like rowing a boat upon dry land. Within one’s own eyes, the sun and moon are concealed.
The first line of the three-line verse:

"In the heavens and across other lands, all are at a loss; the various arguments of the Cakravartin’s inverted doctrines are manifold, yet the towering [Buddha] has not yet reached the Nyagrodha tree."
The second phrase: Linji and Deshan set out on their journey; before they had even crossed into Silla, the staff was already being brandished.
Those who attain realization point recklessly along the way. The third phrase:
Vimalakīrti manifested illness and Mañjuśrī went to visit him; their dialogue of mutual silence shook heaven and earth. This continues until...
Now, as a source of laughter, I shall provide verses on the Five Ranks as requested by the assembly.
Regarding "The Center and the Deviation": At midnight, a black hen crows within the room; beneath the ocean, a lamp illuminates the world; upon a stone, one plants a tree.
The flower on the long branch is spiritual;
it is centered within the partial. When the sun sets behind the western mountains, one beholds a strange reflection; the distinct image reveals the vehicle of the school.
Cease searching for the moon in the well with a furrowed brow.

Coming from the very center: a wooden horse gives birth to a child that fills the nine realms. Advancing and retreating, it moves freely through the path of birds; how could it be compared to the narrow confines of those who dwell in nests?

Reaching the convergence of both: each of these men possesses full spirit and vigor; though spear and shield clash against one another, their edges do not meet. Expanding and unfolding, he lets loose— *Note: This passage is a poetic commentary on Zen practice, utilizing the "Three Phrases" (Sanju) structure of the *Wumen Guan*. The final phrase, "展拓縱" (zhǎntuò zòng), indicates the final liberation of the realization.*
Transversely inseparable, they reach into the midst of both.
Before black and white appear, cease all making and doing. You must clearly see that the pillar has not yet given birth to a child;
do not mistake wild words for the path and wander on.

The entire verse returns from the partial to the correct, reaching the ultimate mystery and profundity. When the correct departs and the partial arrives, principle and phenomena are complete. One must know that the establishment of the correct is not a matter of verbal expression;
its subtle signs belong to the realm of conditions. Simultaneously reaching the past and future, it gives rise to wondrous function; once this simultaneity is attained, why pursue anything further?
Words and explanations—how could their appearance and disappearance encompass the entire world? Vast and without reliance, the bird-path is profound.

Because a monk requested instruction on the Buddha’s dialogue regarding "the bamboo-stem whip beneath the Zhulin Mountain," there have been tens of thousands of Chan practitioners from the north and south; do not be surprised that we do not bow when meeting.
Horse! East and west each have their own destiny. To Li, Prince of the Household: You manifest a thousand, ten thousand, and even billions of bodies;
your compassion, wisdom, and vows are inexhaustible. When among the laity, you follow the ways of the laity; when residing in the palace, you accord with the ways of the palace.
Everywhere there are great protectors; in every place they manifest supernatural powers. Cherish our school with good fortune; many are able to establish the ancient style.
Looking up at the sun on the horizon as it debates, how many times does its pure light rise from the four quarters?
A Great Being with disheveled hair asks Master Zhigong: "The Mahāprajñāpāramitā."
Commentary on Venerable Dushun’s Verse:

“The Ox in Huazhou Eats the Grain” (The River-Sand Worlds); “The Horse in Yizhou Has a Bloated Belly” (The Ants Carrying the Bowl); “Summoning Physicians from All Under Heaven” (Donkey’s Head and Horse’s Horns);
“Moxibustion on the Left Shoulder of a Pig” (Painting a Tiger and Producing a Fox).
A Verse on Winter Idleness. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"The trees of Dongshan are tall; How many years, how many rains? The pine branches of Nanling are lean; Stones grow from the earth beside the stones."
Jinshen saw Gautama. [The numbers] two, three, seven, eight, five.
A monk requested the ancients' "Song of the Twelve Hours," whereupon he composed this verse:

At the hour of Chou (1–3 a.m.), when the cock crows, one encounters people in dreams in a state of utter confusion. At the hour of Yin (3–5 a.m.), at dawn, having awakened, one goes about on the road playing with one's own spirit.

At the hour of Mao (6–8 a.m.), the sun rises; within the brilliance of its blazing radiance, one sits. At the hour of Shen (11 a.m.–1 p.m.), having eaten one’s fill, one still knows this to be the cause of illness.
At the hour of Si (9–11 a.m.), one enters the marketplace to buy and sell, weighing and measuring goods. At the hour of Wu (noon), the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest as objects of laughter.

At the hour of *ri-dyik* (the second watch, approximately 1–3 PM): "Lord Zhang drinks wine; Lord Li is drunk. At the hour of *phu-shi* (the third watch, approximately 3–5 PM): "Reflecting on this, I sit upright, drowsy and intoxicated. At the hour of *nyi-nyir* (the fourth watch, approximately 5–7 PM):

"The thatched hut and bamboo door are propped up with difficulty. At the hour of *huang-hun* (the fifth watch, approximately 7–9 PM): "The sun sets behind the western mountains; foxes and spirits emerge."
Midnight (Zi): A single bright moon, *sūri*. The Hour of Rat (Hai): Mice form their ranks by the bedside.

Essential Sayings of Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan of Chizhou (Second generation under Nanyue; succeeded Mazu). The Master’s name was Puyuan.
He was a native of the Wang family in Zhengzhou. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Old Wang is selling himself."
"Is there anyone who will buy this? At that time, a monk came forward from the assembly and said, "I will buy it.
The Master asked, "Without making it expensive and without making it cheap, how will you buy it? The monk was speechless.

Later, while the Master was drinking tea with Luzu, Guizong, and Shanshan, Luzu lifted up his cup and said, "This very thing existed even before the world was formed. The Master said, "In these present times..."
"Recognizing only this, one does not yet recognize the world. Zhaozhou said, "Yes. The Master said, "Does your brother not share this same view?
Zhaozhou lifted up his cup and said, "Could you speak when the world had not yet been formed? The Master made a gesture of slapping him.

Zong made the gesture of receiving with his palms against his face. When the Master, along with Luzu, Shanshan, and Guizong, took their leave of Mazu and each planned to dwell in a hermitage, they parted ways midway.
As they were separating, the Master thrust down his staff and said, "Even if you can speak the Way, you will still be obstructed by this."

The bandits were utterly defeated. [The monk] pulled down the curtain and departed. He reported this to the Master. The Master said, "I have always suspected this fellow.
A monk asked, "When Niutou had not yet seen the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds carry flowers to offer him? The Master said:
"He has been treading the steps of the Buddha at every turn. [The Master] asked: "After you have seen [the Buddha], why do you not offer him flowers? The Master said:
"Even if he did not come, it would still be one thread’s distance from Old Wang. The Master asked a lecturer: "What sutra are you lecturing on?"

[The student] said: "The *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (Sutra on Maitreya’s Descent). The Master said: "When will Maitreya descend to be born? [The student] said: "He is currently in the heavenly palace;
he has not yet come. The Master said: "There is no Maitreya in heaven, and there is no Maitreya on earth."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Sons, at the age of eighteen, this old monk already understood how to make a living.

Anyone who understands how to make a living, come forth and discuss it with me; only then will you be a true mountain dweller. After a long silence, he looked over the assembly, joined his palms, and said:
"Be careful. If there is nothing to do, each of you should practice for yourselves. The assembly did not disperse. The Master said: "It is like the great fruit of sainthood."
Be wary! Do not underestimate this great man; even he could do nothing about it. For my part, I am not him, and he is not me. How can he possibly affect me?
Those scholars of the sutras and treatises take the Dharmakāya as the ultimate limit, calling it the Samādhi of Ultimate Principle and the Samādhi of Ultimate Meaning.
As for me, in the past I was taught by others to "return to the root and revert to the source. For a time, I nearly fell for that.
Meeting. A calamity. Brothers, these days there are too many Chan masters; one cannot find a person who is dull-witted and simple.
It is not that they do not exist at all, but among them, such people are rare. If there were any, come forth and deliberate with me. At the time of the empty kalpa, were there any practitioners?
If you say there were or there were not, why do you not speak? You usually have clever lips and thin tongues, yet when it comes to this—
When questioned, he remained silent on all accounts. "Why do you not come forward? Do not discuss matters of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
Brothers, people nowadays carry the Buddha upon their shoulders as they walk. Yet when they hear this old monk say that 'the mind is not the Buddha' and 'wisdom is not the Way,' [they are startled]."

They gathered their heads together, intending to push him away, [but] the old monk said, "There is no place for you to push me. If you could bind up empty space and beat me with it as a staff, then feel free to push.

At that time, a monk asked, "From the ancestral masters of old down to Master Jiangxi, they all said, 'This very mind is Buddha' and 'The ordinary mind is the Way. Now, you, Master, say that 'the mind is not Buddha' and 'wisdom..."
"It is not that I am saying so; rather, all you students have given rise to doubt. I pray that the Master will compassionately provide instruction.
The Master replied with a resonant voice: "If you were a Buddha, you would cease to involve yourself in doubt. Instead, ask the old monk:
'Where is there such a person as you who comes to doubt the Buddha alongside others? As for me, I am certainly not a Buddha, nor have I ever met the Patriarchs. You speak in such a manner!"
[The student] said, "I shall go seek the Patriarch myself. The Master said, "When the Master speaks thus, how does he instruct his students to sustain [the practice]?
The Master said, "You must quickly reach out your hand and support empty space. [The student] said, "Empty space has no characteristic of motion; how can it be supported?
The Master said, "By saying there is no characteristic of motion, you have already moved. When has empty space ever said, 'I have no characteristic of motion'? All of this...
“This is your emotional perception. He said, “Even ‘emptiness has no mark of movement’ is still an emotional perception. What did you previously mean when you told me not to rely on anything?
The Master said, “Since you know that one should not say ‘rely,’ where would you intend to support him?

He said, “If it is not the case that ‘this very mind is Buddha,’ then is it the case that ‘this mind creates Buddha’? The Master said, “‘This very mind is Buddha; this mind creates Buddha. This is emotional perception.”
All that is reckoned as existing is entirely formed through conceptualization. The Buddha is a person of wisdom; the mind is the master of accumulation.
Whenever one faces an object, the mind immediately employs its subtle functions. Venerable sir, do not identify with the mind or identify with the Buddha.

Even if you were to identify them, it would be called by others "ignorance regarding the knowable. Therefore, the Great Master of Jiangxi said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. For now, let us...
"If you, my descendants, practice in this manner, will the students of today—who merely don these robes—be able to resolve such idle matters as those you have raised?
[The student] said, "Since it is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing, why does the Master now say that 'mind is not Buddha' and 'wisdom is not the Way'?
I do not yet understand how this is so. The Master said, "It is because you do not recognize that mind is [Buddha]."
The Master said, "Buddha is not the Way; the old monk does not admit the 'mind' even to come forth—where else could it be placed?

[The student] said, "Since it cannot be grasped at all, how is it any different from the great void? The Master said, "Since it is not a thing, what can you compare it to as the great void? Furthermore, who is there to distinguish between difference and non-difference?
[The student] said, "It cannot be that there is nothing; it is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. The Master said, "If you recognize it thus..."

[Zhaozhou] said, "This very act of stopping constitutes becoming a mind-Buddha. [Zhaozhou] said, "Please, Master, explain it. The Master said, "I myself do not know. [Zhaozhou] asked, "Why do you not know?
The Master said, "How am I to explain it to you? [Zhaozhou] said, "Does this not mean that you do not permit your student to understand the Way?
The Master said, "What Way would you understand? And how would you go about understanding it? [Zhaozhou] said, "I do not know. The Master said, "Not..."
"It is better to know how to set it aside. If you take my words as the standard, you will be called a person of 'following through' (yītōng).

Even if you were to see Maitreya appear in the world, he would still pluck the hair from your head. The monk asked, "How will this affect future generations? The Master said, "You should look for yourself; do not worry about those who come after.
The monk asked, "Previously, you did not allow me to understand the Way; now you again tell me to look for myself. I do not yet understand."
"How so? the Master asked. The monk said, "I understand it as a hidden meeting, a wondrous meeting; please grant me your approval. "How do you understand it? the Master asked.
The monk said, "What is this 'wondrous meeting'? The Master said, "Do you wish to imitate the words of an old monk? Even if it were spoken by this old monk, what would you, Venerable One, make of it?
The monk said, "If I were to understand it on my own, there would be no need for the Master's presence. I beg your compassionate instruction. The Master said, "One must not point toward the east."
Pointing west to deceive people: when you were being so complacent and easygoing, why did you not come to question the old monk?
Nowadays, people are clever and cunning; only then do they say, "I do not understand. What are you trying to achieve?

If you emerge into this life and say, "I have left the home-life to become a Zen master," then tell me: what have you actually done since before you left the home-life? Speak! Let us deliberate with you.
[The student] said, "At such a time, I do not know. The Master said, "Since you do not know, do you recognize this 'it is so' right now as being correct?
[The student] said, "If recognizing it is not [correct], is non-recognition [correct]? The Master said, "What kind of talk is this—'recognizing' or 'not recognizing'?
[The student] said, "Having reached this point, I am even more confused. The Master said, "If you do not understand, I shall further..."
"No. The monk said, "I am but a student, so I do not understand. But you, Master, are a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); surely you should understand.
The Master said, "This fellow, when I told you you do not understand, who was I debating with as a 'virtuous friend'? Do not be so clever. Look at it this way:
when the old master of Jiangxi was alive, a scholar came and asked: 'Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-bushel boat.'"
"How is this principle? An elder said, "Here there is neither water nor boat; what need is there to discuss sinews and bones?
When the scholar was about to leave, he did not exert much effort. Therefore, I have repeatedly told you: "The Buddha does not understand the Way;
I practice it myself—what use is knowing? [The scholar] asked, "How does one practice? The Master said, "It cannot be grasped through deliberation. He continued, "Go toward..."
"In the human realm, to cultivate and practice in such a manner is extremely difficult. The student asked, "Does this allow a student like me to practice?
The Master said, "I cannot obstruct you. The student asked, "How then should I practice? The Master said, "If you wish to practice, then practice."
"One must not exclusively seek [instruction] from others. [The student] said: "If it were not for the guidance of a good friend (kalyāṇamitra), there would be no way to attain realization.

As you, Master, often say: 'In practicing the Way, one must first understand before one can succeed. If one does not understand, one falls into the causality of others and lacks the capacity for self-mastery.
I wonder how one should practice so as to avoid falling into the causality of others? The Master said: "There is no need to deliberate further."
[The student] said, "As for cultivation, where can one not go to attain it? The Master said, "How could you possibly go to attain it?
The student said, "The Master has not yet spoken; how am I to seek it? The Master said, "Even if I were to speak..."
"Where would you go? For instance, from dawn until night, even when you suddenly walk east or west, you do not even deliberate whether you can go or cannot go;
others cannot know what you are doing. [The student] said: "When walking east or west, one does not think about it at all—is that so?
The Master said: "At such a time, who would say 'it is' or 'it is not'? [The student] said: "Every time the Master speaks..."
“I do not go anywhere at all; others cannot capture me. This is called the Pervasive Samādhi, the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body. Is this not the principle?
The Master said, “If one speaks in terms of cultivation, where would there be a place not gone?
I do not speak of being captured or not captured, nor do I speak of samādhi. [The student] asked, “How does this differ from attaining the Way of Bodhi through some existent dharma? The Master said:
[The student] said, "I do not discuss whether they are different or not. [The student] said, "The practice taught by my Upādhyāya is quite distinct from that of the Mahāyāna.

I do not know how this is so. The Master said, "I do not concern myself with whether it is different or not; furthermore, you have never studied it. If we were to discuss the study of the scriptures..."
"There are masters of the sutras and śāstras; the other schools are truly formidable. For now, it would be better for you simply to listen.
The student asked, "Ultimately, how should a student understand this? The Master said, "Regarding what you have asked, it fundamentally resides within the realm of causes and conditions.
Look at you—you are truly helpless because you only recognize the phenomena occurring at the six sense gates. You must simply understand the Buddha."
"Come here; let us deliberate together. Brothers, do not pursue things restlessly in this way, nor reject them in this way.
As the ancients said: 'When practicing the bodhisattva path, one proceeds alone.

Māra Pāpīyān, leading his retinue, constantly follows behind the bodhisattva, seeking the place where the mind's activities arise, intending to strike them down. Thus it continues for immeasurable [eons]."
Throughout kalpas, one cannot find even a single thought that exists apart from this; only then do they pay their respects and take leave of their retinue, offering praise and worship.

Even these are but those of the lower grade within the stage of progressive cultivation, yet they are already at their wits' end—how much more so for those who have transcended all effort, such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra?
I shall say no more of them. Brothers, how can you say that practice does not exist? Try to find a single person who actually practices!
"It cannot be attained. Nowadays, people follow others from year to year, seeking nothing but the ultimate.
Why do you vainly flap your lips and produce intellectual interpretations? The student said, "At such a time, there is no name for Buddha and no name for sentient beings.

How could I possibly attempt to calculate or conceptualize it? The Master said, "Your very statement that 'there is no name for Buddha and no name for sentient beings' is already a conceptual calculation."
[The monk] said, "It is also a record of another's words. The Master said, "If that is so, everything belongs to the time when the Buddha appeared in the world;

it is absolutely impossible not to speak of it. The monk said, "How would you speak of it? The Master said, "Even if one were to speak, words would still fail to reach it. The Master said, [continuing]: "..."
"If you say that the Way is beyond words and speech, you are vainly pursuing it in such a manner. Who provides you with an object?
He said, "Since there is no one who acts as an object, who is the person on 'that side'? The Master said, "If you do not cite the scriptures, from where would you discuss the Buddha?
Since we do not discuss the Buddha, with whom would I, this old monk, discuss 'this side' and 'that side'? He said, "Although the fruit is indeed..."
[The student] asked: "One abides in the Way, yet the Way can act as a cause. How is this so? The Master said: "Those were people of old.
Now you must not fail to observe the precepts. I am not he, and he is not me. If you can act like Li-nu or Pai-gu, your conduct will be free and easy.
If for even a single thought you differ [from him], it will be difficult to practice the path. [The student] asked: "In what way does a single thought differ, such that it becomes difficult?"
[The student] said, "For the sake of practice. The Master said, "As soon as there is even a single thought of difference, there are the two faculties of superior and inferior.

This is not the realm of emotional views following along with cause and effect; what further freedom could there be? [The student] asked, "I have often heard the Master say that the Reward-body and Transformation-body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the ones who preach the Dharma.
I do not yet understand how this is so. The Master said, "Because they arise from conditions, they are not [the true Buddha]. [The student] said, "Since the Reward-body and Transformation-body..."
[The student] asked, "Is the Dharma-body not the true Buddha? The Master said, "It is already the response-body. [The student] said, "If that is so, then even the Dharma-body is not the true Buddha.
The Master said, "Whether the Dharma-body is the true [Buddha] or not, this old monk has no tongue with which to explain it.
You must teach me how to speak of it. [The student] said, "Apart from the three bodies, what dharma is the true Buddha? The Master said:
[Zhehan] said, "I have already finished scolding you old men, eighty or ninety of you. What more is there to ask about 'separation' or 'non-separation'?
You intend to drive a wedge into empty space. [The other monk] said, "I humbly understand that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was spoken by the Dharma-body Buddha."
"How so? The Master asked. "What words did you just say? The monk repeated his question.
The Master looked at him and sighed, saying, "If it is the Dharma-body that speaks, where would you go to listen? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "This is most difficult."
"A great difficulty! Look at Master Liang; he is a man from Shu who understands how to lecture on thirty-two scriptures and treatises.
While traveling through Jiangxi to give lectures, he came to visit an elder at Kaiyuan Temple. The elder asked him, 'I have heard that you, Master, understand how to lecture on the scriptures.'"
"Is this so? asked Xuedou. The Master replied, "I dare not. Xuedou said, "With what do you lecture? The Master said, "I lecture with the mind.

Xuedou said, "The mind is like a skilled artisan, and the intellect is like the one who accompanies the performance; how could they possibly lecture? The Master said, "Could it be that empty space lectures?
Xuedou said, "Indeed, it is empty space that lectures. The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Xuedou called out to the Master, and the Master turned back.
The Head asked, "What is it? The Master then attained awakening. "Brothers, see how swift and incisive he was!
A monk said, "According to what the Master has said, this is the Dharmakāya preaching the Dharma. The Master said, "If you understand it in such a way, you have already become a Nirmāṇakāya.
The monk said, "Since it is a Nirmāṇakāya, does it not have one who preaches the Dharma? The Master said, "I do not know. The monk said, "I do not understand."

The Master said, "It is better not to understand; thus one avoids having to explain it to others. A questioner asked, "The scriptures state that where the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas gather, they see the Dharma-body Buddha;
at the stages of the Bodhisattvas, they see the Reward-body Buddha; and those of the Two Vehicles see only the Transformation-body Buddha.
Is this not the principle? The Master said, "My eyes have never looked at the scriptures, and furthermore, I have no ears."
"I have heard it before; you should examine it for yourself. If you maintain this mindfulness, then later on there will be no way to deal with it.

It is like playing with a pearl while describing how its light pervades everywhere: as long as the golden tray is present, one can obtain it; but if the golden tray is suddenly snatched away, where is the pearl to be played with?
Where can one seek whether its light pervades or does not pervade? The student bowed. "Venerable Master," he said.
Xiaoyun said, "Great difficulty! Great difficulty! The ancients would have cursed you, calling you a hunter or a fisherman, or a man who carries away dung.
Go in peace. Take care."

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Ultimate truth is of one suchness; it functions secretly and operates subtly, with no one perceiving it. This is called 'permeating wisdom' (*sēnzhi*), and is also termed 'non-permeation.
It is inconceivable, equal to space, and immovable. Its nature is not the flow of birth and death; this Way is the Great Way of unimpeded *nirvāṇa*.
Its wondrous function is self-sufficient, and from the very beginning, it attains mastery in all spheres of practice. Therefore..."

It is said that within the sphere of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one acts without acting; it is also called the Samādhi of Universal Pervasion (*sarvatraga-samādhi*) and the Manifestation of the Physical Body (*rūpakāya*).
This is simply because no one knows its place of operation, as it leaves no trace; it does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. The True Principle is spontaneously realized.

Wondrous function is self-sufficient; the Great Way is formless; the True Principle has no counterpart. Therefore, it does not belong to seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing, and it is devoid of thoughts of coarseness or subtlety.
As it is said: "Not hearing that there is nothing to hear is the Great Nirvana. Yet this thing called the Way is not merely "not hearing that there is nothing to hear.

A monk asked: "The Great Way does not belong to seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing. I wonder, how may one realize it? The Master said: [The text here implies the Master’s response follows, though the provided excerpt ends at the question.]
It is said: "One must realize that the hidden resonance is self-communicating. It is also said: "The cause of enlightenment does not arise from seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing.
Seeing and knowing belong to conditions; they exist only in relation to objects. This spiritual and wondrous inconceivability is not something subject to opposition.

Therefore, it is said that its wondrous function is self-communicating and does not rely upon external things. Thus it is said: 'This penetration is not a conditioned penetration; affairs must depend upon things.'"

Only then does one begin to see. Therefore it is said: "It is neither light nor darkness; the Dharma is free from existence and free from non-existence. Its subtle principle penetrates the profound depths, yet no one perceives or knows it.
It is also called "mysteriously meeting the True Principle," which is not a matter of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Thus it is said: "When the mind ceases, one reaches the source;
therefore, one is called a Tathāgata Buddha. Ultimately, such a person is independent and self-sovereign; it is also said that the original fruit does not arise from birth.

Regarding that which is produced by productive causes (*janakahetu*), Mañjuśrī said: "It is realized solely through the realization of the revealing cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*); it is not produced by a productive cause.

Since ancient times, the teaching has been nothing other than to lead people to realize the Way (*mārga*) and to seek nothing else. If one attempts to construct a principle through discursive thought, it all belongs to the realm of words and meanings.
The doctrines of the Three Vehicles and Five Natures are all termed "practices" (*pratipatti*), and one receives [retribution] everywhere [according to them].

If you employ it, you will attain it in its full perfection. However, if one discusses it in terms of the Way, it is not so; for if one is single-mindedly attached to it, one is constrained by consciousness.
This is also called "worldly wisdom. The Teaching says: "Those who study the Tripitaka with single-minded attachment act like hunters or fishermen;
for the sake of profit and sustenance, they destroy the Mahayana. It is also said that their greed has become their very nature. Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha did not realize the Way."
I practice for myself; I possess my own wondrous function. This is also called the "True Cause" (*zhengyin*). When one realizes the emptiness of the six *pāramitās*, objects cannot confine me.
Therefore, the Patriarch came from the West fearing that you people would become deluded regarding the stage of cause and effect;
thus he came to transmit the Dharma to save those lost in confusion. Once the nature of the flower is suddenly awakened to, the nature is the very seed-nature of the flower. This is also called...
The Flower of Bodhi. Thus, the Elder of Jiangxi said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
Although our ancestors spoke of "mind itself is Buddha," this was a statement made for a specific occasion; it was like the teaching of an empty fist or yellow leaves used to stop a child's crying.
Nowadays, many people call the mind "Buddha" and call wisdom "the Way," claiming that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all the Way. If...
Those who assemble in this manner are like Yajñadatta, who, in his delusion, mistook a reflection for his own head. Even if he were to recognize it, it would not be his original head.

Therefore, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) rebuked Kātyāyana, saying that to explain the Dharma of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) with a mind of arising and ceasing is entirely a matter of emotional views (*sāṃkleśika-dṛṣṭi*).
To say "the mind is itself the Buddha" is like saying that rabbits and horses have horns; to say "neither mind nor Buddha" is likewise so.
If oxen and sheep have no horns, and your mind is likewise so, of what use would a Buddha be? It is not that other things lack form and characteristics;

by what means, then, could this [mind] be the Way? Therefore, it is not permitted in the teachings. It is better to take the mind as one's teacher than to let the mind be one's teacher. The mind is like a stage performer, and the intellect (manas) is like the conductor of the performance.
Thus it is said that both the mental faculty and the intellect are not the Way. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing all belong to [the realm of delusion].
They exist through causes and conditions; they all exist by illuminating objects, yet they cannot illuminate constantly. Therefore, both mind and wisdom are not the Way.
Furthermore, the Great Way is neither light nor darkness, and the Dharma is free from existence and non-existence. It cannot be reached by repeated conceptualization.
It is like the time of the empty kalpa, when there was no name for Buddha and no name for sentient beings—at such a time it is precisely the Way, yet simply no one awakens to it or knows it.
To see another is to fall short of that other; to call it the "Nameless Great Way" already belongs to the realm of names and phrases.
Therefore, the True Principle is suchness alone, beyond all thought. As soon as there is thought, one is immediately constrained by the aggregates (*skandhas*).

Then there are the names of sentient beings and the names of Buddhas. Since the Buddha appeared in the world, he has been called the "Wise Man of the Three Realms. But consider him when he had not yet appeared in the world.

What would you call this? As it is said: "Wisdom cannot be grasped as either existence or non-existence," yet one gives rise to the mind of great compassion. The Buddha’s appearance in the world is solely to cause people to realize the Way.
Its essence is neither ordinary nor sacred; it is called returning to the source and reverting to the root, the embodiment and understanding of the Great Way.

Since you have today realized the Way in this manner, you will see that throughout immeasurable kalpas, the six realms and four modes of birth have all involved coming and going—these are merely temporary.
Regarding the place where [the Buddha] practiced at that time, the *Saṃyukta-āgama-sūtra* (or *Sūtra on the Original Practices of the Former Sages*) states: "There is nowhere I have not gone.

Although all sentient beings are within such a realm of practice, because they lack the cause of realization (*viniścaya-hetu*), they give rise to greed and desire; this is called being "entangled" (*saṃvṛta*). They do not attain mastery. It is like a brief moment at a crossroads:
as the clouds move, the moon appears to travel; as the boat moves, the shore seems to shift. Through the deluded thoughts of sentient beings, there is no object that does not [appear thus].
Abiding [in this way], how much more so could the principle (li) undergo change? Now that you have reached such an understanding, you must instead practice within;

this is not like the previous stage of realizing the causal factor (hetu-pratyaya) to meet the fundamental fruit. By realizing that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are empty, and that the six pāramitās are empty, one thereby attains mastery.
If one does not practice within, how can one crush and eliminate the five kinds of greed and the two...?
Planting various desires, one does not abide as a Śrāvaka; rather, one follows along with the duration of kalpas.

Therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess the two adornments of merit and wisdom as their cause of realization. They realize that the essence of the six pāramitās is emptiness; this is what they enjoy.
Thus, by not maintaining cognitive views, one first attains sovereignty. If there were cognitive views, one would belong to a specific stage and would possess a limited mental capacity.

Separated by cause and effect, it is called "repaying causes and answering effects. Because the Buddha does not attain sovereignty, the Great Sage rebukes this as the "inner view" and the "outer view.
When the measure of one's emotional intellect is not exhausted, there are the two obstacles and the two delusions; thus, the river of views can sweep away even the fragrant elephant.
Ultimate Truth has no form—how can it be known through seeing? The Great Way has no form—its principle transcends thought and deliberation. Today...
