Only through such enjoyment does one attain freedom; going and staying are sovereign and unimpeded.

This is also called "the adornment of diligent skillful means," and it is also called the "subtle and pure *dharmakāya* endowed with the thirty-two marks. It simply does not permit the mind to harbor any sense of partiality or limitation. If...
There is no such mind. In all spheres of activity, even down to a snap of the fingers or the joining of palms, these are all the true cause.
All myriad virtues are identical; there is no beginning or end, and one attains mastery. For this reason, the celestial Māras and externalists cannot find me.
This is called the "non-abiding mind. It is also termed non-leaking wisdom, inconceivable, wondrous function, and sovereign mastery—Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are all [this].
This is the realm of the practitioner; it all belongs to the category of clarity. If one realizes that from the beginning there has been no such thing as an object, then water cannot wash water.
Why? Because from the beginning there has been no object. Thus the Sūtra says: "In the treasury of my King, there is no such sword. It also says:
"The Goddess of Merit and the Woman of Darkness—a wise host accepts neither. Therefore it is said:
It is neither light nor darkness; therefore, it is said that the ocean of nature is not the ocean of awakening. When the ocean of awakening engages with conditions, it must confront objects.
Its wondrous functioning is such that no one perceives it; this is called the "extremely subtle permeation of the colors and dusts of gold and water.
That which the Bodhisattvas rely upon is called their "receptacle of utility. If water does not wash water, then its substance is neither light nor darkness; it is also called "non-existence."
It is the wisdom of penetration; it is also called unimpeded wisdom. If it is thus, one cannot be constrained by anything anywhere.

Yet now, you seek to establish further meanings and phrases, searching for victory and defeat in intellectual understanding and verbal expression, saying that sentient beings are inferior, that there are Buddhas and sages, that one must save sentient beings, and that one seeks the Bodhi of a Buddha—all of these belong to greed and desire. They are also called precept-breaking bhikṣus who are far from the Way.
A vast distance separates them. The Great Way is without ignorance; it has never known darkness. It is not encompassed by the three realms, nor does it belong to the past, future, or present.
The Tathāgatagarbha is truly not concealed; when has the lion ever been in a cave? The five aggregates are fundamentally empty; when has there ever been a location for them?
Furthermore, the Dharma-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories; the Dharma is immovable and does not rely upon the six sense objects.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The Buddha-nature is permanent; the mind is impermanent. Thus, wisdom is not the Way, and the mind is not the Buddha.
For now, do not call the mind "Buddha," and do not try to understand this through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. This thing is fundamentally non-existent from the beginning.
There are many names; their wondrous functions naturally interpenetrate, and no numerical measure can encompass them—this is the Great Liberation.
Therefore it is said: "The human mind has no place of abiding; its traces cannot be sought. Thus it is called non-outflowing wisdom and inconceivable wisdom.
Consider how Cui Shijun of Chizhou asked the Great Master Wuzu:
"Among your assembly of five hundred disciples, why was it that only the Great Master Neng alone received the robe as a transmission of the faith? Why did the others not receive it?

Wuzu replied, "The four hundred and ninety-nine people all understood the Buddha-dharma, but only the Great Master Neng is a person of transcendent capacity; therefore, the robe was transmitted to him."
Xin said, "Cui says that one thus knows the Way is neither for the foolish nor the wise; he has therefore informed the great assembly that you must all remember this.
The Master said, "Remembering belongs to the sixth consciousness; it is not fit for the state of non-action. Be careful."
He addressed the assembly, saying: "In the time of the empty kalpa, there were no names whatsoever. Only when the Buddha appeared in the world did names come to exist;
thus, one grasps at appearances. The Master further said: "It is precisely because people nowadays cling to words and letters that they limit the Great Way with unequal measures.
In reality, there are no ordinary beings or sages at all. If there were names, they would all belong to the realm of limitation. Therefore, [it is said of] Jiangxi..."
The old master said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. This was intended to guide future generations in their practice.

Nowadays, everyone attempts to grasp the Great Way through the intellect. If one studies the Way in such a manner, even until the appearance of Maitreya Buddha, one will still have to resolve to cultivate the mind before success can be achieved;
what freedom or autonomy could there be? It is just like under the Fifth Patriarch’s assembly.
Of the four hundred and ninety-nine people, all had fully realized the Buddha-dharma; there was only the single person, Layman Lu, who did not realize the Buddha-dharma.
He only realized the Way and nothing else. If one recognizes the mind as the Buddha, the mind is the master that gathers the three realms.
If you take wisdom to be the Way, that wisdom is full of artifice and deception.

When discussing the time of a Buddha’s appearance in the world, he is called a "wise man of the triple realm" who expounds all teachings, meanings, phrases, and principles; these are called temporary implements for use.

If you claim that the mind is the Buddha or recognize wisdom as the Way, both are merely localized attachments. Therefore it is said: "Without mind or intention, there is manifest activity for a time."
Wearing robes of filth and grease, he comes to preach for the sake of others that this is not a thing of ordinary or sagehood.
From morning until evening, it never acts as a cause for others, nor has it ever acted as an effect for others. If it were to act as a cause for others, it would lack sovereignty;
it would be constrained by cause and effect and could not attain freedom. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, no one could comprehend it. If he had not appeared in the world...

Regarding the discourse on the extremes, it is still admitted that there is a partial correspondence; however, this is merely understood through the hidden principle (*mínglǐ*) by oneself. Being without a teacher and so of itself, it is fundamentally without substance.
Consequently, seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are themselves the retributive and transformational [bodies]. Therefore, the thirty-two marks are of a distinct substance.
If one were to depart from that, one would be identical to the Tathāgata; yet, if both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas were entirely struck down, where could anything remain?
This is not to say that they are not permitted; it is simply that even Maitreya acts as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). He vigorously practices the six *pāramitās*, and he is able to go anywhere.
For what reason, then, is he not permitted [to do so]? He has never been obstructed by or attached to the categories of ordinary person or sage. Therefore, that...
Once you have understood this side, you must then practice on that side; only then will you attain a measure of freedom.
Nowadays, many students of the Way choose to leave the household life and refuse to enter it. They recognize what is good but do not recognize what is evil—how can they hope to succeed?

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva practices on non-ways, it is for the sake of penetrating the Buddha-way. As for those others, they are able to dwell with freedom whether they go or stay. It is just like this.
Why? If you know it, you are immediately constrained by that which is known. If it were not so, how could you not allow for it? This "it" has never changed or varied.
If it were not fixed, it would belong to the realm of cosmic creation (*dhātu*). How could that "it" ever have shifted at any time?
Therefore, the twelve divisions of the teachings are certainly not the self; rather, the self is within the twelve divisions of the teachings.
Zhongxing obtained it through practice. If the twelvefold teachings were the Self, they would immediately undergo transformation.

If one discusses the existence of outflows, this refers to the stage of the Two Vehicles; if one discusses the absence of outflows, this is the name for the Mahāyāna. Therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
If it is this very thing, it is not something that can be bound or confined; thus, it secretly penetrates the subtle principle, such that no one perceives or knows it. It is not...
"This is seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Question: "Can it be understood through the intellect? The Master said:
"If it were understood through the intellect, it would be something attained through deliberation. In their own teachings, they also say: 'I call various manifested bodies "measurable.
That which is inconceivable is not something that can be understood by the intellect. It is like having a reflection when there is water; if there is no water,"

What do you call a shadow? The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) receives its name by contrast with the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya). If there were no Reward-body or Transformation-body, where would one recognize the Dharma-body?

The Dharma-body is also called the ultimate pinnacle of the sutras and śāstras; yet it is only when one reaches the Dharma-body and truly enters the ground of principle that one is identical to the sutras and śāstras at any time.
The sutras and śāstras do not concern themselves with how one dispels [delusions]; they simply are as they are.
Furthermore, not arriving here is a great difficulty, a great difficulty.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Since the Buddha appeared in the world, he has done so solely because sentient beings do not understand the Way.

If one does not hear it through a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), it is called 'self-enlightenment without a teacher. If one hears it through a good spiritual friend, one might suddenly cite sutras and treatises to provide proof."

To be the master of one’s own actions requires no recourse to sutras or treatises; this is the most economical use of mind and effort. If one were to cite sutras and treatises, one would be using another’s eyes as one’s own and would lack freedom.
The Great Way is of one suchness; it is self-so from the beginning without a teacher. If one can remain as suchness without change, one has never been deluded.

The Reward Body and Transformation Body are not the True Buddha; do not mistake them for the Dharma Body. The karmic fruits and retributions of both ordinary beings and sages are all [merely conventional].
An image. If you grasp at it, it belongs to the realm of impermanence and arising-and-ceasing. Discussed in terms of the coarse and the subtle, not even a hair’s breadth is established.

When principle is exhausted and nature is fully realized, everything is entirely absent. It is like when the world had not yet formed: vast, empty, and open, with no name for Buddha and no name for sentient beings.
Only then is there a partial correspondence; having directly understood it there, one returns here.
Regarding practice: one does not realize the fruits of the ordinary or the sage. According to the fundamental principle, there is truly not even the slightest dharma to be attained;

how much less so the distinctions of the three vehicles and five natures? These are merely names and numbers based on causes and effects, all of which belong to the impermanent cycle of arising and ceasing.
They are all worldly, provisional designations established for the sake of discourse, having no connection to the primordial reality. The Way is not something that can be illuminated by such means.
Dark objects: do not recognize or cling to anything at all. The Great Way is darkly pervasive; wisdom cannot fathom it. Thus it is said:
"Meeting yet not knowing one another; conversing yet not knowing each other's names. Go well. No affairs. Be careful.
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Since the beginning of summer, I have been unwell; this is entirely due to my transgressions. Those who have died are already dead;
those who remain must now arrange their own affairs. You students today must directly realize that before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were no names at all.
The hidden intent was secretly pervasive, yet no one perceived it; such people were called 'men of the Way. When the Buddha appeared in the world, he provisionally taught the Three Vehicles."
Regarding the five natures: he is not one of those people categorized by the three vehicles or the five natures. He practices from that direction;
he is a free person who understands both present existence and original existence. It is not from hearing it from a Buddha that it serves as a condition for him.

Now, you must directly cut off the phrases of both extremes and penetrate beyond them. Only when you are no longer bound by ordinary beings or sages, and your mind is like a withered tree, will there be a slight measure of realization.

These correspondences and the meanings cited from the sutras are all merely distancing oneself from others and making one’s living within another’s house; ultimately, there is no share of true freedom.
It is just like a water jellyfish that takes a shrimp for its eyes—how could it ever attain freedom? The Buddha is the one who experiences the fruition of retribution.
Nowadays, the ultimate limit of practitioners is merely to recognize the Dharma-body, which is like the moon reflected in water or empty space.
Flowers. Brothers, images do not exist within them; you must simply realize this directly. Not heard from a Buddha, it is self-sovereign without a teacher.

The retributive and transformational bodies are not the true Buddha; the fundamental reality is one suchness, for there is no change or variation. The Dharma transcends the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; it functions through the absence of mind and intention.
If you understand it thus now, you are no longer a mere commoner; this thing does not...
This is neither ordinary nor sage; it is neither foolish nor wise. Yet we forcibly call it "foolish" or "wise," though fundamentally it is not a name.
One must not speak of it; if one speaks of it, then horns will grow upon its head. To call it "Suchness" (tathatā) is already a transformation.
Brothers, you must enter among the heterodox classes before you can succeed. It is a great difficulty! A great difficulty!
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Since the Buddha appeared in the world, he has taught nothing but the Way, for no other purpose.
From patriarch to patriarch it was transmitted down until the Elder of Jiangxi, who likewise taught people only to realize this very Way.

When the Buddha-dharma first reached this land five hundred years ago, Bodhidharma came from the West because he feared that you would become mired in the names and characteristics of the Three Vehicles and Five Natures."

I preach the Dharma to deliver you all from your deluded minds. Now, among the five hundred people under the Fifth Patriarch, there was only one person who did not understand the Buddha-dharma and could not read characters:
the practitioner Lu. That man only knew how to speak of the Way. Students today must likewise clarify that Way;
do not concern yourselves with other forms of wisdom. It is certainly not a thing. The Great Way is formless; the True Principle is—
It is so. Equal to space and unmoving, it is not the flow of birth and death; it is not encompassed by the three realms, nor does it belong to the past, future, or present.
Therefore, while light and darkness come and go, empty space remains unshaken; the myriad phenomena come and go of their own accord, yet light and darkness do not truly reflect it.

Nowadays, there are those who take this mirror-like cognitive awareness and intellectual understanding to be the Way; these are all led astray by external objects, following along with the cycle of birth and death.
Flowing along, when have you ever attained freedom? If one holds such a view, there is truly no possibility of attaining freedom.
Therefore, it is not difficult to see that wisdom is not the Way. One might ask: "What is this wisdom? What is this Way? If we speak of worldly merit and wisdom, they can only be called ornaments;
they are also called the "two adornments of merit and wisdom," and they are also called "requisites for enjoyment."
All of these are remedies. What would you call a Buddha appearing in the world? One could only call him a "wise person within the triple world.
Before he appeared in the world, what would you call him? If one speaks of non-infiltration, it is inherently complete from the beginning; its wondrous function naturally penetrates all.
No one perceives it; it moves in secret and functions in obscurity, its traces difficult to find.
Therefore, for immeasurable kalpas, Māra Pāpīyas and his retinue have sought the point where a Bodhisattva first gives rise to a single thought, yet they cannot find it.
Māra praises it, saying: "The Buddha-Dharma is most subtle and wondrous; I truly cannot fathom it. Now, I shall simply accord with the principle of Suchness and practice directly."
Practice. Why not ask how one practices? Simply realizing that the nature [of reality], which has remained unchanging throughout immeasurable kalpas, is itself practice;
employing wondrous functions without dwelling [upon them] is the conduct of a Bodhisattva. Realizing the emptiness of all dharmas, one possesses mastery over wondrous functions.
Through the samādhi of the form-body, one fervently practices the six pāramitās within emptiness, remaining unimpeded everywhere as one roams through the stages.

The prison is like a garden pavilion; it cannot be said that one lacks the capacity for action. Since immeasurable kalpas past, sentient beings have been deluded regarding their original nature and have failed to realize their own essence.

Like clouds or dust momentarily obscuring the sky, they become attached to various evil desires. It is like the moon appearing to move when the clouds rush by, or the shore appearing to shift as a boat travels.
For a brief moment on this forked path, they fail to attain autonomy and undergo manifold sufferings without even realizing it. Thus...
Up to this very day, it is gathered; the nature from of old is no different from that of today.
If one says "this very mind is Buddha," it is like saying rabbits and horses have horns. If one says "neither mind nor Buddha," it is like saying oxen and sheep have no horns.

Therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha is truly not hidden; the five aggregates are fundamentally empty. Since when has the lion ever been in its den? It is also called the water of nature, and it is also called...
The water of Dharma; the water of Dharma is like waves, and its essential nature is like moisture. Water does not wash water; the Buddha does not deliver the Buddha.

The Lady of Merit and the Woman of Darkness—no wise host accepts either; one simply says that the nature is non-existent.

You must directly realize this through experience and practice it according to reality. Do not say, "I am a Chan master," while letting mere intellectual understanding be settled upon the tip of your tongue.

If both feet are slightly off the ground, do not consider this to be inconsistent with the Way. Brothers, whether coarse or subtle, conceptualizations and discriminations—all such greedy pursuits belong to the realm of objects.
Whether discussing the Three Vehicles or the Five Natures, from a coarse or subtle perspective, they do not transcend the limits of emotional consciousness.
When even a hair’s breadth of thought stirs, one is possessed by a malevolent spirit. He would not permit seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing;
he appears like a dull-witted person with little spirit, for whom it is best to remain ignorant of all things. At that time, Puxian said, "I used my mind to hear.
Manjusri said, "If the initial mind cannot enter, how can you attain perfect penetration? With a single blow, [Puxian] was ground to dust—no more matters. Be careful. Adieu.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Way of Dīpaṃkara Buddha is finished. If one gives rise to all phenomena through the thoughts and reflections of the mind, they are all false and unreal.
Why is this? Since the mind itself does not exist, how can it give rise to all phenomena? It is like distinguishing forms and shadows within empty space;
it is like a person trying to capture sound and place it inside a casket; it is also like blowing on a net in an attempt to make it full of air."
Therefore, the veteran elders say: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. This is merely to guide you brothers in your practice.
According to the teachings, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi and attain the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas;
they naturally acquire all meditative concentrations, liberations, supernatural powers, and wondrous functions, manifesting their physical forms universally throughout all worlds.
He manifests his body, or displays the attainment of perfect enlightenment as a Bodhisattva, the turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma, and entry into Nirvana.

He causes immeasurable beings to enter a single pore; therein he expounds a single phrase for immeasurable eons, its meaning never exhausted, thereby teaching and transforming immeasurable billions of sentient beings.

The Venerable Nanquan, named Puyuan, was a native of Zhengzhou. His secular surname was Wang. He received his monastic training at Mount Dawei and attained the Dharma from Master Mazu I.
He lived to the age of eighty-seven and had fifty-eight years of ordination seniority. He passed away during the Dahan era of Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty.

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "All dharmas are vast and open; what fetters them, what binds them? It is you yourselves who within them give rise to notions of difficulty and ease."
The source of the mind is a single unity, extending continuously throughout the ten directions. Those of the highest capacity understand this naturally and clearly.
Have you not heard Nanquan say: "Such dull-wittedness is rare indeed in this world"? Everything is distinct and clear; neither existence nor non-existence is it.
It is simply that one lacks the resolve of a true man, which leads to such exhaustion as this. Do you wish now to attain ease? From antiquity until the present day, [it remains so].
Not a single ordinary person or sage has ever appeared before you, nor has a single word—whether good or evil—ever reached your domain.
Why is this? It is because when one does good, the good has no form; when one does evil, the evil has no characteristic.
Since there is no self, what is there to grasp as good or evil? What can be established as ordinary or holy?
Do you believe this? Will you take responsibility for it? Where is there any place to evade it? It is just like trying to escape one’s shadow in broad daylight;
can you ever escape it? If it is so now, it was so in the past; when past and present coincide, can you avoid it? This is the Buddha-dharma.
Profound and subtle! Those who have realized this should spur themselves on from within. Do not let minor conditions obstruct the Great Matter. Have you not seen the Way?
It would be better to establish the Dharma for a lifetime than to lose one's conditions all at once. O Benevolent One, do you wish to take the shortcut and meet with Zen?

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Fortunately, you are already pitiable enough; why do you toil so hard to seek out a mere fragment of sound and form, or the cleverness of words and phrases, before others?
Let me ask you: how do you go about seeking those two characters, 'sound' and 'form'?
Do you understand? I say that sound and form are like bubbles. Shall I explain this through for you, or shall I seek out sound and form for you? Try to deliberate on this."
Examine it carefully; do not treat it with ease. With firm resolve and diligent application, if you realize its source, you will find it is ultimately nothing other than yourself.

It is like a round mirror: when a man approaches, a man appears; when a woman approaches, a woman is revealed. This extends even to monks and laypeople, blue and yellow, mountains, rivers, and the myriad things.
According to their forms and appearances, a single mirror reflects their brilliance; it cannot be that there are many kinds of mirrors. It is simply able to reflect objects and reveal them.

O Benevolent One, do you recognize the mirror yet? If you do not recognize the mirror, you will be entirely obstructed by men and women, blue and yellow, mountains and rivers, and the like, which hinder your radiance.
What outlet will there be for your breath? If you recognize the mirror, then even as regards blue and yellow...
Men and women, the great earth, mountains, and rivers; those with perception and those without perception; four-footed and many-footed beings; those born from wombs, eggs, or moisture;
and the heavens and hells—all of these find their respective proportions and the duration of their kalpas within a single mirror, whether they be material forms or empty space.
"And you are able to realize this; it is not some other thing. Have you not heard the meaning of 'all dharmas are like illusions'?

The Earthworm. A monk asked, "Today I dug up an earthworm with my spade; both ends were moving. I do not know where its life-force resides.
The Master took up the spade, struck the left end of the worm once, struck the right end once, and struck the empty space in the middle once.
He then cast away the spade and returned. Later, the Master again [took up] the spade...
Dizi was next. He held up a hoe and looked back at Shenguang, saying, "The matter is not non-existent;

yet as soon as you conceive of it in your mind, you err. Shenguang then asked, "What is this matter? The Master stepped on him, knocking him down across his chest. From that moment, Shenguang attained realization.

It was a fine sight for passersby. Two monks from under the guidance of Linji heard of this and traveled a great distance to seek him out.

Upon arriving, they indeed saw the notice. They entered the gate and reached up with their hands to lift the curtain; as they were about to rise but had not yet risen, the Master shouted, "Watch your step!

Heh! Beneath Mount Zihu there was a potter’s family who, having no son, burned incense every day and made a vow to seek a male child.
The Master went to their house to beg for bamboo; first he asked, “Is it you, husband and wife, who every day...”
One morning, he arose and made a vow, intending to accomplish something. He said, "Because my household has no son, I pray for a male child.
The Master said, "I shall ask you for a certain thing; can it be granted? He replied, "What thing does the Monk require?
Simply give me your command. The Master said, "I do not want anything else. I wish to ask for a load of bamboo, which I will give to you in exchange for a son."
The family rejoiced and said, "This is but a small matter; feel free to chop as much as you wish. The Master chopped large bamboos, nearly a thousand stalks.
Master Tao said, "Venerable Monk, you asked for only one load; why have you chopped so much? The Master replied, "Even this single load is not yet sufficient.
He then took several of the longest large bamboos, split them, and joined them together to form a single bundle. He then carried it away.
Upon returning home, his family experienced a dream that night and subsequently gave birth to a son. For this reason, he was named Shenli Zihu (Divine Power Son Lake).

The terrain was rugged and steep; they ate wood and wore grass. Their monastic decorum remained unchanged.

When the Master first followed his own teacher on a pilgrimage and arrived at Nanquan, while his teacher first performed the ritual greetings, the Master only then began his greetings. At that time, Nanquan was lying down inside the abbot’s quarters.
Seeing the Master coming to visit, Nanquan asked, “Where have you recently come from? The Master replied, “From the Ruixiang (Auspicious Image) Hall.
Nanquan asked, “Did you see the auspicious image? The Master said, “I did not see the auspicious image; I saw the Reclining Tathāgata.
Nanquan then rose and asked, “Are you a novice with a master, or a novice without a master? The Master replied, “A novice with a master. Nanquan said:
"Who is your master? The Master said, "It is still cold in the first month of spring. I humbly hope that the Venerable Abbot’s health and daily life are in every way well.
Fayan then called to the *vina* (chant leader), saying, "This novice should be assigned elsewhere.

After the Master had received his precepts, he heard that his ordination teacher was residing at Huguo Monastery in Xizhu, Caozhou. He returned to the monastery to visit him. Upon his arrival, the Master [his ordination teacher] ordered—
Master Hao said, "The son of your family has returned from his travels abroad;
his relatives and kin are filled with unremitting joy and are waiting for tomorrow to go and see him. Upon hearing this, the Master remarked, "The net of worldly attachment knows no end."
Having already taken his leave to enter the monastic life, he expressed no wish to see him again. That very night, he packed his belongings and set out.
Thereafter, carrying his own water jar and staff, he traveled extensively through all directions. He would often say to himself: "If a seven-year-old child surpasses me, I shall question him;
if a hundred-year-old elder falls short of me, I shall instruct him. When he reached the age of eighty, he finally settled at Zhao.
At the Guanyin Monastery east of the prefectural city, ten *li* from the Stone Bridge, the current abbot has been withered by austerity.
Resolving to emulate the ancients, he has no front or rear galleries in the Sangha Hall and prepares his own meals on the spot. When one leg of his rope bed broke, he used it to burn firewood.
He bound them with ropes. Whenever there were others who attempted to establish new [rules], the Master did not permit it.

During his forty years as abbot, he never once carried a single letter to inform his patrons (*dānapati*). Once, a monk from the south came and asked Xuefeng: "Master, why is it that you have never sent a letter to your patrons?"

"What is it like when the cold spring water flows through the ancient ravine? Xuefeng said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see its bottom. The student asked, "What about those who drink from it?
Xuefeng said, "It does not enter through the mouth. When the Master heard this, he remarked, "If it does not enter through the mouth, then it enters through the nostrils!"

The monk then asked the Master, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? The Master said, "Bitter. The student asked, "And what of those who drink from it? The Master said, "Dead.
When Xuefeng heard these words of the Master, he praised him, saying, "An ancient Buddha! An ancient Buddha! Thereafter, because of this, Xuefeng no longer engaged in verbal discourse.
Later, when the Prince of Yan from north of the River led his army to take the town of Zhenfu, they reached the border.
Above, a diviner of atmospheric phenomena reported: "There is a sage residing in Zhaozhou; if you go to war, you will certainly not be victorious.
Consequently, the two kings of Yan and Zhao laid on a banquet and both ceased their hostilities. They then inquired: "Who is the eminent master of Zhao’s 'Golden Land'? Someone replied:
"There is a Great Master who lectures on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, whose integrity and conduct are solitary and remote. If there is a great drought, they all command him—"
They went to Mount Tai to offer prayers. Before the Great Master had yet returned, a sweet rain poured down like a torrent. Thereupon, he said, "I fear it has not been entirely auspicious.
Someone remarked, "One hundred and twenty li from here lies the Guanyin Monastery of Zhaozhou, where there is a Chan Master of venerable age whose insight into the Way is clear and lucid.
Everyone said, "Could this be the omen? The two princes halted their carriage to visit him. Having arrived—
Inside the hall, the Master sat upright and did not rise. King Yan asked, "Which is more venerable: the human king or the Dharma King?
The Master replied, "If he is among human kings, he is the most venerable among human kings; if he is among Dharma Kings, he is the most venerable among Dharma Kings.
King Yan acknowledged this with a single word of assent. After a long silence, the Master asked, "Which one here is the Great King of the Prefecture? Zhao Wang responded.

[The disciple] replied, "Yes. [This is because] Zhaozhou belongs to the Prefectural Government, so I have sent this to express my respect. The Master said, "I, an old monk, have lived here for too long; I am not worthy of receiving you in person.

After a short while, the attendants requested the Master to preach the Dharma for the Great King. The Master said, "The Great King has many attendants; how can I teach the old monk to preach the Dharma?
He then signaled for the attendants to withdraw. Beside the Master was a novice named Wenyuan.
He called out in a loud voice, "I inform Your Majesty: it is not these attendants. The King then asked, "What kind of attendants are they?
He replied, "Your Majesty’s honorific name is so numerous that the Master did not dare to preach the Dharma. King Yan then said:

The Emperor requested the Zen Master to set aside his taboo name and preach the Dharma. The Master said, "Thus we know that the members of Your Majesty’s retinue in past kalpas were all kinsmen who became enemies.
When our Buddha, the World-Honored One, uttered even a single name, their sins were extinguished and blessings arose.

Yet Your Majesty’s ancestors would immediately give rise to anger whenever anyone touched upon their names. The Master, out of compassionate tirelessness, preached for a long time until the two kings bowed in reverence.

He offered praise at the outset, honoring him with inexhaustible reverence. When it was time to depart the following day, the Yan King sent his vanguard commander to inquire why the Master had not risen.
At dawn, he entered the monastery and rebuked the Master for being arrogant toward a lord. Upon hearing this, the Master came out to receive him. The vanguard commander then asked:
"Yesterday, when you saw the two kings arrive, you did not rise; today, seeing me here, why do you rise?"
[The Master] received him. The Master said, "If the Prefectural Governor were like Your Majesty, I would not even rise to receive him.
When the Vanguard heard these words, he bowed repeatedly and departed. Shortly thereafter, King Zhao dispatched an envoy to invite the Master for offerings.

Upon arriving at the city gate, the entire city’s ceremonial procession welcomed him into the palace. As soon as the Master stepped down from his precious palanquin, the King prostrated himself and requested the Master to enter.

The Master ascended the hall and sat in the position of formal authority. After a long silence, he struck his forehead with his hand and asked, "Who is that official standing at the foot of the steps?

His attendants replied, "These are the venerable elders of the various monasteries, as well as Great Masters and Virtuous Ones. The Master said, "Each of them is a spiritual leader in their own region;
had they been standing at the foot of the steps, I, this old monk, would have risen as well. Thereupon, the King ordered them to ascend the hall. That day, a vegetarian feast was served.
As the banquet was about to conclude, the monastic officials were arranged from the highest to the lowest. One person at a time would pose a question; one person would ask about the Buddha-dharma.

When the Master saw this, he asked, "What are you doing? The official replied, "I am asking about the Buddha-dharma. The Master said, "Right here, I have already sat upon the old monk. Over there, what dharma could you possibly ask about?
Two Honored Ones do not manifest together" (this is a phrase used to express such a meaning). The King then ordered him to stop.

At that time, the Queen and the King were both standing in attendance at their side. The Queen said, "I request that the Zen Master perform the rite of stroking the crown and bestowing a prophecy for the Great King.
The Master stroked the Great King’s crown with his hand and said, "May the Great King live as long as this old monk.
At that time, they welcomed the Master and temporarily stationed him in a nearby monastery while selecting a site to construct a Zen palace for him. The Master—
Upon hearing this, he sent a man to say to the King: "If you so much as touch a single blade of grass, I, the old monk, shall return to Zhaozhou.
At that time, General Dou was willing to donate a fruit orchard valued at fifteen thousand strings of cash;
it was named Zhenji Chan Monastery and was also called the Dou Family Garden. After the Master entered the monastery, the assembly of disciples gathered like clouds. At that moment, Prince Zhao...

He paid his respects. When the memorial from King Yan of Youzhou arrived, the King ordered that ceremonial robes be sent to the governor’s office and that full imperial protocol be observed for the reception.

The Master resolutely declined and would not accept them. His attendants carried a box to the Master’s presence and said, "The Great King has provided these for the sake of the Dharma of the Chan Master."
The king earnestly requested that the Master wear this robe. The Master said, "For the sake of the Buddha-Dharma, I, an old monk, do not wear this robe.
The attendants said, "But please consider the face of the Great King. The Master replied, "How does that concern a secular official?
Thereupon, he personally took the robe and hung it upon his body, accepting the repeated bows and congratulations with nothing but a simple acknowledgment. The Master resided at Zhaozhou.
In his second year, as he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples: "After I have departed this world, burn my body completely;
do not attempt to collect or purify relics (*śarīra*). Masters and disciples differ from the common worldly ways. Furthermore, the body is an illusion; how could relics possibly arise?"
"This is not permissible," [the Master] said. "Let my junior disciple deliver a fly-whisk to King Zhao and convey these words:
'This is something this old monk has used throughout his life and will never exhaust. On the tenth day of the eleventh month in the year of Wuzi, the Master sat upright and passed away.
At that time, at the Sin Garden, the lamentations of the clergy and the laity, numbering over ten thousand people on foot and horseback, shook the very air.
At that time, the rites for the conclusion of his life were performed in full. His tears of lamentation were no different from those shed when the golden coffin concealed its splendor at Kuśinagara.
Everyone raised lofty pagodas and erected magnificent steles in his honor; he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhenji Guangzu, and his tomb was named the Pagoda of Master Guangzu.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the eleventh year of the Baoda era of the Later Tang dynasty, a student inquired [of the master]:
Chan Master Huitong of the Eastern Cloister at the Eastern Capital [Luoyang] was recording the origins of Zhaozhou’s former practice of transformation.
He paid his respects and withdrew, whereupon [the compiler] took up the brush to record it.
The Master asked Nanquan, "What is the Way? Nanquan said, "The ordinary mind is the Way. The Master asked, "Can one still pursue it?"

Xiang said, "No. Quan said, "To intend [to know] is already to deviate. The Master said, "If you do not intend, how can you know this is the Way? Quan said, "The Way does not belong to knowing or not knowing.
Knowing is deluded cognition; not knowing is indeterminate consciousness (*avyākṛta*).

If one truly penetrates the Way that is beyond doubt, it is like the great void—vast, open, and expansive. How could one forcibly impose right and wrong upon it? At these words, the Master suddenly attained profound awakening.
The essence is this: the mind is like the bright moon.
Nanquan was ascending the hall when the Master asked, "Is it appropriate for the light, or is it appropriate for the dark? Nanquan then returned to his quarters.
The Master then descended from the hall and said, "This old monk has been rendered speechless by my single question. The Head Seat said, "Do not—"
The Master said, "The Venerable Dao was speechless. From this it is clear that the Senior Monk did not understand.
He then struck him and added, "This blow should have been taken by the old man at the head of the hall. The Master asked Nanquan, "Where does a person who 'knows' go? Nanquan replied:
“I am going to become a water buffalo at the house of a lay patron (dānapati) before the mountains. The Master said, “I thank the Master for this instruction.
Nanquan said, “Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window. While the Master was serving as the head cook (*lútóu*) at Nanquan, the community was invited to select vegetables.
The Master was inside the hall when he cried out, “Fire! Fire! The entire assembly rushed to the front of the Sangha Hall. Then the Master—
He bolted the door of the Sangha Hall; the assembly had no response. Nanquan then threw the key through the window into the hall.
The Master then opened the door. While the Master was drawing water on the well-pavilion at Nanquan, he saw Nanquan passing by.
He immediately embraced a pillar and hung his feet over it, saying, "Save me! Save me! Nanquan climbed up the ladder and said, "One, two, three, four, five."
After a short while, the Master went back to pay his respects and said, "Just now, I thanked the Abbot for saving me.
At Nanquan, the monks of the East and West Halls were disputing over a cat. Nanquan came into the hall, picked up the cat, and said, "If you can say something [to save it], I will not kill it;
if you cannot, I shall kill it. When the assembly offered their responses, none accorded with Nanquan’s intent. He then killed the cat on the spot.
The child was finished. When evening came, as the Master returned from outside and exchanged greetings, Nanquan recounted the previous story and asked, "How would you have saved the cat?
The Master then took a shoe, placed it on his head, and went out.
Jianquan said, "If you had been there, you could have saved the cat. The Master asked Nanquan, "I do not ask about the extraordinary;
what is the ordinary? Nanquan pressed both hands against the ground. The Master then kicked him over and returned to the Nirvana Hall, crying out, "Regret! Regret!"
Nanquan heard of this and sent someone to ask him, "What do you regret? The Master said, "I regret not having given two more kicks.
Later, as Nanquan was passing by the bathhouse, he saw the bath attendant lighting the fire. He asked, "What are you doing? The attendant replied, "Lighting the fire for the bath.
Nanquan said, "Keep this in mind; I will call for the Water Ox to bathe. The attendant responded with an assent. That evening, the bath attendant entered the hall.
Zhaozhou asked, "What are you doing? [Yu] said, "I am asking the water buffalo to go bathe. Zhaozhou said, "Have you brought a rope with you? The bathmaster had no reply.
Later, when the Master came to pay his respects to Zhaozhou, Zhaozhou recounted the incident to him. The Master said, "I have something to say about this."
Nanquan said, "Have you brought the rope with you? The Master stepped forward and suddenly pulled him by the nose. Nanquan said, "It is so, it is so;
yet you are too crude. The Master asked Nanquan, "Beyond the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, please, Master, speak."
Quan returned to the abbot’s quarters. The Master said, "This old monk usually talks incessantly, yet when questioned, he cannot utter a single word.
The attendant said, "It would not be right to say the Master has no words. The Master then gave him a slap.
Nanquan then closed the door to his quarters and surrounded it with ashes. He asked a monk, "If you can speak, I shall open the door.
Many people offered responses, but none accorded with Nanquan’s intent. The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! Nanquan then opened the door.
The Master asked Nanquan, "It is said that 'the mind is not Buddha' and 'wisdom is not the Way. Is there still a fault here? Nanquan—
[The monk] said, "There is. The Master said, "Where does the fault lie? Please tell me. Quan then cited [the previous exchange], and the Master immediately left.
Later, the Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "This matter is such that even men of immeasurable capacity cannot get out of here.

[The monk] asked about the meaning. The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The Master spoke again:
"When I was ninety years ago, I saw more than eighty spiritual friends under the Great Master Mazu; every one of them was a true master.
They were not like the spiritual friends of today, who produce branch upon branch upon branch. For the most part, they are far removed from the sages; each generation is inferior to the last."
[Zhaozhou] said, “It is simply this. For instance, Nanquan usually said, ‘One must walk among the heterodox. How do you understand this?

Nowadays, those who are like mere fledglings talk of entanglements at the crossroads, seeking food and gain, looking for prostrations, and gathering three or five hundred followers, saying, ‘I am a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); you are students. A monk asked, ‘What is purity?’”
“Jing’s Monastery. The Master said, “A girl with two horns. “How is it to be among those in the monastery?
The Master said, “The girl with two horns is pregnant. Question: “I have heard that you, Reverend, personally met Nanquan;
is this true? The Master said, “In Zhenzhou they grow large radishes. Question: “Where is the Reverend’s native place? The Master pointed with his finger and said, “To the west, even further.”
Facing west. He asked: "Phenomena have no separate phenomena; what is a phenomenon? The Master said: "External emptiness, internal emptiness, and external-and-internal emptiness."
Question: What is the Buddha’s true Dharma-body? The Master said: "What more do you find lacking? Question:

What is the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground? The Master said: "A model for all time. Question: What is the host within the guest? The Master said: "I, this mountain monk, do not ask after my wife. Question: What is the guest within the host?
The Master said: "This old monk has no father-in-law. Question: What is... [the text ends here] The Master said: "... (The response is omitted in the source).
"All dharmas are eternally abiding. The Master said, "I do not deny the Patriarchs. The monk asked again, and the Master said, "Today I will not answer questions."

The Master ascended the hall and said: "Brothers, do not stand for long. If there is something to discuss, let us deliberate; if there is nothing, it is better to sit beneath your robes and bowls and exhaustively investigate the principle.
When I was traveling as a pilgrim, apart from the two times of receiving rice gruel and meals, these were the only places where I applied my mental effort;
outside of those, I had no other place to apply my mind. If you do not act in this way, your departure from the household life will remain far away. A monk asked: "Regarding the myriad things..."
"What thing within is the most solid? The Master said, "If you are cursing me, I will let you have your say; if you are spitting at me, I will let you splash your water.
A monk asked, "What is it like when day and night do not cease? The Master said, "Among the monks, there are no such people as those who pay the double tax.
A monk asked, "What is the one phrase? The Master said, "If you cling to a single phrase, it will only wear you out. The Master spoke again: "If for a lifetime..."
"You have not left the forest; you have not spoken for ten or five years, yet no one calls you a mute.
In the future, even the Buddha will be unable to do anything with you. If you do not believe me, cut off this old monk's head and take it!"
The Master ascended the hall and said, "Brothers, you are currently within the third grievance. Therefore it is said: 'Only change the place where you formerly practiced;
do not change the person who was formerly there. Each of you left home for your own sake. Lately, you have been without concern, yet you still ask about Chan and the Way.
Thirty or twenty people gather their heads together to question me, as if they were actually lacking in Chan and the Way."
"It seems so. You call me a 'good spiritual friend' (kalyāṇamitra), but I am one who has undergone the same interrogation as you.

This old monk is not joking; I fear I might bring trouble upon those ancients, which is why I speak of the east and the west. Question: "How should one apply the mind throughout the twelve periods of the day?
The Master said: "You are driven by the twelve periods, whereas I make use of the twelve periods. Which period are you asking about? Question: [Unrecorded]
"What is the Master of Zhaozhou? The Master exclaimed, "You bucket-binder! The student responded, "Yes, sir. The Master said, "Bind your buckets properly.
A question was asked: "What is the student’s fundamental matter? The Master said, "When the tree shakes, the birds scatter; when the fish are startled, the water becomes turbid.
A question was asked: "What is a person with little spirit? The Master said, "I, an old monk, am not your equal."
The student said, "I do not occupy the position of victory. The Master said, "For what reason are you lacking in spirit? A question was asked: "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty;
it only dislikes discrimination. This is the nest of people of this age. The Master said, "Someone once asked me this, and for five years I could not explain it away.
An official asked, "When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard fall off? The Master [remained silent].

[The Master] said, "When raw things are transformed into cooked ones within an official’s residence, what kind of person is it? [The monk] said, "It is the one who employs others. The Master said, "But he is indeed a master of his craft.
A monk asked, "When the Seer Viśvāmitra took the hand of Sudhana and saw the Buddha-microdusts, what was that like?"
The Master then took the monk’s hand and said, “What have you seen? A nun asked, “What is the practice of a śramaṇa? The Master said, “Do not give birth to children.
The nun said, “Master, do not involve yourself in this. The Master said, “If I were to involve myself with you, what would be the use?
A monk asked, “Who is the Lord of Zhaozhou? The Master said, “The tenant farmer. [Another] asked.
"What is 'The King Requests the *Santapa*? The Master said, "Tell me, what does this old monk want?
Question: "What is the mystery within mysteries? The Master said, "Why speak of the mystery within mysteries? It is seven among the sevens, and eight among the eights. Question: [Untranslated]

[The student] asked, "What about the time of *saindhava*? The Master suddenly rose, bowed, and joined his palms. [The student] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "I dare not. I dare not.
[The student] asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "Imperative! Imperative! Seize! Seize! [The student] asked, "How far is it from Zhaozhou to the Prefectural Capital?
The Master said, "Three hundred [li]. The student said, "How far is it from the Prefectural Capital to Zhaozhou? The Master said, "Not separated."
Question: “What is the mystery within mysteries? The Master said: “How long has it been since the mystery began? The student said: “It has been a long time since the mystery began.
The Master said: “Fortunately you encountered this old monk; otherwise, I would have killed this fellow for good.
Question: “What is the student’s own self? The Master said: “Do you see the cypress tree in the courtyard?”
The Master ascended the hall and said: "If you are those who have long been in the assembly, you must be grounded in reality; you must transcend antiquity and the present.
If you are those newly entered into the community, you must also investigate the principle before you can succeed.

Do not merely chase after three hundred, five hundred, or a thousand followers on this side, nor the two assemblies on that side, so that the monasteries may praise you as a 'fine abbot. For when it comes to being questioned about the Buddha..."
The Dharma is just like trying to make rice by roasting sand; there is nothing that can be done, and there is nothing that can be swallowed.
Yet you speak of others as wrong and yourself as right, your face flushed with anger. This is truly because worldly people utter un-Dharmic speech.

If you truly wish to clarify the meaning, do not fail this old monk. Question: When one is amidst the dust of the world preaching the Dharma for all the sages, it all belongs to the wearing of robes. I wonder, however—?
"How do you instruct people, Master? The Master said, "Where have you seen me, old monk? The student said, "I ask the Master to speak.
The Master said, "A whole hall of monks does not understand this monk’s words. Another monk asked, "I ask the Master to speak.
The Master said, "You speak and I will listen. He asked, "When there are no traces of true transformation and neither teacher nor disciple, what then?"
The Master said, "Who taught you to come and ask? The student said, "No one other than myself. The Master then struck him.
[The student] asked, "How is this matter to be discerned? The Master said, "I am annoyed by you. The student said, "How can it be discerned?

The Master said, "I am annoyed that you do not discern it. The student said, "Can I rely upon it? The Master said, "Whether you can rely upon it or not, look for yourself. [The student] asked, "How is it?"
[The student] was a person who lacked understanding. The Master said, "What matter are you talking about? [The student] asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?

The Master descended from his meditation seat. [The student] said, "Is it not so right now? The Master said, "I have not yet spoken a word. [The student] asked, "The Buddha-dharma has existed for a long time. How should one apply the mind?
The Master said, "Have you seen how the Former Han and Later Han dynasties held the world in their grasp? At the end of their lives—"
"At that time, even a half-cash coin would not have been worth a fraction. A student asked, "Ordinary people consider precious jewels to be valuable;

what do śramaṇas consider to be valuable? The Master said, "Quickly shut your mouth! The student said, "Even if you shut your mouth, will it still be acceptable? The Master said, "If your mouth does not shut," [it will not be acceptable].
[The Master] said, "Who can discern this? A monk asked, "What is Zhaozhou’s one phrase? The Master said, "Not even half a phrase. The student said, "Is there not at least the Old Monk present?
The Master said, "I, the old monk, am not even one phrase. A monk asked, "How can one avoid being deluded by various sensory objects?
The Master extended a foot. The monk immediately took off his shoes. The Master withdrew his foot. The monk was speechless. There was a lay official [who asked a question].
Question: While the Buddha was in the world, all sentient beings took refuge in the Buddha. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, where do all sentient beings take refuge?
The Master said: "When there are no sentient beings. The student said: "I am asking about the present moment. The Master said: "What other Buddha would you seek? Question:
Is there anyone who does not repay the four debts of gratitude within the three realms of existence? The Master said: "There is. The student said: "For example,"
"What is it? The Master said, "You patricide! I reckon you were only lacking this one question. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Master?
The Master said, "There is no place for contrivance."
The Master ascended the hall and said: "Brothers, simply reform the past and cultivate the future. If you do not reform, there will be many places where you will be caught.
I have been here for over thirty years, and never has a single Zen master come to this place.

Even if one were to come, they would stay only one night and eat only one meal before hurrying past, seeking out a soft and warm place to go. A monk asked: "What if one suddenly encounters a Zen master?"
When the teacher arrived, [the Master] asked him, "What would you say to him? The teacher said, "A crossbow that weighs a thousand *jin* does not release its trigger for the sake of a field mouse.
The teacher said, "Brothers, if you have come from the south, I will unload it for you; if you have come from the north..."

He immediately loaded [the goods] onto it. Thus it is said: "If you approach a superior person to ask about the Way, you lose the Way; if you approach an inferior person to ask about the Way, you gain the Way.
Brothers, when a right person speaks a false dharma, the false dharma follows along with the right; when a wrong person speaks the true dharma, the true dharma follows along with the wrong.
Elsewhere, it is difficult to see but easy to recognize; here, it is easy to see but difficult to recognize. Question: [What does this mean?]
The nun asked, "Is there anyone who, having reached the bottom of good and evil delusions, is nonetheless uniquely liberated? The Master said, "Not uniquely liberated.
The nun asked, "Why are they not uniquely liberated? The Master said, "They are right in the midst of good and evil. The nun asked, "Apart from what you have just described, [is there liberation?]"

“Please, Preceptor, give me instruction. The Master scolded him, saying, “The iron pitcher has been baked to pieces. The nun brought the iron pitcher back filled with water and said, “Please, Preceptor, answer my question.
The Master laughed at her. She asked, “When the world turns into a black pit, I do not know where this [person] falls.
The Master said, “He does not occupy [a place]. The student asked, “Who is it that does not occupy? The Master said, “A commoner from the fields. [Another] asked.
"Without words and without intention, one may for the first time be said to have attained it. Since a phrase is already wordless, what do you call a phrase?
The Master said, "To be high without being precarious; to be full without being overflowing. The student said, "Right now, are you, Master, full or overflowing?
The Master said, "What can you do? You asked me. A question was asked: "What is the numinous one? The Master said, "To defecate a heap of dung upon pure ground. The student... [continued].
[The student] said, "I request the Master’s instruction. The Master said, "Do not trouble the old monk. [The student] asked, "The Dharma-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any categories;
may one still speak of it? The Master said, "How would you speak of it? The student said, "In that case, I would not speak of it.
The Master smiled. [The student] asked, "What is the Buddha? What are sentient beings? The Master said, "Sentient beings are themselves [the Buddha]."
" Buddha. A Buddha is precisely a sentient being. The student said, "I do not yet understand which of these two is the sentient being?
The Master said, "Ask! Ask! [The student] asked, "The Great Way has no root; how can one join in its song? The Master said, "You yourself are already joining in the song.
[The student] asked, "If it has no root, then what is it? The Master said, "Since it has no root, where could it bind you? [The student] asked, "As for a person who is practicing correctly..."

[The monk] asked: "Can ghosts and spirits not fathom it? The Master said: "They can fathom it. [The monk] asked: "Where does the fault lie? The Master said: "The fault lies in the seeking. [The monk] said:
"If that is so, then there is no practicing cultivation. The Master said: "There is practicing cultivation. [The monk] asked:

"When the solitary moon hangs in the sky, from where does its light arise? The Master said: "From where does the moon arise? [The monk] asked: "I have heard the Master say that the Way does not belong to..."
"Practice, but do not become defiled. "How is it to be undefiled? The Master said, "Examine both the internal and the external.
[The student] asked, "Is there still something to examine within yourself? The Master said, "Examine. [The student] asked, "What fault is there in yourself that you must examine? The Master said:
"What business do you have?

The Master ascended the hall and said: "This matter is like a bright pearl held in the palm of one's hand; if a barbarian comes, it appears as a barbarian; if a Han person comes, it appears as a Han person.
This old monk takes a blade of grass and uses it as a sixteen-foot golden body, and takes a sixteen-foot golden body and uses it as a blade of grass."
"Functioning. The Buddha is precisely affliction; affliction is precisely the Buddha. Question: "For whom does the Buddha become affliction?
The Master said: "For all people, he is affliction. Question: "How can one avoid this? The Master said: "Why would you need to avoid it?"
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "In this place, I receive people by means of the fundamental matter itself.
If I were to receive people according to their individual capacities, there are already the Three Vehicles and the Twelve Divisions of the Teachings to deal with them.
If they do not understand, whose fault is it? Hereafter, when you encounter those who compose treatises, tell them that I have not failed them; however—"
Someone asked: "I have been engaging people with matters of one's fundamental nature. Question: From the ancients until now, it has been said that 'the mind itself is Buddha.
Is it not permitted for students to deliberate upon this? The Master said: "Setting aside for a moment the idea that 'the mind itself is Buddha,' what is there to deliberate upon?"
Question: "Does an ancient mirror still reflect even if it has not been polished? The Master said: "The previous life is the cause; this present life is the fruit. Question: [Continues]...
"How is it before the three blades have fallen? The Master said, "A dense forest. "How is it after they have fallen?
The Master said, "A vast expanse. Question: "What is one who has transcended the three realms? The Master said, "Nothing can encompass them. Question:
"Before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch, a hundred birds brought flowers to offer him in worship. Why is it that after he saw him, the hundred birds no longer bring flowers?"

[The student] made an offering. The Master said, "Whether responding to the world or not responding to the world. [The student] asked, "When Baiyun is at ease, how is it? The Master said, "How can it compare to the spring breeze, idle everywhere?

[The student] asked, "What is the white ox on the open ground? The Master said, "Under the moon, there is no need for color. [The student] asked, "What does it eat? The Master said, "From ancient times to the present, no one has been able to chew it. [The student] said, "I ask the Master to answer the question. The Master said:
