Only then did the monk prostrate; Feng immediately kicked him down. It was seven years before the monk finally saw [the truth].
The Master said, "It was you who took seven years to see it. The Head (of the assembly) said, "Yes. The Master said, "Give him another seven years and only then will he attain it. The Master.
While at the assembly of Master Yun in Zhongzhe, one day during a tea break, he raised the following koan:
"Master Yun said, 'Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the Dharma; yet the Dharma is apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—how is this so? A monk standing nearby remarked:
"See that all these things currently being seen, heard, sensed, and known are dharmas; yet even these dharmas cannot be apprehended.
The Master clapped his hands once. Yun then raised his head. The Master said, "You still lack one move. Yun said, "When I reach this point, I do not understand.
The Master went to Gongxiang. Gongxiang asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "From Snowy Peak."
Xiangyun said, "I want an urgent statement; bring me one. The Master said, "The other day the head cook came. Why did you not ask him?
Xiangyun said, "Let us set aside the head cook for now. The Master said, "The arrow has already passed over Silla. This was when the Master was staying at Lingzhong.
The Master asked Wòlóng Huángshān: “Does one who has realized their own nature still see that there is a self?
Wòlóng said: “Only when one no longer sees a self does one truly realize the self. He asked again: “What rank of capacity is that which is learned upon the long meditation benches?
Wòlóng said: “The second capacity. The Master said: “What is the first capacity? Wòlóng said: “Tie your straw sandals tight. [The Master] was at Lǐng...
At midday, a monk asked, "What is the matter that lies beyond the Dharma-body?
The Master said, "It would not be difficult for me to tell you what lies beyond, but what do you call the Dharma-body? The monk said, "I ask the Master to examine it for me.
The Master said, "Setting aside the examination for a moment, how do you speak of the Dharma-body? The monk said, "Just so, just so. The Master said, "This is merely the continuous [lineage]."
"What you have learned on the meditation platform—I will ask you this: does the Dharma-body know how to eat? The monk was speechless.
Later, another monk recounted this to the Abbot of Liangjia Hermitage, who said, "Yunmen has truly entered the mud and the water.
Zifu said, "One grain missing is not permitted; one grain extra is also not permitted. When the Master was at Xuefeng, he was with Changqing...
In the West Hall, Xuefeng ascended the hall and said: "The entire great earth is gathered up and made as small as a grain of millet;
it is tossed before you. You lacquer buckets do not understand! Let us beat the drum and invite everyone to look!
Xiyuan asked the Master, "When Xuefeng spoke thus, was there a point where he could not show his head? The Master said, "There is. Xiyuan said, "What is this 'showing his head'?"
"An improper place. The Master said, "One must not always interpret this as the view of a wild fox spirit.
He also said, "The mess is no small matter. He also said, "The seven luminaries shine in the heavens. He also said, "In Jambudvīpa to the south, and Uttarakuru to the north.
One day, the Master and Changqing discussed Zhaozhou’s story of "no guest and no host. [Changqing asked: "When Xuefeng gave him that kick at the time, what was it?"
The Master said, "I am not like that. Qing said, "How about you? The Master said, "The Stone Bridge is to the north.
The Master and Changqing raised the story of Shigong receiving Sanping. The Master asked, "How would you explain this, so as to avoid having Shigong call him 'half a sage'?
Changqing said, "If one does not return the price, how can one distinguish the true from the false? The Master said, "Enter."
In the water, he saw a tall man. When the Master arrived at Dongyan, Dongyan asked, "What have you come to do?

The Master said, "I have come to draw near. Dongyan said, "Why are you wandering about so restlessly? The Master said, "For a moment I was not here. Dongyan said, "To recognize one's fault is sufficient. The Master said, "..."
"What are you doing, Master, wandering about so restlessly? The Master went to Shushan. Shushan asked, "Bring me a single phrase from where you have attained strength.
The Master said, "I ask the Master to question me in a loud voice. Shushan then questioned him in a loud voice. The Master said, "Did the Master eat porridge this morning?
Shushan said, "Why would one not eat porridge? The Master said, "Why are you shouting so wildly? And again.
Shushan addressed the assembly, saying: "Before the Xiantong era, this old monk understood the matter of the Dharma-body;
after the Xiantong era, I understood the matter above the Dharma-body. The Master asked:
"I have heard that before the Xiantong era, you, O Monk, understood the matter of the Dharma-body, and after the Xiantong era, you understood the matter above the Dharma-body."
“Is it so? Sanshan said, “It is. The Master asked, “What is the matter of the side of dharmatā? Sanshan said, “A withered stump. The Master said, “...”
“What is the matter that lies beyond the Dharma-body? Sanshan said, “It is not a withered stump. The Master said, “Do you permit a student to speak of principle?
Sanshan said, “I permit you to speak. The Master said, “Is it not the case that a withered stump clarifies matters pertaining to the side of the Dharma-realm?
Is it not the case that what is not a withered stump clarifies the matter that lies beyond the Dharma-body? Sanshan said, “Yes. The Master said, “Dharma-body...”
"Does it encompass all things? Mountan said, "How is it that it does not encompass them?
The Master pointed to a water pitcher and asked, "Does the Dharmakāya encompass this? Mountan said, "Disciple, do not seek it within the water pitcher. The Master then bowed.
When the Master arrived at Caoshan, Mountan addressed the assembly, saying, "Everywhere else they simply employ restrictive barriers; why not give him a turning word?"
The Master said, "Teach him so that he may go away without doubt. The Master then asked, "Why is it that one does not know what exists in the most profound and secret place?

Sanshan said, "Precisely because it is so profound and secret, one does not know what exists there. The Master said, "How should one approach such a person? Sanshan said, "One does not approach from within the profound and secret place.
The Master said, "If one does not approach from within the profound and secret place, will one still be able to draw near? Sanshan said, "Only then..."
He attained the opportunity for close attendance. The Master replied, "Yes, yes. The Master asked Caoshan, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa?
Caoshan said, "One who eats the crops belonging to the monastery. The Master said, "What about when one departs in this very manner?
Caoshan said, "Are you able to maintain it? The Master said, "I, your student, am able to maintain it. Caoshan said, "How do you maintain it? The Master said, "Wearing clothes and eating food."
"What difficulty is there? Shanshan said, "Why do you not say, 'I wear fur and carry horns'? The Master then prostrated himself.
Later, when Elder Yaotang raised the matter of a Bodhisattva holding a red banner in his hand, he asked the Master, "What do you make of this?
The Master said, "You are an ill-mannered fellow. Yaotang said, "In what way are you ill-mannered? The Master said, "Even a slave of yours, an outsider, could not do such a thing. The Master [said].
He arrived at Tiantong. Tiantong said, "Can you still determine this with certainty? The Master said, "What did the Abbot say?
Tiantong said, "If you do not understand, you are wrapped up in what is before your eyes. The Master said, "If you understand, you are wrapped up in what is before your eyes.
Later, seeing Xinzhou Ehu ascending the hall, he said: "Do not say that those who have not yet attained realization are constantly in a state of restless agitation; even if one has attained it—"
Even those who clearly know where they are going still remain in a state of restless agitation. The Master came down and raised this statement to ask the Head Seat:
"Just now the Master addressed the assembly, saying, 'Those who have not yet attained realization are in a state of restless agitation;
those who have realized it are also in a state of restless agitation. What is the meaning of this? The Head Seat said, "Restless agitation. The Master said, "Head Seat..."
"Sitting here for so long, with hair white and teeth yellow, you speak such words. The Head Seat said, "I wonder, Senior Monk, what would you say?
The Master said, "If you wish to speak, you may; if you see it, then you see it. If you do not see it, do not speak recklessly.
The Head Seat said, "As for what the Abbot said—that one is 'floating and bustling'—what does that mean? The Master said, "The head..."
"A cangue upon his head, and shackles upon his feet. Dazhu said, "If that is so, then there is no Buddha-dharma.

The Master said, "This is the realm of great beings such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. While the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, an official asked, "Do you have a phrase that can settle heaven and earth?
The Master said, "Suru suru siri svāhā. When the Master arrived at Jiangzhou, there was a Chen...
The Minister of State requested the Master to observe a retreat. Upon meeting, he asked: "I shall not ask about the Confucian classics;

you have your own masters for the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. What, then, is the matter of a monk’s traveling on pilgrimage? The Master said: "How many people have you questioned so far?
The Minister said: "I am questioning you, Venerable Sir, right now. The Master said: "Set that aside for a moment. What is the essential meaning of the teachings?"
The Book says: "Yellow scrolls and red-bound volumes. The Master said: "This is merely words and language.
What is the meaning of the Teaching? The Book says: "When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail; when the mind wishes to follow its objects, thoughts vanish. The Master said:
"'When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail'—this is in contrast to having speech. 'When the mind wishes to follow its objects, thoughts vanish'—this is in contrast to deluded thinking. What is it?"
This was the Master’s intention. The Minister remained silent. The Master said, “I have heard it said that you, Minister, study the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Is this true? The Minister replied, “It is. The Master said, “The sūtra states: ‘All livelihoods and productive enterprises are entirely non-contradictory with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Now tell me, how many people in the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought lose their positions? The Minister remained silent. The Master said, “Minister, for now...”
"Do not be so hasty. Regarding the ten sutras and five treatises, even if one were to abandon them and enter the monastic community for ten or twenty years, one would still be unable to master them;
how much less could you, Minister, ever hope to understand them? The Minister prostrated and said, "I, this humble person, am at fault.
When the Master arrived at Guizong, a monk asked, "The great assembly has gathered like clouds; what should they discuss? Guizong said, "In twos and threes. The monk... [proceeded with his inquiry].
[The Master] said, "I do not understand. Zong said, "In threes and twos. The Master then asked the monk, "What is the meaning of Guizong's intent?
The monk said, "The whole body comes thus. The Master said, "Have you ever been to Longya in Tanzhou? The monk said, "Yes."

[Zhaodu] had previously arrived there. The Master said, "A fellow who goes about gathering firewood. Later, because Qianfeng was ascending the hall and said, "The Dharma-body has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance;
you must penetrate each one thoroughly. Furthermore, you must know that there is 'illumination' and 'function' to be applied as the occasion demands.
The ultimate aperture remains above. Qianfeng then remained silent for a long while. The Master stepped forward and asked, "Why does the person within the hermitage not see [the aperture]?"
Regarding matters outside the hermitage, Feng laughed heartily. The Master said, "This is still where the student has doubts. Feng asked, "What kind of mental activity is yours?
The Master said, "I also wish for the Master to understand me. Feng said, "You must be thus before you can sit securely.
The Master responded, "Yes, yes. Gan Feng addressed the assembly, saying: "If you bring up one, you must not bring up two. Let go..."
"One step past it, you fall into the second. The Master said, "The assembly says: 'Yesterday someone came from Tiantai and went on to Jingshan.
Feng said, "The head cook must not be called for general labor tomorrow," and he then descended from his seat.
The Master asked Qianfeng, "Please, Master, answer my question. Feng said, "Have you even reached me yet? The Master said, "In that case, the student is..."
"Too late," [the Master said]. Feng said, "Is it so? Is it so? The Master said, "I thought the monkeys were white;
there are even black ones. The Master arrived at Guankui. At that time, a monk cited Guankui’s words: "The ten directions have no walls; the four sides have no gates.
Pure and naked, bright and clear—there is nothing to grasp. He asked the Master, "What about it? The Master said, "Just so."
“The Way is simply easy; it is the great difficulty that emerges. The monk said, “Does the Senior not approve of the Master speaking thus?
The Master said, “Did you just cite [the story] in that manner? The monk said, “Yes. The Master said, “When will you ever dream of Guǎngxī?
The monk said, “I have the case at hand. The Master said, “I ask you: where there are no walls on the ten directions and no boundaries on the four sides...”
No gate. Purely naked. Utterly bare. Nothing to grasp. Tell me, what were Mahābrahmā and Śakra discussing?
A monk said, "How could it concern them? The Master shouted, "You fellows who eat your rice in line!"
Minister Chen Shangshu asked the Chief Attendant of Yunju, “Is Yunju high or low compared to you, Disciple? The attendant was speechless.
Minister Chen asked the Master. The Master said, “Minister, do not let the conversation fall into error.
When the Master was at Lingzhong, he asked an old master, “How does one discern and clarify throughout all times? The old master said, “What do you call ‘all times’?”
The Master said, "Śākyamuni Buddha has already finished speaking; even Maitreya still does not know.

He also saw an old master ascend the hall and say, "If one is deliberating or attempting to awaken others through conceptualization, it is like a sharp sword held at the gate; beneath a single phrase, there must be both killing and giving life for it to be effective.
The Master stepped out from the assembly and said, "The Master has been in the hall for a long time; the assembly is returning to their quarters. The old master [remained silent].
The former master said, "What do you say? The Master replied, "The sun and moon flow on easily. While the Master was at Lingshan, he asked Vinaya Master Shun:
"When the ancients raised up their whisk and then lowered their whisk, what was the underlying meaning? Vinaya Master Shun said:

[The monk] brushed away [the previous view] and saw [the later one]. He brushed away [the later view] and saw [the former]. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. He also said, "This is an acceptance; this is a non-acceptance.
He also said, "One may know the propriety of the ritual. The Master heard Lopu interrogating a monk, saying, "Where have you recently departed from? The monk said:
Jingnan. Pufu said, "If a person goes in this manner, do you encounter him? The monk said, "I do not encounter him. Pufu said, "Why do you not encounter him?
The monk said, "If I were to encounter him, my head would shatter into pieces. Pufu said, "The Master’s three-inch tongue is very well-guarded."
Later, the Master encountered that monk in Jiangxi and asked him, "Do you still have those words? The monk said, "I do. The Master said, "Luopu would have retreated three thousand li!

When the Master was serving as the head seat (shouzuo) in the assembly of Great Master Zhisheng at Lingshu, a monk asked Zhisheng, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhisheng said, "This old monk has no words."
He then asked a monk, "If one were suddenly to ascend this stele, what words would you inscribe there? At that time, several monks offered responses, but none were in accord with the truth.
Xingshan said, "Go and invite the Head Seat to come. When the Master arrived, Xingshan raised the previous question and asked him.
The Master said, "It is not difficult. Xuedou said, "What words can be applied here? The Master said, "If someone asks, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
simply say, 'Master. Xuedou deeply approved.
I humbly submit this posthumous memorial to the Great Master.

I have heard that the finite physical body cannot avoid the lamentations of flourishing and decay; yet as for the formless true reality (*dharmatā*), who could speak of a time for its transition or change?

Since the flame of a wind-blown lamp or torch cannot be retained, and like the moon reflected in water or flowers in the sky, what purpose do they serve? Thus, I dare not evade the established rites and traditions.

This is my fault. I am about to present my words of casting off this mortal shell. Your servant bows in deep humility and reflects: My origins are humble and lowly; I was born from the common grasses.

From the time I was a mere child, I have ardently admired the Empty Gate (the Buddhist path). With pure sincerity, I vowed to eliminate all other attachments; with keen resolve, I sought only to explore the Inner Classics (the Buddhist scriptures).
On some occasions, I forgot to eat while awaiting instruction, or stood in the snow to seek knowledge; I endured the hardships of wind and frost for seventeen years.
Over the course of a year, traveling thousands of li across the north and south, I finally beheld the heart-monkey cease its leaping and the mind-horse halt its gallop.

My body took refuge in the clouds of Shao-shi, and my hair turned as white as the snows of Chu-shan. Thus, having encountered this auspicious era and repeatedly basked in the imperial grace, I have investigated the Way and discoursed on emptiness, vowing to repay the virtue of Heaven and Earth.
To enlighten the ignorant and resolve their obstructions, I shall travel as swiftly as a shooting star across the waters and clouds.
As one among these followers, I have been able to propagate the causes of benefit solely through the grace of Your Sacred Majesty.

Furthermore, having repeatedly received imperial edicts like those of the phoenix and stood before the Dragon Court on numerous occasions, I have successively been granted proclamations and bestowed with layered honors and gifts. Reflecting upon myself with deep emotion, how could I ever repay them even at the cost of my life?

I do not say that I, a feeble steed, have grown old and can no longer bear Your Majesty’s profound favor; rather, I am suddenly beset by exhaustion and illness, awaiting only the end of day and night.

The journey to the Milky Way is vast; casting my gaze afar, I but just catch sight of the North Star. The waves depart with such speed that a mere turn of the head finds me already swept away by the eastern current.
I humbly pray that the Phoenix Calendar may bring eternal spring, fanning the Imperial Wind through kalpas as vast as the rubbing of stones, and that the Dragon...

I pray that these [teachings] may endure forever, so that longevity may be as eternal as the city of *sarṣapa* (mustard seed). As for this servant, my remaining years are limited and time knows no respite; my humble person is about to depart.
I am unable to hasten to the Crimson Gate to offer my farewell, nor to bid adieu at the Vermilion Court. Your servant cannot bear the intensity of his longing for Heaven and his devotion to the Sage;
with the utmost urgency and trepidation, he respectfully submits this memorial for Your Majesty’s perusal.

Regarding these final instructions: when those of former virtue followed the transformation of the Dharma, there were none who did not leave behind final instructions. Even when the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he likewise left behind a teaching and exhortation.
Although I lack the virtue of the sages of old, I have had the misfortune of having raised the assembly in this region until it is nearly exhausted. Not...
"You may remain silent and show nothing. Since I first resided at Lingshu and moved to this mountain, more than thirty years have passed.

Throughout this time, I have constantly exhorted you morning and evening regarding the ancestral Way. Should there be any words or phrases of mine that have reached your ears or eyes, those with true insight will recognize them;
you must preserve and take responsibility for them. I am now advanced in years and my life-force is nearing its end; change occurs in an instant—take a moment’s rest."
Wait until [my life] is exhausted. Yet, how many times have we been submerged and drowned in birth and death? This is not unique to the present alone.

Since I have taken charge of this monastery, I have greatly troubled you all with the labor of assisting and supporting me; I know only shame for this myself. After my passing, place my remains within the Abbot’s Quarters (fangzhang).
Even if the Emperor should grant a plaque for a stupa, hang it only within the Abbot’s Quarters and do not construct anything else. You must not.

Weeping, wearing mourning garments, and extensively preparing for ancestral sacrifices—these are my earnest concerns. For those who have left the household life, their primary duty is transcendence; they must not act like worldly people.
As for matters such as the administration of the monastery, all shall continue according to established precedent. In receiving visitors, do not deviate from the constant rules.
All disciples should look up to and follow the instructions and admonitions of the elders. As for all the mountain gate’s estates, operations, and utensils...
All these shall be used exclusively for the expenses of this monastery; do not transfer them to other temples. The teachings contain clear injunctions:
even the goods belonging to the eastern and western corridors must not be used interchangeably. You should take this to heart.

If you can follow my admonitions, then the Buddha-Dharma may be made to circulate, the celestial deities will provide protection, you will not fail the four debts of gratitude, and you will be of benefit to the world. Should you violate this...
Such a person is not of my retinue. Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves! The great deadline is drawing near. As I depart, I briefly offer these final instructions:
Strive on! Strive on! Farewell! Do you understand? If you do not understand, the Buddha has clear teachings; practice in accordance with them.
Preface to the Extensive Record of Chan Master Yunmen Kuangzhen:

The ancestral lamp has been passed down in succession for several hundred years, producing masters who transcend their peers, surpassing both the present and the past, exhausting all subtlety and reaching the ultimate spirit.
Those by whom the Way flourished throughout the world were but a few; the Great Master Yunmen was preeminent among them.
In his seizing and releasing, his unfolding and rolling up, his vertical and horizontal transformations, he opened wide the rivers and seas so that fish and dragons found the means to swim and play;
he gripped the heavens and earth so firmly that ghosts and spirits had no path to flee. Even the grasses and trees should bow their heads, and the soil and stones would be moved to do the same.
*Faguang*. Regarding those [records] transmitted to the world—namely the *Duiji lu*, *Shilu*, *Chuidai*, *Kanbian*, and *Xinglu*—some discrepancies may have occurred over the long passage of time.
We have now consulted various sources to revise and correct them, newly carving the printing blocks so that they may circulate forever.

May this further serve as a forge for one’s own fundamental share (*benfen*), sounding like metal and vibrating like jade; may the towering world be shattered like tiles and melted away like ice. This must be so for all the various lineages.
To divide the schools is to unavoidably follow error with error. To discuss merits and record virtues is already to bury the former sages.
To follow patterns and imitate models merely serves to confuse later students. If one has the eye at the crown of the head, where could one ever meet Yunmen?
On the twenty-fifth day of the third month of the Bingchen year of the Xining era, written by the Acting Commissioner of the Two Zhe Circuits and Vice Commissioner for Transport.
Preface by the Official Su Xie.
The Record of the Conduct of the Great Master Kuangzhen of Guangtai Chan Monastery on Mount Yunmen.

The Master’s name was Wenyuan; his surname was Zhang. His family had been natives of Jiaxing in Suzhou for generations. He was actually the descendant of Wang Jiong, the Eastern Secretary of the Jin Dynasty.
Sengcan was a thirteenth-generation descendant of Senghan. From his youth, he possessed a numinous character and appeared in the world in response to the needs of sentient beings.

Thus, even while still a mere child, his aspirations were self-directed; he grew weary of worldly customs and subsequently entered the monastic order as a disciple of Vinaya Master Zhicheng at Kongwang Temple.
Because of his quick-witted nature and innate knowledge, and because his wisdom and eloquence were divinely bestowed, he required no second reading when reciting any of the scriptures.
Hui Cheng deeply admired his profound capacity and fine character. When [Daoxuan] grew up, he shaved his hair and received full ordination at the altar in Piling.

Later, he returned to serve as an attendant to Hui Cheng, where he attended lectures for several years and thoroughly investigated the principles of the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya). Once his mastery of the Vinaya was strict and pure, and his realization had emerged from a deep vessel, he took leave of Hui Cheng to visit Master Daotong of Muzhou.
Daotong was a descendant of Huangbo; recognizing that the Way would not find its match in the world, he [Daotong] drew him in.
Having already established himself, he lived in seclusion at an ancient monastery. Although he withdrew from the world to pursue lofty conduct, he was nonetheless admired by the world.

Whenever he received visitors, his wit and eloquence were so sharp and swift that there was no room for even a moment’s reflection. When the Master first went to visit him, he knocked on the door three times;

just as the door opened and the Master was about to enter, Huizong stopped him, saying, "This is the axle-hole of a chariot from the Qin dynasty. Upon hearing this, the Master was suddenly enlightened and his mind became clear.

He attained awakening. Thereafter, he consulted and studied under him for several years, penetrating deeply into the profound and subtle. [Baizhang] perceived that his spiritual vessel was vast and expansive, and that he was fit to bear the yoke of the Way.
He therefore said to him, "I am not your teacher. You should now go to consult and receive instruction from Chan Master Yicun of Xuefeng.

Do not remain here any longer. Following these instructions, the Master entered the mountain ranges to visit Xuefeng. He refined his practice there for many years until his realization accorded with [the Master's].
Master Cunen [bestowed] the seal of the lineage upon him in secret. Thereupon, he returned to report this to his master.

Having finished his formal attendance, the Master left the mountain range to visit various quarters, investigating and exhausting the diverse paths of practice; his sharp eloquence was so formidable that it became widely renowned throughout the world.

Later, he arrived at the Dharma-seat of Chan Master Zhisheng of Lingshu. Zhisheng had already anticipated his arrival from long ago; suddenly, he beat the drum to summon the assembly and invited him to come forward.
He received the Head Seat (shouzuo). At that time, the Master indeed arrived. Previously, Zhisheng had resided at Lingshu for several decades;

when the Hall was vacant and the Head Seat position remained unfilled, the assembly repeatedly requested that he be appointed to it, but Zhisheng did not consent. He once said, "The Head Seat has only just begun his travels."

When the Master arrived, he was finally appointed as the head of the assembly. Later, when it became known that Zhisheng was about to pass away and intended for the Master to succeed him on the seat, Zhisheng secretly wrote a letter and placed it within a secret casket, saying to his disciples: "After my passing, if the Emperor should visit this place, please present this to him.
Indeed, the Emperor’s carriage did arrive at the mountain. Knowing the Emperor would arrive, Zhisheng ascended the hall and sat in the full lotus position before passing away. When...

When the Emperor arrived, [the Master] had already passed away. The Emperor inquired about the Master’s final instructions. A disciple brought forth a casket and presented it to him. Upon opening the casket, he found a letter which read:

"The Eye and Treasury of Humans and Gods; the Head Seat of the Hall. The Emperor then issued an edict to the Regional Inspector, He Xifan, to perform the proper rites and command the Master’s successor to preside over the Dharma assembly.
Thereupon, the Emperor admired and praised him, repeatedly summoning him to the imperial court, where he was consulted on every occasion.
His responses were immediate and resonant, leaving the Emperor increasingly respectful and submissive. The Emperor subsequently bestowed upon him purple robes and a formal monastic name.

Later, he moved his residence to Mount Yunmen, where he restored the ruins of the former site and extensively renovated the buildings. The Master sat firmly upon the ancestral domain for twenty-five years;
his refined influence spread to the four quarters as he widely propagated the Dharma. Disciples from all over gathered, and those who ascended his gate and entered his chamber were beyond counting.

Now, the Great Master Shishō of Byakusen-san was the foremost among them. On the tenth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Kanna era (1129), the year of Jikyū, the Master passed away peacefully.
Having previously submitted a memorial to take leave of the Emperor and set forth his final instructions, he subsequently sat in the full lotus posture and departed this life.
Shortly thereafter, by imperial decree, the nameplate for his stupa was bestowed; furthermore, in accordance with the Master’s last will, his entire body was enshrined within the abbot’s quarters.
An imperial plaque for the stupa was bestowed; it was hung only in the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) and no separate structure was constructed.

The disciples followed these instructions and interred the Master in the abbot’s quarters to serve as his stupa. The Master had previously entrusted the Dharma to his disciple Shixing, intending for him to succeed to the site of enlightenment.

However, after collective deliberation, it was concluded that Shixing had already transmitted the Way to his own followers, so they changed their decision and appointed the assembly member Fagiu to succeed him.
To succeed to the Master’s seat. Alas! The guide of the age has passed away. For those who have planted their roots in the darkness and practice in obscurity, where shall they turn for guidance?

I, Yue, having had the good fortune to witness the remnants of the Master’s transformative influence and knowing the general outline of his deeds, dare not fail to record them for the sake of future generations.
On the twenty-fifth day of the first month of summer in the year of Jǐyǒu, at the Jíxián Palace, Lèi...
