How can one bear to be attached to the ways of the world? Sentimental ties belong entirely to the foolish. A guest beneath the gate of the Patriarch arrives here to distinguish the finest nuances.
Having visited Master Xinxin, who dwells in the rear chamber of Vimalakīrti, he stands in the snow seeking his heart; he awakens like Sudhana, as the wood grows old and the flowers wither into white.
Clouds swirl in disarray; as the waves settle in a frosty night, the bright moon lingers. To visit the lofty and distant Gate of Non-duality, one must again mount a weary horse and enter the dust.
Seeing off the White-Headed Seat-Holder returning to his hometown—do not ask about the many twists of the road.
Taking the four seas as one’s home is not yet the full view; the single sandal and pure fame belong to Bodhidharma.
The ninefold alliance of the feudal lords was but a laughable feat for Duke Huan of Qi.
In the same rhyme, I respond to Elder Yung of Ganlu:
By nature dwelling in the mountains, he never tires of the mountains; The sound of the water and the colors of the peaks differ from the human world.
If those who know the sound can understand my intent, Then even a perilous height we shall climb together.
Seeing off Zen Practitioner Ren:
The moon upon White Cloud Cliff, the shadow beneath the Tai-peace Pine—when the autumn wind rises in the deep night, it all becomes a single, unified realm.
Seeing off Zen Practitioner Wen for the sake of his parents.
In this life, one’s parents are those whom one should personally attend to; look closely at one’s original father and mother. In every movement and action, they provide full strength;
whenever they are brought to mind, one’s hair stands on end with awe.
I have sent this monk to Huan-huai, where he has gathered with his fellow monks for forty years; now he returns, his path spanning three thousand *li*.
If anyone asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, the water flows through rivers and lakes, and the moon dwells in the sky.
I send this letter to the Honored One;
with one flask and one bowl, simply follow conditions as they arise. This matter must be proclaimed forcefully from time to time. Knowing ones do not come, and spring is gradually fading away;
on a solitary peak, the bright moon faces the cold spring.
In the same rhyme, I respond to Huang Longtu:
The clouds and mountains of Haihui are layered with tangled greens; The dragon pool pours forth azure, its sound cool and clear.
The Prefect begs for a place of peace and leisure, To join the assembly of Chan practitioners in listening through the night.

In the same rhyme, I respond to my elder brother Master Gaotai, who often reads my "Verses on the Joyful Seclusion. Its pure breeze is ever more lovely; sometimes I speak of it to others, yet people of this age do not understand.
Turning my head, I gaze toward Mount Heng; the mountain lies a thousand li away. Walking alone in the slanting sun, I hear the whistling of autumn winds.
Intending to send clouds to convey my thoughts to the Chan practitioner, I seek a spring clearing.
Touching the rocks, they seem about to soar high; before the Terrace of Wang Bo, they pass through the emerald mists. Originally, they have no mind to become rain.

The dew—when has it ever intended to leak the secrets of Heaven? Wind and thunder rely on their momentum for their distant resonance; grasses and trees take advantage of the shade for their lush growth.
Do not say that when the work is done, there is only empty dispersal; when will you return to your secluded retreat in the mountain crags?
Three Poems on Sending off the Dharma Master From the crevices of the crags, clouds burst forth in fragments; Half shrouding secluded rocks, half following the dragon.
Having universally moistened the parched and withered with rain, He now enters the first layer of misty vines.
Do not discuss human sentiments or the sentiments of the Way; for the most part, the principles of things are naturally clear. Beneath Mount Huankong flows a long river;
from antiquity to the present, it surges on, pure to its very depths.
In the courtyard, there is no one to stand with the snow; on the road, there are travelers amidst the dust. Exhausting my heart in this moment, I present these parting colors among the pines.
Together with Guai Chan, we sought grain in the water and found it;
fearing the traveler Guai Chan, we went back and forth by the banks of Yan Creek. Hearing the sound, was it heard or not?

Entrusted to the Elder Dīpaṃkara of Taiping, who wanders extensively through the Five Patriarchs’ Mountains: his speech and laughter are heartwarming; his vision reaches to the horizon with a vast capacity of mind; his deportment is largely spontaneous and free.
Missing my hometown, I wish to return; I do not fear the reproach of others. We shall meet again next year, with no hindrance to our coming and going.
Sent to Dharma-brother Master Gao Tai:
The spring mountains stretch to the horizon for thousands of layers; leaning alone against the precarious railing, who is there with me? In the stillness of night, only the cuckoo knows my heart.
Intention. Every sound resounds within the emerald peaks.
After moving to Baiyun and entering the monastery, he instructed his two or three attendants:
"When climbing mountains, one must rely on a staff; when crossing waters, one requires a boat. When guests arrive, open your face and smile; when there is no sorrow, stretch out your legs and sleep."
In all things, preserve this Way; with a single flavor, trust in past conditions. If one were to compare this to within the red dust of the world, how much would such purity and emptiness be worth?
Sent to mendicants in various prefectures:

sit for a moment and attend to the seven-day retreat. The ancient sages left behind their traces here on this earth and in the Western Heaven; every one of them clearly understood the standard of measure.
Pointing at iron turns it into gold; shouting at a stone transforms it into a wall. As for the mighty Nārāyaṇa—who is it that has personally encountered him?
Two poems addressed to an old acquaintance:

though we have been apart for a long time, this does not mean we are estranged. Does forming a friendship depend on seeing one another frequently? Let the mountain paths below remain as rugged as they are.
Rugged and steep—ten thousand li of moonlight form a single expanse.
The northern wind sweeps away the snow from a thousand crags. On the branches, the red plum buds are about to burst open. Vague, cold clouds drift down from beyond the heavens.
Who can speak of this realm of my house?
Four Verses on Sending Off the Dharma-Messenger What brings this autumn wind into the night’s coolness? The rice blossoms occasionally waft their lingering fragrance.
If you wish to know this true message, Its most profound flavor is found at the very end.
When parting before the Terrace of Lord Wan, the peach blossoms were like brocade and the willows like eyebrows.
On this same day next year, gazing from the railing, there will still be just one or two green branches.
To emerge from the Dragon Gate is not yet difficult; how many can pass through Zhaozhou’s Barrier?
Flakes of white cloud beyond the green mountains, becoming rain and drizzle, they go and then return again.
Emerging from Baiyun Mountain, I carry my staff and walk upon the misty marshes. Within my heart are tens of thousands of thoughts;
only you can understand them. Three Poems Sent to an Old Friend:
The leaves fall in the high autumn as the jade dew hangs down; Before the window, the yellow chrysanthemums gradually begin to wither. Flakes of white cloud welcome the new [season].
The wild goose: Not one who knows the music, to whom can I speak?
The letter has not yet arrived, yet he already gazes toward it; the message has not been delivered, yet I am unaware of it.
Spending my days among the forest springs, free from worldly cares, I knit my brows as I steal glances at the white ape.

The plum blossoms wish to fall but do not; the peach blossoms wish to bloom but do not. Thinking of you, where we once listened together to the cries of the monkeys—a single mass of white clouds drifts down from beyond the heavens.

Occasionally, for a long time, I have wished to paint the wild geese at the edge of the sky; yet, though I observe their plumage, it remains imperfectly rendered. Their cries need not hinder one’s awareness of the seasons;
once they are fully formed, what difficulty could there be in watching them fly away? "Goose, goose, goose"—the pagoda was first occupied by them. Ancient traces, Chan, Chan—entering.

The principle is profound and deep; it is formless and shapeless. Through a thousand hardships and ten thousand difficulties, over many lifetimes and long eons, with a mind as firm as stone, one pierces through it.
Composed in the style of the Patriarch’s Flower, following the rhyme of Inspector Li, three stanzas:
This flower is far removed from that of the human world; It bears fruit and blooms where it is born. If you wish to understand the ultimate point of the Patriarchs, [look here].
The essential meaning: Before anything has even sprouted, Heaven and Earth have already completed it.
This is the name of the patriarchs and Buddhas of this land and the Western Heavens; iron flowers bloom atop the twin peaks.
Though there are countless hands in the world skilled in ink and color, I fear they may succeed in painting it, yet fail to capture its poetic resonance.
The work of creation and the nature of all things: when one is truly in the state of arising, one does not speak of arising. To seek branches and pluck leaves is but a waste of effort;
when a single flower blooms, a Buddha is realized.
In the same rhyme, I respond to the Prefect Peng’s inscription at Seven Peaks Pavilion:

On the slope of the mountain, a small pavilion was built; Therein I have temporarily established my lifelong dwelling. At the summits of three or four perilous peaks, The cries of gibbons are exceptionally clear.
In the same rhyme, I send this to Commissioner Peng of the Ministry of Personnel:

Even if one were to see it with one's own eyes a thousand times, how could that compare to experiencing it personally with one's own hands once? To penetrate this heavy barrier is the very skillful means of one’s entire life.

In the same rhyme, I respond to the Prefectural Administrator of Wu on the profound subtlety of his mountain life: The path winds and turns through peaks; those who return are rare. A single bowl of yellow mustard greens passes the long days;
White hair covers the head, yet the ultimate mystery is realized. Waterfalls cascade before the window around the crags; Mad monkeys howl at the moon upon the ridges.
Soaring upward, he finds his own lifelong contemplation insufficient; how could he know that this floating world is both affirmation and negation?
Composing verses in response to the words of Li Chao-feng, the Vice-Governor of Qi, the essence of truth does not lie in verbosity.
Mañjuśrī’s non-duality was questioned by Vimalakīrti; Zhaozhou’s eye blazes through the four heavens.
Fortunately, there was my fellow practitioner, Laywoman Ling, who inscribed this on the eastern ridge of West Lake for Governor Li, the Secretariat Supervisor:
Tall bamboos and lofty pines gather deep, verdant shade; Green willows and red blossoms fill the gardens and groves. In the end, one must yield to West Lake.
The water is clear and still, like the heart of a gentleman.
On the road to Dongying, I spent one night at Chengjia Village; alone as a drifting cloud, I travel ten thousand miles. My gate remains tranquil wherever I am; when will the worldly path ever cease?
Raising my head, I ask the bright moon; resting my heart upon the Dipper and Ox (the constellations). Why is the time for your return so late? You still wander through other lands.
At Juyuan Pavilion, what the eyes behold is never enough, and what the ears hear can never be exhausted. The waters are emerald and the mountains are azure; who is distant and who is near?
Answer: Relying on the Way, I am old and infirm, negligent and dull-witted; my mind does not retain things. Surely I have never reached the Jasper Forest in a wild dream.
The sounds of water and the colors of mountains shall be my constant companions; let profit and harm be as deep as the sea.
I lingered between the two gullies as they flowed side by side; the azure waters cascaded down like twin ribbons. The waves at Changsha were deep, and the turbulent current surged and overflowed.

In response to Xiucai Shi’s verse on last night’s fierce west wind that tossed the surging billows—leaving not a hair’s breadth of old memories remaining—I leaned upon the railing, finished my laughter, and reflected.
[Verse] Gazing across the vast sky, the moonlight is high.
In parting with Great Minister Zhu, I say:
If the mind is at ease, one is at ease everywhere. Do not be constrained by city or mountain stream. Right and wrong, fame and profit—these are all as nothing.
A Dream. When viewed with the True Eye, it is but a single instant.
Seeing off Lü Gōngfǔ as he departs his guest at Jīnshā:
The path traveled grows ever more distant; pale smoke enshrouds the azure heavens, and thin mist adorns the crimson clouds.
The hundred-tongued wren sings by the new tree; A thousand stalks grow with tender sprouts. Recollecting the place where we parted, I raise my head and see peach blossoms.

As I bid farewell to Huang Jingchun: Autumn clouds and autumn waters, both lingering on; Wild geese cry out as they pass through the azure heights. Most likely they have headed toward Dongting Lake and Qingcao Marsh.
The banks [of the river]—the Chu sky is vast and boundless, and one knows not where to return.
I have met with Guo Gongfu, the layman Jingkong, after a long acquaintance; thirty years have passed in what was but a single moment. Today, beneath the white lotus flowers...

Master Yanshi of Haihui once traveled on pilgrimage to the summit of Baiyun Peak, where he encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) seated upon a lion throne in the form of a bhikṣu.
This teacher performed no action and preached no doctrine. At times, he grasped the clouds and seized the waves, sporting with complete ease;
at other times, he cut through iron and severed nails, his conduct being beyond description. Disciples from all quarters flocked to him, and the fourfold assembly looked up to him with reverence.
They were at a loss to fathom the reason for this, and all were utterly disconcerted. Only the Master gazed steadily at them and smiled; there was no discord in his heart.

Before even an hour had passed, they were granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Heaven and men joined in their praise. From Sifumen (Four Directions) he proceeded to Taiping (Great Peace); from father to son the lineage was transmitted.

From Taiping he came to Haihui (Ocean Assembly), answering questions according to the capacity of the listeners and exalting the Dharma through specific circumstances, without relying on [artificial] sharpness.

Then, he struck his chest two or three times with his hand, called to his attendant, and when the attendant responded, the Master said, "I have a headache today. Take care. A monk asked, "Regarding hearing the sound of the bell..."
[The student] asked: "Is there only this sound, or is there something else? The Master said: "Three catties behind the head. [The student] asked:
"If the true nature does not follow conditions, how can one attain correct enlightenment? The Master said: "Red dust rises from the bottom of the great ocean;

waves overflow the heavens atop Mount Sumeru. [The student] asked: "Who is the person who performs great deeds? The Master said: "Slaying the butcher outside the city wall. [The student] pressed further: "..."

[The student] asked, "What is it like when one does not understand this meaning? The Master said, "A scale of one catty cannot hold it. [The student] asked, "When the Mahāyāna mind is able to bear all virtues, what is it like?
The Master said, "There is no road to ascend to heaven; there is no gate to enter the earth. [The student] further asked, "What is it like when one does not understand this principle?
The Master said, "Gazing toward one's hometown from within Sha-men Island."
A letter arrived from Baoying of Ruizhou, announcing that he had ascended the hall as a Dharma heir. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked:

"When the five petals of the flower have blossomed and the Dharma pervades heaven and earth, what then? The Master said: "On the Double Ninth Festival in the ninth month, chrysanthemums fill the air with fragrance.

The monk pressed further: "In that case, the clouds of compassion provide universal moisture. The Master said: "Vast and empty, there is not a single thing; its radiance shines throughout the ten directions."
Fang. Question: What is the first mystery? The Master said: "The Way is present in the ordinary; every word is profound and mysterious.
Question: What is the second mystery? The Master said: "Where there is a question, there is an answer; the sun and moon shine forever.
Question: What is the third mystery? The Master said: "Why trouble the tortoise with ten questions about its years? Question: As soon as the bell has ceased, the assembly is gathered at the dais.
"Regarding the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, I request the Master to proclaim it. The Master said, "Monks are ranked by their years of ordination; laypeople are listed by their age.
He further asked, "If that is so, then a single rain universally moistens the great trichiliocosm. The Master said, "The sun rises naturally and uniquely;
its radiance illuminates the ten directions. A question was asked: "In the Hall of Good Dharma, I extend this inquiry: I wonder, does the Master still receive [the student] or not? The Master said:
[The Master] said, "Brocade from the land of Shu; observe the cotton wool. The student replied, "If that is so, then I have received the Master’s compassion.
The Master said, "Vast and open, without obstruction; moving freely in all directions as one pleases."
The Master ascended the hall and said: "Virtuous Chan practitioners, a patch-robed monk is a man of penetrating transformation.

If he encounters boiling cauldrons, glowing furnaces, or any manner of calamity and hardship, how could he possibly avoid them? If he cannot avoid them, what name can he be given other than a man of penetrating transformation?"
"What is the phrase that penetrates and liberates one from all manner of calamities? Is there anyone here who can penetrate and liberate themselves?
Try speaking it before this assembly; I shall provide you with verification. If you cannot penetrate and liberate yourself, then ten thousand people will be your tomb."
"No one can replace him. He then descended from his seat. A monk asked, "Master, having ascended the lion’s throne, what is the meaning of the Patriarchs' intent?

The Master said, "Standing is the performance of Buddha-work; sitting is the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*). The monk pressed further, "If that is so, then you have cast your body beyond the three realms."
The Master said, "As for the matter that lies beyond the three realms, how is it? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "This blind donkey will leave even this old monk in doubt.
A monk asked, "The path leading upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages. What is this matter that is not transmitted?
The Master said, "In the hearth, they add more fire yet still complain of cold; on the road, the traveler merely endures the chill. The monk pressed further, "I do not yet understand this..."

"What is the principle here? The Master said, "In winter there is no accumulated snow; in summer there is no surplus grain. The student advanced and said, "If it is so, then I thank the Master for his instruction.
The Master said, "The staff is cast down while chanting at a loud voice; blood is seen atop the head from the blow of the staff. The student bows. The Master said, "So be it."
He was told to stop, yet he refused to stop; he waited until the rain drenched his head. A question was asked: "I have heard it said of old:

'All day long one is in a state of busyness, yet that matter is not hindered. What is that matter? The Master said: "The assembly hears it all at once. The questioner pressed: "What is the principle behind this?
The Master said: "Every traveler carries sorrow. A question was asked: "In the past, Baizhang studied under Mazu and suddenly attained a state where everything was swept away."
"I have no further doubts. Today I have come specifically to request instruction; I beg the Master to employ skillful means to provide a complete presentation.
The Master said, "The Yellow River has nine bends; Shaanxi Province produces iron oxen. The student advanced and said, "A large month has thirty days;
a small month has twenty-nine. I have already received the Master’s instruction on this. But as for the upward-pointing pivot—how is that? The Master said, "I have deeply understood this question."

"Carrying the shackles and passing through the court for your offenses—you have brought disgrace upon your ancestral lineage. The student said, "If that is so, then this student has grounds to pay homage.
The Master said, "When the double indictment is finalized, ten thousand miles of mountains and rivers shall not turn back. A question was asked: "When many hands sift gold, who is it that obtains it?
The Master said, "Look with eyes fixed on the tip of the staff. The student said, "I ask the Master to give his full command. The Master said, "It is indeed so."
He fell into a deep pit. [The student] asked: "When a single horse and a solitary spear leave you to fight alone, what then? The Master said: "Drawing the hairpin from behind the head.
[The student] pressed further: "If that is so, then the general has been defeated and his horses return empty-handed. The Master said: "Accept the silver coins; do not linger long."
In the *Guangjiao Kanbian Yubing Xinglu*, there is a verse concerning the Master’s interrogation of a monk.
The Master asked a monk, “Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, “From Dongjing. The Master said, “Why is your mouth broken?
The monk said, “The Master must also be careful. The Master said, “Seven blows for thirteen; eat them under the storehouse.”

The attendant departed. The Master asked a monk, "At evening you cast yourself into the forest; at dawn, from where did you depart? The monk said, "I am a newly ordained monk who has never studied Chan.
The Master said, "Born with a body that enters hell! [The monk] went down. Later, a monk brought this up to Great Master Mingjiao of Zhimen in Suizhou.
The Great Master said, "Why not say, 'The lock and key are in the hands of the Abbot'? This was due to a monk's service.
There was a letter tube. The Master asked, "What is this? The monk said, "Venerable Sir, you should recognize it for what it is.
The Master said, "So, after all, it is just a lacquered bucket. The monk said, "I ask the Venerable Sir to take it back. The Master said, "Griming one's eyes from inside a coffin.
Later, hearing the sound of a youth reciting sutras, the Master asked a monk, "Do you hear the sound of the sutra recitation? The monk said, "Today I have been tested."
"Broken! The Master said, "An adept. The monk said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. The Master said, "Today I have suffered a loss.
The Master examined five newly arrived monks, saying, "Are you all the attendants from Yunju? The monks said, "Yes. The Master said, "If that is so, sit down all together.
Because a monk entered the room and requested instruction on the story of Master Zhaozhou’s "Cypress Tree," the Master said:
"I shall not refuse to speak with you. But will you believe me? The monk said, "Since the Master speaks with such gravity, how would I dare not believe?
The Master asked, "Do you hear the sound of water dripping from the eaves? At that, the monk was suddenly enlightened; without realizing it, he involuntarily let out a cry of "Aha!"
The Master asked, "What principle have you seen? The monk replied with a verse:

"The water droplets from the eaves, clearly dripping— Breaking through heaven and earth, the mind is stilled in this very moment. The Master was pleased. Later, while the Master was unwell, a monk asked, "The four elements are fundamentally empty;
from where does illness arise? The Master said, "One may discuss medicinal prescriptions all day long, yet it will never be cured. The monk... [remained silent].
[The Master] said, "If you do not understand this meaning, what then? The Master said, "Only the *amṛta* (clarified butter) of the mind-ground is cool.
Once, while walking with three or five monastics and laypeople, the Master was leaning on a white staff. One monk asked, "It is simply that he lacks one skin and five fingers.
The Master then raised his hand and spread out his five fingers, asking, "Do you understand? The monk and the laypeople said, "No."
[The Master] said, "An assembly. The Master continued, "Five wheels upon the fingers emit rays of light. The Master went to the infirmary to visit a sick monk.
The monk asked, "Venerable Sir, the four great elements are originally empty; from where does illness come? The Master replied, "It comes from the place where you, Dharma-heir, ask.
As the monk gasped for breath, he pressed further, "What about after one has ceased asking? The Master said, "Letting go of all, one lies in the vast expanse of space."
The monk said, "Yes," and then passed away. While the Master was walking along with the monk, they encountered a dead person, and the monk asked:
"The cart is here; where are the oxen? The Master said, "You are limping along. The monk said, "If there are no oxen, what is it that you are walking?
The Master said, "Since you have no oxen, why have you bruised your feet? The monk said, "In that case, I have come directly from Ye County.
The Master said, "Do not run about recklessly. Later, while the Master was picking wisteria flowers with a monk, there was...
A monk asked, "On this day we pluck the wisteria flowers; will there be a karmic fruit in the future? The Master said, "To say 'there is' is an error.
The monk said, "In that case, there is no karmic fruit? The Master said, "You are indeed a master.
While the Master was at Shoushan’s assembly, Shoushan one day asked him, "If you call it a bamboo stick, you encounter resistance (*chu*); if you do not call it a bamboo stick..."

He immediately turned his back. [The Master asked: "What should this be called? At these words, the student attained sudden and thorough realization. "Blind! The Master then paid his respects. Later, the Master went to Guangde in Xiangzhou. Guangde gave this instruction:
"Zen practitioners, you must truly be lion cubs before you can succeed. You all possess the nature of lion cubs. The Master then stepped forward and asked:
The Master said, "I have heard the Venerable say, 'Everyone possesses a lion cub.
What is the Venerable’s lion? Guangde then let out a lion's roar. The Master said, "This is still the howling of a jackal.
Bring me the lion! He then gave a shout and struck a palm. Guangde said, "A true lion cub. The Master said, "What kind of talk is that?"
Deyun said, "Ask your brother thoroughly. The Master said, "I must not let him off.
The Master went to Dongshan and asked, "When there is vast emptiness with nothing to rely upon, where does the Dharma return? Dongshan said, "Three times the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).
The Master said, "If that is so, then those who know the sound do not harmonize. Dongshan said, "What is the matter of those who know the sound not harmonizing? The Master said, "Turtle hair."
The whisk was three feet long. [Zhaozhou] said, "Why have your eyebrows and beard fallen off?
The master then bowed. He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Xiangzhou. The master pulled the boy aside, gave him a slap, and shouted, "Get out!"

The Brick Hermitage of Universal Teaching: vast and open, without bounds. Passing the days according to conditions, following one's nature with simple ignorance. The myriad phenomena of the universe are transmitted by both the ordinary and the holy.
Should anyone arrive here, they will find themselves on the western side of Mount Xue.

Seeing off the monk as he departs for Dongjing to escort his elder brother into Liangyuan: The brilliant sun shines through the window, reckoning not the passing years. To report this verse from beneath the forest trees to my Master:
A mindless illumination breaks through ten thousand layers of barriers.
The Master has three verses for the Supervisor of the Sacrificial Department (Cibu), a few of whom know of his whereabouts:
"Resting the mind where it finds repose, there is no further doubt. Should anyone ask about the affairs of my life, I say:
the sun rises in the east, and the moon sets in the west."
The Sacrificial Department perceives that everywhere is pervasive; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are its true style. Let the flower-adorned trees stand before one as they may;
with no-mind, one subdues all things to manifest the True Principle.
The precincts of the Sacrificial Department appear vast and serene; the myriad phenomena of the universe are present before one's eyes. Let others rejoice and delight as they may;
following conditions, I deliver beings throughout the days among devas and humans.
The former master had a verse, which he explained word by word:

"Facing the sun while one's back is to the Yin Mountains" (he said: "Transcendent, there is neither front nor back"). "How is the meaning of coming from the south and going to the north? (he said: "It does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence").

Someone asked about the meaning of the Westward Journey (he said: "From the beginning, there has been no interruption"). At the eastern edge of the Eastern Sea lies Silla (he said: "The great earth can do nothing about it").
The Master, feeling unwell, spoke these two verses:
"I now have this illness; there is neither seeing nor hearing. The principle of pure emptiness is ever-luminous like the sun and moon.
I now have this illness; it is rare to meet one who understands. Even if you were to understand it clearly, you would lose your lifelong realization."
In his old age, he composed a verse:
"The illusory years have reached seventy-three; the true nature does not follow conditions. Vast and open, it is without obstruction; pure and empty, it alone remains tranquil.
When the monks did not ask him questions, he then recounted five verses.
It is you who do not ask questions; it is this mountain monk who does not answer in Chan. The sun is exactly at midday; it splits open the mouth of the local deity.
It is you who do not ask questions; this mountain monk has no way to close his mouth. At noon, he strikes the third watch; the pillar of light preaches the Dharma at night.
It is you who do not ask the question; this mountain monk is truly astonished. After winter, for one hundred and five days, ivory comes from Guangnan.
It is you who do not ask the question; this mountain monk has nothing to hold onto. The nostrils are right here; pick them up and strike him over the head.
It is you who do not ask questions; this mountain monk has nothing to boast of. Vastly following conditions as they arise, Hu-nan produces ramie.
Woodfish song! Woodfish song!
Woodfish song! Lying across the three realms, shaking head and wagging tail, flashing the golden scales—ordinary beings and sages alike.
Transverse and vertical, there is nothing that can restrain him. When the Old Barbarian hears it, he pricks up his ears to listen.

Every sound vibrates through the heart of the Ancient Buddha; carefree and sovereign, there is no partiality or crookedness. As he wanders vast and open, he moves at ease; pointing to the sun and moon, Mount Tai collapses.
Leaping and bounding, the demonic armies are startled; when he bellows and chants, clouds gather in ranks. It is like the sound of a thunderclap from the bottom of the great ocean.
Accompanying the patron, I delivered offerings for the Arhats to Mount Nanyue, where there is a verse:
"Fortunate from past lives, we have here formed a noble connection. The traces of the Arhats remain; the sun and moon shine upon the blue sky, while pines and creepers grow lush and thick."
At the edge of the cliff of inherent nature, where the Way-man walks, mountains and rivers fill the eyes; the white ox in the open field stands vast and without companion.
The myriad phenomena of the universe are right before one’s eyes. If a person does not understand this, where can they meet it? When someone asks about it—
Look directly beneath the arrow.
A verse on inviting a monk to travel the mountains:
The days for traveling the mountains are few and the paths are perilous. Pack your gear and do not hesitate; tomorrow you shall see the mountains in their entirety.
Form: when the mind is directed toward its dwelling place, it is obscured by mountains.
As the master of offerings at the mountain gate passes through seeking verses, many patrons from all quarters come and go.
How is it with the green mountains and blue waters? Śaṇmukha should recognize [his own face].
Ying: "He does not know that the hawk has flown to Silla.
Praise for the true teacher, the true teacher of the second generation of Baoying:
His countenance is ancient and imposing; his speech is direct and decisive. His coming and going are distinct; the myriad phenomena of the universe are all clearly revealed.
Universally saving the hearts of all beings, the Chan practitioners who come and go behold the great mountain crumble into stone.
What need is there for pigments and ink to depict my Master’s true form? His appearance is like the full moon, pervading heaven and earth.
A Verse for Sending a Monk to the Eastern Capital: I see off the eminent monk as he enters Liangyuan;
Spring passes and autumn comes, yet years are not counted. In his vast wandering, there is no path of deviation;

Mountains and rivers offer no hindrance—smiling at the West Heaven. The youth of the Snow Mountains utters a shout beneath a word; Were one to hesitate even for a moment, ten thousand [barriers would arise].
Ten thousand years.
A single lantern, a golden lamp named Linglong. Its four sides and eight facets require no craftsmanship; it illuminates and shatters the darkness of heaven and earth.
The mountains, rivers, and great earth are its true style.

As the patron of offerings and the master of transformation depart for the immortal city, north and south are no different from east and west; transcendent beyond the age of Vimalacitra, they penetrate everywhere, whether horizontal or vertical.
Brightness and darkness are both inherently thus; in silent stillness, heaven and earth are empty. All conditions are suddenly stilled, yet the roar shakes heaven and earth.

On the third anniversary of the late Master’s passing, his true visage is like the sun. The three-year period having concluded, he pervades heaven and earth; standing on one foot for seven days, he fully displays the majestic wind.
The fox-spirits vanish from sight; incense and tea are offered as sustenance. Who can recognize the lacquer-like radiance?
Together with the monks, we look at the mulberry seeds—the seeds are black, the wood is sturdy.
A mindless state is the site of enlightenment (dharma-śālā). When the high monk partakes of a single meal, the fruit ripens of its own accord, fragrant and sweet.

As you escort the patron who offers this felt mat on your journey ahead to spread the Way, do not shrink from hardship. Follow conditions with unwavering resolve, drifting as you may. Let clouds parting and waters flowing be your companions;
from time to time, let your roar shake heaven and earth.
Below the snow are four verses: On this day there is fine snow;
who says it is not pure as ice? White silver like grains of millet—the sun and moon of Silla. On this day there is fine snow;
the myriad people delight in their work. It spreads wide across the vast sky, cutting off the paths of both ordinary beings and sages.
Today is a fine day for snow. What need is there for words? All things are without mind; mountains, rivers, sun, and moon. Today is a fine day for snow;
vast and empty, it vanquishes the thief and fills the universe. Who can discern it?
At the end of summer, I saw off a monk;
a high monk accompanied me through the ninety days. Who can speak of the teachings of the ancestral vehicle? Transcending both the mundane and the sacred, its wondrousness is all-pervasive.
Who could even attempt to deliberate upon it? They would fall a thousand peaks deep.
A monk approached him and said, "I do not know the Master's style. The Master offered this verse:
"The Gateless Teaching has no gate; Transverse and vertical, it penetrates everywhere. When the red dust of the great earth rises, The master of the house is lost."
Rain falls on this auspicious day. Heaven and earth have no path; the sun and moon shine forever. To the West lies the Pure Land.
[These] verses on human affairs and the handkerchief were composed by Shi Jianyi in ten stanzas.
Guangjiao’s hand-towel: neither merit nor ability. Encountered at every turn, it is put to use.
Green mountains and white clouds—Guangjiao’s hand-towel. Spanning from antiquity to the present, silent and vast, it shatters heaven and earth.
Guangjiao’s handkerchief does not accord with the sentiments of the multitude. Someone asked in inquiry: "The Great Peak crumbles its rocks;
Guangjiao’s handkerchief—why labor the mind and spirit? Light and darkness are thus of themselves; green mountains and white clouds."
Guangjiao’s hand-towel; a blink of an eye, presented to one another. The white ox on the open ground—neither ordinary nor holy.
Guangjiao’s hand-towel: who has seen it? Who has heard it? To understand it directly right now is to lose one's entire life.
A broad teaching hand-towel: the sun and moon shine forever bright; lengthwise and crosswise, it is free and at ease.

A person from the land of Silla uses this broad teaching hand-towel; it is not woven through deliberate effort, but follows conditions as it passes the days, floating and sinking according to its nature.
Guangjiao’s hand-towel fills the heavens and earth; the wise and the foolish both understand its meaning—how it makes one laugh at the barbarian monk!
Guangjiao’s hand-towel requires no formal treatises; if you can realize it before words are spoken, your very eyes will be blinded.
A verse for the meal invitation by Master Shengxi of Xichan: Do not delay; do not delay.
From the beginning, this matter has always been just so. Two times the snow has fallen in thick flakes; it is neither caused by human lords nor by Heaven.
The Great Master answered in verse without delay:
"Without delay! The myriad phenomena of the universe are before one's eyes. The clouds gather thickly, blackening heaven and earth;
the white ox in the open field pervades the great thousandfold world."
A Verse on Roaming the Hermitage:
Suddenly beholding the hermitage garden, I am as naturally foolish and dull-witted as ever. When someone arrives here, it is as if separated by mountains and passes.
[I] have prepared a tea service to offer to the Master who provides sustenance; hereafter, I shall recognize each line [of his verse].

Salt without vinegar (the commentary says: like a thief entering an empty house). Vegetables without oil (it says: there is no private self to create a barrier). Floating and sinking according to conditions (it says:
following one's nature as it drifts or sinks). A hundred flavors of rare delicacies (it says: there is attainment in whatever one encounters).
While the monks were conversing, there was this verse:
"One arrival at Xianzhou forty autumns ago; Following conditions, I have rested here in stillness.
Fortunately meeting a high monk as my companion, I have wandered freely and unexpectedly reached the mountain peak."
The monk presented a portrait for the Master, who then composed a verse and inscribed it himself:

Who painted this likeness? (It moves heaven and earth. With a marvelous brush and cinnabar colors, (words flow from the mouth like blossoms. Light and dark are thus as they are; (dry and wet share the same direction. Why labor the mind and spirit?

(Let nature float and sink. My true self is not false; (one finds attainment by touching all categories. The painted image is not the truth; (to conceive of it in the mind is already to err. The features are of humble substance.
(The heavens cannot cover it). Pervading heaven and earth, it manifests forms in response to things.
As his years grew old, he composed a verse on the Sixty-Eight Extensive Teachings:
"Ordinary people and sages alike are extinguished. If someone should come to ask me about it, it is on the Double Ninth Festival of the ninth month."
The sixty-eight sections of the Extensive Teachings—who can truly examine their essence? If you understand them directly right now, there is three catties of iron behind your head.
To the one who provides offerings:
one year’s spring ends and another year’s spring begins. Please trouble yourself to speak of drifting with the current or sinking; the myriad phenomena of the universe are impartial.
Song: A single sound, as soon as it moves, cuts through heaven and earth.
The fan is a broad teaching; this single handle of a fan has, from the beginning, no front or back. Sometimes it is in the hand, yet for the moment, no one sees it.
The mountain monk’s staff is a single cane; its纵横 (zōnghéng) movement is beyond measure. Sometimes held in my hand, its application pervades the ten directions.
*Qiángzhú zhàng* (Bamboo Staff).
The nine-jointed *zhongzhu* bamboo staff extends vertically and horizontally without deviation; it unfurls across the vast sky, severing the paths of both the ordinary and the sage.
When the two head monks of the hall chant the verse, they both issue a downward shout;
the two head monks of the hall simultaneously issue their shouts. To those who are blind, there is no discrimination—this is what is generally called the "guest and host" within the phrase.
What need is there for the labor of tortoise-shell divination to inquire about one's future?
Master Guangjiao’s single word to his disciples has been transmitted by both ordinary people and sages; understand it directly, and the ten thousand li of mountains and rivers are revealed.
The monk requested further instruction:
"Steadfastly following conditions, I let myself drift or sink; I am not bound by spring, summer, autumn, or winter.
Disciple, you who request further instruction on the affairs of your life—go ask Hanshan, and only then will you know."
Zen monk, Zen monk! There is no need for discursive debate. If you can realize it before a word is spoken, you will find "three pounds of flax" behind the head.
When Li Duye asked about the Master’s birthday, the Master composed ten verses:
"On my birthday, everywhere is true; Following conditions, I sit unmoving, drifting with the flow. The myriad phenomena of the universe are impartial."
Verse: The sun rises, naturally illuminating heaven and earth;
Where the mountain monk was born, all is vast and serene. Unconstrained by ordinary or holy, he wanders with ease; Let others before him rejoice and celebrate.
With no-mind, he subdues things and celebrates peace.
This mountain monk was born amidst the azure clouds; sentient and insentient beings share one true reality. When light and darkness are exhausted, there is no path of deviation;
in this luminous clarity, one does not fall before the ranks of sages or commoners.
This mountain monk has few who understand him where he was born; following his nature and随缘 (following conditions), he has passed through several springs.
If someone should ask about his life’s affairs, a stone man beats the drum and a wooden man listens.
This mountain monk issues his command from his place of birth; all Zen disciples of the ten directions are utterly startled.
If one can understand how to take root with the rootless tree, they will be able to draw water from the sea and light a lamp from the bottom of the deep.
Where this mountain monk was born, the True Command is enacted; the village elders sing his praises and spread his fame.
If a person does not recognize the function of the Vajra, they are but a man in a well beside Mount Nirvana.

The mountain monk’s place of birth spans from antiquity to the present. Who can speak of the transmission of the Dharma? Transcending both the ordinary and the sage, his wondrous mastery is all-pervasive;
he draws out his hairpin from behind his head to offer sacrifice to the gods and spirits.
This mountain monk’s place of birth is within the forest; the tiger’s roar by the azure stream displays heroic spirit. Turning back, he startles the lands of the ten directions;
ten thousand li of rivers and mountains enter into a thousand peaks.

This mountain monk was born upon the mountain peak; when Kāśyapa heard the bell, he emerged from the cave gate. Even if my bones were ground to powder and my body shattered for ten million kalpas, it would be difficult to repay the kindness of my teacher through mere reflection.
This mountain monk was born amidst the azure depths; he is unconstrained by spring, summer, autumn, or winter. One must cease at once with a single stroke—dualism severed.
Who could even attempt to deliberate upon this? They would fall ten thousand peaks deep.

When the Master was visited by a monk, he offered a verse that expanded upon a single word of the broad teaching; those who were people of direct realization found this distasteful. When someone questioned him, he replied, "Ten thousand miles of rivers and mountains.
Upon ascending the hall, he recited a verse.
In the forty-fifth year, he was at Xianzhou; sages and ordinary beings intermingle—let the master roam as he pleases.
If someone should ask what the matter is, by the third watch of night, he has arrived at Yizhou.
Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Honored Masters, Volume Twenty-three;
Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Honored Masters, Volume Twenty-four:
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yan of Shending Mountain, the First Patriarch of Tanzhou.
Chan Master Shending, whose name was Hongyin, was the son of the Hu family of Xiangshui. Since he began his travels, he had passed through both cold and heat clad in nothing but a single robe.
Once, while traveling with several senior monks through the region of Xiangmian, there was a monk who was quite agile in discussing the vehicle of the school (zongcheng).
They happened upon a mountain inn where a meal was being prepared; yet the monk continued his discourse without ceasing. The Master said, "The three realms are mind-only. The myriad..."
“The Dharma is consciousness-only; consciousness-only is mind-only. ‘The eye and sound, the ear and form’—whose words are these?

The monk said, “The words of Fayan. The Master asked, “What is their meaning? He replied, “Because it is mind-only, the sense organs and their objects do not reach one another. Because it is consciousness-only, sounds and forms are as they are.
The Master asked, “Are the tongue and taste also organ and object? He replied, “Yes. The Master took a vegetable with his chopsticks and placed it in his own mouth.
In the midst of this, he spoke with indistinct words, asking, "What do you mean by 'mutual entry'? The seated monks were startled; none could answer.
The Master said, "The joy of the journey does not culminate until one arrives home. To have insights that penetrate the subtle is not called 'seeing the Way.
One must investigate authentically; one must awaken authentically. The King Yama does not fear much talk. The monk bowed and withdrew. Later, he returned to Changsha.
The ashes were concealed in the San-sheng Zang (Treasury of Three Lives) at Mount Heng. Later, a wealthy and nobleman from Xiangyin came to visit Fuyan;
seeing that the Master’s chamber was serene and tranquil, with only a single alms bowl hanging on the wall and no other possessions, he was filled with admiration.

He then prostrated himself and entreated him, saying, "Shending is the place where my family has cultivated merit for generations, yet it has long lacked a patriarchal master. I pray that you, Master, will go there with me."

"How is that? the Master asked, smiling and consenting. He immediately placed his own horse on the back of the master. It was not until ten years later that he finally established a monastic community;
there, a single dilapidated bed served as his Dharma seat for preaching.
On the day of opening the hall, he pointed to the Dharma seat and said: "Before ascending this seat, my work of transforming conditions was already complete.
Do you all understand this thoroughly? If you understand it thoroughly, you may disperse and go.

If you do not disperse and go, I cannot avoid ascending this seat and entering the second chapter on 'Skillful Means. Furthermore, you must not blame this mountain monk. He then ascended the seat and offered incense, saying: "This one stick..."

Incense. This first offering is made for the present Emperor, that his holy life may be boundless. The second offering of incense is for the Prefectural Governor, the Academician, and all the honored officials of the entire commandery;
we humbly pray that they may forever illuminate the Sun of the Buddha and eternally assist the Enlightened Sovereign. The third offering of incense:
this incense is not the fragrance of precept, concentration, or wisdom, nor is it sandalwood or aloeswood; it is simply the local soil of汝州 (Ruzhou), fit to be burned here.
He said, "I shall make offerings to Master Shou Shan to repay the milk of the Dharma.
The Master then spread his seat and looked over the assembly, saying, "In the kingdom of Magadha, this edict was personally issued. Does the assembly know where it lands?

A single phrase encompasses heaven and embraces earth, transcending all beyond the extraordinary and standing before all the sages. Therefore, while the five regions have different harmonies, the Sanskrit scriptures..."
They did not bring it with them. Śākyamuni shut his room in Magadha; Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī.
Outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles, there is a single phrase transmitted separately. I dare ask the assembly: what is this separate transmission?
Try to speak for the assembly and let us verify it together. After a long silence, he said: "Even if you could speak it, it would still not accord with the Patriarch’s intent. Now tell me—"
"How can one be said to have realized the intent of the Patriarchs? Brothers, you must rouse your spirits and thoroughly investigate the root source.
When you reach this point, you cannot speak of bodhi, nirvana, true thusness, or liberation;

nor of 'upward' or 'downward,' sitting in meditation, entering samādhi, building bridges, or digging wells—can you do so? Nevertheless, even if it be thus, there can be no lack of words."—Shan [Guang].
When the monk first set out on his travels, he had no fixed intention;
he wished merely to go to the Eastern Capital to listen to one or two volumes of sutras and treatises to supplement his lifelong studies.

Unexpectedly, as he traveled on and on, he arrived at Xiangcheng County in Ruzhou, where he happened upon the "Rising Wind" of Ruzhou that was stirring at Upper Mountain (Shangshou Shan). There, amidst the assembly, he encountered an old master. At that time...
He struck me with a single blow right on the head, which caused sweat to pour down my back. At that moment, I did not even realize I had prostrated;
I regretted it too late. "Great assembly, tell me: what was there to regret? I regret not having dragged him down from his meditation seat and given him a severe beating!
Nevertheless, the official gate admits no needle, yet private paths allow for carts and horses. He then descended from the seat.
Small Assembly Sermon. The Master raised the case: Dongshan said, "Greed, anger, and delusion—how utterly ignorant they are!
Fortunately, this morning I have recognized them. When they walk, I strike; when they sit, I hammer. I entrust them to the Mind-Prince to investigate minutely.
For immeasurable kalpas they have not been liberated. I ask you three: do you know or not? The Master said: "The ancients spoke thus, but at Shending, it is not so. Greed, anger..."
Ignorance. Truly there is no knowing. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, let it be as it may. Walking, it goes; sitting, it follows. Entrusting it to the Mind-King, what could one possibly do?
Since immeasurable kalpas past, it has been fundamentally liberated. Why need one further ask whether it is known or not? The Master raised the three phrases of Zifu.
Regarding the first phrase: "The Patriarch did not know existence. The Master said: "No one understands this. Second...
The first phrase: To act as a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas. The Master said: "The nostrils are in the hands of this mountain monk.
The third phrase: To uphold and promote the patriarchs and Buddhas. The Master said: "I have told you clearly. Case: A monk asked Shoushan, "What is the house style of the Master?
Shoushan said, "A single word cuts off the mouths of a thousand rivers; only before a ten-thousand-fathom peak does one attain the profound mystery. The Master said: "Shou..."
Shanzhi only understands the family style; he does not understand how to employ the family style. A monk asked, "What is employing the family style? The Master said, "Zhù.
He then said, "If the old fellow Shoushan were here, hearing Shending speak like this, he would surely let out a great laugh.
Now tell me, would he approve of Shending or not? Try to deliberate on this, you venerable monks. As for practicing..."

In studying, one must first possess the eye of a true seeker to succeed. If you merely cherish the words and phrases of others, recording them in your conscious mind, you will be unable to cut through [delusion] yourself.
Even a layman might say, "A man of spirit does not need an inheritance divided at the time of partition.
How much more so for a monk—what should he do? Only by exerting your full brilliance can you succeed. Be careful! Case: A monk asked Master Lingquan, "If..."
"What is the Seal of the Spirit Spring? Lingquan said, "Neither transmitted nor received. [The Master] asked, "What about at the time of handing over the succession?
Lingquan said, "The boatman of Huainan looks toward Luoyang. The Master said, "When the ancients spoke thus, what was their intent? Do you wish to understand?"
Neither transmitted nor received. Be careful. Case: A monk asked Lingquan, "What is the melody of Lingquan? Lingquan said, "The stringless lute has its own resonance;
the strings and flutes stir the heavens. The monk asked, "Is there anyone who understands this? Lingquan said, "There is."
The monk asked, "What is it like to be one who knows the sound? Quansou said, "The stone man on the mountain claps his hands together;
the wild old man by the stream is the first to know the sound. The Master said, "Shending is not like this. The monk then asked, "What is the tune of Shending?
The Master said, "If you wish to sing it, then sing it. The monk asked, "Is there anyone who knows it? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "I do not yet know what kind of person it is."

[The Master asked: "What kind of person is this? The Teacher said: "One who is without mind, intellect, or consciousness. The Teacher said: "When Shending speaks thus, how does it compare to Lingquan?
Try to deliberate upon this; you must know that the 'house style' of each is different. Be careful!"
Small Assembly. The Master raised an ancient verse by Jinfeng, which says: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: When smoke appears, one must not yet stop.
Only when the spark of gold manifests Does one return home and reach the ultimate end. The Master said: "Shending does not think so. Studying the Way is like drilling for fire..."
As soon as you encounter smoke, stop immediately; do not wait for the appearance of the golden star. It will burn your feet and then your head. Now tell me:

when Shen Ding speaks thus, does he contravene the ancients or accord with them? Is there some other principle here? You must say: is it better for one to go in this way, or is it better for one to come in this way?
At this point, you must possess the eye of a patch-robed monk before you can understand; do not simply accept [this at face value].
People are deceived. Take care. A small discourse (*xiaochan*).
After a long silence, he raised [the case]: Jingqing was ascending the hall. After a long silence, a monk asked, "How should one sing the Patriarchal Song?
Jingqing said, "Carrying a drunk man home. The monk said, "If that is so, then I have failed you, Master. Jingqing said, "A fierce tiger does not..."
"Eating hidden meat. The Master said, "When the ancients spoke thus, was it clear before the phrase? Was it clear after the phrase? Do you understand?
You should realize it before you have even asked."
Small Assembly Sermon. [The Master] raised a case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is it like when the black bean has not yet sprouted?
Zhaozhou said, “It is good for making sauce. The Master said, “Shending does not say so. If you were to ask me, ‘What is it like when the black bean has not yet sprouted? I would say to him:”
"What can it possibly do? Thereupon, he spoke in verse: "When black beans have not yet sprouted, who says they are fit for making sauce?
When a monk of true character hears this, what kind of appearance would he have? Mount Hua’s peak stands upside down; Sumeru’s foot points straight up.
Do not say there is no Dharma to employ—just look at this very form! He then said: "The ancients spoke thus; Shending composed this verse thus."
Now tell me, does this accord with the ancients or oppose them? Do you understand? Even mixing sauces will not do.
What is the principle here? Only when you have realized it will you succeed. Take care! Case: A monk asked Xiangyan, "What is the Way?
Xiangyan said, "A dragon’s cry within a withered tree. The monk asked, "What is one who is on the Way? Xiangyan said, "The eyes within a skull. Later, there was a monk...
Jian asked Shishuang, "What is it like when a dragon roars within a withered tree? Shishuang said, "There is still joy remaining.
Jian said, "What is it like when there are eyes within a skull? Shishuang said, "There is still consciousness remaining.
The Master said, "Shishuang has consistently cleared away everything, making his living within the realm of emptiness. Later, a monk reported this to Caoshan. Caoshan said, "This Shishuang..."
An old śrāvaka held such a view. Caoshan had a verse that said: "The dragon’s roar from a withered tree is the true seeing of the Way;
the skull, devoid of consciousness, has its eyes first opened. When the faculty of consciousness is exhausted, all news is exhausted; how can a person distinguish the clear within the turbid?"
The Master said, "Understand it thus.
Small Lecture. He raised the following case: When a junior disciple was taking his leave of National Teacher Niaoke, the Teacher asked, "Where are you going?
The disciple replied, "I am going to study the Buddha-dharma. Niaoke said, "As for the Buddha-dharma, I have a little bit here too. The junior disciple then asked:
"What is the Buddha-dharma of the Master? [The Master] reached for a tuft of cloth on his body, held it up to show him, and then blew upon it.
The junior monk suddenly attained great enlightenment. The Master then reached for the tuft of cloth on his body and presented it to the assembly;
he followed this by giving a blow and said, "Do you understand? In the future, do not let me down. Take care."
Small Assembly (Xiaocan). [The Master] raised the case: Layi’s First Seat led the assembly up to Shimen. The Gatekeeper said, “Before the ten-thousand-fathom peak, the stone ox roars;
what is the meaning of piercing the clouds and crossing the waters? Layi had no reply. The Gatekeeper said, “The mountain monk’s duties as abbot are great;
go to the meditation hall. Later, Shimen brought this up and asked the monks to offer a word. He said, “I have long heard of the Master,” and added, “Seeking the Way and searching for...”
Master Ming understood the essential meaning. He realized the source and manifested a wondrous capacity.
He said, "At that time, if the first seat had been able to utter a word of concealment, I would not have regarded him as a student. The Master said, "I did not call him a student."
"What kind of person would you call him? Do you understand? Holding hands, we walk together upon the path of no interval. The Master raised [a case], saying:

An ancient said, "Wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and streams, seeking teachers and visiting paths for the sake of Zen study—since I have recognized the road to Caoxi, I know that birth and death are no longer relevant.
What is the road to Caoxi? A monk said: "It is like one who has attained it drinking water."
[The student] asked, "To whom did you explain this meaning? The Master said, "I know. [The student] said, "I am just like that; what is your intention, Master?
The Master said, "Go out of the Sangha Hall and enter the Buddha Hall," and then he descended from his seat.
