In the past, five hundred sons of elders from the city of Vaiśālī each held a parasol made of the seven precious gems and came to where the Buddha was.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he caused all those jeweled parasols to merge into a single canopy that pervaded everywhere.
It covers the trichiliocosm. Can all you people still believe in it? It is not only the ancients;
everyone today possesses this one canopy. Have you ever even caught a glimpse of it?

If you can catch a glimpse of it, then every step is nothing other than the profound path, and every word is entirely the turning of the Dharma wheel. If this is not yet so, then although this mountain monk is old and clumsy, [this] treasure...
He stood for a long time to assist in proclaiming [the Dharma].
Ascending the hall, the Old Man of Longmen said, "What is it? He further asked, "In the end, who is it? [The monk] replied, "It is you."
He asked again, "What have you accomplished during this summer retreat? The Master replied, "It is difficult to tell you;
I fear you would fall into mere views and hearing. He added, "But speak, there is no harm in it. The Master then held up his staff and said, "To have seeing and hearing is the way of ordinary people;
to have neither seeing nor hearing is the way of the Two Vehicles. Is there anyone who recognizes this? After a long silence, he said, "A pair of mandarin ducks."
"Yang Xiu finished her embroidery for you to see; she did not pass the golden needle to anyone else.
*Chan*. The *Botian* memorial arrived. He ascended the hall. After concluding the expression of gratitude for the imperial favor, he raised the following case:

"Baizhang Huishang said to the assembly, 'You all shall cultivate the fields for me, and I will explain a great principle to you. When the assembly had finished cultivating the fields, they requested the Master to speak of the Great Meaning."
[The Master] spoke of the meaning. Baizhang rose, extending his hands and stretching his limbs. "The ancients attained such directness; do you understand the place of their such expedient means?
Baizhang expounded the Great Meaning; the toil involved is well known. At Longmen there was no fixed principle; the assembly was free from doubt.
The Emperor’s power weighs heavily upon heaven and earth; the Ruler’s grace descends like rain and dew. Is there anyone who..."

A question was asked. [The Master] slightly raised his eyebrows from beyond the clouds. "Why did you raise your eyebrows? After a long silence, he said, "Everlasting spring throughout the ten thousand ages.
Ascending the hall, as soon as the drum sounded, the Dharma meaning was already complete. The assembly came forward, having followed the light until now.
I, the Mountain Man, hold high the ancestral seal; may all of you together set aside your doubts. You must truly overturn the mountains and empty the lakes; by all means, do not seek after branches.
Picking up a leaf, he said: "The reason I say this is that those gathered here are for you who are in the Sangha hall;

those gathered here are for you who are in the private quarters. Do you understand? It is well to study with spiritual teachers everywhere; cease using your former intellectual interpretations of Chan."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The people of Jambudvīpa in the south are mostly noisy and chaotic. Those in the Heaven of No-Thought and the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven have the most sluggish faculties.
Their speed differs as much as heaven and earth; it is difficult to exchange their defilement for purity. Two pieces of five-hundred-cash coins are originally but one string.
String! String! A mute claps his hands and calls out at the top of his voice; the deaf man hears him but feigns ignorance. Heaven!"
The next day, at midnight, Master Zhizhe was lecturing on *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation). The assembly asked, "How is this principle?
After a long silence, he said, "Look."

The donor invited [the Master] to ascend the hall. He raised the following case: When Elder Master Duan resided at Yuan Tong, Yang Cigong and Guo Gongfu would frequently come to inquire about this Way.
Later, when they traveled to Huainan, they constantly sought the essentials of the Dharma.
One day, when Gongfu visited him, Elder Master Baiyun ascended the hall and said: "Previously, I was visited by the great scholar Cigong; for his sake, I..."
Master Tang once recited this once. Today, as Gongfu has arrived, I cannot conceal it; let me recite it once more for you.
These words are truly extraordinary: "The Great Man above, Qiu Yi Ji; he transformed three thousand, seventy scholars."
"You are but a young man. You have eight or nine sons. Your son Jia Zuoren—can he be said to know propriety? Thereupon, he descended from his seat.

"The assembly, though these words may seem coarse and shallow, their principle is in fact most profound. If you do not understand 'The Great Man Above' (Shang Daren), how can you enter the gate of the Sage Confucius?

How can you master the Six Classics, the histories, the works of the hundred schools, and the Odes and Documents? Even if one’s status and reputation are illustrious and successful, if one does not understand 'The Great Man Above,' it is as if [one knows nothing]."
How can one assist the state and bring peace to the realm, so that merit is accomplished and one may withdraw from office?

As for those of the various crafts and arts, the common folk who carry goods for sale, the young children, and the supreme beings—how do they achieve their tasks? Even the mountains, forests, rivers, and seas; the sun, moon, and stars;
and the sages above and the ordinary people below—even these cannot be established by the supreme being. O Great Assembly, how wonderful is this supreme being!
"Do you understand? If a disciple of the Confucian school could recognize this, they would be the foremost person to break the cassia branch and ascend the examination hall.

[The Master] descends from his seat. He ascends the hall and says: "Master Sanping said: 'This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing. The Master says: "Taking earth and molding it into incense."
"Furthermore, there is no sound or form to present to you. The Master said, "People dwell upon old thoughts.

"If within this one understands and there is nothing remaining," the Master called to the assembly, saying, "The place where you stand is solitary and precarious. Essence and function are neither obstructed nor divided.

The Master said, "Go around the hall and observe. He then descended from his seat. After the assembly had finished their circuit of the hall, he spoke to them again, asking, "Is there anyone who understands? He added, "Understand!"
"Is it so? The assembly had no reply. The Master said, "Fools! Fools!
A letter from the Venerable Sīti of Huanglong Mountain arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "The mind of the dead heart has already died; the death of the heart arises from life.
Breaking off the horns of Huanglong, he turns his body over and walks upon the earth. This old fellow has always worn his robe backward."
Wearing a common shirt and carrying his straw hat slung backward, he was coarse and blunt in speech yet gentle and harmonious at heart. He inspected monastic communities and rebuked his students;

though he transmitted the Way of Huìtáng, he favored the Chan of Yúnmén. He used scolding the wind and scolding the rain as his method for training disciples, and planting vegetables and herbs as his daily tasks.
He brought about calamities and inflicted misfortune, being seldom joyful and often wrathful; when foolish people saw him, they would huddle together in fear.
The eyebrows. The Wise One nodded his head in agreement. To go when one wishes to go—truly a master! His leaping forth was originally that of a Miao man;
in sleep, he lost the Old Man Sishin. Alas, how lamentable! A misfortune for the Dharma-gate.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Empty names and empty forms are like echoes in a valley or reflections in a mirror. To discard them without cultivation—how could that clarify their illusory and false nature?
If you do not exert yourself while young, you will be filled with regret in old age. Reflect on this in stillness and weigh it according to your own capacity.

As the ancient masters said: 'It is like an old man of a hundred years performing songs and dances; how could this be the play of a child? Great assembly, do you understand why he spoke thus? He struck the gavel once.
An old man performs a song and dance. Tilting his head and lowering his brows, he listens to the rhythm of the drums.

Although he understands the beat clearly in his mind, his hands and feet are slow and his efforts grow increasingly arduous. He then rises and dances, saying, "Do you understand? It is difficult for an old man to act like a youth. He descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single leaf falls, and all under heaven is spring. There is no path for thought; such laughter kills people!
Below is heaven, above is earth—these words do not enter the minds of those following the current trends. South becomes north, east becomes west; movement becomes stillness, joy becomes sorrow."
"A snake's head and a scorpion's tail—let us test this once. "A live sparrow in a fierce tiger’s mouth. What kind of talk is that? Return to the hall. Entering the hall, he said:
"The eyebrows and eyelashes are most intimately related; the nostrils and lips are neighbors. Why do these closest things not see one another?
It is simply because they are of one body, which is the entire person."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and struck it once. Then, looking around, he said, "Staff! Staff!
You have no administrative duties to occupy your mind, nor do you suffer from illness or pain; yet you are so dark and gaunt—why is this?
He took up the staff and laughed heartily, saying, "What words are these? To see in form or seek in sound is to walk a deviant path. Formerly, Linji...
Because of this, Deshan realized the Dharma and attained the vision of truth; later, illustrious masters of clear eyes relied upon it to guide and deliver sentient beings.
Have you not seen how, during a communal work session, Huangbo said to Linji, "I have gained the full strength of this staff"?
Linji stepped forward, snatched the staff away, and pushed Huangbo down. Huangbo then said, "Help me up!"
"Come! Help me up! At that moment, a monk stepped forward to assist him, saying, "How can you, Master, tolerate such an impertinent, crazed fellow acting with such insolence?
Baizhang then struck that monk several times. Linji then cried out, "Heaven!"
"O Heavens! Great Assembly! That staff which was then in my hands is now in Longmen’s hands.
He then raised it, called to the assembly, and said, "Is there anyone here who possesses the skillful means of Linji? Come forth! Come forth! Longmen, however, let it go;
he then cast down the staff, threw his body flat on the ground, and said, "If there is anyone who can support me, come forth! Liang...
Jiuzhou said, "Since there is no one like Linji and no one to help him up, Longmen rises and falls by himself;
what use is there in that? Return to the hall. He then descended from his seat.
When Master Ganlu entered the mountains, he ascended the hall and said: "If Bodhidharma had not come to the land of Tang, the earth would have been eternal and the heavens everlasting.

If the Second Patriarch had not gone to the Western Heaven, the mountains would be green and the waters clear. When the dragon roars, mist arises; when the tiger howls, the wind is born. Autumn rains hang from the void."
Floating clouds obscure the sun. Do those people with eyes still see? Do those with ears still hear? Since they possess both seeing and hearing, what is delusion and what is awakening?
What constitutes the conditions, and what constitutes the objects of perception?

If you wish to understand the principle of delusion and awakening, rising and sinking, you must ultimately return to your own fundamental teacher and the Way of the Buddhas of the past. As for the physical body, its form belongs to the four great elements; as for the nature of the mind—
They return to the six sense objects. The four great elements are each separate in essence; who is it that brings them together? O Great Assembly:

since body and mind are already like this, what exactly is it that exists now? Lately, those who study the Way have all been rushing about with words and phrases, citing and discussing matters of antiquity and the present, yet they are entirely unclear regarding their own fundamental task.
Consequently, the True Teaching has grown thin and the Dharma has become diluted.

We are deeply moved. It is our great good fortune that you, Venerable Master, have arrived. We humbly beseech you to thunder forth the tide of your voice, reveal the true purport, tear away the heavy cataracts, and manifest the pearl within the robe.
The fourfold assembly bows with utmost sincerity; we cannot bear to refrain from this earnest request.
The posthumous letter from Master Huanglong Linyuan arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "In the past, he inscribed the 'Continuation of the Orthodox' (Zhengxu);
now, he reveals the true return. This is the single path to Nirvana; both practice and teaching lead directly to it. He brightly lit the lamp of Linji and wondrously sang the Way of Huanglong.
The empty ocean has long been clear and still, yet the surging waves are now vast and boundless. Transversely swallowing the great sea, he rides high upon the iron boat. [He remained] hidden.

To manifest their common source: that which unfolds and rolls up without limit—can it be anything other than the spiritual source? The Chan Master dwells on the ground of ultimate realization and abides in the field of original enlightenment.
Although he manifests birth, there is in fact no birth to be manifested; although he manifests extinction, there is in fact no extinction to be manifested.
It is luminous and profound, profoundly and luminously so; true transformation does not shift, so from what direction could there be appearance or disappearance? What...

His final testament served as an instruction; his true message was heard by all. Having brought his life’s work from beginning to end, this single period of his career may now be said to be concluded.

As for myself, at the start of my travels in former years, I encountered him in Longshu. He granted me the friendship of a half-familiarity, and our spirits were so attuned that we felt a deep resonance.

Although it was like jade hidden within the mountains of Jing, I had already met one who possessed true knowledge of its worth. Subsequently, it was as if a pearl were split from the belly of an oyster, or a sword obtained upon boarding a boat. (Ouyang)
Our meeting once again on this peak fulfills our long-cherished wishes even more; our joy at this wondrous occasion is as if we were joined by matching tally-sticks.

From that first meeting until now, during these thirty years, our principles have accorded like a shared breeze and our sublime resonance has been uninterrupted. Why then must we part so suddenly? That you have specifically sent me this letter moves me deeply;

my thoughts dwell upon both the living and the deceased, and this feeling grows ever more poignant. Nevertheless, such is the case: the Buddhas are inconceivable, and they do not permit one to remain forever.
World-honored One, let the great assembly reflect deeply: in the end, it is only this [the Dharma] that is so. Thus, when Ziqi passed away, Boya broke his strings;

this was surely because he grieved that there was no one who understood him as a connoisseur of music. How much more so for this Ultimate Way, which transcends perception and surpasses emotion—there is nothing more harmonious than its accord with the heart.
What indeed can be said? Long ago, someone asked Changsha, "Where has Nanquan gone after his passing? Changsha said, "When Shitou was a novice monk, he studied under the Sixth Patriarch.
[The questioner] said, "I am not asking about when Shitou was a novice monk studying under the Sixth Patriarch;
I am asking where Nanquan has gone after his passing. Changsha said, "Let him reflect upon it for himself. The Master [said]: "He taught him to seek it out."
He then laughed heartily and said, "Do you understand? Do you understand? When the water rises, the boat floats higher; when the mud is deep, the Buddha is large. Come together before the altar;
there is no need for further observation or listening."
The posthumous letter from Master Fojian of Jiangshan arrived. He ascended the hall and said: "Aha! Aha! Elder brother, elder brother!
You emerged before me; you have departed ahead of me. Aha! Aha! Elder brother, elder brother! You emerged before me, allowing me to drive side-by-side and shoulder-to-shoulder;
you have departed ahead of me, leaving me with but a single wing to soar alone. Do you not think of this sea of suffering? [He continued: "The multitudes..."

Those lost have not yet been delivered; how much less so for those of profound learning from the Five Lakes who carry their books upon bamboo frames to attend your assemblies? If you suddenly abandon the boat and oars, who will ferry them across the vast river?
Yet the principles of the Buddha-dharma naturally possess their own causes and conditions; this is simply because sentient beings lack protection, brought about by their meager merit.

Forever separated from the monastic community, the torch of the Dharma has no successor. I have heard that the Tathāgata manifested his parinirvāṇa beneath the twin śāla trees, and I have also heard that Bodhidharma departed for the West with a single shoe.
From Buddha to Buddha, from patriarch to patriarch, their Way has continued unceasingly; how much more so in the case of my dharma-brother Fojian of Zhongshan!
The wondrous capacity [of the Buddha] is uninterrupted; appearing and disappearing in response to conditions, coming and going through birth and death—what concern is this of mine?

Yet I am most deeply attuned to the Master’s school; among the ranks of the geese, we are as brothers with hands joined, our friendship forged in metal and stone, and our spirit thinning the clouds and heavens.
How can I bear to hear these lingering echoes? Reflecting on this decaying body, I realize it is not solid. With one heart and shared illumination, what more need be said?
I still remember when the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe, what other Dharma has the World-Honored One transmitted?
Kāśyapa replied, "Ānanda. Ānanda responded with an assent. Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner in front of the gate."
"Topple the banner pole before the gate! O Great Assembly, if you do not possess this public case, birth and death will burn fiercely.
Master Baiyun said: 'Beyond the golden robe, what else is transmitted? Responding to a brother's call—how could it be by chance? Topple the banner pole before the gate!"
"Exempted from instruction, as before, leaning by the wall. O assembly, do you understand? Leaning by the wall, leaning by the wall;
within the light of quiescent extinction, one pays homage to the white lotus."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The mind-seal transmitted by Great Master Bodhidharma—look, look! It has been swept away until nothing remains. Is there anyone here now who can see Great Master Bodhidharma?
If you can see him, only then will you understand how to take responsibility for it. If you have not yet attained such vision, you must strictly avoid identifying with anything.
Therefore, the True Lineage is plain and simple, while heterodox paths are towering and imposing. Long ago, Attendant Wang visited Master Muzhou."
One day, the Governor asked, "For what reason did you enter the hall so late today? The attendant replied, "I was watching people playing polo with horses, which is why I arrived late.
The Governor said, "Do people play polo, or do horses play polo? The attendant replied, "People play polo. The Governor asked, "Are the people tired? The attendant replied, "They are.
The Governor asked, "Are the horses tired? The attendant replied, "They are. The Governor asked, "Is the pillar tired? The attendant was left speechless and at a loss.
"Yes. He returned to his private quarters and suddenly realized it during the night. The next day, he went to see State Preceptor Zhou and said, "I have understood yesterday's matter.
Zhou asked, "Is the pillar exhausted? The attendant replied, "It is exhausted. Thereupon, Zhou granted him permission. This is the essential tenet of Master Bodhidharma:
the pillar does not understand how to play the ball; why then would it be exhausted? Is there anyone who can clarify this?
"Ma! When the person is exhausted and the horse is exhausted, that is not yet true exhaustion; the exhaustion of the pillar is the true exhaustion.
It is well to realize non-arising beneath the words; do not seek measurements within the words. Had Baizhang not possessed his pair of deaf ears, how could Linji have received the three blows?
They have taken their karmic consciousness entirely as a transmitted tradition; nowadays, people discard this Way like excrement. [He stood for a long time.]
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In the past, there were two people, a head official and a subordinate, who both served Avalokiteśvara at the same time.
One day, the subordinate stole the head official's money and fled. The head official burned incense and prayed to Avalokiteśvara, saying, 'I pray that you may allow me to catch the subordinate.
The subordinate also burned incense and prayed to Avalokiteśvara, saying, 'I pray that the head official may not see me. At that moment, Avalokiteśvara—"
To save whom is it? It is merely to save the head. Yet, if one goes against the subordinate, one merely saves the subordinate; if one goes against the head, one merely saves the head.
If one were to save them all at once, the matters would be in great contradiction. Master Bian of Shan-nan said: "If you wish to practice the Great Way..."
"Taking three steps as one leap. O assembly, these are fine words; I only fear that people will approach them with a coarse mind.
Examine them closely, yet you will find they are difficult to penetrate. Let me analyze them for you point by point. If anyone wishes to understand, they must first recognize Avalokiteśvara.
Do you wish to recognize Avalokiteśvara? It is the heart of great compassion. Furthermore, you must know the heart of great compassion.
From what source does it flow forth? Those who listen to the Dharma clearly and vividly at present do so without deliberate intent, yet from this flow forth ten thousand schools of thought.

If one recognizes the head of the tethering rope, only then will one understand how to apply that rope. Not only does one know how to apply the rope, but one also recognizes the end of the tethering rope.
This "end of the tethering rope" is the end of the rope belonging to the head; apart from the head of the tethering rope, there is no separate end of the rope.
If you recognize Guanyin thoroughly, you will understand that the "subordinate" (shìxià) is made by the subordinate;

not only is the subordinate made by the subordinate, but one also recognizes the "head of the subordinate" (shítóu). This head of the subordinate is the very head of that which subordinates; apart from the subordinate, there is no separate head of the subordinate.
If it is thus, then "head of the subordinate" and "subordinate" are merely empty names; both the subordinate and the head of the subordinate are entirely... [empty].

There is no place of reliance. With a fiercely blazing heart of great compassion, one is uniquely liberated. Having already recognized the master and having also recognized the servant, one must further recognize the money and silks.
When the master sees them, they are the master’s money and silks; when the servant sees them, [they are the servant’s].

This refers to the money and silks belonging to the subordinate messenger. As for the head messenger, his money and silks are separate from those of the subordinate; they do not belong to one another.

One must understand that the money and silks of the head messenger have no concern with the affairs of the subordinate, and the money and silks of the subordinate likewise have no concern with the affairs of the head messenger;

each remains distinct. Although they do not intersect, the money and silks of the head messenger are themselves the money and silks of the subordinate, and the money and silks of the subordinate... [are likewise].
"Silk" refers to the money for the head of the messenger; it is one and the same thing. If it is thus, they are identical;
if it is thus, they are distinct—both are the functioning of the Great Compassionate Mind. Thus, one knows the money and the silk; furthermore, one must clearly understand gain and loss.
When the head of the messenger loses the wealth, it is the head of the messenger who loses it; when the subordinate messenger gains the wealth, it is the subordinate messenger who gains it. Gain.
The loss does not reside within the portion of another. Thus, when the head is lost, it is the time when the handle is gained;
when the handle is gained, it is the time when the head is lost. Although gain and loss differ, they are not distinct; though gain and loss appear separate, they are always the same.
How could there be some other entity that creates sameness or difference? Whether it be the head, whether it be the handle, or whether it be the coin—[it is all one].
Silk. Whether gain or loss, when each and every thing is clearly understood, only then is one named Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. An ancient said:
"Gain, loss, right, and wrong are the wisdom of all Buddhas; if one person lacks the eye of mind, their ears will be deaf."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In Aparagoyānī the drum is beaten; in Jambudvīpa we ascend the hall. The great assembly from the ten directions has arrived together and heard it equally.
The wild guest extols it, and this sound pervades the ten directions, shattering all hearing, seeing, form, and fragrance.
It is truly laughable that Śākyamuni Old Man casually shook the earth and emitted light. Great assembly, return to the hall."
When Master Xu Gong entered the mountains and ascended the hall, he asked: "Where can one seek thorough penetration? The root of doubt is itself extraordinary.
Suddenly realizing that mind is Buddha, one abruptly perceives that the ocean is not salty. On the path of Sudhana’s pavilions, one advances daily toward the crimson heavens.

While ordinary people say it has not yet occurred, I say the Way is constantly revealed. The assembly, it is like one's own face—how could one distinguish its own beard and eyebrows? It is also like...
The eye-faculty does not see its own surface. If it were to see itself, it would no longer be the original head. If the eye-faculty were to see itself, the eye would become identical to its object;

this is why Shigong could find no place to strike when shooting at himself, thereby realizing his entire body. When Pang Gong was asked about the mind, [he replied: "The mind is like the moon reflected in water."
Sucking it all up in a single gulp, one finally attains the truth; this is what is called the undertaking of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Has it not been said: "The great man wields the sword of wisdom; the blade of *prajñā* has the brilliance of a diamond.
It not only shatters the minds of externalists, but long ago it struck down the courage of the celestial Māras. Is this not precisely seeing one's original face and realizing the pure [nature]?
Because his Dharma-eye is pure, he is entitled to be called a Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa).

On this day, we were graced by the arrival of the Palace Attendant (Daifu) of the Imperial Household, whose banners entered the mountains to visit these springs and rocks. Recently, I, a mountain-dweller, followed the example of former virtuous masters and established a field for the giving of the Dharma.

Having resided at this mountain for several years, I have gradually supported its restoration and renovation so that it may serve as a place for practitioners of Chan to cultivate their minds. [The laborers...]

The work being completed, I have ventured to disturb your hearing and sight with this request for a grand and magnificent composition to manifest its imperishability and to benefit those who come after.
I am deeply honored by your gracious response; it is a most great fortune.

Although I, a mountain monk, do not understand the subtleties of doctrine, observing this excellent work, I find it rare in recent times. Is this not a blessing for this land and this mountain, but for all under heaven?
This is a great blessing for the monastic community. Formerly, Layman Xiang lived on forest fruits and drank from mountain streams;

he set down his realizations in writing and sought the certification of the Great Master the Second Patriarch, saying: "Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To toy with shadows is to weary the form;
one does not realize that the form is the root of the shadow. To raise a sound is to seek to stop the echo; one does not know that the sound is the source of the echo. To eliminate afflictions...

Yet they proceed toward Nirvana—this is like seeking a shadow while discarding its form, or seeking the fruit of Buddhahood apart from sentient beings; it is like searching for an echo while remaining silent.
You should know that what is gained is nothing gained, and what is lost is nothing lost. Before I have had the honor of paying you a visit, I have briefly set forth this meaning;
I humbly hope for your reply. The Second Patriarch, the Great Master, replied: "I have fully examined the intent of your letter; it is all as it truly is. It is profoundly subtle."
Their underlying principle is ultimately no different. Originally deluded, one mistook the *maṇi* jewel for rubble; suddenly awakening, one realizes it is a genuine pearl.
Ignorance and wisdom are equal and without distinction; you should know that all phenomena are thus. Out of compassion for those who hold these two views, [I have spoken].
I extend my words and wield my brush to compose this book, observing that one’s own body and the Buddha are no different; why then need one seek that which is beyond remainder?
When the layman received these verses, he joyfully attended upon him. O virtuous ones, the ancients awakened to the mind and set it forth in written characters.
"This is truly rare. Do you still see the matters realized and attained by the Second Patriarch, the Great Master, and the layman?
After a long silence, he said: "Though vast eons may come to an end, this culture shall not perish. He remained standing for a long while.
Ascending the hall: To deliberate and then seek liberation, to reflect and then seek understanding—how can a solitary lamp rival the radiance of the great sun?
It is not the mind; it is not the Buddha. For your sake, I sweep away the den of spirits. A falcon soaring through the sky flies into the clouds;
a thousand miles, ten thousand miles, is but a single bound. *Alalala!* He descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall: Without giving rise to indolence, there is no further cultivation; truly there are no words, and truly there is no seeking.
Seizing the food from the mouths of hungry men, driving the oxen from the hands of the plowmen—truly joyful! Free from a hundred worries! From this point on, one does not return;
yet if one returns, it is attained. On the five lakes, wind and waves surge to the heavens.
When Chen Yuming returned the *Buddhapiṭaka-hṛdaya-sūtra* (Heart Sūtra of the Buddha’s Crown) and requested the Master to ascend the hall, [the Master said]:
"Oṃ cilin oṃ cilin. Oṃ bulin oṃ bulin. Great assembly, what kind of speech is this? What is its underlying principle? Is there anyone here who understands it?
If you say it is speech, it does not even constitute speech. If you say it possesses a principle, it likewise does not constitute one."
In principle, it may be said that words cannot reach it and conceptual discrimination cannot grasp it;
the ancient sages called it "esoteric speech" (*guhyavākya*) and also "true word" (*mantra*). All sounds and voices arise from this, and all verbal teachings emerge from this.
While I was recently examining the scriptures, I obtained the seven-syllable *dhāraṇī*, which can extinguish a thousand calamities and bring about the fulfillment of ten thousand virtues. Now...
He recited this seven-syllable dhāraṇī once for all the people. "Listen attentively," he said, and they remained silent.
He bent his fingers from the first to the seventh and asked, "Did you hear it? Fearing that some might not have heard, he recited it once more. Again they were silent.
He bent his fingers from one to seven and asked, "Did you hear it? "O Great Assembly, only the Buddha and..."
Only the Buddha can know this; all other sentient beings are utterly at a loss.

There is a skillful means, called the "Repetition of Verses," by which I shall now once again clearly explain these seven characters of the mantra. This concludes the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-hṛdaya-sūtra* and the vow for the fast.
O Great Assembly, do you understand the essential meaning within it? Wait, as this mountain monk shall explain it for you. One character.
One must know where the characters land. If one discusses the Buddha, it is simply the person themselves; there is nothing else.
If one discusses the crown, day and night it radiates light, illuminating the realm before one. If one discusses the mind, when observed it has no form, yet when functioning it is profound.

If one discusses the sutras, they can be understood and spoken, yet they are not sound. If one discusses the fast, all that is done and enacted is in perfect harmony. If one discusses vows, they are like...

Dwelling within the Longmen Courtyard, if one speaks of realization, there is no anxiety and no doubt; the mind is luminously clear. When the mind is luminously clear, blessings and longevity increase while calamities diminish.
To measure its merit, it is vast and inconceivable: Mount Sumeru is not large, and the vast ocean is small.
What this mountain monk has just spoken is the True Word (*mantra*). Worldly people know only that there are words, but they do not know that there is the Truth. If not...
To know the truth is to realize that all spoken words are false. What, then, is called a "True Word" (mantra)? Because it can give rise to ten thousand schools of thought, it is called a True Word.
It is also named the King of Samādhis; it is also named the Ten-Thousand-Syllable Crown; it is also named the Subtle and Wondrous Phrases; it is also named the Great Secret Dhāraṇī.
To receive and uphold it with a sincere heart brings great spiritual efficacy—namely, this seven-character incantation of the mountain monk. It is...
Counting on his fingers, he said: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. To recite and uphold this is entirely secret.
It is like a person entering a mountain of jewels in person; all rare and wondrous treasures emerge from it. He stood for a long time.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Can the Way be learned? In truth, it cannot be learned. Can the mind be awakened? In truth, it cannot be awakened.
When there is neither learning nor awakening, the true mechanism is fully revealed. The bright moon shines upon the Sahā world; floating life passes from dawn to dusk.
If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams are dispelled; throughout antiquity and today, there is no gate for entering or exiting. He then called to the assembly, saying: "What is this?"
Ascending the hall, the mountain monk briefly takes this seat so that the great assembly may forever cease their doubts. Each one is a golden-maned lion;

in coming and going, they roar with full majesty. Linji’s high-voiced successive shouts and Deshan’s brandishing of the staff and heavy blows—though there be even a word or a phrase, it shall never be made into another path.
Great assembly, shake off your spirits and put an end to your drowsiness! Act!

"What is this sequence of arising? You have merely confused yourself. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, do I seek for people to arrive, or do I not seek for people to arrive? Try to examine this."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised [this story]: Dongshan said to the assembly, "Brothers, at the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, if you go east or west, you must go to a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass.
He further asked, "But as for that place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass—how does one go there?
When Shishuang heard this, he said, "Stepping out the door is already grass. A monk cited this.
[This resembles] Dongshan. Dongshan said, "How many people can there be within the Great Tang?
The Master said: "Stepping out the door, it is already grass. The old man of Longmen is left idle. Going north to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, Coming south to climb Mount Wulao.
My hair has turned gray and white; I regret not having returned sooner. Standing alone before the autumn wind, I gaze across the river islands with longing. Be well—there is no need for more."
Seeking further, he ascended the hall and said:
"What thing comes thus? Do not hang a bright mirror upon a high terrace. What thing goes thus?
Clearly, there is no need to point it out head-on. To point it out clearly makes it even more difficult; the limpid pool does not permit the blue dragon."
"The dragon coils. "If you understand it thus, you are far too reckless. He then clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "The world of Vairocana in the Flower Treasury is vast.
He then ascended the hall and said, "What a fine group! Does anyone among them see what is within that group? If one is truly among them, they will surely..."
He observed what was occurring therein. After a long while, he laughed heartily and said, "Do you understand?

If it were otherwise, even if one possesses the affairs within, they would not originally be a person of that inner circle; and even if one were such a person, they would not originally have mastered those affairs.
Once one has mastered the affairs within and become a person of that inner circle, what further cause for worry could there be? Have you not seen [the story of] Mount Mushi?"

It is said: "The phrase with a sentence and the phrase without a sentence are like a vine leaning against a tree. At one time, someone asked, "When the tree reaches its end and the vine withers, what then?
Guishan laughed heartily. Furthermore, Qianfeng addressed the assembly, saying, "The Dharma-body has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance.
Only when each of these is thoroughly penetrated can one sit securely. Yunmen stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "As for the person within the hermitage..."
"Why do you not see what is outside the hermitage? Ganyue let out a great laugh. "The assembly, if someone were to ask:
'What was the intent of these two venerable elders? Longmen clapped his hands and laughed aloud. After a long while, he said:
'You all, why do you not set down your bags for me and loosen your bellies to let out a laugh?'"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Śākyamuni Buddha has already attained perfect enlightenment; Maitreya Bodhisattva shall descend to be born in the future.
Old Lu carried [the Dharma] across the southern ridges; Bodhidharma brought it to this eastern land. Each claimed that the saving of sentient beings was complete and their vows were fulfilled."
"How is it that the six realms and four modes of birth still persist? How is it that the mountains of earth and stone have not yet crumbled?
Why do we not encounter the Pure and Wondrous Land? Is it because our power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is insufficient? Is it because the fruits of karma (*karmaphala*) are difficult to exhaust?

Or is there some other principle at work? Can anyone here sever [this cycle]? If you do not sleep in the same bed, how can you know if the lining of the quilt is worn through? Return to the hall; let us go drink tea."
Ascending the hall, he said: “Śāriputra did not understand sitting in the crag; when spring comes, the peach trees are red one after another.
The celestial mechanism is leaked, leaving no place to seek it; it is all because the lamp-stand hangs the lantern. Lamp-stand, lamp-stand—yet it possesses an ancient style.
Lamp-stand, lamp-stand—well able to provide guidance. One day, the nun will be a daughter; in the hall, having attained great enlightenment, go drink tea.”
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind is the root; dharmas are the dust. These two are like scars upon a mirror. When the stains of the scars are exhausted, the light begins to appear.
When both mind and dharmas are extinguished, the nature is the truth. When the faculties and their objects have ceased, the light of the mirror manifests before one.
But when both mind and dharmas are extinguished, what is it then? "The crimson body is free of delusive thoughts; the eyes hear and the ears see, detached from攀缘 (pān-yuán—clinging conditions)."
Ascending the hall, he went out the gate to welcome the rising sun; already he felt himself shrouded in mist and fog.

Braving the moonlight, he returned gazing at the mountains; heavy dew drenched his meditation robe. His heart was silent and still, his steps slow and measured. On the holeless flute, he blew again and again: *li li la, la li li*.
The traveler, hearing this for the first time, has his travel-sleeves moistened; the beautiful lady still sings, her jade brows lowered. Listen further, do not be suspicious.
What song is this? Return to your hall.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A true person who has reached home—what leisure have they to discuss 'home'?
A person who has attained definitive realization—how could they point to what was realized? To discuss home or to discuss realization is the way of commoners and peddlers;
to have neither realization nor home is truly the state of a wandering and forlorn child. Why not arouse a resolute will and open a mind of extraordinary penetration? Observe his every action."
"Go upstream! Do not vainly follow the vulgar and base. Each and every word must flow from within your own breast;
only when it can cover heaven and earth for me will it suffice. If you all act like this, your study of the Way will remain as distant as a donkey’s years."
Ascending the hall: The Sea Gate Mountains, the Chang’an Road—vastly stretching mists and waters join with the green grass.
A traveler atop a tower, a youth upon a horse; hearing the falling plum blossoms, they grieve for their hometown. The spring wind passes by, flowers fly away until they are gone;
butterflies flutter gracefully over the low wall. Listen further: what chapter is this? If you cannot understand it, go to the meditation hall.

In the ninth month of the eighth year of the Zhenghe era, he received an imperial edict to reside at Baoshan Temple in Hezhou. Upon ascending the hall, after the expression of gratitude for the imperial favor was completed, a monk asked:
"It is well known that from a thousand miles away one hears good news; but as for the matter of not traversing the journey, what is it like? The Master said: "Not hanging upon the three inches."
The student said, "A single bright moon shines upon the void; ten thousand miles of clear wind, the universe is vast. The Master said, "Yet there is still deliberation involved.
The student said, "If one suddenly encounters a fellow practitioner on the road and is questioned, what then? The Master said, "What difficulty is there in answering?"
A student stepped forward and said, "When the clouds leave the valley mouth, a thousand peaks show their splendor; when the moon reaches the heart of the sky, the four seas are bright.
The Master said, "Who is such a person? The Master spoke again, addressing the assembly: "Is it not here before us, at Longmen Mountain in Shuzhou?
Was it not just now by imperial decree that I was appointed to Baochan Temple in Hezhou, ordering me, this mountain monk, to go there to transmit the Dharma and serve as abbot? Furthermore—"
What is the transmitted Dharma? Do you wish to know the essential purport of the Buddha-dharma? Without leaving Longmen Mountain, you wish to see Baoshan Temple;
without leaving Baoshan Temple, you wish to see Longmen Mountain. Longmen Mountain is easy to see, but Baoshan Temple is difficult to see.
Is there anyone who can see Baoshan Temple? If you can understand this, then you possess the Buddha-dharma.

The Essential Meaning. If it has not yet been clarified, after a long silence, he says: "The Emperor’s power is as heavy as a mountain; the Ruler’s grace is as vast as the universe. Being without talent, how can I repay it?
At every place, my heart finds peace. He remains standing for a long time. Arriving at Baoshan, he enters the abbot's quarters. The Master takes his seat and says:
"In the past, Chan Master Dingming sat in meditation upon this peak, dwelling in the Great Samādhi. His compassionate salvation and great vows spread their benefits..."

On the other hand, this mountain monk, though unworthy, has followed in the footsteps of my predecessors and continued the bright flame for those who come after. Seizing the ten directions, I shall carry out the ancestral command.
As the drum sounds and I ascend the hall, you must all listen with focused attention.

Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The Sagely Emperor has bestowed upon us this famous mountain; the worthy Prime Minister has proclaimed the Imperial decree, commanding that I, a poor monk, shall transmit the Dharma and reside here as abbot.
Is there anyone among you who can shoulder this heavy responsibility? Come forward and speak. A monk asked:
"An ancient said, 'I borrow a question for a moment to serve as a screen. I do not know how this principle is to be understood. The Master said:
"What kind of mental activity is this? Jin said, "One might say: 'Holding a night-bright talisman in hand, how many know when the dawn breaks?
The Master said, "How many people have you asked about this? Jin said, "At this point, how many people have misunderstood it? The Master said, "And what about you, Dharma brother?
Jin said, "Thirty years from now, there will be someone who understands. The Master said, "That is still somewhat better."
A monk asked, "When a single speck of dust arises and the entire earth is fully contained within it, what then? The Master said, "Two specks of dust.
The monk pressed further, "If that is so, then the realms of boundless lands do not separate self and other by even a hair’s breadth;

ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from this very moment of thought. The Master said, "How do you perceive the affairs within Henshan County? The monk replied, "Mountains."
"The river and the great earth fully reveal the body of the Dharma King. The Master said, "This acharya is indeed worth discussing.
The Master spoke again, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes, but it is difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk. Can you discern this?
Before I came to this place, the Dharma seat of this mountain had long been vacant and the monastic community was not flourishing. At such a time, did you know Dingming Chan?"
"Is this Master your good spiritual friend? Since I have come to this place, the Dharma seat has first been opened and the monastic community has been re-established;
thus, it is certainly Master Dingming who is your good spiritual friend. Therefore it is said: "Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the nature and its characteristics abide eternally.
If you can understand and perceive it in this way, I say that the light of the Way is present. Long ago, there was...
A certain venerable elder, when the assembly had settled, rose and performed a dance, saying, "Do you all understand this meaning? The assembly remained silent.
Jì said, "This mountain monk does not abandon the Way and its teachings, yet manifests the affairs of an ordinary person. The Master then laughed heartily and said, "How extraordinary!
If it were Bāochán, he would not have acted thus. He then rose and performed a dance, addressing the assembly, saying, "Do you all understand?"
"I do not agree," he said. After a long silence, he continued, "Pure poverty brings eternal joy.
He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "Baoshan has only just settled here; it is utterly desolate. Under the white moon and clear breeze, the scene enters the painting.
Though there may be a thousand kinds of pleasure in the human world, none compare to this morning when everything is nothing. Thereupon, he laughed loudly and said, "A fine fellow!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The stone pagoda amidst the clouds rivals the stars. Master Dingming opens his mouth wide.
If you understand the meaning of these words, there is no need to travel the world with your satchel strapped on. He then struck the meditation staff once and said:
"A bird sings freely at the first light of dawn; a dog barks repeatedly upon meeting a stranger. He struck the staff again and said: "Return to the hall."
Ascending the hall, he said: "One knows only today and tomorrow, yet fails to realize that today is but the beginning of tomorrow.
Every matter seems as if pre-arranged; every arrow naturally hits the mark. That which is sweet is sweeter than yellow gall; that which is bitter is more bitter than white honey.
Having tasted such flavors," he said, dancing with his hands, "it is quite alright—*ra-ra-li-li*. He then descended from his seat.

On the first day of the first month, he ascended the hall. Striking once with his staff, he said: "Heaven obtains the One; the constellations Ox, Cow, Maiden, Void, Danger, Chamber, and Net-Ending obtain it.
Earth obtains the One; grasses, trees, mountains, rivers, and all soil and stone obtain it. The Ruler obtains the One; above, below, and in the four quarters, there is none equal to him.
He called to the assembly, saying: "Within the manifestation of the myriad phenomena, there is a single, perfectly luminous sphere."

Throughout the ages, there has been joy and glory, sorrow and grief; there have been enemies and kin, favor and adversity; there have been wealth and nobility, poverty and begging. Of these myriad forms and thousandfold variations, who is the one who orchestrates them?
They are like echoes in an empty valley, emerging in response to whatever conditions arise. Once the embroidery of the mandarin ducks is finished, it is left for you to behold.
The golden needle is not revealed; it is too subtle and dense. Baochan offers this exhortation: each of you must turn your heads back now.
Do not wait until the moment of departure to lament and chatter. Recognize the light of Mahāprajñā; ten thousand ages of eternity are but this very day. [Long pause.]
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Tathāgata has no two kinds of speech. How do you all understand the Tathāgata’s words? What are these two kinds of speech?
You must clearly grasp them before you can attain it. The first is divisive speech; the second is harmonious speech. The Tathāgata is devoid of these two."

This is called the speech of the Tathāgata. What is called divisive speech? When those who are able to hear the Dharma desire to listen and receive it, yet the one who preaches the Dharma does not reveal it to them—this is called divisive speech.

When the one who preaches the Dharma desires to reveal it, yet those who hear the Dharma do not desire to listen and receive it—this is called divisive speech. Although one speaks, there is no one capable of speaking [it].
It can be said that although one listens, there is neither a listener nor anything to be heard. One who attains such understanding is then called one who speaks words of reconciliation.
One should contemplate these words of division and words of reconciliation: are they one or two? Are they the same or different? Thus should they be realized.
One abandons divisive speech and shall attain harmonious speech. As for the Tathāgata, who is free from these two types of speech, he neither speaks nor listens.
Yet, this state of neither speaking nor listening also comprises two aspects: first, that of ordinary beings; second, that of noble wisdom.
Just as ordinary beings have nothing to reveal and nothing to receive, remaining in a state of profound darkness without awakening, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). It is also named...

It is because there is neither speaking nor listening. It is that which is reached by the two types of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). Having reached this state of neither speaking nor listening, one transcends the roles of host and guest and cuts off all practice and understanding.
Abiding spontaneously in the ground of ultimate reality is also called "neither speaking nor listening. Students should skillfully discern this.
Do not harbor divergent views; do not treat this with superficiality or lack of distinction.

[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "I cite the story of Zen Master Zhaozhou. One day, when the Prince of Zhao arrived, Zhaozhou did not descend from his meditation seat and asked, 'Do you understand? The Prince said, 'I do not understand.
Zhaozhou replied, 'Since my youth I have observed the fasts, yet my body has grown old; seeing people, I lack the strength to descend from my meditation seat. [He then] leaped down.
When Master Teng had an audience with Empress Wu Zetian, he looked up at her and asked, "Do you understand? The Empress said, "I do not understand.
Master Teng said, "This mountain monk observes the precept of silence. When National Teacher Huizhong saw Emperor Suzong, he pointed to his head and cap and asked, "Do you understand?
The Emperor said, "I do not understand. The National Teacher said, "The weather is cold; please do not take offense that I have not removed my cap. Monks, [consider this].

Do you understand the intent of these three people? It is like a precious boat reaching the shore; one has obtained great wealth and can cross over with abundance. It is like opening the bolt of a jade door;
yet to ascend the hall and enter the inner chamber, one must still remain outside the gate. How can one blame the jewels for being unable to enter?
To remain trapped in solitary poverty—is this the fault of the precious gems? Do you understand? Bian He had his feet cut off, yet he returned to his hall.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "When someone passes in front of you, you immediately know it is Zhang San or Li Si. But when they pass behind you, why can you not see them?
On this side of the wall, you clearly see a bench or a leaning board; on that side of the wall, why can you not discern anything?
If such is the case within the span of a few feet, how much more so across the ten directions of the world? If students of the Way do not understand this, they shall surely..."
"I know that the matter of our study has not yet been concluded. Time passes swiftly; it has already been ninety days since we entered this temple.
You practitioners from various districts who have resolved to serve as teachers—please broaden your minds and settle yourselves. Then, picking up his staff, he said:

"People from the four directions—east, west, south, and north—are most intimate despite the vastness of the earth and the distance to heaven. Mount Heng and Mount Tiantai connect with the imperial palace. With this, he snapped his fingers once.
[The Master] said: "Lightly snap your fingers; no need for effort. He then took up his staff and said: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the sun, moon, and stars;
grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—all are upon the tip of this staff. Do you see them? After a long silence, he said:
"With a hundred thousand strings of cash girding one's waist, riding a crane to Yangzhou. [He then] stood for a long time.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Zhaozhou had the story about eating porridge; it is indeed a fine story. That monk attained enlightenment on the spot. Do you understand?
The moment you lift your bowl and move your spoon and chopsticks, you have already missed the meaning of the ancients.
The Patriarch has the story of the wind and the banner; why is it that throughout the twelve periods of the day, all of you are like tigers looking at their own tails?"
"It is like water. National Teacher [Huai-rang] said, "There is the preaching of the Dharma by the insentient. According to you all, this should be clearly understood; why then do you not hear it?
If you can understand each and every point, then you are a practitioner of Chan who has found his true footing. Return to your hall.
Ascending the hall to pray for rain, Chan Master Dingming Miaoying preached the Dharma like clouds and rain.

It was not that people of the time did not hear it, nor was it that they were incapable of understanding his words. Such a singular, wondrous efficacy has endured through many cycles of cold and heat.
Even if one encounters withered seeds or scorched sprouts, he employs skillful means to rescue them all at once.
When Prefect Master Zeng and his attendants entered the mountains to pray for rain, he ascended the hall and said, citing the case where Official Liu Yu asked Yunju:
"Where does the rain come from? He replied, "It comes from where you, Official, ask. The Master said, "Where does the rain come from? There is no need to seek it out;
it fills the void, rescuing all that is withered and parched. It is surely a manifestation of wondrous response and spiritual penetration.
Your Excellency, Governor and Scholar, has truly brought this about. Is it not indeed for rain and for drenching? Who would not rejoice and find it good? Now, let us ask these people:"
“Rain of clarity, rain of renunciation, rain for the common people—will one surely obtain it? After a long silence, he struck his staff once and said, “Three.
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he struck his staff once and said, "Assembly! Why did you all hide yourselves inside the pillar last night?
And now that the sky has brightened and you have finished eating your gruel and come up here to listen to the examination of the mind, why are you standing on the balustrade?
Do you see? Even if you were to manifest such spiritual transformations as this, I would still ask further."
Master Yuntali ascended the hall and said:
"To the end of one's life, you insist on traveling as a wandering monk; you stubbornly seek to awaken to your original mind.
This is like drawing legs for a snake—it only exhausts your sinews and bones, bringing shame upon the deep waters of green mountains. Have you not seen how Old Man Deshan told you?"
“Even before he has stepped onto the gunwale, he deserves thirty blows. Everyone here, you too must show some spirit!
Even this rice-bag deserves thirty blows. He then struck his staff once and descended from the seat.
Retiring from Baoshan, he ascended the hall: "Departing once and returning once, cranes atop the pines; Half-open and half-closed, clouds above the ridges.
Leaning on my staff, standing alone beyond a thousand peaks, I offer only the Southern Mountain in prayer for the Sage Ruler."
When Prefect Qian submitted a memorial requesting that he reside again at Baoshan Temple, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:

"By imperial decree, I am once more summoned from my secluded life among the *bìluó* vines; there is no room for quietude—*svāhā*. My official robes and scholar’s cap are most shabby and unseemly, yet here I am, singing ‘Liluo, liluo’ before the people.
(He claps his hands once. "Liluo! (He claps again. He says: "Last year it was plum blossoms; this year it is willows."
The colors and fragrances remain as they were. People grow old; the waters flow ever on. To accord with the Way without artifice—this is the head.

[He] descended from his seat. Entering the hall, he raised the case: Master Lianhuafeng of Anzhai held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying, "When the ancients reached this point, why would they not consent to stay?
He said himself, "Because on that journey, one does not gain strength. Thus it was for twenty years. No...
People could understand these words. Later, an elder heard them cited and said, "It is so, yet there is still room for further progress.
A monk asked, "How does one progress? The elder said, "Just ask what it ultimately is. The monk took these words and questioned the hermitage master.
The master said, "Carrying the knotted staff across my shoulder, I heed no one; I turn back and enter into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. The Master [Zhaozhou] held his staff horizontally.
Resting his staff upon his shoulder, he called out in a loud voice, "Preceptor! Preceptor! Then he said again, "The whole nation pursues him, yet he will not return;
for ten thousand autumns and ten thousand ages, he remains but an empty memory."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: Venerable Yan Yang asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when one brings nothing forth?
Zhaozhou said, "Put it down. At that moment, the Venerable attained great enlightenment. The Master said, "Good assembly, do you see the place of his enlightenment?"
Exhausting one's strength, one cannot let it go; applying effort, one cannot bear its weight. One might think there is nothing at all, yet it is originally one's own.
Having seen what is one's own, the heart is filled with great joy; from this point on, the family estate flourishes, traversing ninety thousand miles in a single stride.
On the first day of the first month of the lunar year, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "All phenomena are the radiance of the mind;
all conditions are but the awakening of the nature. The entire earth is form—what, then, is the mind? The Master said, "Do not try to deceive an old monk.

The monk pressed further, "If the entire earth is the mind, what then is form? The Master said, "How long has it been since you began reciting these words, *ācārya*? The monk replied, "As for form and mind..."
"How can one penetrate these two characters? The Master said, "One knows only how to cross the water, yet fails to realize the depth of the waist.

The student further asked, "In this way, neither side gains any advantage. The Master said, "Let it be as you wish to chew and peck. The Master spoke again, "In a year, there are only these thirty days."
In this second month, when the yang energy begins to arise, does the practitioner of Prajñāpāramitā accord with the Way-seeking mind? Now I have two questions for you all:
one question for those who agree, and one question for those who do not. First, I ask those who agree: [The text continues with the specific questions.]
"How long has it been since you came here in this manner? You must say it has been a long time. I ask you:
since it has been so long, have the sounds and forms before your eyes caused you any affliction or harm? If they have caused you affliction and harm, then the Elder was not yet as he is now.
If they have not caused you affliction and harm, then you have realized through clear insight that they subsequently do not cause affliction."
It is not that one does not perceive through insight; it is simply that one is not afflicted by harm. If one perceives through insight, only then does one see that there is no affliction or harm;
this is what is called "the mind that perceives through insight. It is not yet called "being thus" (in its true state).

If one does not employ the mind that perceives through insight, how could one know that there is no affliction or harm? Based on forming such a view, I cannot answer your first question. As for the second question, he who refuses to consent says:
"How long has it been since you did not come this way? The Master laughed heartily and said, "What an excellent question!
You are an ordained śramaṇa, a disciple of the Buddha. With teeth within your mouth and hair upon your head, you stand tall and majestic. How can it be that you do not come this way?"
In what way do you differ from worldly people? Even if you were truly not like this, it would still be because of being "like this" that there could subsequently be "not like this.
Based on this view, you have also understood; yet I cannot grant you my seal of approval. Have you not heard the Great Master Shitou say:
"To be 'like this' is not permitted; to be 'not like this' is also not permitted; to be both 'like this' and 'not like this' is altogether not permitted"?
There were still those who could not explain it. Mazu Daoshi said to them, "Sometimes I raise my eyebrows and blink;
sometimes I do not raise my eyebrows and blink. Sometimes raising my eyebrows and blinking is right; sometimes raising my eyebrows and blinking is not right. They immediately understood.
The Master remained silent for a long while and said, "Do you understand? When the mud is deep, the Buddha is large; when the water rises, the boat floats."
[The Master] ascends the hall. He takes his seat.
If one has not yet realized that objects are mind-only, various forms of discrimination will arise. Once one has realized that objects are mind-only, discrimination no longer arises.
Since discrimination does not arise, one then abandons the appearances of external phenomena. He then took up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "No."
Can it not be called a "cane"? Yet, how can you explain the principle of relinquishing it? Some people here say, "What is it that you call a cane?
This immediately contradicts the path of the ancient Buddhas, who taught: "Without destroying conventional designations, one speaks of the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Others say, "What further cane could there be? If this were so, then the myriad phenomena of the world would fail to be established.
It is established thus. Furthermore, if one continues to call it a "cane," then all ordinary beings are most unfortunate indeed.

O Great Assembly, when you reach this point, how is it so? You must believe that the stone pagoda in the clouds is not of the human world, and the cloud-covered mountains beyond the railing do not arise from the transformations of the mind.
Wind rubs, rain sweeps; the sun shines, smoke veils. The wondrous function is unleashed.

Transversely, the boundaries of concealment and manifestation are one and the same; thus, one may naturally dwell in seclusion upon the Bird Path, opening up the breast and mind to wondrously accord with the true norm.
When the ten directions are clearly illuminated, it must reach this very point. Yet, you must further know that there is the "aperture of the patch-robed monk" before you have attained it.
What is the aperture of the patch-robed monk? *Pah!* (He strikes the meditation staff) and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an example: Once, while Master Guishan was seated, he saw Yangshan passing before his quarters.
Guishan said, "If you were my late teacher, Baizhang, you would have to receive a severe beating. Yangshan asked, "What about today's matter?
Guishan replied, "You might as well shut that pair of lips of yours. Yangshan said, "This kindness is difficult to repay. Guishan said, "Guishan..."
Dongshan was advanced in years. It was not that his disciples were lacking in talent. Nanquan said, "Today I saw Master Baizhang in person.
Guishan asked, "In what phrase did you see the former master? Nanquan said, "I do not say that I saw him; it is simply that there is no distinction.
Guishan said, "From beginning to end, you are a true adept. The Master said: "From the very beginning down to Baizhang, there has been an 'unviolate decree,' which Guishan deeply realized."
As for its essential meaning: one must be able to walk upon the edge of a sword; Yangshan drank the air to support him, yet he did not violate the blade or injure his hand.
There are some fellows who merely go on brandishing staffs and shouting "Ho!"—do they truly understand his command of non-violation? Have you not heard it said?
From beginning to end, he was a master of the Way. Every day people come and go; where have they seen Baizhang?
He ascended the hall and said: "For a moment, collect your thoughts. Here and there is Maitreya; at every door is Sudhana. In a single moment of thought..."

Earth, stone, mountains, and rivers; tiles, rubble, thorns, and brambles—O Great Assembly, whether manifesting as holy or as ordinary, being able to defile or to purify—they possess such majestic spiritual power and such wondrous function that they are simply like this.
Yet for a guest of Caoxi’s school, even seeing them in this way is not yet the news from Shaolin. As for the news from Shaolin, what should you, guests of Caoxi’s school, do?
"Born [in this world], descend from your seats.
Entering the hall: "Su Wu grazed sheep; though humiliated, he did not bend. Li Ling gazed toward Han; so joyful was he that he forgot to return.
Whether in a foreign land or one's own country, among the Buddha’s disciples, some had their two feet cross a pit, while others listened to the zither."
They rise and dance; some bury their bodies in excrement and soil, while others revile the river deities—these are habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), yet they are also wondrous functions.

As for lifting a staff to strike the ground, holding up a fly-whisk to knock upon a couch, or as Muzhou constantly kept his door closed and Luzu spent his entire life facing the wall—was this acting for others, or was it not?
One can thus know that all ordinary beings are buried within the precious treasury. How different!
What a lack of manliness! Why do you not hoist the sails and set the rudder to cast off from the river and reach the shore?

You must not remain here, lashing the oars while tethered to a stake; when will you ever arrive home? Since you are a person of Caoxi and a native of this very house, do you still see this as something belonging to "home"?

Ascending the hall, he raised an example: "Formerly, when my late teacher was serving as the miller in the White Clouds assembly, one day Elder Master Duan came down and said, 'Do you know of a certain matter?
My late teacher replied, 'I do not know. The Elder said, 'Recently, several Zen guests have come from Mount Lu;
I asked them about it, and they all claimed to have attained realization. When I asked them to speak of it, they were indeed able to speak.'"
Because of this, when the causal conditions were raised, it was also clearly understood by Yi; the words spoken under the teaching were likewise understood.

Master Duan remained silent for a long time and said to his former teacher, "Moutou, you have simply not yet arrived. What do you say to this? Upon hearing this, the former teacher felt uneasy in his heart;
for seven days and seven nights, he could not digest anything. Right in the center of his mind, he then reflected to himself:
Having already attained awakening, I could speak it and clarify it; yet why was it that I had not yet "arrived"? Suddenly, in the middle of the night, I finally understood.
All that I had previously cherished was at once cast aside, and I reported this to Master Duan. The Master rose and began to dance and leap for joy.
I had formerly served my late teacher, who, upon hearing me recount this incident, said to me: [The rest of the passage would follow here.]
Those who study the Way must let go all at once; only then will they find peace and joy. Assembly, do you see this?
If you can let go, it is truly refreshing and liberated. If you cannot let go, you are like an ox pulling a plow.

It is laughable that the ancient masters of all quarters beat the drum and preach Zen without end—without end! Not being startled or afraid—how lamentable! Only one who understands how to tread upon Vairocana [can truly understand].
"Supreme Practice. Even without speaking, it naturally transmits throughout the world.
Good brother! [The Master] ascends the hall and says: 'Citing the case: Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang said to the assembly, "Seal off your throats, lips, and mouths;
bring forth a single phrase! Guishan said, "I beg the Master to speak it himself. Wufeng said, "The Master must also seal it off too."'"
Yunyan said, "Does the Master have it yet? The Master said, "This is a matter that circulates within the monastic community.
Later, Chan Master Xuedou evaluated the words of these three men, noting that each had its own depth; he then requested the Master to speak on them.
A tiger’s head sprouting horns emerges from the wild grass. "The Master has also shut it away. "On the battlefield of dragons and snakes, one observes their stratagems.
"Does the Master have them yet? "A golden-maned lion does not crouch on the ground. Now, among the assembly, some go to seek instruction or to engage in dialogue.
If someone says, "These three lines of speech do not yet accord with Baizhang," this is called suppressing [the truth] rather than...
Yang said, "I request the Master to speak. Baizhang replied, "I do not refuse to speak to you, but I fear that later on it would cause the loss of my descendants.

Is this not suppressing and not revealing? "The Master must also shut it up," [Yang] said. Baizhang said, "In a place where there is no one, I look toward you with bared teeth; where is there any 'acceptance' of him? This is indeed suppressing and not revealing. The Master— [Note:

The text provided appears to be a fragment of a dialogue concerning the pedagogical methods of Chan masters, specifically the tension between withholding instruction to protect the lineage and the necessity of transmission.]
"Is there or not? Baizhang said, "I am losing my descendants. Furthermore, he was unwilling to concede.
As for Baizhang saying, "Close off your throat, lips, and mouth, and bring forth a single phrase," how can that be considered a gradual process?
Since you have closed off your throat, lips, and mouth, what kind of matter are you clarifying? You should also support this; let us descend from our seats.
Upon leaving Baochan Monastery and departing the hospital, he ascended the hall to address the assembly. He cited the Sixth Patriarch Master, who had addressed the assembly, saying:
"All of you, quickly prepare the boats and oars; I wish to return to Xinzhou. A disciple asked: "After the Master departs, when will you return?"
The Patriarch said: "Leaves fall and return to the root; when they came, they had no mouth. The Master said: "What kind of talk is this?
Having gone away, why come back again? Have you not seen how our late master Dongshan said, 'Even the great Great Patriarch still lacks awakening'?
The Master laughed heartily and said: "Do you all understand? Listen to this verse: 'Returning to the root, one attains...'"

What more need be said? At the mouth of the cave, the Qin people half-close their gates; the falling flowers have already drifted far with the flowing stream, leaving only the dense, billowing wild clouds gathered on high.

Arriving at Jiangshan, he ascended the hall and said: "Xuansha’s blank paper was a waste of an envelope; upon hearing the thunderous voice, ten-thousand-fathom peaks sink low. To comfort [the assembly].
Having released his private feelings beyond measure, he could no longer bear to chant "Luo-luo-li. He then laughed out loud with a "He-he," saying:
"The ancients said, 'One must laugh for thirty years. How true these words are!

When I was formerly at Baibuyun, I gathered in the Dharma assembly with my elder brother, Master Foguo of the Hall; that joy was boundless. To this day, that joy remains unspent. Again, he laughed with a "He-he."
He laughed loudly and said: "One hand does not clap alone; both hands make a resounding *glop-glop*. When the intention is raised, it transcends conceptual thought;
looking at one another, we share the same path. Mount Zhongfu rubs the clouds as it rises high; throughout the world, the sun’s disc blazes. The wondrous mechanism is swift as lightning;
the divine pearl is not upon the forehead. Take care, Great Teacher of Gods and Humans! Upon seeing this, the monk’s very soul is lost. Why? Who?"
If you dare to look directly with your own eyes, then descend from the seat.

The three verses on "Pointing out the Way," along with the Preface to the *Zongmen* (School of the Lineage), are presented here at once. Their author lies buried in grievance; the ancient road crisscrosses everywhere—how can one find a footing?

Unless one possesses the keen eyes that know the direction and a transcendent faculty that goes beyond the ordinary, lifting up one to clarify all three, everyone will drift together in the current. Should one merely follow the words...
To be stuck and obstructed is for the illness to lie in what one has seen and heard. To seal one’s mouth and hide one’s form is for the fault to reside in external recognition.

If you wish to decisively seek the Great Jewel, do not act as a petty merchant. Cast off your hands over a precipice; throw yourself directly into the void. How could the hundreds of thousands of samādhis be sought elsewhere?
If you recognize them through words and speech, it is called false understanding. As for awakening beings and establishing tasks, the scales and mirror [of discernment] are about to...

Come! Circling a hundred times and a thousand layers, we have barely managed to coordinate our hands and feet; yet some have fallen into the tracks of illness midway, while others have run out of provisions half the way.

Leading my children along in such a state of desolation is surely due to the inadequacy of the guidebook. This is truly because the moon’s reflection in a clear pool makes its traces difficult to discern.
One must simply sit and cut off all conceptualization at Vairocana’s realm, wandering freely upon the Great Path. Therefore, I have composed three verses to demonstrate the Way.
This serves as a mere fraction of the path proclaimed by the Master; it is certainly not something that can be attained through sequential stages, degrees of depth, numerical quantities, or names.
It is my hope that those who have reached enlightenment will look toward this for mutual inspiration.
Following the stream, the spiritual traces of a thousand sages are upon the tips of every blade of grass. To stand out clearly and let go is called "following the stream";
later teachings for ten thousand ages have no one who recognizes it—this brings to laughter the water-buffalo of Mount Mui.
The tracks coincide;
the moon in the water is the moon at the edge of the sky. North, south, east, and west—there is no difference between them.
When the smith of Silla strikes iron and sparks fly, burning one’s fingertips is called "coinciding tracks."

Chanting in unison, they cut off the ancient pathhead of a thousand differences; they unfurl the boat that rescues beings at the shore of seeds. A single phrase, luminously clear, encompasses all phenomena;
when skillfully chanted as non-sound, how can it be sought?
The six verses and their preface indicate that when the Buddhas appeared in the world, there was no dharma to show people; when the Patriarch came from the West, there was no Way to point out.
