He spoke only of self-awakening, which is called the Sudden Gate. If one still clings to the trap and the snare, it will be difficult to reach a true understanding. Thus, one must forget these expedient means.
It is difficult for those who are deluded to advance upon the path; thus, signs are set up to guide people, so that some may attain understanding.

Therefore, following those gentlemen who speak with elegant words, I have composed six stanzas of verse to illustrate one corner [of the truth], so that there is no need for the threefold repetition. Those who later find a dark resonance with this may perhaps find something worth taking up.

In delusion and awakening, the deluded person is deluded by awakening; the awakened person awakens to delusion. Delusion and awakening share the same substance; only the awakened one knows this. To mistake south for north is a matter of grasping at appearances;
yet the north is fundamentally the south—awakening involves no shifting or error. If one turns back to investigate the conditions of delusion, no place of origin can be found.
Suddenly I realized the correct direction; where could my delusion have gone? That delusion was indeed a delusion, falsely creating high and low;

through the evil perceptions of birth and death, I needlessly suffered like one stuck in glue. Upon realizing that delusion is without falsehood, joy became immeasurable; the thief of ignorance was slain in but a single moment.
In a single moment, one attains dark penetration throughout the great thousandfold world-system; with direct realization, all is perfectly clear. The three periods of time are empty and profound;

from beginningless time until now, everything has depended upon this very day. Until the end of the future, there is no further seeking. At the thought of non-thought, the numinous light blazes ever more brightly.

The numinous flames soar with radiance; the mind knows it cannot be concealed. The numinous source washes the azure depths; the myriad phenomena universally enter. The Ocean Seal manifests its brilliance;

it is unrelated to movement or stillness. Roots and objects do not meet; how could the pearl of the mind be confined? Turning back, one does not observe the self; yet when emerging, there is still something present.

Existence and non-existence emerge together; there are no traces to be found. Although the function of wisdom is marvelous, it still encounters the pursuit of awakening. Awakening itself becomes an obstruction to the Dharma, causing the body to encounter the formless void.
Like a wild dog or a fox in a windless place, one merely exerts oneself in vain by spreading out their palms. The written records of the ancestors are the original family heritage.
The scenery of old days is not something that can be intercepted; with a loose and easy manner, one remains as before in doubt.
Originally there is no illness, so why trouble oneself to speak of medicine? Treading on solid ground, one nods off while wide awake. The vast expanse of the great earth—understand it thus.
Such a Dharma does not depend on Kāśyapa; whose descendant would you be to prattle on with such confused talk?
You understand it as confused talk, but the wise person sees through it at a glance. This gate is vast and great; the fool burns himself. To slander and burn oneself is none of my business.
I am a deluded person; you are spiritually sharp and keen.

As you sit in meditation, the light of your mind reflects in emptiness; its essence transcends both partiality and perfection. Like golden ripples circling one another, movement and stillness are eternally in *dhyāna*. With every thought arising and every thought ceasing, [the nature remains constant].
Do not attempt to stop or sever it; let it flow on spontaneously. When has it ever arisen or ceased? Arising and ceasing are themselves quiescent extinction.
Thus, Mahākāśyapa appears—sitting, reclining, and walking—without a single moment’s interruption. Why does meditation not sit? Why does sitting not meditate? To realize this is to attain suchness.

This is what first came to be called "sitting in meditation" (*zuo chan*). Who is it that sits? What is this meditation (*chan*) that one wishes to sit upon? To seek the Buddha by means of the Buddha is to seek the Buddha where there is no need for seeking;
in so seeking, one only loses him further. Sitting does not involve contemplating a self, and meditation is not an external technique. At the initial stage, the mind is noisy and distracted.
It is unavoidable that one must alternate [practices]; therefore, I employ various methods to instruct them to observe in stillness and sit upright to gather the spirit.

At first, there is turmoil; after a long time, it becomes tranquil and serene. The six sense-gates become empty and at ease; as the six gates slightly subside, discrimination arises within. As soon as discrimination is born...

It appears as arising and ceasing; arising, ceasing, and transforming, all proceed from the manifestations of one’s own mind. One then employs that very mind to reflect back upon it once and for all—once is enough, never again.
A radiant halo crowns the head, and spiritual flames surge with brilliance. Mind after mind is unimpeded, encompassing horizontally and penetrating vertically.
Birth and death are forever stilled. A single grain of elixir turns gold into liquid. The guest-dust of body and mind finds no door through which to leak.
Let us speak of delusion and awakening for now; cease debating the adverse and the favorable. Reflect deeply upon the past, sitting coldly in search; though it is not otherwise, it remains so.
How utterly chaotic! In a single kṣaṇa, neither ordinary person nor sage can believe it; all around, a vast expanse of confusion. One must be most cautious.
If you do not understand this, sit upright and contemplate; one day you will strike upon it. I prostrate myself before you, I prostrate myself before you.
Entering the Way, the Way is fundamentally without flaw; as soon as the mind is directed toward it, one has already deviated. The moment a sign arises, the entire world becomes like empty flowers.

If you wish to grasp it in its entirety, you must simply be given it directly; there is no need for addition. It is a perfected pattern already manifest before you. When the source is thoroughly penetrated, every dharma is complete and perfect.
The numinous clarity is the natural law; it is wondrously beyond the reach of words and explanations. Words cannot grasp it, and even to "attain" it would be a deviation.

It stands far removed from the sense organs and their objects, serving as the standard for all time. When it exists, it is invisible; when it is absent, it faces one directly. Neither existing nor non-existing, the myriad phenomena manifest of themselves.
Outside the mind there are no phenomena; outside phenomena there is no mind. Mind and phenomena shine forth together; object and wisdom are profoundly deep.

When the mind forgets its illumination, it ceases; when object and wisdom come to rest together, they are one and the same path. This single path universally pervades and encompasses all ten directions. Birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally not two different things.
The four modes of birth and the six realms of existence—cease suffering and halt bitterness. In the Great Way of equality, there is neither heterodoxy nor orthodoxy.

Since neither Hu nor Han come [into it], what could serve as a mirror? When the image is empty, the mirror is bright; when the mirror is clear, the image is reflected. When the image departs, the mirror vanishes; even the thousand sages are not "sublime."
This gate is difficult to enter; you must simply cease your own striving. If one enters this gate, half a coin is not worth its weight in gold, nor is half a coin lacking in value.
Ten thousand nations vie to behold it; thus it is said: "The essence of the Great Way is vast."

Seeing and hearing reach their ultimate limit as light is shed; listening is perfect as it encompasses all resonance. If one speaks of seeing and hearing, phenomena become objects of conceptual thought;

yet the light flows through the great trichiliocosm and the resonance is transmitted across the sands of worlds. Manifested in direct presence, it is fully revealed—neither existing nor non-existing. Sound is not sound; form is not form.
Neither form nor sound; the mountain is high and the water is swift. It cannot be seen by the eye, nor heard by the ear. Though neither seen nor heard, it is vividly seen and heard.
Seeing forms and hearing sounds, one transcends the sense organs and their objects. Like the moon in water or images in a mirror, like a dream or a magical illusion, all things are thus arrayed.

In Mañjuśrī’s jewel-adorned land and Avalokiteśvara’s universal gate, you alone pervade the entire dharma-realm. Your person and the land reflect one another, wondrously transcending both the mundane and the sagely.
This innate, celestial truth is neither illness nor health; sing it forth with long melodies and further display this sublime dance.

East, west, south, and north manifest like flowers in the sky; birth-and-death and coming-and-going, coming-and-going and birth-and-death—if it were not thus, there would be much error and many faults.
These words are not yet ultimate; these statements are all the fundamental source. If one points with the finger to show the way, this is the same tradition as the ancients.

Pointing directly at the moon in the water, the most distant is the most intimate. If one claims it can be seen, it still bears a double halo; the moon is bright above, the water flows below—each is independent of the other.
Upon what conditions could they be falsely joined? Sounds echo and reverberate; the target is formed by the drawing of the arrow.

Whose finger-pointing metaphor is more clear? Who can discern the gates [of the teachings]? To the sight and hearing of ordinary beings, the moon is bright while the water is turbid; the waves of the mind and the consciousness of karma flow toward the gate of suffering.
To the hearing and seeing of those of the Two Vehicles, it is like a face in a mirror; facing the image, they are deluded regarding the reality, for they have not yet realized the source.
The water is clear and the moon is reflected; its solitary radiance shines far and wide. One must extinguish this illusory city and press further forward.

A single moon illuminates the heavens; its light swallows the great trichiliocosm. The myriad phenomena suddenly appear, stretching infinitely and boundlessly. All equally contain the precious moon, their intermingling rays vast and transparently clear.

Neither internal nor external, the one and the many are harmoniously integrated. In the nature-ocean of Vairocana, self and other are without obstruction; delusion and awakening, awakening and delusion, mutually vanish yet mutually remain.

A single mote of dust contains ten billion worlds, and ten billion worlds are contained within a single mote of dust. One rushes through the lands of these motes of dust without ever moving from one’s own original body.
The light has vanished and the moon has fallen; how many have groped in the dark? For forty-nine years, he used it all without success. A man of great ambition has his own marketplace;
at the crossroads, he watches others suffer loss. He does not rejoice in the sages, nor does he loathe the common folk.
Holding a winnowing basket and offering a broom; riding a horse or mounting a donkey. If anyone laughs at me, I too shall laugh at them. Should you ask further how it is, I do not know how to read.

In speech and silence, the ultimate Way is beyond words; yet words may also transmit it. Why can they be transmitted? Because they are proclaimed in response to phenomena. Although words respond to phenomena, phenomena themselves are without substance.
When words speak of the insubstantial, the sounds of speech naturally vanish. When the discourse that transcends words reaches its limit, wondrous responsiveness returns to universality.

The Way is neither obscured nor illuminated; speech and silence are equally grasped. Who raises the cry when it is lifted? Every single thing is empty and vast, universally penetrating the great trichiliocosm and pervading the thoughts of the mundane dust.
Though the categories of beings are not one, their voices emerge from the same source. The perfect sound falls resonantly; both ordinary and sage find their place therein.
The myriad species and ten thousand categories are permeated by the seeds of omniscience; thus, this single gateway is called the "Infinite Meanings.

Mountains and rivers proclaim it, grasses and trees raise their voices, and they speak eternally without interruption—what is known as the profoundly deep. Yet, how deep it is! It is profoundly shallow, for it does not stir the perceptions of emotional attachments.
It requires the least effort. Ordinary beings do not realize it; yet this non-realization is most intimate. The wondrous meaning is thus laid bare: when there is joyful speech, there is laughter;
when there is resentment or anger, there is wrath. Wrath is Vajra; joy is Kāśyapa. Within the Flower Treasury of Vairocana, mind meets mind in direct succession.
It is present and visible, yet one cannot see its back. This wordless, secret speech emerges from this very moment. Once it has appeared, who is there to discuss it? It is not heard with the ears;
rather, the six sense-faculties share a single gateway. The wondrous verses are distributed like stars; the myriad scriptures do not transcend a single speck of dust.

It is neither tongue nor eloquence; like rolling thunder and rushing lightning, it is held within the hand—what dharma is not contained therein? Transverse and vertical throughout the three realms, there is not a single leakage.
Yet people of the time do not believe this; they cling to the sickness of verbal expression and rely upon external objects, taking them to be ultimate reality.
"It is certain that this is the mind; it is certain that these are the objects. Driven by mind and objects, one is not a free person.

The sages have spoken with bitter mouths regarding the faults that follow from folly; they have skillfully employed many words and forcibly made distinctions. Yet the Dharma is beyond verbal expression—you must discern this well."
They abandon speech, and the cycle of birth and death is naturally severed. When ordinary people hear this, they find no fault in it;

they grasp at that wordlessness and remain in profound darkness for a long time. Sitting upright in a dark prison, they continue on with the mind alone, turning their backs on speech like mere earth or wood.
To abandon existence for non-existence is to fall into a deviant path; both existence and non-existence are afflictions. When both afflictions are removed, where does one go after their removal?
One does not leave this very place. At this very place, nothing is born. Speech and silence mutually encompass one another; yet in grasping them, one is unaware of whether it is east or west.
To speak is not to speak; to have no doubt is itself doubt. Thus one is called a "Son of the Buddha. An ordinary person who understands affairs—what kind of ordinary person is this?
Go ask Li Hu.
That "other" and "self" are non-dual;
wherever people travel, it is not that I, the Lord, am incapable. Now relying on the power of you, my son, I shall again be of one mind with you.
There is no discrepancy between that and this; we transcend both past and present. The myriad differences are not stagnant waters; birth and death naturally subside into stillness.

In whom could there not be something wondrous? Shaking off the sleeves, one seeks out those who understand. Not falling onto the path of mechanical devices, clarity itself determines depth and shallowness.
Yet, as for those who have not yet awakened, they and I merely cause each other harm in vain.
In movement and stillness, there is always but one source;
from the beginning, one has never been deluded. Why labor to attain awakening today? Guard the city of solitude; know that you would be mistaken to seek it elsewhere.
All the sages of the past were originally ordinary people; how could there be any other path to lead people away from sorrow and suffering?
This very midst of birth and death is precisely the place where the Buddha goes. If someone suddenly treads upon it, what need is there to choose between pure and defiled lands?
He never once looks back; even if called, he does not heed. Though a thousand sages cannot do anything about it, why do you fail to understand these words?
To bring an end to greed, anger, and delusion is itself the mother of all Buddhas.

Only through wondrous words can one truly know the speech of the Buddhas and the Patriarchs. When the flower was held up to show the deluded son, I now utter this discourse; how could you say it is inverted?
When a person is naturally authentic, they are like the water of an autumn pond: not a single thing can adhere to it; how could one use names and designations?
Do not, by any means, seek to recognize it within that state; even if you do so, it is not it. Have you not seen Subhūti? He realized that emptiness is empty, reaching beyond all that.
Realizing that delusion is fundamentally truth, I ask you, greed, anger, and ignorance: where does your home reside? I now intend to send each of you off in separate directions;
consider this well and thoroughly, lest you be caught by the government officials. The eldest is named Greed, who has raised two younger brothers.
The three of us shall dwell together as one, living our lives day and night in common. I shall cause your household to flourish and ensure you are well-governed.
Yet now, my son, you weary me with your distress. I make a vow with you: first, that you must know yourself; second, that you must follow established precedent.
Third, one must give rise [to realization] in its own place. Fourth, one must have the verse of joy: "May we be in harmonious accord with you; each and every thing is free from defilement.
Once awakened, all is understood; why need one remove the veils of affliction? I am the mother of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time."
The distinction between self and others is absent;
the green mountains are my body, and the flowing waters are my life. I nourish them through the four seasons, remaining serene and naturally upright.
I shelter and sustain all sentient beings, cultivating and reflecting upon the Six Perfections within myself. I plant flowers to sow the seeds of Bodhi; I sweep the stones to seek tranquility.
I do not see willows fluttering; there are naturally shadows of grapes. One may gaze upon them without weariness, and in departing from them, there is no resentment or contention.
The single nature is all natures; it is the great round mirror of this Sahā world.
Living together and speaking well, people of the world do not recognize me; they seek me through outward form, yet my form is not like theirs—they merely gaze at a dragon on paper.
If you wish to truly know me, ask the Master. The Master’s household affairs are excellent; every single thing is securely stored away.
The six elder brothers boast of their artistic skills; the three mothers are sufficient in their warmth and kindness. In the southern hall, calligraphy and arithmetic are mastered;

in the northern storehouse, wealth and grain abound. Having lived here, I only feel that time has passed long; being too lazy to go inquire after the Zhangs and Wangs. If you can recognize this for what it is, I shall share the same rafter with you.
Her beauty was once a sight to behold;
since our parting amidst the mountains by the sea, ten years have passed and the spring grasses turn green. My longing remains within my heart; her countenance was as bright and pure as jade.
Yet letters and news have long ceased to come; the peach and plum trees are now thick and ripe. Only that person in my heart causes me to knit my brows in sorrow.

The wondrous countenance is not seen, for throughout the entire body there is no reflected image. It is the bare essence, revealed in full majesty; it is beyond speech and beyond sound or form—how could it ever have length or brevity?

It manifests everywhere, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; thus it is called the King of Dharmas. The Udumbara flower is now in full bloom, yet though one smells it, its fragrance is not perceived.

Lengthening and shortening occur naturally within the spring days and spring mountains; all matters of spring are entirely spring. Spring light shines upon spring waters; spring vapors coalesce into spring clouds.

The spring traveler’s spring emotions are stirred; spring poetry is renewed with every spring. Only those who recognize spring know that throughout ten thousand kalpas, it has always been but one spring.
The tranquil essence pervades all;

the wondrous body is without fixed direction and possesses universal knowledge. Near and far benefit one another without the slightest gap. Roots and objects respond in an instant throughout the sand-grains of the world-realms.
Sitting and cutting off all conceptualization, Vairocana awakens the great potential.

When conditions correspond without error and phenomena are without deviation, this is right cultivation. From this point on, seeing and hearing cease their drifting. Though one exhausts the mind, it has not yet reached the state of the "mindless.
How can the single aggregate of faculties and objects find rest?
The Patriarch plants flowers upon the ground; here are four verses in summary:

The Ground of the Ground is fundamentally without birth; because of birth, one speaks of the existence of the ground. This transmission has flowed from antiquity to the present; it is neither foolishness nor wisdom.
The seeds have never been deluded since antiquity; what is there to awaken to now? It is solely because the seed-nature is profound that there is no other path.
The flower...

There is a seed within the ground of the mind; through causes and conditions, the flower blooms of itself. If you wish to know where the fruit is realized, look back and laugh at the arrival of the Patriarch.
Once the five-petaled flower has fully bloomed, the mountains grow long and the waters grow deep; wild clouds hang across the valley mouth, and the wandering traveler vainly pursues them.
Regarding the six-line verses in six stanzas along with their preface:
each verse exhausts the treasury of merit within one's own mind without the slightest deficiency.
Only by not departing from the six lines while simultaneously transcending them can one truly understand this meaning.
The preceding thought is ordinary;
the preceding thought is ordinary. Cutting cloth to make a shirt, seeing off a guest at a long pavilion, unfurling sails as the sun sets—the subsequent thought is sacred.
The subsequent thought is sacred; a single blow lands it squarely. Amidst the chaos of war, one recovers their very life.
The preceding thought is not ordinary;
the preceding thought is not ordinary. When speech is upright yet words are slanderous, the heavens are high and the seas are vast—every feather and wing is bristling.
The subsequent thought is not the sage;
the subsequent thought is not the sage. The myriad phenomena are a clear mirror, requiring no cultivation through perfuming; they are originally pure.
The preceding thought is simply the ordinary person.
The preceding thought is that of an ordinary person; an ordinary person cannot fathom it. If one wishes to know it, one can never point it out or delineate it.
The succeeding thought is that of a sage;
a sage cannot know it. It is like an iron ox crossing the sea, or a stone woman giving birth to a child.
Regarding the Ten Verses on Recollection and their Preface, I have often said:
"Though the former sages have passed away, their Way remains. If one attains accord with it, I am present here.
Baizhang once spoke of this to Guishan, saying: "It is like suddenly remembering what had been forgotten; that which is called 'recollection' is vividly manifest within the spirit."

I understand. Just as what meets the eyes and ears cannot be mistaken, I have therefore composed ten verses of the "Ten Recollections" (daśānusmṛti) to elucidate my former intent, so that those of a thousand years hence may all believe and accept it;
this is also to show that I have never for a moment forgotten [the truth]. Since I already know this, do you all know it?

Recalling Shao-lin, ever since those three prostrations, the transmission has been wrongly carried on for a thousand ages. Through eternal days no one has arrived; only the whistling wind through the cypress and cedar trees.
Recalling Cao-xi.
After the leaves have fallen and returned to their root, a single drop from Caoxi is profound. Few people come to dwell in the mountains; truly, one must be a fine connoisseur to know this.
I recall Nanquan’s return to his quarters: where can one find Nanquan? Last night at the third watch, the moon shone coldly before the seat.
I recall Zhaozhou, after he never descended from his meditation seat; he spoke no clever words, only matters of ordinary peace and joy—yet these have been vainly circulated through past and present.
I recall Nanyang...
After Danxia visited him, they spoke from then on of Nanyang: the grass turns a lush green, and the spring breeze blows for long or short as it may.

Recalling the Twin Trees—once having entered those Twin Trees—the affairs of the celestial palace become inscrutable; the fisherman does not grow weary of his trade—where else can one behold the Tathāgata?

I recall Han Shan, who after settling on Mount Tiantai, wore only a single layer of coarse cloth that had even torn; though his sinews and bones were exposed, his songs and laughter cannot be fully conveyed.
I recall Master Pang.
After planting flowers upon the stone, one’s life is naturally springtime. If you encounter a question that strikes at the core, I will certainly not spare you.
Remembering my former teacher—after meeting him once, it was both pitiable and laughable. If you ask why this is so: he was eighty years old and yet appeared as a youth.
Remembering you, I remember you;
after remembering you, I laugh and laugh without ceasing. Who knows this intent? There are words that cannot repay it.
Ten Verses on the Ten Practices, with Preface.
The *Avataṃsaka* uses the ten dharma-realms to comprehensively encompass its manifold gates, demonstrating the principle of inexhaustibility.
The Chan school has the "Ten Mysterious Gates" (*Shi xuantan*) to clarify its proclaimed path. Dongshan has the "Ten Non-Returnings" (*Shi bugui*) to manifest transcendental realization.

I, this mountain monk, have set forth the "Ten Practicable Principles" (*Shi kexing*) to instruct future generations, hoping they will assist their cultivation of the Way—just as when mugwort grows amidst hemp, it does not need leaning.

And it is straightforward. Furthermore, it is like a person who has been perfumed with incense; they also carry its fragrance. Those who find even slight benefit herein shall record it hereafter. [This concludes] the *Yanzuo* (Seated in Tranquility).
The principle of pure emptiness ultimately has no body; in a single thought returning to the root, all phenomena are leveled.
Subject and object are suddenly forgotten and the whole body is revealed; herein, one does not calculate progress or stages.
Entering the room to ask about the Way, one hastens to the Master’s seal to realize one's own mind. Entering the gate, one must seek out a true companion of realization.
If in this life one does not tread the path of Caoxi, what will one have to transcend antiquity and the present when reaching old age?

In the communal labor of gathering firewood and selecting vegetables, the master is the true craftsman; by advancing in practice and cultivating the self, one encounters the ancients. If you travel to various quarters, you must examine things with thorough sincerity;
at Longmen, this Dharma is the universal ford.

When the board sounds three times for the rice gruel, birth and death are severed; when the Buddha’s name is chanted ten times, past and present are united. Opening the mat and unfolding the bowl, one must personally and clearly grasp this;
do not be coarse-minded or oblivious to suffering and emptiness.
When dust arises on the swept floor, it is cleared away at once; in the quietude of the corridors, we dwell together in peace. Incense is burned and the ground is swept—there is nothing else to do;
silently radiant and concealing its brilliance, it reveals the wisdom-gem.
When washing clothes by the stream, do not be negligent or indolent. When entering the assembly, garments that are soiled are improper.
Having been pressed shoulder-to-shoulder with neighbors above and below for a long time, how can the movements of mind and body fail to be melted away?
The stone path for walking meditation among the trees is level as a bird’s track; with nothing to do after the midday meal, I walked it briefly.
Returning, I asked my like-minded companions: "How was it today? What was it like?"
Reciting the sutras deep in the stillness of the night, one recites them within; with no afflictions in the mind, the demon of sleep is awakened.
Although it is a dark room where no one sees, the dragons and devas naturally listen with their ears pricked.
Prostrating before the Buddha removes the defilement of arrogance; through this physical act, one attains refreshing clarity. The words of Xuan Sha are worthy of refuge and respect:
"This is for you, not for others"—the principle and the fact are profound.
Meeting on the Way, speak of the Way; do not be full of empty pretense. Speak with bold words and loud voices, laughing at those of superior station.
If you can, beneath these words, exhaustively investigate the root and the branch, would you ever consent to form friendships based on what is meaningless?
Two Poems on Spontaneous Inspiration The physical form is but an apparition in space; the self is but a body in a dream. Within this dream, do not seek after the world or one’s station.
Piteous is that single stream before the crag, flowing into the human realm from antiquity unto the present.
Dreams, illusions, and empty flowers are known only to oneself; in silent reflection, I realize my errors of twenty-nine years.
Where the setting sun meets the fragrant grasses—the places I once trod—who would have thought that red lotuses would follow at every step?

When Haihui took his leave of the Old Monk, there were no words for his coming; nor was there anything known or heard of his departure. Who can harmonize with this melody? It resounds forth from amidst the white clouds.
The Fifth Patriarch, Old Monk, sent this "Song of the Iron Ox" to the Master (appended):
Last night before the third watch, the iron ox plowed the fields through; Having grazed on the spring grasses, it now exhales its breath into the azure sky.
There are no fences and no enclosures; whether facing the front mountains or the back mountains, one acts according to convenience. Never has one recklessly damaged the crops in the fields.

Cherishing the skin and fur, one does not treat them with contempt. Suddenly, a great clap of thunder resounds, and only then does one realize that what was previously attained has been fully manifested.

The Master harmonizes; before the primordial chaos was divided, he first made his discernment. His creation does not rely on the forging of yin and yang. With its horns already manifest, it is a fine bull;
its hide and fur need no further changing. Before one's eyes lies a level field where not an inch of grass grows; hungry, it eats; thirsty, it drinks. No [obstacles].
Birth and old age—Ayuṣmat-rāja Buddha is just like this now; what sentient beings are there to seek out? A single roar causes heaven and earth to tremble.
For those who have realized the Way, my [teachings] are of no use. Sitting and cutting off all, the world of Vairocana is vast.
It is simply that the eyelids of the patch-robed monks are heavy. Once they meet a true知音 (one who understands), the harmony begins. All others are merely idle attendants.

The mountains were tranquil and still; sitting quietly by the brazier, I reflected on the joys of forests and springs in the world beyond for forty years, and how vastly different they were from the trivialities of this mundane world.

Reflecting deeply until reaching the ultimate Way, I have thus composed these mountain verses to encourage myself and to show to all fellow practitioners of meditation, so that you may not turn back as late as this old man.
The moving world pervades the entire Sahā universe, and it brings about oppression. Settle your mind in one place and sit; from this, the white light of emptiness will emerge.
What is it that oppresses? Oppression; the grease and fire searing the soul. What is it that is empty and white? Emptiness and whiteness;

the vast teaching spreading solitary wings. How excellent is the mind of the tranquil one! To them, even the four seas are too narrow. Compared to those men of action, how vast is the distance between heaven and earth!
Therefore, let us examine this thoroughly. Both [extremes] are equally biased and deviant. To abandon that and rush toward this—how could there be any profound benefit?
From where does pleasure come? To where does suffering depart? When the roots and origins of suffering and pleasure are forgotten, it is because one has strayed onto the byways of the journey.
If there were no taxes on the roads and lanes, one would dwell contentedly in one’s own home. Previously, one did not loathe the rubble; how could one now prize gold and jade?
That gold and jade are prized does not mean the rubble should be cast away. To call rubble "gold and jade" would imply that killing and stealing are not rebellious acts.
Gold and jade are called tiles and pebbles; the traces of the sages and worthies have vanished. Gold and jade remain gold and jade; tiles and pebbles remain tiles and pebbles.
Suffering and pleasure are each equal; every dharma is without borrowing from another. The great emptiness is free from all conceptualization; reality is without change.
In pleasure there is no mark of pleasure; in suffering there is likewise no trace of suffering. Suffering and pleasure are identical with the ten voids;

the gate of the mind is opened wide. The dragon roars and the phoenix cries; from the heavens and the abyss, the golden elixir emerges. Yet people do not contemplate the various paths; their famished mouths vainly seek food.
When it comes to this first matter, Caoqi is called the supreme guest. Thinking thus of the worthy sages, I cannot sleep through the remainder of the night.
The time is now; let each of you exert yourselves. Advancement and decline lie but a hair’s breadth apart.
Inscription on the Stupa of Chan Master Simian Fazhi:
"O you of precious numinous awareness, Continuously extending through past and present, The person dwells beyond the myriad sages; The stupa is locked within the depths of chaotic clouds."

The colors of the cypress and pine in the azure void; the roars of tigers and leopards on the crimson cliffs. If you can turn back the light and arrive here, you will surely perceive the Master’s mind.

Like Mokeji (Wang Wei) responding to guests while sitting cross-legged at night amidst the four walls of the city, and like Old Lu (Huineng) with a mindless heart beyond the clouds—on this deep night, the moon is bright and the wind is clear.
Sitting. Leaving the household life requires no effort at all.

To the monk who asks about the meaning of the scriptures, I show that its phrases and principles manifest beyond this shore; the five thousand-plus scrolls are all contained therein. Why do you not seek the root?
Meditate: Look at how the leaves on the branches turn yellow.
Regarding the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), there are two verses:
Empty names and empty words have been passed down for a long time; True words and true traces are shown to later generations. The distinction between the empty and the real is clearly known below.
Falling. A pure breeze reveals its fragrant traces through the ages.
Before every door is a torch; at midnight, the foolish man speaks of what is similar. The blue sky is like water, the moon is like a hook;
throughout antiquity and today, it is but a name left adrift in idleness.
To the monk planting pines:
"An inch of numinous sprouts planted by your own hand; on the ridges before and the mounds behind, they shall become fine timber.
Daring to transmit this imperishability to future days, I hold only these evergreen hues for those who come after."
Three Verses Spontaneously Composed in the Mountains Clearly discerning yet failing to understand, one instead falls into delusion. To whom shall these boundless splendors of nature be entrusted?
If one gains a firm footing upon the land of one’s own home mountain, then naturally, everywhere is inconceivable.
Past events have become empty and can no longer be pursued; take this old mind and contemplate it once more. From ancient times to the present, there has not been a hair’s breadth of separation;
to realize this is truly marvelous.
When it is time to rest, simply rest; then you may roam freely through the traces of the Five Lakes. Do not begrudge that your livelihood is meager;
this very state of *muni* is what brings one to the ultimate end.
Addressing the assembly:
Seeking the mind, the mind is not yet realized; Waiting for people, no one comes. Rocks and flowers, after the morning rain— In silence, for whom do they bloom?
Three-Phrase Verse.
At Longmen Temple by the Cave of Yu, he seeks pearls and wishes to question the dragon. The black pearl has been swallowed into its belly—how can it be retrieved? (Please provide the final line.)
Day after day, hour after hour, I read the *Song of the Twelve Hours* by Lingyuan. The Old Man of Longmen knows this in his own heart.
The Master would often show this to practitioners: a set of six dice, each of whose six faces showed six dots. Furthermore...
Three verses composed:
Six dice fill the bowl with red; no need for contrivance, it is simply so.
If you intend to step forward to seek understanding, it is much like heading west while facing east.
Six dice fill the bowl with red; dust, ink, rivers, and sands cannot exhaust it. Who can unfold the Vajra-hand?
Even the Patriarchs and Buddhas come to sweep away their traces.

Six dice fill the bowl with red. A horse carries a donkey; one throw is empty. When the crimson poverty arrives, there is nothing with which to compete. "I ask you to manifest your spiritual powers from this point on.

(A monk asked, "When the six dice fill the bowl with red, what is it like? The Master said, "No one can compete. The monk asked, "What if such a person were to suddenly encounter this? The Master said, "Come out evenly.
The monk said, "I ask you to manifest your spiritual powers from this point on. How do you manifest them? The Master said, "The dice are in my hand.")

Meeting Bodhidharma by chance, he traveled through Liang and Wei with confident steps; seizing the moment, he departed from Shaolin. The guests in carriages and on horseback in Chang’an harbor boundless hearts for profit and fame.
[This was written] because of Fayan’s verse.

"Regarding curses, poisons, and the perversions of form and sound—if the eyes and ears were to perceive them directly, where would the person go? The Master again versified this: The Root asks: Where does the person go?
Anointing and cutting are equal; forget both the favorable and the adverse. Though conditioned phenomena are false, their nature is eternally true.
All dharmas are without dependence; this is called auspiciousness."
Inanimate things preach the Dharma;

this preaching by the inanimate differs from the blind and the deaf. Those who hear it possess the supernormal powers of the eye and ear. Not only do they perceive nearby objects, but even distant lands;
having reached all ten directions, their full power is revealed.

Cold Food Festival Rites for the True Image of the Former Master, Five Poems Seeking this school through clouds and waters, I have spent ten years polishing the great void. Exhausting my humble efforts, I have returned to the original state;
only then do I know that all phenomena are fundamentally the same.
Once you awaken to the mind of our Teacher, it immediately ceases; the gate of faith has no entry point through which to enter. For twenty years the matter remained as secret as ever;
toward others, he never exerted a thought or a bit of effort.
The predecessor speaks the Dharma and the successor listens; from the beginning, both have been devoid of sentience.
It is solely because mouth and ear are alike that the transmission flows on and the Way is spontaneously realized.

Those who have departed have gone with earnest instructions; those who remain maintain the lineage without interruption. When one encounters a true connoisseur and there is a moment of resonance, one then knows that both departing and abiding are ever-sufficient.
On the Qingming and Hanshi festivals, together with all people, we pay homage to the First Patriarch, whose body remains unmoving. All dharmas are inherently tranquil, and the mind is likewise so;
who among those who come after will truly attain my essence?
Two Verses on the Chief Seat Hegui:
Discussing only intimacy, not the time; turning one’s smile upon the "tiger-trap" ruses of all quarters.

Not even a single word was permitted as a response before the sail had already caught a favorable breeze and returned home. At every turn there is a path fit for treading; in every thing there is no discrepancy—do not [neglect it].
Abandoned and estranged, I failed to see the extraordinary man at Huangmei; yet Master Lu was able to receive the Patriarch’s robe.
I am ashamed that you sought me out to recognize the endurance of winter, not begrudging the thousand turns of the perilous path.

Having once visited you in person with a note left in your hall, how could you, in your secluded mountain dwelling, have dared to deceive yourself? Under the moonlight, you surely composed verses alone, sharing the world within the alchemical elixir-flask.
Who watches? The great function at the opportune moment fully encompasses both gathering and releasing;
why need one fuss over grasping a ball of snow? Seeing off Grand Master Guo as he departs for Juyue:

for half a year he enjoyed the pleasures of fisherman and woodcutter; after three years of traveling north, his parents have come. At the Golden Horse Gate and the Jade Hall, a mere snap of the fingers.
Entering, the jeweled pavilions and fragrant galleries open all at once.
Inscribed by Chen Zimei on the Hall of Resting in the Shade:
"Deep and clear are the cold streams; layered are the mountains. To rest in the shade in my final years, I have attained leisure of body. The flowers of Wuling are beautiful; spring is eternal."

Fishing and singing songs, pure matters that concern nothing else; beneath one's eyes, children and grandchildren may attain wealth and honor, yet before the wine-cup, one lets one’s hair turn white and streaked with gray.
Daily, the celestial mechanism brings true news, as I frequently permit Chan monks to come and go with me.
Inscription for Sun Qinzhi’s “Nurturing Simplicity” Studio To nurture well is not to instruct;
sounds and sights do not disturb it. The plain silk is unstained—this is true nature.
Sometimes I come to sit within this studio, Becoming a person of undifferentiated simplicity, free from artifice.

The Dharma Master Zhihai, having sought verses and begged for alms in the mountain city, returns to the imperial capital. The food from Vaiśālī is fragrant and delicious; do not long for the spring peaches and plums of your old garden.
Further investigate the meaning of the Westward Transmission from the Superior Land.

Pointing to the monks gathered around the brazier, sitting silently and wordlessly by its side: regardless of whether one is coarse or as common as a city dweller, observe the color of the fire within this space;
the Patriarch’s Heart-Seal has been personally transmitted.
Inscription on the Wall of Old Man Xu Si Old Man Xu’s livelihood is as natural as the heavens. In his old age, he has neither joy nor anger. Take up the mulberry tree standing before you:
Heaven and earth do not transcend a single speck of dust.
**Inscription for Jiyuan Hermitage** Who dwells here in Jiyuan? It is said to be Tong the Hoe-Maker. Beyond things, bamboos by the hermitage; among men, winds at one’s ear.
The dew-drenched fields are lush and green; the misty marshes are verdant and hazy. In this very place of hidden mind, it is clearly the same as the ancients.
In summer, as soon as I disperse [the heat], I fall ill. Being both ill and distressed, I have thus written these mountain verses to show the practitioners of Chan:
ten thousand kalpas are but a single instant; though dust and sand remain unmoved and unshifted, if one were to discuss the past and future, they are all entirely subsumed within timelessness.
The sea is vast and the waves still roll; when the mind penetrates, it may equal the Buddha. This wooden pillow at the head of the bed is pushed forth for fear that people might be deluded.
Inscribed on the Incense Forest Pavilion in the Attendant’s Quarters:

At the Ge Kitchen, beneath the pine pillow, the midday window is cool. Lying down, I watch the winds and clouds; the fragrance of grasses and trees fills the air. With a snap of the fingers, one travels throughout all lands and worlds.
All is exhausted; on the mountain path home, one smiles at the winding sheep-tracks.
The Attendant, returning west to visit his kin, originally traveled from Mianzhu through the south.
Following his previous route back, he enters Mianzhu once more; his well and dwelling remain as they were in former days.
I dwell here; the mountains and rivers remain as they were in those days. When my neighbors see me, none are struck with alarm;
my kin welcome me, and I have severed all discursive thoughts. When asked about what was gained in the South, I lean briefly upon my slender cane.
The junior disciple Chongjian requests a verse:

"When affairs are concluded, one must seek the Way; only then will you clearly understand your original nature. The gate of Chan has no locks or keys—it requires only that you apply your mind to open it."
Spontaneous Verses at Longmen, Five Poems How bright and clear is the moon!
Throughout the long night it enters my chamber. It illuminates the heart of ten thousand ages; I contemplate this physical form of a hundred years.

Wind and dew drip through the window; I wrap myself tightly in my coarse woolen robes. I lie awake for a long time, unable to sleep; the last light lingers upon the eastern wall. The forest birds cry out incessantly;
I strip off my clothes and sit up in the middle of the night. Shifting the embers, I realize the truth of my life: the exhaustion of the spirit returns to its state of decay.
The matter is clear, yet people remain deluded; who can harmonize the winding and the plain? Thinking of this, I never forget it; the gate stands open, yet few come to pass through.
Alas, alas, the flying squirrel cries; those of this age find no joy in it. When their desires are met, they call out to one another; when the desire departs, they should simply let it cease.
Good fortune and misfortune arise from this; I have yet to see the logic behind it. These words are like something never heard before: Great Plum possesses the fundamental teaching.

Coolness arises early in the first watch of night; a thin cloud rolls away across the vast void. A lamp hangs amidst the dew of pines and bamboo; the curtain is drawn back by the wind through the *bìluó* vines.
How laughable are the affairs of a thousand years; one can penetrate them all with a single thought. When meeting a Zen guest who inquires, I speak at length of my own school.
Whenever I reflect on the matters within my heart, I repeatedly open the pearl within my palm. I wish to rely on the wild geese of heaven to carry it, waiting for the fish in the water to deliver it.
This meaning is ultimately difficult to express; these words cannot be fully written down. Though I hold my brush, all is silent; the trees surrounding the house grow lush and spreading.

I inscribed this on the wall of the Lingguang Terrace in the seventh year of the Zhenghe era. A separate Lingguang Terrace was constructed below the Southern Mountain, upon which a pair [of pillars] was erected.
The stūpa faces west toward the place where the sun sets; this signifies the principle of returning to the root and gathering in [the essence].
One stūpa is dedicated to the remains of the successive patriarchs and masters after their transformation and passing;

one stūpa is used to enshrine the bone relics of the Chan monks from the ten directions following cremation. These two serve to manifest the Way of Quiescent Extinction (*nirvāṇa*), though they follow different paths.
They share the same destination; it is where the myriad spirits all assemble. My own withered bones shall likewise be enshrined here.
Generations after generation, you should observe this, so that it may endure for all time, equal in longevity to empty space. This is the reason these twin pagodas were built.

On the day of the Cold Food Festival in that year, the mountain dweller Qingyuan recorded this and composed two verses, saying: [The verses follow] On the day of the Cold Food Festival in that year, the mountain dweller Qingyuan recorded this and appended two verses.
At first, I intended to speak of the True Constant; yet I feared that the True Constant would flow on in secret. It is better not to speak, so that people may know it together.
When people wish to know it, they instead exhaust their thoughts. On the cliff’s edge, the stupa reveals its form;

atop the terrace, wild clouds fly without staying. Wandering alone, one might perhaps follow; from within the brocade valley, I return to my dwelling. (The ancient saying goes: "Wandering alone atop the four mountain peaks...")
Wandering through the three great paths, on this day the hundred limbs crumble and scatter; it is said that a single thing eternally lives, a remark for another time.

On this day, that which eternally lives may still be known, but when at another time the limbs have crumbled and scattered, upon whom shall it rely to be raised up? One can know that there is thus arising and ceasing; only by understanding how to raise it up can one truly forget.
Giving and taking: radiant and silent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges. Be careful not to speak of "you" and "I" therein.

The stone tortoise on Flower Mountain does not reckon the antiquity of the years; though its old record has perished, its name still remains. Beside the road, the verdant tree grows old with the frost.

Snow. Wild grasses by the mountain stream follow the seasons of spring and autumn. Misconceptions have been passed down through the careful reading of the *Huayang zhuan*; of sacred traces, only those of Bhikṣu Yao are heard of.
One may rely on the power of meditative concentration to verify the present and the past; all other human affairs are but empty and lingering delusions.
The wooden fish strikes this gong without cause; the bells and drums blend together without confusion. The perceiving subject and the perceived object are not two conditions;
through this and that, they are mutually exchanged. Why do ordinary people create such clinging? How can the realized one achieve [liberation]?
Through the contemplation of wisdom, one may compassionately flow into *sarvajñā* (omniscience). Even while intoxicated by sleep, such is the case; like fish strung on a line, they are cast out.

Reading the scriptures, one is unstained yet stained, for the root of delusion is inherently void. Being stained yet unstained, there is nothing remaining; because the root is inherently void, it is naturally capable of accomplishment.
As for phenomena, how can their pure essence hinder the manifestation of myriad differences? When delusion is severed and the true mind is realized, how could it ever cease?
To say it is neither true nor false makes wisdom seem circuitous; to understand both truth and falsehood as unimpeded—this sovereign, perfect luminosity is only then the pearl.
He did not sleep in the house of the layman in Vaiśālī; within a space of ten *hū*—a mere wall-enclosure—he contained as many as the sands of the Ganges.

Eighty-four thousand high seats and a multitude of beings were, in an instant, provided with flowers perfumed by celestial incense. Though far-reaching, they do not reach those who are deluded by obstructions; yet, moment after moment, he constantly enters their hearts.
There is no difference. Mount Sumeru and the four great oceans—I see them as a single grain of millet or a sesame seed.
Rising early, I grow old;
the more I observe, the more my mind finds no worldly affairs. The night is long, and I especially know that my spirit grows cooler. In the shallow hearth, there is still—

The fire has died down; the moon over the distant mountains still hovers above the wall. I attempt to inscribe in silence the verses of the Nāga-like Samādhi of Extinction, yet my calligraphy is but the trivial carvings of an insect.
Suddenly startled by the crowing of a cock, I am abruptly cut off, and all at once I return to right contemplation.

Rising late, stretching out the feet and then drawing them back; a hungry mouse cries out. Closing the eyes and then opening them, once more the dew glistens. Only upon waking does one realize the events of the dream;
how could that which was dreamed be known after awakening? In the blink of an eye, the yellow millet is still not yet ripe; the butterfly flutters on.
Madly flying, I don my robes and sit alone at high noon. Let me ask: how does this differ from the time of midnight?
Composed two verses while wandering through the Myōdō and Anzō courtyards:
In the Great Being’s place of seated meditation, In the spring of Thousand Pines Courtyard, The gates are deep and the pines and cypresses are ancient; The events are old, yet the seasons are new.
People offer incense and lamps at night; birds sing and flowers rain down at dawn. It must be upon these meditation rocks that going and staying alike transcend the divine.
A white stupa amidst the clouds on the path, a clear sky above eaves beyond the birds’ flight—these fine mountains enter my gaze forever, and I sit here all day without weariness.
How many bamboos grow from the rocks? A few branches of blossoms reflect upon the curtain. Having never before reached Chang’an, divine power stirs both the flying and the hidden.
Quoting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*’s "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations," he composes this verse:
The Sugata clearly knows it is direct and not crooked; One must exhaust the deluded consciousness as a flower in the sky. Thus he causes Ānanda to investigate the mind.

The eyes: when first observing the superior marks at the start of his renunciation, why was it that within [the body] the liver and stomach were obscured? When their mutual correspondence is sought outside, yet another discrepancy arises.
Comparing the lapis lazuli to the eyes, they share the same objective realm; closing them creates obstruction, while opening them brings clarity without limit.

Where they meet, form arises accordingly, making it difficult to fixate on a substance; root and object are intertwined like drifting weeds and hemp. In all things of the world, there is no attachment—whether on water, land, or in the air.

One's actions become like a cataract or a flaw; for seven lifetimes there is no refuge, and one loses all composure. From this point on, one must begin to encompass all that is as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
To express my own state of mind and show it to students:
reflect deeply upon the events of fifty-three years, integrating them into the mind throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night. You must believe that every moment passes by.

Not yet; there is not even a hair’s breadth of further seeking. As past karmic roots are extinguished one by one, they are first severed; the path that forever cuts off new calamities has already become profound.
This is the place where one establishes the body and sustains life; therefore, I blow a single tune to repay those of like mind.
To Guangdao, while ill, I showed:
"My illness has no form and cannot be seen; Mañjuśrī alone attains deep knowledge of it.
If you wish to convey news on two or three occasions, push out the wooden pillow from the head of the bed.
At Mount Jangshan, seeing Officiant Wuzhuo depart for Shuzhou:

Having already paid homage to the stupa amidst the clouds, He now gazes once more upon his teacher within the hall. I think of the time when we were together north of the river By the western side of Dinglin Monastery.
A single phrase contains nothing more; amidst a thousand differences, never doubt. Upon reaching home, be diligent in its protection; this Way is known by few.
Sending off a Chan practitioner entering the capital:

amidst throngs of thousands and tens of thousands, be without joy or anger, for your ears and eyes will be unobstructed. If you wish to know the Venerable Fu of Taiyuan— *Note: The final line is a fragmentary imperative or rhetorical question directed at the practitioner.*
Seated. The bells and drums of the six streets resound with a tumultuous *dong-dong*.
Having once again received the imperial decree to retire to Mount Baoshan, I compose three verses on his behalf for Mr. Qian, the Governor of Wuhua.
Having long suffered from the "frost-and-mist illness," I have now been granted leave to return to the herd of deer. Your profound kindness toward me remains truly unrequited.
In response: Deep in meditation, I merely burn incense before the burner once more.

Your family possesses the enduring virtue of loyalty and tranquility; thus, with Dingming, you have opened the conditions for the Way. Whether in another age or in this present time, how could this be merely a matter of human intent?
To govern a thousand li with a single command is a tradition passed down through your lineage.

Emerging from the mountain peaks with a sense of ease, he also rides upon his inspiration; weary of flight, he returns at will, knowing how to go back. With a mind, one knows how to reach the realm of non-mind;
the bird yearns for its old forest, and the clouds remain upon the mountain.
Eulogy for the Image of Śākyamuni Tathāgata Emerging from the Mountains:

His wondrous form is not a physical body; his appearance is universal. Before he had descended upon Jambudvīpa, he was already beheld at the Twin Trees. Vast is his salvation, and profound is his merit.

For six years he practiced austerities; his marks and signs were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges across ten billion lands. When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Buddha-sun is at its zenith.

Those with right mindfulness receive its light, while the deluded seek it outwardly, carving sandalwood or weaving silk. Yet the image has not yet reached the stage of infancy; this present model is the very mold from which it arises.

The transmission comes from antiquity; the elephant-tread emerges from the mountains. The pearl of wisdom gushes forth from the river; the water-moon suddenly becomes clear. The gate of awakening is flung wide open.
Beholding it and gazing up at it, how could one dare to be self-disparaging? It is eternally present and imperishable—these words cause my hands to dance with joy.

Eulogy on Avalokiteśvara, Two Stanzas Throughout vast kalpas, you have been free from all suffering; Moment by moment, you have forever severed all conceptual discrimination. Wherever there is hearing, it is true hearing yet no hearing at all;
Though speaking when it is spoken, there is always no speaking. The Dharma-body manifests universally to both ordinary beings and sages alike; The faculty of hearing perceives the sound.
The sound ceased. In this Sahā world, there is the greatest affinity; with a single thought of cool clarity, the fever of affliction is removed.
Through vast eons, it has never been false; every word is therefore entirely true. Responding to thoughts, light descends as swift as a flash of lightning;
seeking out sounds to save from suffering, it rushes like a gale. Myriad chapters and ten thousand phrases transcend all characters; diverse rhythms and unique tones are bestowed.
Secretly revealed, manifested signs proclaim it when the time arrives; those who see or hear it find their minds liberated, rejoicing this very day.
A Eulogy on the Images of the Three Great Sages of Tiantai:
Majestic is Mount Tiantai, vast and expansive as the universe. The Great Sages are not "me"—they cannot be grasped even at the tip of a hair. The traveler from Shu’s heart is frantic with devotion.
A single speck of dust, a single thread—counting on one's fingers, clapping one's hands. Amidst pines, rocks, and fierce tigers, what sustenance is there in life?
Passed down through antiquity and today, I sit in quiet contemplation within this empty hall; it is not that I claim this is without benefit.
The Master Dharma’s eulogy shook the Liang and Wei dynasties;
he weighed the skin and the marrow. Who would say that his coming from the West was nothing more than an empty coffin? In the bare walls and empty hall—
At Shaolin on Mount Xiong’er, the Great Master Baizhang praised the continuation of the lamp of wisdom.
May this blessed precinct be opened wide and remain forever in the world. Like the moon in water or an image in a mirror—this is what is called a "congregation" (conglin).
The Great Wisdom Master Baizhang and the Monk of Yangqi praised him for displaying his performance atop the pole in the bustling marketplace,
startling the eyes of all who witnessed it; they lauded him for swallowing the thorny *liji* and *pulu* fruits whole, a feat that left everyone throughout the various quarters in awe.

At Xiushui in Yiyang, there was the floating fruit; at Yangqi, after the rain, clouds stretched across the sky. With heaven high above and earth below, Master Baiyun Yuan praised the manifest clarity of the fundamental principles.
Never forgetting the transmission of the dharma, his pure space is boundless, like the sun in midday. If you wish to investigate the root source, look here.
Beholding him at Longxiu:
Master Wuzu Yan’s eulogy says, "When encountering an enemy, he treats them as a kinsman;
his transmission is truly authentic. He has hard and tough teeth and guts of cast iron; his influence clears the regions of Huai and Chu."
The Way is truly the core of the patriarchal tradition; were it not for wisdom and compassion, how could descendants turn toward it?
Master Yuanshan Yuanjian praises the iron cavalry of Bingfen:
the old man rests in the desolate mound; the clouds have spread and the rain has ceased; the flowers fall and the waters flow.
Eulogy for Chan Master Dingming of Baoshan:

Renowned throughout the four seas as a master of the Tang, he emerged from Huayang and never rose from his meditative seat; soaring through the imperial capital, his fame became one with the mountain itself.
The Way flourishes with the times, saving the people and aiding the state. It can bring rain and it can bring sunshine; the poor obtain wealth, and those oppressed by heat find coolness.
That the masses of the ignorant turn to it is truly because it shall not perish.
Wu Shouzuo depicted my illusory physical form and further requested a eulogy for it:

"Vast and empty, there is no sage; solemn and majestic, there is a countenance. Bright and clear, it is free of all traces; subtle and dense, it leaves its tracks. In the past, he cherished his treasures."

A withered tree harbors a dragon; now he reveals himself to the world. Upon the great mountain stands the lofty pine: the dragon swallows the myriad species, and the pine flourishes through the three winters.
Divine and unchanging, it is surely followed by wind and clouds. My form has already attained its perfection, and your Way naturally gathers here. The road through Baoshan and Xishan is perilous.
The Han River flows toward the capital;
the head seat Guī seeks a eulogy.
Like a *gui* and like a *zhang*, you are not I. You are both humble and unrefined; in me, this may be fitting, but you now transmit it from me.
The clumsy becomes marvelous; things resonate and spirits meet. As the form moves, the mind follows; the gathered clouds do not fly away, and the cold moon shines down in reflection.
Who would call this ordinary? Who would call it sacred? I am just like that: the marvelous and the clumsy share the same thread. With joyous laughter, I await the literary expression.
Before the Great Simplicity had dispersed, one followed along with knowledge stored within, seeking praise for the colors and lacquer inside;
thus, the form was not seen. It is for this reason that my true self is remote within the shadows. My true self certainly exists, yet it is not a form.

Obstruction. To manifest illusory objects for the sake of ordinary people, once these objects are revealed, the Way becomes ever more fresh. One need not prize that Superior Man who came from the West;
the Chan practitioner Yuan seeks a eulogy.
Resembling others, resembling others; classifying me, classifying me. To whom do I further refer? Like fire meeting fire—it cannot be captured by sketching, nor can it be reached by pursuing.
To transcribe this at Longmen would bring calamity upon the patch-robed monk.

If one seeks to find a master who could serve as a worthy comparison, such a person is rare; yet his manifested form remains universal. He can appear in a single instant and illuminate the depths of a thousand ages. Like clouds rising from a dragon’s song.
The wind rises and the tigers roar; words to praise this are utterly exhausted. Gazing upon it, what can be seen?
The worthy Head Monastic (Kuan-yüan) requested a eulogy: "Pervading the entire realm, nothing is hidden;
at the tip of a single hair, there is singular wondrousness. Though he has not yet let out a sigh or a groan, he has already begun to smile. This, my son, is what you must recognize."
The moon in the water shines forth; not even a speck of dust is left behind. This is the essential core.

Who is it that seeks the "shoulder" (the Venerable Wei-na) and recognizes me? Observe the ultimate reality! Who says it is mere ink and color? To toil in search of it is but a vain effort. Severed clouds rest upon the mountain peaks.
The bright moon is on the wall; it is vividly alert. Awaken to this profound stillness.
A diligent practitioner of Chan seeks a eulogy:
"A single drop from the vast ocean is salty without end; a speck of dust upon the thick earth is expansive beyond measure. For what reason does one depict such a humble countenance?"
It is so. It is simply because your traces were found in Longshu that you, Attendant Xin, sought to praise my conduct.
You followed me; when I called, you responded. This following and responding—neither lacking nor superfluous—is how I came to know you.
This image is indeed intimate. Beholding it in stillness, its Way is truly beyond compare.
The original attendant requested a eulogy:
Though his Way is radiant, his form belongs to the mountains and wilds. Carrying a broken-legged cauldron, he dwells in a secluded aranya. His rustic tone has nothing to commend it; yet, it is so.

Whose humble likeness shall be painted? It has always been present at my side. My attendant Jueyuan and his junior disciple Chongjie requested a eulogy for this portrait, yet it was soon neglected and subsequently lost.
Vast and empty like space, as bright as the sun—looking upon these pigments that depict a physical form, who could have caused it to be so?
I have searched for it in vain.
Where is the man of non-attachment who seeks praise?

Where does he stand with staff in hand gazing at the clouds? Standing alone in the empty mountains, my heart is filled with emotion; I am ashamed that I am so desolate and possess nothing. I thank you for this.
Adorned and mutually perfected.
Professor Feng Jichuan requested a eulogy:

"In heaven and earth there is no 'thing' or 'self,' and for me there is likewise no 'thing. Hidden or manifest, empty clouds appear and disappear according to their course; who here has realized the profound mystery?"
A person. Amidst a flash of lightning, he roared a single "Du!
Wu Gongming sought a eulogy for him, wishing to know the old man Tanran.
He is a native of Longmen; his fame has spread throughout the four quarters. He has spent ten springs in this very place, sitting and reclining.

Having met Master Yi’an, who has departed, what prevents us from beholding his sublime form and true essence? Throughout our lives, we shared a karmic affinity through the incense and lamps; to perceive this correspondence is itself a spiritual power (*abhijñā*).

When Zhang Gongshou requested a eulogy, he first visited Mount Dongshan and later attended closely at Longxiu. Years have passed through cold and heat, and people have changed from old to new. Yet the "poisoned drum" continues its long resonance.
"Do not smell the *udumbara* flower; sit in stillness facing it all day long. The disciple Gongsu Daijuji requested a eulogy for the painting, which everyone recognizes:
"Meeting on the road behind Qiyun Peak, we remember our frequent comings and goings; the more we meet, the closer our way becomes."
The Abbots’ Hall of Longmen constantly requests a eulogy from me, the True Knower (Zhizhi).
Vast and formless, what is Longmen? There is a path that points the way, utterly free from the marks of axe and hatchet; it is through causes and conditions that one comes and goes.
Leaving matters to be discussed by others: the cold pools of Yellow Bamboo are bright in the morning and dark again at night.
*Recorded Sayings of Ancient Worthies*, Volume Thirty;
*Recorded Sayings of Ancient Worthies*, Volume Thirty-One.
Recorded from the Small Assembly (Xiaocan) of Master Fuyan of Longmen in Shu Prefecture, compiled by Shanwu, Dharma heir residing at Yunju in Nankang. The Small Assembly discourse says:
"What an excellent turning phrase! Is there anyone who can answer it? After a long silence, he said: "Question and answer are both complete."
Therefore, the ancients said: "One who preaches the Dharma should preach it according to the Dharma. But how does one preach according to the Dharma?
Since you all are raising waves where there is no wind, we cannot help but take what is non-existent and treat it as existent.
Thus it is said: "The one who preaches the Dharma has neither preaching nor demonstration; the one who listens to the Dharma has neither listening nor hearing. Since you all have no listening...
And listen. Here, where I am, there is speaking without speaking. If you can attain such a state, not a single dharma can be apprehended before your eyes.
Why? Listen for a moment: outside of what is spoken, there is not so much as a hair’s breadth of listening; outside of what is listened to, there is not so much as a hair’s breadth of speaking.
Thus one is able to penetrate both barriers simultaneously, such that no dualistic marks remain. It matters not whether there is speaking or no speaking, listening or no listening—of itself...

Yet the great earth, mountains, and rivers, as well as form, emptiness, light, and darkness, are not separate dharmas at all. This may be called "penetrating beyond the dust and toil" and "suddenly dwelling on the ground of reality.
Although one is currently within the three realms, one is intensely transcending the three realms;

although one is currently amidst sounds and forms, one is intensely transcending sounds and forms. Now, while speaking and listening with you all at this very moment, how can one speak of that which is "not"?
To explain the principle that cannot be heard, one must know its ultimate point and attain clear awakening before it can be realized. Have you not seen the ancient sayings?
"That which is neither form, sound, smell, taste, touch, nor mental object"—this destination is indeed extremely difficult to reach.

For those who study the Way, unless they have reached this stage, there will inevitably be a dharma before their eyes. Since there is a dharma externally, there must be a mind internally. Internally...

Through external conditions, one is submerged in the three realms. It is from this that the various sages appear; it is for this reason that the Dharma came from the West, appearing specifically on this earth.
Do you still know where these sages applied their minds? It is simply the mind of all people; there is no other mind, nor is there any other dharma. Therefore it is said:
"The Bhagavans of the ten directions share a single path to the gate of Nirvana. This is truly and without deviation.
Only then will you know that there is neither delusion nor enlightenment, and that one is neither a sage nor an ordinary person.

If you truly attain such a state, you should conceal your brilliance and hide your traces, treading upon the profound path of the sages. If this is not yet the case, you must certainly maintain constant vigilance.
Have you not seen how Master Zhaozhou said, "During the twelve periods of the day, I allow you one period for external study"? A monk then asked, "I am allowed one..."
At that time, the outsider asked, "I do not yet understand what you study. The Master said, "I study the Buddha; I study the Dharma.
The outsider replied, "If even the Buddha and the Dharma are considered 'external studies,' then what else can one possibly do during the twelve periods of the day? This is truly difficult to fathom.
For this reason, when I now meet with all of you, it is called "discourse at an improper time. Since it is discourse at an improper time, it is like...

How can you go away so easily? A person who has attained the Way is like one who can melt vases, platters, hairpins, and bracelets into a single piece of gold, or stir together butter, curd, and clarified butter into a single flavor.
For such a person, what does it matter whether the time is right or not? Everything will hit the mark. I exhort all of you: investigate this thoroughly and quickly.
During the twelve periods of the day and night, distance yourselves from worldly attachments and do not give rise to divergent thoughts. Is this not so?
I have heard that in the past, there was a man atop a high tower who saw two bhikṣus passing before the tower.
Two ghost-messengers were sweeping the road together, while another two ghosts followed behind scattering flowers.
When the two bhikṣus turned back, the next two ghosts again shouted and spat at them from the front, while the other two ghosts followed behind to sweep away their footprints. That man then...
He went downstairs to ask the two bhikṣus the reason for this, and they were only then filled with regret. Having attained awakening, they said:
"When we left, we were discussing the principles of the Buddha; yet by the time we returned, we were speaking of trivial matters.

O virtuous practitioners of dhyāna, although this was a coarse circumstance, if one examines it closely, it is a matter of great importance for those who study the Way. Why? It is simply because a fleeting thought arose."
Arising. When external objects appear before one, if thought does not arise, no object can be apprehended. Therefore, the Way of the ancient sages takes non-thought as its fundamental principle.
Now, there is merely the absence of the dualistic thoughts of ordinary and sage; likewise, there are no various mental constructs, no afflictions to be severed, and no enlightenment to be sought.
In birth there is no birth; in death there is no death. One does not perceive the [distinction between] the past and the present.
While Master Shàn was strolling with his senior teacher Mì on a mountain excursion, they suddenly saw a white rabbit spring from the grass.
Mì said, "It looks very much like a man in white robes being invested as a high minister. Shàn said, "Old man, old man, you are making such talk! Mì replied, "..."
"What about your elder brother? Shan said, "For generations he has worn the official cap and sash; for a moment he has fallen into disarray.
How can this koan be resolved? Tell me, what is the principle here? If you can understand how a commoner may be ennobled as a high minister," [he continued].

Thus, one walks alone upon the crimson heavens, forever transcending the common flow. If you can understand this, then you will know how to seize the food from the hungry and drive away the oxen of the plowmen.
Do you fully comprehend? Even if you were to comprehend every detail with absolute clarity, it would still not apply to anyone’s own portion.
What, then, is the matter regarding each person’s own portion? Try to judge for yourself.
After a long silence, he said, "What kind of rabbit are you hunting?

Take care. The Master returned to Dongshan to pay his respects. The assembly requested a small-scale sermon (*xiao can*), to which he replied: "I briefly descended from Lotus Peak and lightly counted my fingers; in the blink of an eye, three years have passed again.
Although there has been not even a hair’s breadth of separation, how can this compare to coming personally before the seat? [Signature] Xi.
I humbly recall that several days ago, I accompanied Master Taiping on his carriage as he ascended Mount Lian once more.
Upon returning to attend upon our Great Master, the Elder, while gazing upon his compassionate countenance, one must know there is a matter of "meeting. I venture to ask the assembly:
what is this matter of meeting? It cannot be that you see me or that I see you; such would merely be a mutual encounter.
Seeing. If it were like this, there would be no place at all where one gains power through the Buddha-dharma.
Why? Because within the various realms of the world, subject and object persist; one remains constantly within birth and death, with no ground for liberation.
Therefore, Master Xuefeng said to people: "I have already met you at Wangzhou Pavilion; I have already met you at Wushan Ridge."

"I have already met you before the Sangha Hall. If one relies on such an instruction, how could one wait for voices and countenances to meet, or for words and breaths to intermingle, before considering it a meeting?
Venerable elders, those who are students of the Way must truly possess a place of departure before they may succeed.
Do you understand yet? Nowadays, I dare say that though we share the same wind from a thousand miles away, meeting face-to-face is actually easier.
Meeting. Though you face one another, it is difficult to know. Why is it difficult to know? Old Man Jia Shan said:
"Before my eyes there is no Master; upon this seat there is no old monk. Although all those who have come are present here, how can you see that "before my eyes there is no Master"?
The Teacher, the Great Abbot, is seated in the hall, serving as witness for all the assembly. How do you act [in such a situation]?
