"How can you see that there is no old monk upon this seat? You must not pass through this casually, nor treat it as a trivial matter.
Day and night, you are buffeted by the winds of seeing and hearing; bound by the sense bases, the elements, the aggregates, and the spheres of perception, you find no freedom.
The matter of birth and death is great; you must attain a point of entry through awakening before you can succeed. Even so, this is the Way beyond the categories."
People truly encounter strange laughter. Why? You must know there is a point that transcends [the ordinary]. Wait for another day or time, and I shall break it open for you all.
Because I recall that in the past, the two venerable masters Nanquan and Zhaozhou were both those whose realization surpassed the mundane world and whose fame spread throughout the realm.
At that time, there was a monk who went into the mountains and saw a Chan master there.
He sat in a meditation hut atop a flat stone. A monk then asked, "Nanquan has appeared in the world with such great renown;
why do you not go there to pay your respects? What is the point of sitting here in vain? The master of the hut replied, "Do not speak of Nanquan appearing in the world;
even if the Buddha himself were to appear in the world, I would still not go. The monk took these words and went to see Nanquan. Nanquan was greatly astonished and subsequently sent Zhaozhou to him.
He went to investigate. Upon arriving at the abbot’s quarters, he walked from east to west; the abbot paid him no heed. He then walked from west to east;
the abbot still paid him no heed. Guo-zhou then stood directly in front of the door and said, "Abbot! You are defeated!
The abbot still paid him no heed, so Guo-zhou pulled down the curtain and walked away; the abbot still paid him no heed. O Great Assembly, this one episode—

Regarding this causal condition: how do you all truly understand it? Is it that Zhaozhou and Nanquan failed to reach the master’s ground, such that they were instead exposed by him and fell into his "trap for tigers"?

Or is it that although the master had no personal attainment, he lacked the ability to shift and exchange [his means] when the moment arose, resulting in a "corpse on level ground"? You gentlemen— *Note:

This passage is a classic Zen kōan inquiry, likely from the *Wumen Guan* (Gateless Barrier) or a similar collection of koans, examining the dynamic encounter between the masters Zhaozhou, Nanquan, and the Hermitage Master.*
This is simply not the principle. Generally speaking, a traveler on the path must have clear insight into the Way before they can succeed.
If one’s insight into the Way is not clear, one has already had one’s eyes changed by Nanquan, Zhaozhou, and the Hermit—there is not even a slight point of accord.
If, however, one’s insight into the Way is clear, then Nanquan, Zhaozhou, and the Hermit are themselves...
"Elder, do you have no other view? Do you not agree with this? Have you not heard it said: 'Having once traversed the great ocean, one ceases to boast of water;
were it not for Mount Sumeru, all else would be but dust'? You have stood long enough."
The *Xiajie Xiao-chan* (Small Summer Retreat Sermon) states: "One, two, three. The wordless youth speaks incessantly. Three, two, one.
Above, below, and in the four quarters, there is no equal. The livelihood of the patch-robed monk is devoid of even a hair’s breadth; the glorious legacy of ten thousand ages is this very day."

"Great assembly, what is this 'presently manifest certainty' of today? With monks and laypeople from east and west gathered here, lamps and candles glowing brightly—how can you see that matter which is utterly devoid of even a hair’s breadth of existence?
If you can see it here, you will realize that throughout kalpas of time it has been solitary luminosity, never once clouded or obscured.
Only then can you believe the saying: 'Bodhidharma did not come to the land of Tang, and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Thus it is said.
This concerns the matter of these people who have turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the dust of sensory objects.
Having wandered for a long time, their light of wisdom has been unable to manifest; therefore, they travel abroad to seek the Way and visit various masters.

If one can see clearly beneath even a single phrase, only then will one know that the affairs of immeasurable kalpas are found right this very day. Yet, the matters of today are also extremely difficult.
Understand this thoroughly. Why? It is because for all people, that which manifests as discrimination is the mind’s original, fundamental reality.
By mistakenly identifying with discrimination, one turns away from the true source. If one simply lacks this manifold discriminating mind, it will naturally be manifest at all times.
Regarding this very matter, does it still require expedient means or not? I, the mountain monk, have an expedient means to bestow universally upon the great assembly. Thereupon—
He raises the whisk and says: "Do you see it? If you say you see the whisk, you have blinded both eyes.
If you say you do not see the whisk, you are born-blind and have lost both eyes. Setting the eyes aside for a moment, tell me: does this whisk exist or not?
If the whisk exists, then there are dharmas external to the mind. If the whisk does not exist..."
This destroys the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). When it comes to this, how can those who study the Way provide any theoretical justification?
To point things out in such a manner is to excessively degrade the noble by treating them as base. If one were a truly authentic person on the Path, there would not be so many such matters.

Therefore, when our Śākyamuni Tathāgata was in the world, he established a gateway of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*), yet even then there were not so many such matters. Every time the retreat concluded...
They completed their retreats and did not visit one another, each seeking to realize the fruits of the Path. During the ninety days, some attained realization while others did not;
some harbored doubts while others were free of them; some incurred offenses while others remained blameless.
Upon reaching the day of the summer retreat’s *pravāraṇā*, they would then proceed to the Buddha’s dwelling to present their respective views and seek the Buddha’s seal of approval;

hence it is called *pravāraṇā*. Since the Great Awakened One concealed his radiance, the minds of men have become turbulent, resulting in various perceptions and knowledges—such as morning consultations and evening petitions—which prevent one from attaining accord with the original source. I recall when the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove.
In the vihāra, he entered the *varṣā* retreat together with the great bhikṣus.
When the day for the *pravāraṇā* arrived, the Venerable Upāli observed that the great assembly was as pure as the ocean, without any transgressions or violations;

however, there was only the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī who took no pleasure in his place of residence, preferring instead to roam through villages and thus violating the prohibitions and precepts. At that time, Upāli [related this] in full detail.
He informed the Buddha that he wished to expel Mañjuśrī. The World-Honored One said to him, "If you can expel him, then go ahead and expel him.
Thereupon, Upāli assembled the congregation and struck the *ghanṭā*. Yet, those to his left and right, above and below, were all Mañjuśrīs;
throughout the entire realm of empty space, every place was entirely Mañjuśrīs. The World-Honored One said to Upāli, "Which Mañjuśrī do you wish to expel?"
At that time, Upāli struck the *gandi* and prostrated in repentance, saying: "I am of little virtue and little wisdom;
I did not recognize the realm of the Great Being. O Great Assembly, it was truly regrettable that he was let go at that moment. I would rather have been one who delights in the Lesser Dharma.
Had he struck even a single blow, let alone Mañjuśrī—even the Old Man Śākyamuni himself would have had no place to stand."
Do you all know where the single blow lands?

If you can know it, then all sentient beings throughout the entire earth—the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence—will at once crumble like ice melting away, leaving not even a hair’s breadth to be seen.
Should there be a monk who comes forward and says, "Please, Master, try striking me," you should say to him: "Movement is not as good as stillness; let go."
One step beyond. Why? "The setting clouds fly side by side with the solitary wild goose; the autumn waters share the same hue as the vast sky. In a small *pratyaya-samādhi* (small *chan*), he said:
"The ancients said, 'If it were Tao Yuanming, he would knit his brows and turn back. Now I dare ask the assembly:
Is knitting one's brows and turning back a matter of having eyes, or not having eyes? If it is having eyes, why does he turn back?"
"You lack eyes. For what reason did you go back? As for those who went away, let them say as they please.
But as for those who have now returned here to circumambulate—do they possess eyes or not? If they possess eyes, why do they circumambulate? If they lack eyes,"

Why is it surrounded? Is there anyone capable of discerning this? If one can discern it, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of omission, and comes for an audience once every five days, it would truly be a rare occurrence for people to trouble themselves to seek this out.
Yet, since people do trouble themselves to seek it out, is it for the sake of worldly sentiment, or is it for the practical application of the Buddha-dharma? If it is for the sake of worldly people—
"Friends, we who are śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya cannot allow this to circulate as mere worldly convention.
If it were so, what benefit would there be? If it is the enjoyment of the Buddha-dharma, how do you perceive the principle of that enjoyment of the Buddha-dharma?
Is there anyone here who understands? Is it not the case that all of you have come from before the gate to inquire, with palms joined?"
Is standing on one’s hands the Buddha-dharma? If so, it calls out though it has no form, and it responds though it has no sound;
is the inexhaustible enjoyment in all places the Buddha-dharma? Is it not that he is not like this? Nothing can encompass him; the eyes do not see him, the ears do not hear him;
are these myriad apertures, all hollow and open, the Buddha-dharma? Is it not that you, Master, speak in such a way?
"Is it the Buddha-dharma for people to listen in such a manner? Is it not that, fundamentally, there is nothing to do? Why bother with such things?
It is very much like adding a head atop one's own head. Is it the Buddha-dharma simply to act according to the times and seasons?
Is it not that the two words 'Buddha-dharma' need not even be spoken? Mountains are mountains; waters are waters; monks are monks; laypeople are laypeople. For now, let us..."
"To establish a teaching gate to guide beginners—is this the Buddha-dharma? O assembly, this is certainly not the principle;
do not err! If it were so, then the Buddha-dharma would merely consist of what is driven about by the mouth and the mind.
If it were only like that, where would the Buddha-dharma be? It would all be meaningless speech, unreal speech, and deceptive speech—slandering Prajñā."
This is a grave offense, truly beyond bearing. It would be better not to have attained realization at all, for then one would remain free from trouble for kalpas.
By all means, do not claim to have attained what you have not; do not give rise to great arrogance and treat those who have gone before you with contempt.

If you have truly found a place of peace and joy, you must recognize some measure of good and evil, and distinguish some measure of the heterodox and the orthodox. You must not remain in a state of delusion, confusion, or superficiality.
This is merely self-deception and self-delusion. This mountain monk, however, is truly not deluded regarding the various sages.
Being here now, I do not begrudge my verbal efforts as I deliberate with you in this manner. I call this "discussing the real, not the unreal.
I simply desire one person whose understanding is clear and who has attained thorough awakening; I do not want all these various displays of wondrous activity.
Especially so. His spiritual pivot was profound and absolute; he applied both staff and shout simultaneously. One such as this cannot be grasped by mere conceptual extraction. Why?
Even before you had entered the gate, thirty blows were already administered to the soles of your feet.
Yet you come here again, raising your eyebrows, moving your eyes, snapping your fingers, and waving your sleeves, then departing and saying, "I am not being petty; there is nothing more to say."
[The Master] said, "Assembly! When you sweep your sleeves and walk out, I will indeed follow you. But how can this lingering doubt be resolved so that you may see the Truth?
Let me ask you: when you sweep your sleeves and walk out, you say it is finished. Yet why do you not sweep your sleeves when attending to the two necessities of nature?
Why do you not sweep your sleeves when eating porridge or rice? Why do you not sweep your sleeves when meeting others and exchanging greetings?"

When it is necessary to speak the Buddha-dharma, what is the meaning behind the gesture of waving one’s sleeves? If one point is penetrated, a thousand points and a hundred points are all penetrated at once.
Do not take offense at these harsh words; do not say they are mere empty chatter lacking flavor. I do not seek after your fame, reputation, or material gain.
It requires nothing more than for you to attain awakening, so that you may repay the Buddha’s kindness; beyond this, there is no other matter.
If you truly have a point of entry, you will know that this mountain monk does not treat you with partiality. Those who have already attained it should nurture the sacred embryo;
those who have not yet attained it should strive to resolve their doubts with speed. Have you not seen how Yaoshan did not ascend the hall for a long time? The monastery...
The attendant said, "The assembly has long been waiting for the Master’s instruction. Dōyō said, "Just strike the bell.
The head of the monastery struck the bell, and when the assembly had gathered, Dōyō closed the door of his quarters. The attendant said, "The Master promised to preach the Dharma for the assembly;
why do you not come out? Dōyō replied, "Attendant, there are sutra masters for the sutras, treatise masters for the treatises, and vinaya masters for the vinaya..."
"Venerable Vinaya Master, why do you find it so strange? Great Assembly, look at how extraordinary this ancient one was!
How could he be compared to those teachers of today who merely chatter away with their two flaps of skin, as if they were teaching from a book?
What benefit or salvation is there in that? Everyone, please disperse. Take care. After the assembly had dispersed, the Master spoke again: "Great Assembly, thirty years hence..."
One must not err in citing [the teachings].
In a *xiaocan* (small session), he said: "People of the present day must indeed honor themselves and value themselves; they must achieve self-reliance before they can succeed.
If one can do so, only then will there be a place of rest. Although there is a place of rest, there is also no measure of that rest. If...
It is not like this. To close one’s eyes and see flowers is to perceive things erroneously from the start. You need only recognize the mountain monk’s whisk and you will have it.
But how do you recognize the whisk? He held it up and said: “Do you see it? If you see it, you still do not recognize the mountain monk’s whisk.
If you do not see it, you likewise do not recognize the mountain monk’s whisk. Furthermore, what is self-respect?”

Regarding this principle of self-importance: recently, brothers have come to regard mountain wandering as "visiting the Way," viewing scenic sights as "studying under a teacher," and calling it "tramping about.
But does this truly constitute the business of tramping about?

You wish to see Mount Wutai and Qingliang, the capital, the two provinces of Jiangnan and Jiangbei, Mount Lu, Hunan, Tiantai, and Yandang—fine mountains, fine waters, and fine monasteries throughout the south and north. [He] picks up [the whisk].
[The Master] raised his whisk and said, "Look closely. A lifetime of traveling as a mendicant is now complete. "If you have toiled and traveled on foot, it is truly a matter of self-depreciation.
O assembly, you must by all means honor yourselves and value yourselves. Consider what it is that can be placed upon this state of dignity and nobility.
There is nothing more to do; there is no need to stand for long. A nun is originally made of womanhood; an elder sister is originally..."
"Brother-in-law! Good brother! Return to the hall! The Master Poshuo said:
"The Dharmakāya has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance. Only when each of these is thoroughly penetrated does one know how to sit securely."
Furthermore, at the assembly on Mount Lengyan, the Tathāgata spoke of fifty kinds of illnesses of meditation.
As I tell you people now, it is only by being truly without illness that one succeeds. The Way of Longmen speaks of only two kinds of illness: first, riding a donkey while searching for a donkey;
second, having already mounted the donkey, refusing to dismount. You say, "Having already mounted the donkey, one still searches for a donkey"—is this not utterly ridiculous?
A great illness! This mountain monk tells you not to seek it. A person of keen intelligence recognizes it immediately;
once the sickness of seeking is removed, the frantic mind comes to rest. Having recognized the donkey, yet mounting it and refusing to dismount—this is the most difficult illness to cure.
This mountain monk tells you not to mount it: you yourself are the donkey. The entire world is this very donkey.
"How do you ride? he asked. "If you ride, I guarantee your illness will not depart. If you do not ride, the ten directions of the world will open up and fall away;
these two illnesses will depart at once, and with nothing remaining in the mind, one is called a man of the Way.
What further matter could there be? This is why Zhaozhou asked Master Nanquan, 'What is the Way? Nanquan replied, 'The ordinary mind.'"

This was the Way. From this point on, Xiangzhou suddenly ceased his frantic seeking; he recognized the sickness of the Patriarchs and the sickness of the Buddhas, and there was nothing he did not penetrate.
Later, he traveled extensively throughout all regions, and no one surpassed him. This was because he had recognized the sickness.
One day, he went to visit Zhunai, walking with staff in hand from east to west and from west to east. Zhunai asked, "What is it? Xiangzhou said:
[Zhaozhou] probes the waters. Nanquan says, "In my place, there is not even a single drop. What is there to probe? Zhaozhou leans his staff against [a tree] and walks out.
Observe how he reveals some of his standards; it is truly extraordinary. Nowadays, monks generally take their illnesses as their dharma.
"Do not let the mind's illness flourish. [The Master] stood for a long time.
The Master said, "Is it not the case that one who does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion has transcended worldly toil? The mind does not know the mind."
The eye does not see the eye. Since it is absolute and without counterpart, when seeing forms there are no forms to be seen;
when hearing sounds there are no sounds to be heard. Is this not the transcendence of worldly toil? One enters where there are no paths; one sees where there are no seams or gaps.
Even the Buddha-dharma has no east, west, south, or north. It is not said that you are the disciple and I am the teacher. If [one is] oneself...
It is personally manifest and clear; there is nothing that is not so. When attending upon a teacher, one does not perceive a teacher; when attending to oneself, one does not perceive a self.
When reading the sutras, one does not perceive the sutras; when eating, one does not perceive the food; when sitting in meditation, one does not perceive the sitting.
In daily life, there is no deviation; not even a hair’s breadth of a characteristic can be found. To see it in this way—this is true seeing.
Is this not being free and at ease? [The Master] stood for a long time.
The Master said: "If you do not ask, it cannot be; yet as soon as you come to ask, you have already made light of yourself. If you do not ask, how can one know?"
You must also understand the question before you can attain it. I have just prodded you at the crown of your head with a awl to make you recognize pain and itch;

it was like peeling off the scab from a moxibustion sore. A person of keen faculties would immediately know this, and only then would they have attained it. Do not deceive yourself. I am not deceiving you.

I have not seen an ancient ask: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? A venerable elder was greatly startled and said, "Why do you ask him about the meaning of his coming from the West?
Why not ask about your own meaning? What is your own meaning? He replied: [He remained silent.]
One should contemplate the secret function. What is this secret function? An elder demonstrated it by opening and closing his eyes.
How many times did the ancients speak with such bitter urgency! Yet later descendants do not act in this way either;

as soon as someone enters the gate, they simply shout, without any further deliberation or hesitation, fearing most that you might not understand—there is such a matter, so why do you not recognize it?
Take this up. Elsewhere, people are fond of having others examine *kōan*s; here, I present a *kōan* that is already fully realized, which you should observe well.

Do not let it be "seen through," for then you will miss the great matter, whether large or small. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, your state is nothing but deluded thoughts, worldly toil, and mental preoccupations.
Wisdom has not yet arisen. All that is disseminated comes from within the mental faculty (*manas*). What use would there be for it?
When wisdom is like the rising sun, there is nothing that does not become bright and clear; this is called the manifestation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
You must reach such a realization once and for all. From this point on, you will have a place to set foot and a share in the words spoken to you. If it is otherwise...
"Delusory thoughts and worldly toil—where I, this mountain monk, have no place to set hand or foot; truly laughable, truly laughable!
To speak of the east and enter the west, to speak of the west and enter the east—I can do nothing for you. If you can turn your head around and your wisdom opens, then you will understand:
'The Master has always been speaking for me,' and 'I too have been speaking for the Master. When you shake your head..."
It is a matter of tailoring one's practice to suit oneself. You all vainly claim to have been practicing Chan for ten or five years;
when have you ever truly applied yourselves with such effort? It is merely to satisfy a fleeting impulse. When you first came here, were you willing to look into yourself?
If so, your practice was not yet matured, and there was no flavor in it. Now that you are here, spend ten or five years applying yourself.
When your practice becomes mature, you will surely attain awakening. I usually teach people how to practice;
the words I speak all accord with those of the ancients, not differing by a single character. Once you have mastered this, you will know the affairs of the ancients.
Do not say, "The ancients spoke thus, but I understand it differently"—that would be incorrect.
As for what the ancients said—"It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving; it is the mind of the worthy one moving"—how many words have reached your own station?
Are they right? Are they wrong? Furthermore, they say, "I am you; you are me. There is nothing beyond this.
Again, when someone asked Yunmen, "What is the student’s own self? Yunmen replied, "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth."
"Childish and fond of [conceptual] likes and dislikes. To say 'this exists' or 'that does not exist'—if mountains, rivers, and the great earth were to depart, how could you see your own self?
If they do not exist, how can you say they are non-existent right now while these mountains, rivers, and the great earth are manifest? The ancients have already explained this to you;
you simply fail to awaken to it and remain ignorant. Longmen constantly tells you that this is the matter of original possession, which is currently active and functioning within your own sphere."
Do not cling to seeking; do not cling to arranging; do not cling to cultivation or realization. It requires only that you have a single, deep faith;
this is extremely effortless. Such a person is hard to find. When my late teacher was in Baizhang’s assembly, Master Wuzu often said:
This Way is the wondrous state of natural spontaneity attained by oneself; it is because there is a matter of innate knowledge.
When I saw my former teacher, for ten years I could not speak of it, simply because my doubt was so deep. Later, I came to understand it thoroughly; now, altogether, no effort is required.
It is not a time of deliberation, yet it is also not the case that there is no deliberation. This is the Buddha-dharma.
It is not so. As for the matter beneath the *kāṣāya*, do not let it be buried by this mountain monk.
If you do not withdraw to reflect and investigate, your entire life will be buried; how could there ever be such a message? At present, your eye of the Way is not clear.
"Those who have transcended the world are many. A transgression! A transgression! How would one dare to occupy the high seat for others? [The Master] raises his whisk to show it to people;
'Agh!'—it would frighten people to death. He is like one who is blind or deaf; he is neither startled nor terrified, merely pursuing what is before his eyes.
He has no anxiety for future lives; he beats the ghosts on their buttocks. Suffering! Suffering! You people possess the causes and conditions of merit."
When awakening the mind, you must by no means become a world-transcending person. A disaster! A disaster! If there were any genuine reality, its fragrance would naturally manifest.
Look at how many superficial Chan masters there are; as time passes, they become worse day by day.
It is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood—when it is finished, it still reeks only of filth. You all seek liberation from birth and death.

Seeking the essential way of transcendence, one must strike so that [the mind] becomes a single piece. It is not that you and Rong become a single piece; rather, it is through this striking that they become a single piece.
If one were to try to make them a single piece by teaching, they would certainly never become a single piece. Long ago, there was a monk who had studied under Master Ju Dao.
One day, while traveling in the mountains, he asked: "Master, Xianglin said: 'For thirty years, I have sought to become a single piece...'"
"A single piece cannot be found. What is the meaning of this? Jue Daoshi said, "The old monk is also like this," and then asked the monk, "Do you understand?
The monk replied, "I do not understand. Jue Daoshi then gave the monk another verse, saying:
"The Fragrant Forest forms a single piece; The old monk is also like this. Before this month has ended, I shall once again break it open for you. At the end of the month...
Jǔdào (Lifting the Way) subsequently passed away. You tell me, what of this "single matter"? Is it good or not? Xianglin has become a single expanse;
Longmen is also thus. To inform all you practitioners of Zen: do not let it slip past you right before your faces.
Each of you, depart. [He remained standing for a long time.]
The Master said: "Many have seen it, yet they are helpless. Now, having seen it, why are they helpless?
It is simply because they do not recognize it; therefore, they are helpless. If one sees it and recognizes it, then one can deal with it.
Yet, when one resolves to practice Chan, one wishes to understand it immediately—who does not desire this? It is only because there is no point of entry that people try to force an understanding."
It cannot be attained. It does not accord with anything; the conditions everywhere are at variance. Even if you exert effort to grasp it, you will not attain it. After a long while, he said:

"In all twelve hours of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, in your turning, moving, bowing, or looking up, and in all manner of activities—everywhere there is that matter which transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs. Yet, the very moment you wish to understand it, it is already gone. Truly.
"This one is 'no. If you attempt to settle upon it, you have already turned your back on it. Therefore it is said: 'Seeing it is simply being helpless.
Is it not the case that when you do not apply the mind nor give rise to intellectual understanding, you attain it? To turn it over and over like this is even more impossible.
If you cannot attain it through understanding, how much less so without understanding? If it were a person of keen intelligence, as soon as they hear this mountain monk speak—"
If you can see with wide-open eyes upon encountering this, are you not a person of immeasurable capacity?
It was said, "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination," and it was also said, "Where wisdom does not reach.
If it were not so, how could it be called the Buddha-Dharma? Nowadays, you brothers merely present your intellectual understandings and your personal views as the Way.
In principle, when has anyone ever understood it as coming from such a source? When has anyone ever reached such a state?
If there is a person with the seed-nature for the Way who is willing to look into it in this manner, they must investigate it deeply and examine it closely.
If, all of a sudden, they can manage it, then doubt will vanish. You all do not understand because of the twelve hours [of the day].

In the midst of this, you are snatched away by miscellaneous discursive thoughts. This is because you desire to study worldly affairs; seeing things, you fall in love with them, and seeing texts, you fall in love with them.
As time passes, you are led astray by these pursuits. How, then, can your spiritual practice be accomplished?

For all who study worldly affairs, each has their own proper time. Once one is over thirty, it is no longer possible to learn them; even if one does study, they will be difficult to master. To study...
If you have attained it, what further use is there? If your own task is accomplished, even study can remain; this is because you have already been enlightened.
If your own task is accomplished, how could you possibly be willing to study? If one is in their twenties or so, they may still be able to study;
however, even those who are sharp-witted and mindful of birth and death will not be willing to study. Furthermore, in all cases of Zen practice, one must first have a level mind.

Straightforwardness. It is the correspondence between mind and mouth; because the words of the mind are straightforward, such is the state of the stages from beginning to end, without any element of deviousness.
Do not say, "I understand," or "How could I possibly attain it? If you were to somehow attain it, why would you go anywhere else to ask others?
Just now you said you understand Chan. People are watching your every move and observing your speech and actions.
Why, then, do you ask, "How is this? and "How is that? If you truly understand Chan, how can you still be struggling with ignorance?
Take for instance the saying, "Silent radiance conceals its brilliance"—how is that? "Hiding one's name and obscuring one's traces"—how is that? Not...
How can you say that the minds of others are not the Way? Each of you should examine your own conditions and refrain from speaking of right and wrong.
For instance, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; advancing, retreating, bowing, or looking up—every single moment is transcending the Buddhas and surpassing the Patriarchs.

The water buffalo before the mountain possesses the Buddha-dharma; yet the moment you begin to investigate it, it is already gone. Why do you not recognize it in this way? We have stood for a long time.
The Master said: "The livelihood of Longmen is the very marrow of the thousand sages. There has not been a single thought in which I have not spoken to you all;
it is simply that you yourselves are unwilling to accept it, and thus it has turned out that I am deceiving you.
Furthermore, where is there any place where I am not speaking to you? Zen practitioners say, 'This monk does not teach people to engage in deliberation.'"

I do not teach people how to understand or interpret; I do not teach people to deliberate upon causes and conditions; I do not cite the ancients or the present. To do so would be merely to pass the time in vain.
If I were staying at another place for a summer retreat, I would certainly have to clarify two or three public cases (gong'an) or listen to a certain text.
If you wish to deliberate upon them or cite the ancients and the present, then please go elsewhere; here with me, it is otherwise.
It is simply the single flavor of Chan; therefore, it is called the marrow and bones of the thousand sages.
Let me ask you: why did you just now inquire after the Holy Monk? When you were inquiring, did he verify you? Did he grant you his assent?

If you say it is a matter of certification through the seal, then you and he are but ordinary monks; how could they understand certification? If you say it is a matter of assent and approval, then how could you understand assent and approval?
Since you do not understand assent, approval, certification, or the formal greeting, why do you ask this question?

Is it within the realm of benevolence and righteousness? Is it a matter of perceiving appearances to give rise to goodness? If it were within the realm of benevolence and righteousness, then for a member of our lineage of patch-robed monks—

How could there be benevolence and righteousness? How could there be the perception of forms that gives rise to goodness? Is it not the case that these matters are unavoidable, and that one merely follows the crowd in offering greetings?
Furthermore, what principle does this establish? Reaching this point, one must clarify each and every thing before it can be attained.
Have you not seen how the Great Master Changsha one day turned his head and saw the Holy Monk, whereupon he suddenly knew his homecoming and said: "Turning my head, I suddenly see my own nature"?
The coming body and the original body are neither seen nor real. If you take the original essence to be the same as the true essence, you will wander through kalpas enduring bitter suffering.
Do any of you understand this principle? Take care.
The Master said: "Sometimes when questioned, monks all say they do not know and do not understand; they merely say, 'When hungry, I eat;
when tired, I sleep. What remedy is there for such talk?
Furthermore, they say they do not know the size of the months nor heed the intercalary days of the year—who would attend to such matters as these? Let me ask you: what is it?"
Sheng spoke of a principle that is "not knowing. When you see someone speak thus, do you immediately say the same?
Have you ever truly realized that principle of "not knowing"? An ancient said, "He who does not know knows nothing that is not known;
he reaches everywhere that is not reached. To call it "not knowing" is to lead you, people of the present day, to that state of "not knowing. This is...
The realm of the sages—how can it be compared to the blind ignorance of today, where one calls their lack of understanding "not knowing"?
If everyone were like this, saying, "I do not know and I do not care," then should someone suddenly question you, how would you transmit the single path of Caoxi?
I fear there would be no one left to carry on the lineage. You must not act in this way; you must diligently investigate and discern for yourself. Be careful!
[The Master] said: "In antiquity, there was a Chan master who asked an elder: 'What is the essential point for transcendence? The elder replied:
'Smoke rises from beneath the Venerable One's feet. At these words, the Chan master suddenly attained the fundamental meaning. Do you all still understand the matter of transcendence?"
"Ma! If you give rise to a conceptual understanding, you have already missed it. Later, a venerable master said, "I dare not fail the Master;
smoke is rising beneath my feet. Furthermore, when Beiyuan Tong took his leave of Dongshan, Dongshan asked him, "Where are you going?
Tong replied, "I am going into the mountains. Dongshan said, "The Feiyuan Ridge is steep; you must look well [at it]. Tong hesitated, and Dongshan said, "Tong!"
Tongyìng responded, "Yes, Shīlācārya. Dàoshān said, "Why do you not enter the mountain pass? At these words, Tongyì suddenly attained the essential meaning beneath them.

The ancients were extremely direct in their dealings with others; whenever someone came to them, there was nothing they would not show him. When he said, "Enter the mountain pass," what was the meaning?
People today do not understand this clearly and must create some point of comprehension for themselves, using a mere fragment of understanding as... [the text ends].

This has been clearly separated. One is permitted only to investigate its essence; one is not permitted to rely on intellectual understanding. Once the essence is realized as one, there is no further doubt. Nevertheless, it is not easy to maintain this state.
If you can enter into this, there will be no falling back or loss. Therefore, it is said that where there is understanding, clarity is attained.

It is better not to see it in a state of non-attainment; there is also a portion that can be relied upon, where there is no longer any time of failing to attend to it or any time of not understanding it.
Therefore, the ancients said: "The ordinary mind is the Way. Can one still direct oneself toward it? If you intend to direct yourself toward it, you have already deviated.
Seeing this, he does not permit you to direct yourself toward it. Furthermore, how can one rely upon it? It is not easy; it is not easy.
Is this not indeed the matter of transcendence? If you seek a place of transcendence, it is what is called "bitter distress.
Xuansha said: "The entire earth is hell; one dwells there for kalpas. If you do not attain clarity beneath this thread of robe-cloth, that is great bitter distress."
This is no matter to be taken lightly; you have stood here for too long. The Master said:
"The Third Patriarch, the Great Master, taught: 'Do not seek the Truth; simply cease your views. He further said:
'As soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes confused and loses the mind. These words are precisely where you people of today should apply your practice."
Furthermore, when you see him say, "There is no need to seek the Truth," you immediately reply, "Then there is no need to seek it at all. This is precisely what is called "seeing without cessation";
with such conflicting views, one will never arrive at the mind that has no seeking, but will merely form intellectual interpretations. This is the way of those who study the Way nowadays.
Examples are all like this. When you encounter a turning phrase, you must find a point of insight within that phrase;
then you will say of all words and sentences, "There is nothing that is not this very matter.

To thus store it in your heart and claim it as your own possession, without realizing that you have given rise to intellectual views and lost your true mind—clinging to it and refusing to let go—you are a truly great fool. You must [realize this].

Have you attained the mind that has nothing to seek? Simply do not give rise to various views; it is not a matter of being in a state of dark oblivion where nothing is understood that one calls "seeking nothing.
If, throughout the ordinary twelve periods of the day, you do not clearly comprehend what is before your eyes, it is because your mind of views is engaged in grasping and rejecting.
Furthermore, how could you know the mind of non-discrimination? Therefore, the former sages said: "Are there differences between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

The answer was: "There are no differences. Heaven and earth, rivers and seas, wind and clouds, grasses and trees, birds and beasts, humans and things, birth and death, and transformations—all these appearing before one's eyes are called the marks of the conditioned. The Way of the unconditioned is tranquil and motionless, beyond all form.
It has no name; it is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). How can one attain non-differentiation? Master Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature;
the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. These two are distinct; how then can one clarify the principle of their identity?
One must realize the mind that seeks nothing, and thereby harmonize and integrate them into the state of non-action. 10.

The fifth stage among the stages is the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā). This means that true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) and conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are extremely difficult to attain simultaneously;

at the moment of entering this stage, both are equalized, and for this reason it is called the Difficult to Conquer Stage. You fellow students on the path of training, throughout the two six-periods of the day and night, you should skillfully grasp the teachings and so forth.
Then, recognize: "Is this not something projected by your own non-conceptual mind? It is like a painter who produces various forms through his painting.
Beauty and ugliness. One paints out the five aggregates; one paints out humans and devas. At the very moment of painting, no external power is borrowed;

both the painter and the painted lack any discrimination. Because of this failure to understand, various views arise—viewing self and viewing others—and one spontaneously generates beauty and ugliness.
Thus it is said: "The master painter paints hell, with hundreds of thousands of hideous forms. When he lays down his brush, look from the beginning: it is truly..."
The cold of the ground-bone hair: if one knows this is merely a painting coming forth, what is there to fear? The ancients understood this clearly; it is fully manifest in all places.
When the Great Master Xuansha was felling wood, a tiger leaped out at him. His attendant said, "Tiger! Tiger, Master! Xuansha shouted, "It is you who are the tiger!
Furthermore, while a monk was prostrating, Xuansha said, "Because of me, you have come to pay homage."
This expedient means deeply accords with the Buddha’s intent. When Master Fayen pointed to the dog before him and said, "A painting has been carved out;
when you all look at it, do not seek its meaning upon the dog's body. You must bring it back to your own self and look there before you will succeed.
Only then will you understand his saying: 'As soon as there is right and wrong, confusion arises and the mind is lost. Recognize this well!"
[The student] stood for a long time.
The Master said: "If one can right now directly believe that 'it is so,' one is already called 'inept.
How much more so if one cannot directly believe it—what use is such a person? Even if one directly believes that 'it is so,' why would one be called inept?"
As for this, from all that long time past, where have you been coming and going? You must know that you have already lost a peg;
thus, what was previously unresolved becomes, in turn, an extraneous view. I observe that among the ancients of old, there were those who attained enlightenment from delusion;
all that has been disseminated is the Dharma-gate of attaining enlightenment from delusion. There are those who, having attained enlightenment, understand...
Regarding those who are deluded: all that is propagated for them is the dharma-gate of awakening by understanding delusion. Regarding those for whom there is neither delusion nor awakening:
all that is propagated for them is the dharma-gate of neither delusion nor awakening. Next, regarding those who come from outside delusion and attain awakening:
These are also very numerous, and thus are not worth mentioning. Moreover, those who do not understand awakening and fail to comprehend delusion are precisely the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
From the masters of old such as Nanquan and Guizong, this was called the "view of neither delusion nor awakening.
Nowadays, students merely pursue the words "neither delusion nor awakening" with their mouths; how could they have ever arrived at its true meaning? Do not speak of it lightly.
He said, "It is because you have doubts. I shall now ask you a question: when first entering the mother's womb, what object did you bring with you?
At the time of your coming, there was not a single thing; there was only this mind-consciousness, which has neither form nor appearance.
When it comes to the time of death, one casts off this burden of the five aggregates, yet there is still not a single thing—there is only this mind."
Consciousness. It is like this now when you travel as a wandering monk and enter among the assembly; this is the sovereign master. I ask you now:
you received the vital energy and the essence-blood of your parents, and that which grasps and maintains it is called "my body. From the moment of birth, it gradually grew until it reached maturity;
this body was entirely considered to belong to me. But tell me, does it belong to you or not? If you say it belongs to you, then at the very moment of first entering the womb—
Nothing has been brought here from elsewhere. When did these parents’ vital essence and blood ever belong to you? Furthermore, they should have remained with you for a hundred years;
yet, as before, they are cast off as a corpse—so when did they ever truly belong to you? If you say they do not belong to you, how is it that now, not even a single step can be taken without them?
When scolded, they understand how to cease their anger; when in pain, they are able to endure it. How, then, could they not belong to you?
If you can deliberate and examine whether it exists or not, you will certainly be unable to remain indifferent to the distinction. This is because the root of doubt has not been severed.
As for the notion that it "exists," from the time of birth, as one gradually grows—reaching three years, five years, and even up to twenty years—[the sense of self persists].
It is certain and unchanging that by the time one reaches forty or fifty years of age, this body undergoes transformation and decay from moment to moment; it is impermanent from instant to instant.
It is certain that this is called "existence," and one cannot say it has come from "non-existence. All its various movements and functions can be performed, yet one cannot say it is non-existent.
Long ago, there was a man who lost his way while traveling and stayed overnight in an empty house. At night, a ghost appeared.
A ghost arrived carrying a corpse. Shortly thereafter, another ghost came and said, "This is my corpse. The first ghost replied, "I brought it here from that place.
The second ghost forcibly seized the corpse. The first ghost said, "There is a traveler here who can testify to this."
The two ghosts approached and asked, "Whose corpse is this that you have brought? The traveler thought to himself, "Both ghosts are malevolent;
surely one of them will harm me. I have heard that those who do not speak falsely at the moment of death will certainly be reborn in heaven.
He then pointed to the first ghost and said, "That ghost brought it here. The second ghost was greatly enraged and tore off the traveler's four limbs, while the first ghost felt ashamed.
The man replied, "If you will provide me with testimony for these words of mine, I shall cause your limbs to become incomplete. He then restored the corpse limb by limb;
however, the head, the heart, and the abdomen were taken away again by a ghost from behind. The first ghost then restored them one by one using the corpse.
Thereupon, the two ghosts scrambled on the ground to devour the flesh until it was completely gone and departed. At this, the traveler’s eyes—
Previously, he saw that his parents’ bodies had already been devoured by two ghosts; he then looked back at the body he had exchanged and wondered:
"Is this me? Is it not me? Does it exist? Does it not exist? Thereupon, his mind became utterly deranged.
He ran to a monastery and saw a bhikṣu, to whom he recounted all that had happened. The bhikṣu said, "This person is easily transformable."
Dudu already knew that this body is not existent; he then had the essential points of the Dharma briefly explained to him and subsequently attained the fruit of the Way.
You people merely speak of "investigating Zen" (chanzhen) and, upon citing a kōan (yinyuan), immediately call it the Buddha-Dharma, claiming it is the very marrow of Zen.
Why do you not investigate by harboring such doubt? Do you understand? Your body is neither existent nor non-existent; existence is the mind.

"There is [existence]. When the body exists, this mind has never existed. There is no [non-existence]. When the body is absent, this mind has never been absent. Do you understand? To speak further of the mind:
it is neither existent nor non-existent. Ultimately, it is not you. That which originally existed is now non-existent; that which originally was non-existent is now existent.
This is the view of permanence and annihilation. Stand firm for a long time."
