Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Masters, Volume Thirty-two:
The Universal Discourses and Record of Master Fuyan of Longmen in Shu State.
Compiled by Shangu, Dharma-heir residing at Yunju in Nankang.
The Master stood before the meditation seat and said, "I, this mountain monk, stand here waiting for you all to grasp it. Can you grasp it?
After a long silence, he sat down and said, "Even having seen it, it is not easy to establish a true mastery. Have you not seen the ancients?"
He called out to a monk, "Upādhyāya! The monk turned his head back. An ancient said, "A fellow carrying a wooden board.

At such a moment, how can one act as a master to avoid being called a "fellow carrying a wooden board"? This matter is not easily grasped. It is called the vast expanse of karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Thus, it is said that Muzhou asked Yangshan, "All the people in the great earth have a vast expanse of karmic consciousness; what about you?"
"How do you distinguish them? Yangshan said, "I have a way to test it. Guishan asked, "How do you test it?
At that moment, a monk passed by in front of them. Yangshan called out, "Venerable sir! Venerable sir! The monk turned his head back, and Yangshan said:
"This very thing is precisely what is called 'the vast expanse of karmic consciousness' (*karma-vijñāna*).
The Master said, "At this very moment, how can you act as a master to avoid being told that you are in the 'vast expanse of karmic consciousness'?
Some Chan practitioners forcibly attempt to act as masters, saying, "When he calls, simply do not respond, and he will leave. But why would you respond to him? You are not him!
"Wooden head. Some are not like this. They raise a fist and utter a "Tut! and call this "forcibly assuming mastery. But let me ask you:
when you raise a fist and utter a "Tut" here, it is indeed up to you;

however, what will you do when someone suddenly questions you while you are preoccupied with the front porch or the back eaves? You cannot simply utter another "Tut" and raise a fist. Raise [your hand].
"A single blow! But it must be real before it will do. This matter is truly impartial; it makes no distinction between noble and lowly.
You see, Minister Chen Cao was a mere secular official. One day, while he was on his tower with his subordinates, he saw several monks passing by with their bundles packed.
One official remarked, 'Several Zen guests. Chen said, 'I am not yet convinced; I shall wait to examine them.'"
The monk approached the front of the tower. Cao called out, "Upādhyāya! The monks all raised their heads. Cao looked back at his subordinates and said, "I told you so.
At such a moment, how could one act as a true master to avoid being seen through by him?
Setting aside for a moment the 'board-carrying' fellow mentioned by the ancients, consider this: when that monk turned his head upon being called."
"Head. Why, then, does it become a "carrying a board"? How do you understand this? When the Buddha-dharma reaches this point, one must know that there are profound and far-reaching depths;
one must soak in it for a long time and must not forcibly assume mastery. [The Master] stood for a long while.
The Master said: "In general, practicing the Way requires one to be free from discursive thought. This gate is the most effortless of all; it simply requires that you abandon emotional attachments.
Only when you clearly realize that there is no dharma within the triple world can you truly practice. To practice outside of this is merely laborious and arduous.
Have you not heard of an ancient monk who observed the precepts for his entire life? One night, while walking, he stepped..."
He noticed something making a sound; it was a frog with countless eggs within its belly.
He was filled with incessant regret and alarm, when suddenly he fell asleep and dreamed that several hundred frogs came to demand his life. The monk was seized with profound fear.
When dawn broke, he went to look at it and found it was merely an old eggplant. At that moment, the monk’s doubts were instantly extinguished;
only then did he realize that there is no dharma within the three realms, and only then could he understand how to practice through actual realization. I ask you all:
when he stepped upon it in the night, was it a frog or was it an old eggplant? If it were a frog, [then... at dawn...
At dawn, it is seen to be an old eggplant. If it is indeed an old eggplant, even before daybreak there was a frog seeking its life;
can you cut this off? Let the mountain monk try to settle this for everyone: "The frog’s emotion has already been shed, yet the eggplant’s understanding still remains.
To attain freedom from the eggplant’s understanding, strike noon with the evening bell. [He stood for a long time.]
One day, when the assembly had gathered, the Master came forth and walked two circuits before the multitude.
He let out a long sigh and said, "The mountain monk has already run two laps through the bellies of you all. Do you know it? It has not been otherwise even today."
It is constantly moving back and forth within the bellies of all of you. Do you know it? It is called the "mind that has no deceptions.
It is truly so. This mountain monk knows fully whether you are good or evil.
Therefore it is said: "Where all of you know, Liang-sui knows all; where Liang-sui knows, all of you do not know. Master Liang-sui was...
This master of exegesis, however, clearly understood this matter. One day he went to see Magu.
When Magu saw him coming, he paid him no mind and simply took up a hoe and entered the vegetable garden.
Liang-sui followed after him as well, but Magu still ignored him and returned to his quarters, closing the door behind him. Thereupon, as he reflected deeply, his spirit suddenly attained clarity.
He then said, "Preceptor, do not deceive Liangsui! Do you all now still manage to be like this? It is not easy to grasp.
Furthermore, there was Master Guling under Baizhang; having attained the Dharma, he returned to receive his former teacher.
This was not only the case with ancients; among people today there are also such as this. Have you not seen that forty or fifty years ago, there was a man of tea...?
When National Teacher Lingyu was serving as the abbot of a mountain monastery, a monk from Mount Lu arrived. During their conversation, the teacher raised a case for him:
"A monk asked Faden, 'How does one advance further atop a hundred-foot pole? Faden said, 'Ugh! From that point on, Lingyu investigated this matter daily."
Even while eating porridge or rice, he never for a moment parted from this thought.

One day, while traveling on an invitation to another place, he was riding a donkey across a bridge when the bridge gave way and the donkey’s leg fell in. Unconsciously, he uttered the word, "Agh! and suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He then composed a verse of realization, which says: "I have a bright pearl, Long shrouded by various defilements. Today, the dust..."
The Light of Exhaustion arises, illuminating and shattering mountains and rivers, flower by flower. This is the very model; it is called "studying with reality.
People of the present day should simply study in this manner. If you rely on words and intellectual understanding while wishing to clarify this matter, you will never succeed.
It is clear that this cannot be grasped. To attempt to match the words with the meaning is to miss the point; it simply cannot be matched. You must know that there is a cause for awakening.
If you are truly studying the Way, simply look in this manner. Even if you rely on your current understanding and rest content with having mastered a few phrases, that will suffice.
All of you have been traveling as pilgrims to resolve the great matter of birth and death; you must not rely on your present state.
If you simply stop at meditative concentration, you must become like those ancients; you must seek for yourself a point of awakening.
Only then will you have the true capacity for study and practice. I shall now take my leave.
The Master said: "As for this inherently existing nature, why do you not understand it? The Buddha-dharma is not something vast; it simply requires taking the direct shortcut.
It does not teach the eradication of delusive thoughts or the suppression of body and mind. To close your eyes and say, 'This is it,' is not how this matter is.
You must examine what the present reality actually is. Why, then, have you become deluded? It is like this."

This is most intimate and direct. Suppose, for instance, that before this old monk has spoken to you, and before you have ever heard it—was there at that time any distinction between coming and going?
At such a moment, you must by all means avoid forcing a rational interpretation. This applies even up to the Buddhas.
Down to all things, it is entirely like this. Therefore, the holy and the ordinary are equal; the heterodox and the orthodox are equal;

birth-and-death and nirvana are equal. Now I ask you people: as for the Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa of the past, and the three periods of time throughout antiquity and the present—what kind of person’s domain are these?
As for the contaminated lands of the ten directions—what kind of person’s domain are these?
[The Master] said: "As for this matter, I, the mountain monk, say that you will all realize it thirty years from now. Only then will you know that what the old monk of Longmen has spoken is true.
You must by no means claim that you already know it. If you do so, this is called the view of a heterodox teacher. [I shall now] take my leave."
The Master said: "If, when questioned by others today, you are unable to speak, where does the fault lie?
It is because you perceive form where there is no form; you hear sound where there is no sound; you forcibly construct principles where there are no principles;
and you forcibly assume mastery within that which has no master. When these cannot be resolved here, it is called 'the cataract still remaining,' and the 'confused blossoms in the empty sky'."
It falls away. Why? It is simply because the mind exists that one cannot speak it. The Buddha-dharma is not something vast;
it requires nothing more than to be able to speak a single phrase plainly and straightforwardly. Now tell me, what is this plain and straightforward phrase?
If someone asks me, the Mountain Monk, I will simply say two phrases to them and finish. Do you understand? The ancients said: [The text ends here.]
The Way is something beyond the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it has been explained clearly and in detail.
Yet, when one arrives at this point, for the most part people become confused and muddled, failing to awaken. If you do not see this, you are simply a person nodding off while standing upright.
All people are constantly within the light; they see clearly with their eyes open, yet they do not know it. How can I, this mountain monk, deal with this?
[The assembly] stood for a long time.
The Master said, "In this way, I have been raising examples for you from east and west, saying that I am teaching you Chan. Yet, as soon as you turn your feet..."
Simply take this and circulate it as worldly convention. If you remain within it moment after moment, there will be a portion of awakening.
Look closely: for the most part, one merely misses it in the realms of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and touching.
You must, without departing from the discriminating mind, recognize the non-discriminating mind; without departing from seeing and hearing, recognize that which is beyond seeing and hearing.
It is not merely closing one's eyes and shutting them tight upon a long bed that is called "non-seeing.
Rather, it must be that within the very act of seeing, there is non-seeing. Therefore it is said: "Abiding in the realm of seeing and hearing, yet seeing and hearing do not reach it;
abiding in the ground of thought and deliberation, yet thought and deliberation cannot attain it. [The Master] stood for a long time.
The Master said: "What do you all who have come here seek? You must provide for yourselves; do not listen to what others say.
An ancient said, 'At eighteen, I already knew how to provide for myself. You all must likewise know how to provide for yourselves before it will do.
What kind of livelihood do you propose to provide? Simply do not seek elsewhere."

Nowadays, many people love to move their hands and feet; they do not understand how to manage their own livelihood and have already abandoned their home and scattered their property, drifting aimlessly.
They clearly lack true understanding, yet they persistently seek it out, merely learning a few fragments of intellectual knowledge.
To record a few words and phrases is called "carrying manure in. When you reach this point, you must have your luggage properly arranged;
only after long days and deep months, through thorough soaking and maturation, will you come to understand. An ancient said: "In every place it is you;
going east, it is you; going west, it is you. Who are you? If you say, "I am so-and-so," this is [the error].
Regarding intellectual consciousness (*vijñāna*), one must penetrate through it before one may attain realization. Long ago, Vasubandhu asked Asaṅga:
"Brother, when you went to the Inner Court, what Dharma did you see Maitreya expounding? Asaṅga replied: "He was expounding this very Dharma. But tell me, what is this Dharma?
One must be able to discern it before one may attain realization; do not mistake it for this [intellectual object], for most people are trapped by this very thing.
The sentence conceals it as well. Therefore, it is said that illness is the Dharma; for this reason, one is called a "pityable person.
[The student] stood for a long time. The Master said: "Do not say that what is being spoken now is it. It is not yet. If there were a 'it,' there would also be a 'not-it.'"
It is so. This is why it is said: "All words and phrases are entirely inconsistent with this matter;
you must simply accord with it. This matter does not reside in another person. Have you attained such resonance yet? For whom do you resonate?

If you say you resonate with the ancients, the ancients have already passed away. If you say you resonate with a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), that good spiritual friend has nothing to do with you.
This is the negotiation. Thus, the various sages compassionately announce and inform us, teaching that one must accord with the source of one’s own mind.
But tell me, what is this source of the mind with which one accords? If there were a mind that could be accorded with, it certainly could not be so accorded;
it must be through the mind of no-mind that one accords. [I have] stood long.
The Master said: "Within the twelve periods of the day, you must have a point of resonance and accord; only then will it be achieved.

Have you not seen how Lingyun, upon seeing a peach blossom, immediately attained resonance with this matter? And how Xiangyan, upon striking a bamboo, immediately stilled his mind? As the ancients said:"
If you do not accord with this matter, then the mountains, rivers, and the great earth will deceive you; the lanterns and the pillars will cheat you.
Today, the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence are vast and turbulent precisely because this matter is not understood. I urge you, my brothers:
first, eliminate coarse attachments. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you harbor various distractions—thinking of clothing, brooding over food, and all manner of miscellaneous anxieties.
It is like the flame of a lamp; it does not pause for even a single moment. Only the coarse conditions are removed, while all subtle ones naturally exhaust themselves.
As days and years pass, they naturally vanish. This is not a matter of deliberate cultivation; it is called "resting the mind and forgetting conditions.
One does not set oneself in opposition to the various sensory objects. Therefore, the sublime intent of the West lies in self-illumination. Long... [of] Longmen.
I, old as I am, have no Zen to give you, nor any Dharma with which to deliberate. It simply requires that each of you realize it for yourselves.
Within the gate of study, the only essentials are to forget external conditions and still the thoughts; this is the fundamental principle of our predecessors.
Did not the Patriarchs say, "Take non-thought as the school and formlessness as the essence"? If one merely utters a shout or delivers a blow, what is there [to gain]?
[The guest] said, "I have long stood here waiting for an opportunity.
The Master said, "To propagate the Way, the mind must remain ever detached; to follow worldly affairs, the consciousness must race about.

I only wish that one may be rich in the Way while poor in body, and thin in emotion while thick in virtue. Here in this mountain monk’s place, it is thus every day and thus at every moment. Now tell me—"
"What is it like? Apart from the conceptualizing mind, consciousness, and intellectual speculations regarding words and phrases, bring forth a single phrase.

This matter is not something you can understand through intellectualization. At present, whatever involves mental deliberation or observation is all subject to some form of intellectual understanding.
Yet, when you turn back to investigate your own eye and reflect upon the very mind that thinks and deliberates, why is it that people [fail to realize it]?
If you do not understand this point, you will say that from the very beginning it has been neither blue, yellow, red, nor white;
it is without marks and without form. Let me tell you: what I have spoken to you is called "language"; it is not your original mind. How can the original mind be deliberated upon?
How can one's own eye see itself? At the very moment of turning back to observe, there is likewise no one who is able to see. There is someone...
Go right here and swallow it all in one gulp; then the eye of wisdom will open wide, and you will suddenly reach your native land.
How can people of the present age reach the place where there is neither seeing nor hearing? At present, the myriad dharmas are fixed and vast;

yet when one sees people or houses, and the various ten thousand phenomena, they are like boiling water surging upward, never for a single moment coming to rest. It is just as when one was an infant—one still heard sounds.
They also see forms, yet they do not understand how to discern them. As soon as they become aware of things, they immediately begin to listen for and discriminate them;
from that moment on, they have been divided throughout their lives. When one reaches this state, it is difficult indeed to find anyone capable of organizing it.
Those who have attained the Way do not perceive walking when they walk, nor do they perceive sitting when they sit. Therefore, the Tathāgata said: "The eye sees forms."
It is like being blind; hearing sounds with the ear is like hearing an echo. How can one say it is "like being blind" or "like an echo"?
When hearing a sound, there is no sound to be heard; when seeing a form, there is no form to be seen. All that is seen and heard is like an echo.
Furthermore, when dreaming, one sees all manner of realms; upon waking, are there still so many varieties? If there were, then [the bed]...
Above, it was merely a matter of being given a pillow. If you say there are not so many varieties, yet you can recall them clearly in your mind and speak of them;
what is seen and heard during the daytime is likewise the same. Therefore it is said:
"The matters seen by the eye and heard by the ear may be learned from the sutras and treatises, but as for the numinous hall (the mind), how can it be learned? [The Master] stood for a long time.
The Master said: "Where is the Elder Śākyamuni? [The student] replied: "What? What? The Master spoke again:
"Where is the Great Master Bodhidharma? [The student] replied: "Just here. How difficult it is to clarify the principle of "just here"!
If one can understand this, only then will one know that the True Dharma abides eternally. For the most part, among Zen monks...
I simply say that the very place where it is raised is it. But what if your body were to perish and your life end?
Or what if you were ill and unable to speak? You must realize and enter [this state] before you can attain it.
Have you not seen how a monk asked Deshan, "Where have all the sages of the past gone? Deshan said, "What? What? Is it that "what" itself is the sages? No.
If you all do not understand this through words, you will fall into the flow of his sounds and echoes.
Even if you do not fall into his sounds and phrases, you will fall into his state of wordlessness and silence. This reality is truly beyond your intellectual interpretation or conjecture.
If you harbor even a single thread of thought, it becomes a point of orientation, and you are estranged from yourself. Even if you employ profound mysteries—
The wondrous meaning departs to accord with others; it will certainly not accord if one does not apply oneself. Yet, if one does not reflect upon it at all, that is also unacceptable.
One must personally realize it; only then can one clearly see it and be free from doubt. I shall take my leave.
The Master said: "People of the present day err in their study of the Way, and their errors do not go beyond two kinds of illnesses.

The first is to take the cave-dwelling of the five aggregates as the goal—a state that is wordless and speechless, formless and partless, a place of profound stillness and immovability—and then to say, 'Even if all Buddhas and patriarchs were to appear, I would simply remain thus.
This is one illness. The second is to identify with the capacity for speaking, the capacity for talking, and the capacity for hearing, and to apply oneself to these functions."

To engage in activities such as walking, standing, sitting, or lying down is itself another sickness. Do you still recognize that movement is the root of suffering and is sustained by the power of the wind?
If there is someone who can free themselves from these two sicknesses and understand how to investigate the essence, this person must have a moment of awakening.
If it is not so, there will be no way to bring order to one's practice. Furthermore, there are two other kinds.
Good spiritual friends provide bitter-mouthed instruction as a skillful means for two types of practitioners.

There is one type of practitioner who constructs their own intellectual systems and spouts out their own private messages; they advance and retreat, raising their fists or joining their palms, taking these to be the Way of Chan.
When the good spiritual friend sees them acting in this way, he speaks to them with bitter words: "You have misunderstood! You are needlessly being stubborn."
To recognize this as such is itself a form of spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Furthermore, there are certain students who say, "I do not understand;
I do not know. One does not yet know how to proceed; they have no point of entry whatsoever.
Therefore, when the spiritual friend perceives them in this state, he says to them: "You have nothing to do; why do you seek understanding or seek entry?"

This, too, is a kind of spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). For those who study both the former and latter approaches, if they hear the spiritual friend speak in this manner and are able to skillfully turn their light inward to investigate it, they will surely attain clarity.
If you merely say, "I do not understand," you are simply giving rise to self-defeat;
even after a thousand years, it will remain just as it is. If you are fortunate enough to be among those who practice within this, yet still say you do not understand, [you have missed the point].
Seeking a point of accord—what end will there ever be? Do you wish to understand? You must not establish any limits;
you must grasp it directly and immediately. Long have you stood here.
The Master said: "Tonight I shall give you all a parable.
It is as if you each possess an eye capable of perceiving all forms—long and short, square and round—and yet why is it that you cannot see this very eye?
You may recognize long and short, square and round, but if you wish to see the eye itself, it is impossible. Your mind is just like this; its radiance..."
It shines forth, penetrating throughout the ten directions and encompassing all that exists. Why, then, does it not know itself? Do you wish to understand?
Simply recognize these matters of shining and so forth; if you see a "mind," that will not do. As the ancients said: "A blade does not cut itself;
a finger does not touch itself; the mind does not know itself; the eye does not see itself. This is the reality. [I shall now] take my leave.
The Master said: "All of you have been standing here for so long; have you seen even one true spiritual friend? You must not depart in vain.
I simply call them 'false elders. As the former sages said: 'I use only provisional names to guide sentient beings.
The Buddha was an old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven; there is no need for you, honorable ones, to trouble yourselves."
To discriminate and grasp at signs: who is this old man Śākyamuni? And who is that Great Master Bodhidharma?
At this time before the Patriarch had yet arrived, was there still the Buddha-dharma? How can you say there was none? If you say there was none, you are merely deceiving yourself.
When [Bodhidharma] sat facing the wall at Shaolin, were there already so many verbal teachings and public cases? It being thus...
To see through this is to take a shortcut by many degrees. When you did not come up here, neither I, the mountain monk, saw you, nor did you, the Upādhyāya, see me.
You did not see me, and I did not see you; how then can one discern the truth? If you can understand this, [you have attained it].
Furthermore, what matters are there? Before the Buddha appeared in the world, it was thus; after the Buddha appeared in the world, it was thus;
even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was thus. If you reach such a state, there is truly not a single speck of a thing.

When you all walk, stand, sit, or lie down, when you eat when hungry and drink when thirsty—how can you say there is "nothing"? Unless one is a person who has seen the bottom [of reality], it cannot be so.
Only then can one understand it thus. Formerly, when Mahākāśyapa was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he prostrated before the Buddha.

Seeing that the great multitude stood there with solemn dignity, he immediately attained a point of realization and said: "Now, this great assembly is as if they have never existed before. What do you say of this meaning?
Previously, while you were down below, you did not see so many people; yet now that you have come up here—
Clearly, there are many people here. How can you say that it is as if they have never existed from the beginning?
Long ago, an elder asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "From the city. The elder said, "Where are you now?
The monk replied, "In the mountains. The elder said, "I have a question for you; if you can answer it, you shall stay; if you cannot answer it, you must leave."
The Elder leaves the city; within the city there are few Elders. The Elder arrives at the mountain; on the mountain the Elders abound.
If there were no Elder in the city, then the Dharma would not be complete within the mind. If the Elder abounds on the mountain, then there is a Dharma external to the mind.
The assembly remained silent. If you people can investigate and examine this thoroughly, it is what is called "not falling into the two extremes of annihilationism or eternalism."
Upon seeing this, the six sense organs become serene; whether walking or standing, one remains silent and still. The single mind does not arise, and all conditions are simultaneously stilled.
If it were otherwise—following after existence or non-existence—one would fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism. It would be like abandoning one’s father and fleeing away.
Reaching this point, truly, I do not require you to expend even a single thread of effort; simply understand it as it is. If you wish to bring these things into harmony...
Regarding this matter: when there is no seam or crevice in the teaching, it has already been torn asunder.

In the past, I pondered this matter and thought that it would only be after two or three lifetimes that one could attain awakening. Later, I heard of those who were "dispatched" [to realization] in a single moment.

Whoever possesses the right perspective will immediately realize that even people of today can attain awakening and understanding. The weather is cold; examine your conditions and see what you can accomplish.
Clearly investigate your own person—this is a matter of great importance. I have stood for a long time.
The Master said: "If someone were to ask you, 'How would you respond? would you be able to say anything?
What use is it for you all to engage in deliberation and mental calculation to produce a single phrase? How would you respond at the third watch of the night?"
When you rise at dawn, how will you speak? When you are in the front corridor or the back eaves, how will you speak? Can you say it yet?
You must have clear eyes before you can succeed. [He stood for a long time.]
The Master said, "Just now the attendant reported that the rain would not stop. Had we entered into meditation then, I feared the assembly would not hear it.
Now that the rain has stopped, do you all hear it? I say that when the rain did not stop, it was most intimate.
Why? It was simply because you lacked the mind to listen. As for what is shown to people everywhere, they say the sound of the rain is..."
"You have preached the Dharma. Is it truly so? "The mountain monk does not say so. The sound of the rain is your preaching of the Dharma. Do you understand?
If you can see through this directly, there will not be even a single hair's breadth of anything remaining.
Nowadays, those who travel as monks must wait to find a phrase that accords with their spiritual mentor; acting in such a way..."
Why do you trouble yourself with such contrivances? I shall ask you further: what is that "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) you seek to accord with?
If you wish to accord with the intention of that good spiritual friend, simply recognize your own mind. I ask you again: what is this mind of yours, and how is it to be recognized?
One cannot understand it through forced intellectualization; one must experience a sudden awakening to it before it can be grasped. Thus spoke the ancients.
Having no choice, one provisionally establishes verbal designations where there are none, and skillfully applies expedient means where there are no expedients.
One day, Xuansha entered the mountains and encountered a tiger; his attendant reported, "Master, a tiger! Xuansha said, "That is your tiger.

Currently, mountains and rivers face one another, and lands stretch out in all directions; yet through conceptual discrimination and thought, they appear as a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions. How [can this be otherwise]?
I have spoken of that which is your own principle. If you do not realize it here, you will be obstructed and stifled everywhere.
It is simply because you have followed after sensory dust for kalpas and have been turned by external objects. Try, then, to point out: what is that object?
"What is it that you are? Thus, there was a monk who asked Xuansha, "A student has newly entered the forest; I beg the Master to point out a path of entry.
Xuansha said, "Do you hear the sound of the Yan River water? He replied, "I hear it. Xuansha said, "Enter from here."
People nowadays do not understand clearly; they merely say, "The nature of mind is all-pervasive. But who is it that hears this?
What relevance does such talk have? You must truly be naked through and through, with not even an inch of thread hanging upon you, before you will succeed.
"Furthermore, I ask you all: have you put on your robes? After a long silence, he said, "How can you be so shameless? He stood for a long time.

The Master said, "As soon as you apply intellectual reasoning, it becomes difficult to understand; you must not apply intellectual reasoning at all before you can succeed. There is a certain kind of person...
Upon hearing such words, you immediately say, "I have no speech and no principles," yet you do not realize that this is precisely the very principle itself.
Now, I shall establish a single definitive agreement with you: to clearly perceive one's own mind is the ultimate standard.
This single phrase is the Buddha-dharma within Longmen Mountain. As the ancients said: "The mind does not [arise] by itself..."
"I know. The mind does not see itself. How do you people go about seeing clearly? One's own mind is difficult to see.
All the sages of the past were people who clearly saw their own minds. My late teacher was likewise one who clearly saw his own mind.
Consider, for instance, at that time in my late teacher’s assembly: how many brothers who had come from all quarters could there have been who truly possessed this?"
To clearly see one's own mind is extremely rare. The mind does not see the mind; it must be that this very mind is not seen for it to be attained.
This is the realm free from thought. If I were to speak of this matter to you people now, you would say I am disparaging the various traditions of the quarters.
Yet, if I do not speak of this matter, it is likewise difficult to clarify and understand. There are certain masters who tell people, "You fools! This one piece..."
Matter. Why do you not understand? First, take your own mind and make it into a nest; then, use that mind to seek realization.
This is called "driving in a stake and then running around the stake. Thus it is transmitted; thus it is received.
When one strikes the meditation seat or raises the whisk for practical use, it is called "using the mind with the mind. Furthermore, there is a certain kind of master who...
Regarding the human path: do not engage in calculations or rationalizations; as soon as you open your mouth, there is no connection, for it does not correspond with it at all.
Recognize it before the empty kalpa; it is utterly beyond words and descriptions, just like sitting upon a ball of breath.
"There is a place of profound peace and bliss. Furthermore, it is like a frog puffing out its breath. You hold such a view;
before you, it is as if a black mist has completely shrouded everything. This mountain monk exhorts you with utmost sincerity. It is not a false statement;
it is not a matter of intellectualizing, nor is it a means of ensnaring people, refusing others, or suppressing the worthy. This mountain monk does not speak in such a manner at all.
As for the principle: if you simply recognize it as such, that is up to you; if you say, "I also see it this way," that is up to you;
if you say, "According to my own view, I have attained it all," that is up to you; if you say, "My mind is not yet settled," that is also up to you.
You must simply not deceive yourself. How many masters are there in the world who speak...?
Chan and the Way require careful scrutiny: whether one deceives oneself or not, and whether one deceives others or not.
Long ago, when I was in my late teacher’s assembly, I served as a fundraising monk in Luzhou. While traveling past Yindu Temple, I encountered muddy rain;
suddenly, I slipped and fell. Distressed in mind, I said to myself: "I am on pilgrimage, yet I cannot even practice Chan."
From morning until now, I have not even eaten a meal; yet you continue to undergo such hardship. I heard two people scolding one another, saying, "You still remain in a state of affliction.
Upon hearing this, I was suddenly filled with joy, yet I could find no place that was not afflicted.
This was because I had failed to break through my state of doubt. It was only after four or five years that I finally understood it. Now...

Brothers, you must apply yourselves with such care and attention before you can succeed. This summer, we have discussed the kōan of "Inanimate Things Preaching the Dharma," yet those who misunderstand it are many.
You see what is inanimate and call it inanimate; you see what is animate and call it animate.
If you, who are practitioners of Zen, do not understand the preaching of inanimate things, how will you ever complete your journey as a wandering monk?
Regarding this matter: as one who acts as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), if you do not know how to preach the Dharma through insentient things, how can you receive beings and benefit them?
I exhort all of you to investigate this thoroughly and bring it to awakening. If you have not yet reached a point of realization, then for now, study it slowly; do not be in a hurry.
I shall stop here for now. Long standing.
The Master said: "My late teacher often spoke of a parable. It is like two men from a foreign land coming to the Great Court to investigate affairs.
Upon first entering the border, the two consult together and then each takes a separate direction—one goes east and the other goes west.
From one prefecture to another, from one county to another, they travel back and forth until suddenly they arrive."
Inside the city of Dongjing, two people collide at the palace gate. [One looks at the other; the other looks at this one.

Without a single word being spoken, all the matters they had previously deliberated regarding the affairs of their own country appear vividly and clearly as they pass shoulder-to-shoulder, with no one noticing.
How strange! Everyone, tell me: what is it about such a collision?
"How is it when one is 'clad' [in realization]? It is just like a Chan practitioner applying effort: today they grasp something, tomorrow they investigate something;
through this exhaustive inquiry, one day it manifests before them, much like suddenly bumping into someone at the palace gate.
This is called "resolving" the matter; one must have such an experience before it can truly be called "wandering in search of the Way" (xingjiao).
The task is accomplished. It is like returning to one's hometown after many years and encountering the old lord in a bustling marketplace;
one recognizes him without doubt, nor is it necessary to ask others whether he is indeed the lord or not. Brothers, simply maintain your practice in this manner.
Do not treat this lightly; time does not wait for anyone. The Patriarch said: "Do not let the passing moments go to waste;
each of you should exert yourselves. [The Master stood for a long time.
The Master said: "The ancients said: 'In the bell there is no sound of the drum; in the drum there is no sound of the bell. How is it with the students of today?"

Having reached such a state, sometimes when entering the room and seeing a brother offer a turn of phrase, and even when further pressed, he simply insists, "I have already responded to that; there can be nothing else.
How very clear! Yet, practicing in this way—what basis for realization is there? You fool! Have you not seen?
The Way of the former sages: every word reveals the Truth, every phrase returns to the Source. You have not yet understood it, yet you persist in making arbitrary claims.
From now on, when entering the room for instruction, do not act like this. It would be better to say, "I do not understand," and then receive correction. [He stood for a long time.]
The Master said: "To be called a Zen guest (chanke), one must first be a person who believes what others say.

If one does not believe, then even if one teaches people a thousand or ten thousand times, it will be of no use. Ha ha! If you do not believe, you merely go on listening to others speak; how can you be called a Zen guest?
As for a Zen guest, when the wind stirs the dust or the grass moves, they understand everything. Even before a sign has arisen and before it has fallen away, they comprehend it."
Recognize it immediately when the pathways of thought have not yet stirred; only then can one be called a Chan guest.
Why? Such a matter requires a person who does not hesitate for even a moment to confront birth and death.
Have you not seen how Yunyan studied under Baizhang for twenty years without clarifying this matter, until Daowu bit off his finger for him? Look at this!
The ancients, though they did not understand, felt no anxiety. Thinking "I do not understand," their minds never ceased their effort, nor did they run after words and phrases.
Furthermore, it is like Xuefeng, who went to Touzi three times and ascended to Dongshan nine times.
While at Touzi, one day he pulled back the curtain and entered the hermitage. Seeing him coming, Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood up. As Xuefeng hesitated, Touzi—
He then took his leave and departed. Huifeng was left in nothing but tears. Later, he went to Dongshan, but still could not resolve his doubts.
He then went to Deshan and asked, "Do the various sages of the past have any share for a student like me? Deshan struck him with a staff and said, "What are you saying?
At that moment, Huifeng felt as if the bottom had fallen out of a bucket. Even when he reached Aoshan, he still remarked, "I still have doubts. Observe this.
The ancients of old simply broke through the "doubt-mass" (yiquanzi) and only then did they find rest; they would then say, "The matter is finished," and their intent also ceased.
This very thing has always been all-pervasive wherever it touches. Nowadays, when brothers in the lineage come to seek instruction, most rely on words to give rise to intellectual interpretations.
Chaos acts as the sovereign. Otherwise, you would call the place where the ancients attained awakening "causes and conditions. Where would you look for that?
To call it "empty talk"—what connection could there be? It is just like Xuefeng going to Touzi three times and to Dongshan nine times.
This is certainly not for the sake of mere words. Brothers, you must simply step back and investigate. How do you step back?
It is not that I am teaching you to sit with eyes closed on a long couch, forcibly suppressing body and mind as if you were wood or clay;
such practice would be of no use for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. If you wish to step back, take those words you do not understand and those matters you have not resolved.
The causal conditions are suddenly right before one’s face. Stepping back to look at oneself, why is it that one does not understand? After a long silence, he said:
"The monastics say that one must not engage in deliberation, yet one must not refrain from deliberation either. This leaves people wondering how they are to look."
I tell you this: simply look by retreating. After a long while, he again sighed deeply and said, "How stifling! How difficult to understand!
What is this 'stifling' that you speak of? Who is it that is stifled? If you look by retreating in this way, you will gradually become awakened;
day by day there will be light, and you will gradually see the vastness. Yet, you must not grasp at it as a single thing."
If you recognize it within this very state of going toward [the goal], you will say it is settled;
yet even so, you would still be pinned down and killed—what use is that? You must apply some wisdom and observe. The ancients permitted you to manage and direct a single path;
if you thus rest and step back, you will surely find a principle. This is because you do not understand at all, and there is nothing...
As for those who know: there are also those barbarians of confused speech, those who prattle on about "how" and "what.
You should simply step back and look: what is it that you are saying so confusedly? Only by thus turning the light inward and reflecting upon yourself will you find the truth.
If you practice with such single-minded effort, there will eventually come a time of awakening. If you do not believe this, then...
There was nothing that could be done about it. When this mountain monk first attended upon Master Sheng, he was instructed to contemplate:
"What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? At the edge of the city of King Chu, the Ru River flows east. He was further told to contemplate the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner.

Upon coming down here to attend upon the Old Monk, I asked him: "The ancients said that sound and form are pure and true; yet though you, Old Monk, have explained it a thousand times and ten thousand ways, it remains merely—"
He did not understand it. Later, [the Master] again asked him, "What is this extraordinary matter?
He replied, "What do you say? Thereupon, he felt pleased; for he had found a way to grasp it. Consequently, he constantly investigated, asking, "What is this extraordinary matter?
[The Master] replied, "What do you say? He pondered alone, thinking, "What did I say? I said, 'It is extraordinary.'"
Furthermore, he saw nothing extraordinary about it. After studying for three years without understanding, he departed to travel in Zhejiang.

On his way back, he was told to contemplate the cases of "killing one's father and mother" and "repenting before the Buddha. Then he was asked, "Where would you repent for killing the Buddha and the Patriarchs?
Yunmen said, "Exposed! This koan remained like a ball of red-hot iron in his heart for seven years.
Having exhausted all hardships, only those who have long practiced among the assembly truly know this; let me tell you more.
When Huitang first studied Chan, he came from Gui Prefecture and first met Master Yunfeng Yue. For three years he did not understand his words.

He then went to study under Chan Master Nan, where for two years he likewise did not understand. He subsequently spent the summer retreat at the abbot's quarters of Guoshan, where, while reading the *Transmission of the Lamp*,...
Recorded: A monk asked Duofu, "What is Duofu’s grove of bamboo? Duofu said, "One stalk, two stalks, leaning.
At this, Huítáng attained enlightenment. People nowadays merely call this a dialogue; this is because their application of effort is not thorough.

"You do not understand the skillful means of the ancients. I, this mountain monk, urge you, my brothers: since you are now beneath the forest trees, each of you should study the Way and not let time pass in vain;
take awakening as your standard. [He stood for a long while.]
The Master said: "To draw near to virtuous friends is the earnest entrustment of the former sages.

Students of the present day must rely upon the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, seeking out a teacher to investigate and resolve their doubts; only then will they succeed. If one does not do so, how can they be called a student?
If you wish to clarify this matter, you must give rise to doubt and engage in investigation. If you harbor deep doubt regarding this matter, that itself is the wisdom of *prajñā*."
Manifest before you. Why? The purpose of traveling as a mendicant is solely to bring the state of doubt to rest. If you do not give rise to doubt, how can the state of doubt be brought to rest?

Have you not seen that when our former teacher was thirty-five years old, he shaved his head and immediately went to Chengdu to study the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) and the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha* (Exposition of the Hundred Dharmas)?
There, upon hearing it said: "When a Bodhisattva enters the Path of Seeing, wisdom merges with principle, and the object merges with the spirit," he...

When [the master] divided [the process] into the means of realization and the object of realization, the non-Buddhists raised an objection: "If you do not distinguish between the means and the object of realization, then by what means is there realization?
At that time, no one was able to respond; they ceased the sounding of bells and drums, turned their robes inside out, and departed. Later, the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty arrived there.
Jiuzhi explained this meaning as follows: "When wisdom merges with principle and the object meets with the spirit, it is like a person drinking water;

whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves. He then reflected to himself: "The coldness and warmth may be understood, but what is this matter of 'knowing for oneself'? How could one not harbor deep doubt?
Consequently, he asked a lecturer, "I do not understand the principle of knowing for oneself; how does it work? The lecturer was unable to answer. Thereupon—

[The Master] said: "The Head of the Assembly must clarify this principle. I, however, have not yet reached it. In the South there are venerable elders who transmit the Buddha-mind school and do know this matter.
You must travel on foot [to seek them] before you can attain it. Thereupon, the former master set out on a pilgrimage, traveling through the capital and the two provinces of Zhejiang.
Whenever he encountered a venerable elder, he would inquire about this matter; none failed to respond. Some spoke of it, while others provided a verse.
Yudi said, "It was simply that my state of doubt had not been resolved. Later, he went to Mount Fudu to see Yuanjian.

Observing his ascending the hall and entering the room, Yuanjian spoke entirely of matters within [Yudi’s] own mind. Consequently, Yudi stayed there for one year, being instructed to contemplate the words, "The Tathāgata has secret words;
Kāśyapa did not conceal them. One day, [Yuanjian] said, "Why did you not come sooner? My age..."
"You are old now; you should go to consult Master Baiyun Chenguan. When my late teacher went to Baiyun, one day he ascended the Dharma Hall and attained great enlightenment.
"The Tathāgata has secret words; Kāśyapa did not conceal them. Indeed! Indeed! Wisdom merges with principle, and the objective realm accords with the spirit.
It is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves. Truly, these words are so! Thus it is said:
A verse on seizing the opportunity says: "Before the mountain lies a stretch of vacant land; with palms joined, I earnestly question the patriarch:
'How many times have you sold it only to buy it back? It is for pitying the pines and bamboos that draw in the pure breeze.
When Master Duan looked at this, he nodded his head. Everyone, is this not a matter of deep doubt? Only by drawing near to a spiritual friend can one attain clarity. As for the former...
The Master traveled on foot to visit spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Later, he said: "How is it that you ask about the patriarch?
How is it that you sell yourself only to buy yourself back? You must know that there is nothing left over. An ancient said, "It is all you," and he also said: [the rest].
I have never given you so much as a single phrase. If I had given you even one phrase, what would you have been able to do with it?
If you all wish to break through your doubts, you must also be like the former Master once; only then will it be achieved. I have stood for a long time.
The Master said: "Just observe how when Mazu Daoshi saw a monk descend the steps, he called out, 'Virtuous One!
The monk turned his head, and Mazu said, 'From birth until old age, you have been nothing but this fellow. Why do you turn your head and twist your brain?
At these words, the monk attained realization. What is the principle here? 'From birth until old age, you have been nothing but this fellow. Tell me, who is that?"
This fellow—just as soon as you give rise to the thought that you wish to see this fellow, you no longer see him.

This fellow is difficult to see; he is a thousandfold difficult, a ten-thousandfold difficult. People nowadays merely say, "This is that very fellow. But who else could it be? It cannot be anything other than this.
Out of every hundred people, ninety-nine understand it in this way. What kind of grasp do they have? If it were like that...
How can you clarify the matter from birth until old age? How can you see that it is simply this very person?
If you do not see this person, you will remain entirely ignorant of where the four elements and five aggregates have gone.
For instance, right now as you preach and listen to the Dharma—is there preaching and listening, or is there no preaching and listening? If you say, "You stand and I sit; I am speaking..."
Listen! Even people from a village of three households understand how to speak like this; how could they dare to call themselves Zen practitioners?
If you say there is neither hearing nor speaking, yet it is also said that from birth until old age one is nothing but this very person.

Therefore, upon reaching this point, you must seek out someone who has attained thorough realization to resolve your doubts. When I was formerly unable to clarify this for myself, I was utterly helpless.

Having understood this, he then requested further instruction from his former teacher. As soon as he asked about it, the former teacher simply said, "I do not understand; I do not know; I am not your equal.
He asked again, "Is Zen ultimately easy to investigate or difficult to investigate? His teacher replied to him, "You have nothing to do; why ask whether it is easy or difficult?
Investigating Zen is called the 'gold-and-dung' method: when you have not yet realized it, it is just like gold; when you have realized it..."
"It is exactly like excrement. This monk does not approve of these words. Yet, reflecting upon them now, although the language is coarse, the underlying meaning is not shallow.
These are all men of thorough realization; every word or half-phrase they utter is never in vain.
Whenever they acted for others, they never gave instructions recklessly, nor did they grant their approval haphazardly. There are those nowadays who...
Only then can one know them. At times they speak correctly; at times they speak without any basis. How is this principle to be understood?
It is because they themselves have not yet attained full realization. Sometimes they grant that a person is right, and sometimes they say they are not.
If it is like this, how can one clearly realize that from birth until old age it is only this very man? Look closely at people nowadays.
It is simply the person of former times; the activity of the present time is also simply the activity of former times.
Even amidst a thousand transformations and myriad changes, it is only necessary for you to attain self-acceptance here—only then will you achieve realization.
That people of the present day fail to realize this is simply because they lack decisive discernment. What is the state of lacking decisive discernment? It is simply taking...
To interpret the words and phrases of the ancients and use them to prick and bore into oneself—this is precisely how it is.
Even when Maitreya descends to be born in this world, you will still not understand it. Why? Because I tell you: as soon as you turn your head or shift your gaze, it is already no longer so.
At this point of effortless ease, there is no further need for "how" or "what. Realize it directly right now. You all, first...

Bringing intellectual reasoning forward, you use the words and phrases of the ancients to entangle and bind yourself, as if you were a pure and pristine expanse, yet it is like sprinkling a handful of dirt upon it.
The other day, when I entered the room and gave instruction, I said: "Now that you have arrived here, you must not be like you were just now; you must have something."
It is only at the place of assembly that it can be attained. Some say: "When you first came, it was just like this; even now, it is just like this.
You have already entered into the realm of intellectual consciousness; how can you blame anyone else? How compassionate the ancients were toward you!"
"Walking is the Buddha's walking; sitting is the Buddha's sitting. All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; all sounds are the Buddha's voice.
You have misunderstood this, and so you say that all sounds are truly the Buddha's voice and all forms are truly the Buddha's form.
Since such an understanding is not permitted, how then is it so? I tell you: as soon as one involves oneself in [conceptualization]..."
At the very moment a sign or omen arises, you have already become fragmented and disjointed. When you wish to use wisdom to illuminate it, it has already become dark and obscured.
Now, simply do not rely on my words; let each of you practice according to your own means.
You may examine the ancestral precedents, you may sit in stillness, or you may investigate in all places—all of these are sites for your cultivation. One.
Every place is the place where you realize entry. Simply be single-mindedly focused on one place; as days pass and months go by, it must be resolved by you.
Have you not seen how when Master Guling returned from his travels, his teacher asked him, "You have been away from me traveling?"
