It is simply because seeking never ceases. Everywhere is seeking: contemplating principles is seeking;
examining the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients is seeking; looking at the Chan manuals is seeking;
even if you sit in stillness, for thoughts not to abide is itself seeking. Do you understand? Then that very seeking of yours—
This is not a matter of frantic seeking. Within this, it is extremely difficult to gain faith and enter; it is difficult to apply effort; and it is difficult for those who do not find peace and joy.
This is because you are either sinking or floating. Therefore it is said that you do not understand how to go about it.
Now, how can you avoid sinking and floating? When that single thought arises, is it a flow of birth and death? Is it the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*)? Or is it not?
"Is it movement? If you look at it from this perspective of turning it over and examining it, there is some measure of principle. [The assembly] stood for a long time.
The Master said, "Sharing the same bed and blanket, yet dreams differ for each. As the former sages said: 'Within the same Dharma, one does not attain this matter.
For instance, within the single Dharma of birth and death, one must enter into birth and death without being bound by birth and death."

Those who dwell in birth and death and are bound by birth and death share the same single Dharma; yet one person is bound while another is liberated—is this not like a dream where each experience is different?
You usually take birth and death as one side and the absence of birth and death as another side;
you take deliberation as one side and non-deliberation as another side; you take speech as one side and the absence of speech as another side.
To speak of "action" is one extreme. In this mountain monastery, there is neither the business of the patch-robed monk nor matters of the "upward direction.

We discuss only the matter of transcending birth and death. It is not enough merely to say a single phrase and leave it at that; you must perceive the absence of birth and death within birth and death itself.
Have you not seen how Master Yongjia, upon meeting the Sixth Patriarch, said: "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence..."
"Swift. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Why not realize non-arising? Is there anything that can be called swift?
Jia said: "Realization is itself non-arising; fundamentally, there is no swiftness. Furthermore, when Caoshan took his leave of Dongshan, Dongshan asked:
"Where are you going? Caoshan replied: "I am going to the place of non-alteration. Dongshan asked: "In the place of non-alteration, how could there be going? Caoshan... [replied].
It is said: "Going, it does not change or alter. Is this not one who has attained realization? Your deliberation constitutes one side;
your non-deliberation constitutes another side. Beyond verbal expression, you attempt to construct a state of non-expression.
Even if you clearly understand this state of non-expression, as soon as there is verbal expression, it immediately obstructs you. Day and night, whether walking, standing, sitting, or...
"Lying down—never walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Why do you not investigate in this way?
Sometimes when monks come here, I utter a phrase and give a single clap. How can that serve as a realization that does not fall into the two extremes?
You must go and contemplate it: 'I am clearly within birth and death; how can I attain freedom from birth and death? Do not simply say, 'It is just this.'"
It is so. Originally, I have no birth and death; it is not through your single phrase that this is realized.

There are those who, upon hearing others say there is no birth and death, immediately declare, "It is so; originally there is no birth and death. If one forms such an understanding, it will be difficult to comprehend.
Since you do not permit people to construct rationalizations or give rise to intellectual interpretations, yet you also do not permit them to simply negate [the teaching], it is like this:
"What effort is there to be made? Have you not seen the ancients say: 'I simply take what you have brought and show you a point of entry'?
Be careful! The Master said:
"When I look at the brothers in the monasteries nowadays, it seems as though they all do not speak of this matter at all. Only...

Throughout the world, wherever there are monasteries and those who claim to be masters of Zen, whether entering the room or ascending the hall, there is nothing they do not discuss regarding this matter.
Why, then, do you say that it has never been spoken? It has indeed been spoken, yet it was spoken without hitting the mark.
Not only was it not hit, they do not even understand how to look at it; they do not understand how to apply themselves to such practice, but merely speak of "issuing the correct command."
A total presentation: cutting off the ten directions. Strike the Buddha if he comes; strike the Mara if he comes.
Though I have been speaking of Chan all along, I have never spoken of its most essential point. What I speak of here is that which has been cast aside and discarded by others everywhere.
I casually pick it up from a heap of refuse and present it to people, yet they are unable to speak of it. It is simply this.

Nowadays, there are those who have entered the room and asked the Way, claiming they have attained understanding. When they see the incense altar, they wonder: "Is it the incense altar, or is it not the incense altar?
If you say it is the incense altar, you are no different from ordinary people. If you say it is not the incense altar, then to whom is the incense altar entrusted?
When questioned gently on this matter, they immediately fall apart like scattered flowers and broken threads. This is because, in their daily lives...
Go altogether to a quiet place and apply yourself to practice. Let me ask you this:

setting aside for a moment your coming into the assembly, before you had set out on pilgrimage or entered the community, when you saw an incense altar, what did you call it? He replied, "I called it an incense altar.
The Master said again, "Everyone calls it an incense altar; why do you not contemplate why it is called an incense altar? Zen must be like this.
"Consider this! You must clarify the matter from your beginningless past. Master Daoxiu practiced the Way yet did not perceive the original Dharma; such obstruction has been his lot from the start.
If a person possesses such obstructions, they will undergo thousands of cycles of delusion. As our former teacher said: 'It is like a person who has fallen fast asleep.'"
He placed a bit of excrement on the tip of his nose. At first, he was unaware of it. When he stood up, he either smelled an odor or noticed it upon smelling his vest;
thinking it was the vest that smelled, he took off the vest. Upon picking up the object, everything emitted a stench.
He did not realize the smell was upon his own nose. Suddenly, a wise person said to him, "It is nothing else."
Regarding this matter, Gang himself did not believe it. A wise man said, "Just take your hand and rub it against your nose to see. Gang refused to do so.
Had he been willing to rub it once, he would have known that he was already slightly ahead. He then washed it with water, and there was no odor at all.
If one smells any object, it originally has no odor whatsoever. It is the same with Zen meditation: one simply refuses to acknowledge it.

Cease your efforts and look within yourself. To seek out intellectual interpretations below these words, to search for logical connections, or to engage in mental calculations—all of this is entirely incorrect.
If you are willing to turn the light back upon yourself and examine it, there is nothing that will not be understood.
As it is said: "Once the single root returns to its source, the six functions cease to operate. If you simply observe in this manner, there will certainly be a portion of awakening and clarity.
He stood for a long time.
As soon as the Master sat down, he laughed heartily and said, "You still do not understand. After a long silence, he spoke again:
"I have explained it to you in this way, yet you still do not understand. If you go elsewhere, how will you understand there? You are not going to run off to all those other quarters."
I do not make you act; I do not settle you in sitting. Here, I neither cause you to exert yourself nor fix you in stillness;

it is truly effortless and easy to understand. Why, then, do you not understand? It is only because you employ a thousand schemes and myriad expedients, artfully constructing rationalizations, that it becomes difficult to understand.
The Buddha-dharma is a dharma that is easy to understand and brings peace and joy. Although it is easy to understand, [you fail to do so].
It is simply that it is difficult to enter and difficult to apply effort. If you can settle yourself in the various quarters [of practice], you will have a place to apply effort;
if you can move about freely, you will have something to chew upon. Brothers, when you say, "I do not dare say it is so," how is it that you do not dare say it is so?
Why not look into it in this way? I only fear that you...
Previously, you were confused in your understanding and haphazard in your comprehension; I simply wanted to teach you that one may attain clarity without stirring a single thought.

Furthermore, there is another who says: "According to my own view, though a thousand things may be right and ten thousand things may be right, this very state is precisely like the sprout of parched grain."
It is like a rotten seed that will never sprout again; you have already said as much. How can it be saved? You must harbor deep doubt regarding this matter.
Therefore it is said: "Ordinary people are prone to vacillation. Furthermore, there are those who understand it yet cannot speak of it;
even if they could speak of it, it would not constitute the true principle. Do not be hasty; investigate it thoroughly, I, the mountain monk, advise.
I am practicing together with you. If I have attained realization, you must also attain it; if you do not attain it, I, this mountain monk, likewise have not attained it.
Have you not seen how Xuansha pointed to a white spot before him and asked a monk, "Do you see it? The monk replied:

[The Master] said, "I see. The monk said, "I see too; you see too. Why then do you not understand? There was a fellow practitioner who had paid respects to the Senior (the Master) and had been with the late Master for a year and a half.
Whenever he entered the room [for instruction], the Master would simply say to him, "Senior, can you distinguish between black and white?
Time after time he went, and time after time it was the same. How can one understand such talk? It is like this...
"What kind of practice can be done now? In these times, there are no venerable masters who act in such a manner, nor are there any senior practitioners who inquire with such earnestness.
Were it anyone else, they would have left in frustration. One day, he heard his late master ascend the hall and say, "Those who enter and exit the same gate are enemies from past lives.
At this, he was utterly bewildered, as if a heavy scale-weight had fallen into the depths of his heart.
It is similar. From the previous perspective, it was like seeing flowers in the sky;

from now on, having seen the Truth, you must practice in this way and realize awakening in this way. Zen must be investigated in this manner. It has already been one month since the beginning of summer.
It is truly not seen that brothers have any place where they can perceive or touch [the truth]. You must simply exert your spirit with utmost discernment.

If it were such that no one had spoken of it and no one had revealed it, it would be difficult to apply oneself to practice. Since you have encountered someone [who has taught it], you may well apply yourself to practice.
One must first distinguish between the monastic and the lay before this can be achieved.
[The assembly] stood for a long time. The Master said: "Nowadays, you traveling brothers may indeed believe that there is such a thing as sudden enlightenment.

The various quarters may also say that there is such a thing as sudden enlightenment. If there were no such thing as sudden enlightenment, how could they be called 'forests' (monasteries)? This is because—"
It has been traditionally handed down that one merely examines the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients—perhaps one or two cases—until a slight degree of knowledge and understanding arises.
If there are points that cannot be comprehended, one further seeks out the seams and fissures to probe and investigate until a realization is attained.
Having already understood it, he said, "This matter is simply like this," and it was circulated throughout the monastic communities.
Yet, none of them spoke of the matter of sudden enlightenment. Without the matter of sudden enlightenment, how could one dispel the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms?
How could one cause the state of doubt to fall away? Recently, there was a monk who came and said:
The Way is such that seeing and hearing are not obscured. To simply go about recognizing seeing and hearing and say, "This is it," is to fail to see that which is the unobscured state.
If so, one will not know the affairs of other worlds when questioned, nor will one penetrate the matters of the sense faculties and their objects when questioned.
"How can one take the limited capacity of an ordinary person's mind and equate it with the matter of sudden enlightenment? Today, this mountain monk addresses the great assembly:
simply have faith that there is such a thing as sudden enlightenment. It is like a common villager who, while plowing his field, picks up a grain of the Golden Elixir;
after consuming it, his entire family ascends to the heavens. It is also like a layman being appointed as a high minister. As it says in the scriptures:"
To speak of your ordinary, worldly capacity is like an unbaked clay brick; it cannot be used at all unless it has been fired in a great fire.
It must pass through the firing of a great fire before it becomes fit—much like attaining a sudden enlightenment.
Since I came from Sichuan, I have studied under only one person, and I know that this man’s speech accords with the ancients.
He was an ordinary person. Once he asked his former teacher, "I have heard that within the Chan school there is awakening to the Way; is this true? His former teacher replied, "It is so.
If there were no awakening, how could you exist here? Just investigate slowly and steadily. Thereupon, I [the mountain monk] began to investigate with a relaxed mind.
There was another head seat who possessed clear and penetrating insight; for this reason, I often went to consult him.

He would always tell me, "You must provide for your own livelihood; do not come to ask me. One day, he cited the case where Zhaozhou held up a firebrand and showed it to a monk, saying, "One must not call this fire.
What is it? I harbored a deep doubt over this: it was clearly fire. Just as...
"Why do you not call it fire? He looked at it thus for three years, constantly reflecting:
"How would I dare, with the limited capacity of an ordinary person, inquire about that which the Sages have realized? Furthermore, he had heard the *Lotus Sūtra* say:
"This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination. He constantly maintained this single thought. Now, brothers, this is precisely what our way is.
This very thing has already been explained for you all together; even so, you would still not understand. Furthermore, our former master once went to the residence of Inspector Li.
After the Inspector invited him into the library to burn incense, he presented the *Transmission of the Lamp* record to the former master.
Although I am a layperson, I have long applied my mind to this Way. Whenever I read this record, there are many points I do not understand;
I hope the Venerable Master will explain them one by one. My late teacher said: "This matter is not to be understood through intellectual reasoning; one must attain awakening first.
If there is a place of awakening, there will be nothing one does not understand, and one will naturally have no need to ask others. If there is no awakening, then [it remains as it is]..."
"Even the place where they meet is not it. The Provincial Inspector said, "My teacher has explained it correctly.
Furthermore, as for my own life's work, I realized it while serving as the guest prefect (zhikè) by the hearth; since then, there has been nothing I have not understood.
Brothers in the assembly must realize the matter of sudden enlightenment before you can succeed. Nowadays, it is the custom in monasteries not to speak of this at all."
[The monk] stood for a long time.
The Master said, "In my own portion, there is nothing that is not so. If there were even a single thread of what was not so, how would I dare speak it to others?
How would I dare point it out to others? When I am in my own portion, there is no mind that can be 'so'."

Furthermore, there is no dharma that can be affirmed as "this" such that one would dare to speak of it to others. If we examine the state of each person, it is clear that there are points where one is not [in accord with reality];
this is why I come to you to seek discernment. If you were already enlightened, when would you have time to go ask others?
However, here in my mountain monastery, I simply point out that which is "not this" for you; if you are not [enlightened], I will never stop until you are.
"I dare say you are so; I wait for you to be so. This mountain monk agrees with you only because you are so.

"Great assembly, there is no one whom this mountain monk does not recognize. Whether someone has come before me, whether they have attained realization or not, and whether they possess understanding or not—I know them all.
It is like a skilled physician of the world who recognizes a disease at a single glance, knowing whether it is cold or hot."
"A physician cannot [diagnose this]; one must inquire into each case individually to know it. This is like the case of the mediocre physician mentioned previously.
When Fayan pointed at the curtain, two monks went to roll it up. Fayan said, 'One has gained, one has lost.
You must not say there is any such thing as gain or loss here. He also said: 'One person understands that coming and going to roll it up is "gain," while the other does not.'"
To come and go and roll [the scroll] is a failure. If it is like this, how can one understand medicine?
That you have not yet attained clarity now is because your realization of the mind is not yet definitive. It is like a physician who does not recognize the illness;

such a person does not recognize whether others understand or do not understand, and they cannot distinguish between the presence or absence of insight. How, then, can such a person benefit others? How can they speak to them?
A person must penetrate to the very marrow and investigate until the truth is realized before they can succeed.

If one is willing to penetrate to the marrow and investigate until the truth is realized, there is nothing that cannot be understood. Have you not seen the ancient say: "You need only sit and investigate the principle;
if after twenty or thirty years you still do not understand, cut off my head and use it as a urine bowl! When monks sometimes say "It is so," they have reached the point of penetrating to the marrow.
To investigate the reality, you instead move about restlessly, like looking at a horse through a window; it passes by in an instant.
You must become like two or three thousand catties of iron—neither able to pull forward nor push backward—only then will you know what is real.
As soon as you are shaken by others, you already move; if they apply even a little more force and push once more, you will fall over. You must...
This is penetrating clarity. Suddenly one sees the three hundred and sixty joints and the eighty-four thousand pores all opening up at once.
Both the internal body and the external world—every phenomenon—is the primordial Dharma; there is nothing that is not so from the very beginning.
Only now can the teachers and monks rely upon this and be able to speak of it. If everything were removed all at once, there would be no place for them to settle. It is also said:
It has already passed. For all of you, there is no time better than this. Since you are already within it, you must steady your spirit and strive with diligence to realize it. Take care.
The Master said: "If we discuss equality, nothing surpasses the Buddha-dharma; only the Buddha-dharma is most equal.
If you say 'I understand while you do not,' that is not the Buddha-dharma. If you say 'You understand while I do not,' that too is not the Buddha-dharma.
The scriptures state: 'This dharma is equal, with no high or low'; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. My own realization accords with this."
All people are equal; the way all people perceive is also equal to that of this mountain monk.
Furthermore, an ancient said: "What all people know, Liang-sui knows entirely; what Liang-sui knows, all people do not know. For what reason, then, do they not know?

This is truly because your mind, O Benevolent One, harbors high and low; failing to rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom, you consequently perceive this land as filled with earth, stones, mountains, and impurities.
Only by relying on the Buddha’s wisdom can this be realized. What the Sages have taught is precisely the Dharma of equality.
It is also said: "The four modes of birth—egg, womb, moisture, and transformation—and the nine categories of beings—I shall cause them all to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and attain liberation.
Though I thus liberate immeasurable sentient beings, in truth, there is not a single sentient being who attains liberation.

Is this not the Dharma of equality? An ancient said: "Nirvāṇa is named 'Broad Deliverance'; it gathers all within the single flavor of non-remainder. This includes egg-birth, womb-birth, and so forth.

Moisture and transformation, emptiness and existence, as well as sinking and floating—when the *sattva* can descend and abide within these, the path to Bodhi is naturally complete. Yet, in an instant, even a tiny speck remains;
this is forever lingering on "this shore. As soon as there is even the slightest hair’s breadth that is not exhausted, it is precisely "this shore. It is also said:
In a single instant, it flows into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) and becomes the very root of birth and death. How could one recklessly claim realization or give rise to false understanding?
An ancient venerable master once said to people: "Each and every one of you possesses the original mind.

When first resolving to set out on the pilgrimage, one must necessarily resolve for the sake of birth and death; one may resolve because of weariness with suffering, or because of being pressed by worldly circumstances.
Even those who resolve their minds out of necessity or compulsion are all said to have "aroused the mind. Why is this? It causes people to look at that very first moment of arousal;
it means that the single thought-moment you first aroused is not easily changed. When you turn back toward it, it possesses the greatest power. This is the Chan you are investigating.
When it manifests before you, it is simply this mind, luminous and pure. In the interim, seek out and visit masters of the lineage.
Day and night one investigates and scrutinizes; this is simply to nurture and sustain this mind. Even upon attaining awakening, one sees that it was not lost even before the mind had been awakened.
The Patriarch Aśvaghoṣa called this initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) identical to original awakening (mūla-bodhi).

Original awakening is non-awakening; the non-duality of the original and the initial is termed ultimate awakening (atyanta-bodhi). It is further said that at the very moment the mind first awakens, one achieves perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). This means:
First, one realizes the fruition—the maturation of the Buddha’s six perfections and myriad practices.
Therefore, I ask you to investigate only that initial mind of aspiration. Furthermore, my own realization is no different from that of everyone else; why do you not understand it in this way?
[I shall now take my leave. Long standing.
The Master said: "A man of clear eyes has no fixed patterns. That which you usually fail to grasp is simply because your eyes are not clear.
If your eyes were clear, you would indeed be able to grasp it. Therefore it is said that 'a man of clear eyes is hard to find. As soon as you say 'it is,' [you have already missed it]."
To act in such a way is precisely to fall into a conceptual trap. If one were a person of clear eyes, they would not act thus.

Have you not seen how Deshan addressed the assembly, saying: "Tonight I shall not answer any words; anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff"? This was possible only because he was a man of clear eyes.
How can one grasp it? As soon as one fails to grasp it, one falls into conceptual thought, which immediately becomes a sign.
Therefore, throughout his life, only Yantou was able to grasp it. Thus it is said: "One must be a person with clear eyes to achieve this. I have stood for a long time.
The Master remained silent for a long while, then addressed the assembly, saying: "The Patriarch truly knows those who can hear his music.
Hehe! I laugh! He continued: "It can only be explained in this way. Those who understand it will personally experience its benefit and immediately possess a place to tread upon.
If you involve yourself in principles, calculations, or verbal explanations, then you do not understand; nor will you personally experience its benefit."
When you are walking back and forth in the corridor, or when you are washing clothes and sorting garments in the quarters, do you still recognize the true, good connoisseur—the Patriarch?
It is simply because you have not seen him that, when questioned, you become flustered and bewildered.
Where does this sickness lie? It lies in your habitual state of constant deliberation and calculation; you have not attained it through direct experience.
As for their practice, they all sit upon long bedsteads with eyes closed and pupils hidden, calculating and deliberating until they have exhausted their thoughts.
They may reach as far upward as the Milky Way and as deep downward as the Yellow Springs before they can utter a single phrase or two;
yet once they reach a place of leisure, they no longer know where it has gone. Everything before their eyes becomes an obstacle; if questioned even lightly, they are unable to proceed.
Now, let us speak according to the facts; do not speak recklessly. Let me ask you this: when you had not been given rice gruel or food for three days, were you able to move?
Certainly you could not have moved. Only after you had eaten some gruel and food could you finally move.
If that is the case, it is all merely the "qi" (vital energy) of rice gruel. To reach such a state, if you wish to truly attain a person [of realization], you must also...
Only when you see that this is not a matter of mere worldly sustenance can you truly attain it. Zen must be investigated in this manner;
only then is it called "decisive discernment" (*nirṇaya*). Having eaten your rice gruel, you ought to support yourself by taking up this very matter and investigating it.
Yet, you remain entirely ignorant of it, instead wasting your time on trivialities—discussing right and wrong and meddling in affairs that do not concern you.

Matters—whether deliberating or scheming—are all too precious, yet you waste them all in reckless confusion. You do not realize that the very moment you form a thought, it is already the world beyond;
in a single kṣaṇa, it flows into the realm of the mind and becomes the root of birth and death.
Furthermore, while this body of the five aggregates still exists, you do not even know its nature; once the hundred bones have scattered, where will you seek it? Lately, there has been one who...
Simply sitting like this all the time: at first one is alert, but after a short while one falls asleep; nine out of ten people sit there and fall fast asleep.
It is truly painful that they do not know how to apply themselves to the practice. How can one hope to attain realization by forcing oneself to sit rigidly?
That is not the principle. How, then, can it be seen? Dana (Danxia) held up his whisk; Layman Pang (Pangjushi) raised his mallet. Dana—
He threw down his whisk; the layman set down his mallet. Again he asked, "What about yesterday's koan? Danxia threw himself down and lay there.
The layman then departed. Is this not true intimacy? How could it allow you to speak recklessly?
How could it allow you to add footnotes? Furthermore, Yantou said: "As for those who are śramaṇas, each must [realize] from within themselves..."
It must flow forth from one’s own breast, covering heaven and earth, before it can be attained.
Where, then, is there any need for quiet sitting and conceptual deliberation? As the former Master said: "Investigate while sleeping; investigate while eating. Furthermore, as the ancients said:
When sitting, there is the principle of sitting; when standing, there is the principle of standing.
Have you not seen how Touzi asked Cuimi, "May I hear the secret instruction of the West? Cuimi stood still and looked back at him. Touzi said, "I do not yet understand the profound words;
I beg the Master to point them out again. Cuimi replied, "You wish for a second ladle of foul water to be poured over you. Touzi...
The disciple then attained realization. [The Master said: "If people cannot make use of this within the twelve periods of the day, they miss how many good things!
Therefore, I say that the Patriarch was truly one who knew the true sound. After a long silence, he spoke again:
'The Way of the Patriarchs is like the bright sun in a clear blue sky. Why is it that some lose their way? He stood for a long time."
The Master said: "You all cannot understand. Where does the fault lie? It is simply that you do not understand;
it is fundamentally a lack of understanding. Yet you still seek a place where you might understand. An ancient said, 'Do not abandon this side to cling to that side.
If you act like this, it becomes even more difficult to understand. I tell you that it is fundamentally a lack of understanding—why do you not look at it in this way? As it is said:
When Fayan was traveling on pilgrimage, Dizang asked him, "Where are you going? Fayan replied, "I am traveling on pilgrimage.

Dizang asked, "Do you understand the matter of traveling on pilgrimage? Fayan said, "I do not understand. Dizang said, "To truly understand the matter of traveling on pilgrimage, it is precisely this state of not understanding.
From this, Fayan attained awakening. I ask you: since you do not understand, how can it be so? There must be a point of entry; only then will you know that it is not otherwise.
Those who understand forcefully have a thousand clever ways of understanding; yet you do not understand at all from the very root.
What use is that? You must apply your mind and investigate it. Do you see how this "not understanding" comes about? Do you wish to know? This "not understanding" of yours—
Fundamentally, there is no place from which it comes. Since there is no place from which it comes, how can it not be "not meeting"?
When you have clearly realized this, you will see that there is no place to which it goes. If you look at it in this way, you can be certain that you must realize it.

It is simply because you do not know how to act as a practitioner of the Buddha-dharma; you have consistently applied your mind only to worldly matters and have never for even a moment investigated this matter.
How can one possibly understand it? When confronted by a question, people speak in gibberish and ramble on;
this is not the matter at hand. Long ago, I heard an old monk say that when Master Xianglin saw a monk approaching, he said:
"What you have said is certainly not without merit, yet as soon as you step down two or three paces, it is no longer so. Do not speak in confusion. You!
Look! How did the ancients, whose faculties were exhausted, treat this as their task? There is no principle in the Buddha-dharma that is wasted.
Understand it! Understand it! Be careful!
The Master said: "Master Yunmen said, 'If you have truly not yet grasped it, for now simply follow the principle and recognize it.
Those who study within the monastic community must also advance in accordance with this principle; one must not dare hope for a matter that transcends it.
Generally speaking, students today treat phenomena as one side and principle as another side, which is why they are unable to find peace in body and mind."
How pleasant! Why not simply teach that all affairs should always accord with principle? We have not yet discussed matters from beginningless kalpas;

we are speaking only based on a single thought-moment entering the mother’s womb, whereupon the sense-faculties, the physical body, and the vessel-world are suddenly transformed. From that point onward, there has been nothing that is not an affair.
Within a single retributive body, there are all manner of things—how could there ever be a single dharma that is not an affair? How, then, can you now manage to dismiss them?
This matter proceeds in accordance with principle. Now, phenomena have form and substance, whereas principle has no marks or characteristics.

Once the ancients attained this principle, phenomena immediately became integrated and harmonious with that principle. Have you not seen how a man of old, upon hearing the sound of a wooden board, clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "I understand!
I understand! Is this not learning in accordance with principle? Why do you not [do the same]?

Furthermore, practice such investigation throughout the twelve periods of the day. When you have performed this kind of work for a long time until it reaches maturity, it will naturally accord with the principle (*li*).

"When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? He replied on his behalf: "Ask me. He said again:
"I deeply appreciate your question, Master. One day, after finishing his gruel, he addressed the assembly, saying: "So many people..."
[The Master] ate congee. Not a single person could grasp it, so he simply rose and left. Case: One day an ancient worthy did not go to the hall.
The attendant said, "We request the Master to go to the hall. The worthy said, "Today I have been eating oil-cakes at the manor.
The attendant said, "The Master has never gone out; why do you say you were eating oil-cakes at the manor?"
"Come, Dechen. You simply go and ask the master of the manor. Just as he was about to leave, the master returned and thanked the Master, saying, "I am eating oil-cakes at the manor.
[The Master] spoke on his behalf, saying, "It is indeed so. Hearing the cry of a flying squirrel, an attendant monk asked, "The ancients said..."
"This is this very thing; it is not another thing. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "This old fellow does not know good from bad. Why do you speak for others?
He further said, "When you are in your quarters, prattling here and there as usual, is there any good or ill fortune in that?
Question: "How can the butcher with the broad forehead put down the butcher's knife in his hand? The Master spoke on his behalf: "There is no need to put it down."
[The Master] said, "Yes. Question: "What is this before one's face? He spoke on his behalf: "Nothing. Question: "The Sixth Patriarch was illiterate.
Why did he write 'Recorded by Old Lu in the second year of the Longshuo era' upon the waist-stone? He spoke on his behalf: "One must be even more thorough and precise. Questioning an attendant monk:
"Since you serve and support me in this way, with what shall I repay you? He spoke on his behalf: "Thank you."
The Master replied. While looking at the moon, he asked an attendant, "Where has that other half gone? [The attendant] pointed his finger at the moon in response.
He asked, "How can all the sentient beings of the great earth be delivered? [The attendant] replied, "There is a way to deliver them.

The monk said, "How do you deliver them, Master? The Master said, "Do not concern yourself with them. Because a monk had passed away, he asked the assembly, "After the midday meal, we shall cremate him."
"You too? How about you? [The Master] replied on his behalf: "Matters do not arise in vain. He said again: "It is not only I. He said yet again:

"I deeply appreciate this question. The Master said to an attendant monk: "I have always told you this, yet it has resulted in a transgression. [The Master] replied on his behalf: [The same as above].
