When Xie the Abbot sent him a gift, he received only half of it. The Master then instructed his attendant to deliver a message, saying, "Keep the other half for me, the old monk.
One day, the Master went before the stupa of Master Baogong and suddenly said, "Master Yunguang was a fine Dharma teacher.
Why did he place horns on his head? Since he was Master Yunguang, why did he place horns on his head? [The attendant] answered on his behalf: "He was wearing them as a hat."
"In the humble alleys, one does not ride a golden horse; returning, one puts on a tattered robe. The Master was sitting in the abbot’s quarters when he saw a monk approaching.
The Master said, "You have not yet entered the room; it is your turn next. [The monk] spoke on his behalf, saying:
"If that is so, then I, your servant, respectfully withdraw. While the Master was taking medicine, he asked a monk: "Just now, it felt as if there were something in my chest. Now—"
"What thing is the Way? A monk replied, "It is the breath of the lungs. Another said, "There is still this here. Yet another asked, "What is this? and then abruptly walked away.
The Master said to a monk, "The shop has been opened; buy in the east and sell in the west. The monk said, "Fine tea.
The Master said, "Take back your cheap wares yourself. The Master asked a monk, "When you suddenly die..."
"How is it? The monk was speechless. The Master laughed heartily. A monk asked, "What is the state of affairs before any signs have yet arisen?
The Master said, "Why did you not ask sooner? One day the Master said to a monk, "It cannot be supported;
even ten thousand people could not support it. After a long silence, he added, "There is only one person who can support it. The monk said, "I do not know for certain."
"What kind of person is this? The Master said, "One who has no power. The Master asked a monk, "Where did you get this lantern?
[The monk] answered on his behalf, "The proof is right before your eyes. He asked a monk, "What if you suddenly encounter tigers, wolves, swords, or blades?

[The monk] answered on his behalf, "They are tigers, wolves, swords, and blades. He asked a monk, "How will it be for you hereafter? [The monk] answered on his behalf, "It will be just like today. He asked a monk, "Following conditions..."
"One who attains" means there is forever no falling back or loss. To perceive one's own self here is also to give rise to an enemy. Do you understand?
A monk asked, "What is it like when one does not even see one's own self? The Master said, "Then who would you have to describe it to? The monk was speechless.

The Master spoke on his behalf: "It is still cold in the first month of spring. The Master cited a case: A monk asked Xuefeng, "When one knows there is a matter above, and thus first has a share in speech, what then?
Xuefeng raised the monk’s hand and said, "What is this? The monk was speechless. [The Master] spoke on his behalf:
This caused the Old Monk to reach such a state. [The Master] raised a case: A monk asked Faden, "At the top of a hundred-foot pole, how does one make further progress?
Faden said, "Agh! He then asked the monk, "What words would you have offered in response? [The Master] provided the following on behalf [of the monk]: "An immortal upon level ground."
Case: Yaoshan said to the novice Gao, "I hear that Chang’an is very bustling. Gao replied, "In my country, all is tranquil.
The Master asked a monk, "What is my country? [Substitute response: "Four or five hundred lanes of flowering willows and poplars;
two or three thousand pavilions of pipes and strings. The Old Monk Wuzu would often extend his hand and ask people, "Why do you call this a hand?"
Daiyun said: "You have deceived me too much.
To show the essential point to those of the Zen mind, one should not establish limits within the boundless void. If one were to establish limits, that would be the boundless void itself.

This is the fallacy of self-conceit. Thus, one who understands emptiness has no notion of emptiness. If a person attempts to grasp the mind through words and designations, they will ultimately not find the mind;
yet, if they do not attempt to grasp the mind through words and designations, they likewise will not find it.

Words are originally the mind itself; because one attempts to designate them, one does not find it. That which is without words is originally the mind itself; because one does not designate it, one does not find it.
All various encounters and circumstances do not accord with one’s own mind; the Patriarchs of old said it is simply a matter of silent resonance (*mòqì*). It is like this:

if the Way has not yet been realized, there is nothing to do but eliminate deluded thoughts. If a person recognizes these as deluded thoughts and attempts to suppress them through intentional effort, [they will only create further distraction].
This is because one perceives the existence of deluded thoughts. Knowing that there is the mental activity of deluded thoughts, one observes so as to perceive the correct principle;

yet, even this observation reveals the existence of deluded thoughts. When one knows that delusion is fundamentally the Way, then there is no delusion. Therefore, for one who has realized the Way, there is nothing to be attained.
If one gives rise to the intention to seek the Way, the Way is immediately attained; it is simply a matter of not seeking elsewhere. To know that there is no confusion or delusion is called "seeing."

Regarding the Way: in recent times, everyone says that there is nothing that is not the Way. This is like sitting beside a grain basket and talking about food; one will never be satiated because one does not actually put it into one’s mouth.
As for realization (*sākṣātkāra*), it is the severing of subject and object. It is not that there is some separate, mysterious principle existing elsewhere.
In the midst of ordinary daily activities—such as when seeing forms, this is the moment of realization; when hearing sounds, this is the moment of realization; when drinking water and eating...
Consciousness [of the ultimate] is the time of realization. Each instance is utterly devoid of subject and object. This is not something achieved through long-term practice;

it does not depend on cultivation or refinement. It is simply a matter already present. Yet worldly people do not recognize it, and thus they are called "wandering. Therefore it is said: "Only through realization can one know that it is difficult to fathom.

Those who study the Way clearly know that such a thing exists. Why, then, do they fail to grasp the essential meaning and remain in perpetual doubt? It is because their faith has not yet reached its ultimate limit. Doubt arises from this.
It is not yet profound. Only that which is profound and ultimate, whether as faith or doubt, is the true reality.

If one does not understand this and instead reflects erroneously, one will fall into confusion and lose track of the source. To falter midway and yet be able to reflect upon oneself—there is no second person capable of this.
Since this is called "the matter," how could it be something further known? To know it is a deluded thought; in this matter, one simply does not lose it.
The Way does not wait for explanation or demonstration before it becomes manifest; rather, its essence is eternally revealed.
Explanation and demonstration are merely the provisional application of the Way's function. Even for those who achieve awakening through them, these are but temporary detours.

Whether one realizes through explanation, enters through demonstration, or returns by means of spontaneous self-awakening, in the end there is no difference in the matter attained, for all lead to the ultimate source of the mind where one comes to rest.
People say that one must first attain enlightenment before practicing cultivation; this belongs to the gate of remedial measures (*pratipakṣa*).
Although the Zen school also permits the use of correct knowledge and vision to counteract [delusions], for the person of realization themselves, it is not necessary to be thus.

That the Buddha-way is long and distant, requiring the endurance of diligent suffering over a long period before it can be accomplished, refers to its continuity throughout the three periods of time, where ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness; therefore, it is said that "the Buddha-way is long and distant."
No divergent views arise, and there has never been any abandonment. Therefore it is said: "Having long endured diligent suffering, ultimately there is no separate dharma.

Therefore it is said: "Only then can it be accomplished. This is the task of a Great Man. People do not recognize this when they ask; thus, they answer according to what was brought before them. They do not realize that they are asking themselves:
"To whom do you wish to give an answer? People do not recognize the answer; thus, they give rise to views based on words. They do not realize [the truth].
He then answered himself: "What purpose or meaning could there be in that? Therefore it is said: 'It is all for you to look upon, to look upon. Someone might say:
'Since time immemorial, the instructions and teachings pointed out by the ancient sages and Buddhas have been disseminated throughout the world, each one clearly elucidated.
Why, then, do you say it is all your own deep failure to heed the bitter-mouthed compassion bestowed by the ancient sages of old? To this, I now reply:"

I follow the fundamental intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; you are the one who bears the burden, not I. If you claim there is something to be said, that is precisely to slander the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Do not become the last person to sever the seeds of the Buddha. If you do not turn toward what you yourself know as your refuge, then all that you do will result in the fabrication of falsehoods.
Even if you were to memorize as many words as the sands of the Ganges or exhaust every grain of ink and brush, what benefit would it bring you? Therefore, it is said: "Bring forth..."
"Regarding 'hearing and upholding the Buddha': why does the Buddha not hear for himself? To hear by seeking outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like you.
An elder said: 'I can now offer you a single phrase, which is not difficult; if you can realize it in a single word, you will still have some merit.
But if you do not understand, I, this old monk, would instead become a liar. Nowadays, students compete with one another to ask questions.
Answer: This is a crucial point within the Chan school. Not realizing that it is the mind of conceptualization that performs taking and rejecting—alas!
Scholarship that pursues both principle and phenomena is merely the talk of those who dwell near the gate. Even if one has a slight degree of comprehension, one must not yet rest.
Have you not heard that in the Way of Nirvana, all calculation and measurement are utterly severed? One must simply understand how to examine oneself before one can attain it. People are deluded.

It is because of the mind that one advances on the Path. Having come to the mountains and forests, one meets a spiritual friend and mistakenly thinks there is some other path that can bring peace and happiness.
One does not realize that returning to investigate the very point where one was previously deluded is the foremost of all practices. If one fails to reach this, [there is no attainment].
To enter the mountain forests and not return is to act in vain. It is extremely easy to become lost therein, yet difficult to enter;

thus the former masters said it is "difficult to believe and difficult to understand. They also said, "This is the teaching of the Sudden School. To reflect back upon what has already transpired is already a state of straying; how much more so is it when one does not do so?
Later generations have consequently treated these words as ordinary and mundane, regarding them as a single flavor of reality.
This is another point where later students lack clarity and fail to discern what is appropriate for their practice. Since ancient times, there have been two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*):
the skillful means of reality, which refers to the teaching that there is no interval [between delusion and enlightenment];

and the skillful means of artifice, which refers to the wondrous response to the various capacities of sentient beings. If one enters through the skillful means of reality, there is no need for deliberation; the nature itself is divinely liberated.
There shall never be any regression; its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

If one enters through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), attains the seat, and dons the robe, yet looks back upon oneself and finds that what has been attained is still insufficient, taking this to be the ultimate—these two types of skillful means are, in fact, one single Dharma.
One must not lose this for even a moment; let the student reflect on this. Xuefeng instructed people, saying: "Do not let me be old..."
The Master said: "The monks have a single phrase that reaches your own station. If there were a single phrase reaching your own station, what could it possibly do?
This was merely because the ancients had no other choice. Later people did not understand the intent of the ancients and simply claimed that within their own station there was no such talk;
thus they misunderstood. Nowadays, many people take this..."

At present, the function of discerning awareness is taken as the ultimate standard. This is why Xuansha said to people: "In a deep mountain, utterly remote and devoid of human presence—do you say there is anything there?
To realize the mind and see into one's nature, one should be like Xuefeng and Xuansha;
to tread the path and practice the truth, one should be like Nanquan and Zhaozhou. Nowadays, students merely take the skillful means of the ancients to be the Way of Chan.
One cannot participate in the realization of the ancients. It is like a strong man carrying a load of one hundred and twenty catties across a single-plank bridge;
he does not tilt or sway. What sustains him in such a way? It is simply because his refinement is free from admixture.
It is the same for the Way. As it is said in the sutras: "For example, when a lion seizes an elephant, it exerts its full strength."
Even when catching a rabbit, he preserved his full strength. Someone asked, "What strength did he preserve? He replied, "The strength of non-deception.

If one perceives even a single hair or a strand of fur as different from the mind, then one loses one's own life. Therefore, for the person who has attained the Way, there is nothing that is not [the Way]."
This power is exceedingly great; however, because it is eroded by boundless unwholesome thoughts, its functional efficacy becomes impaired.
If there were not so many diverse phenomena, diverse forms, diverse conditions, and diverse mental objects, it would transform according to the mind, sovereign and unimpeded.
The Way is not to be sought through hardship; if one seeks it, the Way is lost. Affairs do not depend on arduous dissolution; if one dissolves them, affairs arise.
When there is neither seeking nor dissolution, the Way and affairs meet. Thus, what affair is not the Way?
It is like a person with clear vision who enters a treasury of jewels but does not know the skillful means [to retrieve them], because they lack the illumination of fire, torches, or light.
Upon entering, one is immediately struck and wounded, damaging one's own head and body, thinking it to be a venomous hole rather than a treasury of jewels.
One who possesses wisdom enters within, holding a lamp or candle to illuminate it, and seeing the various kinds of jewels, selects them at will; having obtained the jewels, they exit.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, one must employ the light of wisdom so that the six sense-objects do not cause self-injury through contact. Thus spoke the former Head Seat, Yong.

He departed from Fenyang together with Ciming, yet Yong never fully exhausted the subtlety of his teaching. He followed Ciming for twenty years, yet in the end he remained unable to attain liberation.
One night, while they were gathered around a brazier deep into the night, Ciming struck the charcoal with a pair of fire tongs and said, "Venerable Yong!
Venerable Yong! Yong then rebuked him, saying, "Wild fox spirit! Ciming then pointed at Yong and said:
"Yàláng, you have gone off in this manner once again. It was through this that Yǒng finally attained ultimate realization. From then on, he followed [Címíng] until the end of his life.
Whenever Címíng posed extraordinary or challenging questions during their daily interactions, none of the assembly could respond; only when Yǒng arrived would Címíng nod his head in approval.
This is what is called "medicine for those without illness," the essential point of which few students have grasped, let alone those of later generations.
How could those who merely understand through intellectual views and interpretations grasp this matter? One must attain it like Yongjia, and apply the medicine like Ciming;
only then can one hope to succeed. To find stillness amidst the clamor is for a village to become a mountain forest;

to realize that afflictions are themselves bodhi is for all beings to achieve perfect enlightenment. Beginners in the study of the Way generally say they have attained and understood this, yet they treat it as a mere concept.

One plants the seeds of impartial knowledge and vision; yet when the mind is set free, ordinary people and sages remain as before, divided into two types, their stillness and agitation serving different functions.
Clearly understanding this is "comprehension," but one must first attain a state of stability before the single flavor can be realized. One must not force such comprehension.

In recent times, many have treated question-and-answer sessions as the hallmark style of the Chan school. Failing to understand the affairs of the ancients, they pursue only the superficial without ever returning to the source. This is lamentable.
Strange! Truly strange! People of old, because they were deluded, asked questions; thus, they sought realization within the very place of questioning.

Upon obtaining a single word or half a phrase, they took it as their task, investigating it until they had penetrated through to the end. This was not like the people of today who ask at random and answer offhand, only to be laughed at by those who have attained realization.

Those who have reached such a state study the Way throughout the twelve hours of the day, never abandoning it for even a moment. Even if such a person has not yet attained entry, [they are far superior to others].
Every thought-moment is already cultivation. What is commonly called cultivation does not go beyond the purification of the three karmas and the six sense faculties;

however, in the Gate of Chan, it is unnecessary to be thus. Why? Because in the gate of meditative concentration, every thought-moment is equal to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and thus there is naturally no fault or affliction in any place.
When, after a long time, the mind-ground becomes transparent and luminous, [the past...]

When both are fully perfected, it is called the Samādhi of One Practice. People of the present day rely entirely on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) yet fail to open the eye of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Consequently, all their instructional phrases and circumstances merely result in contentious debate and the mental activity of arising and ceasing. Now, the study of Chan is no trivial matter;
one need not necessarily transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs, yet once the essential point is grasped, such transcendence is not difficult. —Sūn Chéngwù of Gāoyóu.

He wrote a letter asking: "It does not fall within the realm of conceptual thought, nor does it reside in existence or non-existence. How then may one proceed? The Master replied: "If you ask 'how,' it is not permissible;
yet if you do not ask 'how,' it is likewise not permissible. Thereupon, the intoxicated guest was suddenly awakened, and the divine pearl of his mind shone forth with natural clarity.
How could one possibly plan for this in advance and then receive it?

For those of the highest caliber—those who are sharp and discerning—if they fail to find this single thought through their investigation, it is difficult for them to see it for themselves. To see it is precisely it; there is no other divergent path.
Ordinarily, people take the preceding thought to be correct and use the succeeding thought to examine it. Thus, they chase after past and future, using mind to employ mind, and the mind becomes...

This constitutes the perfected object. Generally, once the mind and its objects have been fully understood, they become increasingly untenable; as with subsequent thoughts, if one does not grasp them, they naturally lack any place of arising or ceasing—they are liberated in their own place.
Since thought is fundamentally non-arising, how could there still be the conceptual notions of existence or non-existence to act as obstructions?
To awaken to the mind in a single thought-moment is what is meant by attaining perfect enlightenment. Thus, in every thought-moment there is no birth; in every thought-moment...
It is signless and equal to empty space. When it touches things or encounters conditions, all are the wondrous functioning of the Buddha;

there is not even a thread’s breadth of duality. The jewel in the robe shines alone; the affairs of the worlds of the ten directions can be understood through direct perception, without waiting for a deliberate thought before knowing them.
This is truly the undertaking of a great man, which must be accomplished. To grasp its essential point, there is indeed...
It is not that the Dharma acts as an obstacle; rather, the desire to attain mindfulness arises precisely because one has lost mindfulness both before and after.
Day and night, one lacks self-mastery. One desires to be in accord with the Way, yet there is not even a slight point of accord. The more urgent one becomes, the less one accords with it.

The illness lies in grasping at one thing and rejecting another, failing to apply the mind skillfully, and lacking the essential method. Utterly bewildered and ignorant, day by day one moves further away from the Way.
If one sits in composure and settles the spirit, there is no need for strenuous effort. Thus, Master Bodhidharma said to Yang Xuanzhi:

"One does not abandon wisdom to approach ignorance, nor does one cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment. One traverses the Great Way beyond measure; one penetrates the Buddha-mind through transcendence.
Not entangled with either the ordinary or the sage, one is loftily named a Patriarch. This is not a matter of attachment or abandonment.
One side is precisely one side; know that it is luminously manifest, luminously functioning, supported by meditative concentration, and capable of apprehension.
It transforms the mundane into the sacred and transmutes iron into gold. This essential shortcut must be investigated in this way.

I only fear that people will run in two directions—neither achieving the first nor being the second—failing to recognize the profound principle and laboring in vain to contemplate stillness, like those of the Two Vehicles who sever [the defilements].
To attain realization while still possessed of afflictions is called "partial cultivation"; it is not as swift as transforming through mindfulness into unsurpassed awakening.
When a practitioner of the Way encounters the arising of afflictions, how should they respond? An ancient said, "Treat them solely with right knowledge and vision.
I, however, do not say this; I treat them simply by means of the afflictions themselves. Looking at it in this way, one does not even perceive their existence.
This is also regarding afflictions (*kleśa*). Why? One cannot further treat afflictions with afflictions; it is like fire not burning fire, or water not further wetting water.

Their essential nature (*dharmatā*) is identical, and nothing can be manifested therein. This is the realization that afflictions are fundamentally empty; one does not cling to them nor seek to dispel them.
If one gives rise to wisdom to sever, treat, or suppress them, this instead becomes a separate mental engagement (*cittopayoga*) involving duality and opposition, whereby one is overcome by them.
Second, regarding the shifting of objects: even if one were to attain them, it would be circuitous and limited. It is best to follow a direct path. As the ancients said:
"The kalpa-fire has once blown upon the breathless; no effort was required for it to wither instantly. This is what that means.
At times when sitting in stillness, the mind wanders and scatters; or when facing actual events, one completely loses [the realization].
This is entirely because one has not yet attained direct personal realization, falling into duality or triad, which leads to errors and successive failures.
As the ancients said: "Movement and stillness are non-dual; truth and falsehood are non-dual. Vimalakīrti clarified that all dharmas enter the gate of non-duality. If one understands this...
Essential. All movement is inherently quiescent and extinguished. For instance, the eye does not reach the form; the form does not reach the eye. Sound does not reach the ear;
the ear does not reach the sound. It is thus for all phenomena (*dharma*). Originally, they are the treasury of merit within one's own mind, where there is nothing to be grasped or rejected.
When one accords with this, where can one go that is not beneficial? This is precisely the Great Samādhi of the Nāga. Now, having emerged from it...

Those who are willing to study the Way must have planted roots of goodness in previous lives and possessed a fundamental basis; thus, they are able to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and are also able to resolve their doubts and attachments.
By investigating within themselves, and because their afflictive hindrances are thin, they possess the necessary causes and conditions; such individuals are easily transformed and delivered.
If one has not yet permeated this mind, right faith will not arise; even if they hear the teaching, they will not give rise to doubt, but merely—
It was like the wind passing by one's ear; even when exhorted, he gave rise to anger and added further slander. On what basis, then, could this be made manifest?
Thus, among thousands or tens of thousands of people, there are but one or two such as this.

If one can personally understand how to make a living and manage to gather these [virtues] together, then life after life one will proceed from here, becoming increasingly clear and sharp, never again falling away from one’s merit. One lifetime will be superior.
Throughout one's life, one enters the domain of all other Buddhas and remains constantly in accord with this reality. Whether in the human realm or the heavens, it is exactly thus.
Even when confronted by the five desires, the eight winds, and all sensory objects, one accords with the principle; one does not travel the paths of the three miserable realms.
With the single flavor of equality and right knowledge and vision, what further matter could there be? One must realize that birth and death are not something to be feared. One must understand.

This section concerns the truth and falsehood regarding birth and death. Only when one attains peace and happiness can one be free from transgression; otherwise, body and mind become a burden. The body is like shackles;

one should know the places where the body comes and goes. The mind is like a monkey; one should know the places where the mind arises and ceases. From where do these two come and go, and arise and cease?
When this is understood, body and mind are perfectly luminous, and the internal and external are as one. Furthermore, as for the mind...

The mind is internal; the body is external. The body is internal; external objects are external. The National Teacher said: "Body and mind are of one suchness; there is nothing remaining outside the body.
Thus, one does not perceive birth and death as having any reality within the sphere of feeling. This may be called liberation on the Great Way.
Therefore, it enables people such that upon seeing or hearing, they cannot help but be liberated; their conceptual thoughts cannot help but cease; and the realm of objects cannot help but dissolve.
What more is there to doubt?
First, reflect upon yourself:
this physical life is like a white colt passing through a crevice; what leisure is there for idle sentiments or to recklessly engage in trivial affairs? Since [life] is already flourishing...

O Śākya, examine closely the lineage of your ancestral tradition and its established standards. Second, your path of practice is not yet complete and the time since the Sage has passed is far removed;

you must truly not abandon the instruction of virtuous friends and teachers. Exert yourself spontaneously, mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, knowing this for yourself alone, and let not your great resolve falter.
Third, the conditions of retribution are empty and illusory and cannot be forcibly altered; how long is this fleeting world?

Whether one’s household circumstances be abundant or meager, whether one encounters suffering or joy, adversity or favor, the Way lies within them. Whether in motion or stillness, cold or warmth, one should feel self-reproach and repentance.

Regarding inquiries and dialogues, I caution that many contemporary practices invite ridicule and slander; this is largely because people do not understand the intent behind extending an inquiry to resolve doubts and seek instruction.
Successive generations have transmitted [the tradition], frequently employing words of benediction and seasonal greetings; these are not established within the core teaching (zongcheng).
For example, when an ancient asked, "How can one escape the three realms? or asked, "How can one penetrate through sound and form?
or asked, "Regarding this school's core teaching, how do you, Master, discourse upon it?"—these were all matters of on-the-spot resolution before the assembly. Lately, however, elder brothers...

Brother, advancing ten or five turns of "speech without a handle" (moba bi yu)—whether offered to officials present in the hall or prepared as an offering for lay donors—neither possesses the true flavor of a monk.
Furthermore, withdrawing from the assembly and speaking a few words [is likewise not it].
At times it was said: "So-and-so does not speak in such a manner. It was also asked: "Why does the Master not speak?
Now, one who engages in dialogue seeks to stimulate and exalt the ultimate mystery; it need not be prolix, consisting of no more than three or two turns of speech.
The aim is to inspire faith in others, ensuring that one does not lapse into frivolousness or become an object of ridicule for worldly people.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Zen Master Fuyan, Volume Thirty-Four Since the Venerable Teacher Fuyan attained the Dharma from Dongshan,
he has occupied the seat of enlightenment three times and carried out the ancestral command for over twenty years.
Throughout the Huai region, monks from the four quarters flocked to him like spokes converging at the hub of a wheel; to fail to reach Longxiu was considered a futile return.
The Master dwelt serenely in his quarters, making the transmission of the Way his sole responsibility. He pointed directly at people with unmistakable clarity, never weary from morning until night.

Whether ascending the hall or entering the inner chamber, he pointed directly toward the source. In his total employment of great capacity, he delivered general discourses and small-scale sermons, skillfully employing expedient means to instruct and enlighten others.

To eliminate the illnesses of meditation, one must cause the student to attain sudden enlightenment to their original mind. The great earth, mountains, rivers, and the myriad phenomena of the universe have never been external objects.
The Buddhas of the ten directions and the ancestral masters of successive generations are none other than oneself. Outside the mind there is no dharma; the mind itself is also without mind.
A single ray of spiritual light appears everywhere; naturally, there is no dharma to be grasped, and no dharma to be...
Let go. Do not perceive a single dharma as non-existent or existent, as contrary or compliant. Do not perceive a single dharma as internal or external, as departing or arriving.
When both subject and object have vanished, the myriad differences are revealed in their uniqueness.

The previously existing evil thoughts, emotional views, delusive imaginings, and worldly toil are, in their very substance, transformed into the subtle and wondrous samādhi. In every particle of dust and every world-system, whether sentient or insentient, all are...
This is established as the true, original substance of oneself. If one reaches this secure and profound field, one may manifest transformations at will and act spontaneously.

Within the non-dual Dharma, one manifests immeasurable differentiated realms, enabling people to perceive the fundamental source amidst a thousand heads and a hundred faces; without shifting by even a hair’s breadth, one then—
Unmoved by the myriad objects of the sensory world, he moves out and enters alone, penetrating and liberated with total freedom. Such spiritual powers are fully recorded in this collection;

every word is a direct command, and every sentence is the perfect essence of the school. Although it has been carved onto woodblocks for public display, one must take care not to call these words mere "sentences.
If anyone opens this volume and clearly perceives its ultimate aim, they will know that Master Fuyan remains present to this day.
He has never passed away. On the eighth day of the eighth month in the seventh year of the Xuanhua era, Feng Jie of Suining respectfully wrote this preface.

The Epitaph for the Stupa of the Late Chan Master Fuyan of Baoshan, Hezhou, was composed by Li Misan, a Xiaojun Lang who formerly served as the Superintendent of the Chongfu Palace at Mount Song in the Western Capital.
To the south of the Yangtze and Huai rivers, there was a great Chan Master known as Fuyan. His spiritual practice became renowned at court, and by imperial decree he resided at Baoshan in Hezhou.
After more than a year, he declined the position due to illness and returned home, retiring to the Eastern Hall of Jiangshan, where people from near and far flocked to him.

Those who have sought the Dharma by observing the etiquette of a disciple are beyond counting. From famous mountains and great monasteries, messengers continue to arrive without ceasing to invite him.

On the day before the winter solstice in the second year of the Xuanhua era, after finishing his meal, he adjusted his robes, sat in the lotus posture, pressed his palms together above his forehead, and passed away with a serene expression.
His disciples mourned him with deep longing, as if they had lost their guide across a vast expanse.

The Liang dynasty was like one who has lost their boat and oars, not knowing where to find salvation. The Dharma-brother of the successor, the Great Master Foguo Keqin, described the Master’s conduct and said to Misan:
"The Master took delight in you upon merely hearing of your reputation; he reached a profound accord with you in a single word. Now that he has passed away, you have truly witnessed this.
No one knows the Master better than you; it is fitting that you compose the inscription. Thereupon, he composed the preface and the inscription, saying: [The inscription follows.]
The Master’s surname was Li and his given name was Qingyuan. A native of Linqiong in Shu, he left home at the age of fourteen and received full ordination.

He had previously relied upon the Vinaya, having thoroughly investigated its doctrines. Later, while reading the *Lotus Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination.

Taking this up, he questioned a lecture master, but none were able to provide an answer. Thereupon he said: "The study of meaning and the nomenclature of names are not [the means for understanding] this."
Having resolved the great matter of birth and death, he abandoned his former habits and traveled south through the Jianghuai region, visiting various Chan seats in succession.
Hearing that the Master Yan of Taiping in Shuzhou was a preeminent teacher of the age, he went directly to his quarters to serve him with reverence and earnest inquiry.
As time passed, his resolve grew ever firmer. Yan marveled at his depth and deemed him capable of upholding the Dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti), remaining steadfast and unyielding like a wall.
I hope that you will attain profound realization. For seven years, the Master never uttered a single word in vain. One day, he attained a moment of awakening;
his insight became penetrating and transcendent, and his sharp, swift eloquence was such that none could withstand its edge.

From then on, monks vied with one another to seek him out as their teacher, yet the Master remained increasingly silent and self-effacing, never considering himself to have achieved anything. He lived in seclusion at Dazhong Hermitage on Mount Simian during the Tianxia era.
When the new Chongning Wanshou Monastery was about to select a person to reside there, the Governor of Shu, Lord Wang Huanzhi, invited the Master to serve as its abbot;
however, the Master declined and departed. It happened that the seat at Longmen was vacant, so he was appointed to fill it. He remained there for twelve years before moving to reside at Baocan.
Having presided over three famous monasteries, he caused them all to flourish wherever he went. During his tenure at Longmen, his reputation for the Way...

His reputation spread even further. Scholars from all quarters all said, "I must take Longmen as my teacher. Consequently, they gathered there like clouds until there was no space left to accommodate them.
Without rising from his seat, the Master transformed the cramped and humble site into a magnificent monastery.

The strong contributed their physical labor, the wise provided guidance and measurements, and the wealthy offered their resources; he never grudgingly withheld anything. The Master was dignified, upright, serene, and grave, living in a state of profound detachment.
He was sparing with speech; his smiles and movements were governed by ritual propriety. When he did speak, his words were harmonious and measured, causing others to receive them with deep reverence.

His teaching was simple yet profound and subtle; it cut off all paths and transcended written characters. It did not linger in empty or diffuse doctrines, nor did it take pride in learning, reputation, or rhetorical skill.
Its purpose was to enable people to penetrate the true source and tread upon the ultimate reality. This was not...
He attained profound realization and did not grant his approval lightly. In his daily life, he took the Way as his sole responsibility and did not involve himself in worldly affairs.
He once said, "An elder need only sit upright in the abbot’s quarters and transmit the Way. When associating with scholars and officials, he was never swayed by power or profit;
if their principles accorded with the Way, he would joyfully visit them, but otherwise, even if they passed his door, he might not be seen.
The high officials and great men held him in high esteem. When the State Councilor Deng Xunwu heard of his reputation, he memorialized the throne to grant him purple robes and a monastic title.

Upon seeing the Dharma discourses transmitted by the Master, the Censor-in-Chief Chen Gonguan sighed and said: "The heart-essence of all Buddhas and the ocean of the nature of sentient beings—Master Yuanyong has immersed himself in these depths profoundly.
Yet even they did not truly know this Master; how much less so those who have personally been bathed in his presence? He was indeed like a Buddha.

Guofojian was a peerless and harmonious fellow-disciple of Dongshan. Their reputation for the Way surpassed one another, and the world spoke of them as "the two Dings and the one Yuan of the Eastern Mountain.

He once expounded upon the meaning of the *Bai-men* (One Hundred Gates) and composed the *Yuanrong Liwen* (Text on the Ritual of Perfect Fusion). Furthermore, he excerpted from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra* to compose the *Pumen Lizì* (Characters for the Universal Gate Liturgy);
both works circulate in the world today. Among those who studied under him and attained the Dharma, there were no fewer than several dozen people, including Shiguī and Shanwù.
He was the foremost among them. The practitioner from Susong, the Daoist Nianfo [Lifang], reached a profound depth of his teachings.

The Master’s age was fifty-four, and his years as a monk were forty. As he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples, "The venerable elders of various regions invariably leave behind verses when departing this world.
Can the world be abandoned so easily? Moreover, where shall I go? Upon reaching the end, he did not utter a single word. Initially, while at Longmen, he composed...
The Lingguang Terrace was built to hold the cremation of the bhikṣu. He composed an inscription for himself, saying: "In the future, my remains shall also be interred here.
Later, his disciples enshrined his bones in a casket and returned them to Longmen. The people of Longmen were both moved by grief and filled with joy.
He served it as if it were alive. On the *renyin* day of the first month in the third year of the Xuanhua era, the stupa was completed.
The inscription reads: Great Wisdom is but the mind; there are no Northern or Southern patriarchs. Once one departs from its source, one opens windows and doors [of sectarianism].
Those who guard the mystery still seek conformity; those who cling to interpretations follow their own inclinations. Paths diverge and streams branch out; once overturned, they cannot be traced back.
Vast and profound, all blended together; he expounded it until its essence was perfected. The Master then succeeded him, and the Way became even more honored.
Like gathering the entire tide so that no individual wave can be distinguished, or lifting up the whole earth so that all things are displayed therein.
He utilized obscurity to manifest clarity, and his reputation spread in all four directions. Awakening the deluded and unraveling errors, those far and near relied upon him.
In the relinquishing of use, who can fathom it? His every movement and word follows a disciplined rule. He disciplines himself with rigor and reveals the pivot of opportunity through equanimity.
Dwelling alone amidst the groves, he takes only the Way as his standard. His transformative conduct is cultivated; he does not seek mere silence.
He greatly revives the Dragon Gate, adorning what was decayed and ruined. He penetrates the true source and deeply treads upon the ultimate reality.
The Perfectly Interfused Universal Gate, Shining equally upon all while benefiting both self and others; In his final teaching, he did not establish even a single verse.
Alas, O Master! Who can discern where you have returned? The deep pool is clear and the moon appears; As the boat moves, the shore shifts.
With a single movement of the hand, you manifest great compassion; The original pearl is right before us, yet the formless void cannot perceive it.
Who among later scholars shall be their teacher? The Inscription for the Spirit-Light [Pagoda].
Revised by Shi Gui, Dharma Heir and Abbot of Yongquan Chan Monastery on White Cloud Peak at Gushan, Fuzhou.
