The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shenzhao, the Founder of Dasui, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuande of Western Shu. Upper Section.
Entering the Hall, he said: "Have you not seen it said that a single mote of dust contains the Dharma-realm? Therefore it is said that there is a wise person who shatters [it]."
A scroll emerges from within a mote of dust; its measure is equal to a trichiliocosm. Do you wish to break it or not?
I now lift it up; let everyone seek this matter. The three thousandfold world-system is gathered within a single minute mote of dust;

the waters of the four great oceans are returned to a single drop. Mount Sumeru is contained within a mustard seed. If you seek your own true self, it resides in but a single hair. If you [seek it] as one—
Even when seeing it within a single hair, the three thousandfold world-system becomes a single scroll. It is simply that you yourself cannot move this realm;
therefore, the true state does not manifest. What need is there to speak of even a hair’s breadth of awakening?
It is all merely leaning against a blade or dodging an arrow—fearing the realm and hiding one's form. Brothers, what do you call this? It is like grass being pressed down by a stone.
It is similar. Or perhaps you might set aside the stone, yet the habitual tendencies remain as before. You must settle it thoroughly in every situation;
only then can you become the master of the environment and avoid being driven by external objects. This is extremely difficult, extremely difficult—thousandfold difficult, ten-thousandfold difficult.

This is merely an empty shell. Afterward, who will suffer from carrying the bell and bearing the saddle? As soon as there is even a slight touch of awakening, one immediately intends to act as a teacher to others—this is a great error.
You must speak of the ordinary until the ordinary is exhausted; you must speak of the sacred until the sacred is exhausted.
To cite one case illustrates all others: it is nothing but this. It is not easy; it is not easy. Take care! Take care! [The Master] descended from his seat. A question was asked:
"What is the matter of 'great following' on one side? The Master said: "There is no east, west, south, or north. Question: "What is the matter within birth and death?

The Master said: "A bubble floating on the water; inside and outside are not seen. Question: "What is the single phrase of the central principle? The Master said: "Neither from the exterior nor from the interior.
[The student] further asked: "How is it when the Master has resolved his will? The Master said: "Know it beneath a word."
Yin. He asked, "What is the place where the Way is applied? The Master said, "Do not deceive yourself. He asked, "The subtle *ālayavijñāna*..."
"How do you distinguish it upon reaching this point? The Master said, "Your eyes only know how to observe form; do they also know how to hear sound? Question:
"The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? The Master said, "The myriad dharmas originally do not return. Question: "How is it when the six states have not yet been pacified?

The Master said, "The ministers' efforts are rendered futile. The questioner pressed further: "When the Way of Ruler and Minister is perfectly harmonized, what then? The Master said: *Note: The final response by the Master is left as "The Master said" to indicate the end of the recorded dialogue.*
"I do not see any sovereign or ministers. A questioner asked: "What is 'sovereignty'? The Master said: "Non-sovereignty. The questioner pressed: "How is it when there is non-sovereignty?
The Master said: "Then one is sovereign. A questioner asked: "When the snow falls upon the jade steps, what then? The Master said: "One does not loathe the worldly realm.
A questioner asked: "What is the matter regarding the single path of Caoxi? The Master said: "I, this old monk, say it is like a pit of impurity."

The student asked, "Why is it so? The Master said, "The paths of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are two; they do not interfere with one another. A questioner asked, "Having long dwelt in the cold crags, why does the sun not shine upon you?
The Master said, "It does not shine upon the cold crags; the cold crags will never come out to meet your sunlight.
A questioner asked, "Apart from light and shadow, what is the nature of the Master? The Master said, "I spit it out along with the light. The student pressed further, "Do not..."
[The monk] spoke in a ghostly voice. The Master struck him. He asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "Is this the end or the beginning? [The monk] asked again.
"How is it that one follows along with objects? The Master said, "It is not like you, student. He asked further, "Why do you not speak? The Master said, "Not so.
He asked, "What is the primordial place? The Master said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization. He asked, "When the waves ceaselessly surge, what then?
The Master said, "Pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem. He asked further, "Why is it that when the waves subside and stillness prevails..."

[Sand and stones] grow ever more numerous. The Master said, "I shall cut them off for you. A question was asked: "When a student is like drifting clouds, using a mirror to catch light—where can it be arranged?
The Master said, "Be the master of the clouds. A question was asked: "How is it when not even an inch of grass has grown? The Master said, "This old monk has no rice to eat;
I will never leave Mount Daisui. A question was asked: "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? The Master said, "They are the same."
[The student] said, “Different. The Master said, “Not investigating the beginning; not looking toward the end. [The student] asked, “What is it like when one encounters an ancient Buddha on the road?

The Master said, “If you were to encounter a camel, a donkey, an elephant, or a horse, what would you call them? The Master continued, “The virtuous ones of former generations all sought the reality; they did not deceive themselves.
How can they be compared to moths flying into a flame, injuring and destroying themselves? He was clearly enlightened and was [thus] treated.”
Constrained and obstructed by the cycle of birth and death, one is unable to attain it; thus, consciousness cannot cognize it and wisdom cannot know it.
One does not hear the Way. Śākyamuni closed his room; Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth; Subhūti spoke without speaking;
Śakra and Brahmā listened without listening. This matter is most difficult, most difficult. Take care.
Ascending the hall, he was asked: "All phenomena arise from the mind; I wonder, from what does the mind arise? The Master said: "A stone ox runs along the river;
beneath the water, fire burns the sky. He was asked: "What is Mount Daisui? The Master said: "The ears do not hear; the eyes do not see. He further asked:
"What is it like to be among those on the mountain? The Master said: "In a crowd of a thousand people; in a crowd of ten thousand people. ...not [one].

"I do not face one person; I do not turn my back on one person. A question was asked: "If one digs one zhang and finds one zhang of empty space, and then takes that one zhang of earth to fill that one zhang of empty space—where does the emptiness go?
The Master said: "Do not take this principle to be the Buddha-dharma."
"Go out! Go out! A question was asked: "The Buddha-dharma pervades all places; I wonder where you instruct students to set foot? The Master said: "The great ocean allows the fish to leap;
the vast sky permits the birds to fly. A question was asked: "Having smashed the pearl of the black dragon, I ask the Master to clarify the living treasure.
The Master said: "Setting aside the living treasure for a moment, what is this pearl of yours that you have smashed?"
The monk remained silent. [The Master] asked: "The three bodies of the Buddha—Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya—are also not what is spoken of.

What is the primordial body? The Master said: "The wish-fulfilling jewel at the bottom of the sea; from beginning to end, there is nothing it does not respond to. [The Master] asked: "What is the mark of a great man? The Master said: [He remained silent.]
"No sign posted on the belly. The Master asked a monk, "Where are you going? The monk said, "I am going to live in a hermitage on West Mountain.
The Master said, "If I call for you from East Mountain, will you come at once? The monk said, "No, I would not. The Master said, "Then you have not yet attained the ability to dwell in a hermitage.
[Someone] asked, "When birth and death arrive, what then? The Master said, "When you meet tea, drink tea; when you meet rice, eat rice."
Jin said, "Who receives the offering? The Master said, "Close your bowl. Beside the Master’s hut was a tortoise.
A monk asked, "All other sentient beings have skin over their bones; why does this sentient being have bones over its skin?
The Master then took his straw sandals and placed them over the tortoise, then asked, "Do you understand? The monk was speechless. [Another] asked, "What is the Dharma of all Buddhas?"
"Essential! The Master raised his whisk and asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The fly-whisk.
A monk asked, "What is the student's own self? The Master said, "It is my own self. The monk pressed further, "Why then is it the Master’s own self?
The Master said, "It is your own self. A monk asked, "What is the seamless stupa? The Master said, "One chi high."
5. [The student] advanced and said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “A whole brick. [The student] asked, “What is the emptiness of all-knowledge?
The Master said, “The emptiness of the mind is it. [The student] advanced and said, “If there is further coming, what then? The Master said, “It is not emptiness.
[The student] advanced and said, “Does this accord with the matter above? The Master said, “Not so. [The student] asked, “After the Master passes away, to whom shall the Dharma be entrusted?”
"With whom [is it]? The Master said, "The pillar and the brazier. [The monk] further asked, "Does it still receive [it] or not? The Master said, "The brazier and the pillar.
A certain attendant leading a group came to the Master's place. The Master asked, "When one who has attained realization calls 'East,' what does he call it?
He replied, "It cannot be called 'East. The Master scolded him, saying, "You stinking donkey! Then what do you call it?"
The practitioner remained silent, and the assembly all dispersed. A question was asked: "There is but one Dharma which the ears do not hear and the eyes do not see;
it is entirely light and shadow. What is the person within the light and shadow? The Master rebuked him, saying: "Do not be irreverent! Do not be irreverent! A question was asked:
"What is it like when principle cannot be expressed through words? The Master said: "Words and expressions are themselves the principle. A question was asked: "What is the house style of the Master?"
The Master said, "Painting a winnowing fan with red earth. The student asked, "I do not understand how this principle works.

The Master said, "The winnowing fan has a rim; the rice cannot leap out. The Master asked a lecturer, "What scripture are you lecturing on? The lecturer replied, "The *Śata-dharma-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas).
The Master picked up his staff and said, "From what does it arise? The lecturer replied, "It arises from conditions. The Master said, "Alas! Alas! The Master [continued].
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you been? The monk said, "I went to pay respects to Samantabhadra.
The Master raised his whisk and said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here. The monk drew a circle, threw it behind him, and then spread out both hands.
The Master called to his attendant, "Give this monk a bowl of tea. He then asked, "I heard about the great waters of Dawsui from afar; having arrived, I see only this."
"This is a flax-picking pond. The Master said, "You see only the flax-picking pond; where do you see the waters of Daisui? He asked, "What are the waters of Daisui?
The Master said, "They are so bitter and astringent that it is difficult to get them down one's throat. He asked, "Can they be drunk? The Master said, "If you drink them, you will die immediately.
Once, while burning a mountain, the Master saw a snake. He prodded it with his staff and cast it into the fire, saying, "Hmph!"
The Master said, "This physical form is still not being relinquished; you will die right here, like one who finds a lamp in the darkness.
Thereupon, a monk asked, "At this very moment, is there still sin or not? The Master said, "When the stone tiger roars, the mountain valleys echo;
when the wooden man bellows, the iron ox is startled. The monk then took leave of the Master by sending a letter, asking: "I, this student..."
[The monk] said, "I am leaving. I do not know what words the Master will use upon arriving there. The Master said, "Speak well so that you may attain thorough understanding.

[The monk] asked again, "As I am about to part ways and it is late, I request the Master to grant me an instruction. The Master said, "Go home early; there is nothing to do. A monk came from Mount Wutai.
The Master asked him, "How is Mount Wutai compared to Mount Daisui? The monk asked, "What is Mount Daisui like? The Master said:
The monk turned his back. The Master called out in a loud voice. The monk called out in a loud voice: "What is Mount Dàsui?

The Master said, "Whether it be a thousand mountains or ten thousand mountains. [The monk] asked: "What is it like when a fish swims on dry land? The Master said: "In a place where it cannot be bent."
"This is what the *ācārya* values. The monk asked, "What is it like when one descends back into the green depths?
The Master said, "It is difficult to clarify the matter of standing on one's feet. The Master examined a monk, asking, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I have come from Sichuan.
The Master said, "Before entering Sichuan, where were you staying? The monk said, "Nowhere. The Master said, "Is it not that there is a place?"
[The monk] asked, "Is it excessive? The Master said, "If there were such a place, it would blind people's eyes.
The Master continued, "Heaven and hell occupy but a single *zuoju* (seating mat) of space; they are like a drum lying in a pit that sounds of itself without being struck.
What use are they? A questioner asked, "When birth and death arrive, can one still avoid them? The Master said, "Eat when hungry; put on clothes when cold."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Now, for a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya, if one regards existence as non-existence, only then can one accord with ordinary beings and sages at all times, and accord with liberation.
Only then does one have even a slight degree of 'going forth. If it is not like this, it is a great difficulty, a great difficulty! Take care!"
Ascending the hall, he was asked: "The great earth and the sun and moon—when their time comes, all return to exhaustion.
There has never been a single thing that has not been swallowed by impermanence. Is there anything, then, that cannot be swallowed? The Master said: "What do you call 'impermanence'?"
The monk continued, "That which is not ultimate is impermanent. The Master said, "Impermanence is, in fact, ultimate; it is you who are not ultimate.
The monk would not accept this, so the Master struck him. The Master then examined a layman, asking, "What kind of mourning attire does this body wear?"
The scholar said, "Both my parents have passed away. The Master said, "Go and drink tea. The layman responded with an assent and went out.
The Master called him back and said, "Tsk! You have been deceiving this old monk. Your parents are still here;
do not speak of studying the Unsurpassed Way when you do not even know your own parents. Get out! Get out! [The scholar] asked, "What is the profound principle? The Master said, "Straightforwardly."
"Xuanyan, go. The student asked, "What is the mystery within the mystery? The Master said, "Do not turn back to go.

A questioner asked, "When the ancients stood in the snow and cut off their arms, what Dharma were they seeking? The Master said, "The ancients did not cut off their arms. The student pressed, "But the ancients did cut off their arms!"

[The student] asked: "For what reason did he not sever his arm? The Master said: "He simply took pleasure in the midst of the snow. [The student] asked: "What is it like before the golden rooster has crowed?
The Master said: "One loses track of King Weyin (Vipaśyin). [The student] further asked: "What is it like at the very moment it crows?"
The Master then smiled. A question was asked: "When an insect in firewood dies within the firewood, how should one deal with an insect in water?
The Master said: "All things are as they are. A question was asked: "When a golden goose sends a letter, why does it not reveal its wings? The Master said: "Empty messages are not passed through."

Question: "Who is capable of discerning the offering of jewels at the site of enlightenment? The Master said: "Empty space is capable of discerning it. The Master suddenly manifested a slight illness and did not receive visitors.
At that time, a monk asked through a curtain: "Why is it that we do not see one another when we are but a few feet apart?
The Master said: "We see each other right now; why do you not ask about it? The monk then asked: "What is this matter of seeing each other? The Master—
[The Master] said, "This old monk is unwell. What state of mind do I have to face you?

He ascended the hall and said, "At ease, one wanders through heaven; in stillness, one returns to earth. A question was asked: "When there is not a single tile above and not a needle’s point of space below, what then?
The Master said, "Where are you residing right now? A question was asked: "Impermanence is swift; it does not—"
[Question: "When one has made an appointment with another, and they suddenly arrive—how is it then? The Master said: "Ask quickly! Ask quickly! [The monk] stepped forward and asked:
[The Master] said: "You were far too slow. [Question: "Regarding 'the simultaneous pecking and hatching'—how does one behold this? The Master said: "Is it movement? Is it stillness? [Question:
"When emerging from the shell—how is it then? The Master said: "Is it the branch? Is it the root? He added: "Do you see? [Question: "Universal..."
[The student] asked, "Why does the rain not moisten? The Master said, "It rains everywhere. [The student] asked, "When a drop of water turns to ice, why did the ancients disapprove of it?
The Master said, "The ancients were exactly like this. As for me, I would say: hang a broken lapis lazuli bowl in the midst of empty space.
[The student] asked, "Since he is a lion, why was he ridden by Mañjuśrī? The Master said, "He was tamed by himself."
[The Master] was present. A question was asked: "The solitary cliff has no embroidery; how is it with this matter of direct penetration? The Master said: "The solitary cliff has embroidery;
the matter of direct penetration is manifest. Question: "Why does a fish living in water die of thirst? The Master said: "It is simply because the fish does not apply its mouth [to the water].
Question: "Father and son are most intimately related; what is it like when they part ways at a fork in the road? The Master said: "Because there is a father."
A disciple. A layperson offered a bowl to the Master. He asked, "Before you were given this bowl, what did you use?
The Master said, "I used the one who was very last. A monk wished to leave the mountain to beg for alms on behalf of the community and took his leave of the Master.
The Master said, "If you can utter a single phrase, I will let you go. If not, return to the hall to rest and attend to your own matter."
The Master asked, "The entire empty realm of the ten directions is the patronage of this old teacher; I wonder what kind of people he transforms?
The monk said, "I only ask the Master to provide the draft, and I shall speak for him. The Master said, "First attend to your own affairs.
[Another] asked, "What is it like when one slanders the Buddha and reviles the Sangha? The Master said, "What fault has the Sangha? It is the Buddha who has wronged you."
"What is this? You are slandering him. The monk was speechless. Entering the hall, the Master said:
"In these times, a śramaṇa must first discern the fruit within the cause, and the cause within the fruit, before he has attained it. A monk then asked:
"What is it like when there is a person who belongs neither to cause nor fruit? The Master stepped forward, seized him firmly, and said: "I am one of these times!"
The śramaṇa had just been distinguishing the fruit within the cause and the cause within the fruit. You say that one person does not belong to cause and fruit;
you speak separately, you speak separately! The monk was speechless, and the Master struck him out.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, “I do not ask about the past or the future; what is the present? The Master said, “Can empty space accommodate a grinding stone?
A monk asked, “When coming there is no obstruction; when going there is no hindrance. At this very moment, I beg for a word from the Master.
The Master said, “Empty space has no boundaries; the great ocean is as level as the palm of a hand. Prajñā.”

"Nature and so forth. He ascended the hall and addressed the great assembly, saying: "Do you all know that there are three places where one does not stand? First, substantial obstruction and the presence of conditions;

second, the two limits being indivisible; and third, how could one know coming and going? The Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms are not absent even among those who are not sages; as for the Eight Liberations and Six Supernatural Powers..."
The extraordinary is not something that exists [independently]. Although all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, can one treat these wriggling creatures as equal to the Buddha?

Nevertheless, there is no partiality in their high or low status; it is only that there are differences along the path. This body is difficult to obtain, while birth from womb or egg is easily achieved.
How much more so for those who are disciples of the Śākya, and even descendants of his lineage, whose bodies are covered by the three robes, having cultivated themselves through past kalpas.

Come. As for the four requisites of support, this has not been the case from today alone. His outward appearance was entirely like that of a high monk, and even his speech was superior to that of a worldly person.
To call him by name is to refer to him as a *śramaṇa* who transmits the Dharma. Yet, if one reflects carefully, what exactly does he transmit?
He consistently disparages the scriptures and teachings; though possessing eyes, he is like one blind. He is purely a slanderer of our ancestors; though possessing a mind...
It is just like wood or stone; unable to reflect upon one’s own virtuous conduct, one indulges in ignorance all day long.
With a heart devoid of shame and remorse, how could one ever awaken while remaining in such a daze? Once this body is lost, one will sink into the depths for eternal kalpas.

Not only is it difficult to regain a human body, but even to attain the status of a fortunate beast is hard to find. Question: When playing with the moon’s orb atop a solitary peak, what is there to do?
“How is it? the Master asked. The student said, “Why do you not settle the matter of the solitary peak? What is the point of playing with the lunar disc?

The Master said, “What is the matter of being transparently clear both inside and out? The student replied, “It is so. The Master said, “How is it that you are transparently clear both inside and out? The student remained silent.
"There is nothing that is not illuminated. The Master rebuked him, saying, "This dull donkey even intends to learn the gallop of a horse.
The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again: "I ask you, you traveling monks from all quarters: do not say that I, this old monk, have any Buddha-dharma here to preach to you.
When you were traveling on foot through all quarters seeking out spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), what did they say? And what did you take away from them?"

What? Do not say that one simply rises after performing three prostrations and approaching to inquire. Even if one attains realization at the moment of speaking, they are still not yet a person who has reached the ultimate end.
Do not seek excellence merely through verbal cleverness; for those who are the eyes and lamps of humanity and heaven, this was not achieved in a single or two lifetimes.
It is entirely the result of merit accumulated and fruition perfected over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Only then does one attain such a state.
This is why I have manifested myself here within this forest monastery. It is solely for the sake of you people of the present day who practice with diligent effort.
I only fear that you renunciants will lose this human body; do not let your days pass in vain.
What Dharma do I, this old monk, have here to preach to you all? It is simply because you yourselves have come up the mountain and said:
I am practicing the Way. I am one who stands above the Buddha. Let me ask you:
what is the appearance of one who is below the Buddha?
It is not that I, this old monk, have some "one above the Buddha" or "one below the Buddha" here whom I am telling you about. If you do not speak, I cannot know what is in your belly. Or perhaps...
If you ask this old monk, I shall speak to you according to your own capacity; I cannot be made to speak in a confused or arbitrary manner—can you not understand?
As for when I was traveling on pilgrimage, I did not discriminate between monasteries, whether they had offerings or not.
One must simply observe whether his eyes show even a slight resemblance to true capacity and whether he possesses some measure of spiritual vessel;
only then will one allow him to stay for a summer or a winter. If his faculties are base and inferior, he departs after three mornings or two days.
Calculating it, among the sixty-odd great masters I have studied under, there are not even one or two who possess the great eye; as for the rest, how could they truly have it?
This "true knowledge and vision" is merely a means for you all to provide offerings, hoping to receive blessings and rewards.
But what blessings and rewards do you have to give him? You must not come forth from the household life merely to join the crowd and eat your fill. Nevertheless, this is so.
Who can escape this body composed of the four great elements? Even if the mind transcends the realm of the sages, the body remains that of an ordinary person;
furthermore, it is merely a provisional construct sustained by cultivation. Nowadays, people instead bury their human bodies within the inner depths [of conceptualization].

Do not deceive yourselves with mere verbal fluency, for that results in slandering the Buddha and destroying the Dharma. What you see must be seen as it truly is; what you hear must be heard as it truly is.
Only then can it be attained. Even if you speak with words as sharp and decisive as cutting through iron or nails, you must first ensure that in the midst of daily life you do not deceive yourself;
otherwise, even a single mustard seed on a cart has not yet been touched upon. When you arrive, you immediately say, "I am an inconceivable person."
Even if one were to eliminate the coarse and heavy [afflictions] surrounding oneself, one would still remain ignorant of the subtle remnants.
If one is already unaware of the coarse and heavy, how can one speak of the Dharma of liberation? Even the Buddha does not know that which is the most subtle among the subtle;
how then could deluded ordinary beings fathom it? Whatever exists within the world arises from inversion; yet, one desires to attain liberation.

Regarding worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), there is nothing better than self-examination within the mind. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is the Dharma-body of liberation. Reflect upon this minutely: furthermore, who possesses it and who lacks it?
This old monk is neither a drunken commoner nor a hypocritical sage; it is simply that my habitual tendencies have not yet been eliminated.
Above, I accord with the heart-seal of all Buddhas; in the middle, I accord with all humans and devas; and below, I accord with all wriggling and moving sentient beings.
Master, those who don the Dharma robes of the Tathāgata must seek liberation; time does not wait for man, and every moment passes in an instant.
Take care! Take care!
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "The Dharma-realm of True Suchness takes samādhi as its incense and flowers; it pervades the entire universe and is likewise one single family.
Why is there no overnight guest at the Dragon Gate? Why is there such an abundance of frogs in the turbid waters? The Master said:
The Dharma-realm of True Suchness does not take samādhi as its incense or flowers; it pervades the sands of the world without a fixed home.
Is the one questioning before my eyes not Master Zhizhuan? The Master replied, “I am. The Teacher said, “This very thing is like a shrimp at the bottom of a shallow stream.
The Teacher spoke again, “Cast away your former livelihood and recognize the life-sustenance of the original source. The Master was speechless.
[The student] spoke. The Master said: "The Sutras have Sutra masters; the Shastras have Shastra masters; the Vinaya has Vinaya masters.
What should you be discussing throughout the twelve periods of the day? On what basis do you maintain such an appearance?
You must not form groups of three or clusters of five, preying upon robes and plundering food. Everywhere you go, you cannot avoid disturbing the donors' sleep and rest. [What is on your] mind?"
It is difficult to surpass the donor. Even if you were to leap and bound through the void of space, it would still be within the sovereign’s domain.
One must not merely recite a single scroll of scripture at times when observing the fast or upholding the precepts as a way to repay the four debts of gratitude or the three realms of existence.
How could such things ever suffice as a repayment? This is simply a matter for individuals during their own time; one must practice until reaching the stage of a Pratyekabuddha.
Only then can one truly deserve the offerings of devas and humans. Ordinary people of this mundane world are merely those who differ from the secular;

yet, having consumed these offerings, they remain unaware of shame. In vain they pursue speech, claiming themselves right and others wrong. Their words seek to sever the life-force of others, and their very breath acts like that of a venomous serpent.
When speaking of themselves, they claim there is nothing in the three realms superior to them; when disparaging others, they do so with utter contempt.
Like insects and ants. If these ancient Buddhas possessed such signs, one might now wish to imitate them slightly;
yet if from the beginning there were none, then from what cause would they have arisen? To allow such indulgence—how can this be called pure virtue?
If you do not penetrate the source, you will inevitably remain subject to the dripping [of defilements]. To change your skin and replace your bones in the bitter sea of *niraya*—who could bear it?
You must all exert yourselves to the utmost; you must not pass your days in negligence. It is not that you lack the capacity to study Chan and study the Way. But tell me:
is there a Chan that can be investigated, or a Way that can be studied? If you say there is something to be studied—
This is impossible. If you say there is no more learning (*aśaikṣa*), this too is impossible; one cannot simply depart with a vacant mind.
You must return from where you came upon the ground, and you must clearly establish the foundation to exhaust the very root of birth and death.
Even if you are reborn among the various classes of beings, you must never fail to realize your own numinous spirit. The four elements combine to form what is merely you.
This is their cave-dwelling. When you depart from this side, you have already been born on that side; when you depart from that side, you have already assumed another form here.
Do not merely speculate; look and see which of these is your original body. You must investigate this within that very state.
Do not wander aimlessly through the southern and northern regions, for there will never be an end to it. Time passes swiftly; take heed!
Take heed.
Ascending the hall, he said: "This nature is originally pure and replete with myriad virtues. It is only through following the two conditions of defilement and purity that distinctions arise.
Therefore, the sages awaken to it and, by applying it exclusively toward purity, realize the path of enlightenment. Ordinary people, however, are deluded."
It functions solely in defilement, drowning one in the cycle of saṃsāra. Yet its essence is non-dual; thus the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:

"Without duality, there is no division; it is without distinction and without interruption. At that time, a monk asked, "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, I wonder:

does this very nature perish or not? The Master said, "It perishes. The monk pressed further, "If that is so, then it must follow along with them [the destruction]. The Master said: [He perishes. (Note: The original text here ends with "師" [Master], implying the Master's response continues.)

The Master said, "It follows him; it follows him away. The monk remained silent. At that time, more than three hundred monks in the assembly all refused to accept this, saying, "Since the beginning of our tradition, it has only been taught that the nature is indestructible. Why does the Master say, on the contrary, that it is destroyed?
The assembly was each filled with anxiety. Then, one monk came forward and addressed the Master, saying, "Just now, a monk asked the Master—"
The monk continued speaking. The Master replied to him. The monk seemed unwilling to accept the Master’s answer. The Master said, "It is only this one monk who is unwilling;
what if there were others who were also unwilling? The monk said, "There is only this one monk.
The Master said, "Even if all the people in the three thousandfold world-system were to be entirely unwilling toward me, it would still fall short by a small measure."
It was not only this monk. Later, that monk went to the place of Master Touzi. Touzi asked, "Where have you recently departed from, Venerable?
The monk said, "I have come from afar from Daisui in Western Sichuan. Touzi asked, "Is there any venerable elder there?
The monk said, "There is a Zen master residing on Mount Daisui; he currently has more than three hundred followers. Touzi—
The Master said, "What words or phrases do you use to engage people? Try reciting them for this old monk.
The monk said, "Yesterday I asked Dawsui, 'When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, I wonder: does this very thing [the mind] perish or not?
He replied, 'It perishes. The Master asked, "How did Dawsui answer? The monk said, "Dawsui answered, 'It perishes. The Master said, "I asked further: 'If that is so, then it follows him.'"
"He has gone," said Daguī. The monk replied, "He follows him; he follows him as he goes. Zhaozhou asked, "How do you understand Daguī’s words?
The monk said, "I do not accept these words. Zhaozhou said, "You have already made a mistake, Reverend.
When Daguī said, 'He follows him; he follows him as he goes,' how would you respond? The monk said, "To this day, I have not reached a decision. Zhaozhou—
He then called his attendant to prepare incense and spread out his sitting mat. Facing the Great Sui Mountain in Western Sichuan, he performed three prostrations from afar and sighed, saying:
"This is not merely the Abbot of Great Sui; he is an ancient Buddha. This is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
You must go there quickly to repent and seek instruction. I do not possess such a Dharma to speak to you; go at once!"
"Go quickly. Thereupon, the monk returned, only to find that Master Daguī had already passed into *parinirvāṇa*. He returned again to Tōji, but Master Tōji had likewise passed into *parinirvāṇa*.
The Ruler of Shu bestowed upon the Master purple robes and a posthumous title, and dispatched the inner attendant Zhu Yanpu to serve him.
The Master did not accept these honors. The Master further remarked, "This mountain monk has resided here by chance for no long time; I dwell among the crags."
Living by the water, he nurtures the Way and preserves his true nature. Who could have falsely brought such renown as to cause the King to bestow such extraordinary favor?
We thank you for coming from afar; we are troubled that you must return to the King. This old monk can only cover his body with plain cloth; there is no need for famous garments upon him.
Though the King’s grace is profound, how can this decrepit old man endure it? Thereupon, the imperial messenger returned and reported this three times.
He brought it forward, but the Master would not accept it. The Master spoke again, saying: "I have not come here for the sake of fame or profit; I must find someone who is truly worthy.
I cannot pursue you through the green mountains and white clouds to settle matters of right and wrong. In a future age, after casting off this physical body,"
They do not eat much grass either. When the Golden-Maned Lion asks them something, they simply bray like donkeys or neigh like horses.
You worthy ones, when I was traveling as a pilgrim to various places, there were often assemblies of a thousand, or at least seven hundred or five hundred people.
Some stayed among them through winter and summer, yet they did not realize their time was passing in vain; they were merely following the assembly at Mount Mui.
He worked in the kitchen for seven years and served as a wood-gatherer in Dongshan’s assembly for three years. He would always take on the most difficult tasks first;
he simply sought to realize his own nature—what concern was that of others?

He knew that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas had undergone diligent austerities for countless eons, relinquishing their status as Wheel-Turning Kings and even sacrificing what they held dear: their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains.
Material things—kingdoms, cities, wives, and children—are beyond counting. This is why he first earned the name "Buddha. What did those various *ācāryas* ever actually renounce?
What did they ever actually achieve through their arduous efforts? Yet they would simply say, "I understand the supramundane Dharma.
When they have not even understood the mundane Dharma, and some slight state of realization manifests before them, they immediately knit their brows and glare in anger.
[The Master] said: "This eye cannot tolerate it. What do you mean by 'teaching the Dharma of liberation'?

Sitting upon the long continuous bed, not moving a single finger, and having consumed the offerings of the faithful, one closes one's eyes and mouth and says: "I have practiced and cultivated the Way; such is the fruit I have attained."
It would merely be a waste; it would only be deceiving yourself. For instance, when Master Baizhang established the monastic hall, he sought only those who could "accomplish the task.
Dharma brothers, what kind of task can you accomplish? Among them, there are those who do not even move a hand or body.
"One can spend ten thousand taels of gold in a single day. If one were truly able to 'spend' [the Dharma] in such a way, how could one have such a limited understanding?
Is it not so that [the Buddha] did not come from his mother’s womb? To merely understand worldly dharmas is itself called the supramundane dharma.
If you do not even understand worldly dharmas, how much less so the Buddha-dharma? It is just like the entirety of the Great Canon."
"This is what was proclaimed from the golden mouth; it is the secret of the Tathāgata. If you recite it from your own mouth, it all becomes the speech of Māra—how could it ever be realized?
Why is it not realized? If it were realized, Bodhidharma would not have come from the West.
Now, when Bodhidharma had not yet come to this land, was there still no Buddha-dharma? Furthermore, how can you say there was none? It is, for example, like a person..."
There is a treasure that has fallen into the mud. Though one may toil and suffer for many kalpas seeking it, it cannot be found.
Suppose there is a person who knows well the location of the treasure; they simply extract this treasure from the mud and show it to the one who lost it.

As soon as the one who lost the treasure sees it, they recognize it as their own original possession, realizing there is no gain or loss at all. The coming of Dharmatrāta from the West was likewise so.
It is so. It is not that only this old monk is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); all sentient beings throughout the world are spiritual friends.
It is simply that their awakening-perception (*jue*) has not yet been clarified. One cannot say they do not exist.

If one were to say they do exist, would you people be willing to prostrate to these crawling creatures as Buddhas? It is like a bright pearl fallen into the mud; it has not yet met [with a discoverer].
How could there ever be an end to this? To have such sentient beings is like being insentient; they are no different from dull, inanimate objects.
Since you are now beneath the three robes, you must personally draw near to those of true knowledge. It was only after cultivation over many lifetimes that you first attained this state;
you must not, on the contrary, fall back into the cycle of the six realms of existence. If one has attained true mastery, what more is there to discuss?

The cauldrons of boiling water, the furnace coals, the mountains of blades, and the trees of swords—within these realms of the four modes of birth and the six paths of existence, one would eat them as if they were fine delicacies.

If you have not yet attained such [liberation], you will truly undergo this retribution. Once you lose this human body, even if you seek one like it for ten thousand lifetimes, not one in ten thousand will be found.
Do not claim what you have not attained as attained; do not claim what you have not realized as realized; do not claim what you have not heard as heard. Do not deceive yourself and delude yourself.
One loses the precious moments of time and vainly prolongs the days and months; shifting and turning about, one merely bears the heavy burden of ignorance.
It would be better to remain a layperson, following the natural flow of circumstances to pass the days, so as to remain free from karmic debt. Now, having become a śramaṇa, you have a task every day.
What is this task? That which you tread upon is the ground of kings; that which you wear is the clothing of donors; that which you eat is...

This is food provided by donors and believers. Flesh and bone are the very substance of one's parents. If you do not understand this, how will you repay them? Therefore, it is said that there is karma.
As for me, an old monk, I am certainly no one who has reached final realization. When I cast off this retribution-body, I shall proceed according to my karma;
who can say for certain what will happen? Only a Buddha and a Buddha can know this. At that time, a monk asked: "Without depending on..."
"How can one know [the meaning] through words and phrases? The Master said, "If you do not even know them when they are merely provisional words and phrases," and the monk was speechless. He bowed.
One day, as the Master ascended the hall and the assembly had gathered, he feigned the symptoms of a wind ailment and addressed the crowd, saying, "Is there anyone who can cure this old monk's mouth?
The monks vied with one another to bring medicine, and when the laypeople heard of it, many also brought medicine.
The Master would not accept either. After seven days had passed, the Master himself pinched his own mouth to straighten it and said, "For all this time, these two pieces of skin have been beaten;

Sitting upright and composed, he passed away.

This is the *Biographical Account of Zen Master Shénzhào, Founder of Dàsuí*.

The Master’s name was Fazhen. His appearance was ancient and majestic; his eyebrows hung down, covering his eyelashes. He had often heard the elder masters say that he was an incarnation of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
He was born into the Wang family in Yanting County, Zizhou, Jiannan. His clan was originally of noble lineage.
Having attained awakening at an early age, he resolved to seek out a teacher at Huìyì Temple—now known as Zhúlín Monastery within Hùshèng Temple.
It was so. After the Master had received full ordination, he traveled south. He first visited Yaoshan, Daowu, Yunyan, and Xiantong;
subsequently, he went to the assembly of the Venerable Damei outside the Ling Range. For several years there, his food did not suffice to satisfy him, yet he did not seek warmth when lying down.
He refined his practice through austere asceticism, and his conduct was beyond the common. Upon first seeing him, Dayi held him in high esteem.
One day, Dayi asked, "Since you have been among my disciples, you have never asked a single turning word. The Master said, "Where would you have me begin?
Dayi said, "Why not ask, 'What is the Buddha? The Master then made a gesture with his hand.

Baizhang covered Muzhou’s mouth. Muzhou sighed and said, "My son has truly grasped the marrow. From that time on, his fame spread beyond the mountain ranges and his reputation resounded throughout the world.
Thereafter, he returned to Western Shu and took up residence at Longhuai Temple on Mount Shan Kou in Tianpeng.
For three years, he brewed tea by the roadside and bestowed it upon all who came. One day, while wandering toward the rear mountains, he saw an ancient monastery named Daisui Mountain.

The peaks stand tall and magnificent; the mountain stream flows clear and cool. In the midst stands a tree, over forty feet in circumference, its roots coiled around the kalpa-stone and its form soaring toward the clouds.
It opens a single door to the south; the interior is spacious and unobstructed—a natural hermitage, fashioned without the aid of axe or hammer.
The Master then took up residence there; it was comparable to Kāśyapa’s Three Peaks and not far from Vimalakīrti’s chamber.
People of the time all called it the Wooden Meditation Hermitage. The Master lived there for over ten years, his shadow never leaving the mountains and his traces never appearing among the laity.
His moral integrity became increasingly prominent, and his reputation spread far and wide. Those who knew him came from all quarters, not hesitating to travel thousands of li.

They crowded together like the teeth of a comb within the space of a fathom, attending him in the morning and seeking instruction in the evening; they went forth with empty hands but returned with fulfillment. At that time, the Prince of Shu held the Master’s name in high esteem, yet he declined three successive summons.
The King admired the Master’s solitary integrity but had no means to meet him in person.

Consequently, on the fifteenth day of the tenth month of the first year of the Guangtian era, he dispatched an inner attendant to present the Master with purple robes, a title of honor, and a temple plaque. The Master would not accept them. Although they were delivered three times, the Master resolutely declined them.
The King’s admiration for the Master’s virtue grew even deeper, and he again dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree stating: "It is my heart's desire..."
"I pray that this time, Master Hui will likewise refuse as before; it would then be Your Excellency’s fault, and Hui will surely execute you.

The celestial messenger, bearing the imperial decree, went once more to the Master’s dwelling. The Master again refused to accept it. The messenger, with earnest devotion, prostrated himself and said:
"Master, if you do not accept the imperial command this time, I shall surely be executed. I pray that you, out of compassion, will spare me from this calamity.
The Master, having no other choice, accepted it. Once the Master had accepted, the messenger informed him again, requesting a memorial to express gratitude for the imperial favor.
The Master said, "Since I have been living in the mountains, I have had neither paper nor ink. You should convey my words to the Great King orally."
"You must preserve this well. Whether governing a household or a state, affairs must not be partial or biased. Receive these transmitted words and do not let them be forgotten.
As for when you wish to seek an audience, follow the Master’s instructions and return to the palace to report them to the King.

The King was deeply pleased and again dispatched a celestial messenger to the mountains to attend upon the Master. The Master would not accept this either, saying further, "I, an old monk, shall not act as such."
"What is the use of fame and profit? You must find someone to do it; why are you so distressed? The Master then temporarily detained him.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Qiandé era (the Jīmó year), before the midday meal, the Master took his leave of the assembly, sat upright, and passed away.
His secular age was eighty-six, and his monastic seniority was sixty-six. When the King heard of this, he mourned the Master with such deep longing that his heart could not endure the grief.
An imperial decree was issued: "Let Wang Zongshou, Director of the Palace Secretariat, be dispatched with incense, candles, and all necessary ritual implements to the mountain to perform sacrifices.
His remains shall be enshrined in the stupa. His divine manifestations were numerous and cannot be fully recounted.

It is simply because all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to the law of arising and ceasing; thus, one returns to true quiescence and forever severs the cycle of sinking and drifting.
I, the disciple Zongshou, though fortunately of weak and mediocre capacity, have long admired the expanse of your virtue and am deeply devoted to the benefit of transcending the mundane world.
I was about to exalt his ability to transcend defilement; how could I have anticipated that the Dharma-boat would so suddenly reach the other shore?

Now that the date for the relocation of his spirit and the enshrinement of his remains has been determined, I regret my lack of skill in the monastic arts to compose a final testament for the rest of my life. I venture to present this offering of pondweed and algae.

Master Touzi’s name was Datong; he was a native of Shuzhou and belonged to the Liu clan. He received his formal training at Baotang Monastery in Luoyang and attained the Dharma from Master Cuiwei Wuxue.
He lived to the age of ninety-six and was the fourth generation in the lineage of Master Shitou.
He entered nirvana during the Qiánhuà era of the Wǔdài Liáng dynasty.

whether going against or with the current, one does not leave the water. This being so, how should you act? Brothers, do not allow yourselves to suffer such humiliation.
"Do not sink and drown yourself. Once you have arrived here, there is nothing to be done; it will simply result in a field of deluded thoughts. What business is there? Come forth!
At that time, a student asked, "How can one study so as to attain the non-deluded true mechanism?
The Master said, "In what kalpa have you ever been deluded? The student asked, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master to point it out directly. The Master said, "Blind your eyes."

[The Master said: "Can you do it? [The student] asked: "When one is submerged in the wheel of birth and death, how can one escape? The Master said: "How much time have you spent within it? [The student] asked:
"'Exhausting the command yet still holding the mainstay'—this is still the howling of a jackal. What is the lion’s roar? The Master then struck him on the mouth with his palm. [The student] asked:
"When the six states are not at peace, how does one restore order? The Master said: "I have never sat in the ancient hall. Where [else would I look]?"
[The student] was unsettled. The student asked, "How should I understand this? The Master said, "It is you who do not understand. The student asked, "What is the Great Perfect Mirror?
The Master said, "It has never reflected anything. The student asked, "How does it discern? The Master said, "Since it has never reflected anything, what would there be to discern?"
Question: "Regarding one's own portion [of realization], how should one speak? The Master said: "If you are not a traveler on the road, what words would you utter?
The student said: "Is it still spoken in this way? The Master said: "It is you who speak in this way. Question: "This seat is high and vast; I cannot ascend it.
I wonder, what kind of person can ascend it? The Master said: "How long has it been since you contracted this illness?"
At that time, Xue said, "I request the Master's medicine. The Master said, "This dull-witted fellow. A monk asked, "When one’s own matter is not yet clear, how can it be made clear?
The Master said, "That is ever-unconcealed; when the mirror reflects the finger, the face reveals itself.

A monk asked, "Among the sages of the past, were there any who did not rely upon a teacher? The Master said, "By whom did you, O *śrāmaṇera*, [receive your training]? The Master continued, "Brothers, since the emergence of the various sages..."

This is because people generally misunderstand. They say that the Buddhas expounded the Dharma and the Patriarchs sang of the profound mystery only because they were dim-witted by nature from birth, which led them into delusion.
Therefore, the teachings could not reach them, and the Patriarchs did not come from the West. But as for you, O benevolent ones—what is it in your own portion?
Each has such a matter; do not be disheartened. Do not merely step forward to seek it. If you seek it...
It is immediately lost. What was close becomes distant. Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there has never been a single pinch of earth that could cover it.
Brothers, each of you must exert yourselves. Return to the hall. Take care.
The Master ascended the hall before the Buddha Hall as the great assembly gathered like clouds.

The Master took his seat, surveyed the assembly, and then stood up again; after a short while, he returned to the Dharma Hall. After the monk had followed the Master to the rear of the Dharma Hall, the Master asked him:

"The opportunity has passed and cannot be discerned; standing on opposite banks, it is difficult to see clearly. How do you understand this, worthy one? The monk was speechless. The Master then asked: "What is [the meaning]?"

"The ultimate truth does not rely on verbal expression. The Master said, "When will you ever understand this? It would take as long as a donkey's years! A questioner asked, "I do not ask about strength or weakness;
what is the Way of everyday ordinariness? The Master said, "Why have you reached such a state?

The student said, "Have I attained that ordinariness yet? The Master said, "Do not let the bowl ring out its sound. A questioner asked, "Regarding the matters of the Dharma-lineage, I beg the Master to provide an instruction."
[The Master] says, "Tear it apart! The Master asks, "What is this? He then calls [the student] to come forward. This is "tearing apart" (*tisī*).
You must not call this a matter of the "Dharma-vehicle" (*zongcheng*). The student asks, "I do not yet know: what is a matter of the Dharma-vehicle?

The Master then strikes him with a staff. Question: "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master says, "Look beneath the brush of the stone man. Question: "What is 'making'? The Master says, "... (text fragment)
[The Master] said, "Disciple, why are you traveling on foot? The student said, "If it is so, then I have no doubts.
The Master said, "Where did you find a master [to teach you]? Question: "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "From where have you gathered it?
Question: "What is the final phrase? The Master said, "Why do you weary yourself? Question: "When departing..."
At this juncture, he requested a word from the Master. The Master said, "I shall by no means fail you. The student asked, "A thousand-year-old pine tree still has drooping branches;
though this student wears the robe of the assembly, he does not yet understand the path that transcends the mundane. I beg the Master for a skillful means.

The Master said, "Though the Nine Heavens differ from this world, in the end they remain profoundly beyond comparison. The student asked, "What is it like when one comes forth with such majestic dignity? The Master— [replied: "... (The text ends here).
[The Master] said, "Majestic and imposing, yet one can do nothing about it. A questioner asked, "When one’s own matter is not yet clear, how is this verified?
The Master said, "Heaven and earth do not conceal it; it is people themselves who are deluded. A questioner asked, "What is the place where the student stands firm?

The Master said, "It is not obtained from the various sages. [The questioner] said, "If one proceeds in this very way, what then? The Master said, "That is still merely the point where people of the present age advance. The student said, "..."
"How is it when one does not fall into the direction of phenomena? The Master said, "Is there still any turning back?
"Venerable masters, in general, when traveling on pilgrimage, you must recognize and discern the essential style of our school. Do not merely seek after words and chase after phrases;
there will be no end to it. As Master Xuefeng said: 'The Buddhas of the three periods cannot chant it; the twelve divisions of the teachings cannot contain it. Therefore, Master Gushan said:"
There was once a person who came along in this manner; he had never before been informed of this news.
When I spoke to him in this way, he took a lump of yellow clay and stuffed it into my mouth. Is it right to resent him? Fearing that people might recklessly stuff others' mouths, I therefore say:
"Gushan has a phrase for not crossing the stone gate. How would you speak of it? At this point, one must truly be such a person.
"O people, do not speak in confusion. At that time, a student asked, "What is the matter of not stepping across? The Master struck him over the mouth with his whisk.
The Master then asked, "Do you understand? The student said, "I do not understand. The Master then exclaimed, "This is not the handiwork of such a person!
The Master continued, "If your own matter has not yet been revealed, even if you can discern it from others, it will remain copied in scrolls or recorded in books."
"Writing it down—what is the use? It is better to clearly realize one's own matter. To clarify the Way is 'virtue' (de); to practice it without interruption is 'conduct' (xing).
When virtue and conduct are both complete, one is called a 'sage' (dian) in this age. Furthermore, as for another person—how is he?
You monks, do not fail to distinguish between mud and water, nor discern the clear from the turbid. In this age of the Dharma’s decline, the world is in a state of frantic turmoil. Elder brothers..."
That you, my younger brother, may share this forest and spring with me, eating and chewing together with your fellow practitioners—this is indeed something for which one must feel great joy.
You must strive earnestly day and night; do not let your precious time pass in vain. Each of you, return home. Take care.
The Master ascended the hall before the triple gate and asked a monk, "Suppose there is a person who comes from the edge of a pond and immediately turns back;
what do you make of that? The student said, "The Master must also grant him permission. The Master struck him across the back with his staff.
"How do you do it? The student had no reply. The Master said, "To say 'I am unqualified and respectfully withdraw' is also the talk of a hollow man.
A monk asked, "What is the first phrase that does not rely on words and speech? The Master said, "I give you thirty blows.
A monk asked, "Without rising from one's seat, what is the lightning-fast pivot? The Master said, "Are you drunk? A monk asked, "Whatever words or phrases there are, they all fall into..."
[The Master] held up his finger and asked, "What is the moon? The Master said, "Do you know shame yet? A monk asked, "By what eye do you digest the offerings of devas and humans?
The Master said, "Blind fellow! A monk asked, "Before reaching the original source, how does one practice?
The Master said, "How far apart are they? The monk said, "But how can I resolve my doubts, Master? The Master said, "Whose fault is it? A monk asked, "I am still merely on the road."
"Please, Master, give me instruction. The Master said, "How long have you been on the road? He replied, "Thank you for your instruction, Preceptor. The Master said, "Do not defile others.
He asked, "Regarding the place of bitterness and astringency, please tell me. The Master said, "Take it up well.
He asked, "How should one tread throughout the twelve periods of the day so as not to fail oneself? The Master said, "One must simply not fail."
[The Master speaks of] the Self. A question was asked: "When the source is clear and the waves are stilled, why does the true form not manifest?
The Master said: "Where could it be gathered up? [The monk] said: "Ultimately, what is it like? The Master said: "It is not ultimate;

I will not communicate with you, O *śrāmaṇera*. [The monk] said: "Is there no skillful means (*upāya*)? The Master said: "Whose domain is skillful means? A question was asked: "I have heard the Master say that [you] do not permit..."
The student asked, "If one is not permitted to select words when examining a saying, how can one practice so as not to violate what the Master has entrusted to me?

The Master said, "Do you feel shame within yourself? A question was asked: "Beyond the peaks of the nine heavens is the moon; within the room is a single wheel of a lamp. What is this single wheel of a lamp?
The Master said, "The banks and valleys are windless; it is in vain to stare with wide-open eyes. A question was asked: "Regarding names, phrases, and wondrous sentences... [The text ends here.]

[The student] said: "That which is expressed by the net does not involve the three categories (*triskandha*). I beg the Master to speak directly. The Master said: "It has never been transmitted [even as far as] behind the elbow. [The student] asked:

"How can one reach the ultimate realization of birth and death throughout the twelve periods of the day? The Master said: "Bring me birth and death. The student said: "If it is so, then there is no place of ultimate realization.
The Master said: "It is like your way of speaking. [The student] asked: "In practicing Zen and studying the Way, one must surely be..."

A student came in this manner and requested, “Please, Master, speak directly. The Master said, “Why do you act so blindly distracted? The student said, “I thank the Monk for his instruction. The Master said, “I grant you twenty blows.
A student asked, “Everyone says they come to seek benefit; I wonder how the Master provides such aid? The Master said, “People of these times find it difficult to accept the truth.
A student asked, “By what standard may one act so as not to turn away from the Way? The Master said, “Those who rely on their own noses find it hard to agree.”

In the past, the Master said, "One cannot avoid departing. The student said, "I thank the Master for this instruction. The Master said, "Then you shall receive a blow of the staff. A question was asked:
"Of the thousand hands and thousand eyes, which one is the true eye? The Master said, "What need is there for the true eye? Another question was asked.
"What is the present function? The Master said, "What is the present function right now? The student said, "I do not understand. I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master said, "The person of the bare ground does not tread upon it. A question was asked: "When neither of the two extremes is established and the middle way does not exist, what is this?
The Master said, "Where is it right now? The student said, "Is there not a way for the Master to act on behalf of others? The Master said, "..."

[The Master] asked, "For whom am I teaching? The student said, "Where is there any need for such courtesy? The Master then gave him his staff. [The student] asked, "An ancient said, 'When meeting, one does not lift it up;
by raising the intention, one knows it exists. What is meant by 'knowing it by raising the intention'? The Master said, "Who is it that raises [the intention]?
[The student] asked, "What is the most intimate and most essential point for a student? The Master said, "Why do you engage in deluded thoughts?"
The student said, "Is it still appropriate? The Master said, "Put it away! What kind of talk is this? A question was asked: "What is the wooden horse and stone man riding?
It does not turn its back on the Seal of the Empty King. The Master said, "Where the mud ox walks, the blind merely exert themselves in vain.
A question was asked: "What is moving one's countenance to reveal the ancient road? The Master said, "I do not wish to engage in deliberation. A question was asked: "What is..."
"What is this matter of the separate transmission? The Master said, "You cannot catch a toad's mouth.
The Master said, "Each of you monks has such a thing for yourselves; do not feel aggrieved. It has never been lacking, nor has there ever been a single inch of soil that can cover it.
Why, then, do you fail to understand? You go further forward, treading upon the path again and again."
"Earth. You do not understand what is within the room. Furthermore, as for the matter within the room, how is it? You merely wish for someone else to speak for you;
this is your own affair. Why then do you not understand it yourself? You only manage to understand the affairs within the houses of others.

This is nothing but consuming the spittle of the old masters from your neighbors' homes, forming interpretations within the realm of consciousness. What connection does that have to the Way? To travel on foot..."
Since one does not encounter such a person, it is said: "To be constrained by the initial recording of a single word, one becomes a wild fox spirit for kalpas.
If you are truly sharp and perceptive, you need not rely excessively on the teacher. [The Master] stood for a long time. Each of you must exert yourselves. Take care.
On one occasion, the Master ascended the hall and said: "At all times, when the bells and drums are struck like this, what are you seeking by coming up here?
Is there any matter of grievance or injustice? Have you not seen the ancients say, 'This is entirely a band of fellows who have eaten nothing but dregs of wine'?
[The ancients] would have taken up their staffs and driven them all down at once. Guishan now, out of sheer compassionate concern, says: 'If anyone has doubts, come forward and ask.'"
At that time, there was a student who asked, "I have recently entered the monastic community but have not yet attained realization. I beg the Master’s compassion to provide me with instruction.
The Master said, "I do not dare to deceive you. The student asked, "What is this matter of not deceiving? The Master struck him with a staff. [The student] asked again.
"What is the direct statement? The Master said, "Most direct. The student asked, "What is that which does not rely on verbal expression?
The Master said, "Right now, how much is there? A question was asked: "I have heard the ancients say: 'Within the body with form is the body without form.'"
"How is it that there is a formless body within a body with form? The Master said, "Right now, what kind of body is this?
The student asked, "How is it that there is a path of non-arising upon the road of ignorance? The Master said, "Right now, what kind of road is this?
A student asked, "I am destitute; I beg the Master for deliverance. The Master said, "What trouble is there? The student said, "How can one endure such destitution?"
The Master said, "One suffers for kalpas. A questioner asked, "I have heard the ancients say that it cannot be obtained through clever explanations, but is transmitted only through the mind.
What is this transmission of the mind? The Master said, "What do you say? The student said, "I do not understand. The Master then gave a shout and sent him out.
Another asked, "How is it when one turns upon meeting the opportunity? The Master said, "How would you turn? As soon as the student stepped forward, the Master gave a shout.

[The Master] went out. A question was asked: "The Great Matter has not yet been accomplished; what serves as the verification during this time? The Master said: "During this time, one must not take a step.
The student asked: "How can one attain correspondence? The Master said: "Non-correspondence. The student asked: "Why is there non-correspondence?
The Master said: "It is not for you. A question was asked: "At the point of urgency, I beg for a word from the Master. The Master said: "Devadatta did not grant his consent. A question was asked.
The Master said, "It is as the ancients have said: 'The great body is vast and boundless; the small mind does not admit even a speck of dust.
What is meant by 'the great body is vast and boundless'? The Master said, "Large and small. The student asked, "What is meant by 'the small mind does not admit even a speck of dust'?
The Master said, "Why have you come to such a state? A questioner asked, "I have heard the ancients say: 'All sentient beings use it daily, yet they do not realize it.'"

[The student] said, “I understand. What is the matter of daily life? The Master said, “Whose words are these? [The student] asked, “When two dragons struggle for a pearl, who is the one that obtains it?
The Master said, “Where is the pearl? [The student] asked, “I have heard the ancients say, ‘One flower opens into five petals;
the fruiting occurs naturally. What is this fruiting that occurs naturally? The Master said, “Right now.”
"What is it? [The student] asked: "Regarding the ancestral vehicle (*zongcheng*), I request the Master to point directly. The Master then rebuked him. [The student] asked:
"Before the various sages had arisen, what served as the eye? The Master said: "Where is your eye, *ācārya*? [The student] asked: "The Master is compassionate; how may one realize this?
The Master struck him with a staff. [The student] asked: "As for when a monk asked Dongshan, 'Among the three bodies (*trikāya*), which one...'"
"The body does not fall into any categories. Dongshan said, "I have always been earnest about this. [The Master asked:
"As for Dongshan saying, 'I have always been earnest about this,' is this falling [into categories] or not falling? The Master said, "You are again playing with your life here!"
Question: "Throughout the day, one is in motion or at rest; why is it that one does not clarify oneself? The Master said:

"Precisely because one is throughout the day in motion or at rest, one does not clarify. The student asked: "What is it like when one is neither moving nor resting? The Master said: "What is this? Question:
"When Master Shanran saw a monk prostrate, he would immediately strike him with a staff. What was his intention? The Master said: "Why did [the monk] not..."
[The Master] went on a pilgrimage. A monk asked: "Nanquan struck his knee with his hand and said, 'Here it is easy.
Then he said, 'Here it is difficult. Another monk asked, 'As for that movement of the hand, is that not the proclamation of the Dharma-treasury (zongcheng)?
The Master then struck his knee with his hand and said, "Why would this not be the proclamation of the Dharma-treasury? The student asked, "As for that movement of the hand, what was its meaning?"

[The monk] said, “It has arisen. The Master said, “Look for yourself. [The monk] asked, “What is the first phrase? The Master then took up his staff and made the gesture of thrusting it across [the monk’s] mouth.
[The monk] asked, “When it is deep without bottom and shallow without source, what then? The Master said, “How long has it been since you contracted this illness?
The Master said, “Lately, monks only love to cite the sutras and treatises, speaking of the Perfect and the Sudden.”
Therefore it is said: "The Sūtras have masters of the Sūtras; the Śāstras have masters of the Śāstras; the Vinaya has masters of the Vinaya.
There are cases and titles; there are sections and volumes. By day they are kept bright by windows, and by night they rely on lamps and candles.

Since there are people who transmit and uphold them, what does this have to do with you, monks? Tell me, for whose sake was the *Yuan* (Perfect) established? For whose sake was the *Dun* (Sudden) set forth? Because—

To speak of the partial as the complete allows it to become the Perfect and Sudden; yet it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected from the beginning, not because of this partial speaking. This is the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
As for how it functions within the realm of the patch-robed monk—each has their own distinct allotment. Do not destroy the Hu lineage. Each return to your hall.
Take heed. The Master asked a question to test the monks:
"The ancients said, 'Biting the tip of the arrow, even in a donkey’s year one would not understand it. What did the ancients mean by this? The Master said, "The ancients were speaking of the Way."
There is harm and there is benefit. The Master asked a monk from Silla, "What are you doing coming up this mountain? The monk replied, "I am here to pay my respects to the Master.
The Master said, "The world is entirely unmarked; where do you intend to pay your respects? The monk replied, "I pay my respects where it is unmarked.
The Master said, "Out of consideration for your being a man from Silla, I let you off with thirty blows of the staff. He asked, "A junior monk of Jingshan says, 'Jingshan...'"
The verse says: "Turning one's head to return home, one cannot find the way back. The Master said, "Returning—this is what people do.
Is this not so? He replied, "It is. The Master said, "He did not obtain your 'return. Is this not so? He replied, "It is. The Master called out, "Venerable Yan! He replied, "Yes, Master!
The Master said, "Is that returning, or is it not returning? There was a monk who compiled the *True Record of Xuefeng*.
[The Master] said: "Every time the Master ascended the hall, after a long silence, he would look out at the assembly and then say, 'What is this?

The monk asked, "Did Xuefeng have only these words, or was there something else besides? The Master said, "There was something else. The monk asked, "What was it? The Master said, "It was the case of Yuan."

He went down the mountain. [The monk] asked: "As soon as this student performs the three prostrations, I immediately know there are twenty blows of the iron staff. I do not yet know whether the ancestral vehicle from above is authentic and unerring regarding my original inquiry. I beg the Master for a skillful means; I pray you will grant me a definitive judgment. The Master then gave him a blow with the staff. The monk returned to the hall and refused to accept it. you must investigate until you reach the bottom and look through until you see clearly. Only when not even a thousand sages can provide proof will the true man of great capacity be revealed.
