He then cited an ancient saying: "Naked and bare, bright and clear; in the four directions there is no obstruction; above and below, there is nothing to grasp."
The Master said: "I traveled to Mount Luofu in the morning and returned to Mount Tante in the evening—let us not speak of that for now.
How do you express the phrase beneath the heels? He raised an example: Layman Pang asked Mazu, "The person who is originally present is not obscured; I ask the Master to cast his eyes wide open."
The Patriarch looked directly up. The Layman said, "This is a single-stringed lute; only you, Master, can play it exquisitely. The Patriarch looked directly down. The Layman bowed.
The Patriarch then returned to his quarters. The Layman followed after him, saying, "Today, playing for cleverness has resulted in clumsiness. The Master said:
Now tell me: did the guest bring about his own clumsiness through cleverness? Or did the host bring about his own clumsiness through cleverness? Is there anyone who can discern this?
If you can discern it, thirty blows of the staff—each blow is beyond measure. If you cannot discern it, next year there will be new branches;
the spring wind, causing such vexation, will never cease. It is said in the Teachings: "Where there is contention, there is birth."

"Death. When there is no contention, that is nirvana. The Master said: "Even if you achieve a state where the wind blows and the grass bends, where echoes follow sounds and harmonize, and you seek nothing from the sages nor value your own spiritual nature, such that not even a speck of dust remains—this is still a dharma of contention.
So, what is the dharma of non-contention? He cited: "An ancient said, 'The Buddhas of the three periods do not know it exists. The Master said: "Like a worm..."
"Eating wood. The wildcat and the white ox, however, know it exists. The Master said, "Adding frost to snow. He cited the case: Deshan asked Longtan, "I have long heard of Longtan.
Now that I have arrived, the pond is not seen and the dragon does not appear. Longtan said, "You have personally arrived at Longtan.
Deshan then desisted. The Master said, "Do you recognize Old Longtan? As the monk hesitated, the Master [struck him].
[The Master] struck him across the mouth with his whisk. A monk entered the room. [The Master] raised the case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "The myriad dharmas return to the One;
where does the One return? The Master immediately shouted. The monk was left bewildered. The Master then asked, "What did Zhaozhou say?
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk. [The Master] raised another case: A monk asked Zen Master Zhimen Zu, "What is the Buddha? Zhimen said, "Tread upon it."
"Tearing up his straw sandals, he walks barefoot. "What is the matter that lies beyond the Buddha? The Gatekeeper said, "On the tip of my staff, I carry the sun and moon.

The Master then asked a monk, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master then showed him this verse: "Sandals worn through, walking barefoot; Let the patch-robed monk cease his grand talk.
Sun and moon carried on the staff's tip— Facing south, one looks at the Northern Dipper. The monk then... [proceeded].
[The monk] bows and departs. The Master says, "Come! Come! The monk then turns his head. The Master says, "Do not let him bump into the pillar. He cites [the following]:
The verse by Master Guishan Lingyou for the Abbot’s Quarters states: "The Abbot’s quarters of Guishan are steep and precipitous, difficult to ascend;
if a person should tread upon them, their spirit is like that of General Fan. The Master said: "A master of the school possesses this naturally.
A monk asked: "How about you, Master? The Master gave him a verse: "The Abbot’s quarters of Cuoyan have never had any obstructions; as soon as a patch-robed monk enters, [he is met with...]"
Upon seeing the Master, the monk bowed and rose. The Master asked, "Do you see this old fellow of Cuoyan?
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him across the mouth with his whisk. The Master then cited a case: A monk asked Xianglin, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe?
Xianglin replied, "In the twelfth month, fire burns the mountains. The Master then asked the monk, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said:
"Why do you deceive this old monk? The monk remained silent for a long while and then said, "I, too, have my own way of understanding.
The Master said, "Xianglin shall also receive a blow of the staff."

Small Assembly Sermon. The Master raised an example: In the past, Baizhang, at the end of the year, addressed the assembly, saying, "You young monks, you certainly do not know the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras.
You have entered the community to practice Chan, yet you do not understand Chan either. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how will you settle the account?
The Master said: "Truly, O Zen practitioners, the time since the Sage has passed; human hearts have grown thin and indifferent."
Looking at the monastic communities (conglin) of today, they are even more unacceptable.

Wherever they may be, there may be three hundred or five hundred disciples gathered together in great numbers, yet they consider their prosperity to consist merely in abundant food and comfortable quarters.
Among them, not a single person is diligently devoted to the Way; even if there were ten or five such individuals, they would merely be running back and forth, half...
Half blue, half yellow. When they meet, they all claim, "I have attained it. Each one considers themselves to be grasping the jewel of the divine serpent;
who would be willing to admit their error? Yet when pressed and prodded to the limit, there is not even one in ten thousand who succeeds. How bitter! How bitter!
It is said that the forest of Prajñā withers year by year, while the wild weeds of ignorance grow longer each passing season.

Among these, the younger generation of the present day, as soon as they enter the monastic community, immediately sit upright with hands folded in a gesture of submission, accepting the offerings of others.

Everywhere they go, they do not select a single stalk of vegetables nor carry a single bundle of firewood; their ten fingers never touch water, and they have no concern for any of the hundred affairs of the monastery.
Although one may find momentary satisfaction for a single day, how can one avoid the burden of the three miserable realms upon the body? Have you not seen what is taught in the scriptures:

"It would be better to have red-hot iron wrapped around one's body than to accept the robes of a person of faith; it would be better to have molten copper poured into one's mouth than to accept the food of a person of faith"?
Elder, if you were to depart, even if you were to transform the great earth into gold and churn the long rivers into ghee—
Offering curd to the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) is not even considered an extraordinary act.

If that were not enough, then for even a drop of water or a thread of silk, one must bear fur and horns, pulling the plow and dragging the cart to repay them before it is finished. Have you not seen the Patriarch say:

"If one enters the Way but does not penetrate its principle, one must return to the body [of an animal] to repay the faithful offerings"? This is a matter of certainty; it will never be in vain. All of you—
Venerable Elder, time is precious; it does not wait for man. Do not wait until the day your eyes fall to the ground.

Then the wasteland will have lacked even the labor of a single basket of earth, and the Iron Ring Mountains will close with the agony of a hundred punishments. Do not say you were not told. Take care.
Verses on My Original Dwelling (Two Poems) I hang my staff upon the western peaks;
In the profound stillness, I struggle to find the way. A thousand crags shed their accumulated snow; Ten thousand trees naturally turn toward spring.
In the warm valleys, the sound of springs carries far; in the secluded forests, the birdsong is fresh. I recall with regret the single sandal left behind and laugh deeply at the people of Luoyang.

Hanging my staff upon the western peaks, who else can join me in shaking forth this tradition? With the curtain drawn, the sun shines over a thousand ridges; sitting upon a rock, I lean on my single bamboo cane.
On the Snowy Peaks, there is no written word; from Hengyang, no letter can pass. Looking back beyond the pure scenery, clouds and birds pass to and fro in endless succession.
Three seals are but one seal—impressed upon the mud, known alike by the wise and the foolish. The nostrils are torn and turned; a golden mallet strikes the crown of the head.
Sealing water with a single seal is merely flapping one's lips; one has not yet crossed the shifting sands, and vast waves rise in competition.
Sealing space with a single seal is the bright moon and clear wind, the *śakrāloka* eye, and the bell tolled after the midday meal.

Reclining in Leisure on a Spring Day (Four Poems) In the season of spring beneath the forest trees, All things flourish in a state of vibrant harmony. Beholding the power of this mild warmth, Who would not call it the universal ford?
In the springtime beneath the forest trees, the realm of this secluded dwelling is doubly pure. Morning clouds divide the hues of the peaks; flowing waters carry the song of the orioles.
In the springtime beneath the forest trees, the sun lingers as the days grow warmer. Unaware that there are those who sing of the Way, the springs and rocks find their own natural ease.
In the springtime beneath the forest trees, who can share this heart? Wild flowers bloom without end; the mountain cypresses stand cold and dense.

—By Baguā Héshàng (Five Poems) He is unrestrained and does not observe formal protocols, spending his days trailing through mud and water. Vast and boundless, he ultimately knows not where he returns. Teach him!
From whom shall one seek vindication?
When exhausted, he clutches his bag and remains silent; bystanders are all filled with doubt and suspicion. I cannot help but present this to you all:
what a trivial, ruined household tool it is!

This poor monk has originally nothing to shield or protect. Looking up, I see you are at a loss for words. How pitiful that in the second and third months, everywhere bees go wild and butterflies dance.
Do not marvel that my robes are tattered; entering the marketplace, I have no taboos. Lying across the main road, I wait for others—who is it?
Thus one understands the underlying pattern.
At dusk, he loves to wander through the poor districts; how could this be for the sake of some petty profit? I clearly inform you all:
the winter waters and frost fill the earth.
Mixing mud with water (five verses):
I have a path that not even a thousand sages have reached. Running north and rushing south, one buys a hat to fit a head. What kind of path is this?
Clouds stretch across the azure peaks;
I have a single discernment. Wind arises from the face of the mountain; a thousand differences appear at a glance. Knowing that you do not realize it—what kind of discernment is this?
Regarding the Sangha hall and the Buddha hall, I have another saying:
"One who well knows the proper timing—if a person understands this, it is like adding a wedge to their own eyes. What kind of saying is this?
Cold in spring, hot in autumn. I possess a sword;
its cold radiance is like a length of silk. When the tiger roars, the wind arises; flying clouds and streaks of lightning flash forth. What kind of sword is this?
With dust on his head and earth on his face, I have one device known to both sages and commoners alike: remove the nostrils and lift up Mount Sumeru. What kind of device is this?
Yuanming knits his brows.
To the students (three verses):
Within the brilliant light of the sun, who does not see clearly? This majestic matter enters the weeds; carrying staffs and bearing satchels, what bitter toil!
The mind that enters through the gate is not the treasure of the house. To expound the vehicle of the school and uphold the teachings of the patriarchs—how can a thousand-year-old dry bone be chewed?
Return from the north, south, east, and west; you have grasped the nostrils but lost the mouth.
The sutras are not read; Zen is not understood. All day long, huddling by the brazier, one nods off to sleep. Zen students from the Five Lakes vie with one another to come;
they raise their eyebrows at the three gates.
Cuiyan does not understand Chan; he looks up at the blue sky. The Great Tang Empire is shattered; Old Nanquan is made to laugh to death.
On account of the snow, he addresses the assembly (two verses):
Snow! Snow! Flakes fly together without ceasing for a moment. Ten thousand li of mountains and rivers are leveled as one. The vital ford is blocked and held fast.
The ultimate timing, the seal of Mañjuśrī, the secret instruction of Samantabhadra—though the bright sun is high in the sky, it still leaks forth.
The silent youth recites *mahā*; Kauṇḍinya sticks out his tongue.

The fundamental meaning of the school has barely been revealed, yet its implications are already far-reaching; in vain do they employ their consciousness to discourse at length. The fisherman sings his way home to the misty island at night;
the woodcutter walks through the falling blossoms in spring.

The six characteristics—formation and destruction, totality and particularity, identity and difference—interlace like Indra’s net in these six meanings. Grasping up the great earth, mountains, and rivers, they transcend the worlds of past, present, and future.
Mañjuśrī raises his eyebrows within a dream; Samantabhadra snaps his fingers in the void. Thirty years hence...
Look for yourself! For now, let us simply mix mud with water.
Twelve Verses on Ancient Cases:
The pouring of water does not fill the cup; The shoveling of snow does not fill the well. Alas, the blue-eyed man! He has traveled far across the Pamir Mountains.

Having failed to achieve results through abstaining from grain, what realization can come from carrying grain for grinding? When the one flower and five petals bloom, the monkeys howl atop the various peaks.
Why must one discern the "coming mechanism" upon entering the gate? This weary monk does not know himself;
he stubbornly points to the cypress tree in the courtyard, only to cause everyone to drive needles and awls into level ground.
Embracing simplicity at Shaolin for nine years, Zhaozhou suddenly grew the cypress before his courtyard. How pitiable are the countless people who wait by the stump;
in solitude they sit facing the colors of a thousand peaks.
The ordinary mind is the Way. Taking a step, one enters the wild weeds; I sigh anew for Master Wáng, who, in the end, could not understand it.
Let the jade hare and golden crow fly and run as they please.
Once you have seen the peach blossoms, there is no doubt; noble ambition has always been his very nature.
If you ask Xuan Sha whether his words have reached the ultimate, the evidence before your eyes is something you know for yourself.
Zhaozhou had a saying: "Go drink tea. All those with clear eyes have been misled by it; yet if they are not misled, they are still not granted permission.
How laughable that Heshan knows how to beat the drum!
The bamboo-stem whip beneath Mount Zhànglín—whether taken from the head or the tail, it is always the same.
Do not wonder that Xuánshā did not cross the ridge; his house was originally a fishing boat.
Among those who speak, he is the discerning, aged Chan master. He goes straight up the path to Mount Tai without missing his way. Having been thoroughly tested, he returns;
let no one question him. The boatman of Yueyang sails upon the waves of Lake Dongting.
Treading upon the scale-beam as hard as iron, the dazed Chan practitioners have not yet glimpsed it. On the mountain peaks of the three winter months, fiery clouds arise;
in the long sky of the sixth month, a great snow falls.
Du Chanhe, Du Chanhe! A single sesame cake—what can one do? Let your head touch the ground as you prostrate;
the boatman of the Eastern Sea sails off to Silla.
Dongshan had a saying: "Three pounds of hemp. The patched-robed seekers clasp their hands, seeking to cross the ford. This makes me recall watching his cursive script in years past;
after Zhang Zhiyan’s madness, there has been no one else.
Cease asking about hiding one's body within the Northern Dipper; it only provokes vexation in the pillar. Leaping and crashing into the lantern, he pierces through the Elder of Hunan.
Because the Sangha raised up the verse of Letan, he then offered this verse to demonstrate it:
"The Dipper concealing its body—the matter is not in vain; Shaoyang was still but a mangled corpse.
Yet today, those who cast their lines in the marshy lands still use the stench of raw meat to deceive the deluded."

The monk who remained in attendance at my teaching station for two or three autumns has now departed; though I have diminished my worldly attachments from the start, the Way remains unfulfilled. For what reason do you shed your robes so lightly to take your leave?
Your alms-bowl bag still hangs from the tip of a tree branch.

The prayer beads fall one after another, circling in the hand; vast and boundless, one knows not how to leap forth. Although they are fundamentally perfected from the start, what can be done about that single aperture within?
When let go, the Tathāgata radiates light; when held fast, Vaiśravaṇa’s brilliance is eclipsed. Sometimes he seizes it and...
Held in his hands, it is precious yet brings laughter from the patch-robed monks.
The Lion of Nanfeng’s mountain form rivals that of Xihe; majestically he presides over the northern peak. His claws and fangs remain concealed; foxes and hares naturally hide their tracks.
Yunmen ascends to the hermitage;
the thatched hall stands precariously west of Ruoye. In the secluded dwelling of the nine summer months, the scenery is wondrous: The curtains roll back upon the chaotic peaks after the first rain;
White clouds and flowing waters follow one another of their own accord.
Sending Off the Dharma-Messenger (Two Poems) The opening and closing of the gate of transformation do not occur at the same time.
To leave the frontier, one must first sever the myriad affairs of state. When the Way prevails, he returns once more to his days beneath the forest trees;
Rolling up the curtain, he idly watches the mountain clouds drift home.

I see off the Chan practitioner Wen, who parts from me to visit the Southern School. How many layers of mountains and rivers lie between Wu and Chu? Do not say there is nothing to part with at this crossroads;
the Ten-Thousand-Year Pine stands upon Mount Rongfeng.

Sending off Head Seat Ning: A single word penetrates all mysteries; it opens the provisional gate for transformative teaching. The staff is held aloft, and the whisk is brandished. The three robes are worn with dignity, and the bowl is carried with ease. The great matter is settled; the small matters are forgotten. The four winds blow, and the five flowers bloom. The ten thousand phenomena are all present; the myriad forms are each distinct. The head is shaved, the body is clothed, and the feet are shod. Shaking his mendicant’s staff, he returned to Shao-shi; once again he knocks upon the bamboo gate. No words are needed to proclaim the Patriarch’s intent; the brilliance of the Great Sun overflows the eyes.
To the Chan practitioner Hua who sees him off:
not a single character emerges from the head; not a single stroke is raised from the foot. What a pity for those of Shaolin—they sit upright, yet lack discernment.
Who says he has cast away his gold and tin? Holding it aloft, he returns to his native land. A pure breeze stirs vast and boundless through the void.
As he sends off Master Cong, one who never dwelt in his homeland nor paused even briefly in a foreign land—shoulder slung across a single staff of tin—where shall one inquire of his traces?
To Master Ciji:
Amidst the piercing icy winds of this twilight scene, you sit alone by your hut atop the twin peaks. Vast and boundless are the six directions, yet you have never sought to know them;
the moon casts its reflection upon a thousand rivers and ten thousand streams.
To Chan Master Fuyan (Two Poems) Traces are hidden in the cold crags where clouds and birds have ceased;
In the shaded cliffs, the flowing water and flowers faintly bloom. Last night, the celestial wind swept clean the stone bed;
In vast silence, I sit facing the moon of three lifetimes.
When a single leaf falls, the world turns autumnal; the affairs of men, past and present, drift aimlessly on. The Emperor’s grace was magnified by his threefold refusal of the throne;
the true spirit of a thousand years is still sung without ceasing.
Entrusting this to Chan Master Peng of Yungai:

when attachments are forgotten, it is permitted that the Way may be shared between us. Who would say that the distance of the journey is too great? The moon is bright and the five peaks reflect the white waters of the Xiang;
clouds rise from Shilin, where the dew is especially abundant.
I am grateful that Master Nanhua Ciji has sent this letter from Caoxi; it suddenly brings to mind my years at Dayu,
where there were countless matters both laughable and tragic— sweet melons growing bitter gourds.
To grasp grass and call it gold is not yet remarkable; who knows the wind-bone of Shao-yang? Having grown old and frail in recent years, I am utterly useless;
facing Master Lu, I can only knit my brows alone.
Elder Kishokusan has carved this stone;
cease your boasting, for it merely nods its own head. To whom shall the Dharma-way of Wuling be entrusted?
Having grown weary of opening my eyes in recent years, I sit alone at Longmen and behold the nine provinces.
Sent to Elder Jin from the Dragon King:

The Way of dwelling in the mountains of the south and north is no different; yet even if it is no different, the common path has not been attained. On the Dragon Peak, the climate is warm and the flowers must flourish;
on the Stone Peak, the clouds are cold and the ten-thousand-fathom cliff stands solitary.
I bid farewell to you, my fellow traveler Li;
you have been away from home for a long time, longing to practice Chan meditation. You do not mind the rugged paths—truly pitiable. I tell you:
you must quickly return to your native village. Before winter ends, plow and reclaim the fields of your youth.

Traveling in late winter, my thoughts dwell on the snow-laden, strange pine branches that seem ready to break. Worn out by illness and fearing the cold, I keep the brazier constantly burning; as I sit for a long time adding more fuel, my eyes suddenly close.
Lying prostrate, I do not realize the mountain moon has already reached its decline.
The mountain man of Zhanmuping stands atop the peak, his robes like drifting clouds;

his countenance is refined by the pure breeze and ancient in its bearing. Before a single bubble has yet formed, ten thousand mechanisms arise as fine threads. The Way reaches its ultimate in simplicity.
His conduct was so profound that it transcended all rules; I bow my head to Master Muping.
Without the toil of axes or chisels, this Chan man has painted my true likeness, yet he insists on a eulogy for me—a face with a high crown, rounded cheeks, and clenched fists.
This is a grievance against the Patriarchs and Buddhas; with lips too thin and a nose too short, it is a blemish upon the Chan courtyard, detested by all people under heaven.
This old fellow—fifteen, sixteen;
the celestial wheel and the terrestrial axis; the face of the sun and the face of the moon; where gods cry out and ghosts wail.
From his youth at Shaoshi Mountain, when he played bamboo horses in the wind, until now—do not ask about the Hu family’s tune! (Pah!)
I have composed this one verse for myself:
A tattered robe once worn has covered my snow-capped head; Pine and bamboo around the hall coldly encroach upon me. In the empty hall, the night grows long and half is spent sitting;
Before the crags, how many layers of falling petals do I know?

Four Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains Fragments of withered red petals drift upon the distant waters; Tender smoke-touched trees bear the slanting sun. Holding my staff across a stone, who would ask me?
A single cry of a monkey resounds, long as it stretches beyond the heavens.
Listen silently as the cool breeze circles the cave stream; gradually, the autumn colors enter the profound and subtle. The fisherman parts the moonlight of the Xiang River;
the woodcutter tramples through the pine cones on his way home.
Layer upon layer of mountain wheat are shrouded in purple mist; a time of great peace reveals a bountiful year. Wild clouds suddenly disperse and a solitary peak emerges;
the branching streams fly across, falling as spring water into the ravine.
Holding onto the roots of the cliff, the snow remains thick; the evening clouds idly lock the distant peaks. In the earthen stove, firewood crackles as it burns high;
in the stone kettle, tea is brewed for a single cup.
Reply to Great Master Yunfeng Zheng (Two Poems) The snow deepens before my eyes, the mountains and rivers vast;
In this traveler’s courtyard, the cold hues still linger darkly. I am especially glad that beyond the phenomenal world there is a noble affinity;
From time to time, your excellent words comfort this heart of mine.
In my bamboo study, leaning on a pillow, my illness has just begun to recede; lo, spring rice-cakes with plum blossoms have suddenly been sent to me.
How shall I repay this precious kindness? I shall lean upon my staff and ascend the stone pavilions from time to time.
Entrusting this to my fellow traveler:
drifting clouds have vanished and flowers have fallen; in the end, the bright moon is one's true livelihood.
With the heavens stretching across the six curtains beyond a thousand mountains, where is there a pure breeze that does not belong to one’s old home?
Facing the chrysanthemums with serene detachment, golden blooms reflect the autumn light. For what reason does no one raise the jade cup? I recall instead Tao Qian’s old pond;
would he have allowed the flowers to wither like weeds past the Double Ninth?
Retired Residence at Chengtian Monastery: An Occasional Composition (Five Poems) My Way is thin;

I often feel ashamed before the legacy of my ancestors. I have retired to the crags and valleys to let the years pass as they may. At the time of my midday meal, there is naturally but a bowl of soup and rice;
Throughout the six realms, the pure breeze never ceases.
My Way is thin; I am always ashamed that I have failed to succeed my ancestors. The golden hue of his eyes has already become a hollow legend.
Yet even now, he still wears the saṃghāṭī robe, sitting upright on Chicken Peak to deceive later worthies.

My Way is thin, and I am always ashamed that I have not continued the ancestral lamp. In my old age, I laugh beneath the forest trees at Lu Neng. With arms around his waist, he held a stone three feet long;
he was truly no inferior to the monk within the Huangmei assembly.

The Way has grown thin; I am constantly ashamed that my heart has not succeeded to the Patriarchs. For nine years, what was the reason for severing ties with those who understand? In the end, there is nothing but helplessness as I turn my head back;
skin and marrow remain in chaotic confusion even unto this day.

The Way is thin, and I am ever ashamed before the ancestral gate; following the family’s abundance or scarcity, I shall simply rest in poverty. The sun and moon move across the palm of my hand while Mount Sumeru runs beneath my feet;
grasping the Southern Star, I face the Northern Dipper.
The Song of the Twelve Hours:

The Cock Crows at Chou (1–3 AM). Before the first signs of dawn appear, one still runs about in confusion; within dreams, one deliberates upon tens of thousands of matters, yet when day breaks, there is nothing—only empty words.
At dawn, the hour of Yin: mountains, rivers, and the great earth are held in the palm of one’s hand; amidst the vajra flames, one snaps the fingers in emptiness.

The blue-eyed barbarian monk has yet to arrive. At sunrise, the hour of Mao: the blazing majestic light leaves nothing behind; the vast and boundless universe knows not where to return, as all vie toward the path.
In the midst of strife, one employs clever stratagems.

At the hour of the meal, who among the north, south, east, or west is truly kin? Failing to encounter the fragrant food of the Scent Accumulation (Gandhakūṭa) within the alms bowl, I feel deep shame for having falsely assumed the life of a renunciant.
At the hour of Yuzhong (Yi): Whatever the hand grasps, there is nothing that is not so. Yet one remains deluded, wandering from South Street to North Street.
For whose sake has the straw sandal been worn until it is worn through?
At the hour of Rimmian (Wu): Turning out the bag, there is not a single thread to be found. Do those with copper heads and iron jaws know or not? The grass bows before the wind.
Their conduct stands for a thousand ages.
Before the sun has even set, cease your talk of True Suchness and ultimate reality. The authorities do not permit travelers at night;
who taught you to fall asleep drunk on the street?

The hour of *shen* (the seventh watch). A traveler comes forward to ask for the essential ford; though the alms bowl has been broken, it is but a trivial matter, yet he grows angry because the tea and salt are insufficient.
The hour of *you* (the eighth watch).
Morning audiences and evening invitations—when have they ever truly existed? It is better to sit in stillness and recite the *Vajracchedikā*; let others laugh.
Tearing open the mouths of monks:
at dusk, in the hour of the dog, a single cold lamp illuminates the secluded chamber. Amidst the clamor of tolling bells and drums, it is all a scene of commotion.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
At the hour of Ren-ding (Hài), the mechanism of the "peck and hatch" was met with derision and strangeness. Since those chaotic times, how many years have passed?
I have never owed even a single coin to anyone.
At the hour of Yi-ban (Zǐ), to remain wide awake while wetting the bed like this—this old barbarian still wanders through such rugged difficulties; the stone pagoda is empty.
He remained to preside over Xiong’er Mountain.
In the seventh month of the seventh year of the Jiayou era, as the Master was about to manifest his passing, he ascended the hall and delivered a verse.

He had dwelt in the world for sixty-five years and served as a monk for fifty-seven summers. His profound disciples could not fathom his ultimate destination; they were like those who, having lost their noses, seek to find their nostrils.
The Great Head Facing Downward.
Volume Forty-one of the Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters:
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunfeng Yue.
The words of Chan Master Yue are like green mountains and white clouds, where opening and closing are at his own will; like a clear pool and the bright moon, which one must grasp to truly know.

Like iron and stone crumbling from a precipice, or a frost-bitten bow splitting a flying arrow, he did not receive the prediction of Dīpaṃkara, but personally upheld the three seals of the orthodox lineage.
Even if ancient Buddhas were to appear, he would strike them down with a single blow to settle the matter. Thus, he first inspired the old master Huineng.
Emerging from the stagnant waters of Ledu Tan, he received the seal of transmission from Ciming; later, he exhorted Chan Master Zuxin to stir the cold ashes of Dayu to behold Huangbo.
Observe these two moves of mine: they must be met by a master of the world’s chess, who first breaks through this single speck of dust.
To bestow the eye upon the patriarchs of the four seas. For those who harbor doubts, this is because they are unwilling to accept the Elder of the Valleys;
he intends to present the teaching in its entirety and first rescue Layman Wuwei. Written by Huang Tingjian.
Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Honored Masters,
Volume Forty-Two The Record of Chan Master Yun’an Zhenjing of Baofeng while Residing at Shengshou Monastery in Junzhou Compiled by his Dharma heir, Fashen
On the day of opening the hall, after the proclamation of the memorial (sūtra), the Master said: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas;

yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood. Today, surrounded by the fourfold assembly, the Buddha-dharma manifests before us—does it so manifest or not?
After a long silence, he said: "Wishing to travel a thousand li, one step is the beginning. Thereupon, he ascended the seat and offered incense as a vow.
The Master concluded the formal session. Again, he held up the incense and said, "Great assembly, do you know where this single offering of incense falls?
Without further concealment, I burn it directly for the former Zen Master Huanglong Nan, sending it into the brazier. Thereupon, he sat cross-legged.

After the mallet struck to signal the end of the session, the Master called to the assembly, saying, "You must observe for yourselves. If one observes in this way, it is called right observation. If..."
To view it otherwise is called false viewing. Before the false and the correct have been distinguished, there is doubt, and thus he asks a question. A monk asked:

"When the successive patriarchs ascend the hall and worthy lords press their invitation, we pray that the Master will proclaim the supreme vehicle of our school. The Master said: "Six times six is thirty-six."
The monk stepped forward and said, "I always remember that in the third month of the south, where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant. The Master said, "What fine news!
The monk said, "Today the Langzhong has received this blessing; I now withdraw and prostrate three times to thank the Master's kindness. The Master said, [silently].
[The Master] said, "Profound. The monks prostrated. A monk asked, "Both speech and silence are easy to discern.
Whose Dharma heir have you now become? The Master said, "I told you already this morning. The monk pressed further, "In that case, you are a true son of Huanglong and a direct grandson of Linji.
The Master said, "You are still merely speculating. The monk pressed further, "Now, the four seas are as clear as a mirror; [you] walk..."
"No one makes an enemy of the road. The Master said, "Quickly, prostrate three times. A question was asked: "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, Brahmā and Śakra followed him.
When you, Langzhong, invite the Master, with what will you repay him? The Master said, "One rain falls everywhere; all things flourish.
He further said, "A single word is born from beneath the brush; it falls among humanity for ten thousand ages. The Master said, "As for matters among humanity, how are they?"
The student said, "When the waves subside, they return to the water; when the moon sets, it does not leave the sky. The Master said, "Idle words.
The practitioner asked, "Heaven and earth treat all things as straw dogs; the sages treat the common people as straw dogs.

I wonder, Master, with what do you treat [people] as straw dogs? The Master said, "A dot. The student said, "Calamity has entered the gates of the Sangha. The Master said, "It is so. The practitioner was about to—
The Master gave a shout. The attendant prostrated. The Master said, "How can you be so one-sided, having the beginning but no end?

A monk asked, "Today, humans and devas have gathered in great numbers, and the Governor is present at the assembly. The Patriarch’s intent came from the West; I beg the Master for its definitive meaning. The Master said, "Definitive.

The monk pressed further, "I have already received the Master’s instruction on this single phrase. As for the ultimate vehicle of the ancestral school, what is it like? The Master said, "The downward-pointing one."

The student said, "If one does not ascend the tower to gaze out, how can one know the depth of the vast ocean? The Master said, "Too much. The student said, "The fourfold assembly has received your grace;
I, this student, offer my thanks. The Master said, "You still lack one move. The student said, "The bystander looks on with shame. The Master said, "..."
[The Master] let go. A monk came forward and said, "What place is this? The Master said, "Ask well; do not be hypocritical.
The monk asked, "What is the phrase that is hypocrisy? The Master said, "This hypocritical fellow! The monk was speechless. The Master then gave a shout.
As the monk prepared to offer further words, the Master said, "You have brought me to utter frustration! The monk stepped forward and said, "A truly good spiritual friend! The Master said, "..."

"You have no choice but to do so. He spoke again: "Let us set aside these questions for a moment. You know only how to ask about the Buddha and the Dharma, yet you do not realize the source from which the Buddha-Dharma comes.
Tell me, from where does it come? Then he lowered one foot and said: "In the past, Huanglong personally issued this command;
none of the Buddhas of the ten directions dared to disobey it, nor did any of the ancestral masters of successive generations."
The sages and worthies dare not transgress it. Among the immeasurable Dharma-gates and all subtle meanings, the tongue of the Old Monk of the World has been, from beginning to end, a single seal;
none dare differ from it. Let us stop for a moment regarding this lack of difference.
Where does this seal reside? Do you see it? If you see it, you are neither monk nor layman; without partiality and without faction, it is entrusted to each and every one. If you do not see it—yet...
I withdrew it myself; then, withdrawing my feet, I shouted: "The army follows the seal; the general pursues the talisman.
As for the Buddha’s hand, the donkey’s foot, and the circumstances of birth—old man, you deserve thirty blows! Is there anyone in this assembly today who does not feel this bitterness?
If it exists, it is indeed extraordinary; if it does not exist, then this new elder is merely deceiving you all.
Therefore, our Great Awakened World-Honored One, in the past, on the eighth day of the twelfth month in the kingdom of Magadha, at the moment the morning star appeared, suddenly realized the Way.
All sentient beings of the great earth attained Buddhahood simultaneously. Now there is the Śākya śramaṇa Kewen, who—
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month, at the time when the blazing sun appeared, within the city of Jinyang in the Great Song Dynasty of Eastern Zhendan—what else was realized?
[The Master] drew a line with his whisk and said: "I do not dare slight you;
you shall all become Buddhas. He then descended from his seat.
In the eighth year of the Xining era, the Master accepted an invitation at Dongshan. Before the Dharma seat, he held up a document and showed it to the assembly, saying:
"The very first phrase—everyone must know it! Do you understand? After a long silence, he said: "When the tally arrives, the decree is carried out."
When the *vinaya-dhara* had finished proclaiming the notice, the Master said, "Great assembly, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they all simply attend to a particular season.
But tell me, what season does this poor monk attend to today? He then pointed to the Dharma seat, called to the assembly, and said, "From ancient times to the present, it has never fallen away;
it is clearly right before one's eyes. He then ascended the seat and said, "Is there anyone who would ask?"
[The Master] said, "What is it like? At that time, a monk asked, "I have heard an ancient saying: 'Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata; only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara.
What is this matter of being 'self-sovereign' (zìzài)? The Master said, "Piercing through seven, piercing through eight. The monk pressed further.
When the dragon meets the water, its spirit increases; when the tiger encounters mountain scenery, its fierce majesty grows. The Master said, "Dark.
The student advanced and said, "Deep within the snow of the village ahead, last night a single branch blossomed. The Master said, "Idle talk. A question was asked:

"The patron has respectfully extended three invitations; what is the matter at this assembly today? The Master said, "In the cave of Xinfeng, the waters flow murmuringly. The student advanced and said:
"If that is so, you have heard what was unheard and departed. The Master said, "But tell me, what is the matter you have heard?
The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master said, "A fabricated Chan practitioner! The monk stepped forward and said, "The assembly bears witness; I, this student, offer my thanks.
The Master then sighed repeatedly and said, "Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? After a long silence, he shouted, "In days of yore..."
"The Great Awakened World-Honored One rose from beneath the Bodhi tree and went to the Deer Park, where he turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five bhikṣus;
it was Kātyāyana alone who first realized the Way. Today, this poor monk goes into the cave at Xinfeng and turns only this staff.
He then took up his staff and placed it to the left of the meditation seat, saying: "Is there anyone here who has realized the Way from the very beginning?"
After a long silence, he said, "One may truly say that a man of integrity possesses a will that soars toward the heavens; he does not walk where the Tathāgata has walked.
With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Upon first entering the monastery and ascending the seat, a monk asked, "Heaven and earth are suffering from a parching drought; we pray that you will grant us a rain.

The Master said, "There is naturally that which brings coolness. The monk pressed further, "In that case, all living beings shall have their reliance. The Master said, "Those who recognize this kindness are few. The monk pressed further.
When the clouds disperse, the moon is in every house; when spring comes, flowers bloom everywhere. The Master said, "Not easy to recite from memory.
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Shengshou? The Master said, "The old buildings stand in uneven rows; only those who arrive will truly know.

The monk pressed further, "What is the person within the realm? The Master said, "It is as if we do not know one another. The monk continued, "I have already received the Master’s instruction on both the person and the realm."
"What is the matter regarding the vehicle of the upward-pointing lineage? The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master said, "One shout was not enough.
A monk asked, "In the past, when the World-Honored One appeared in the world, he sat and cut off heaven and earth. Today, when the Master appears in the world, what is your intention?"

The Master said, "Surrounded by the fourfold assembly. The student stepped forward and said, "The great assembly bears witness; I, this student, prostrate. The Master said, "Why do you not ask further?
He added, "The green mountains and clear waters cannot detain one; the white days and red dust return of their own accord. Now there is no avoiding it;
for now, blend with the world and harmonize with the light, with head like ash and face like earth. Even those who dwell beneath the forest trees must laugh at this!"
[The Master] laughs. "If you understand this laugh, it is truly marvelous! On the crossroads of the city, he has picked up a coarse cotton robe;
shaking off the dust, he shows it to all people. Is it good? Is it not? Do you understand? Or do you not? Let him sing and shout from the butcher’s block!
[He lets out] a shout and says, "Turn your heads and look back!"
Evening *sōdan* (evening discourse). A monk asked, "It is ever serene right where one is; if you seek it, you will know it cannot be seen.
I do not ask about 'seeing'—what is this matter of being 'not separate'? The Master said, "Pour out your heart and bare your soul.
The monk stepped forward and said, "If one does not ascend the tower to look out, how can one know the depth of the vast ocean? The Master said, "As for that matter of being 'serene,' what then?"
[The Master] said, "Born. Jin said, "The three gates and the Buddha hall face each other; green bamboos and pines in the wind fill the courtyard with cold.
The Master said, "Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality. Jin said, "One must still examine this thoroughly. The Master then gave a shout. He continued, "Maitreya is truly Maitreya;
his body manifests in hundreds of thousands of millions of forms. From time to time he shows himself to those of this age, yet those of this age all fail to recognize him. [He] took up his staff.
[The Master] said, “Do you recognize it yet? Among thousands and tens of thousands, simply recognize this one. He threw down his staff and descended from the seat.
Because the Head Seat, the Rector, and the Director of the Abbot’s Quarters had requested him to ascend the hall, he asked, “The flowing water descending the mountain has no intention;
the drifting cloud returning to its cave is fundamentally without mind. What is the phrase regarding being without mind? The Master said, “Are you with mind, or without?”

[The Master asked: "Is it the mind? The monk replied: "The layered stone peaks are high and precipitous; white clouds emerge from the old pass. The Master said: "Do not say that being without mind is good. The monk bowed. The Master said:
"Thirty years from now, you will come to your senses. He spoke again: "The three virtues and six flavors are offered to the Buddhas and the Sangha.
In the kitchen of Fragrant Accumulation, skillful seasoning is held in the hand. The Buddhas of the three periods [of time] face the sound upon the mortar and pestle."
"Correspondence through sound. But tell me, with what do you correspond? After a long silence, he said, "Go ask the first seat in the hall.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "When the colors of dawn have not yet parted and all gaze toward it, once the sky has truly broken, what is the meaning? The Master said:
"Do you see? The attendant replied, "Though the city god’s abode is humble, the Way is shared intimately beneath the forest trees.
The Master said, "What kind of place is this? He continued, "There is advancing and retreating; there is urgency and leisure. The Way lies in adaptability; thus affairs are brought to completion.
The head of the monastery bears the burden with all his might; the lay attendants employ skillful means to transform others; and the guest prefect provides guidance as the occasion demands."
The Elder cited the facts and closed the case. "Is there anyone who does not fall within this category? After a long silence, he said:
"Next year there will be new branches again; the spring wind shall never cease its turmoil."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "If the real is illusory, and the illusory is real, once both reality and illusion are removed, where does the Way return?
The Master said, "If there were a specific location, what could it possibly be used for? The monk pressed further, "A thousand rivers have water, and each has a thousand moons;

ten thousand miles of solitary boat, ten thousand miles of solitary body. The Master said, "Yet it is not like this. The monk pressed further, "The fisherman on the river merely casts his line in vain."
[The monk] bowed his head. The Master said, "What did I just tell you? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "A fine shout! The monk shouted again.
The Master said, "After two shouts, what then? The monk prostrated and said, "I still feel it is too little.
The Master then sighed repeatedly and said, "To the assembly: I have been well for some time. I have been preoccupied with various affairs for several days and cannot greet each of you individually."
Expressions of gratitude. If rituals are too numerous, they lead to confusion. Once you understand this matter, simply let it be.

But tell me, what matter is this? Suddenly he picks up his staff and says: "The wind does not whistle through the branches; the rain does not break the clods of earth. The wind of Yao sweeps vast and clear;
travelers yield the road. The myriad people sing in joy. Within the city of Yunchang, whose hearth has no smoke? When Lord Zhang drinks wine, Lord Li..."
[Zuò] leaned on his staff and said: "Hanshan and Shide.
He then ascended the hall and said: "Yesterday there was a monk who came from Letan and is now heading toward Yangshan. Suddenly, he picked up his staff and said:
In the city of Jinyang, at Shengshou Monastery, the drums were beaten for a communal tea service.
Ascending the hall, a master of transformation asked: "An ancient sage once said: 'Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil.'"
"A sovereign attains the One and thereby governs the world. I do not yet know how it is when a monk attains the One.
The Master said, "He is skilled at transforming and guiding others. The monk further asked, "In that case, there are no idle guests on the dusty road of the mundane world?
The Master said, "Every household has Avalokiteśvara. The monk bowed. The Master said, "You must still exert effort. He spoke again: "I contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma..."
"The law of the king is thus. [The Master] suddenly picked up his staff and said, "I have pierced through the nostrils of you all and replaced your eyes.
Return to me the Dharma of the Dharma-King! He then shouted, "To err by a hair's breadth is to miss by a thousand li!"
He cast down his staff, descended from his seat, and ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma. What is this One Vehicle Dharma?"
The Master said, "A hundred-foot flagpole points its tip toward heaven. The student said, "I, this disciple, step back three paces.
The Master said, "Under his heels, they run wild in every direction. The student said, "Moonlight blends with the clouds into white; the sound of pines carries the chill of dew."
The Master gave a shout. The monk also shouted. The Master said, "This wild fox spirit! He spoke again:
"To the great assembly, ten thousand blessings! It was but recently the beginning of summer, yet already it is early autumn. This morning at dawn, the first day of the seventh month has arrived.

Alas! Time flows as swiftly as lightning; the four seasons shift and change. All things are impermanent, and people likewise grow old. Is there anyone who does not involve themselves in the concerns of old age and youth?"
[The Master] said, "What? After a long silence, he said, "An eighty-year-old man wearing embroidered boots.
On another occasion, when Elder Xiaoyao arrived, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "A single phrase clearly transcends ten billion worlds.
I do not ask about that single phrase; what are these ten billion? The Master said, "A Daoist fastening his sash. The monk pressed further, "In one hall, the wind is cold."
Faint. The meaning of a thousand ages is clear. The Master said: "A foreigner wears a crown on his head. The student stepped forward and said:
"May the assembly bear witness; let us first pay three prostrations. The Master shouted: "Blind fellow! He then added: "A man from deep within the green mountains comes here into my world of dust."
The red dust is momentarily unseen; white clouds and flowing waters remain. What distinction can there be for the ears and eyes between floating fame and fleeting profit?
Is it the red dust that is false, or is it the green mountains that are true? Between these two paths of right and wrong, how many disputes have not yet ceased?
Fortunately, we have encountered one who dwells in carefree ease; let us expound the principle of carefree ease.
[Descends from the seat. Enters the hall: Heaven and earth share the same root with me; the myriad things and I are one body.

From head to tail, horizontal and vertical, in every direction—when fire breaks out on the continent of Uttarakuru, it burns the eyebrows of Śakra, and the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea suffers the pain.
Unable to restrain himself, he let out a thunderous clap of lightning that caused the mountains and rivers to overturn and the vast sky to darken with clouds.
At that moment, Old Zhao of the Crossroads, while intoxicated, suddenly woke up, clapped his hands, and laughed heartily, saying, "Lately there have been few thieves in the city of Jinyang.
He then took up his staff and said, "Thief! Thief! and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The gate of Yunmen is opened; it is sevenfold and eightfold passable. Yet you must know that there is a bolt to be turned.

If you do not know this, though you are alive, you are as if dead. The present Huanglong Dragon undergoes a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, yet you must further reach his hidden lair.
If you do not reach it, though you have eyes, you are like the blind. Venerable ones, I contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King—the Dharma of the Dharma-King."
Thus it is. One who possesses eyes discerns and grasps.
Because the Elder Qingliang arrived, he ascended the hall; once the heat and affliction were exhausted, coolness manifested before him, and no further discrimination arose.
"Empty clarity illuminates itself; only then shall I press my finger. The Sea-Seal (Sāgaramudrā) emits its light. As soon as you stir your mind, the dust of affliction first arises.

He then shouted, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time—strike them all dead with a single blow! Fill the ditches and block the gullies! Cast them east and west, wherever you please; let everyone look!
Suddenly, he took up his staff and said, "The Buddhas of the past were also like this. The Buddhas of the present..."
The Buddhas of the past were thus; the Buddhas of the future will be thus. He then threw [the object] down and said, "Look!
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the pearl? The Master said, "Its blazing radiance is right before your eyes.
The monk pressed further, "The entire city is full of those who know it; let us compose a new poem for all to see. The Master said, "Who is the one who knows it?"
The monk said, "The great assembly bears witness; this student prostrates. The Master said, "A man of empty talk. He spoke again: "A single leaf falls, and the world turns autumnal.
This old monk is too weary to shave his snow-white head. The wind roars and the waters flow; the busy are busy, the idle are idle.
The azure hues of Zhongnan Mountain lean against one another; on the banks of the Xiang, the orange clusters hang like red hooks. O Zen adepts!"
If you understand, you will immediately put it into practice on the road; if you do not understand, let it circulate as a worldly truth for now. Holding up his staff, he said:
"This is not for practice on the road—how then shall it be transmitted? After a long silence, he shouted: "The night is still and the water is cold; the fish does not bite."
Returning under the bright moon with an empty boat full.
Master Yuehua ascends the hall: At Vulture Peak they spoke of the moon; at Caoxi they pointed to the moon. Today at Shengshou, we give thanks to the moon.
Tell me, between you and the ancients, who is close and who is distant? Is there anyone who can discern this?

If you can discern it, then offer this very body and mind to every dust mote and land; this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. If you cannot discern it, the hornless iron ox sleeps at Shaoshi;
the childless woman gives birth at Huangmei. This will make the Pine-Planting Wayfarer laugh to death. *Chan.*
Ascending the hall: It has only been seven months since the fifteenth day [of the seventh month], yet it is already the Mid-Autumn Festival of the eighth month.
