Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The ancient worthy said, 'Those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure.
But what, then, is the family treasure? [He suddenly took up his staff and called to the assembly: 'Do you see it? He then struck the incense stand and sighed repeatedly.
Śākyamuni cannot be killed by blows from a staff; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra will not turn their heads even when called. Stop! Stop! It is a waste of effort."
Furthermore, follow the current and wait for the right moment to arrive. When a single leaf falls, the whole world knows autumn. Entering the hall:
Under the gate of Dongshan, if you wish to walk, you walk; if you wish to sit, you sit.
To defecate in the alms bowl or spit into the water pitcher—such is the practice of those who cling to the Dharma and cultivate it like an ox pulling a millstone. *Chan* (Examine)!
Ascending the hall, he thanked Huangbo for having preceded him, saying: "Branching out and dividing into schools, we together propagate the ancestral tradition;
fully upholding the Patriarchal Command, each adapts to circumstances as they arise. By raining down the single rain of Huanglong, withered trees flourish anew; continuing the legacy of Duanji."
The true lamp flares up once more, its light illuminating my predecessors’ awakening and advancing those who come after. I am overcome with joy and celebration.

As for this unworthy person, how could I have anticipated such a swift arrival? You, Venerable Sir, having distanced yourself from Vulture Peak and delved deep into Dongshan, have specifically sent this letter to recount the lineage of our dharma-milk.
Having been so thoroughly bathed in your diligent care, I look up to you with gratitude that knows no end. Again, he brandished his staff and called to the assembly, saying: "Truly..."
It is said: Though we were born from the same root, we shall not die from the same root. *Ara ara*. How truly marvelous! Calculating it, we are both sons of men;
yet while sleeping on the same bed, each dreams his own dream. From ancient times to the present, few have understood this principle.
Few people know this. Entrust it to Xianchi to transmit back to Vulture Peak, where you may clearly present it to the Master.
He ascended the hall and said: "Under the gate of Dongshan, if one wishes to speak, one speaks; if one wishes to act, one acts. One might save the eyebrows, yet lose the nostrils.
He then gave a shout and said: "Long rains have not ceased. Retreat! (Chán).
Upon returning from the county seat, he ascended the hall and said: "To say that one who has not been seen for three days cannot be looked upon with the old eyes—what kind of talk is that?
For several days now, Dongshan has not been seen; yet when we meet, it is still just the person of old. He then joined his palms and said:
"I hope you are well, all Buddhas of the past, present, and future. After the session, they drank tea together.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Under the gate of Dongshan, sometimes he blends mud and water; sometimes he stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
If you all intend to see Dongshan in the place where he blends mud and water, Dongshan is not to be found there.
If you intend to see Dongshan in the place where he stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, Dongshan is likewise not to be found there."
"Regarding the 'place': if you intend to see Dongshan in all places, Dongshan is not actually present in all places.
You need not seek to see Dongshan; his nose is already in Dongshan's hand. If you intend to nod off to sleep, he will pull the nose-rope taut.
You will see only his eyes flicker, yet you still do not recognize him. I do not require you to recognize Dongshan; rather, you must recognize yourself."
"I have attained it myself. Descend from your seat.

[The Master] ascends the hall to express his gratitude to the Chief Administrator (Kanyuan). A monk asks: "When it is time to act, one acts; when it is time to withdraw, one withdraws—what of that? The Master says:
A brand-new sun and moon; a distinctively extraordinary heaven and earth. The student said, "When the dragon meets the water, his spirit increases;

when the tiger encounters the mountain scenery, its fierce majesty grows. The Master said, "For now, let there be peace throughout the world. The student said, "If that is so, then the Way is so prosperous that the Emperor's edicts need not be transmitted.
The Master said, "I have been thoroughly outwitted by you, old monk! He then added, "The body is radiance itself."
The Banner. The mind is the treasury of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*). The great assembly, each of you, take care of yourselves; rouse your spirits.
Now, manifesting meditative concentration—monks are thus, laypeople are thus, Śākyamuni is thus, and Maitreya is thus.
Is there anyone who can believe this? If you can believe it, it is not considered extraordinary. If you cannot believe it, it is nonetheless not lacking.
[Omission]. Faith and lack of faith. Light Banner. Treasury of Supernatural Powers. Each of you, go to the hall. [The Master] descends from his seat. He ascends the hall and says:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the patriarchal style of your house? Yunmen said, "When a scholar comes, send word.
"Virtuous ones, a thousand hearings are not equal to one seeing. But how do you see it? After a long silence, he said, "It is simply because..."
How extremely clear! Yet it causes what is attained to be delayed.

Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "Under the gate of Dongshan, there are eight hollows and nine elevations; they intersect and overlap, winding and twisting, rugged and precipitous, towering and craggy.
Water and clouds obscure one another, mists and vapors layer upon layer. There is a single, direct path for those who observe."
"Among those who travel, nine out of ten take their very first step and have already lost their way.
Is there anyone among them who does not lose their way? He then shouted, "Tell me, where is the entrance to Dongshan’s path?"
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: "In the past, at Tiantai Guoqing Temple, while they were roasting eggplants, Shide took a bamboo skewer and struck the back of the *weina* once.
The *weina* called out for the *zhisui*, saying, 'Look at this madman!
Shide said, 'Heaven! Heaven! Hanshan asked, 'Why did you strike him? Shide said, 'It was a waste.'"
"How much salt and sauce? O virtuous practitioners of Chan! When Shide beat the *vinaya-dhara*, he truly meant that too much salt and sauce had been wasted;

there must surely be another principle here. Let a clear-eyed monk come forth and judge it! First, to resolve the doubts of the assembly—both those who already understand and those who have not yet awakened.
Second, to manifest one's own study of the Way and discern right from wrong. To speak of entangling vines while sitting in the cold is to be disparaged.
"Peeling back the past and present—this is no easy task. Is there anyone capable? If not, I, this old monk, shall resolve your doubts for you.
The steward pleaded repeatedly to retire, yet after being entreated three times, Hanshan and Shide were retained. Everything was entrusted to them: those who sweep were told to sweep;
those who tend the fires were told to tend the fires. "Let none of the sons of the various quarters pass their time in vain," he said, his eloquence abundant.
He has come all the way here. I, this old monk, have already examined him for him.

The head monk, the rector, the steward, and the overseer—you must also know what the surnames of Hanshan and Shide are. If you do not even know that, one day at some future time, you will all be led by the nose by him.
(He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.)
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The light shaves the head; the pure washes the bowl. If it is good, one dwells; if it is evil, one departs.
O virtuous practitioners of Zen, do not use worldly views to bury the mind of the Way."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Dongshan is deep, secluded, and solid. For a thousand years, the forest trees have given rise to mist and fog. Within these woods are countless branches of entanglement;
reaching left and right, they are difficult to avoid. To turn away is to further involve oneself; otherwise, one remains fixed in their place. He-he-he!
I thought Dongshan was full of entanglements, but it turns out they are actually the *Cantong Qi*. [The Master] then gave a shout and said: 'Clear! "
"O monks, do not take this lightly.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "If you merely know how to follow the custom and eat your fill, you might as well get three coins to buy straw sandals.
But what about 'the new bride riding the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it'? Even if you can say something for this, I shall further ask: how long is the patriarch’s nostril?"
"It is somewhat there. [The Master] descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall: "The trousers have no crotch; the breeches have no opening. Three or five pecks of green ash upon the head—Old Zhaozhou is showing off too much.
Nevertheless, 'In the state of Guoqing, the talented are noble; when a family is wealthy, the children are spoiled. Alas, the grain and millet do not ripen in the sun!"
"Flames! People compete to plant peach and plum trees in spring, yet this only causes those who toil in the fields to become half of the flower-sellers.
Entering the hall, [the Master] said: 'To simply leave behind all that is false and delusive is called liberation; however, in reality, one has not yet attained total liberation.
What is total liberation? He suddenly picked up his staff and said, 'The barrier. He spoke again: 'Master Yunmen was on the staff...'"
Leaping upon the tip of the staff—do you still see Cuiyan’s eyebrows? If you do not see them, Dongshan shall explain them for you.
Changqing arrives; he then throws down [the staff] and says: "The flute is blown and the drums are beaten; let us all go forth and look!"
Ascending the hall, he thanked the Hall Master and the Supervisor of Collections, saying:

"The superior practitioners who investigate the mystery and the eminent persons who savor the Way find that, amidst the daily activities of movement and stillness, all things are manifest and all requisites are complete. Yet, one must know the source of each and every thing.
Therefore, the ancients said: 'It is like the great earth; what thing is not born from the earth? The Buddhas point only to the One Mind. What...?
The Dharma does not arise from what the mind establishes. It is a matter of the region’s divisions; what the earth produces may be wheat or hemp, or beans or rice.
Yet, were it not for the right person, these could not be brought to fruition or established. Once they are established, one need not exert mental effort.
Even though such effort is exerted, not a single grain falls elsewhere. Tell me, where do they fall?
"Where? He then took up his staff, threw it down, and called to the assembly, saying: "Do you see it? Who is without their share?
Do you know its place of origin? If you do, you may be said to be elegant even where there is no elegance."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Those of long-standing training under former worthies are not limited by these constraints; those who are beginners or new to the path need not harbor deluded thoughts.
Upon what else could you rely? Why not clear away the obstructions from the spiritual source within your own mind-ground and let forth the radiance of your supernormal powers?"
Flowing forth in an unceasing stream, they accomplish the Buddha’s work—how joyful this is! [The Master] suddenly grasps his staff and says, "This is not supernatural power or radiance.
He then strikes the incense table and says, "This is not the Buddha’s work," whereupon he hurls it down. After a long silence, he lets out a shout.
He said: "At midnight, who snatched away the black hen? At dawn, it is caught amidst the snow and pointed out. Entering the hall, he said:
"To arrange things with conscious intellect and to fabricate through effort is to pursue external conditions exclusively; thus, one's own fundamental matter falls into ruin.
If you do not believe in the Perfect and Universal Knowledge of our own house, you will not attain true enlightenment even after kalpas. He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following cases: Sansheng said, "Whenever I meet a person, I come forth; when I come forth, I do not act for the sake of others.
Xinghua said, "Whenever I meet a person, I do not come forth; when I do come forth, I immediately act for the sake of others. The Master said, "Look at these two ancient worthies!

Having stolen a mere fragment of Linji’s livelihood, each has demarcated his own territory and established his boundaries, their vital energy piercing the cosmos, so as to deceive those with clear eyes."
Monks, this is simply a matter for good laughter. All you practitioners of Zen, tell me: why do you laugh? Do you know where it lands?
If you know, then let yourself go seven ways up and eight ways down as you please. If you do not know, then for now chew upon the tangled vines of Sansheng and Xinghua.
[The Master] descends from the seat.
The small *chán* (meditation) talk on New Year’s Eve says: "On the night when the year is nearly spent, there are those who have not yet returned from ten thousand miles.
Tonight, this entire assembly consists entirely of children from foreign lands. For what reason do you not return? A-he-he! Even if you were able to return, having returned, there would be no home.
This is precisely the place where all of you belong. Can you return? Have you not heard Master Pang say: 'The ten directions...'"
Gathering together in this assembly, each person studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas; with an empty mind, one returns having passed the imperial examination.
(With his whisk, he struck the meditation seat and rose.)
Ascending the hall on the first day of the year: "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata; only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara.

O virtuous practitioners of meditation, today everyone adds a year to their age. Do you see it? If you do not see it, yet I say again that everyone adds a year to their age—if you do see it, where do you place it?
Once you have seen its place of abiding, you will see its point of emergence. Since the point of emergence...
Only through clarity can one attain mastery over the phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

When Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva went to buy sesame cakes (*húbǐng*), what he held in his hand was actually steamed buns (*mántóu*). How wonderful, O virtuous Chan practitioners! One year adds one year; one year is one Tathāgata.
Holding up his staff, he said: "Even this staff will become a Buddha. Look!"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "As for the two words 'Buddha-dharma,' do not speak of them. To speak of them is to give rise to horns. The ancients only knew how to kill people;
they did not know how to bring them to life. Why not say that these two words, 'Buddha-dharma,' are each and every one already fully realized? O virtuous Chan practitioners!"
If you wish to know the Buddha, it is simply these people. If you wish to know the Dharma, it is simply that which these people use in their daily lives.
Is it so? It is so. This is truly marvelous. Not so? This is also truly marvelous. To kill or to bring to life—if one does not penetrate this single point, [one is lost].
In both places, effort is lost; in both places, there is no penetration. Encountering every path, one encounters stagnation.
Upon returning from the prefecture to ascend the hall, matters in the mountains and within the city remain mutually unknown. There is a single phrase that I have not yet dared to reveal its intent;
I shall wait until I have visited each of the quarters, where I will deliver it directly to each person face-to-face. It is truly a matter for the moment; each must apply yourselves with diligence.
[The Master] said, "Do not let it slip away. He ascended the hall and said:
"Fenzhou, do not forget; Jueyi, raise your finger. The matters of the Buddhadharma, ancient and modern, come to rest all at once here.
Rest! Rest! Yet I recall Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman—where there was no artifice, there was artifice. [He] took up his staff.
Zhaozhou said: "Exerting one's utmost strength for the sake of the assembly.
After the Master of Transformation had ascended the hall, the beggars packed their belongings after more than a month. They troubled the administrators, the head seat, and the great assembly;
whether moving or still, how could they not have been fatigued? Yet, such exertion is simply the natural lot of a man of the Way.
This is not a matter of mere Buddhist ritual. What is meant is that coming and going are boundless, and movement and stillness share a single source.

If one attains spiritual resonance within movement and stillness, then there will be no obstruction in coming and returning. When neither mental activity nor physical traces arise, what fault can there be in favorability or adversity?

This is to have no mind regarding the mind and no affairs regarding affairs; how could it hinder the diligent engagement in movement, stillness, coming, and returning? If one should attain this, it is indeed correct.
"The mind: he who loses it becomes disordered in his nature. Thus, gain and loss are inherently distinct; it is not that movement and stillness differ.
[The Master] then picked up his staff, threw it down, gave a shout, and descended from the seat."

Ascending the hall, he said: "To let one move pass is to fall into the second rank. As the mid-spring gradually warms and the scenery becomes bright and beautiful, all you eminent practitioners—how are your daily activities?
Is there anyone among you who does not encounter the conditions of spring? After a long silence, he said:
"Holding an empty bowl on a distant road, treading upon falling blossoms in the deep mountains."

Ascending the hall: It has been ten days since we parted; returning once more to the midst of mountains and waters, my eyes open as if awakening from a dream—these matters are for the most part empty.
(He lets out a shout. He descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season.

In ancient times, people pointlessly drove stakes into empty space to deceive and delude later generations. Today is the first day of the fourth month; it is the season of early summer, and the long rains have not ceased."

I humbly wish that the administrative officers, the head seat, and the assembly may enjoy ten thousand blessings in your physical well-being. What further need is there to seek the meaning of Buddha-nature?
Each of you possesses eyes, a nose, a mouth, and ears; why do you not disperse?
Do not hinder me as I move east and west. [Descend from the seat.]
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case: Yunmen said, “Zha! Long rain, no sun. The Master said:

“Although Yunmen was skilled at adapting on the spot like a leopard changing its spots—brandishing his staff here and there—he could not avoid muddying the waters. Let us set aside for a moment this ‘muddying the waters.
As for Yunmen saying, ‘Zha!’—what kind of character is that ‘Zha’? Is there any monk with clear eyes who recognizes it? If you recognize it, then [Yunmen’s]”
The gate has a certain breath. If you do not recognize it, what breath does a patch-robed monk have?
Only those with nostrils can discern this very breath. Descend from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The World-Honored One held up a flower; Kāśyapa smiled. Now, picking up his staff, I say:
'Dongshan picks up this staff—what do you all intend to do? He then struck the incense table and descended from the seat."

Ascending the hall, he said: "This matter is like a bright pearl on a tray; it turns of its own accord without being nudged. There are those who nudge it but it does not turn, or press it but it does not come alive.
How can one blame the old monk for this? Do you wish to recognize the bright pearl? Each of you return to your quarters and drink tea."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Holy Monk has been speaking to you all every day, penetrating to the very bone and marrow. Just now, when the drum was struck, he proclaimed it once more.
If we wait for the Elder to open his mouth and move his tongue, what would that even amount to? I, this old monk, speak thus."
This is like drawing legs for a snake.
On the day of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "The ten directions assemble here; once every three months we hold this retreat.

It serves to stifle the heart of wild arrogance, to eliminate the heat of suffering and affliction, to attain supreme coolness, and to realize great nirvana. Reaching the shore of *pāramitā*, one leaves the tracks of birth and death behind. By means of this holy..."
It was established for this reason; thus, it is not set forth in vain. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas neither see nor hear it. The Buddhas of the three periods can only know it for themselves.
Even patch-robed monks cannot leap out of it; they are caught within its intricate patterns. To move is to open one’s eyes and urinate on the bed—to speak dreams within a dream.
For now, seek a way to live for ninety days under the gate of Dongshan.
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: "In the past, Salt Official (Yanguan) constantly taught his monks the Dharma-gate of seeing one's nature.
Hearing that Daopei did the same, he secretly dispatched two monks to investigate him. Upon arriving at the master’s seat, they failed to recognize any of the teachings or proclamations made.
They consequently gave rise to a sense of arrogance. One day, they encountered Xiaoshijia, who said to them, 'Do not be careless. Xiaoshijia then drew a circle."
He held his hands out in front of them as a gesture. The two monks did not recognize it. Little Śākyamuni said, "Do not be so careless," and then he rose and departed.
The Master said, "Little Śākyamuni’s samādhi—did those two monks not know it? Is there no one among the disciples of Dongshan who knows it? What kind of samādhi was this?
After a long silence, he said, "To grind flour, one must use the wheat of that specific region; to sing a song, one must..."
He was a native of the Imperial Capital.
Ascending the hall, he struck the bell and then beat the drum; the sun was precisely at its zenith. Shide said to Hanshan, "Painting a dragon, one ends up with a tiger.
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "The two words 'Buddha-dharma' are truly difficult to encounter.
There are those who do not believe in their own Buddha-work, relying instead on a mere shadow of the ancients—on the realms of knowledge of semblance-prajñā and on dharmas of fixed characteristics.
As soon as they move, they turn their backs on awakening and join with the dust; they become stuck and cannot escape. Or when students come, it is like a seal stamping clay. Only...
To transmit the seal of realization in this manner is not only to deceive oneself, but also to mislead others. Under Dongshan, there is no Buddha-dharma to give;
there is only a single sword. To every person who approaches, he cuts them off one by one, so that their life-force is extinguished and both seeing and hearing are obliterated.
Only then does he meet them before their parents were born. As soon as they step forward, he—
"It is for the purpose of severing. Now, although a sharp sword may be keen, it does not cut those who are innocent. Is there anyone who is innocent?
Even so, they should still receive thirty blows of the staff."
Ascending the hall on the twentieth day of the twelfth lunar month: "The entire assembly of Xinfeng—this is the very nose of the patch-robed monks. A drop of water, a drop of ice. Ascending the hall:
"When a man is poor, his wisdom is short; when a horse is thin, its hair is long. Zhaozhou said, "I made a cloth robe in Qingzhou that weighed seven pounds.
The Master said: "He has years but no virtue. Dongshan saw the hare and released the hawk; he knew of birth, but did not know [the end]."
"O Great Assembly! Those who wish to transcend birth and death do not wade through existence or non-existence. When the Great Function manifests before you, do not follow after words.
I invite the Head Seat, the Steward, and Master Xiaoyao to come. To ascend the hall: Without moving from the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), one establishes a locus for all phenomena.
Yesterday’s title was 'Director of the Monastery'; today’s name is 'Head Seat. Conditions respond in hundreds of thousands of ways; this is the head of the established locus."
"Head Cook! When you hold the handle of the ladle, you must attend to each detail as the occasion arises. If you can harmonize the mouths of the assembly, you shall wander at ease along the same Way.
The standing place of all dharmas has now been revealed. How would you explain the principle of 'the unmoving true limit'?
He gave a shout and descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Within the gate of the Buddha-dharma there is both yielding and seizing. To yield: 'Four or five hundred flower-and willow lanes; two or three thousand pavilions for pipes and strings.
To seize: 'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. But what about when there is neither yielding nor seizing?
After a long silence, he said: 'I always hold the flute for returning home; at night deep, I blow it across the Mùluó River.'"
[He] descended from his seat.
Because the Master of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra had arrived, [the Master] ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-realm is the fundamental substance of the bodies and minds of all sentient beings.
Then, picking up his staff, he said: "This is not the Dharma-realm; it is the numinous clarity that has been vast and open within you all since beginningless time."

Thoroughly penetrating the wondrous essence of vast emptiness and stillness, the lands of this world and other realms, the heavens and the hells, the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of sages, and all things sentient and insentient, are one and no different.
They are neither destroyed nor mixed, like the bright pearls of Indra’s net, mutually interpenetrating and interfusing.
Thus it may be said that within the boundless realms of all lands, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth.
Throughout the ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, nothing is ever apart from the tip of the staff.

If this is so, then it is more than merely casting the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters or containing Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed. Now, the ten billion suns and moons, the ten billion Mount Sumerus, and the ten billion worlds are all contained within this very staff.
[The Master] then throws it down and says: "I cast it right upon the faces of you all!"

[The Master] said, "Did you see it just now? Do you believe it? This inconceivable power of liberation, this playful exercise of supernatural faculties, these wondrous functions manifesting before you—none of them rely on external arts;
they are all the constant attributes of our own mind. He gave a shout and descended from his seat.

Upon returning from his journey through the prefecture, he ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said: 'Going, going, yet truly not going; on the road, do good deeds. 'Coming, coming, yet truly not coming;
on the road, do not fall into peril. These ancients did not see through to liberation; they needlessly created complications that have confused later generations.
Dongshan is not like this. When coming, I simply say I am coming; when going, I simply say I am going. What fault is there in that? Old [Master Dongshan].
When monks enter a prefecture, they stay as soon as evening falls and depart at dawn; what more is there to do?
On the road back, they rest when weary and eat when hungry; what harm or danger is there in that?
Now, meeting you practitioners here beneath the forest trees, what further business is there? After the session, let us drink tea together.

Ascending the hall: It is the extreme cold of late winter. I prostrate myself, wishing that the administrative officers, the head seat, and the entire assembly enjoy ten thousand blessings in your honored persons.
Mid-winter has already passed; early spring has not yet arrived; late winter is now present. The past is truly past; the future is truly yet to come.
The present should not abide; since the three periods of time do not linger, where would the four seasons go?
If this is so, then what fault is there in the gate of the patch-robed monks’ being right and wrong, long and short? He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "I have been in the prefecture for barely ten days; I have been out of the county for only two mornings. If this mind is free from contrivance, then both movement and stillness are *xīyāo* (carefree/liberation).
Holding up his staff, he said: 'This staff must also be *xīyāo*. After a long silence, he said: 'Do not move it!'"
If you stir a single hair’s breadth, I shall break your donkey’s back.
Evening Sermon / Ascending the Hall. The Master raised a case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, “What is it like when one comes face-to-face?

He replied, “Hand it over to the head cook. Again he asked, “What is that which has outflows (*sāsrava*)? He replied, “A bamboo sieve. “What is that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*)? He replied, “A bamboo sieve.”
"A wooden ladle. The Master said, "The bamboo sieve and the wooden ladle are both handed over at once to the steward; do not seek them elsewhere. Each is already fully present.
Although the objects are of ordinary form, their excellence lies in the person. There are those for whom these things are right before their eyes, yet they cannot pull them toward themselves."
One cannot push it away. Even if one were to drag it here by force, one would still harbor a thousand doubts and ten thousand anxieties, not daring to employ it.

There are those who, reaching out with their hands, drag it forth—transcending the present and surpassing the ancient. Thus, a monk asked Yunmen: "What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs?"
The Gatekeeper said: "Steamed buns. O practitioners of Zen, you who value economy of effort: this is indeed so, but does it possess the principle of transcending Buddhas and patriarchs?
Try to decide. If you can decide, then in the Sangha hall you may bite as you please—horizontally or vertically.
If you cannot decide, trouble will fall upon the new and old administrative officers (Dianzuo).
Ascending the hall, the Master raised this case: "In ancient times, there was a monk who cried out loudly at midnight, saying, 'I have attained enlightenment!
A monk standing nearby grabbed him and asked, 'What have you realized? The monk replied, 'A nun is originally made of woman. The Master said, "Excellent! Truly excellent!"
"How many people has he deceived! Yet one must know there is a place where he deceives others. Dongshan also had a moment of awakening; tell me, what did he awaken to?
The master of ceremonies was originally acting as his disciple. How exquisite it is! How many people has he made laugh!
Yet one must know there is a place where he makes others laugh. 'Deceiving' and 'making laugh'—these two phrases are presented together for the sake of the thoroughly trained monk."
An attempt to distinguish between the near and the distant.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "The verse of Xinfeng, the melody of Yunmen—throughout the world those with true knowledge can join in and continue it.

As the assembly stands before the dais, we pray you will clear our ears and eyes. The Master struck the meditation seat once with his right hand. The monk stepped forward and said: "A wooden man claps his hands."

Ascending the hall on New Year’s Day: "Last year’s poverty was not yet true poverty; this year’s poverty is truly poverty.

truly, one could say his style of conduct has reached the pinnacle of our own house. O virtuous Chan practitioners, when Dongshan acted in this way, was it not [the case that]..."
Do you side with the ancients? Or do you support the ancients? Try to discern this!

Thereupon, he struck the incense stand and descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: Great Master Wuben said, "The ancient road is level and smooth; who has placed their foot upon it? No one understands how to sing the tune of returning home.

The assembly believed him. He struck the incense table again and said, "This is not the tune for returning home;
how then shall it be sung? If you can sing it, the five notes and six scales will find it difficult to compare; step by step, one wanders freely, reaching one's native land.
But if you cannot sing it, guarding the stump under the moon is but a trivial matter, and I fear you will let a lifetime slip away in vain. With a shout, he descended from his seat.

Lifting up the north, one knows the south; lifting up the monastic, one sees the layperson; lifting up the sage, one clarifies the ordinary person.

By means of the new, one perceives the old; by means of the sutra, one reveals the casebook. How fitting it is that each and every dharma established therein is both-and-yet. Though both-and-yet, it does not involve duality.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, and the temple administrator’s eyebrows and whiskers fell out. Furthermore, the scriptures state:

[He said,] "Ma. After a long silence, he said, "If there is no one else, only the Head Seat, Master Cheng, deeply understands this principle.

Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "In Jiangxi, they use the Buddha’s hand and the donkey’s feet to receive people;

Chanhe. [A student] stepped forward and said, "Thirty years from now, there will be someone who brings up this story.

"Protecting this [Dharma] lies within you. By taking the cause toward the fruit, all shall attain the Buddha-way. Thereupon, he sat in the full lotus posture. Striking the gavel, he said:

"Are these two? After a long silence, he said: "The superior person resolves everything in a single decision;

those of middling and inferior capacity hear much but have little faith. If you have doubts, please ask. A monk asked: "In the past, the Brahma King invited the Buddha for the sake of the deluded masses.

it is a convergence of pure conditions. The Grand Chancellor, Duke of Jing, and the Vice President of the Council have offered their residence, gardens, and groves.

Thus, there is a separate transmission outside the teachings, which directly points to the great assembly: "See your own nature within this very mind and become a Buddha. Does the assembly believe this?

However, because one has been deluded for a long time, it is truly difficult to gain conviction upon hearing these teachings all at once.

Consequently, one fails to realize that the good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the past and present throughout the world, as well as all methods of Chan and all spoken words, are likewise established by the spiritual friends flowing forth from within their own Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
That which flows forth is the root; the Buddha-nature is the source. The state of the Buddha-dharma in recent times is truly lamentable.

Most people abandon the root to pursue the branches and turn their backs on the correct to cast themselves toward the deviant. They merely recognize that all the words of the ancients constitute Zen and the Way, but what connection does this have?
In truth, even when Bodhidharma came from the West, there was no Zen to transmit;

he only desired that the great assembly would awaken for themselves and become Buddhas for themselves, establishing all things of the Zen and Way for themselves—let alone supernatural powers and transformations, which are for sentient beings.
It is inherently complete; there is no need to seek it externally. Yet nowadays, most people seek it outwardly because they fundamentally lack realization within themselves.
They are merely working as outsiders, counting the treasures of others—all of which is empty and illusory—and in the end, they cannot escape the cycle of birth and death.
