when the Great Matter of the person manifests in its entirety, one is naturally alive—striking against everything, clashing with everything, gnashing and grinding like a tiger wearing horns.
A-he-he! Descend from the seat.
Entering the hall: O virtuous practitioners of Zen, if you can detach yourselves from all marks, you will certainly enter the house of the Dharma King. Such is the path of the Dharma King’s Dharma.

Vast and boundless, his majestic virtue is sovereign, subduing all manner of heterodoxies. With a mind of singular emptiness and stillness, his wondrous functions are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
[He] ascended the hall and said: "Seventy parts, eighty parts, ten billion wondrous gates—these are the legacy of the old adept Huanglong, passed down to his descendants.
Thus, only by knowing gratitude can one understand how to repay it. Is there anyone here who understands how to repay it? You are a man of substance; as soon as you hear of 'repaying'..."

I would rather say this: you have only managed to express seven or eight parts; it would be better to drag you down to the ground, spit in your face, beat you to death, and throw you to the dogs—would that not be delightful?
It would not even be considered excessive. A-he-he! In vain do I take this intention of not returning and speak it to those who seek the Way.
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: One day, Linji and Puhua were at a donor’s house for a meal.

Linji said, “A hair swallows the vast ocean; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. Is this the wondrous function of spiritual powers, or is it simply the natural state of things? Puhua then kicked over the table.
Linji said, “You have attained it, indeed, but you are far too crude. Puhua said, “What kind of place is this that you speak like this?”
He spoke roughly about the details. The next day, he went to another house for a vegetarian feast. Nanquan again asked, "How was yesterday's offering compared to today's?
Yunhua again kicked over the table. Nanquan said, "It is fine, it is fine; you are simply too crude. Yunhua replied, "Blind fellow!"
"The Buddha-dharma speaks of both the extremely coarse and the extremely subtle. The Master said, "In ancient times, those who practiced Chan equally attained liberation;
their insight was clear and, when it came time to act, they acted immediately without any deliberation.

Why was this? It was because they were not hindered by the conceptual knowledge and views of the Buddha-dharma. Is there anyone present now who is likewise unhindered by the Buddha-dharma? After a long silence, he shouted, "Even if there were such a person!"
Furthermore, it is struck within the armor of non-action.
I request the Head Seat to ascend the hall. One instance is new, one instance is old; the new and the old must mutually support one another to achieve fulfillment.
O Zen practitioners, tell me: what is it that is accomplished? Is it the accomplishment of Buddha-work? Is it the accomplishment of the Dharma site? Is it...?
"Is this the tradition of the monastic groves? If it were accomplished in such a way, how could there be a 'separate transmission outside the teachings'?
He then picked up his staff and said, "As for this—does it belong within the teachings or outside the teachings? Is it new or old? You must not call it a 'staff.
If you can grasp it as such, then it is truly accomplished. He then cast the staff down and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master laughed heartily. The monk pressed him, saying, "Why do you laugh?
The Master said, "I laugh because you give rise to intellectual interpretations based on words. The monk replied, "I have simply met with misfortune.

The Master then called out loudly, "No need for prostrations! The monk immediately returned to the assembly. The Master laughed again and said, "Giving rise to intellectual interpretations based on words. He then added, "Excellent, great assembly!"
There is no Chan; there is no Way; there is no mystery; there is no subtlety. One must clearly understand this single aperture to be truly at ease.
If this single aperture is not clear, it will bring one to the brink of despair. As soon as you move, you rely on others and end up mixing excrement with urine. *Can* (the kōan).

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Dharma has no fixed principle; its depth or shallowness accords with the capacity of the individual. To those of penetrating understanding, it can only be known by themselves.
Is there anyone here who is such a person of penetration? He snapped his fingers, gave a shout, and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "This student has a lute that is not made of ordinary wood. Today I bring it forth; I ask the Master to play a single melody.
The Master said: "The assembly, lend me your ears. The monk continued: "I shall now hear what I have never heard before.
The Master asked: "What kind of fingering technique is this? The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master said: "Alas! Alas! How short is your life!"
[The Master] said, "Short. The student said, "For now, let us rejoice that there is no further engagement. The Master said, "Not a true connoisseur. The student said, "It is better to go back;
someone at the Pamir Mountains remembers [the lute]. The Master said, "How can you forget the *jiaotong* (burnt-cock) lute?
The student said, "It is right here. The Master said, "Put it down. He then added, "Just now, when you played a melody, everyone was at a loss. Play it once more; you must do so quickly."
"Listen. He suddenly picked up his staff and held it crosswise. After a long silence, he said, "One tune, two tunes—heard or not heard?
Where has the mournful wind and flowing water gone? He struck the ground with the staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Chang'an is very noisy; my kingdom is at peace. Suddenly, he took up his staff and said, "Master Yunmen is coming! Zha!
"Long rain without sun," he said, striking the incense table with his staff. "Silla is to the east of the sea. Linji’s little page possesses but a single eye.
Puhua, that thief of a fellow, feigns madness and pretends to be demented. What a nuisance is Fenggan!"
[The Master] spoke at length. He pointed out Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

Ascending the hall [he said]: "The mind turns according to the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound. If you recognize your nature while following the flow, there will be neither joy nor sorrow.
"Excellent, O Zen masters! It may be so, and it may not be so; it may be both so and not so."
"Generally accepted. The Tathāgata says that a 'unified whole' (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) is precisely not a unified whole.
Subhūti deserves thirty blows of the staff.

[The Master] descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "To realize it before the sound is not yet to be a master; to take responsibility after the shout is still to be a dull-witted fellow."

The student came forward and said, "I request that the Master grant me an audience. The Master said, "A child is spoiled when the family is wealthy. The student said, "That too is merely speaking of principles.
The Master said, "I will give you one coin. The student said, "Today I am not in luck. The Master said, "This is the very reason for raising a son.
The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "Do not cry. Do not cry. He asked, "In the past, there was the household of a State Councilor..."

"Today I have visited the abode of the Buddha and the Sangha; I do not yet know whether they are the same or different. The Master said, "The moon over the White Egret Shoal. The monk continued, "I do not understand your pivot;
I pray you will grant me a skillful means. The Master said, "Tie your straw sandals tight. As the monk hesitated, the Master said: "No more talk."
Layering the mountain passes. He spoke again: "Of all the myriad arrangements, none surpasses the ordinary;

it does not startle the world, yet it endures for a long time. Well said, O virtuous practitioners of Zen! Where the ancients spoke, and where the present-day practitioners walk—it may be likened to the earth upholding a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness;
or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawless purity. After a long silence, he said: "I only fear..."
"It is not jade. If it were jade, it would be truly marvelous.
[The Master] ascended the hall and said, citing: "Sansheng asked Xuefeng, 'What does the golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net eat?
Feng replied, 'Wait until you have emerged from the net, and I shall tell you. Sansheng said, 'A teacher of fifteen hundred people... [He left the sentence unfinished.]
He did not even recognize his own head. The Master said, "Excellent! Excellent! How joyful! How joyful!
You are just like a hawk; do not let it be startled. Baoning said, "I am not like that. What does a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net eat?
I will tell you once it has emerged from the net. When he said this, [the Master] remarked, "The head-word of the teacher of fifteen hundred people!"
"I do not know. I simply dragged him outside the triple gate with my staff and struck him. Then I said, 'This too is a fine way to be happy!
He is just like a tiger; do not provoke him! Zen friends, tell me: how does Baoning’s happiness compare to Sansheng’s?"
"Is there anyone here who is truly happy? Come forward and let us settle this matter. After a long silence, he gave a shout and said, "I take his hand, yet he cannot be pulled back.
He then ascended the hall. A monk asked, "The incense smoke rises upward and gathers beneath the seats of the fourfold assembly; is this a supernatural power (ṛddhi) or a Dharma?"
[The monk] said, "Is it that way, or is it not so at all? The Master said, "You have already spoken for the entire assembly.
The monk stepped forward and said, "When there is spirit, one adds to the spirit; where there is no elegance, one is elegant nonetheless.

The Master said, "How do you understand this? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "You are a clumsy meditator. The monk shouted again. The Master threw down his whisk and said, "What [is this]?"
"I will not strike another blow. The monk hesitated, and the Master said, "A dragon is not formed upon a staff.

A monk asked, "In the realm of True Purity, a single thought-moment is already eight thousand years on Jambudvīpa. May a student as I be permitted to call myself 'True Purity'? The Master said, "Permitted.
The monk pressed further, "If that is so, then one will drift for eternal kalpas, never finding liberation. The Master said, "A hundred..."
"Pick out the old monk from atop the grass. The monk stepped forward and said, "In that case, the small has emerged to meet the great.
The Master said, "Do not mistake this, monk. The monk bowed. The Master said, "As expected. He spoke again: "The two words 'Buddha-dharma' are also very difficult to clarify.
The Buddhas of the three periods have passed right beneath the soles of your feet. If you intend to see them," [you will never find them].
Already, the eyes have fallen to the ground. Suddenly grasping his staff and casting it down, he said: "Tell me, how far apart are the Buddhas of the three periods of time and this staff?
After a long silence, he gave a shout and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised [the precedent]: Xuefeng said, "On South Mountain there is a tortoise-nosed snake;
you all must look well when entering and leaving. The Master said, "Xuefeng lacked the bearing of a great man. Furthermore, a snake does not move without a head.
"Changqing was just like a new bride who fears her mother-in-law; he immediately said, 'In the hall today, many have lost their lives.'"
[The monk] lost his life. Yunmen dragged his staff and lunged in front of Xuefeng, making a gesture of fear.

The Master said, "Drawing legs on a snake. Xuansha said, "What is the use of the Southern Mountains? The Master said, "To say that my realization is intimate does not exempt me from remaining within the nest;
there is not a single person who possesses even a trace of natural spirit. — From Baoning Monastery.
Is there not, at the very least, someone here with a natural air of integrity? I do not dare hope that you will suspend the sun of wisdom elsewhere or alone shake the profound wind;
yet, it is difficult to find even one who can perceive a trace of the vital breath upon the "hawk-stink" robe of the ancients.
Ascending the hall, he raised his staff and said, "It is raised! The numinous light shines through with penetrating clarity, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.
Then, leaning it askew, he said, "It is lowered! The essence reveals the eternal reality, unbound by words and letters.
Neither raising nor lowering, what else could it be called? He then cast the staff down and said, "Look! After a long silence, he let out a shout and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The ladle handle of the eastern house is long; the ladle handle of the western house is short. Picking up the black-lacquered basin, it turns out to be a white porcelain bowl.
The Emperor of the Great Tang laughs without ceasing; the grasshopper in the fire has three eyes. *Chan*."

On the day of the opening of the assembly at the Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu, after the proclamation of the petitions was concluded, the Master held up the incense and sat cross-legged. Once the Elder of Xiyan had struck the gavel, a monk stepped forward and asked:
"Sitting alone in a thatched hut, who would recognize such extraordinary家风 (family style)? A staff held horizontally across the void—what is its meaning?"

"What is the essential meaning [of this]? The Master said, "Five elders in the clouds; the waters fill the two streams. The student said, "If that is so, then the sword leaves its precious sheath because of injustice;
the medicine comes from the golden jar because of the need to save the sick. The Master said, "A single line breaks the color of the green mountains.
The student said, "Suddenly encountering five horses on a spring day, when the harmonious breath of ten thousand households arises—what then?"
The Master said, "I have been caught by you, Dharma brother. He advanced and said, "The sea god knows its value but not its price;

it remains for the human world to illuminate the night. The Master said, "A sharp and clever monk. A question was asked: "A single sound of the flying staff shakes heaven and earth; where the incense smoke rises, it pervades the entire universe.
On this day, opening the hall for the sake of the nation, with what Dharma will the Master repay the Imperial Grace? The Master [remained silent].
[The Master] said, "The news is at the Yaśas Stūpa. The student asked, "I have received the Master’s indication regarding the Imperial Grace;
what of the matter when the court officials arrive at the assembly? The Master said, "There is already rain following the carriage; why need one stir the dragon of the earth?

The student said, "If that is so, then the tiger crossing the river occurs on this very day, and the pearl returning to Hepu is celebrated this morning. The Master said, "One must know how to acknowledge grace."

"How many people? he asked again. "The mind-seal of all Buddhas has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch; what is called 'the separate transmission outside the teachings' takes its essence from this very point.
This essential and wondrous Way resides in the person, not in the vehicles of the teachings.

It is for this reason that Elder Guizong attained it, and used the seal of the wondrously luminous mind to seal the great assembly of monastics and laypeople alike, such that there was no distinction between self and other, and all were brought to completion together."
Regarding the Buddha-way: can you still believe it? The Prefectural Governor has attained it.

By using the seal of the wondrously luminous mind to stamp upon the affairs of the entire prefecture and its thousand *li*, all paths naturally converge at the same point—a single hair-tip—where each and every thing is clearly understood and each is without error.
Only then does one attain mastery in unfolding and rolling up [phenomena], granting or withholding them as the occasion demands; all of these are the constant domain of one's own mind, and not...

It does not rely on external arts. Du Guan, the Commissioner of Judicial Review, attained this; he used the seal of the wondrously luminous mind to seal the ocean of the Flower Treasury worlds of the ten directions within a single hair-tip.

Whether walking or sitting, going or coming, roaming mountains or playing by the water, selecting beautiful sites or seeking secluded depths, the joy of the Dharma and the delight of meditation are all the constant nature of my own mind—they do not rely on anything else.
The Art: When the various officials obtain this, they each seal it with the wondrous and luminous Mind-Seal (*cittamudrā*). Then, affairs of state and civil matters are understood one by one;
each is without error. Thereafter, what may be done is done, and what may be ceased is ceased—all of which are the constant nature of my own mind, not dependent on any other artifice.
When the Chan masters of the various mountains obtain this, [they realize] the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Gate. Seal each with the wondrously luminous mind-seal, and then every dharma will be clearly understood and each instance will be without error.
Thereafter, responding to capacities and engaging with beings, adapting and transforming according to the occasion—whether manifesting as the sun-face or moon-face, the Buddha-hand or donkey-foot;

whether raising the whisk or striking the mallet, or scolding the Buddhas and reviling the Patriarchs—performing these great Buddhist services are all the constant functioning of my own mind. Thus he took up [the whisk].
He struck with his whisk and said, "Cutting through the tangle. He then threw it down and asked, "What is this? After a long silence, he gave a shout and descended from his seat.
While the Master was at Jiufeng in Junzhou, he took leave of the assembly for the evening *zanchan*. He then raised his whisk and said, "In the past, the World-Honored One held it up..."
The flower. Kāśyapa smiled. Tonight, Guizong raised his whisk; the assembly was silent. Is it this silence that is it? Or is it the smile?
And what, furthermore, is this? Consider this: is Guizong’s raising of the whisk the same as or different from the World-Honored One’s holding up the flower?
If you say they are the same, there is no such thing as a "sameness" in the Dharma. If you say they are different, how can there be two distinct things? For a long time...
The former masters of old understood immediately upon hearing the mention [of the case]; however, those of later generations and beginners must be thorough and meticulous.

After a long pause, he said: "Every dharma returns to the source; when facing circumstances, one must adapt with skillful means. At the place where the wondrous source is clear, there dwells the impartial master.

When the Master first entered the temple and ascended the seat, a monk asked: "The Dharma-banner of Master Huiyuan has been raised; the Zen Master now responds to the occasion. The Patriarchal Command is being put into practice."
“Skillful means point toward the deluded masses. The Master said, “Profound. The student asked, “And what is the meaning of profundity? The Master said, “Shallow. The student asked, “How so?”
"How does the student understand this? The Master said, "A dot. [The student] said, "May the assembly bear witness. The student bows in thanks. The Master said:
"The old monk has lost ground today. [The Master] was asked: "Having left the abbot’s quarters of Jiupeng, you have now arrived at the practice site of Guizong.
What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said: "Where the partridge cries, the flowers of a hundred species are fragrant.

[The student] further asked: "Withered flowers are swept away by the wind; fragrant waters are brought by the rain. The Master said: "It is so now; it was so in antiquity. [The student] said: "If that is so..."
[The Master said: "This one will cause the news of Shaolin to be cut off; yet now its traces remain perfectly intact. The Master asked, "What is the news of Shaolin? The monk bowed.
The Master said, "To point at it is to miss it. The Master said, "The essential mystery of the Buddha-dharma simply lies in returning to its source.
If you return to the source, naturally there is neither 'can' nor 'cannot'; everything is manifest, and the Ocean Seal manifests itself."
Guang: "Now, together with the great assembly, we have returned to the source and abide at the fundamental limit of equality. May I venture to ask: what is this source?
What is this essential subtlety? After a long silence, he said: "Precisely because it is so utterly clear, that which is attained is made all the more slow."

Ascending the hall, he addressed the newly appointed and former abbots, saying: "The old ones have returned; the new ones have taken their places. As the new and the old support one another, let us pass over this point.
[He then] took up his whisk and said: 'It must not be understood in terms of new and old. Since it is not understood in terms of new and old, where does it fall?
If you know where it falls, its utility will be inexhaustible; if you do not know where it falls, [it remains ungrasped].'"
Furthermore, its enjoyment is inexhaustible. If one knows where it falls, then its inexhaustible enjoyment can be understood;
if one does not know where it falls, for what reason is its enjoyment inexhaustible? Let the clear-eyed monk try to judge this.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: "When Red-Eye saw a snake, he cut it in two. A monk standing nearby said, 'I have long admired Guizong;
it turns out you are merely a monk of coarse conduct. Red-Eye replied, 'You are coarse; I am coarse. The Master said:
"The assembly only knows that Red-Eye cut the snake and told the monk, 'You are coarse; I am coarse. But what was the ancient’s point of view?"
He then raised his whisk and said, "Today Guizong raises his whisk; is this the same as or different from Guizong cutting the snake at that time?
After a long silence, he said, "Every person has their own true Buddha-nature, yet they remain entirely unaware of its wondrous, all-pervading function."
Today, [I] point clearly and all at once: who else could it be that brandishes the whisk after slaying the snake?
Entering the hall: The Stone of Dhūta is enveloped in moss; the Peak of Thrown-Pen is entangled by ivy.
At the Arhat Hall, three novices are ordained each year; in Guizong Monastery, one drinks tea after the formal session.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Today is the second month of the fourth season. Have you not heard the ancient saying: 'To let one move pass by is to fall into the second'?
Although it is the second, it cannot avoid being just as it was before: 'In the early summer, the heat gradually increases. Then, laughing heartily, he said:
'Whether there is profit or loss, one does not leave the marketplace. West River, Chengdu Prefecture—leak-proof baskets."
"A single coin, three or five coins—scattered before everyone, each one capable of curing an illness.
Yet, no one knows the price of rice in Luling."
Ascending the hall, the Master proceeded to the Dharma seat, surveyed the assembly, and then returned to his quarters.
Ascending the hall again, he said: "Nanquan’s beheading of the cat and Guizong’s beheading of the snake—these are subjects for discussion within the monastic community.

Is there a distinction of superiority or inferiority between them? Let us set aside the question of superiority and inferiority for a moment; but as for Zhaozhou putting on his straw sandals and walking out—what does that mean?"
If one can clearly realize this, what fault would there be in Deshan reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs?

If one does not clearly realize this, Xuedou’s eyebrows and whiskers will fall off when Danxia burns the wooden Buddha. Thus, fortune and calamity have no fixed gate; they are summoned only by oneself.
(He lets out a shout and descends from the seat.)
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you have a staff, I give you a staff; if you have no staff, I take away your staff.
Great assembly, this is a cash transaction—do not let others deceive you. Do you understand? Whether there is profit or loss..."
"Not departing from walking in the marketplace. Aha ha! Yet I recall Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman; even where there is no elegance, he is elegant.
He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised this case: A monk asked Yunmen, “What is the single song of Yunmen? Yunmen said, “The twenty-fifth of the twelfth month.
Suppose someone were to ask Guizong, “What is the single song of Guizong? One would simply say to him, “The twenty-fifth of the fifth month.
Now tell me, how do the intentions of Guizong and Yunmen differ? How far apart are the present and the ancient?
"How many? he asked. He also said, "As for 'chanting,' what is it like? Yunmen replied, "For now, proceed slowly. Suppose someone were to ask Guizong, "What is 'chanting' like?
Tell him, "Do not err; do not err. Now tell me: is Guizong right and Yunmen wrong? Or is Yunmen right and Guizong wrong?
Then, giving a shout, he said: "Set aside both right and wrong; realize it within right and wrong."
Ascending the hall, he threw down his whisk and said, "Guizong threw down his whisk, and the entire assembly saw it at once.
Even those with the eyes of a hawk or the pupils of a dragon must still be caught in its snare. He gave a shout and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall: Today is the twentieth day of the seventh month. The autumn wind has grown cool and piercing.
All Buddha-dharma is manifest before us, yet it naturally does not enter the ordinary mind. He then raised his whisk and said, "The whisk has already entered.

It is because they lack the understanding of the Buddha-dharma’s insight and vision. You all, seeing that there is no Buddha-dharma’s insight and vision, immediately say, "In a large month, there are thirty days..."
The tenth day. The month has twenty-nine days. Let us engage in a discussion on being "without affairs. He lets out a shout and says, "Blind fellow! He ascends the hall and cites:
A monk asked Master Wuben, "When cold and heat arrive, how can one avoid them?
Wuben said, "Why not go to a place where there is no cold or heat? The monk asked, "Where is that place where there is no cold or heat? Wuben said, "Cold..."
"At times of cold, the *ācārya* is killed by the cold; at times of heat, the *ācārya* is killed by the heat.
The Master said, "If you all can understand this, you will be able to sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) at all times, such that cold and heat do not interfere with one another.
If you do not understand, you must simply pass through winter and summer within the realm of cold and heat. He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall: On the mid-autumn of the eighth month, the cool breeze is sweeping. The coming and going of patch-robed monks is like clouds or cranes.
From the north of the mountain to the south, there is a path that leads through; they carry a single staff slung across their shoulders. It may be so, yet it may not be so.
Whether you realize it or not, you must by all means avoid following the old tracks of others. (He lets out a shout. Descending from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Today, Seat-Holder Yuan has prepared the rice of Daowu and served the tea of Zhaozhou.
He has brought forth the single great volume of the Tathāgata to bring you all to the end of exhaustion. Suddenly picking up his staff and casting it down, he said:
'The rice of Daowu, the tea of Zhaozhou, and the single great volume of the Tathāgata—these three Dharma-gates are all scattered upon the tip of this staff.'"
It is opened! East, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—all are freely subject to transformation and adaptation; one may enjoy them with sovereign ease.
After thirty years, you must not fail Master Yuan. If you do not know this, the rain will soon turn cold and the autumn winds will gradually grow chill.
(He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.)

The donor relinquished his Dharma robe and ascended the hall. To the great assembly: "Those who obtain the Dharma robes of the Buddhas transcend the three realms, depart from the five desires, realize the Great Way, and deliver sentient beings.
He then held up the robe and said: "When it is raised, the bitterness of hell ceases and the asuras halt their battles.
When it is lowered, Śakra shakes his head and the devas suspend their music. Neither raised nor lowered, it pervades the ten directions."
"The Dharma-realm—sentient and insentient beings alike attain the Buddha-way. I do not yet know: what does one who bestows a Dharma robe accomplish?
After a long silence, he said: "Since Old Lu gathered it back in, you must believe that everyone possesses it."
The Abbot of Chang’an returned to the hall and addressed the assembly: "A strand or two of silk, a bolt of brocade—each and every one emerges from the mouth of the silkworm.
From its mouth it spits forth to provide for the world. How is it that the patch-robed monks do not all perceive this?
If they did perceive it, then within the door of every household is the Hanyuan Palace. He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
On the day of opening the furnace, he ascended the hall and said: "Ordinary people are hindered by form; those of the Two Vehicles are hindered by emptiness.

For Bodhisattvas, form and emptiness are without hindrance. Before one's eyes, the myriad phenomena are arrayed in their full splendor; principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated and sovereign. Furthermore, warm fires have been added to the Sangha Hall;

high-minded practitioners from the ten directions gather here together. There is no need to further distinguish between self and other; we are all one true Dharma-realm. He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the twenty-fifth of the tenth month. You must know there is a Dharma that transcends words and phrases;
it is fundamentally luminous and fundamentally wondrous, requiring no cultivation. A group of ancient Buddhas have gone into the hall."
"Elders, after winter, the first yang arises; heaven and earth resolve and transform. You patch-robed monks must not sit and wait for the rabbit.
We are all men of integrity; day by day, the true source is alive. Everyone can see it for themselves—why then do you ignore it? Instead, you follow along with external objects.
(He lets out a shout. Down from the seat!"

Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Festival of the Sage’s Enlightenment: "The sun of Shun and the sun of the Buddha shine ever-bright together; the wind of Yao and the wind of the Patriarchs blow side by side.
It is said that when one person has cause for celebration, the myriad people depend upon it. This is precisely the time to offer prayers for the Emperor’s long life.
Then, he calls out: "Ten thousand years! Ten thousand ten thousand years! He then descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the expanse of the universe, there is a single treasure hidden within the mountain of form.
Setting aside the mountain for a moment, what is this treasure? The Master said: "You, O *dārala*, ride a cow all day long yet do not recognize the cow.
The monk pressed further: "If that is so, then from this day forth I shall return home. The Master asked: "What is that one treasure? The monk was silent.
[The Master] then shouted. The teacher said, "Three by three in front; three by three behind. What about that? [The monk] stepped forward and said, "Thank you for the instruction.
The teacher, however, shouted back and said, "If you do not recognize the pivot of Yunmen, you will end up rubbing your eyes with grime whenever you casually move them. He added further:
That one treasure is neither of this age nor of antiquity; it is neither monastic nor lay, neither male nor female.

Throughout the twelve hours of the day, its radiance blazes forth. Is there anyone who can appraise its value? If there were someone who could appraise its value, they would not fail the lineage of Guizong after thirty years.
Is there no one who will appraise it? This group of people, throughout the twelve hours of the day—
"What is this? He let out a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the middle of the tenth month; the moon in the sky is full. He then took up his whisk and said, "Is this whisk not round?
He further struck the meditation seat and said, "How could it ever be partial? "Great assembly, this very path of partiality and roundness is the sound [of the Dharma]."
The realm of form is vast and tumultuous; the eyes and ears merely hear it. Do not ask the Old Man Guizong. He ascended the hall and said:
"Within the gate of the patch-robed monks, there is nothing that is not a trans-measure realm of sovereign meditative concentration. Then he gave a shout.
He said, "Is this not the realm of transcendence? Then he coughed once and said, "Is this not sovereign meditative concentration?
A-he-he! To take this profound mind and offer it to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Good snow, everyone! Rice, flour, firewood, charcoal—everything is now manifest. When cold, we gather around the hearth toward the warm fire;
when weary, we pull the blanket over our heads and sleep. Good assembly! Just now you came from the Sangha Hall, and now you go back to the Sangha Hall.
He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Great assembly, cease! There is no end to it. Come together beneath these trees to study non-action;
with the same shoulder-carrying *kāṣāya* and a single whisk, how much time can we spend meeting one another? He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
The Great Master of the Illusory City arrives. He ascends the hall and says: "There is no peace within the three realms; it is like a house on fire.

Having escaped the burning house, yet not having reached the place of treasure, one must remain in the illusory city. Today we meet at this illusory city, yet we do not see where the place of treasure lies.
Originally, it was simply the former Elder Yuan. Assembly, originally all of you were simply the people of old. [He prostrates.]
Please take care.
[The Master] ascends the hall and addresses the assembly: "An ancient said, 'The entire earth is this Dharma-gate of liberation.
Yet you mistakenly take it to be the Buddha-dharma. Do you not see that mountains are mountains and waters are waters? Guizong, however, says otherwise: the entire earth..."
This is a dharma-gate of liberation. Do not interpret it through the lens of intellectual understanding or views. At times, when seeing a mountain, do not call it a mountain;
at times, when seeing water, do not call it water. O Great Assembly, you are all men of integrity; do not allow yourselves to be deceived by others.

Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly: "Guizong does not lack Chan to discuss, nor is there no Dharma to be spoken. However, as it is currently snowing and cold, it is not fitting to stand for long.
He then gave a shout and said, "Return to the hall to warm yourselves by the fire."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the fifth day of the first month. I cannot help but raise this matter once more for you. The new sun and moon are clearly distinct;
let the practitioners of Zen not be reckless. Is there anyone here who is not reckless? Tell me, what is it?
He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall: "This morning is the tenth day of the first month. The weather is clear and warm, and the spring breeze blows gently.
The Dharma-gate of unimpeded perception before one's eyes—everyone, enter this realization all at once! (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "O Great Assembly! As for these two characters, 'Buddha-Dharma,' neither side has found a way to gain the upper hand. Is there not among you a lion cub?
I do not dare hope that you will let out a single roar, causing the eyes atop the heads of the entire assembly to open at once."
Furthermore, do not chew on the leftover soup and rancid rice of the ancients; it is difficult to find such things. Today, Guizong shall deceive you all.
Suddenly seizing his staff and casting it down, he said: "The turtle-nosed snake of the South Mountain—those who know how to handle it, take it up."
A shout! Descending from the seat.

Entering the hall: In the middle month of the second lunar season, the weather gradually warms; as the time arrives, the myriad things vie for their loveliness. Do not wait until the peach blossoms bloom to awaken to the Way.
Stepping out the door, the fragrant grasses grow lushly. (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
Entering the hall for formal discourse, he cites the teaching: "Not seeing even a single dharma is a great calamity. (He lets out a shout and says: "What calamity is there?
Suddenly picking up his staff and striking it down, he says: "What affliction is there? Then holding the staff horizontally across his chest, he says: "This is Deshan’s staff."
Linji gave a shout. "In all the world, who can grasp this? Heaven is high, earth is vast, and the myriad phenomena are at rest; this is entirely a good season for monks.
He then threw down his staff and said, "What kind of season is this? He let out another shout and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Samādhi of the World-Honored One was not known by Kāśyapa; the Samādhi of Kāśyapa was not known by Ānanda. Why were they not known?
It is simply because there are differences in depth. The three virtues and six flavors, offered to the Buddha and the Sangha, reach all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm."
Universally making offerings together, the *śrāmaṇera* in samādhi is such that the great assembly does not know him. Why do they not know? Because they do not recognize one another face-to-face.
When opening their mats and unfolding their bowls, picking up the spoons and setting down the chopsticks, the great assembly is in samādhi, each unaware of the others.
Why do they not know? Aha-ha! Again, he takes up his staff and holds it crosswise, saying: "I contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is like..."
[He] did so. [Master] Zhuo leaned on his staff, descended from the seat, and ascended the hall.
Holding up his staff, he said: "The mind of nirvana is easy to understand; the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify.
An ancient said: 'If you have a staff, I give you a staff; if you have no staff, I take it away from you.'"
“Staff-holder,” said Guizong, “it is not so. When you have a staff, I take it away from you;
when you have no staff, I give it to you. Great assembly, while the Bānyu [Banyan] is thus, Guizong is not thus.
Now tell me, which is it—thus or not thus? He threw down his staff and said, “What is this? After a long silence...
He said: "This is the Dragon Girl who attained Buddhahood instantaneously; this is not the same as Shanxing, who fell into ruin in his very birth.
He ascended the hall and said: "Today the monastery is making offerings to the Arhats to repay the heart's vows of donors from the ten directions.
May the deceased be reborn in heaven, and may the living obtain blessings. He called out, "Assembly! Simply follow the custom and eat your rice; do not question it."
"Whether human life be short or long," he said, then picking up his staff, he declared: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life is established;
what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence. The three realms cannot prevail against him; he is worthy of the offerings of devas and humans.
He then added, "This lot of young monks from the forest retreats—each of them deserves twenty blows of my staff! With a shout, he descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly: "Though self and other differ, and though the faculties and objects vary, the nature itself is inherently equal—there is no one who is 'equal.
Since even equality does not exist, how much less can there be inequality? He suddenly took up his staff and said, "Sentient and insentient beings share a single body;
everywhere is the same true Dharma-realm. He then cast the staff down and said, "Falling, it is nothing other than this."
Tell me, what is this thing? (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
Elder Longqing arrives; he ascends the hall and addresses the assembly:

"The teachings state that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who act as good spiritual friends are all seen as having come to see the Buddha. Nevertheless, such good spiritual friends are not easily encountered."
"A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) must not be treated with contempt; Master Longqing is a case in point.
The old monk, together with the administrators, the head seat, and the assembly, shares in this great joy. He then gives a shout and says:

"Of the Tuxi lineage, the descendants of Longshan—Longqing of Jizhou, who has grandly opened the Zen gate. As the ancients said: 'Those who enter through the gate [do not see the mountain itself]...'"
"This is a family treasure. He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Is it a family treasure, or is it an external object?
Great assembly, I ask Master Longqing to decide this for us. He threw down the staff and descended from the seat.
The special envoy from Kaifu arrived, and he ascended the hall. "Recently someone came from Chengdu, who brought news from Tanzhou;
they said that the price of rice in Luling was high. He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "The wind blows and the grass bends. He then threw it down and said: [silence].
"What is it? He gave a shout, descended from his seat, and ascended the hall.
Days pass and months come; long months and short months roll on. As time has already slipped away, birth and death draw ever closer.
The entire assembly are guests under the gate of the Patriarchs; you must know that birth and death are not mutually related. Now tell me, how does Guizong [respond] in this way?
[The Master] spoke. He asked, "Is there also a 'passing over'? After a long silence, he said, "My parents would not permit it;
I could not leave the household life. Ascending the hall, he raised an ancient precedent: "In the past, on the road to Mount Tiantai, there was a woman.
Whenever a monk asked, 'Where does the road to Mount Tiantai lead? the woman would say, 'Go straight ahead. When the monk prepared to walk, the woman would say, 'What a fine master! And then—"

"Going like this," [the Master] said. The Master continued, "Those who travel to Mount Tai come and go in such numbers that they cannot be counted; yet there is not a single person among them who has not been deceived by her.
Only one day, Zhaozhou said to the assembly: 'The old woman under Mount Tai has been exposed by me.
O Great Assembly, although you yourselves may not be deceived by her, if you were to subject her to a critical examination, she would be well worth a beating."
“Zhaozhou’s staff is in my hand. Tell me, where does Zhaozhou’s fault lie? If you know Zhaozhou’s fault, only then will you understand how not to be deceived by others.
Is there anyone under Guizong who is not deceived? With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, said: 'If you cannot realize your own mind, how can you know the Right Path? Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Hanshan said:
'In a single thought, realize your own mind; open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Great assembly, what is this? Realize it directly!
Holding up his staff, he said: 'Who does not see? Who does not know? Knowledge and vision are perfectly clear. He then struck [the floor]."
The Chan Master said, "Who has not heard this? Who does not understand it? To realize the equality of the mind—if one contemplates in this way, it is called right contemplation;
if one contemplates otherwise, it is called false contemplation. He struck his staff once and descended from the seat.
He ascended the hall. After a long silence, he said: "The boatman went down to Yangzhou; throughout the great earth there is not an inch of soil.
The sound of a snake biting a shrimp—there is further suffering for sentient beings. He suddenly seized his staff, threw it down, and said: "Today is the twenty-fifth. He let out a shout.
Descend from the seat. Ascend the hall.
This morning is the first day of the sixth month; all things change with the seasons. The earth is fertile and eggplants abound; the rains are sufficient and sweet melons are cheap.
Red peaches are as large as fists; green plums are round as pellets. Who recognizes the Great Way mind of Guizong? [He] picks it up.
When individuals arrive one by one, it is difficult to discern them. [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff and says:
"If you have a staff, I give you a staff; if you have no staff, I take your staff away. How will you discern this?
If you can discern it, you will not have come in vain to spend the summer retreat at Guizong. If you cannot discern it, I shall have this meditation seat take your place and receive [the blows].
*Phat!* He struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Entering the hall, he said: "The Great Way does not depend on carving or engraving; why must the human mind contrive? Know simply that everything is occasioned by the moment."

"Whatever is brought forth is nothing but a wondrous medicine. He suddenly picks up his staff and says, "Is this not wondrous? Then he throws it down and says, "What fault is there in tossing it here and there?
He then lets out a shout: "As soon as there is right and wrong, the mind becomes chaotic and lost."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "The ancients possessed great wisdom; they were at ease according to circumstances, with nothing that was acceptable or unacceptable.

Thus, when a monk asked an ancient worthy, 'What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? he replied, 'Walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles. The monk said, 'Are walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles not insentient?
The worthy replied, 'They are. The monk asked, 'Can the insentient preach the Dharma? The worthy replied, 'They always do.'"
He spoke; he spoke with fervor, without interruption. The monk attained great enlightenment beneath these words and realized that insentient beings preach the Dharma.
The Master said: "The body and mind of the ancient Buddhas were like drinking *amṛta*; their thirst was forever stilled. How extraordinary! How truly extraordinary!
As for peace and happiness, they were certainly not hindered from being peaceful and happy. Yet, had they been the illustrious descendants of Deshan or Linji, they would not have swallowed this."
"Paṇḍa rice. Why? It is not something he eats. Furthermore, what do those of the lineage of Daowei and Linji eat?
After a long silence, he sighed repeatedly. "Within the gates of the Buddha-dharma, it can truly be said that 'diāo' and 'dāo' cannot be distinguished, and 'yú' and 'lǔ' are difficult to tell apart.
He then descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "This morning is the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month. Do not ask about transcending the Buddhas or surpassing the Patriarchs; simply rest content when you are satiated with rice gruel and meals.
Day and night, morning and evening, naturally revolve and intermingle. He suddenly took up his staff and said: "Revolving and intermingling, or not revolving and intermingling?"
He walked out through the three gates of the Buddha Hall, leaped over the kitchen and storehouse of the Sangha Hall, and pierced the nostrils of everyone with his staff.
Turning back, he again interacted with them, then cast the staff down. After a long silence, he said, "Otherwise, remain in your respective positions. He let out a shout.
Descend from the seat.
Ascend the hall. "A single leaf falls; the world is autumn. From the north of Mount Lu to Jiangzhou—suddenly grasping his staff and casting it down, he said:
"If you know that what has fallen is not a thing other than yourself, you must believe that you attain freedom whether moving forward or sideways."

Dissolving the Summer Retreat, he ascends the hall: "On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, the summer retreat is entered; on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the summer retreat is dissolved.

Within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is autumn and summer, there is dissolution and entry. But within the gate of the Buddha-dharma, there is neither right nor wrong, neither gain nor loss.

Everything is nothing but wondrous function. At times there is entry: for ninety days, it is as impenetrable as water being poured through a sieve; the paths of sages and ordinary beings are blocked."
"Severed! Who dares to cough? If you were to cough, it must be that you understand coughing before you can do so.
Even when you understand it, such that the ten directions are thoroughly penetrated and coming and going are free and easy, you must still know the path and the destination before you can succeed.
But tell me, how is it when there is neither understanding nor binding? After a long silence, he let out a shout and descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season. Yesterday, the bell was struck to escort the Dharma-eye into the stupa;

this morning, the drum is beaten to assemble the Zen community for this ascent to the hall. Among a thousand kinds of seasons and ten thousand varieties of conditions, none fail to be contained within this very thing.
Great assembly, tell me: what is this? He then gave a shout and said: "The views of ordinary beings."
The grasping at a self differs from one person to another. Furthermore, how can you old monk be so strange? He ascended the hall and said:
"Today is the Mid-Autumn Festival of the eighth month; it is precisely when the full moon faces the door. As the saying goes: 'The blind do not see.'"
It is not the fault of the sun or the moon. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low. Those who are deluded are deluded of their own accord;
those who awaken awaken of their own accord. The great assembly should know that you must not be reckless or superficial.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "All sentient beings possess, in their entirety, one and the same wondrous clarity; in daily life, there is no partiality.

Yet, in the ordinary course of things, they are led astray by false teachers, who insist that there is a separate Chan that came from the West. He suddenly took up his staff and said, "Tell me, is this the Chan that came from the West?"
"This is the wondrous, luminous ground of the mind. He then threw it down and said, "Try to cut it off! He let out a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the first day of the ninth month; the night brought a chill of frost. You should know that every path outside the gate leads straight through to Chang'an.
He let out a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mendicants from the various provinces have been gone for years; now they return one after another and present their petitions.
We beat the drum and invite everyone to bear witness together. Today is the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month.

It is not that there is no need for the assembly to bear witness, but you must know that every grain of rice in this alms bowl was obtained through bitter toil. The flavor of the rice in the bowl is known by all of you, yet Guizong says: 'Now...'"
On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month at dawn, how could it be otherwise? After a long silence, he called to his attendant:
"When the formal session concludes, invite the abbots from the various districts for tea. He gave a shout and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "This morning is the first day of the tenth month; throughout the world, the warming stoves have been opened. Yet the eye atop the crown of the patch-robed monk remains as shrouded in dust as ever.
As the years and months pass away, birth and death inevitably arrive. A new layer of straw has been added to the bedding; let the snow pile up as it will.
He then took hold of a corner of his *kāṣāya* and said, "O assembly, everyone has their share; you must open the eye atop the crown of your head."
[The Master] finally attained it. He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Upon ascending the hall, he said: "As the ancients said, 'All day long one is in a state of constant bustle, yet that matter remains unimpeded. The Master remarked: "How simple and essential!"
It is simply like opening the sitting mat and unfolding the alms bowl, picking up the spoon and grasping the chopsticks, raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes—what harm is there in this?
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining; whether moving, still, going, or coming—what difference is there? [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff, strikes the incense table, and says:
"What does it hinder? He then throws it down and says: "One must not call this 'busyness'. He then asks the assembly: "As for that matter, what is it?"
"How is it? After a long silence, he let out a shout and descended from his seat.
He ascended the hall and said: "This day has passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly; like a fish in dwindling water, what joy can there be?

Only those of the Two Vehicles find joy in the stillness and extinction of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); this is their true joy. But for Bodhisattvas who study Prajñā, there is the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of meditation."
To take pleasure [in this] is true pleasure. The Buddhas of the three periods of time take the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—as their pleasure;
this is true pleasure. Shishuang Puhui said, "Rest! Cease! Be cold and still!
This refers to the pleasure of the cessation and extinction of the Two Vehicles. Yunmen said, "All-encompassing wisdom penetrates without obstruction," and he raised his fan.
"It is said that Old Śākyamuni has arrived. This is what is called the joy of the Dharma and the delight of Zen.

The staff of Deshan and the shout of Linji are the joy of the compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and relinquishment of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Apart from these three kinds of joy, there is no joy. Now tell me:
does the entire assembly at Guizong reside within these three kinds, or outside of them? After a long silence, he said: "Today, the monastery..."

The Master serves steamed rice and distributes alms money. After the assembly has retired, he calls for a general invitation to tea within the Sangha Hall. He lets out a shout and descends from his seat. Entering the hall, he says:

"The myriad dharmas are the radiance of the mind; all conditions are but the clarity of the nature. Originally there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires this [present moment]."
The day has ended. Good assembly! The realization of Master Xiu and the realization of the great assembly are no different in their daily application.
The realization of the great assembly and the realization of Elder Guizong are no different in their daily application.

The realization of Guizong and that of Master Yunfeng are no different in their daily application. The realization of Yunfeng and that of Head Seat Shen are no different in their daily application. Thus it is said:
He shouted, "Do not distinguish between self and other. Self and other are without difference; the light of the mind shines together, a marvel for daily use.
He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Who does not see this? Who does not understand this? He struck the incense table and said, "Who does not hear this?
Then he threw it down and asked, "What is this? He gave a shout and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised [the following]: Layman Pang said, "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return as the valedictorians. The great assembly are all people who have come to select a Buddha.
Now that you have arrived under the gate of Guizong, you must each return with an empty mind as the valedictorians; you must not act like long-line monks who merely consume gruel and rice. He...
This renunciant has departed from the secular world. Who says that the Patriarch alone possessed the Southern Can [the Dharma of Neng]?
Entering the hall: "Today is the fifth day of the first month of the winter solstice. Having a matter for you, I shall speak directly. Master Lingtang has arrived."
To provide relief, he opens the great treasury; he dispenses rare treasures without parsimony. Whatever is desired is selected as the occasion demands.

Although each thing returns to its source, it does not hinder the distinction between guest and host. He then shouts, "Tell me, is this the guest or the host? He shouts again, "Guest and host are clearly distinct.
Even those who have long practiced and reached this point must still be crude and unrefined.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single tree does not form a forest; everyone knows this well. Once a Buddhist monastery is established, everyone must lend a hand.
He suddenly took up his staff and said, "A torch before every door. He then threw it down and said, "Each of you look for yourselves!
With a shout, he descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall: "This morning is the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth lunar month. Yunmen’s single song is raised once more. The donkey’s feet and the Buddha’s hand are both manifest before us;
yet many bright-eyed monks are still muddled and reckless. With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The realm of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra fills the eyes; it is clear and distinct right here and now. The Way is everywhere.
He suddenly picked up his staff, threw it down, and said: "What fault is there in tossing it back and forth? He gave a shout and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "In the middle month of the second lunar season, the weather gradually warms. As the time arrives, the myriad transformations are most pitiable. Everywhere the peach blossoms are red and the willows are green;
even the stone produces warm smoke. Suddenly grasping his staff, he threw it down and said: "When one has spirit, add more spirit!"
Where there is no elegance, he is elegant. (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat. Ascending the hall:
The numinous light shines alone, utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects; its essence reveals the true and eternal, unconstrained by words and letters.
This was proclaimed by the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang. "The assembly, how do you understand this? After a long silence, he said: "At home, one suspects it is so."
Guests from other lands become kin. (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat. Entering the hall:
The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa take sound as the Buddha-work. This is what is meant by "The true essence of the teaching in this land is pure in hearing sounds.
Therefore, the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of scripture, totaling five thousand and forty-eight fascicles—
Each and every thing is produced from sound. Even the various Chan paths of the successive patriarchs and the elder monks throughout the world are all produced from sound.

The cypress tree in the courtyard, the North Star hiding its body, Deshan reviling the Buddhas and ancestors, and Linji’s shout—how could these not be produced from sound? How much more so for everything that exists in the mundane world!

Since all phenomena are not accomplished through sound, thereafter sound is inexhaustible, its exposition is inexhaustible, its seeing and hearing are inexhaustible, and its benefit and joy are inexhaustible.
If one enters this Dharma-gate, one attains the sovereign ocean of the *svādhiṣṭhāna-samādhi*.
After a long while, he cried out: "Arhats of the ten directions! He let out a roar and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall: This morning is the fifth day of the third lunar month, precisely the season of Qingming. It is not only that travelers come and go;

there are also bees intoxicated with flight and butterflies dancing about. One must believe that their sovereign spiritual powers and their mutual true nature are wondrously endowed within all things.
In general, this is not annihilation. For a monk to seek Zen awakening elsewhere is to abandon the root and pursue the branches. [He] lets out a shout and says, "When will it be donkey-year?
He descends from his seat. Ascending the hall: Today is the tenth day of the third month. Notice: After long rain, the sun does not shine. The Boatman went down to Yangzhou; the Eastern Sea.
A carp struck with a blow; waves surge to the heavens within Lake Dongting. One must know that the Great Way is fundamentally without partiality.
*A shout.* He descends from the seat. Entering the hall:
Today is the fifteenth of the third month; once again the moon is full, facing the door. As for the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings—do they differ?
"Just watch the chicken, cold, climbing the tree. He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "In spring there are no three days of clear weather; in summer there are no ten days of rain.
He then threw it down and said, "At every turn, green willows are fit for tethering horses; at every household door, one passes through to Chang'an.
With a shout, he descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has said: 'Because a bodhisattva has achieved awakening, they are neither bound by dharmas nor do they seek liberation from dharmas.
They do not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor do they loathe those who violate them. They do not value long-standing practice, nor do they disparage beginners. Why is this so?'"
All are ultimately awakened; because both this and that achieve Buddhahood, it is thus.
It is thus for the Sangha, thus for the laity, thus for the ordinary, thus for the holy, thus for the wise, and thus for the foolish. [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff and says:
"The staff is also thus. He throws it down and says: "Thus, thus!"
Ascending the hall, he raised this case: "In the past in the Western Heaven, there were seven sisters who were wandering in the Śītavana cemetery.
They saw a corpse, and the younger sister asked the elder sister, 'The corpse is here; where is the person? The elder sister said, 'Sister.

The younger sister responded, 'Yes. The elder sister said, 'Where [is that]? Thereupon, flowers were scattered from the air. The sisters asked, 'Who is it that scatters flowers from the air? The voice replied, 'It is I.'"
This was Śakra. Seeing that the Venerable One had eloquently expounded Prajñāpāramitā, he was moved and came specifically to scatter flowers.
He said, "Venerable One, what do you require? I shall provide it for you. The woman said, "I have no other need; I simply want a rootless tree.
