Because the self-nature of nirvāṇa is without attachment, I now respectfully request that you do not follow the way of the śrāvakas, but rather enter a three-month retreat together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas.
For the sake of cultivating the great causal conditions for the unsurpassed, wondrous awakening of a bodhisattva, you shall maintain pure brahmacarya, free from all defilements. If you are able to...
Thus it is. It is said that just as a lotus flower is not defiled by water, the purity of mind transcends even that.
[The Master] ascended the hall. The Great Master Qingze, the Honorable One, had spent several years in Zhejiang on account of the stone sluice, ritual implements, and other matters.

I am filled with boundless joy that you have returned from the mountains. However, from the perspective of a practitioner of the Way, all actions are performed without intentional effort (*manasikāra*).
Since there is no intentional effort, this is the Dharma-gate of great liberation through non-exertion (*anābhoga*); it is what is called "acting without acting.
Whatever comes to hand is grasped effortlessly, without taxing the mind or strength. Thus, the various sacred images and the various scriptures—
"Scrolls, various adornments, various ritual implements, and various Buddha-activities—all are present upon the tip of this staff. [The Master] suddenly picked up his staff and said:
"Surging eastward and sinking westward; surging southward and sinking northward.

When it is cast wide open, from the hall above to the storehouse below—the Buddha Hall, the Sangha Hall, and all the various quarters—are variously adorned and variously pure, filled with the joy of Dharma and the bliss of Zen. Thus he spoke.
He cast it down and said: "Though struck, it cannot be broken; though washed away, it does not disperse. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
There is no formation and no destruction. When a carp of the Eastern Sea is struck with a single blow, the rain pours down like an overturned basin. If you do not believe this, [you shall suffer]."
Within every single mote of dust in all the worlds of the Flower Treasury, the entire Dharma-realm is manifested; jewel-lights and emanated Buddhas gather like clouds.
This is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field. I return this to the Great Master Qinggong; I humbly pray that you will take care of yourself.
Ascending the hall: This morning is the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month. To inform the Zen community, do not be reckless or crude.
The green mountains and clear waters are right before your eyes; each and every one is clearly the Buddha’s Pure Land. If you conceive a thought, it is already impure.
But if you do not conceive a thought, what then? Return to the hall for tea.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In an instant, it is already the fifth month. The seasons intersect; the universal and the particular, the same and the different, arising and ceasing, layer upon layer—each and every one is harmoniously integrated and radiantly pure.
He suddenly picked up his staff and said: "At all times, everything is right here on the tip of this staff.
One does not see a single speck of dust or a single sentient being who has not attained Buddhahood. Now tell me, as for this entire assembly at Lestam Mountain—"
"Is there anyone who does not attain Buddhahood? There is none. He then threw down [the staff] and said, "This is formation; this is destruction.

With a shout, he descended from his seat. Ascending the hall: "Today is the fifth month, again the Double Fifth Festival. According to the dispositions of sentient beings' minds, I distribute these rice dumplings.
Although this accords with what is known, one must necessarily know the place from which each one comes. But tell me, from where do they come? Suddenly, he picked up his staff.
Zhaozhou said: "If you know the place from which this staff comes, you will know the place from which all dharmas come. Therefore it is said:
'In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, they appear according to the measure of what is known; they manifest following one's karma. Now, from where do you all manifest?
Every single thing is clearly present before your eyes. If you know how they manifest, it is truly extraordinary; if you do not even know this, [you are lost]."
"What is called 'leaving home'? He then threw down his staff and said, "This very last stroke is also extremely difficult to comprehend.
He gave a shout and descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said:

"Today is the fifteenth day of the fifth month. For the sake of the assembly, I shall make a definitive decision. Let us all join in the communal labor to achieve Buddhahood; there is no need for wonder."
"Old man, descend from the seat.
After leaving the hall and returning from outside, he ascends the platform again. As the ancients said, "All things are in flux"—this is the common condition of human beings.

If such conditions do not arise, then this old monk’s coming and going, his movement and stillness, would be devoid of the activity of departure and arrival; thus, human affairs would naturally be carried out with complete thoroughness. Furthermore...
What prevents one from sporting in the treasury of supernormal powers and delighting in the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna?
Thus, together with the great assembly, one dwells within the Tathāgata’s ocean of quiescent extinction, the ultimate awakening. (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall: Today is the first day of the sixth month. To inform all of you, do not humiliate yourselves;
every moment of daily life is nothing other than the gate of great wisdom—Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The numinous wisdom of Prajñā rescues one's parents and returns them to the Buddha-land; the sincere faith of the śramaṇa provides a single meal to satisfy the Zen monks.
Since the causes and conditions are present, how can the merit ever be exhausted? He suddenly took up his staff and said, "What is called the numinous source is bright and pure;
its branches and tributaries flow on in darkness. He then threw it down and said, "The mind of non-duality is the same as the *Cantong qi*; return to the hall."
"Go drink tea. [He] gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Entering the hall: "Today is the twentieth of the sixth month; yet I sigh that time passes with such urgency. Look, look—the summer retreat is drawing to a close."
Wiping down the staff and the hat—every action is nothing other than the wondrous application of spiritual power; it is entirely the mind realizing and entering the mind.
There is no need to rush outward in search elsewhere; do not abandon your own city.
Ascending the hall, he said: "This morning marks the first day of the seventh month once again. Summer departs and autumn arrives, yet they lose sight of one another.

Each must awaken to the fact that one's own nature is unborn; every person has already attained Buddhahood in this very moment. O assembly, do not say that I am not being splashed with this foul water.
Nowadays, many in the monastic communities hold such an interpretation."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient precedent. An ancient worthy asked a monk, "What sound is this? The monk replied, "The sound of snakes, eels, and frogs.
The worthy said, "I thought all sentient beings were suffering; yet there are even more suffering sentient beings. Furthermore, another ancient worthy asked a monk, "What sound is this?
He replied, "The sound of raindrops on a banana leaf. The worthy said, "Do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma. The Master said: "There is one..."

A turning word can bring peace to the realm and stability to the state, with a sagacious sovereign and worthy ministers. There is one turning word: "When the country is peaceful, men of talent are honored;

when the family is wealthy, young children are pampered. If you can discern this, I grant that at the crossroads, without storing a single grain of rice or planting a single stalk of vegetable, you may receive and attend to all who come and go as true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). If you cannot discern it, [you shall not].
A hat made of scorched fat; a coarse cloth shirt reeking of hawk-skin. For now, just go this way and that way. (He lets out a shout and descends from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Simply settle the mind through the Zen gate and enter suddenly into the power of non-arising insight.
He suddenly took up his staff and said, "This is not non-arising; it strikes right into your nostrils! When the carp of the Eastern Sea is struck with a single blow, the rain falls like a basin."
"Everyone! This is not a matter of intellectual understanding or views. Who would not be clear about it? Who would not be fully endowed with it?
Who would have no share in it? It is not a matter of sudden entry. Old Man Yan laughed heartily and said:
"If the assembly here at Lestam Mountain can realize this, you will all become the brilliant descendants of Yunmen. If you cannot realize it, you all belong to Old Man Yama."
[The Master] cast down his staff, descended from the seat, and ascended the hall.
"Yesterday someone came from Yuanzhou and received news from Hongzhou, saying that the price of rice in Chang'an is high and the lychees on the Fujian road are ripe.
Three before, three after. Five days at Lestam Mountain."
One bow. Descending from the seat.
Ascending the hall: Today is again the first day of the ninth month; the heat departs and the cold arrives, spring follows autumn.
One must believe that each person’s single matter does not follow the shifting flow of the seasons. Since it is each person’s single matter, why is this so?
There are those who have faith, and there are those who do not. It is said that when the World-Honored One was not present, a single rain moistened the three types of grass and two types of trees.
[The Master] ascends the hall and cites: An ancient said, "It is like a pearl on a tray; it turns of itself without being pushed.

Now, consider when the assembly opens their mats and spreads their bowls, picking up spoons and grasping chopsticks—among all the activities performed at all times, what need is there for anyone to push them?

Only after that would there be a turning. Even down to Yunmen’s "stale cake," Zhaozhou’s "pine tree," Deshan’s staff, and Linji’s shout—what need is there for someone else to prompt them before they respond?
It is simply because you people have failed to awaken and have misunderstood them;
it has nothing to do with those stale cakes, pine trees, staffs, or shouts. Have you not seen the Great Master Huineng say: "You should, in a single..."
Reflecting on this, one knows it is not so. One’s own numinous light is constantly manifest.
Entering the hall, the Master raised an example, saying: "The Great Master Yunmen said, 'The entire earth is this gate of liberation.
Yet people mistakenly take it to be the Buddha-dharma. Why do they not see mountains as mountains and waters as waters? The Master said: "How great was Yunmen's error!"
I would give him thirty blows. Now, since you do not call it "mountain" and do not call it "water," what then do you call it?
If there is a clear-eyed monk who can discern this, I shall return those thirty blows to Letan;
if he cannot discern it, I shall deliver those thirty blows to you, O Acharya. (He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.)

Ascending the hall, the Master raised [the following] passage: The Patriarch said, "When speaking of knowing and seeing, knowing and seeing are themselves the mind; when the mind is present, it is knowing and seeing;

knowing and seeing are right now. The Master said: "If you say this is the separate transmission outside the teachings, and you also say 'it is right now,' then consider this one mind of knowing and seeing:
is it the very mind of knowing and seeing that everyone possesses right now, or is it something else?"

"This is the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas. If you say that these people right now possess this one-minded knowledge and vision, some will not agree, as they speak instead of "mind" and "nature.
If you say it is the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas, then what difference is there? Try to settle this for Letan and see.
If you cannot settle it, you will have wasted the offerings of the faithful in vain.

Ascending the hall: This morning is the eleventh month; the seasonal weather is once again bitter cold. In an instant, the light of time passes away; you must observe for yourself the cycle of birth and death.
Once this day has passed, one’s life-span likewise diminishes accordingly. Like a fish in scant water, what joy can there be in this?
You must know that upon each person’s bare lump of flesh there is a thing that can transform along with all phenomena, yet does not wither with the four seasons. Furthermore—
"What is the Way? [The Master] lets out a shout and descends from his seat.
He ascends the hall and says: "A monk asked Yunmen, 'What is the student's own self? Yunmen said, 'Wandering through mountains and enjoying the waters.'"
The Master said: "Now tell me, did Yunmen answer this monk or not? Do not slander Yunmen! If you say he did not answer him, where is the place where he did not answer?
Most among the assembly rely on their teachers' lineages and intellectual learning; those who merely receive the words lose the meaning.
Even if one does not dwell on written words or language, one may still fall into a state of 'nothingness. This is what is called being stuck."
Words are delusion. If you can recognize Master Yunmen, you will recognize yourself.
Whether visible or invisible, when one dharma is realized as such, only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Patriarch came from the West to transmit a separate teaching outside the scriptures. It is like a cow pulling a cart:
if the cart does not move, one may strike the cart, or one may strike the cow. Great assembly, each person has a water buffalo that pulls a cart;
it is only that their coat colors differ and their mental dispositions vary—some are red, some white, some blue, and some yellow."
"Those who are black—do not wait for the next lash of the whip. Each of you pull your own cart and go to the hall to drink tea.
He descended from his seat.
On the first day of the New Year, he ascended the hall. After the questions were finished, the Master said: "Each question and each answer are all the individual responses of those present."
The supernormal powers and radiant light, the pure and wondrous mind—each and every one is brought forth from within oneself and manifests brilliantly before us.

It is only because sentient beings are deluded in their emotions that they fail to perceive or know this. As we welcome the dawn of a new year, I prostrate and wish the administrative officers, the head seat, and the entire assembly all the blessings in the world.
After a long silence, he says: "Yesterday’s affairs and today’s are not the same; everyone relies upon..."
The original master and host, though equal, add a new year; dream and awakening are fundamentally all empty.
Being empty yet not empty, the twenty gates of emptiness are originally unattached; the single nature of the Tathāgata’s body is common to all. (A shout.)
Descend from your seat.
To offer to the Arhats, he ascended the hall and said: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.
There is not a single dharma that does not arise from the mind. If the mind were extinguished, all dharmas would be extinguished. Therefore, the past mind cannot be apprehended."
The future mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended. Since the three periods of time do not exist, from what could a single mind arise?
O Great Assembly! Simply exhaust all floating thoughts, and you will fully realize arhatship. If floating thoughts are not exhausted, you will remain entirely adrift in the cycle of birth and death.
(He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: An ancient said, "The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom.
Yunmen said, "All-encompassing wisdom is unimpeded. He raised his fan and said, "Śākyamuni Buddha has arrived!"
Again, picking up his fan, he said: "Leaping up to the Thirty-three Heavens, he strikes the nostrils of Śakra.
A sea bream from the Eastern Ocean receives a blow of the staff, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. How excellent is the purity of the knowledge of all modes!

It is non-dual, without division; it is without distinction and without interruption. The Buddha’s hand opens the donkey’s hoofprints; east and west, conditions arise in different places. *He shouted.*
A shout. Descending from the seat, he ascends the hall and says:
"Today we make offerings to the Arhats. Last night, distinguished guests from the four quarters recited the 'Chapter on the Peaceful Practices' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* once.
Assembly, what is this 'Peaceful Practice'? To even conceive of it is already to deviate."
"Peaceful and joyful, it is understood! He then gave a shout and said: "Is this not the Practice of Peaceful Joy? What is 'penetrating the Dharma-body'?
Hiding one's body within the Big Dipper—is this not the Practice of Peaceful Joy? What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
"The cypress tree in the courtyard—is this not the practice of peaceful dwelling? What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs?

A steamed bun—is this not the practice of peaceful dwelling? Thus it extends to the entire assembly of monks and laypeople, each abiding in pure radiance and maintaining the Dharma—is this not the practice of peaceful dwelling?
Even down to a single Buddha, two Bodhisattvas, or each of the Arhats—[is this not the practice of peaceful dwelling?]
"A single Pratyekabuddha has no abiding in the true mark that is not pure; this is what is called 'Peaceful Practice.
O Great Assembly, I have only the jewel within my topknot which I do not give away recklessly. Although I do not give it, it is fully present in every person.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, its radiance blazes forth. Who lacks it? Do you understand? Return to the hall for tea. *A shout.*
A shout. Descending from the seat.
Ascending the hall. Within the gate of the patch-robed monks, there is guest and host. At times, as the guest, one harmonizes with the light and blends with the dust.
In four or five hundred flower-and-willow lanes, there are two or three thousand pavilions of pipes and strings. Sometimes he is the master;
he seizes the thief’s horse and slays the thief. With hair and horns, he enters the marketplace; the *utpala* flower blooms amidst the flames. Great assembly!
Just as when host and guest have not yet been distinguished—how is it? This morning, on the fifteenth day of the third month, the Elder of Zhangjiang came;
he ascended the hall and raised [the following]: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?"
The Gatekeeper said: "The mountain flows upon the water in the East. Letan was not like this. If someone were to ask, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?
you should simply say to them: "Far removed from Hongjing, one enters deeply into the Jewel Mountain.
Assembly, tell me: are these the same or different? Suddenly, if a monk comes forth and says, "What kind of place is this, to be speaking [like this]?"

To speak of this in a way that distinguishes it from others is difficult to attain; one must truly reach this stage before it can be achieved. If you have not yet reached it, do not act with such haste.
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the student's own self? Yunmen said, "Wandering through mountains and enjoying the waters."
Nowadays, most people interpret this as referring to themselves. Those who rely on the words lose the meaning; since you do not interpret it as referring to yourself, how then do you understand it?
Those who cling to the phrasing are deluded. When Deshan entered the gate and immediately struck with his staff, the monk hesitated, and Deshan said, "Do not interpret this as a blow.
Since you do not interpret it as a blow, how then do you understand it? Linji’s single shout was not a shout.
As for its function: since it is a single shout, why not employ it as the function of a single shout? What is its essential principle (*zhongzhi*)?

This essential principle is the separate transmission outside the teachings of all Buddhas and patriarchs; it does not belong to written characters or verbal phrases. These written characters and verbal phrases are but the dharmas of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) external to the mind.
Since it does not belong to conceptual proliferation, one must realize it directly through self-awakening. If one awakens by oneself, then [the matter is resolved].
The same family. If it were otherwise, the paths of self and other would diverge. (A shout. Descent from the seat. Entering the hall:
Today is the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month; rice planting gradually spreads across the southern fields.
Half-hungry, half-satisfied, with plain rice and soup, amidst mud and rain—how pitiful! Only the eminent monks remain entirely unaware. Each return to your own place.
"Go to the hall for tea.
He ascended the hall and said: "In the school of the patch-robed monks, there is spring and winter, autumn and summer, yin and yang, day and night.
Heaven covers and earth sustains; the sun and moon circulate, bringing the four seasons to fruition and nourishing all things. One must know this well."
The wise observe the capacities of beings to establish their teachings and provide medicine according to the ailment, employing various skillful means to bring sentient beings to maturity;
it is just like this. Therefore, do not speak before those who lack wisdom, or you will have your head smashed and your forehead split open.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Śākyamuni Buddha said: 'The continuous cycle of birth and death for all sentient beings arises entirely from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity.
By employing various deluded thoughts, and because these thoughts are not true, there is transmigration. O Great Assembly!
If you wish to ensure that birth and death do not continue, and to extinguish the deluded mind, you need only directly recognize your own eternal [mind] right here and now."

Abiding in the true mind, which is a body of pure and luminous essence, one naturally becomes unconnected to birth and death, and both [the practitioner and the teacher] experience a sense of joy and liberation;

this is what is meant by "once attained, it is attained forever. If one does not believe this and refuses to listen or accept it, one will sink into the ocean of ignorance within the consciousness of karma.
[The Master] lets out a shout and descends from his seat.
**Offering to the Arhats: Ascent to the Seat** "O Great Assembly! All phenomena are the Dharma of all Buddhas;
all minds are the mind of all Buddhas; all speech is the speech of all Buddhas; all paths are the path of the Arhats. This is the Dharma, and this is the mind."
It is speech; it is the Way. Now tell me: is it one, or is it two? Are they identical, or distinct? Two exists because of one, yet even one must not be clung to.
When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The second month followed by the third month—each responding to its own season. Willow threads play in the spring breeze; pear blossoms are white as snow.

Gate after gate is the Dharma-realm gate; every phenomenon transcends words and speech. He suddenly took up his staff and said, "If you wish to know the place where they intersect, look at all the Buddha-lands upon the tip of the staff.
Then, throwing it down, he said, "It does not hinder being cast here and there; it is all within the hands of everyone."
[The Master] ascends the hall, addressing the assembly:
"Today is the fifth day of the third month. Throughout the heavens, there is fine rain.
Not only do the common people sing songs of joy, but even this old monk dances with his hands free. Why is this? Have you not seen how when the Gandharva King played music, Kāśyapa rose?"
[He] dances. Suddenly, Mount Sumeru becomes towering and the waters of the sea surge with waves. He abruptly picks up his staff and says, "O assembly!
When a single wave stirs, all waves follow; the myriad dharmas all return to the one dharma. You monks, let us all realize this together:
even the seven topsy-turvy states and eight inverted positions are all radiant. He throws down the staff and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall: This morning marks the midpoint of the third month. With body and mind free from conceptual thought, one ascends to the other shore.
By extinguishing all causes and conditions, one returns to spontaneity. Two fives make ten. (He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised this case: The World-Honored One asked King Prasenajit, "By what characteristic do you contemplate the Buddha?

The King replied, "I contemplate the true characteristic of the body; my contemplation of the Buddha is likewise so. My contemplation of the Buddha’s true characteristic is likewise so for all dharmas. This applies to the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings."
Root and root, dust and dust—all are utterly pure. Great assembly, if you wish to recognize the Tathāgata’s Great Nirvāṇa, simply exhaust all objects of perception.
(He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.

Closing the Ma Zu Pagoda, he ascended the hall and said: "Under the patriarchal lineage, there is always a pivotal mechanism. In responding to stimuli and engaging with beings, there must be both opening and closing.
If one can open but cannot close, the family is lost and the strategy fails. If one can close but cannot open, who can distinguish the coming and going?
To be able to close after having opened is to be free to play; to be able to open after having closed is a layer upon layer of goodness."
"Or when it is neither opened nor closed, how then? [The Master] said, "Great Assembly!
In the Sangha hall, according to custom, one bites into the soft cakes—biting them crosswise or lengthwise. [He] gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. What do you call 'the Old Śākyamuni'?
He suddenly raised his staff and said, "The thirty-two marks are but provisional names; even the eighty minor characteristics are empty sounds.
All that exists among humans is but a forced designation. He struck the ground with the staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The celestial mind attains mastery; in the height of heat, it is cool once more. If a patch-robed monk can realize this, take care—he is the King of the Dharma.
He gave a shout and descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, the Buddha said: "To leave home and renounce the world is difficult; to study the Way and realize one's nature is difficult. Originally, leaving home and renouncing the world is difficult, and studying the Way and realizing one's nature is even more difficult.
Nowadays, those who study the Way are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet those who realize their nature are not even one or two.
The Buddha further said: "When nature is perfected, the unsurpassed Way is attained. Yongjia said: "The self-nature is the original, heavenly Buddha. Cloud...
Yunmen said, "Nowadays, those in all quarters mostly speak of mind and nature; there is little of this in the teachings. The Master said, "Yunmen also did not permit speaking of mind and nature.
The Buddha said that nature accomplishes the unsurpassed Way. Now tell me, is it what the Buddha spoke that is correct?"
"Yunmen’s teaching is this: 'The multitude, a hair's breadth off, and you are a thousand miles in error.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The administrators, the head seat, and the assembly go out and come in, passing one another; yet upon returning, they are as they were before.
South Mountain faces North Mountain. The busy are busy, the idle are idle; busyness and idleness have nothing to do with one another. As before, they remain amidst the waters and clouds."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an example: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Yunmen said, "When spring comes, the grass grows green of itself.
Another monk asked Shoushan, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Shoushan said, "At the foot of the city of King Chu, the Ru River flows east.
If someone were suddenly to ask Letan, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? I would say to him: "For a long time..."
The rain does not stop. These are three turning words. One turning word can serve as the Dharma-medicine of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas to cure the illnesses of all sentient beings.
One turning word can serve as the secret barrier of the patriarchs and the direct, essential path for Bodhisattvas.
One turning word can serve as the great site of liberation for the patch-robed monks.
"This is the place where the practitioner relinquishes body and life. Great Assembly, if you can discern it, it is like a long-traveling guest returning home;
if you cannot discern it, it is like a traveler who has lost their way. With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Buddhas and Tathāgatas have taught that within the bodies of all sentient beings there are three greats.

What are these three? The Greatness of Essence, the Greatness of Characteristics, and the Greatness of Function. Furthermore, an ancient worthy said: 'In the ten directions there are no walls; on the four sides there are likewise no doors.'"
Bare and naked, stark and clear, there is nothing to grasp. Since there is nothing to grasp, what can you call the "Three Greats"?
Is there anyone who can discern them? If you can discern them, you are no small hand indeed;
if you cannot discern them, sentient beings use them every day without knowing it. (He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.)
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly: "Good rain, drop by drop, falls nowhere else.
Tell me, where does it fall? Does it fall before the Dharma Hall? Does it fall upon the fields and wilds? Does it fall amidst the mountains and forests?
For one who has attained thorough penetration, their spiritual powers and wondrous functions allow for neither 'can' nor 'cannot. Yet there are a certain kind of people..."
They no longer seek wondrous enlightenment, but merely cultivate a straightforward, ordinary, and solid understanding. This is also called being a person who does not wander astray.
Yet such an understanding has not yet emerged from the common stream. A person with wondrous enlightenment and clear vision knows the origin of each thing and knows where each thing lands;
they do not remain muddled or vague. O Great Assembly, tell me: where does this fall?

[This is] the section on the "Abode. Those who have long studied under the former masters may understand this at a single stroke; however, for beginners and those of recent entry, it is more appropriate to examine it with great care.
Once, while ascending the hall during a snowfall, the Master cited the karmic occasion of Layman Pang’s departure from Mount Yaoshan.

The Master said: “Chan guest Quan, failing to cut it off when you should have, you instead met with its confusion. Now tell me, what words should Chan guest Quan have spoken at that moment to avoid [this outcome]?”
Having been thwarted by Master Pang, is there now anyone who can support the Buddha’s work?
Come forth and open the eyes of the assembly, and thereby manifest your own state of mind as a seeker. If there is none, I, this old monk, shall explain it for you.
Today is the tenth day of the first lunar month; as the monastery attendants were clearing out their quarters, someone suddenly asked: "What about all [the monks]?"
"What if the beggar is already inside the lodging? After a long silence, he shouted: "When we meet, do not dismount from your horse;
each has his own path ahead."
Ascending the hall: This morning marks the first day of the third month once again. Since time immemorial, how could the Great Way ever have gain or loss?

Wherever the peach blossoms bloom, there is the mind of Lingyun; yet he laughed at Xuansha for being unable to produce it. That very inability to produce it—rare indeed is one who meets a true connoisseur.
Ascending the hall: This morning is the first day of the seventh month, autumn; the seasons turn in cycles, and summer has come to an end.

The livelihood of a patch-robed monk rests upon the tip of his staff—whether to go or to stay, there is no fixed necessity. To go or to stay is entirely free; yet tell me, is the intent of the Patriarchs the same or different?
As for the ancient saying, "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it enters the water"—what is the meaning of this? *Shouts.*
One shout. Descending from the seat. Ascending the hall, Yunmen said: "The rain has lasted long and does not stop. *Zha* (a written note). Great assembly, tell me:
is this one *zha* of Yunmen the same as Deshan’s staff or Linji’s shout? Or is it different? If you say they are different, how could there be two kinds within the school of our ancestors?"
If you say their Way is the same, how can you account for the differing "house styles" of Deshan, Linji, and Yunmen? When a patch-robed monk arrives here, how does he discern them?

If he can discern them, it may be said that the realms of boundless lands are not separated by a hair’s breadth, and the ten ages of past and present do not depart from a single stroke. Today is the twenty-fifth day of the third month.
Each person returned to the hall to drink tea. [The Master] ascended the hall and said:
"I cite the case where Dharma Master Yinzong asked Layman Lu: 'Virtuous one, while you were at Huangmei, what teachings or essential principles were transmitted to you?
Lu replied: 'That which was pointed out and transmitted to me concerned only the realization of nature to become Buddha; it did not speak of Chan.'"
“Samādhi, liberation, non-thought, and the unconditioned. Zong said, “Why do you not speak of samādhi, liberation, non-thought, and the unconditioned?
Lu said, “Moreover, these are two dharmas; they are not the Buddha-dharma of non-duality. Zong asked, “What is the dharma of non-duality?
Lu said, “If you, sir, were to expound the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and clearly perceive the Buddha-nature, that would be called the Buddha.”
"The Dharma is the Dharma of non-duality. The Master said, "At that time, the minor arts of Chan and the Way were already halfway gone.

Nowadays, in the monastic communities, people mostly discuss only meditative concentration, liberation, non-thought, and non-action. Now tell me: is it the Sixth Patriarch’s way that is correct, or is it the way of today?
If you distinguish between them, there will be opposition and compliance; if you do not distinguish between them, there will be..."
This involves affirmation and negation. If one does not distinguish them, nor discern the heterodox from the orthodox, one buries and obscures our own school’s transmission.
It is like the roads of the world: some are straight, some are circuitous; some are perilous, some are easy. Those who travel these paths proceed when they may and stop when they must.
"Great assembly, do you still recognize the old monk of Letan? After a long silence, he said: "Offer this profound mind to the dust of the world."
"Kṣa! This is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. [He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
When the Master was serving as the Head Seat at Mount Yangshan, he gave a small *can* (private sermon) for the summer retreat, saying:

"Is there anyone who is a true lion cub? Come forth and roar before the assembly! At that time, a monk came forward and prostrated. The Master said: "I do not know whether you are one or not. Are you?"
This is truly most extraordinary. A monk asked: "The moment the bell tolls, the assembly gathers like clouds; now that the period of *jinzu* (the summer retreat) has arrived, how do you instruct us?
The Master said: "Everyone is right here. The monk pressed further: "Is this not the very point where the Master benefits others?
The Master said: "Most people turn away from it within the words themselves. The monk continued: "A single hall, its wind cold and still; for a thousand ages..."
[The monk’s] mind was clear and discerning. The Master said, "Do not speak so confusedly. A monk asked, "I have heard it said of old that 'sentient beings use it daily yet do not know it.
I wonder, what is it they do not know? The Master said, "Speak! The monk pressed further, "What is it like after one suddenly knows it?"
The Master said, "One hundred and eight thousand. The monk held up his sitting cloth (zuoju) and said, "What can be done about this? The Master then gave a shout.
The monk said, "That was a fine shout, yet it has not yet reached a final resolution. The Master said, "Wait for another time to receive a blow of the staff.
He spoke again: "Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? After a long silence, he said, "I almost let him pass. He then shouted. He further raised his whisk and said, "Ye! (Yes!)
Indeed. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether ordinary or holy, monastic or lay, grass or wood—all turn toward the base of this whisk and become Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Without before or after, they are liberated all at once. Is there anyone who is not liberated?
If there were, their life would hang by a thread. Again, he claps his hands and says: "Those who know this are few. Therefore, this...
In matters of practice, one discusses reality, not illusion. One must investigate with genuine investigation; one must awaken with genuine awakening.
If there is even the slightest hair’s breadth of incompleteness, one falls entirely into the realm of demons. Have you not seen the ancients say: "On level ground, there are countless dead people;
to pass through the thorn-brake is to be a true adept"? Nowadays, most people merely attain a state where body and mind are stilled and the past and future are severed. One...
"Think of it as ten thousand years gone—resting, ceasing, like an incense burner in an ancient temple, cold and still.
To take this as the ultimate is not to realize that you have instead been obstructed by this sublime state, which veils your own correct knowledge and vision so that it cannot manifest before you;
thus, spiritual powers and radiance cannot be revealed. Or again, one may cling to the notion that 'everything is level.'"

To take the ordinary mind as the Way and regard it as the ultimate principle is to say that heaven is heaven, earth is earth, mountains are mountains, waters are waters, the monastic community is the monastic community, and the laity are the laity;
that a large month has thirty days and a small month has twenty-nine.
This is merely clinging to grass and perching upon wood—remaining ignorant and unconscious, led straight away into delusion. Suddenly, one asks him: "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?"
[The Master] said, "This is the Master's hand. [The monk] asked, "What is my foot like? [The Master] said, "It is a donkey's foot.

[The Master] continued, "Everyone has a place of birth-connection (*jōen*). Which one is the place of your own birth-connection, Venerable? [The monk] replied, "I am a native of such-and-such a province."
What words are these? Do not misunderstand them. In all actions and undertakings, one must take the ordinary path as secure and reliable;
one must resolve to follow it and remain united with it, not daring to shift a single step further for fear of falling into pits or ravines.
For a long time, one should be like a person who is doubly blind walking along a road, never letting go of the single staff for even a single pace.
It cannot be so. You must grasp it firmly and carry it forth; at every step, you must rely upon it. One day, if your Dharma-eye opens wide, you will suddenly realize your former errors.

You will cast away the staff, open both hands, and find the ten directions vast and empty. Moving freely in all eight directions, whether east, west, south, or north, there is nothing that is not permissible.
How could you ever continue to rely solely on another’s gateway or follow in another’s footsteps? There is [no such thing].
"How very refreshing! But what, after all, is one's own state? Have you not seen how the Great Master Yunmen said:

"Most of the old monks in the world today rely on their teachers' lineages and scholarly interpretations; they spread out conceptual entanglements, produced by striking from a printing block or casting from a mold.
If a person were to go about with clarity, why not deal with everything as it arises in the moment? Furthermore, have you not seen Linji?
The Great Master said: "In my place here, this is the living meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.
It is taken up and used immediately; every point where one stands is the truth. He does not say, 'How was it in the past? or 'How is it now?
Nor does he say, 'This word is permissible,' or 'That word is not. Where is the false? Where is the real? Bring forth even a hair's breadth of a truly real principle for me!"

Look! This is simply because one’s own eyes are not open; having no place of one's own from which to see, one has consistently accepted empty echoes and engaged in a hundredfold taboos, binding and entangling oneself.
Even if one were to speak in this way and suddenly perceive things with clear and bold discernment, it would still be like staring blankly from within a coffin.
Now, is there anyone who possesses teacherless wisdom and spontaneous wisdom? No.
One who dwells as a companion to the myriad dharmas is a resplendent great man, with teeth gnashing and grinding, manifesting a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes.
Seeing me speaking such nonsensical words, you should have come forward and slapped me right in the mouth, pulled down my chair, flung it outside the main gate, and shouted to disperse the assembly.
Would that not have been delightful? Is there anyone who can do so? After a long silence, he said: "If there is no one..."
"Behold this old monk riding the mountain of the altar; leaping into the eyes of you all, he goes about laughing at the Buddhas and reviling the Patriarchs, falling headlong in every direction.
With a shout, he descended from his seat.

When the Master arrived at Chongsheng, the assembly requested a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*). A monk asked, "Before one has clarified the seal of the mind-ground, it is difficult to pass through Zhaozhou’s barrier.
What is Zhaozhou’s barrier? The Master said, "Pass. The monk pressed further, "Is this not precisely where you, Master, benefit people?
The Master asked, "How do you understand this? The monk drew a perfect circle. The Master said, "For now, let us say there is no connection."
The student said, "One must not suppress the noble to make them base. The Master then shouted. He asked again, "Is there anyone else who has a question?
After a long pause, no one came forward. The Master said, "Without an event, wisdom does not grow; yet it is not an obstacle to speak of such matters."
The principle of explanation is also unimpeded. To repay those who study the Way, do not conflate principle with phenomena.
A-he-he! If you wish to attain length, you must enter the water. Amidst right and wrong, within sounds and forms—letting one fall and supporting another up—is this what constitutes the school?
La-la-li! [Suddenly] picking up the staff and drawing a line, he said: "Where have all these preceding complications gone?"
"Go! He then raised his staff and said, "Let this staff transform into Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and pour the water of ambrosia into the crowns of all of you.
Is there anyone here whose eyes are opened and heart awakened, whose spirit is clear and breath is refreshed?
He then shouted, "Do not engage in false imaginings! It is alive and well! Suṃmeru Mountain—seize it and smash it! With that, he threw down the staff.
"Ye! Ye! Thus it was said. The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three were unaware and unperceptive. Śakra, dwelling in the Sudharmā Hall, preached the Dharma to the devas, exhorting them, saying:
"O you ṛṣis, all of you have taken refuge in the Buddha and taken refuge in the Dharma of Jambudvīpa."
Take refuge in the Saṃgha. Refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants;

abstain from eating meat. Practice generosity and uphold the precepts, extensively performing virtuous deeds. By doing so, you will be reborn in this realm and experience various kinds of supreme and wondrous happiness.
You sages, you must not remain solely deluded by such exquisite pleasures; you must know that impermanence is ceaseless, moment after moment. Moment after moment...
"Passing away and perishing; swift, oh so swift! This is precisely arriving and being on the verge of falling.
You all should seek that which neither comes nor goes, neither arises nor ceases—the ultimate liberation and the bliss of pure nirvana. The Master then sighed deeply.
"Today I have exerted my utmost for the sake of the assembly. Yet calamity arises from within one's own gate, leaving the mouths of monks wide open with laughter.
Even so, one must not be careless. Thereupon, he stroked his knee and descended from the seat.

The Master arrived at Jiufeng Mountain. The assembly requested a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*). A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'Three threes before, three threes after. I do not ask about the three threes before;
what are the three threes after? The Master said, "The very thing (*de*). The monk stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then I have taken three steps forward.
The Master said, "The barrier (*guan*). The monk said, "The great assembly bears witness: you are a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The Master said, "..."
The fabricated monk further showed the assembly: "If this matter were to be fully brought forth, it would necessarily cause the monastery to fall into ruin and the community to disperse.
It would overturn Mount Sumeru with a fist and trample the four great oceans underfoot.

The Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, the old monks of the world, and the twelve divisions of the teachings—all would be used to fill the ditches and block the ravines. Even so, [it is] all...
The Dharma has no people; it is merely propagated according to worldly convention. Within the gate of transformative teaching, this would not be permissible. He then held up his whisk and said:

"The Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, the old monks of the world, and the twelve divisions of the teachings—all are fully present, differentiated upon the tip of this whisk.
A cow in Huai state eats grain; a horse in Yi state suffers from a bloated belly. Seek throughout the world...

The physician performs moxibustion on the left shoulder of a pig. Striking with the fly-whisk on the left side, he says: "The great void is the drum; Mount Sumeru is the mallet. He then shouts: "Dong! Dong!
Recognize the Son of Heaven in the bustling marketplace! Taking error for truth, he strikes with the fly-whisk on the right side, saying:
"The great earth is the bed; the long sky is the canopy. He lies prostrate and falls asleep at the tips of the hundred grasses.
He offered incense for his ancestors, saying: "The sick bird perches upon the reeds. Alas! For nine years he sat facing the wall in vain; clapping his hands, he did not turn his head back.
This made the onlookers laugh to death. Is there anyone here now who is an onlooker? After a long silence, he gave a shout, saying:

"In the end, you have merely prolonged your imprisonment to increase your cleverness. He then raised his whisk and said: "I have pierced through your nostrils; now come out from beneath your own heels!"
"East, west, south, and north—vast lands where people are sparse. Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. "A-la-la!
He then cast down his whisk and said, "What is this? He then descended from his seat.
The Master arrived at Dayu. The assembly requested a small discourse (xiaochan). The Master said: "In these two or three months, the weather has been mild and warm;

all things grow and flourish, and the myriad birds sing in harmony. Peach blossoms are red, plum blossoms are white, and everywhere the lush greenery of the gardens blends with the colors of the wilds."

While young people everywhere enjoy the springtime by appreciating the beauty of the landscape and walking upon the green grass, there is only an old monk at an ancient temple sitting facing the courtyard cypress trees.

He then strikes his meditation seat with his whisk and says: "Breaking the shackles and striking the locks; pulling out the nails and extracting the wedges. There are many who are foolish and obstinate, fearing to swallow hot iron. This supreme flavor of clarified butter awaits its proper time.
Zhaozhou’s stone bridge follows the path and keeps to the ruts; Baizhang— (Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "Baizhang," implying a reference to the famous Chan master Baizhang Huaihai.)
The wild fox shall decide this for you once and for all. All doubt shall be utterly cleansed. With eyes flashing like lightning, who can distinguish north from south or east from west?
Is there anyone here who can distinguish them? Come forth and try! [The Master] claps his hands and laughs heartily, then performs a somersault as an offering to the assembly.
First, it is a celebration of a lifetime’s fulfillment; second, it serves as a signpost for all people under heaven. There is.
"Is there? Is there? It is simply because the arising of emotion obstructs wisdom and the shifting of conceptions alters the essence.
Here, I cannot help but tear down the eastern fence to patch up the western wall. [With the whisk, he draws a line and says: "The worlds of the ten directions are shattered into a hundred fragments;
where else could there be mountains, rivers, or the great earth? Look, look! The waters of the four great oceans flow surging before you all."
The earth; its phenomena are of myriad forms, and fish and dragons undergo transformations. Do you see them? If you see them, it is not that there is nothing to see.
Suddenly, suppose a sea-roaming yakṣa were to come forth and say, "Zen practitioner, what is the phrase for escaping birth and death?
What would you say to him? If you do not say anything to him, he will strike you dead with his staff and feed you to the fish.
The turtle eats. At this very moment, what constitutes the body? What constitutes the mind? What constitutes the person?
What constitutes the self? What constitutes the Buddha? What constitutes the Patriarch? What constitutes Zen? What constitutes the Way? Do you understand?
After a long silence, he said: "Rising early at the fifth watch, there are still those traveling by night. He then struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat.
*Recorded Sayings of Ancient Worthies*, Volume Forty-Four.
Recorded Sayings of Ancient Honored Masters, Volume 45.
Verses and Odes by Chan Master Yun’an Zhenjing of Baofeng.
Compiled by his Dharma heir Fushen.

The monks asked about this. The Three Sages asked Xuefeng, "What does the golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net eat? Xuefeng said, "Wait until it has passed through the net, and I will tell you.

The Sages said, "A teacher of fifteen hundred people and he does not even recognize the head of the matter! The Master [Zhaozhou] presented this with a verse: The golden-scaled fish has passed through the net; It eats the clouds and drinks the wind. If you ask what its food is, I say: wait until it emerges from the net, and then I shall tell you.
The Great Master of fifteen hundred disciples— He does not even know the head of the matter!
The weary old fisherman sits upon his fishing platform; golden-scaled dragons, magnificent and vast, surge forth with the waves.
As the sea-gate opens wide and he casts his net, a clap of thunder resounds and heaven and earth part asunder.
Xuefeng said: "When this old monk presides over the affairs of the monastery, letting go and gathering in are matters of his own freedom.
He is fit for both the sublime and the ordinary. Pity those who remain stuck in phrases and cling to words;
they argue about right and wrong until their hair turns white for nothing."
The monks asked: "What was the meaning of Danxia riding the Holy Monk?
To undergo a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, to be sevenfold topsy-turvy and eightfold upside-down—to ride off with the Holy Monk and trample down Shaolao. Then Śākyamuni rose up."
The bhikṣu awakens to the Way. If one understands this meaning, when the cold comes, one puts on a heavy robe.
When the monk asked Xuefeng about the karmic conditions of the "tortoise-nosed snake," it was like beating a drum and playing a lute;
meeting thus, they form a single household. Yunmen is able to harmonize the melody, while Changqing knows how to follow the heterodox.

The ancient song is not a matter of musical meter; it is the turtle-nosed snake of the South Mountain. Who knows its wondrous secret? You, my disciple, are Xuan Sha. A monk asked Master Nantai Yuan about the "Tortoise of Daisui" koan.
Yuan turned his hand over and showed it to him, but the monk was not satisfied. He then went to question the Master (Zhaozhou), who explained it with this verse:
The tortoise of Daisui has no head; Its tail is hidden within its belly. If you wish to see the whole body, Look at the hand that turns it over.
The wondrous secret of Shaoshi was transmitted in secret after observing the student's capacity; Da sui once leaked the mechanism, and Nan tai also made a mistake.
Like turning over one’s hand or the place where one removes shoes or dons a tortoise shell—this is a clear transmission beyond words; how could faith be limited by past or present?
Casting down the golden bell, rolling the iron drum; the water flows east, the sun sets west.
A monk asked Great Master Ma about the "Sun-Faced Buddha" and the "Moon-Faced Buddha.
Sun-face, moon-face—when the barbarian comes, the Han appears. A single point of numinous light undergoes ten thousand transformations and a thousand changes.
A monk requested further instruction. The monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma? Yunmen said, "It is universal, yet free from all intentional mind;
it naturally accords with the Great Way. Its application depends on the occasion; do not distinguish between the sublime and the ordinary."
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen said, "On the water above the Eastern Mountain;
there is a path before one's eyes. Who understands how to pass through it? On the water above the Eastern Mountain, seekers wander in confusion."
The place where all Buddhas emerge: water flows uphill on the eastern mountain. A single snap of the fingers before one’s eyes reveals everything with perfect clarity.
Passing beyond the faces of the sun and moon, the Buddha’s hand and the donkey’s feet are displayed. All receive this very power; beyond words, it delivers those lost in delusion.
The monk said, "Among the assembly, many discuss 'non-affairs' (wúshì). Master, you have again composed a verse that mostly interprets it through non-affairs:
'Non-affairs weary the human mind; do not dwell on either existence or non-existence, and you may naturally discern the numinous sound.'"
"Vast and expansive, though responses differ; remote and silent, they need not be sought. It is fitting that the source of the myriad transformations belongs entirely to this very moment.
The monk asked: "The monk questioned Shoushan: 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?'"
Shan said: "Beside the city walls of King Chu, the waters of the Ru River flow eastward;
when the trees fall and the vines wither, the laughter does not cease.
It is truly wonderful that since Touzi departed, no one has been able to speak of the 'you-you' [flowing] state."
The assembly raised the dialogue concerning the cypress tree in front of Zhaozhou’s hall;
some said these words were spoken, while others said they were not. The Master resolved it with this verse:
"The cypress tree in front of the hall— Zhaozhou did not speak these words. If one is a person of true substance, I do not grant my seal of approval even now."
"The cypress tree in the courtyard"—this was the saying of Zhaozhou. To inform my fellow practitioners: how can it be brought forth when face-to-face?

A monk cited Yunmen’s "hiding one's body within the Big Dipper" and "emerging from the east and sinking in the west. Hiding one's body in the Big Dipper is the decree of the Dharma King; its virtue has no neighbor.

Zhaozhou’s discernment of the old woman was neither mad nor sane—this old man Zhaozhou! Whether ordinary or holy, he is difficult for people to understand. Right and wrong, long and short, are left to your own judgment;
the old woman has been thoroughly exposed by him.
The old woman said: "What a fine master! Yet you go on like this;
at the crossroads there is both water and fire. When encountering the lowly, it is immediately noble—truly most excellent. The path to Mount Tai is without deviation;
how many travelers will cast off their fetters?"

Two Verses on the Cypress Tree Before the Courtyard The cypress tree before the courtyard— I say it is not as good as the pine. Its withered branches break and fall to the ground, Striking last year’s palm fronds.

The power of transformation is impartial and requires no thought; each and every thing is a verdant hue, the very color of the year’s end. Long and short, large and small—all are present before one's eyes.
How laughable that people of this age cannot understand!
The Verse by Huanglong Shanshi: Hanging down his staff, the Master showed the Buddha’s hand and the donkey’s hoof.

As for my own hand, how does it compare to the Buddha’s? Turning them over and over, who can distinguish the beautiful from the ugly? Were one not the cub of a lion, a jackal would vainly attempt to open its mouth.
My feet are like a donkey’s feet; hidden and manifest, a thousand differences and ten thousand errors. Desiring to open the adamantine eye, look at the good and evil right before you.
Every person has their own place of karmic affinity; yet if you fixate upon it, you will lose your way as before. When the clouds break across the vast sky, the radiance of the sun shines forth.
Open! East, west, south, and north—follow Your Honor wherever you go.
The Chan Master Niaoke blew on a tuft of cloth;
Niaoke blew on a tuft of cloth. The red sun is high at midday. Because King Zhao was fond of swords, the people of the entire state wore blades.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the mechanism of the simultaneous pecking and hatching? Yunmen said, "Resonance.
When asked again about the mechanism of pecking and hatching, Yunmen replied, "Resonance. Yesterday thunder shook the heavens; last night the mountain streams rose high."
Baoshou opened the hall. Sansheng pushed forward a monk;
as he flew in on his steed, he was struck by the staff. A blind man turned the whole city of Zhinzhou upside down.
"Peace is brought about by the general, yet the general is not permitted to see the peace."
In the flash of a stone-toss, a film of light divides; a wrathful thunderclap follows, shaking heaven and earth.
Countless people are deaf and blind—among them, who is one who knows gratitude and understands how to repay it?
A monk asked Fengxue, “What is the Buddha? Fengxue said, “The bamboo-staff whip beneath Mount Zhanglin;
the bamboo-staff whip beneath Mount Zhanglin. Water in the deep ravine, moon in the sky. A fine horse does not know where it is.”
Go. Ānanda remained as before before the World-Honored One.
Lingyun saw peach blossoms and awakened to the Way, exclaiming:
"How marvelous! Once I have seen the peach blossoms, I shall no longer doubt the myriad distinctions. Only Xuansha’s words remain unspoken.
Chè: How many of your descendants are true sons?
When Lingyun attained awakening in the past, there were branches upon branches of fragrant buds and crimson calyxes. Now they bloom everywhere once again;
when meeting on the road, to whom can one speak of it?
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, "No.
The monk said, "From the Buddhas above down to the ants below, all possess Buddha-nature. Why does the dog have none?
Zhaozhou said, "Because it still possesses karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*)."

It is said that the "karmic consciousness" remains; who would say that the meaning is not profound? When the ocean dries up, its bottom is finally seen; when a person dies, their mind is no longer known.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the 'hair-blistering sword'? Yunmen said, "Whose skeleton do you think the hair-blistering sword sharpens?
Yunmen’s "skeleton" is indeed worth knowing: once power is in one's hand, wait and see when the command is carried out.
A monk asked Longya, "What principle did the ancients realize that they simply stopped and rested?
Longya said, "It is like a thief entering an empty house;
buying a hat to fit the head, measuring one's talent to fill a post. Even a clear-eyed monk does not recognize him before his very eyes."
A monk asked Changsha: "When one has realized it, karmic obstacles are originally empty; if one has not yet realized it, one must still repay former debts.
As for the Second Patriarch—was he realized or unrealized? Changsha said:

"Emptiness at the opportune moment requires no cleverness; when one attains the meaning, there is no need for effort. Yet people do not understand this; hearing of 'emptiness,' they immediately take it to be a void."
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when one brings nothing at all? Zhaozhou said, "Put it down!
Move from high to low; let go of authority and power. The gate of liberation opens—how pitiable that one cannot attain the true wondrousness of the Empty King!"
Instruction: Movement follows sound and form, being led astray by them.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? Yunmen said, "A steamed bun."

A discourse that transcends Buddhas and surpasses patriarchs—presented face-to-face, who can receive it? Not realizing the arrow has already passed over Silla, they idly dispute over a piece of rice cake while the earth shakes.
This is the pivot of Yunmen’s gate.
The pivot of Yunmen’s gate: few people know its secret message. Sometimes, with a single nudge, the whole great earth is covered in rheumy eyes.
Yunmen draws back; Yunmen draws back.
There is a reason for this. If not even a single point reaches you, then rest—rest, rest, rest!
Linji asked Huangbo about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times;
three times he was struck, yet he did not add even a grain of spiritual provision. As the years have passed since that crossroads, I fear the path has grown ever more distant.
Having been struck three blows of the staff directly upon him, last night he slept as before amidst the reeds.
When Linji reached Dayu’s place and attained awakening, he said, "Huangbo did not have many dharmas. A great man would surely not act contrary to himself;
those two fists beneath the ribs clearly showed his conviction—they were not bestowed by Huangbo."
A monk asked Shoushan, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Shoushan replied, "The daughter-in-law rides the donkey while the mother-in-law leads it.
Zhang Dian was not as eccentric as Shoushan; without moving a single hair, he manifested every manner of marvel. Yet even so, Huanglong could still pick it up once more.
He goes out. How shall one transmit this to those with clear eyes in the four quarters?
The new bride rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads it. She lowers her head and picks up a single coin. At the crossroads, she claps her hands and laughs.
Old Wang from the eastern village has a hole in his roof.
Yunmen said: "A cricket in the fire swallows a large insect;
the axle-pin of the Qin dynasty penetrates the drill-head. The Great Gate of Bestowal opens, its wondrousness inexhaustible. The cricket in the fire remains as lively as ever;
who can take it up and let their heroism run free?"
A cricket in the fire swallows a large tiger; last year was not as destitute as this year.
When the miasma of yellow reeds breaks out, snow presses down upon peach blossoms everywhere red.
While Linji was hoeing in the tea garden, he saw Huangbo approaching. He immediately stood with his hoe supported in his hand.
Huangbo said, "This fellow, are you exhausted? Linji replied, "I haven't even started hoeing yet; what is there to be exhausted about?"
Huangbo struck him with his staff. Linji caught it and gave it a shove; Huangbo fell down and cried out, "Venerable Director, save me!
The Venerable Director stepped forward to support him and said, "How can you allow this madman to be so insolent?
Huangbo then turned the staff around and struck the Venerable Director. Linji then—
After plowing the ground several times, he said: "Everywhere else they practice cremation; here, we bury them alive all at once.
Seizing the banner and pulling the drum requires true spirit. Though father and son are close, the Dharma is not close. To report this to the practitioners of Chan from the four quarters:
do not casually act like those who wait by the stump."
Bai Zhang’s second visit to Mazu:
The traveler’s feelings turn with every step; Great majestic light cannot manifest. Suddenly, one shout deafens both ears;
Natha’s eyes open, and Huangbo’s face appears.
When Xinghua struck the rector Kebin, he said, "A man of stature should be decisive;
you do not understand decisiveness. Xinghua was a man who had reached the ultimate bottom of human nature. Let it be taught that later his own eyes will open.
Having been caned and fined, he was expelled from the monastery.
Yunmen’s Twentieth-fifth of the Twelfth Month:
A single melody transcends past and present. The great radish of Zhenzhou grows deep within the earth.
A monk asked Yunmen, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still any transgression? Yunmen said, "Mount Sumeru does not give rise to a single thought.
Mount Sumeru within the sea—take it up and use it; there is no need for any other needle or chisel."
Baizhang’s Wild Fox:
"Not falling into the hidden point" and "not being dim regarding the division"—he intended for him to shed his fox-body from this moment on.
Everyone they meet says, "I have resigned from office," yet not one person has ever been seen beneath the forest trees.
To the Head Seat Baizhang Shi:
Baizhang’s majestic peak leans against the azure void; Within it, the ancient and modern paths are not solitary. I know not whether that single phrase fell into the trap of the fox— May I ask:
did it exist at that time, or not?
There are those who, having heard nothing, laugh heartily; they do not come to inquire because they are not true connoisseurs. Do not easily leak the ancestral mechanism;
wait until their fox-eyes open of their own accord.
Latent potential unfolds in activity, secretly meeting the opportune moment; such talk of "falling into the weeds" is indeed possible. Under my words, one rarely encounters a true lion cub;
for the most part, there are only packs of wild foxes.
In response to the Commissioner Jiang’s request for verses on ancient cases, I offer these eight stanzas:

The Dharma banner of Yangshan and Miaoyan has long since been toppled; From the very beginning, it is raised up once again. Who would have known that this was transmitted through the severing of an arm?
To manifest this matter, one must rely on a person of great wisdom.
At times, father and son reveal the hidden intent; their spiritual transformations and miraculous powers remain unknown to one another.
To call back those whose karmic consciousness is vast and wandering—this makes the old, ancient master of Mt. Mui laugh to his heart's content.
Shushan’s great laughter is difficult to discuss; the tree falls and the vines wither—there must be a cause for this question.
Even if one were to attain awakening beneath Mingzhao’s words, once the eyes are opened, it is still just that person of old.
From this point on, he took up his stringless lute and retired to hide away amidst the deep, verdant mists of Shushan.
There was a lay practitioner named Jiang from Jingxi who, having heard of him, came specifically to seek out one of like mind.

Mount Moshan, Mount Moshan—its summit that towers above the clouds is never revealed. Its towering majesty, from ancient times to the present, stands before one’s very eyes. It is also said that the Way is fundamentally without the marks of male or female;
were it not for you, who could discern the lotus within the fire?
Neither form nor mind, neither karma nor action; it manifests as male or female according to conditions.
Now, whether monastic or lay, or among all classes of beings, each is clearly manifest and entirely without partiality.

Dongshan covers his ears; once again, the scope of his vision is opened wide. (When Jinbu arrived at Dongshan, he left behind a verse that said: "Only when hearing with the eyes can one truly know. He mistakenly used the character for "ear," hence the remark.

Vast and empty, there is no dharma that is not seen as such. Mountains, forests, tiles, and stones speak freely and spontaneously. If you approach this with ordinary sentiments, it will be difficult to gain conviction.
Inspecting the districts, one need not hesitate to visit the Way in leisure; a single night’s stay in Xinfeng was but a discussion of the superficial.
Beyond the clamor of water and the hues of mountains lies the world of dust—will you find us again when the carriage arrives?
Five Verses Sent to the Elder of Yunju:
At the summit, Yunju is aligned with the Northern Dipper; Yunmen’s insight is held aloft. Do not interpret this through ordinary understandings of penetration;
One must, at the critical moment, leave the mud and water behind.
The summit reaches the clouds, level with the Northern Dipper; hiding one's body within the Dipper is most difficult to grasp. The monastic communities all offer ordinary interpretations;
countless eminent monks have sunk into the mud.
The summit reaches the clouds, level with the Northern Dipper; this extraordinary message requires a person of caliber to uphold it.
Among those who have not yet mastered the school’s transmission, there is nothing but mud filling their eyes as they engage in wondrous deliberations.

The summit reaches the clouds, level with the Northern Dipper; amidst the shimmering light, he is extracted from the midst of clamor. Holding his head high and wearing horns, he boasts of his skillful understanding;
each and every one is further instructed to apply fine plaster.
The summit reaches the clouds, level with the Big Dipper; three across and four down, held up before one’s eyes. The falcon’s gaze in the void is utterly unimpeded;
it yet laughs at the fierce serpent that cannot leave the mud.
On a snowy morning, he ascended the hall. He cited the karmic occasion of Layman Pang’s departure from Mount Yaoshan and further versified its meaning to instruct the practitioners:
"In the realm of Master Pang, a drop of water freezes solid; when the *karmic trigger* does not strike, Master Yaoshan’s two eyes remain fixed."

A dream of entanglement; fundamentally, it is naturally true. Who understands how to employ it? In his room, the Master asked a monk, "Have you understood yet? The monk said, "I have not understood. The Master said, "Have you finished eating your congee yet? The monk said, "I have finished. The Master said, "And yet you say you have not understood. He spoke again: [The Master said: "If you have finished eating your congee, why do you say you have not understood? If you have not finished eating your congee, why do you say you have understood? Speak! Speak! The monk was at a loss. The Master struck him once and drove him out. Later, the monk went to another teacher and reported this. The teacher said, "This old fellow has a bit of a hook, but he lacks the ability to cast it. The monk returned to the Master and related what had happened. The Master said, "That fellow has a bit of a hook, but he lacks the ability to cast it. The monk asked, "What about you, Master? The Master said, "I have both the hook and the ability to cast it. The monk said, "Please show me. The Master struck him once and drove him out. The monk later went to another teacher and reported this. The teacher said, "This old fellow has both the hook and the ability to cast it. The monk returned to the Master and related what had happened. The Master said, "That fellow has both the hook and the ability to cast it. The monk asked, "What about you, Master? The Master said, "I have neither the hook nor the ability to cast it. The monk said, "How can that be? The Master said, "When there is no hook, who needs casting? The monk was greatly enlightened. He bowed and withdrew. The Master called to him. "What sound is that outside the gate? The monk said, "The sound of rain. The Master said, "And you say it is not yet understood.
He asked again, "What is that before you? The monk said, "A screen. The Master said, "And you say it is not yet understood."
He spoke again: "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. He then said: "Listen to this verse:
'In accordance with conditions, every matter is resolved; in daily life, what is lacking? All things are simply ordinary; naturally, there is no inversion.'"
Seeing a monk approaching, he struck the brazier with his fire tongs. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master then offered this verse:
Fire tongs strike the brazier; In daily life there is nothing more. Spreading the mat and unfolding the bowl— Wherein lies intimacy or estrangement?
The monk asked again, "When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted the mind-seal alone; how was that?
He then composed a verse:
Striking the brazier with the fire-tongs, Direct pointing—there is nothing more. Opening the robe and spreading the bowl, Each and every one is a radiant heart-jewel.
In the master’s room, he asked a monk, “What is the single phrase that is without words? The monk was speechless.
The monk then asked, “What is the single phrase that is without words? The master said, “What is the price of rice in Luling?
He also said, “The screen is right before your face.”
Each and every thing is transcendent; each and every thing is profound. Do not allow your conceptual mind to linger therein. From the beginning, the Great Way has been without words or letters;
there is no need for contrivance—this is what is called Chan.
The monk said, "Dongshan’s Chan is difficult to study. The Master then composed a verse:
"Dongshan’s Chan is not difficult; For you, it is repeatedly and ever at ease. The staff strikes open the eyes of heaven and earth:
Behind one mountain range, another mountain range."
Two verses for the assembly: There is not a single dharma that exists; it is simply present as the occasion demands. Seize it and apply it immediately—do not hesitate further.
You should be free and at ease regarding the Dharma; do not seek it elsewhere. With the sword of killing and giving life in your hand, you attain elegance wherever you go.
In the three contemplations of the dharma-realm, as expressed in these six verses, form and emptiness are unimpeded.
With sovereign mastery of will, the myriad phenomena are arrayed, their reflections appearing both within and without; they emerge and subside, coming and going.
In this land and other realms, the mind-seal is vast and empty; it is harmoniously integrated and expansive, where principle and phenomena are unimpeded.
With sovereign mastery as one desires, one can grasp Mount Sumeru upside down and set it upright within a single speck of dust. This is the pure Dharma-body.
A single lump of earth is perfected; a single point of light from a mirror is the oceanic assembly of the ten directions.
All phenomena are unimpeded and sovereign as one wishes within the unmoving site of enlightenment. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the east surges while the west subsides.
A thousand differences and myriad wonders: a cicada in the fire swallows a crab. In every matter there is no obstruction;
all is as one wishes and free. Holding a pig’s head in hand while reciting the pure precepts, he drives [the beast] out of the brothel.
Without yet having repaid the debt for wine, one unties the cloth bag at the crossroads;
in every matter there is no obstruction, and all is as one wishes and free. Picking up a single hair, the myriad realms of phenomena are fully entered in a single thought-instant.
The ocean of boundless lands is right before one's eyes;

whether manifest or hidden, if one does not understand each and every thing, who can perceive emptiness and form? When both principle and phenomena have ceased, the iron boat descends into the sea—like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning.
"Alas! How distressing! I lay my Mo-he sword across my lap; the demons' courage is shattered.
To read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra*: 'This Dharma is equal, without high or low.
If the Buddha’s intent were not guided by the verses of Master Fu (Bodhisattva Daishi), there would be many divergent interpretations. Therefore, water and land are equally true."
At the ultimate limit, the flying body is one and the same; thus, the Way of Buddha after Buddha is identical.
Believing this, I have composed a verse to show all practitioners of dhyāna that the various classes of sentient beings are equal:
they are deluded by the causes of the seven realms of existence; drifting aimlessly, they never awaken at last; in their turmoil, they merely follow after the dust.
Relying on my ordinary nature, by what cause have I attained the Dharma-body? Though my supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are not yet complete, becoming a Buddha is likewise natural and true.
This short song is sent to the Venerable Duan:
Deep is Vulture Peak; bitter is Huangbo. Having come once, one knows its flavor and then returns; having gone, one does not look back. The great earth...
Where has there ever been so much as an inch of soil? My chest is vast and empty; the universe within is wide and open. Why is it so difficult for the east to surge up and the west to subside?
I have long said I would go to Mount Xiaoyao, yet I hear you are already in the vicinity of Yuancheng. This makes me think back to sitting alone on a cold, snowy night.
The pines rustle in the wind, adding to the air of refined detachment. Master Duan, Master Duan, listen to my words: the jade key is in your hand;
you must hold it firmly.
Entrusted to another...
