One, two, three, four, five. When the drum beats for the peaceful era, Dao Wu dances. His feet tread upon the golden boat as the sea moon rises high.
Beneath the rootless tree, dragons and tigers crouch. The *utpala* flower blooms amidst the flames. The precious mirror of Xuanyuan is buried in dung and soil.
To repay the virtuous woman of Yingchuan, who faithfully accepted Māyā, the mother of a thousand Buddhas:
I send this Chan practitioner to Nanxiong to beg for alms—whether seen or unseen, encountered or not.
Ten thousand miles and ten thousand leagues within the perfect radiance, he gazes left and right across the ocean of the Flower Treasury.
Lifting lightly and pressing heavily opens the blind and deaf; this wondrous thing—whether one exhausts it or not—it is here that the flowers fall red upon the gardens.
The creation of heaven and earth has its own seasons; do not compare it to the wind of benevolence that knows no interval. Suddenly, Śākyamuni! Maitreya! Do not be arrogant!
Since he is a man of great capacity, so am I; it all comes down to a single hair-tip.
One can also manifest billions of bodies at will, responding to each situation without a moment’s hesitation. It is truly laughable that people of this age either recognize it or do not.

I present to the Chan practitioner Qing a hundred and eight *bodhi* beads and a six- or seven-foot *khakkhara* staff from Shicheng (Qing was skilled at painting). The Elephant King’s trampling is boundlessly moist;
Bodhidharma left behind but a single sandal. To this day, the whole world prizes gold; it makes even Hanshan and Shide laugh to death.
Shide, Guanyin’s compassion, Pudu’s simplicity, and Vimalakīrti’s inquiry where Mañjuśrī was fit—these myriad wonders and strange forms are inexhaustible.
Who clearly understands this principle? The people of Shicheng are mostly virtuous and good; upon your arrival, O Benevolent One, they all bow in greeting.
If someone asks about the Old Man of Xinfeng, you must strictly avoid accepting his words and falling into duality or three.
The Chan practitioner Songsheng begs for arrows in Yuanzhou to pierce the shadow of the red sun.
The mountain ghost seizes the qilin colt. Dou Ba tears his cloth shirt; the sea god brings forth coral branches.
Whether one penetrates Linji’s Three Barriers or not, whether one knows Yunmen’s Single Character or not—let me ponder this in leisure.
Those who practiced together in the past, laugh until they fall over—the old, ancient adept of Xinfeng. Little Śākyamuni, Great Zen Buddha; beneath Mount Jiyun lies a nest of crookedness.
When meeting, one must discern right from wrong; do not blindly follow human sentiment and suffer in vain defeat.

The turtle-nosed snake, the falcon soaring through the vast heavens—ask everywhere for those with true knowledge: what is this thing? How marvelous! He strides down the lower ridges with noble bearing. How excellent!
He carelessly disregarded his future path.
He followed the Chan practitioner from Luling (who was a disciple of Shishuang from Min) as he begged for alms.
Upon Mount Gusang, clouds formed a canopy; at Shishuang, the waters were as clear as a mirror; within the cave of Xinfeng, he stretched out his legs.
Sleeping. Opening the eyes and rising, heaven and earth are vast and distant. Clapping hands, laughing "he-he" without ceasing. The old barbarian in the hall has the secular surname Zheng.
The price of rice in Luling rises and falls again. One must personally carry the rabbit-horn staff.
If one wishes to traverse all realms and every gate, know that the secret chamber is as rotten as mud.
Sending off the Elder Chang to beg for alms at Mount Yunfeng in Yuanzhou:
four rattan staffs. Who else could attain such carefree ease? The ten-thousand-year-old pine atop Mount Zhurong is a famous landmark throughout the world.
The Five Ranks of Xinfeng are carried upon the tip of the staff. Transverse and vertical, three and four; east, west, south, and north—everywhere.
Coming from within, going forth in the Middle Way; meeting the lowly, one becomes noble; encountering the base, one rises high.
Having bumped into an old woman in a village of three households, he snapped her skirt-belt. At the crossroads, the tipsy old man helped her up and tied her sash for her.
Whether right or wrong, it is all a jumble of scribbling; cease speaking of the patriarchs’ secret intent, and do not inquire after worldly toil. Thus it is said:
The livelihood of a person: their conduct is worthy of praise. *Tu!* With this profound mind, serve the lands as numerous as motes of dust;
though the sons wear different robes, Mount Sumeru stands high amidst the seas, with the sun and moon towering above.
I present this to the Chan practitioner Ya, who begs for a chicken at Shicheng;
he does not seek the sustenance of those who have attained nothing. When the waters rise, the boat rises high; things return to the mind that possesses the Way. With much mud, the Buddha grows great.
Deshan scolded the Buddhas and reviled the Patriarchs, yet he was once led past by Yantou before the Sangha hall. This is the path of the Terrace Mountain.

Regarding the "Old Lady at the Top": there was Zhaozhou who, without even leaving his door, exposed her through his investigation. Only Yunmen, that ancient adept, possessed a mouth that could speak without hindrance:
"Fire is fundamentally no fire. Those who rely on words are muddled; I myself do not agree with this.

It is not that the Way is not penetrating, nor that principle and phenomena are not resolved. For one who has penetrated the unity of principle and phenomena, there is nothing that cannot be used to benefit living beings. Since this is so:
There are indeed those who understand how to establish [the teaching] according to the occasion, yet they are not adept at providing immediate containment.

They can only employ their good intentions directly, little realizing that they will instead meet with calamity. Among the sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age, how many are there who truly know gratitude?
"Yazhan, you have created this old woman’s tangle for me. Do you understand?
Sent to Wei, the Retired Scholar of Nankang, with tea:
In Nankang there is a retired scholar named Wei; from birth his mind has been pure, like a blooming lotus. The wondrous mind of the lotus is empty and void."

All things can perform the Buddha-work like grains of sand and dust. Though the seeds of Buddhahood in sentient beings do not sprout of their own accord, there is none who, upon beholding these forms, does not give rise to the sprouts of the Path.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are naturally worthy of veneration; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are praised by all people.
Is it only the compassionate Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? Are they not also the wrathful and fierce Nāthas? At times they have human heads and ghostly faces; at times they have tiger [skins].

Leopards, tigers, dragons, and snakes—each can manifest transformations as the occasion demands; each response is perfectly appropriate, never missing its mark. Know that all this is sustained by this very power.
Does the Master not know this? He knows it himself. This has always been the most wondrous thing: yet at the first decisive stroke, he was outdone by Danxia.
Who says there is north and south between monk and layman? I say that the holy and the ordinary belong to one and the same family.
The sound penetrates regardless of whether one recognizes it or not; whenever meeting someone, one simply offers Zhaozhou’s tea. Let this assist my daily activities as a Buddhist service.
Those who sip it only complain of its bitterness and astringency. But how can that bitterness and astringency ever be exhausted?
Mud and water give rise to boundless possibilities. All human affairs are themselves Buddha-activities: what is right remains right, and what is wrong remains wrong. Reflecting thus upon the past...
The Old Master Dongshan asked about the Buddha’s understanding of the Way: "Three catties of hemp.
He sent [this] to Qingping at the Ox-Crossing Hermitage in Jizhou;
within the hermitage, he knows nothing of what lies outside. Who recognizes the ox-crossing? It is the conditions for the arising of joy. Sometimes he extends his donkey's steps upon the wasteland.

*Caos*. Again, he opens his "Buddha-hand" before the assembly. In every instance it manifests, yet in every instance it is distinct. Originally, for those who have stepped across [the barrier], there has never been partiality.
Fattened seedlings and tender crops flourish wherever one turns. Though satiated, the ox does not eat—how pitiable! In ten thousand households of the Great Harmony, blue smoke rises;
in a single melody of pure peace, there lies the Chan of clarity. When a guest comes wishing to distinguish the color of the ox’s fur, they see only its length.

The old hermit sleeps within his hut; ordinary people may recognize their own oxen. Its hair and horns are distinct, its head and horns complete; as it strides along step by step, it relies entirely upon another's power.
Do not inquire whether there is some other mystery apart from this state of clarity and peace.
The Chan practitioner Jing was sent to beg for alms in Nankang;

wherever he encountered people, he would come forward. He simply extended whatever principle was appropriate, piercing with a single needle and striking with a single probe, seeking to meet those who truly understand. He did not resort to the artifice of "three heads and two faces."
Let the dust of the passions arise as they will; the Way does not belong to contention. How could the Dharma have a cause? Since the mind has no abiding place, the Way is the thoroughfare.
In the teaching of Nankang, all people are treated with equality: the wealthy are not made wealthy, and the poor are fundamentally not made poor—whether male or female.
The Buddha is also naturally so. Whether wise or foolish, their nature is the Dharmakāya. Who is "other" and who is "self"? Who is distant and who is kin?

Each and every one is luminous and wondrous; each and every one possesses spirit. When facing affairs, they are lively and active; responding to conditions, they are subtly manifest. Yet, they do not themselves realize this awakening.

Chasing after pleasure leads to complacency; I point this out from the very beginning so that you do not drift into ruin. You practitioners of Chan, like Haijing, must not shrink from hardship and toil.
I send these words to the Chan master Longyi, who traveled south to Huineng to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch’s true likeness.

I have heard it said that "Bodhi originally has no tree," and it is also said that "one flower opens into five petals. Whether one can discern the truth between right and wrong depends on having eyes.
May my Way thus flourish with brilliant splendor. As the branches of Caoxi flow together into the sea, the verdant peaks of Baolin Mountain join one another in the human realm.
Within them dwell the true bodies of the Buddhas in their pagodas and temples; we must go there together to pay our respects without ceasing.

Furthermore, having heard that since they were men of great capacity, so am I, I ought not to give way to self-doubt or cowardice. Moreover, have you not seen how the ancient sages regarded their own spiritual nature?
Not even [the teachings of] the masters are valued; how much less do they seek the liberation of the patriarchs? Great Man! Great Man! Whose numinous light is not brilliantly radiant?
When the great function meets the occasion, one is free from intellectual understanding. In every action, how could one ever tread the path of conceptualization?

It is fundamentally not of words and does not belong to the teachings; nor is it the way of Chan—do not be deluded by it. Clearly and distinctly, each thing is free from all marks. Yet people stubbornly cling to delusion.
The head is a paste of flour. As for the practitioner of the Second Dhyāna—whether he is so or not? If he is, there is no harm in going south to see Old Lu.
Send the practitioner of the Eleventh Dhyāna to travel through various regions;
his manifested body is a precious banner of light, and his mind is the treasury of supernatural powers. Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality. A thousand words...

In the end, it all returns to a single point. If you wish to know the separate transmission outside the teachings, this is precisely the model of the Western Arrival. Its spiritual powers benefiting beings are manifest;
its radiance shines brilliantly wherever it reaches. It does not belong to the languages of the various quarters, nor is it concerned with the myriad phenomena of the universe.
Great capacity and great function are innate and natural; whether right or wrong, they transcend all measure. Once attained, clinging to objects of perception is forever severed;
there is no further dharma with which it can be compared. Only this one matter is true; everything else is entirely false and illusory.
May all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm together awaken to this unsurpassed mind. The eleventh dhyāna is the transformative practice of the majestic Great General of the Dharma King.
Later, another person was added for the ten-thousand-year karmic connection, making eleven in total;
with the addition of his son, they became twelve. Whether there was profit or loss, they never ceased going to the market.
The wooden pagoda is the old woman’s Chan; the bride of He-yang is a child. These are universally resolved as the madness of the wind.
Now I shall point directly: to the Layman Li Gao, who requested a verse—O Elder Li!
O Elder Li! Your wise nature naturally penetrates; you know the body is illusory and false, and that dwelling in the world is entirely empty. Whether noble or base, high or low...
Meeting for a brief moment, we are like morning dew; all are like spring blossoms, vanishing in an instant. Who, then, am I?
Only the mind is the Buddha—its spiritual wondrousness is inexhaustible. It is eternal life, free from death; this human nature is the same for all. It is clearly manifest in our daily lives.

Lacking self-confidence, they do not honor [the truth]. Awakening reveals there is neither "this" nor "that"; delusion perceives "west" and "east. Elder Li, Elder Li! You have long cultivated roots of merit.
Your entire household is sheltered by your grace, and auspicious blessings are ever-prosperous. Your descendants delight in goodness, their minds harmonious and pure in their right faith.
Within the teachings of all Buddhas, whether praised or reviled, one remains like the blind or the deaf;
thus, all demonic afflictions naturally melt away, and the resolve for the Way becomes firm and steadfast from beginning to end.

I send off the Chan practitioner Zhao with his teeth chattering and grinding. People say I am malicious; they judge right and wrong. I say that people do not act; they neither act nor refrain from acting.
Neither aversion nor delight; the joy of Dharma and the rapture of dhyāna. Shedding stickiness and untying bonds—this is the house style of Huanglong. Buddha’s hand, donkey’s feet:
descendants of later generations must open up their own path for themselves. Greatly opening the three barriers, the final stroke, though it involves words and language.
It does not reside in dregs; it is a pure and luminous source. What difference is there between this and that? It is spiritual power and radiance, the perfection of Great Enlightenment.
One must strictly avoid conceptualization. To respond to the illness, one administers the medicine.

Chan Master Fang requested that his teacher personally write a verse for him to take as a keepsake, insisting that it be handwritten by hand and not composed by another. [The teacher replied: "When both parties possess the *yongyi* (as they wish), one administers medicine according to the illness."
In the midst of clamor, what prevents the Buddha’s hand from opening? Before you can even deliberate, the donkey’s hoof has already stepped forth.

Even a blue-eyed barbarian would surely lose his way at this point. This is not for the sake of deliberately distinguishing between the clear and the turbid; it is a living surging and a brilliant clarity.

Fundamentally natural from the start—why need one bind oneself? Those who can harmonize with the melody of "Returning Home" are rare; when encountering the marketplace, Ganmu merely plays for amusement.
[This is] sent to the beggars of the various prefectures.

For the beggars of all districts, there is no distinction between "this" and "that" on the Way; they cut straight to the root—what more is there to deliberate? Nature is fundamentally a single source, and its functioning is without duality.
Simply exhaust all ordinary sentiments, and there will be nothing else but the supreme meaning. In every encounter with objects and conditions, everything is none other than the Buddha-work.
Whether there is profit or loss, he never leaves the marketplace. Carrying dry wood with him, he performs his art wherever the occasion arises. Sometimes contrary, sometimes compliant;

sometimes wrong, sometimes right; one as host and one as guest; one seated and one rising—his illumination and function are applied according to the moment, and his methods of granting or seizing have their proper basis.
The descendants of Linji; the core essence of the patch-robed monks. They teach and transform sentient beings, bringing their capacities to fruition.

In every household is Avalokiteśvara; at every door is Mahāsthāmaprāpta. For children and adults alike, spiritual powers are their livelihood. Those who understand have no doubts—the Dharma King has passed away.
I see off the Chan practitioner De as he begs for alms in Pingjiang.

A single stream flows eastward through Pingjiang, piercing through thousands of gates and ten thousand households; the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma is clearly manifest, yet people of this age simply ignore it.
Only when it reaches the vast ocean does it finally rest—vast and surging, without beginning or end, flowing on of its own accord.

Lingyuan also appeared to have attained great enlightenment through Zen meditation. If his mind-ground were thus transparently clear and the Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye were fully revealed, what would prevent him from bringing forth the family treasure?
He could then go wherever he saw fit to save sentient beings according to their capacities. He was told that if he returned on this same day next year, he would be permitted to do so;
otherwise, he was to remain in his current position.
Nantai and Foyan have joined the elders for the summer retreat;

this summer at Nanyue and Nantai, the evening meal is so restricted that not even a drop of water can pass through. The pine and cypress trees vainly draw in the cold wind, and the ground is unclean with moss.
It is said that one must "restrain the feet" for ninety days, yet every person has a tongue in their mouth. As for those who observed the summer retreat last year...
It is all exhausted. From now on, it will be entirely cast as iron. Little do they realize that there is Buddha and there is Dharma;
how could one possibly know how to shift the concave to become convex? One simply waits to don this hemp robe, prepared for the summer heat of the coming year.
A Parting Gift for the Daoist Master Ye:
A single leaf falls; the world turns autumnal. The evening sun sinks westward as the waters flow east. When the Yellow River clears, a sage appears.
How vast and distant are the affairs of three thousand years! Rarer than rare, fewer than few— They have caused me to live in vain and grow old time and again.
Now we all rejoice in dwelling in a time of great peace; what prevents us from studying the Buddha and seeking the Way in leisure? Return! Return!
Old Lu need not remain at Huangmei; the Mind-Seal of Puguang is a treasury of spiritual powers. In daily life, the eyes open clearly of their own accord.
I send the practitioner Qi to act as a mendicant monk among the ranks;
seizing or relinquishing as the occasion demands, the numinous serpent is held in his hand, he rides upon a fierce tiger, and whenever there is a beard, he plucks it at once.
If there is no tail, do not pursue; let it go to prevent thirst. Hold it fast to recognize hunger. Guest and host are easy to see; hidden and manifest are difficult to conceive.
This is the Great Way of the Chan school; the Dharma-eye is compassionate.
Seeing Master Xian-official depart for Huanglong to visit his teacher, I write:

Tranquil and serene, a single mass of auspicious clouds leaves the sea mountains. Rolling up and unrolling, appearing and disappearing, it follows its own course; How could it be like thin mist lingering around a fisherman’s cove? Tranquil, tranquil—his feelings and demeanor turn toward the southwest.
Huanglong has long made an appointment, waiting for him to bring forth rain. I... (Note: The final character "我" [wǒ] appears to be an incomplete or fragmentary ending to the verse.)
Now, let us follow Hu Gaopan’s parting gaze as he harmonizes with Old Monk Huangbo’s verse on Layman Li treading upon the broken scale-beam;
the two sections are clearly distinct. I shall speak directly for you: Huangbo’s bitter words were often resented during the three months of winter.
"Where is there no snow? [The Master replied: "Difficult! Difficult! It makes me recall Master Pang and his children, who lived together with their heads close, neither marrying nor taking brides.
The Layman Zeng of Jizhou and his brothers have come down from the mountain;
they go back down from the mountain. When it is time to travel, they travel at dawn; when it is time to stay, they stay at dusk."
On the road, he is with his brothers; at home, he is with his wife and children. Do not find these words too ordinary;
they are precisely the most essential points for you. As for these essential points: three, four, five—Sumeru leaps and Kāśyapa dances.
Sent to the Venerable Jingin of Fuyan:

At present, atop the Southern Terrace, white clouds enshroud the lofty peaks and the bright moon illuminates the shallow waters. Who would say it is the same as the sun? Only one who shares a common understanding can truly recognize it as such.
A man from the borders of the Northern Ridge; a child atop the stone of the Southern Terrace. He saved Old Lu’s head, yet lost the teeth of Shaolin.

He sends forth a Chan practitioner to beg for the heart of a Buddha-child in Yuanzhou, where not even a hair or a speck of dust clings. An bottomless basket overflows with dragon pearls within the city of Yuanzhou.
Letting others set the price, one day he returns, riding backward on an iron horse,
to escort Chan Master Yan to the state of Jizhou so that the Buddhist disciple Xin may beg for alms.
With great joy and great renunciation, he calls a tortoise a turtle and points to a deer as a horse, drowning out the sound of the Xian River waters.
The price of rice in Luling; each and every dharma-gate; seizing the dead snake to bring it back to life.

Sending the Chan practitioner Qing to beg for the heart of a Buddha in Chongyang—there is nothing that does not benefit and bring joy. Within the realm of sentient beings, he administers medicine according to the ailment, sometimes manifesting the Buddha’s hand.
Or perhaps a donkey’s hoof emerges; my school stands resplendent. Do not err, do not err!

The Zen practitioner Tai has sent word seeking rice—the heart of a Buddha-son is capable of bestowing such grace. When the grain ripens before the mountains, the rice among men shall be pure white; ten sheng shall yield one dou.
The two elder brothers, though merely exhausting their ordinary worldly sentiments, did not let a single coin go to waste.

They channeled their hearts toward the Buddhist disciples engaged in the construction of temples; they performed as the occasion required and acted according to circumstances as they arose. Thus, they were always able to fulfill their intentions regarding the Buddha Hall and the three gates.

Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are accomplished with a mere snap of the fingers. At Jiufeng Mountain Temple, I passed by Yijing Village where the venerable Mengcai requested a verse on the ancient Buddha’s家风 (household style).

It has always been known to oneself; it is not a matter of exerting mental or physical effort. When, suddenly, a flash of lightning bursts forth— At that moment, the ancient Buddha’s household style is present. It is not something to be sought through intellectual deliberation; it is the very state where one does not labor the mind or body. When the sudden flash of insight occurs, the ancestral tradition is revealed. It is not found in books or in the words of others, but in the spontaneous realization of one's own nature. This is the true lineage of the Buddhas and patriarchs. It is not a matter of gradual cultivation or external achievement, but of recognizing the original face within the midst of daily life. When the conditions are ripe and the karmic connection is met, this truth manifests like a bolt of lightning, illuminating the darkness of ignorance. Thus, at Jiufeng, I have inscribed this verse for the sake of the Dharma, so that the true spirit of the ancients may endure. It is not a fabrication of my own making, but a direct pointing to what has been so from the beginning. May all who encounter it awaken to their own inherent wisdom.
Having already become a guest of Shao Yang, you ought to be a cub of the lion. Before your eyes, whether ordinary or holy, do not harbor a single one of them.
Furthermore, for the request of Zhuangzhu Man, I offer this verse:
The wise are able to stand alone; When flowers bloom, spring comes naturally. Do not be a companion to the myriad dharmas; How could you consent to be a person halfway through the path?
How vast is the expanse of heaven and earth! How fresh is the majesty of sun and moon! Amidst the ordinary act of casting them aside, who recognizes this as the true nature?
Sent by Rao Shou to Zou Ji-sheng:
This body is a collection of filth; it cannot be otherwise. The wise know it to be an illusion; food and drink merely provide temporary nourishment.
Within this lies the pure Dharma-body; who can recognize its brilliant, refined, and wondrous nature? You and I are no different; once attained, it is attained forever. To Official Ye:
Two Poems This mind is difficult to perfect, yet I shall forget all artifice;
how much more so now that I am amidst the robes and caps of the wealthy and noble. Day after day, I eat my plain rice, content with my lot.
Attained. This floating life is empty and illusory; to whom can it be explained? I am able to express my awakened intent only through these verses;
I do not harbor the sentiment for chanting to compose further poems. This one kind of dwelling at home transcends the mundane; even Māgha of the Western Heaven was like this.
The path of contemplation nears and grows ever more manifest; that which was previously attained is profound. The true nature of reality is empty and pervasive;

the mind named "Pure" is bright and clear. What hindrance can royal affairs pose? The toils of the mundane world no longer invade. The wondrous spirit dwells within daily life; who is ancient, and who is modern?
To Zhang, the District Magistrate of Yichun, who has sent this letter:

The myriad classes of beings are in a state of bustling activity; each and every one is inherently true and fundamentally non-abiding. Is it that only you, Illustrious Sir, possess this wondrous clarity?
I, too, have attained spiritual awakening from within this very state. Sentient and insentient beings, as well as the holy and the ordinary—when the gate of liberation opens, they are all one.
The entire path—both king and subject—can be known for themselves. This is the Tathāgata’s own direct entrustment.
You, O Master, have paid homage to the Teacher and requested a verse;
there was a monk who recently came from Mount Lu and suddenly asked me for a Zen verse. Since I had to improvise on the spot, I composed it for him.

Penetrating. A human head with a ghost’s face transcends words and meanings; how much more so when the Buddha-dharma has no fixed capacity for those to be taught? In the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), there have always been those who have attained penetration.
You, my son, must have long experienced the monastic groves (Conglin); what you say, though appearing disheveled and rambling, is neither right nor wrong.
The Chan Master Zhang’s Jiaman:

His nature is empty and luminous, free from discursive thought. Dwelling here in constant quiescent illumination, all phenomena are within the perfect radiance; pure and serene, they are one in wondrous subtlety.
He has opened a pond to nurture white lotuses, and his gate faces the path of the marketplace. I have no mind for human affairs; thus, human affairs do not reach me.
Entrusting this to the Daoist Zhang of Tangpu:
worldly dust and toil have now been thoroughly exhausted. Like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon, you have refined yourself through hardship until this present day;
let not the precious moon of your body and mind ever depart. Death and rebirth arrive in an instant; as for this illusory and transformative body and mind—
Spring Snow. Only the Way-man possesses a moon-like mind; throughout daily life, it is vast and eternally pure and bright.
One day, while the Magistrate of Jing’an, Official Cheng Jietui, was touring the mountains, he found that the names of the various halls and quarters were vulgar and redundant.
He accordingly changed each name according to its function, renaming them as Incense Cultivation, Diligent Progress, Vast Clarity, and Realization.

Regarding the topics of Essential Nature, Emptiness, the Limit of Reality, Non-duality, Definitive Meaning, Dharma-patience, Sublime Function, Harmonious Gathering, and Clouds and Cranes, this old fool has composed a verse for each.
Furthermore, I have composed a general verse; these thirteen pieces are hereby sent for your perusal.

One cultivates and perfects the path to Bodhi through habitual practice; it is only through such cultivation that success is achieved. Although the principle is realized instantaneously, the task requires gradual elimination of defilements.

A mirror depends on repeated polishing to become bright, and gold must be refined again and again to become pure. It is advised that one first benefits oneself, and only thereafter benefits all living beings.
To reach the six perfections of diligence, first board the vessel of prajñā. Abiding naturally in non-abiding, how could there be any further traces?
The courageous and brave can achieve Buddhahood; the indolent will not reach the goal. Relying on your shared exertion, may all practitioners cultivate with total vigor.
Kuo Ran always sat in silence whenever he came; his breast was vast and open, as expansive as the measure of heaven and earth. His mind encompassed the sun and moon.
Although Master Pang has passed away, Old Cheng again finds a kindred spirit. Listen now to this rain that nourishes the world; it is hoped that external protection will be profound.

To realize the essence is to reach the Buddha-mind essence. When there is not even an inch’s deviation, then practice and understanding correspond. Beholding and honoring establishes the relationship of teacher and disciple;
carving jade shall produce a vessel. Do not ask about the whetstone—every single command of the patriarchs who came from the West is exactly like this.

The nature of emptiness is the nature of both Buddhas and sentient beings; their perfectly luminous essence is fundamentally identical. Seeing and hearing are shared by all; grasping and rejecting are entirely non-empty.

Abiding within phenomena, it can remain hidden; when meeting the capacity of the occasion, its understanding manifests adaptability. Whether discussing Chan or managing secular affairs, each instance reveals its complete efficacy.

The limit of ultimate reality is the wondrous, profound dhāraṇī; it is the body of luminous awakened nature. To those living at home, it seems like a stranger; yet to those from another land, it is a kinsman.

Gradual inducement ultimately fails to inspire faith; when held up high, it only redoubles their anger. Now, in this final age of the Dharma, if I were to teach as a human being, [how could they believe?]

With non-dual equanimity, he regards all his children; the gate of the household opens as one. There is no fixed destination on the traveler’s journey; wandering traces all return home. The Dharma-treasure is named "Wish-Fulfilling";
the companions of Chan are called "Good Wealth. Together they roam the Flower Treasury Realm; the entire universe is contained within a single speck of dust.

Having realized the ultimate meaning, one who was once deluded by the head now recognizes it as but a reflection; once fully awakened, all that was previously grasped is seen as non-existent. Only the Way-mind remains, with no further reliance on the ailments of Zen.
Amidst stillness, one hears the water flow past; in leisure, one watches the bees fly. Each is a matter of natural spontaneity—whom can they share as their common home?

The mind is ever tranquil when facing the objects of *dharmakṣānti*; the numinous source is fundamentally unborn. Events respond according to high or low, and capacities are assessed according to shallow or deep.
To discern and reveal such divine function, and to gaze and penetrate such luminous awareness—there is nothing that is not the power of *dharmakṣānti*. Do not seek further outward for its sound.

The wondrous application of spiritual powers and the wondrous application [of wisdom]—in welcoming and seeing off, and in attending and accompanying—require no further instruction from others; they come spontaneously according to circumstances.

The illusory body is like grass and wood, while the pure nature transcends all dust and defilement. I offer my deepest thanks to Layman Cheng, who has called back my lost head from its state of delusion.
The Dharma-gate of harmony and integration is fundamentally non-dual; wherever one arrives, that becomes home. The shaven head is like a sandalwood tree; the square robe is like a lotus flower.
With the six harmonies as companions and the four means of attraction as a boundless path, how could it be that only the practitioners of Chan alone ascend the Great Jewel Chariot together?

Clouds and cranes pass by at dawn; in the evening they take up lodging. In this mountain hall, one is free to go or stay. A solitary cloud can be as it pleases; a lone crane moves with even greater ease.
The *zhilin* staff opens the green eyes; the *kāṣāya* robe accompanies the white head. Failing to clarify the meaning of the Western Patriarch, my drifting traces wander aimlessly.

Entrusting this to those who possess penetration—what need is there for such people to discriminate? Each and every path is without partiality; should one attempt to distinguish between superior and inferior, one will surely fall back into the fetters of delusion.
Mind after mind is identical in becoming Buddha; dharma after dharma together discusses Chan. Simply exhaust all ordinary sentiments, and the eastward-flowing waters will fill the valley.
Ten Verses on the Meditation Pavilion:
To gather the mind is called pure precept; meditation is named *pāramitā*. Having reached the shore, one still leaves behind the raft; practicing compassion, one further delivers others.
Awakening the heart brings birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; seeing one's nature is knowing Amitābha. Right here beneath this bright pavilion, there is *bodhisattva mahāsattva*.
Second: Although delusion and awakening are distinct, they are one in the mind of equanimity. Do not seek it in Yunmen; do not look for it in Linji.
When flaws are eliminated, white jade is formed; when ore is exhausted, pure gold is found. Peerless and inconceivable, the wondrous source is most profound.
Third: Originally we were all Buddhas together; it is only through deluded thoughts that we remain entangled. If you do not cultivate the Way today, when will you be able to cast off these fetters?

It is best to return at once to the Treasury of Jewels; cease further mistaking empty fists for treasure. Within each and every one, the true nature is manifest: a lotus flower blooming amidst the flames.

The fourth: The original source from the West was not two; the variations transmitted throughout the world are but differences. There is not much to the Buddha-dharma, yet how many schools and gateways there are!

The roles of host and guest distinguish the hare from the horse; blows and shouts discern the dragon from the serpent. Students should examine these matters with great care; alas, the present state is truly lamentable.

Fifth: The various patriarchs transmitted the mind-seal; when has there ever been a separate "Chan"? When the vehicle of the school is misunderstood, differences arise; when the Buddha-dharma is realized, there is no partiality.
Precious enlightenment is vast in every person; the spiritual mechanism is perfect in every circumstance. Do not seek out extraordinary doctrines, lest you let your own field fall into ruin.

Sixth: Those of the Hinayana do not perceive the nature; they seek meditation as something separate from the mind, falsely manifesting the bliss of Nirvana. Thus, deluded, they are ensnared by afflictions.
How could they know that the moon at the bottom of the deep pool is originally the sky above the house? Yet they further take the words of the ancients to be a marvelous transmission.

The seventh is the power of sporting in supernatural transformations (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita-bala*). Each and every one is fundamentally unborn; the Bodhisattva can personally realize this, while the Tathāgata is even more wondrously luminous.

The Śrāvakas hear it but do not yet believe; the Pratyekabuddhas perceive it and are still startled. Only those with the vessel of the Mahāyāna find that as soon as the spiritual source is activated, it becomes pure.
The eighth: The Buddha-nature is a matter of natural truth; who says there is another teacher? Where a man snaps his fingers, a woman emerges from meditation.
Without expending the slightest effort, how has she ever moved her thoughts? All sentient beings are entirely equal; yet in daily life, they harbor many doubts.
The Ninth:
In studying the Way, one must first clarify that there is awakening. The Dharma-seal of the Dharma-King stamps all things without partiality;

when brought forth, every matter transcends the ordinary; when held up, every mind is entirely free from conditions. Because sentient beings possess inverted understandings, they do not contemplate the patriarchs of old.
Coming to transmit [the Dharma], we sport together in the Lotus World; master and attendants intermingle before these reflected images. Tenth:
the place where dragon-elephants delight in dhyāna from dawn to dusk is profound and surpasses this windowed chamber. The mind is the play of supernatural powers.
The treasury: the body is the banner of luminous wisdom-illumination. Though it appears dual according to the high and low capacities of beings, its return to the source is fundamentally non-dual.
If one can perceive this as identical to the true reality, even externalists and celestial māras will bow their heads in submission.

In the Great Dharma Hall, there is no great meaning and no written words. Who says that the Dharma was transmitted? This mind is originally pure and wondrous; this Dharma is fundamentally luminous and perfect.
Every person who has a basis is a Buddha; every thought-moment is Chan without birth. Spreading the sitting mat and unfolding the alms bowl—one by one, they are lotuses amidst fire.

The second: The Great Meaning is the very dwelling place; it encompasses all within a single morning. Saints and ordinary beings alike enter quiescence; leaders and attendants together wander in leisure. A little speech yields great spiritual power;
much learning brings abundant wisdom and understanding. When meditation is over, roam the Garden of Awakening; friends, let us invite one another to join.

The nature of the Illuminating Pavilion is fundamentally bright and wondrous; how could it ever be defiled by delusive conditions? Its constant radiance is eternally still and illuminating; its pure wisdom and pure emptiness are perfectly complete. All beings are equal within this state;
when the opportune moment arises, everything is manifest before one. This excludes only those who lack faith—for how could that which is outside the teachings have been transmitted in vain?
The second:

The teaching transmitted outside the scriptures from the West relies on words to bring about awakening. The mind is the treasury of spiritual powers; the body is the pavilion of wisdom-illumination. The Dharma is the seat of equal emptiness;
skillful means are the gate of total retention (*dhāraṇī*). Its great significance is spiritually inexhaustible; each school of Chan has its own source.

In the Dharma Hall and Lanxuan Studio, the evening responds to the season of cool clarity. Flower buds emit the fragrance of the nation; the lineage of the Xie family was short-lived, yet the teaching tradition of Confucius endures long.

Possessing such virtue, who else could rival them? Even without anyone present, they remain naturally fragrant. In the Lanxuan Studio, there are many practitioners of Chan; their Buddha-nature and precepts are as pure as ice and frost.
The second:

Even without people, it is naturally exquisite; how much more so when planted in the family of the Brahma-kings! The monastic community shares in pure karma, and white flowers bloom in the courtyard of meditation.

Their dialogues constitute dharma assemblies, nurturing the sands of the obstructed stream. This is truly like a practitioner who constantly applies the cultivation of precepts and meditative concentration.
In both spring and autumn there are orchids; I have again composed a verse to clarify this:
The crane is white and the crow is black, yet the mind is the source of transformation. Though the two polarities possess form, the single vital breath is fundamentally wordless.
All things fulfill their natures; the four seasons return to their abodes. Autumn flowers and spring blossoms—their fragrance ever fills the orchid pavilion.
Five Verses Sent to High Sheriff Gao of Jingnan:
If you grasp at the mind as something to be discarded, who would there be to distinguish host from guest? Not knowing the nature of delusive thoughts is itself the mark of a wise person.
It requires only self-awakening; suddenly forget the duality of subject and object. Simply observe the Buddhas and Patriarchs—one by one, they are all transparently true.
(2) The power of knowing and seeing non-arising has already realized the mind within the Zen gate. It was not obtained from Bodhidharma; how could it be sought from Śākyamuni?
Do not be drowned by the wordless; you must prevent yourself from sinking in the verbal. That which is already perfected is ever-present; only through awakening does one realize its depth.

(3) Those of the Lesser Vehicle cultivate minor dharmas, falsely manifesting a desolate dhyāna. They strive for stillness and delight in non-thought, detesting clamor and fearing the presence of conditions.
Not knowing that the Buddha-world is one's own field of mind, one rises and sits as bright as the sun; all sentient beings share in this luminous clarity.

(4) Among those who study the Way, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who can seek it within themselves? Two people find delight in the nature of dhyāna; their minds are as bright as the moon over a thousand li. (5)

Its brilliant clarity is shared by both monastics and laypeople; its spiritual penetration spans both past and present. Do not attempt to explain it through mundane arts; it would be a pity to let it remain buried and lost.
(5) The ambition of a true man and a great hero is to cultivate his own field. Do not pursue the words of Yunmen; do not rely on the Chan of Linji.
Every person is fundamentally complete; every dharma is inherently perfect and round. Simply act as the master of masters; in every gate, you are the sun and moon deities.
Harmony opens the way for Elder Fuku to escort the Chan practitioner Kyō with these seven verses:
whether moving against or with the current, all is eternal youth. Whether right or wrong, the spirit remains unmoved; it constantly follows along with sounds and forms.
Turning back, one again obscures the person of original nature.
When the single breath first harmonizes with it, all things are springtime. Without laboring at effort, how could one labor the spirit? It is beyond speech, beyond phrases, and beyond words.
In this moment of joyful ease, there is a master present.
Most cling to the ordinary, dreaming of spring within their dreams; relying on others' false calculations, they injure their own spirits.
Yet they further transmit the words of Linji and Yunmen, discussing these "extraordinary" matters until they bring sorrow upon themselves.
In Yunmen and Linji, the hundred flowers bloom in spring; each and every spiritual mechanism possesses its own divinity. In the end, it has nothing to do with the affairs of words and speech;
to transmit erroneously or explain wrongly is to mislead others.
Directly cutting through to the root, the teaching is beyond the scriptures; who is not a sage, who does not penetrate the divine?
Nevertheless, though you have left the den of the serpent upon hearing the Way, you act as one who is mindlessly perpetually intoxicated.
To claim that fresh words and phrases are "spring" is mere superficiality; to take the ordinary as practical for settling the mind is to hope for the Way while refusing to seek awakening.
To further use such dregs to instruct others is a grave error.
Since awakening, there is nothing that is not spring; within the thicket of briars, one knows how to nourish the spirit. The constant and the inconstant face each other in emptiness;
when the opportune moment arrives, bringing it forth depends entirely on the person.
I stayed among the cliffs of Fushan with the two venerable monks Huan and Da.
If you were truly a golden-haired lion, why would you remain confined to a den? Striding east and west, you should alert all creatures;
at times, crouching upon the ground, let out a single roar, suddenly startling the hawks of the vast heavens into flight.
What they eat is not the remains of what has been carved; their play consists of nothing but handling living creatures. One cannot help but sigh in pity for the mange-ridden dog—how foolish it is!
Everywhere in desolate gardens, it gnaws at dry bones.
Seeing off Master Xuan, a man of the vast and empty gate:
his mind is empty and the dharmas are also empty; with a *zhilu* staff slung over his shoulder, he wanders south, north, east, and west.

When I was at the ancient Zen barrier on the banks of the Gao'an River at Dayu, I entrusted this to the Head Seat Jishui. My ancestor once cleared away the weary countenance [of those seeking the Way]; though several hundred years have passed, the true traces remain.
They shall long await the return of our descendants.
In response, I offer this verse on the "Perfect Circle" (yuanxiang) sent by Moneyi, the Langzhong of Jun Prefecture, as he departs to reside at Dongshan:
Before it was named "Difficult," its form could already be placed before us; now, perfect and complete, it manifests before our eyes, providing a path for the multitude who were lost.
As you, Master Rong, depart for Huangbo to pay respects to the Old Monk of Jicui Hermitage, know that both the favorable and the adverse are skillful means;
yet among the masters of our school, those who misunderstand these are many.
If you wish to resolve the seal of the mind-ground, go and inquire of the old Chan monk at Vulture Peak.
When the day arrives, you must ascend step by step; entering the realm of the square, it is wondrously worthy of contemplation.
Layer upon layer, inexhaustible and each distinct from the last—rely on you, my friend, to examine each one with meticulous care.
The Head Seat Hezhen offered tea;
few can discern the ground from its sprouts and know the sound. Only our Master Jian is most perceptive; having brewed something extraordinary, he distributes it universally.
How many people will attain full awakening through its flavor?
Venerable Liu Zhen, you have wandered freely through famous mountains and sacred traces; your heart for admiring the sublime has surely grown weary and ceased its toil.
Dwell well within the ancient cave of Xinfeng, and together with us, propagate the Buddha’s work as the seasons pass.

Relying on the ancestral masters’ mind-seal and the "iron ox" pivot, one must directly confront the fray to settle right from wrong. Before the lightning strike has even been withdrawn, the thunderclap roars;
who among those encountered can truly be called a man?
South Terrace, Stonehead, the True Hall;
on the rocks of South Terrace, the *peng-peng* sound. Who among men, past or present, can equal this? In days of yore, the true axe remained in the hermitage;
tonight, the bright moon falls into the stream before us.
When I sent a letter to the Venerable One, you were at the Prajñā Terrace;
you went when you wished to go and stayed when you wished to stay. Your coming and going were ordinary, and with whom did you converse?
Now you are once again at the Prajñā Terrace, yet without money to take a wife, you mend your own clothes.
Master Xiangyan’s Stone Chime:
For long it was hidden by clouds deep within the chaotic mountains; were it not for one who knows the sound, it would be difficult to discern. One day it was hung high in the meditation hall;
its resonance at all times chills the myriad functions of the mind.
The tinkling bell announces the dawn and the morning tea service; directly and without partiality, it awakens all people. Each person has diligently finished brewing and sipping;
alas, the subtle resonance is once again presented in vain.
Seeing the śrāmaṇera Daoyan off on his alms-rounds to Nankang:
Step by step he ascends the heights; the bird-path is profound. Mind after mind unfolds like a lotus from fire.
With the character of a śrāmaṇera and the conduct of a śramaṇa, He has finally understood that his transformation of Nankang is karmically destined.

When sent forth, the superior man is like a trapped fish in a pond or a bird perched on a reed; yet this Great Man vigorously brandishes his two fists, each movement emerging entirely from within his breast.
Covering heaven and earth, he pours forth the essence of *amṛta*.
Sending Zen Master Chuan to Guangnan to beg for alms:
Daruma left behind a single sandal; Old Lu held fast to the robe of the patriarchs. Before every door, the sun and moon blaze forth;
in this Great Peace, there is no need for the majesty of a general.
I present this to the Chan practitioner Wén as he departs for Jízhou to beg for alms:
let his own mind follow the mani-jewel according to its colors; do not inquire whether the price of rice in Lúlíng is high.
Should he wish to travel further throughout the entire Huázhàng realm, it shall all return to the single eyebrow of the Benevolent One.
The Venerable Jian of Tayuan in Chuzhou Qianjiao invited me to stay overnight at his thatched hut, but I was unable to reach the ultimate subtlety of awakening.
For now, I shall rest at the "Thatched Hut on the Way. Do not think that because you have no [deluded] mind, you may simply stop there.
There are three threes before, and three threes after.
Within the hermitage, one knows nothing of the mundane world; how many can truly possess such a mind?
Beyond the city walls of Jiao, at Black Dragon Mountain Temple, the path enters green forests hidden by emerald mist.

In harmony with the Vice-Censor Li Dafu, we share the same hometown, the same surname, and the Way of Penetrating Mystery. Responding to the thoughts of the deluded masses, he manifests his body once more;
at this time, within the hermitage, he unfolds ancient treatises, which, following the nature of the Dharma-realm, reside even within a single mote of dust.
Though his official duties involve overseeing the grain transport of Jiangxi, his staff of mugwort clearly reveals the form of an elder. One must believe that this mind is capable of mastery;
thus, even serving as an external official is entirely free from worldly dust. (Master Li himself claimed to be a descendant of the Elder.)

Furthermore, I offer this to the upright and public-spirited Li, the Judicial Commissioner, as an act of lifelong giving. All the more so, for I have heard that his lofty integrity remains unblemished to this day. Who can recognize how he benefits the people and the state?
It is truly the compassionate heart of an ancient Buddha.
The bamboo torch, once lit, has its brightness exhausted; the lamp of wisdom, once kindled, shines infinitely. Thus one knows that the numinous light of Prajñā is wondrous;
where it is practiced, it radiates brilliance, and wherever it reaches, all is unobstructed.
To Elder Lètán Qián, who has sent me a poem.
Old man Lètán Qián and I, the venerable Zhēnjìng—our white hair is equally covered by frost and snow. For a man of the Way, there is no need for us to meet again;
from across a thousand li, we shall forever share the same breeze beneath the moon.
Long have I loved the dust of Mount Moshan beyond the mundane world; now old and useless, I hide myself even deeper. Such is the nature of all things in the human realm;
who among those in mountain caves will share with me this single incense offering?
In response to the request of the Magistrate of Xinchang for a verse on Perfect Penetration (Yuantong):
What prevents you from recognizing the true host? The wondrous nature is empty, yet its function is not empty. Though royal affairs grow ever more complex, they are all naturally resolved;
Never have I heard that Pei Kai was uniquely pure and unobstructed.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Zhao:
where the colt has trodden, the waters and clouds are deep. Seeking the Way, he travels everywhere in his quest. Parting from me, he heads toward the Third Patriarch;
to catch the fish, one does not stay in a single clear pool.

In parting with the scholar Yang Chuan, his poetic lines are fresh and clear, already transcending the mundane world. He is even more intimately connected to the ancestral Way that came from the West.
Although he wears a black silk cap upon his head, his heart remains a member of the Lotus Society.
The Dragon Pool reaches toward the heavens, its four sides steep and azure; within it lies a dragon pool amidst a mound of overturned rocks. Often before the mountain, rain and hail fall;
surely it is from here that wind and thunder arise.
To Wang Zhengyan, High Counselor for the Transport of Jiangxi:
When you have washed away all defilements and shattered all doubts, and in that vast clarity have recovered your original mind, then you may pluck weeds from the wasteland without discrimination;
wielding life and death, you act with sovereign freedom in the wind.

On New Year’s Day, I shaved my hair and was startled to find snow filling the blade; one must believe that the passage of years shows no mercy. To escape life and transcend death, strive diligently to become a Buddha;
do not say, "I will do it tomorrow," or "the day after."
Sent to Chan Practitioner Hua:
This mind is originally the sovereign within the Dharma; whether north, south, east, or west, how could there be any fixed direction?
If you encounter wind and clouds or a crashing thunderclap, let the flock of geese be as they will, unable to form a row.
Entrusted to Attendant Cheng:
Though old, one must know the body that does not age; walking and sitting together, there is spiritual vitality.
Although it is without form and without countenance, it can act as the master for all living beings.
On the central road between Yun and Hong, there is a post station named Dàtōng. Beside it is a vihāra called Zhúxià (Beneath the Bamboo).
Having arrived there to lodge, I inscribed this:
A temple by the roadside named Zhúxià, One station from Hong, before Dàtōng. Having happened to come here to lodge, The moon fills the window.
The moon accompanies me in the vast silence of the eternal night of meditation.

At dawn, the transformation-master gazes upon the magnificent mountains and rivers atop Tengwang Pavilion; within the city of Hongjing, all affairs are at rest. The ancestral intent that came from the West is fundamentally pure.
Pure. There is no need to further distance yourself from human society.

The immortal’s wanderings, the Pavilion by the Foolish Creek, and its utility for all ages flow on without end. Who within this pavilion is not a silent person? If this mind were like the Foolish Creek—
Water. Throughout the vast expanse of the world, all ultimately rely on the Real.
Having observed the verse by the scholar Peng for the Elder Huangbo at Juelin Monastery, I have thus composed this eulogy.

The nature of awareness is luminous and stainless; the mind is vast, empty, and perfect. The power of its arising is like the earth; the cultivation of its practice is like a forest. The Layman is great from the very beginning;
the Chan Master returns to the source with profundity. Meeting within one family, both monk and layman inspire extraordinary reverence.
Ascending the seat on a snowy morning, a monk asked, "What is the matter regarding the traces upon the snow?
The Master said, "Each flake has no distinct color;
because of the snow, the eminent monk asks. The Elder commands that this be put into practice: each flake has no distinct color; in their profusion, their nature is equally luminous."

A single yang has already announced its arrival; the myriad things await their generation and completion. It is not merely a matter of relying on the joy of dhyāna; when the moment arrives, one must exert oneself to the full.

Visiting the Stupa of Master Huanglong, I lament: "How swift was your passing into extinction! Now only this stupa remains here within these walls. While other monks wander idly through the four seas with their staffs, who else shall experience the 'Wind of Nine Years'?"
Beyond the birds, a thousand peaks encircle it; among men, a single path leads through. Vast and silent from dawn until dusk, there is only the white cloud as its companion.

The new lotus reveals to its followers that though born of turbid mud, it remains forever unstained—how much more so when grown within a Buddhist temple! Its pure nature makes the pool azure; its subtle fragrance fills the hall with clarity.
Round and round it first reflects in the water; short and short, the stalks gradually divide. Wait further for the lotus to emerge, and the wondrous Zen mind may be clearly revealed.

In my old age, I show this to the assembly amidst the mountain colors of Jiufeng. For one as clumsy as I, the thatched hut is deep. Having grown old, I have become negligent and indolent; when asked about Zen, disciples come seeking me out.
If you wish to know the Way of the Patriarchs, it does not transcend the minds of the multitude. Since both self and other alike attain Buddhahood, I shall offer this direct pointing in verse.

Regarding the cypress tree at Qingju, those of old once pointed it out; now the fragrance of the ancient path is transmitted. Rely on you to awaken to the intent of the Patriarchs; let my Zen-mind be made alert.
Thus I know it is no ordinary thing; it remains ever-present in the monastic courtyard. How many times have the common trees aged? Yet its lofty standard remains as green as before.
Presented to Magistrate Xu Chaoyi by Junchen, in response to his command regarding the Nine Peaks, two verses:
I left my home to follow the Way of the Sages; Useless now, I delight in the natural truth. How could I have thought I was so utterly foolish? I still feel ashamed of this old and sickly body.
Unable to transcend the world, I shall simply be a man at leisure. I beg to be released so that I may return to the mountains and spend the remaining hundred springs in tranquility.
A period of sixty-four years has passed; returning to leisure is already late. This single body has its ultimate limit, yet the myriad affairs of life never come to an end.
One who studies the Way should seek stillness; it is likewise fitting for one to be a monk. The virtuous Governor of Shu River surely understands the need for such external protection.

Zhang Wenjie, having been reappointed to the Wangdu Palace in Hongzhou, once again encountered his sovereign and ministers. He was not censured for declining the post in Nan Yue, but rather was praised for serving his elderly parents.

The mountains and rivers stretch for a thousand miles as of old; guest and host are newly united at this moment. I once conversed on Chan with fellow seekers, yet I am ashamed not to be the one who provided the lodging.

At the mountain hall of Daining, the Chan practitioners are able to maintain inner stillness. The dwelling place is a deep mountain; though affairs outside the gate are turbulent, those within the seat remain at ease.
I hear the songs of fishermen at the distant creek; a flight of geese descends upon the front bay. This very thing is nothing other than that; what prevents it from being right here in Hongfu?

At Sanzhu Pavilion, every single fragment is divided by the dragon’s mouth; the pavilion facing the window is named "Scattered Pearls. If one were to gather them all up, I fear they would soon cease to exist forever.
The round moon over Hepu is similar; the courtyard of the Sui palace is no different at night. Not only is it capable of bringing benefit, but all things possess their own craftsmanship.
In imitation of Wang Yuanze’s “Phoenix Terrace”:
The phoenix has flown away, yet the terrace remains long; The gardens and groves connect with distant isles. Moved by the affairs of my former kingdom, I wish to study the Chan of the Old Lu.
The land is a clear, polished, and limpid river; the lingering sunset scatters like brocade across the sky. The people of the Six Dynasties no longer behold it;
my gaze reaches the old mountains and rivers. I entrust this to Master Fayan of Xianan Monastery:

within the monastery, one hears nothing of affairs beyond its walls. Who understands this intent? At the point where the paths through woods and valleys end, it is the moment when the worldly mind is exhausted.
The sound of the bell comes from the old temple; the moonlight descends upon the new pond. I laugh, however, at those who merely follow the wind—how can they, in their petty efforts, ever grow old?
The mind of Jixuan is inherently still; there is no need to further discuss Chan. I wish to bid farewell to many affairs; who will come to share these few remaining karmic ties?
Amidst the verdant mists of the Ten Thousand Pines, Beside the azure peaks of the Five Elders, In this foremost place of secluded seclusion, Lies a minor celestial grotto on Mount Lu.
Inscribed here at the Tranquil Retreat Pavilion of the Layman Tian-shui, a place for stilling the mind and abiding in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing:
Tranquility does not reside within the mountains; In winter, warmth comes from a single brazier’s fire; In summer, coolness is found in a breeze from three sides.
The conditions for sending [this] are already meager; how can the aspiration for the Way have any limit? Do not inquire after worldly affairs; the toil of life is entirely empty.
Master Dongshan sits silently in his hermitage, speechless.
Who knows this mind? The separate transmission has come from of old; it has been secretly entrusted down to the present day.
Above the fields and gardens of the Hu family, deep within the grottoes of Lei Family Cave, stands the hermitage of a high monk. Who will seek out Nan?
Leaving this inscription at Dongxuan:
The Buddha-son’s extraordinary conduct is hidden away; yet when opening the window, there is a proper method—thus one welcomes the night moon and likewise awaits the morning sun.
The smoke from the many trees is just beginning to warm; the hidden orchids are in full bloom. As I sit, my meditative nature grows serene, while the bees and butterflies remain light and flighty.

After Master Shun of Xiangcheng passed away, leaving behind his spiritual insight, the sacred mountain was protected by divine powers. The site of practice remains ancient for a thousand ages, yet the Dharma assembly has been renewed many times.
How can things be discarded? They arise because they reside within man. Moreover, you, Master, are a former adept who does not mingle with the dust of the multitude.

Entrusting myself to you, your attendant, for seventy-six, seventy-seven, or seventy-eight years—time passes and we are renewed together. Green smoke rises above the willows by the pond; white hair appears in the mirror.
The years pass by as the flowers turn; how can one know the reality of Buddha-nature? I address you, Master Cheng: when there is wine, simply sing of spring.
In response to the two poems inquiring after my illness by Magistrate Huang of Jing’an:

Your letter has come, bringing me comfort and inquiry. Why is the power of external protection so partial? I beat the drum to assemble my cloud-like companions; incense is burned as I unroll this snowy stationery.
Lotuses fill the pond, emerging from the water; the moon rises high in the sky. It is like newly woven brocade—its patterns have few equals.
Old age and illness arise in succession; how could one forget being entangled in suffering? Though the hundred members of the body are decayed, this one thing remains sharp and luminous.
Though the old house may lean and collapse, my idle mind remains level and calm. I need only know how to walk the Great Path; I am too weary to ask further about the journey ahead.

Lodging in the room of the venerable Master Bin, I have few entanglements with worldly affairs. This is also because my dwelling is secluded; I do not let the days pass in following the worldly stream, but constantly find peace in self-abiding meditation.

The wild colors of the countryside meet the suburban springs; the crowing of roosters links with the sounds of the marketplace. This body remains old, yet it is a day of warm breezes and apricot blossoms.
I wish to roam through the places on Mount Dongshan where Master Mao did not reach;
idly, I desire to seek them out everywhere. I intend to take the moon of Xinfeng and return it to my awakened original mind.
In the Chan gate, there is the nature of non-attachment; in the immortal’s abode, there is one who understands. I have heard it said that the Cold Rock exists;
Tiantai is the foremost in its depth.
I visited Donggu Temple;
Donggu and Xigu lie before the Kaixian Waterfall. Mount Lu’s enclosure does not complete its circuit, and its momentum leans further toward the southern side.
I traveled to Jingfu Temple to visit the Elder Saeng.

Human life passes in the blink of an eye; the spring colors have already returned to the east. A new patriarch now presides over the chamber of ten feet square, amidst the ancient bamboo of the Chan gate.
Fragments of mountain clouds drift by, and mountain streams flow with a gurgling murmur. All these are things of natural truth; the high monk’s mind shares in this same leisure.
I dwell in the abode of Su Ziyou at Jixi;
how joyful it is! Who would say that Jixi is a desolate place? As long as the clouds and mountains remain, let the secular world busy itself as it pleases.
Three fathers and sons in literary talent; two virtuous and worthy men in conduct. Yet I fear that the new Son of Heaven may find no room for this old stone hut.
Su Ziyou has cleared a "Eastern Gable" (Dongxuan) and expressed the sentiment of Yanzi’s humble alley; I therefore send these verses to him.

Though my talent is submerged, my dwelling is likewise humble; though the Way resides within me, I am not poor. Yet, before the rains have washed the slopes of Mount Fu-yan, I must still endure the dust of Yan-huan’s alley.
With a vast mind, I find joy wherever I am; as a great vessel, I follow my natural spontaneity. The moon over the eastern eaves at midnight—how few among those toiling in life can truly belong to it?
I visited the Elder Baoyun, and upon meeting, we laughed heartily.
The fallen leaves are many in the gardens, yet the color of the green pines still remains. How is the Way of you, O Benevolent One?
Worldly conditions change from morning to evening; the splendor of the season follows after silks and brocades. You, a son of mountain-dwelling dhyāna and silence, do not weary of my frequent visits.

The Sūtra proclaims that this Buddhist monastery shall extend its pavilions to accumulate merit for the people of this region. May auspiciousness increase day by day, lasting for a thousand or ten hundred years, ever as fresh as two or three springs.

The hearts of those seated within are tranquil; all things surrounding the eaves are authentic. The monastery proclaims the sacred names of the Buddhas; may the Son of Heaven bring blessings to the common people.

Entrusting myself to the worldless recluse, worldly affairs are inexhaustible; yet with a mind nurtured in loftiness, one remains naturally at ease. The vegetable garden opens onto the green fields; the groves and thickets border the blue mountains.

I am too weary to add fire to the cinnabar furnace; I am too indolent to fasten the door of the cloud-cave. There must surely be some secret art to cultivate, for at seventy my complexion remains as ruddy as vermilion.
At Kuai-ting, the paths are lined with aged pines and cedars; time flows on in leisurely stillness. This is the true realm of the Dharma King, the ancestral mountain of the Chan practitioner.
The Patriarch’s intent has been transmitted for a long time; human sentiments naturally diverge. How can one satisfy my heart? The sound of water fills the hall.

The Qingliang Pavilion is a place for escaping the summer heat. Its windows and doors face the mountain clefts. The mountain stream rinses on without end; the breeze from the bamboo comes all the more.

"The hundred limbs have shed their weariness; what is the intent of the Patriarchs? Sitting for a long time, I hear the fish playing, stirring the clear waves from time to time. While the Master was at Shuangling, at dawn, the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) came to inquire after him and said, "It is silent and still.

The Master replied: The hundred limbs have shed their weariness; what is the intent of the Patriarchs? Sitting for a long time, I hear the fish playing, stirring the clear waves from time to time. While the Master was at Shuangling, at dawn, the *vinaya-dhara* came to inquire after him and said, "It is silent and still. The Master replied:
The affairs of a solitary monk have thus resulted in this verse, which stands apart with its own unique way of life;
few who follow this path understand it. The affairs of a solitary monk are quiet and still, while the minds of the worldly are noisy and clamorous.

Long have I suffered the burdens of children; do not weary of the depths of water and clouds. Simply rejoice in the meaning of the West’s arrival; worldly toil has long since settled of its own accord.
On the road, I met three scholars from Jianzhou—peach blossoms and willows are green.
Heaven and earth, the rain has just cleared. A lute and a sword for these three men of talent; a jar and a bowl for this one old monk.
His literary works were submitted to the Northern Palace; his path of cultivation followed that of the Southern Neng. We met by chance upon our journey, though we had never known one another in life.

Seeing Master Zhou Return to Lingxi Hermitage: The emerald peaks of Mount Kuanglu are deep and vast; The pines by the mountain streams mostly form spreading canopies. Every cascade from the cliffs sounds like a lute.
The immortal does not merely consume elixirs; longevity can be cultivated through the mind. If in future years you find the Way, may we follow you as you strike your staff and seek me out.
Seeing off Assistant Prefect Zhang on his journey to Kaishan:
Walking into the midst of green pines, a winding path leads far away. Gradually one enters the realm of the Flower Treasury, Deeply hidden within the palace of the Dharma King.

The Way differs from that of the immortals; man is not the same as the worldly. If you wish to know the intent of the Western Patriarch, look at the ancient cypress in the courtyard in the spring breeze.
Xie Xinchang, the Magistrate of Quan, visited me upon my return from the autumn examination for candidates.
With towering talent fit for high ministers and generals, he rode his horse to enter the mountains at the place where the paths diverge across the bridge.

The district magistrate gazes idly at the empty expanse; the forest monk can be accompanied in his stillness. When will the drizzling rain be spread, so that the withered roots throughout the world may be revived?

Seeing Master Ran depart to transform and guide others—once I heard him play the Xinfeng melody, the sound of raindrops dripping from the eaves was like the blowing of a holeless flute, providing for those born with karmic affinity.

If you wish to shatter the darkness of others' delusions, you must first open up the clarity of your own awakening. When the spring breeze brings life to all things, how can one adequately praise the beauty of the Way of Heaven?

Master Qing has long since stilled his thoughts of wandering; dwelling in his hermitage, the Way may be approached. Though it is clearly inhabited by its master, it is so profoundly still that it seems as if no one were there at all.
The lotus in the pond grows old; affairs at the gate renew themselves. Who can understand this mind? The courtyard cypress faces eternal spring.
An Inscription for Master Shao’s Studio of Silent Illumination:
The secluded studio is named "Silent Illumination. Within its embrace, the four seas are tranquil. Though the scenery undergoes the tints of change, the master’s countenance remains unchanged.
Wild springs clarify the space beyond the railing; fragrant mists rise between the eaves. In this cool night, who is there to converse? Vast and silent, the moon fills the mountains.
*Seeing off a Guest to the Secluded Realm of Nanyue Temple:* One by one, the emerald cliffs divide; near and far, the pines join together. High and low, the bells are heard as one.

Spiritual birds occasionally play music; fragrant rocks daily enshroud themselves in clouds. When I think of the places where you walked in meditation, your path shines forth, distinct from the common herd.

Xiucai Lei has composed "Quietly Structuring a Pavilion Above the Southern Pond": "The various blossoms benefit us; the orchids still receive the dew and rain. Beneath the pines, weeds and brambles lie hidden."
Seated in a circle amidst the scenic beauty of mountains and rivers, our spirits are open and our resolve is bold. As scholars, we possess this vocation;
why worry that the cassia branch is too high?

At Shanglan’s Qingliang Hall, observing the capacities of others, I preach only the Dharma. With every hearing, there is refreshing clarity. Desiring to exhaust the illnesses of all sentient beings, I shall open the field of ambrosia.

Deep and secluded behind the abbot’s quarters, it lies in partial shadow beside the prefectural gate. Should one ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey, the melody of the horn atop the city wall lingers on.
A Visit to Taoyuan Presented to Master Liu Jushi:

It is truly like the residence of immortals; one suspects there is no trace of the mundane world here. The people’s dwellings are amidst mountain colors, and the path to their gates is amidst the sound of flowing water.
Willow down hangs together with the green; peach blossoms reflect one another in red. The misty light is perfectly mild and warm; how can the desire for pleasure ever end?
Conversing with a Daoist about longevity—people grow old together in this vast expanse.
Who, then, truly understands how to pursue it? How could one believe in the Way of Longevity? It is clearly the indestructible mind.
The soul flies far to the Jade Palace; dreams labor deep within the Sea Mountains. To those who speak thus while lost in their direction, there is no need to compete over every passing moment.

This was written on the wall of a Daoist: the study of immortality is mired in much talk; one should rely on the critique of the Annalist (Laozi). Only by being without mind can one return to the Great Way; otherwise, there will be gain and loss regarding longevity.

In all things and in myself, the True Master is one and the same; how can the categories of "intimate" and "distant" be applied? How excellent! The source of all wonders resides in each and every instance of forgetting worldly emotions.
I leave this as a gift to the Elder Chun of Xiangcheng:
The mountain colors unfold as the curtain is rolled back; the meditative mind shares in the moon’s radiance. Deep within the temple of Xiangcheng, lies the dwelling of the venerable Lingguan.
The summit altar remains; the overflowing milk has long since vanished. Now, those who follow the pure path recite the *White Lotus Sutra*.

The short cockscomb flower, pristine white and distinct from other blossoms, stands before the steps where the sedges grow in unison. Viewing it at dawn while still wet with dew, it lacks only a single cry.
Visiting Yonggu Temple again, I wander far beyond the world of dust.
