Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhenjing Yun’an of Baofeng, written by Su Che of Meishan on a day in the third month of the eighth year of the Yuanfeng era.
Water flows upon the earth and manifests as grasses and trees; whether salty, sour, sweet, or bitter, it is all water.

Fire is transmitted through firewood and transforms into food and drink; whether rice, cakes, soup, or sliced meat, it is all fire. The mind resides within humans and is revealed in the hundred members of the body; whether seeing, hearing, speaking, or moving, it is all the mind.
The sages of antiquity extended this principle to its full application: from the vastness of heaven and earth and the mountains and rivers down to the minute details.
Yet, within the autumn hair and the subtle mote of dust, this mind is omnipresent and all-seeing. Therefore, one sees the great within the small, and the small within the great;
one becomes ten million, and ten million become one. All of this is simply the mind; it is the natural law of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and nothing is created therein.
Thus, when pointing to the mind-dharma to instruct others, there are those who manifest through the marks and signs of radiance (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*).
People [enter the Way] by means of food, drink, bedding, and clothing; some by means of gardens, groves, pavilions, and open spaces;

and some by means of silence, non-speaking, and non-demonstrating. Indeed, there is no phenomenon that is not the Dharma. Yet, there are gateways of cultivation consisting of hearing, reflection, and practice, through which sentient beings enter.
These are like a great thoroughfare—both direct and easy to traverse. Since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West, the successive patriarchs...

I received [this teaching]. All [these things] are used to enlighten others through words. Once the ground of the mind is clear, every utterance is the Dharma. It is like an ancient tree from which life-force has emerged;
its flowers and leaves are countless, and whether they lean toward or away, whether they are lush or slender, long or short—there is not one that is not acceptable.

There was a Chan Master, Master Wen, who studied Confucianism in his youth. At the age of twenty, he left the household life to seek the Way.
He received the Dharma from Huanglong Nan and preached the Dharma at various mountains in Gaoyang. In his later years, he resided at Dong...

Shan Shishi was a successor to the realization of the fundamental source; his eloquence was vast and unimpeded, and disciples gathered to him from afar. In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, I came to the south on account of my offenses.

Upon meeting him once, he treated me as an old acquaintance. Later, his disciples showed me their recorded sayings (*yulu*); reading them, I found them to be纵横放肆 (transcendent, unrestrained, and bold), which left me utterly bewildered and lost.

Although I was unable to challenge him with arguments, I knew this: [...he was one who had attained the Way. (Note: The final clause is reconstructed based on the context of the preceding passage regarding the realization of the fundamental source.)
He was one who realized the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and attained the Samādhi of Līlā (Mastery).
Therefore, I have inscribed this as the postscript to the beginning of the *Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhenjing Yun’an of Baofeng*.

Then, once again, he struck a clear tone. His natural bearing was majestic; his mechanism for "slaying the snake" was steep and formidable. As the Patriarch’s command was strictly enforced, even those with the eyes of hawks and the pupils of dragons were subjected to his critical scrutiny.

Jian. Hung up in the monastic communities: the self-nature is truly spontaneous; this flavor is fundamentally without distinction. Through hundreds of thousands of samādhis, all quarters may each invite [the Dharma] to their temples.

The Recorded Sayings of Master Jue of Mount Langye in Chuzhou.
The disciple Yuan Ju, having gathered the assembly, addressed them, saying:

He addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you who have spent the summer retreat here with me—I shall point out five kinds of illnesses for you."
1. You must not go to a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not even an inch of grass. 2. You must not dwell alone on a solitary peak. 3. You must not draw a bow and set an arrow. 4.
You must not establish yourself outside of all things. 5. You must not be obstructed by birth or death. Why?
If you are obstructed in even one of these places, it will be difficult for you to save yourself; only when you are unimpeded in all five places can you be called a true guide. You all—
If you, O man, should travel to various places and encounter a master of clear vision, convey this message to me, so that the ancestral wind may not fall into decline.
As for ordinary people, they must simply cease their activity. Why? Because to boast of one's finery within the land of the naked—surely you are far too ignorant of the times.
The Master ascended the hall. A monk came forward and drew a perfect circle. The Master struck him and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk said, "I do not speak;
I do not speak. The Master struck him again. The monk said, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time do not transcend this. The Master struck him once more and then said:
"O Great Assembly! In the teachings of the Middle Way, pointing a finger at a bhikṣu constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Today, this mountain monk enters hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
One day, the Master ascended the hall and said: "The late master Fenyang said, 'Under Fenyang’s gate there is the Lion of West River.'"
He sits occupying the gate; as soon as anyone comes, he bites them to death. By what skillful means can one enter the gate of Fenyang and see the person of Fenyang?
Here at Langye, there is also a bit of this: Langye has a lion that occupies the seat;
if anyone comes, they immediately lose their body and life. By what skillful means can one enter the gate of Langye?
"To meet a man of Langya"—these two turning words: can you all examine them thoroughly or not?
If you can examine them thoroughly, only then can it be called the "eye that discerns dharmas. If it is not so, you will have no place to settle your body or establish your life.
(He struck his staff once and then descended from the seat.)
Ascending the hall, he said: "Self and other are without difference; form and mind are not two. He then took up his staff and said:
"If you call this a 'staff,' you have eyes but are as if blind. If you do not call it a 'staff,' it is no different from avoiding drowning only to leap into fire.
If you can understand it through direct realization, simply know it as a 'staff. He struck the ground once with the staff and then [descended].
Descend from the seat.
Ascend the hall. [The Master] cites: The World-Honored One said, "If you see that all marks are non-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.
He then held up his staff and said, "I call this one a 'staff. Which of these is a mark? After a long silence, he said, "Look downward."
The discourse was lengthy; he reserved it for another day. He struck once with his staff and then descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Sometimes this mountain monk’s single blow brings forth the birth of all Buddhas;
sometimes this single blow turns the Great Dharma Wheel; sometimes this single blow enters parinirvāṇa. Now tell me: what is the birth of all Buddhas?"
"The turning of the Great Dharma Wheel and the entry into Parinirvāṇa—how much time lies between them? After a long silence, he said, "Do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Dharma Wheel. Take care."
Small Assembly. A monk asked, "When you let one move pass, light arises in every eye; when you block off the vital ford, ten thousand trees wither away.
As a student who has come before you, I ask the Master to grant us an instruction. The Master said, "I, the old monk, step back. The monk said, "Letting everyone pass is entirely up to the Master.
The Master said, "Dharma brother, step forward three paces. The monk said, "If I do not enter the tiger’s mouth, how shall I..."
[The Master] saw Tiger Tooth. The Master said, "At the crossroads, one looks toward the void and offers a prayer.
Again, a monk asked, "When it is said, 'Ten years to grind a single sword, yet the frost-sharp blade has never been tested,' what then? The Master said, "A master of the fundamental division.
The student then gave a shout. The Master said, "I have lost out. The student said, "Exactly so. The Master then laughed heartily. The Master then cited the former Liang dynasty...
Shan said, "To those coming from the south, I give thirty blows; to those coming from the north, I give thirty blows. Even though it is thus, it does not accord with the essence of the school.
The Master said, "Liangshan treats a great ingot of pure gold as if it were common iron and sells it away.
Langye is not like this: 'To those coming from the south, I give thirty blows; to those coming from the north, I give thirty blows. Let him do so!"
"The patch-robed monks of the world all criticize [this].
Take care. He ascended the hall and said: "Now, a bodhisattva who studies Prajñā must have the contemplation of wisdom manifest before them;

only then will there be some slight correspondence. Therefore, the former sages said: 'One should contemplate the past as being like a dream, for it cannot be obtained. One should contemplate the future...'"

Because it is like lightning, it cannot be fixed; one must observe the present. Because it is like clouds, it exists only as a semblance. Now tell me, how should a Bodhisattva practicing Prajñā observe?
Do not use discursive thought; it is difficult to find even by bowing one's head. [The Master] struck his staff and descended from the seat.
Later, while the Master was touring the quarters, he raised the following: "Whenever the Baguā Monk was in the marketplace, he used torn paper..."
He wrapped a piece of dried excrement in cloth. Whenever he saw someone, he would present it to them, saying, "The one from Tuṣita Heaven!
The one from Tuṣita Heaven! He then had his disciples offer comments on this; they produced various remarks. Finally, the Master offered the comment: "Maitreya Bodhisattva.
He further cited that whenever Baguaoshang (Pūnyabhadra) saw someone, he would strike them once with the back of his hand as soon as the person appeared. As soon as [the person]—
He turned his head and said, "Give me one coin. He then had his disciples offer responses. Finally, the Master said, "Just throw one coin to him."
Ascending the hall, he raised [the following]: "Our late master Fenyang said: 'A Bodhisattva studying Prajñā must investigate the living word;
do not investigate the dead word. Nowadays, people immediately say that 'encompassing heaven and earth' is the living word, while 'cutting off the myriad streams' is the dead word.
If you understand it in this way, have you not failed our late master Fenyang? Among the assembly, there is a certain class of 'guests' seeking the Dharma."
"Measuring the Path. What is the living word? "Today the sky is fine and clear. What is the dead word? "Ten thousand miles of precipitous cliffs.
If you understand it in this way, even if you study until the year of the donkey, it will still be a dead word.
I, this mountain monk, have shattered them for you all at once. What, then, is the living word? Thereupon he struck the ground with his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Those who study the Way must have true wisdom manifest before them, so that their discernment is without error.
It is said: 'To err by a hair's breadth is to miss by a thousand li. As soon as there is a divergent view, it is called a heterodox path. Thus, there are two kinds of views within heterodox paths:
those concerning causes and conditions and those concerning spontaneity. Because one clings to these as absolute, they become heterodox. This is what is meant:"
Thus, there is no beginning; through conditions, there is no end. Furthermore, according to the Way of the former sages:

"All dharmas are not born of themselves, nor are they born from another, nor from both together, nor without a cause. For this reason, it is said that there is no birth. Although I, this mountain monk, speak thus, you must not understand it in such a way.
If you understand it in such a way, you will enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow. Take care!
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an example: A monk asked Mazu Daoshi, “What is the Buddha? Mazu said, “The very mind is the Buddha.
[The monk asked,] “What is the Way? He said, “No-mind is the Way. [The monk asked,] “How far apart are the Buddha and the Way?
Mazu said, “The Buddha is like an open hand; the Way is like a clenched fist. The Master said, “The expedient means of the ancients were indeed not to be dismissed, but here in my own place—”
There is also this: if there is no one to buy it, I, the mountain monk, shall sell it and buy it myself.
What is the Buddha? Abundant auspicious herbs before the cliff. What is the Way? Plentiful spiritual sprouts beneath the stream. How far apart are the Buddha and the Way?
A few wisps of white cloud enshrouding an ancient temple; a single ribbon of clear water winding around green mountains. Be careful!
The Master, on account of a small-scale *sancha* (informal discourse), was asked by a monk: "If one realizes it before words, one betrays one's lifelong practice;

if one takes it up after the phrase, it becomes a deluded view. I wonder, how does the Master guide people? The Master said: "Horizontally carrying the sun and moon; vertically encompassing heaven and earth."
The monk said, "A true teacher for students. The Master said, "An authentic patch-robed monk. The monk then gave a shout. The Master sat in silence. The monk said, "Finished.

The Master smiled and said, "I could not strike you. The Master then raised the following case: A monk asked the former master Fenyang, "When one seeks a meeting in a state of extreme urgency, what then?
Fenyang said, "Hugging Śāriputra in the water. He asked again, "When one seeks a meeting in a state of extreme urgency..."
"What was it like at that time? Fengyang said, "Naked, he saw Ānanda. The Master said, "There is one turn of phrase that cuts off the tongues of everyone in the world;
there is another turn of phrase that can open people's eyes. If you can discern which is which, I will give you a staff.
He threw down the staff and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an example: "When the Elder of Sansheng went to visit Deshan, as soon as they met, he unfolded his sitting cloth.
Deshan said, 'No need to unfold it; no need to unfold it. Here there is no leftover soup or stale rice.
Sansheng said, 'If there were, where would you put it? Deshan remained silent. Sansheng took up his sitting cloth and went to the hall. Among the assembly..."
"Measurement. It is said, 'To the utmost,' and so forth. Have you not heard the Way? If it were not for Luan Bu, how could one have seen Han Guang?
Take care. He ascended the hall and said: "Virtuous ones, before you have even left the Sangha Hall, the Holy Monk has already understood you.
Before you have reached the Buddha Hall, he speaks this verse again. Upon arriving at the Dharma Hall, when the three beats of the drum have ceased and a single stick of incense has been burned."
You should now disperse. Why? Have you not seen that in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), the waterfowl and the forest trees all recite the Buddha’s name?
In the Heaven of Satisfaction (*Tuṣita*), the trees press against one another, expounding upon suffering and emptiness.
When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, am I degrading the noble to the base, or am I speaking according to the truth? If you do not agree, I invite you to come forward before the assembly.
I, this mountain monk, provide you with proof. If there is no going away, gather up your straw raincoat and bamboo hat from the side;
take your fishing line and return home. Take care.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The phrase that exists and the phrase that does not exist are like a vine leaning against a tree; when the tree falls, the vine withers. At such a moment, one deserves a blow of the staff.
Tell me, where does the fault lie? After a long silence, he said: "If it were not for the hand of Monk You, one would merely be speaking of mastery in painting."
He struck the ground once with his staff and then descended from the seat.
Entering the hall, he said: "Those who come in this manner shall be accommodated in the upper section; those who do not come in this manner shall be registered in the lower section."
When one who is a person of the higher path arrives, they cross the river alone and silently. Yet there is yet another person—where shall they be placed?
After a long silence, he said: "The fishing pole is worn out, so plant bamboo again; do not calculate the labor, but rest when the opportunity arises. Take care!
The Master ascended the seat. A monk asked, "I have heard the Master say: 'Those who come in such a manner are assigned to the upper quarters;

those who do not come in such a manner are registered in the lower quarters. But as for those who come in neither of these ways, what then? " The Master said, "Today I have encountered a patch-robed monk.
The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "Eating your meal in front of the kitchen. The Master then said, "The former sages spoke of clarity."
I offer my humble thanks in the dark. Cold and heat alternate; things flow and change—this is the common nature of humanity. Furthermore, the *Fàngguāng* (Radiance) Sutra says:

"Dharmas have no coming or going, for they do not move or shift. If this is so, then even as whirlwinds topple mountains, the sun and moon traverse the heavens, rivers compete to flow, and wild horses gallop and swirl, there is no actual movement.
If one contemplates thus with true discernment, tell me: what is it that remains distinct and singular?
"How do you say it? After a long silence, he said: "A spark of flint burns the mountain at night; the great earth joins its palms in unison. Be careful.

Ascending the hall, he raised an example, saying: "The Patriarch said: 'The true nature is the treasury of the mind-ground; it has neither beginning nor end. It responds to conditions to benefit all beings;
for convenience, it is called wisdom. The Master said: 'Since it is for convenience that it is called wisdom, tell me, what ultimately is it called?'"
"What are you doing? After a long silence, he said, "Let the vast ocean change as it may; I shall never communicate with you. Take care.
He then ascended the hall and said, "The Samādhi of the World-Honored One was not known by Kāśyapa; the Samādhi of Kāśyapa was not known by Ānanda; the Samādhi of Ānanda was not known by Śāṇakavāsin;
and I have my own samādhi, which you likewise do not know. The Master said, "It is for this reason..."
"What is it that is not known? It is not that one does not know; the principle simply ought to be thus. If a person can realize this, then north, south, east, and west are all accounted for.
If it were not so, where else would you intend to go? He struck his staff once.
Ascending the hall, he said: "All of you, simply follow conditions as you eat and drink; let your nature drift or sink as it will. Abiding in the state of a sage, there is no increase;
dwelling among the common folk, there is no decrease. If you can act in this way, then the imperial wind will sweep vast and clear, and all places will be tranquil.
He then added: "I have spoken quite enough. You must still examine this closely before you can truly attain it. Take care!"
Ascending the hall, he raised [this topic], citing the former Sage: "If one extensively seeks out textual meanings, it is like seeking a form within a mirror;

if one further ceases thought to contemplate emptiness, it is like fleeing from one's shadow in broad daylight. "All you practitioners of Chan, how do you speak when neither of these two paths is involved?
After a long silence, he said: "Look, look! Spring has arrived; the ice melts, the fish swim, and the birds fly in disorder. Be careful!"
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the verse by his late teacher, Fenyang: "The Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish;

Having attained the essential meaning, one forgets the Way and it becomes easy to approach. A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena; On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh.
The Master then gave a shout and said, "Which mystery is this? After a long silence, he said, "You have no measure of transgression, and I too have no measure."
[The Master] committed an offense. He struck his staff once and descended from the seat. Entering the hall, he said:
"The union of ruler and minister is still a matter on the level of the Dharma-body. Do you not see the ruler? Do you not see the minister?
This is still a matter above the Dharma-body. To speak of 'above' and 'below' only serves to make the mind restless. For now, let us [rest]."
“What is the Dharma-body? After a long silence, he said, “Even with the hand of Gu Kaizhi, it would be difficult to paint the true likeness of Master Zhigong. “Take care.
Ascending the hall, he said, “If one discusses this matter, what need is there to speak of Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, Āryadeva, or Śāriputra?

Though their eloquence may flow like a hanging torrent and their wisdom like a running stream, none can know it. In Mahādeva’s room, the door was closed; even with many hands, it is difficult to sift through. Vimalakīrti...”
Silence. How is it that this very state is so? Baizhang rolled up his mat; various quarters speak of this and that.
The Patriarch faced the wall; the monastic groves are vast and wide. If you can discern this point, I shall give you a staff.
If you cannot discern it, I have a phrase that penetrates all directions. But tell me, what is this phrase that penetrates all directions? After a long silence, he said: "The Hand."
Taking his single sandal, he departed for the Western Heaven.

"Take care! [With these words,] he ascended the hall for the discourse. He raised the example: A former sage said, "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast.

It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither along with the four seasons. The Master said: "What a fine verse! Yet it has become two separate pieces. If there were someone to examine it..."
[The Master] said, "I grant you one eye. Take care. He then ascended the hall and said:
"If you wish to seek the Buddha, the mind itself is the Buddha. If you wish to seek the Way, no-mind is the Way.
Because there is no-mind, dharmas do not arise; because it is the mind itself, it remains eternally firm through the kalpas. If this is so, then every dharma..."
There is no difference. Mind after mind continues without interruption. Thus the ancient masters said: "You need only follow conditions like the wind;
though it flies sand and rolls stones, it does not deviate from space. Simply remain unburdened by affairs amidst all phenomena; when seeing forms and hearing sounds, you need not be deaf. Take care.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring wind whistles; it is the sublime teaching of the ancient Buddhas. The green water murmurs; it is the livelihood of the practitioner.
If you understand it in this way, you shall be banished to Yuzhou. How would a monk of true substance discuss this? After a long silence, he said:
'Truly, one hears the heart-rending cry of the monkey. Take care!"

Ascending the hall, he raised [this case]: The World-Honored One said, "All sentient beings delusively take the four great elements to be the characteristics of their own bodies, and the shadows of conditions from the six sense objects to be the characteristics of their own minds.
Now, I ask you, worthy ones: that which is in the eye is called seeing; that which is in the ear is called hearing;

that which is in the nose smells fragrances; that which is in the tongue knows flavors; that which is in the hands grasps and seizes; that which is in the feet runs and moves. Yet, these are not called the [self].
"Birth is not called Buddha-nature either. Tell me, what would you call it? After a long silence, he said:
"Xiangyan received the staff with tears; Yangshan smashed Miaoshan’s mirror. Be careful!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "When receiving words, you must understand the fundamental source; do not establish your own rules and regulations.
If anyone can produce a sentence that penetrates all directions, I shall cut my own throat to express my gratitude to them. Take care."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised an example, saying: "Xuefeng said, 'If one discusses this matter, it is like a mirror:
when a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears; when a Han person comes, a Han person appears. A monk asked, 'What if a bright mirror were to come?

Xuefeng said, 'The barbarian and the Han would simply vanish. The Master said: "Have you not heard it said? 'To test a person at the point of certainty, one need only speak a word to know them. Take care!"

Ascending the hall, he said: "This mountain monk, while reading the *Huayan Jinsiierzhang* (The Golden Lion Chapter of the Avatamsaka), came upon the ninth section, 'The Gate of Skillful Accomplishment through the Revolution of Mind.
It further explains: 'It is like a one-foot mirror that receives a multitude of layered reflections.

If this is so, then it is acceptable to say it exists; it is acceptable to say it does not exist; it is acceptable to say it is neither; and it is acceptable to say it is both. Nevertheless, even though it is thus, furthermore—"
"You must know that there is a single aperture at the tip of the staff. If you do not understand this, the staff will pass through the lanterns and enter the Buddha hall;
it will strike Śākyamuni and knock down Maitreya, while the pillar claps its hands and laughs aloud.
Tell me, what is it that he laughs at? He struck the ground once with the staff and then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised [the following] case: A former master said, "In my early years, I accumulated learning; I also once investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and treatises.
Discerning names and characteristics, I knew not when to stop; entering the sea to count the sands, I merely exhausted myself in vain.
I was then bitterly rebuked by the Tathāgata: 'What benefit is there in enumerating the treasures of others? Now I ask you all: what are your own treasures?"
If you do not understand, the staff will go forth to cry out its grievance. *Knocks the staff once.* "Take care. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Through the eternal night and clear evening, what is there to do?
The green water flows on, never ceasing in the mountain stream; white clouds drift in fragments, flying over the ridges. Take care."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The former masters said: 'From ancient times to the present, it has never fallen; it is clearly before one's eyes. A single cloud arises in the late valley;
a solitary crane descends from the distant sky. The willows by the bank hold smoke-green; the flowers by the stream are fresh with rain.
Who understands this meaning? It makes me recall Nanquan. The Master said: "Tell me, what was Nanquan’s meaning? After a long pause, he said:
The two eyes have already closed along with the blue peaks;
the double brows still wear the frown of wild flowers. Be careful.
[Ascending the hall,] the Master raised his staff and said: "I, this mountain monk, call this thing..."
"O staff! You people, what do you call 'the objective realm'? If you can say it, I, this mountain monk, have a phrase that penetrates all directions;
if you cannot say it, I shall give you seven hundred coins. Take care!"

Ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, even if one’s eloquence were like a cascading torrent and one’s wisdom like flowing water, it would still have no connection to that reality.
Formerly, a monk asked Master Fengxue, 'What is the Way? The Master replied, 'Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion.
[The monk asked,] 'What is one who is on the Way? The Master replied, 'Ask the City Guardian. The Way and the one on the Way—"
"A man of average capacity—how far apart are they? The Master said, "The moon is like a mirror in a gauze screen; the stars are like lamps in the mist.
The Master continued, "There has been much deliberation among the assembly on this. Today, I shall provide you with a verse for it:
'The moon is like a mirror in a gauze screen; The stars are like lamps in the mist. The pure assembly filling the hall— They are all monks sitting in meditation. Take care!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "As the World-Honored One Śākyamuni said: 'One should know thus, see thus, and believe and understand thus, so as not to give rise to the marks of dharmas.
The Master then picked up his staff and said: 'I, this mountain monk, call this thing a "staff. What here is a "mark of dharma"?
He struck the ground with the staff and descended from the seat."
Ascending the hall, he said: "I have always told everyone: to conceive a thought is to err; to stir a single念 (mental movement) is to be mistaken.
Without conceiving or being mistaken, I leave you all free to criticize and dissect it as you please. But tell me, what is there to criticize and dissect? After a long pause, he said:
I suspect you were not made of gold teeth; how else could you draw your bow to shoot Wei-chi? Ascending the hall, he raised a case:
A monk asked Caoshan, "The snow covers the thousand peaks; why does the solitary peak stand out alone?

Caoshan said, "You must know there is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary. The monk pressed further, "What is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary? Caoshan said, "It is not covered."
Qianshan Peak. The Master said: "Caoshan’s compassion is profound and thick; he guides all sentient beings. If you wish to understand him, it cannot be done.
Here in my place, it is not so. What is the 'extraordinary within the extraordinary'? Petal by petal, plum blossoms fly down to the ground. Be careful."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "At times, this mountain monk uses a single blow of the staff as a net that covers the heavens to strike the handsome hawks and falcons;
at times, he uses a single blow as a fine-meshed net to scoop for shrimp and gather clams;
at times, he uses a single blow as a golden-maned lion; and at times, he uses a single blow as a frog or an earthworm. This mountain monk strikes you all."

"A single blow. But how shall we deliberate upon this? If you can distinguish the black from the white, then it will be no hindrance for the eye at the tip of the staff to open and illuminate the four quarters of the world.
If you have not yet attained this, let it remain standing by the side of an ancient screen, waiting for the brush and ink to enter the painted image. Be careful."
Ascending the hall, he raised an example: "Whenever Luzu saw a monk coming, he would simply sit facing the wall. Among the assembly, there was much discussion on this point.
My late teacher, under whom I studied at Liangshan, once had a verse: 'Luzu’s samādhi is most effortless; as soon as he sees a monk coming, he faces the wall.
If one is of like mind and has realized the Way, there is no need for a raised brow to understand each other.'"
I, this mountain monk, am not like that. The Patriarch faced the wall and spread his influence throughout all quarters; countless Zen practitioners vainly attempt to measure it.
With nothing to do, I stand late in the evening by the river, where several withered cypress trees lean against the setting sun. Take care.
The Master raised this case: Once, while traveling on pilgrimage, he was engaged in discussion with an elder among the assembly.

He then cited this: A monk asked Master Changsha, "Where has Nanquan gone after his passing? Changsha said, "He became a donkey at the eastern neighbor's house and a horse at the western neighbor's house.
The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is the case? Changsha said, "If you want to ride him, ride; if you want to dismount, dismount."
The venerable elder then asked the Master, "Is it not responding to his words? The Master said, "No. "Is it not fulfilling his question?
The Master said, "No. "Is it not pointing out his words? The Master said, "No. "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said:
After the sound of the *qing* bell has ceased, one is not permitted to change the price. Thereupon, he composed a verse and showed it to the assembly, saying: "If you wish to ride, then ride;
if you wish to dismount, then dismount. After the sound of the *qing* bell has ceased, one is not permitted to change the price."

The Master ascended the hall, held up his staff, and showed it to the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas and World-Honored Ones of old said, 'To contemplate the emptiness of the nature of phenomena is the supreme wisdom.
I, this mountain monk, call this very thing a 'staff. How do you all contemplate it? Those with wisdom do not require advanced age;
those without wisdom labor in vain for a hundred years. He struck the ground with the staff and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The ancients said: 'Sometimes there is illumination first and function later;

sometimes there is function first and illumination later; sometimes illumination and function are simultaneous; and sometimes illumination and function are not simultaneous. If it is illumination first and function later, one reveals the claws and fangs of the lion-king.
If it is function first and illumination later, one unleashes the majestic ferocity of the elephant-king. If it is illumination..."
When simultaneous function occurs, it is like a dragon obtaining water, bringing forth rain and surging clouds.

If illumination and function were not simultaneous, it would be like lifting up a pampered child or caressing a beloved son. O virtuous ones, is this the way the ancient masters established the Dharma gates? Is it indeed thus?
It is not fitting to be thus. If one were to be thus, it would be like Ji Xin mounting the nine-dragon carriage. It is not fitting to be thus.
If it were like Xiang Yu losing his thousand-li steed, Wui, would there still be anyone to vent their indignation on behalf of Langya? If there were none—how could this be right?
The mountain monk speaks for himself and departs. He plants his staff upright and descends from the seat.
Entering the hall, he says: "A student of the Way must not be obstructed by nature or characteristics before they can succeed. If one speaks of nature..."
To speak of characteristics is to be stuck in characteristics; to speak of nature is to be stuck in nature.

Here, one must have both nature and characteristics completely vanish, and principle and phenomena merged into one, before one can understand that "phenomena are principle" and "nature is characteristics.
At such a time, it is like ten fingers on a fist—extending or contracting at will. Then, picking up his staff, he said: "The staff has gone off to Silla and Goryeo!"
While in the midst of the assembly, he became heavily intoxicated and announced, "This year the price of rice is high; the earth spirits resent this and have given rise to anger.
My staff is now entering the earth! He then threw down his staff and descended from his seat. A monk asked, "What is it like when the Great Matter has not yet been resolved? The Master said:
The golden lamp shines through the night; one does not notice the bell of the fifth watch. A student asked, "What is it like when the Great Matter has already been accomplished?

The Master said, "Only when walking barefoot upon ice and snow does one realize the cold that penetrates to the very bone. A student asked, "To speak of the Truth is to oppose the mundane; to follow the mundane is to deviate from the Truth.
Apart from these two paths, I ask the Master to proclaim the Dharma. The Master said, "The stone ox roars from the bottom of the water; the auspicious [deer] is within the wood."
The flowers bloom. The student says, "If that is so, were it not for observing the Big Dipper, how could one see the Southern Star?

The Master says, "In times of chaos, slaves deceive their masters; in years of decline, ghosts play with people. He then lets him off with thirty blows of the staff. He then cites Master Dayang’s address to the assembly:
"The phrase of ordinary non-arising; the wondrous, subtle, and impartial phrase; the phrase of the luminous and inexhaustible essence. Afterward, there was...
A monk requested instruction, asking: "What is the phrase of ordinary non-arising? "White clouds cover the green mountains; the summit of the green mountain is not revealed.

"What is the phrase of wondrous mystery and lack of partiality? "In the jeweled palace, there is no one who does not stand in attendance; by not planting the *wú-tóng* tree, one avoids the arrival of the phoenix.
"What is the phrase of the luminous essence that is inexhaustible? "When the finger points to space, heaven and earth turn; returning along the path..."
The stone horse emerges from the gauze cage—this, you must express in the first phrase. The lion yawns—this, you must express in the second phrase.
The lion crouches on the ground—this, you must express in the third phrase. When it comes to its leaping forth, it pervades the ten directions;
when it comes to its seizing, it sits in one place. At this very moment, how will you understand? If you cannot understand, come forward!
In the morning, he went again to see the King of Chu, then descended from his seat.
Entering the hall, he said: "Yesterday, because a practitioner requested instruction on the Three Phrases of Master Dayang of Yingzhou, I spoke.
As I once attended upon him as his attendant, today I must not fail to repay that kindness of Dayang."
The Master has departed. This mountain monk also has three phrases. What is the phrase of ordinary non-arising?

Before words, there is no definitive meaning; after the phrase, all seeking ceases. What is the phrase of wondrous mystery and lack of self-interest? The golden phoenix does not perch on a shadowless tree;
how could the jade hare ever descend from the azure heavens? What is the phrase of luminous essence that is inexhaustible? Three...
In winter, the withered tree puts forth its splendor; in the ninth month of summer, the snowflakes are red.
With these three turning words, I offer them to Master Dayang. Nevertheless, one must not fail my late teacher Fenyang.
This mountain monk also has three turning words to offer to my late teacher Fenyang. What is the phrase of ordinary non-arising? *Chui*! (A spurt/splash). As if...

"What is the wondrous, profound, and impartial phrase? *Zhuo* (Peck). What is the phrase of the luminous essence that is inexhaustible? *Hao* (Good). The Master then spoke in verse: "Pecking and striking—how good!
In the forest, the Three Elders were questioned; They did not eat the peaches of the Queen Mother of the West, But possessed the jujubes of the immortals themselves.
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised an example, saying: "An old master said, 'Linji’s shouting as soon as he entered the gate is like striking the bell after a meal;
Deshan’s staff as soon as he entered the gate is like falling into a pit on level ground.

You gentlemen might say, 'This is fortunately a matter of no concern,' but you are merely gouging sores onto healthy flesh and forcibly creating knots upon branches. With such a view, how much more..."
"You must buy twenty or thirty pairs of straw sandals before you can even begin. Furthermore, there was a certain elder who said:

"When Linji enters the gate, he shouts; when Deshan enters the gate, he strikes. Reaching this point, the paths of ordinary and sage are cut off; not even a hair's breadth is established. He cuts off the tongues of everyone in the world.
If you hesitate or deliberate, you will lose your body and forfeit your life. Such a view as this is... [a mere drop].
It is difficult for water to be digested. Therefore, the former master said: "Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout alone shake the universe and sweep across all things.
Langya, however, was not like this: "When Linji enters the gate, he shouts; you must not be careless. When Deshan enters the gate, he strikes with his staff; you must be even more meticulous.
But what does he mean by telling you all to be meticulous? He says: [The text here appears to be incomplete or ends abruptly.]
"Detention of prisoners increases wisdom; nursing of the sick ruins the body. [The Master] struck once with his staff and ascended the hall.
Holding up the staff, he said: "The descent of the Buddhas of the ten directions occurs upon the tip of this staff.
The turning of the Great Dharma Wheel occurs upon the tip of this staff. Their entry into Parinirvāṇa also occurs upon the tip of this staff. You..."
"How do you all thoroughly understand this? After a long silence, he said, "One must not wait for conditions to seek fish from dry wood; when seeing danger, one must risk one's life.
He struck the meditation staff once and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Now, those who study must have their eye of wisdom opened and clarified before they can succeed.

Case: Yantou asked Deshan, "Is this ordinary or is it holy? Deshan then gave a shout, and Yantou bowed.

Case: Xinghua said, "This single stick of incense—had I intended to succeed Sansheng, Sansheng would have been too remote for me;

Case: A monk asked Shushan, “What is the Dharma-body? Shushan said, “A withered stump. The monk asked, “What is that which transcends the Dharma-body?

[The monk] asked everywhere. Caoshan then struck him. Again, a monk asked Caoshan, "What is it like when the full moon draws its bow?
The Master said, "A skilled archer misses the mark. The student asked, "Why does he miss the mark? The Master said, "If it comes from the left, he hits the left;

Case: A monk asked Master Dongshan Chu, “What is the Way? Dongshan said, “A table leg. The monk said, “What if I try to reach for it?

Case: Yunmen said, "When Old Śākyamuni was first born, he looked in the four directions, pointed one finger at heaven and one finger at the earth, and declared:

The Master held up [the case] and said: "To offer this body and mind to every dust-mote world—that is precisely what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
He then cited Caoshan: "Do not travel the path where the mind dwells; do not don the garment of original nature. Why need one act further in such a way?
One must strictly avoid the time before birth."
The Master held up his staff and said, "How do you express the phrase that does not harm the meaning of things?

Case: Chan Master Xian addressed the assembly, saying: "When thoughts do not arise, there is originally no substance.
When the great function manifests, time and season are not mentioned. Later, when he was about to pass away, he asked his attendant, "Who is it that sits?
The attendant replied, "Sengga. He asked again, "Who is it that stands? The attendant replied, "Senghui. Thereupon, Chan Master Xian walked seven paces and lowered [his head].
He passed away with his hand [extended].

When Zhaozhou was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at a country temple. After staying for ten days, as he was about to depart, he took leave of the temple master. The temple master—
The abbot asked, "Where are you going? Zhaozhou replied, "I am going to Mount Tai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī. The head monk said, "I have a verse to see you off, which says:
'Where are the green mountains that are not sites of enlightenment? One must surely take up the staff to pay homage at Qingliang.
Even if a golden-haired lion appears amidst the clouds, when viewed with the True Eye, it is no auspicious sign. Zhaozhou then asked, "What is this?"
"Right Eye. The head monk was speechless.
The Master picked up the case and said: "Crying until the blood flows is of no use.
He then cited the following: Once, when Miceang and Baoshou were attending a banquet hosted by the Provincial Governor, the Governor ordered the guest master to deliver a message, requesting—

Excerpt. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The various bodhisattvas each spoke of the dharma-gate of non-duality. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī said:

Citation: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that Subhūti asked Śāriputra, "What constitutes the Buddha-eye? Śāriputra replied, "Emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) constitutes the Buddha-eye.

The Master picked up the case and said: "Looking toward heaven, one does not see heaven; looking at the earth, one does not see the earth.

The Master picked up the point and said: "It is fundamentally pure and serene;

how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? He then cited Master Zhao: "The whirlwind topples the mountains yet they remain eternally still; the rivers rush toward one another yet do not flow;

The Master held up the case and said: "Master Zhao spoke in this way, yet he too is a man who falls into the pitfalls of the level ground.

Case: When Wuzhuo arrived at Mount Wutai in the presence of Mañjuśrī, they were drinking tea together.

Mañjuśrī said, "What do you usually use to drink your tea? Wuzhuo then simply withdrew.
The Master held up [the staff] and said: "If you say it is so, it can be called snatching food from the tiger's mouth;

Miaoyan laughed heartily and returned to his quarters. That evening, he ascended the hall and said to the assembly, "There are worms in the rice!"

He then cited the following: When Head Seat Tai arrived at Dongshan’s place, Dongshan personally attended to him by arranging fruit for him in the evening.
Dongshan then asked, "Head Seat, there is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth; it is as black as lacquer and is always in motion."
"Within activity. It cannot be contained within activity. Tell me, where does the fault lie? The Head Seat said, "The fault lies within activity.
Dongshan called out, "Attendant! Take away the fruit table; you shall not eat the fruit."

Case: Shuilao Can asked the Great Master Mazu, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
He was kicked down by Mazu; upon rising, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily. He attained great enlightenment on the spot and subsequently became a successor to the Great Master Mazu.
Later, when he was residing there, a monk asked, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Shuilao said, “Since then...”
After the Master of Horses gave him one kick, he has been laughing without ceasing until this very day.
The Master took up the case, saying: "Venerable assembly, tell me: did Shuilao ever attain enlightenment or not?"
Case: Layman Pang asked Master Ma, "The original body is not obscure; I ask the Master to cast his eyes high. Master Ma looked straight down.
The Layman said, "This is a single-stringed lute; only you, Master, can play it wondrously.
Master Ma looked straight up. The Layman then bowed. Master Ma immediately returned to his quarters, and the Layman followed him in.
The Abbot said within the quarters, "Seeking cleverness, one obtains clumsiness.
The Master commented, "He committed a theft all night long, unaware that dawn had broken.
He then cited the following: When Nan-yuan saw a monk approaching, he held up his whisk. The monk said, "A failure. Nan-yuan lowered his whisk.
The monk said, "There is still this one remaining. Nan-yuan then stopped. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented:
"A mad dog chasing a clod of earth; a lion biting a man. He then cited the case:
Nanquan addressed the assembly, saying, "The Way is not outside of things; that which is outside of things is not the Way. At that time, Zhaozhou came forward.
He then asked, "What is the Way beyond things? Nanquan struck him. Zhaozhou caught the staff and said, "Preceptor, do not strike me;
there may be others later whom you will strike in error. Nanquan said, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes, but difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk.
He then threw down the staff and returned to his quarters.
The Master held up the case and said: "Has it not been said: 'When wine meets a kindred spirit, it is drunk; when poetry meets one who understands, it is recited'? He then cited the following:
Shunde asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "From Sanfeng. Shunde said, "Where did you spend the summer retreat?
The monk replied, "At Wufeng. Shunde said, "I grant you thirty blows! The monk asked, "I do not know yet—where does my fault lie?"
"What place? De-yun asked. "I shall lead you out of one thicket and into another.
The Master commented: "A sickle for cutting vegetables. Case:
A monk asked Guang-de, "What is the Buddha? De replied, "The painted halberd gate opens and one sees the falling immortal. The monk hurried away.
These words reached Wukong at the prefectural seat. [Guangde] asked, "The painted halberd gate opens and one sees the falling immortal—what is the meaning of this?
Wukong replied, "Even if you were to see Śākyamuni in person, the wise would all say he is not the Buddha.
Later, when Guangde heard of this, he gazed toward the city from afar and prostrated, saying, "Wukong is an ancient Buddha; how could it have been merely twenty sheep?"
The Master picked up the case and said: "Guangde drives in a nail behind the head; Wugong pulls out a wedge from the eye.
Although they were skillfully in accord with the occasion, I dare say their own houses were not yet thoroughly penetrated."
Case: While Xuefeng and Xuansha were walking along, Xuefeng pointed to a patch of ground and said, "A fine place to build a seamless stupa.
Xuansha asked, "How high should it be? Xuefeng looked up and then looked down.

Xuansha said, "While the karmic rewards of humans and devas are certainly not lacking, as for the prediction of enlightenment at Vulture Peak, you have not even dreamed of it yet. Xuefeng asked, "What about you? Xuansha—
[The Master] knocks on the sedan chair and says:
"Lift! Lift! The Master comments: "At Guoqing, the talented are noble; in a wealthy household, the young child is cherished.
He then cites the case of the Hermit of Tongfeng: An old man came to visit him, and the Hermit asked, "Where have you come from? The old man—
"Not so," the Master said. "Excellent at responding to the occasion! Excellent at responding to the occasion! The old man then picked up a blade of grass and showed it to the Abbot;
the Abbot gave a shout, and the old man bowed. The Abbot then returned to his hut.
Following after him, the old man looked at the Abbot and said, "In this way, you leave the whole world in doubt."
The Master picked up [the case] and said: "Has it not been said? 'If one should cut but does not cut, one will instead suffer from the resulting chaos.

The Verse on the Ancient Case by the Monk Donglin and the Hermit Yunmen, recorded by Attendant Wuben:
Before the World-Honored One left Tuṣita Heaven, he had already descended into the royal palace; before he emerged from his mother’s womb, he had already saved sentient beings.
The discourse on man is finished.
A verse by Donglin:
"Entering crosswise into the sea of right and wrong, Wandering freely amidst a pack of jackals and tigers. Do not bring right and wrong to judge it."
I have spent my life carving and boring through things that are unrelated.
Yunmen’s verse says:
"There is honey on a sharp blade, do not lick it; there is water in a house of venomous spirits, do not taste it. Do not lick, do not taste—both are avoided."
[The Master] committed [an offense]. With a dignified air, he returned to his hometown wearing brocade robes.

Case: As soon as the World-Honored One was born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, walked seven steps, looked around in the four directions, and said: "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the most honored."
The Donglin Verse:
Even the Old Barbarian could not avoid emerging from the womb; He too came before people in such a manner. Pointing to the earth, pointing to the heavens, he claimed to be number one;
Sentient beings suffered for forty-nine years.
Yunmen’s Verse:
As soon as this old fellow was born, he was already in a hurry; He took seven steps, acting like one who has lost his mind.
He has deceived countless foolish men and women, Who open their eyes wide and enter the boiling cauldron.
Case: When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude.
At that time, the assembly was all at a loss, except for the Venerable Kāśyapa, who broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa."
Donglin’s Verse:
The sea waters overturn the void, surging as a bottomless current; Fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs drift up and down by their own accord.
Pitiful is the golden-colored ascetic, Who even unto this day has not ceased his laughter.
Yunmen’s Verse:

Holding up a single branch of flowers, The true lineage style flows forth from within the house. If one speaks of the transmission of the mind-dharma, Matters throughout the world are as numerous as hemp seeds.

Case: An outsider asked the Buddha, "I do not ask for words, nor do I ask for wordlessness. The World-Honored One— *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "世尊良" (The World-Honored One...). This appears to be the opening of the well-known kōan regarding the silence of the Buddha.*
After a long time, the outsider offered praise, saying, "The World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter.
He prostrated himself and departed. Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What realization did the outsider have that he said he had 'entered'?
The Buddha replied, "It is like a fine horse that, upon seeing the whip..."
Walking in shadows.
A verse by Donglin:
Before the skull of delusion and enlightenment, it is but a vain effort to raise the whip again; one merely maintains the precepts of chickens and dogs, and does not study the Chan of the Patriarchs.
Yunmen’s Verse:

At both places, the sturdy barriers strike and do not pass through; Without the slightest movement of dust, one naturally deviates from the source. Suddenly, the karmic mirror shatters into a hundred fragments;
The Yellow-Faced Gautama loses his trace.
Citing the Great Master Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall, Donglin’s verse says:
"Before the mountain of Shaoshi, the wind passes by the ear; For nine years, human affairs have followed the flowing stream. If this were not playing in the tide," [it would be nothing at all].
O people! You must by all means refrain from entering the surging waves.
Yunmen’s verse says:
"When the golden tortoise once pulls [the net], the vast ocean is exhausted; in vain one drifts aimlessly upon a small boat. Today, amidst the misty waves, there is nothing to be found.
Fishing: There is no need for a new moon to serve as a hook.
Lifting [the theme]: The Second Patriarch stood in the snow for a long time. Bodhidharma asked him, "What do you seek?
The Second Patriarch said, "I beg the Master to pacify my mind. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall pacify it for you."
The Second Patriarch remained silent for a long while and said, "I have searched for the mind, but it is utterly unattainable. Bodhidharma said, "I have finished settling your mind for you.
Donglin’s verse:
When the Second Patriarch established Shaolin in his day, snow accumulated in the courtyard deep as the waist. With hands folded at his chest, there was nothing to do;
he neither sought nor searched, nor did he settle his mind.
Yunmen’s Verse:
Seeking the mind, there is nowhere it can rest; I have chewed to pieces a ball of glowing red iron.
Even if you were to open your eyes and display your spirit, How could you compare to one who is not deceived by the Old Barbarian?
Case: Once, when the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, there was a woman sitting near the Buddha who entered into samādhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "Why is it that this woman is permitted to sit near the Buddha while I am not?
The Buddha said, "Simply awaken this woman and cause her to emerge from samādhi."
"Arise! You shall experience this yourself. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times, snapped his fingers once, and then lifted her up to the Brahma Heaven;
yet, despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he was unable to bring her back down. The World-Honored One said:
"Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they would likewise be unable to bring this woman out of her samādhi.
Forty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of lands below here, there is the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti (Maming), who can bring this woman out of her samādhi.
In an instant, Vimalakīrti emerged from the earth, prostrated to the World-Honored One, and said:
The World-Honored One commanded Wangming to bring this woman out of samādhi.
Wangming went before the woman and snapped his fingers once; thereupon, the woman emerged from her samādhi.
Later, an elder asked a monk, "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas. Why did he bring this woman out of samādhi?"
It certainly could not have been attained [by others]. It was precisely because Wangming was so exceptional that he was able to emerge from it.
Donglin’s verse says:
"Without relying on Mañjuśrī’s supernatural powers, there is no need for Wangming to snap his fingers. At that moment, in the assembly on Vulture Peak, the woman...
Arising from meditative concentration, Yunmen’s verse says:
"To emerge or not to emerge—this is concentration, but not the true concentration. Wuming and Mañjuśrī have both lost their very lives."
Case: One day, Master Rang said, "Daoxi is preaching the Dharma for people in Jiangxi, yet I have not received a single word from him. He then dispatched a monk to Mazu’s place.
He waited to see him ascend the hall and simply went forward to ask, "How is it? He told the monk, "Wait until he speaks, and then remember what he says.
The monk followed these instructions and went to question him.
The Patriarch said, "Since the time of chaos, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce."
Donglin’s Verse:
"For thirty years I have been at a loss; there has not been so much as a pinch of salt or a drop of sauce. The Great Master Mazu of Jiangxi and Reverend Letan of Nanyue.
Yunmen’s Verse:
When seen with clarity, one recognizes the intimate; yet even bringing it forth still involves a long journey.
Even those who do not err by so much as a hair’s breadth are merely people licking their fingers after picking up crumbs.
Case: Baizhang visited Mazu for a second time. Mazu held up his whisk. Baizhang said, "Is it used right here?
Or is it apart from this? Mazu hung the whisk back in its original place.
After a long silence, Mazu said, "In the future, when you open your two flaps of skin [to speak], with what will you save people? Baizhang took up the whisk and held it up.
The Patriarch said, "Is it this very function? Is it apart from this function? Baizhang then hung his whisk back in its original place.
The Patriarch then gave a shout, which left Baizhang deaf for three days straight.
Donglin’s Verse:
A single shout from Jiangxi shakes heaven and earth; The full power of the Great Function is the extinction of the lineage.
Three days of deafness as the wind passes through the trees— It brings disaster upon Huangbo, causing him to lose his descendants.
Yunmen’s Verse:
The horse’s neighing has extinguished the family wind; From this point on, news shall pass through the four seas.
To grasp the moon from within a fierce flame— Majestically, he sits alone atop the Great Hero Peak.
Case: One day National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang called to his attendant. The attendant responded.
This was repeated three times, with the attendant responding each time. The National Teacher said, "I thought it was I who was failing you;
it turns out it is you who are failing me."

On the worldly path, amidst wind and waves, I have not seen you; Each time we meet, my spirit is wounded. I know not where the flowing water and falling flowers have gone;
Beyond the mountain cave, the Peach Blossom Spring is a springtime all its own.
Yunmen’s Verse:
A mute person has a dream—whom can they tell it to? Rising up, they face one another, eyes dazed and blurred.
They have already laid bare their innermost hearts before others; Let them now seek their own advantage.

Shushan asked, "What if the tree suddenly falls and the vine withers? Guishan laughed heartily and returned to his quarters.
Shushan followed him, saying, "I have sold my hemp cloth for three thousand *li*!"
"Single-mindedly! I have come specifically for this matter. How could you, Reverend, deceive me?
Guishan then called to his attendant and said, "Bring some money to give to this elder.
He then instructed him, saying, "In the future, there will be a 'One-Eyed Dragon' who will come to pierce through [his delusions] for you. Later, he heard that Mingzhao had appeared in the world.
He went straight to pay his respects. Zhao asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the Seven Circuits of Min.
Zhao said, "Have you ever been to Dayue? He replied, "I have. Zhao asked, "What words or sayings did Dayue have? Shanshan then recounted the previous conversation.
Zhao said, "Dayue’s head is right and his tail is right; it is simply that he did not meet a true connoisseur. Shanshan...

A phrase, no phrase—a vine leaning against a tree. Originally, white rice is made from grain. A flute is blown atop a high tower;
willows are like mist. Spring winds fill the earth as flying花絮 fall.

If one were to use these words to fix the fundamental principle, One would fail the Mingzhao, the One-Eyed Dragon. Suddenly, within a smile, the paths of mud and water are divided;
Only then does one know that from a thousand miles away, we share the same wind.

The seventh [case]: The *yutu* has lost its tail; The breath of one who devours an ox is already enough to boast of. The monastic communities clamor and dispute with their lips and mouths;
How many travelers will actually reach home?
Case: Nanquan addressed the assembly, saying, "The Great Master Mazu of Jiangxi says, 'This very mind is Buddha.
I, Old Wang, do not speak thus. It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
In speaking this way, is there any fault?"
The Donglin Verse:
Lifting up the whisk, he traveled thirty thousand li; Now, he has rested for eight thousand years.
I shall clearly raise it once more from the beginning, Leaving it to all quarters to transmit it as they please.
Yunmen’s Verse:
I have emptied my belly and poured out my heart to tell you; I do not know for what reason you still linger in hesitation.
Now, seize it with sudden force, And entrust it to those in the world who are free from affairs.
Case: Master Nanquan addressed the assembly, saying, "The mind is not the Buddha;
wisdom is not the Way. Donglin’s verse comments:
"The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. Green mountains and white clouds; falling flowers and fragrant grasses. If you are truly quick-witted..."
Master, you will never turn your head or change your mind.
Yunmen’s verse says:

After the rain has scattered and the clouds have cleared, There stand over thirty towering peaks. Leaning on the railing, looking back again and again— To whom do you turn your head? To whom do you return?
Case: Huangbo addressed the assembly, saying, "All of you here are nothing but wine-dregs swillers.
Traveling on pilgrimage like this, how could you have reached this day? Do you know that within the Great Tang Empire there are no Zen masters?
At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "As for those in various quarters who guide disciples and lead assemblies..."
"Furthermore, what do you say? Huangbo replied, "I do not say there are no Chan masters; it is simply that there are no teachers. Donglin’s verse says:
"In the land of the Great Tang, there are no Chan masters; Having paid obeisance, they return to their quarters without further doubt. How laughable is the bride of Heyang!"
My son, you are not like that little page of Linji.

"Only by putting on clothes upon one's body can one avoid the cold; merely speaking of food with one's mouth will never satisfy one's hunger. Within the Great Tang Empire, there is an old woman.
Zen. Today I have explained it through for you.

Donglin’s verse on this is:
A single shout reaches up to the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven; Linji originally did not understand Chan.
Everyone says the morning sun rises outside the door, yet they do not know the night moon falls before the steps.
Yunmen’s Verse:
“Upon entering the gate, he immediately shouts; he has no clue at all. He has led his descendants to dally with the vapors of rice and gruel.
Case: While Linji was sitting, Magu asked him, “Of the twelve-faced Avalokiteśvara, which one is it?”
From the front: Mazu descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Where has the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara gone?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Magu turned around and sat upon the meditation seat. Mazu took up his staff and struck him;
Magu caught it, and they grappled each other back to the abbot's quarters.
The Donglin Verse:
The Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara reveals his true face; An official does not permit even a needle, yet a single thread passes through. The rat drags the gourd—how busy he is!
The ghost contends over the lacquer bucket—no one can praise it.
Yunmen’s Verse:
Blinding oneself to that one move right before one’s eyes, Dragging it here and there, the teeth are bared.
If one does not know the hand of Wang Wei, Who else could paint it to completion?
Case: Linji asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk immediately shouted. Linji bowed and motioned him to sit. The monk hesitated;
Linji struck him. Another monk came; Linji held up his whisk. The monk prostrated; Linji struck him. Yet another monk arrived;
Linji stood there holding up his whisk. The monk did not [respond].
Guru: "Ji also struck.
Donglin’s Verse:
Both host and guest fall into the third mechanism; In every formation they raise their banners, yet do not unfurl them. Within the flash of a stone-tossing spark, victory is divided.
Failure. Riding backward upon an iron horse to Mount Sumeru.
Yunmen’s verse:
Written at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month; may all malicious mouths and venomous tongues be utterly eliminated. Furthermore, with even greater urgency, act according to the law.
[The Master] gave an order: "There is no need to paint a spider on the gate.
[Later,] Linji said: "Upon this ball of red flesh, there is a true person of no station who is constantly entering and exiting the gates of your faces.
Those of you who have not yet realized this—look! Look! At that time, there was...
A monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the true person of no station? Linji descended from his meditation seat, seized the monk, and said, "Speak!
Speak! As the monk hesitated, Linji pushed him away and said, "What is this 'true person of no station'?
It is nothing but a dried-up piece of shit!"
*East Lin Gatha*:
Entering and exiting through the gate of the face is difficult to perceive; The true person of no station is but a foot away. On the path ahead, one’s body is as light as a leaf;
One’s lofty reputation is as heavy as a mountain for a thousand ages.
Yunmen’s Verse:
Seeing the jowls behind the head—this rustic monk! He opens his eyes wide and yet dreams on. Though he manages to catch the rat, A single blow shatters the oil jar.
Case: Zhaozhou visited Linji. Just as Zhaozhou had finished washing his feet, Linji came down and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Zhaozhou said, "It happens to be the time when the old monk is washing his feet.
Linji stepped forward and listened intently. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, then understand; why do you keep picking at it? Linji shook him off.
Xuè immediately departed. Zhòu said, "For thirty years I have traveled as a mendicant, yet today I have mistakenly provided a commentary for others.
Dōnglín’s verse:
There is no further arrangement for washing feet; listening closely at such times is not a matter of mere grasping and chewing.
When the two elders Zhaozhou and Linji met, how could they ever have failed to provide their annotations?
Yunmen’s Verse:
One man’s eyes are like drumsticks; another’s head is like a wooden ladle. These two old fellows know no shame;
to this day there is nowhere to put them.
Case: Zhaozhou asked Nanquan, “What is the Way? Nanquan replied, “Ordinary mind is it.
Zhaozhou asked, “Is there still any need for directed effort? Nanquan said, “To intend to direct yourself is already to deviate. Zhaozhou said, [“...”]
He did not conceive of it. Furthermore, how could he know that this was the Way? Quan said, "The Way does not belong to knowing, nor does it belong to not-knowing.
Knowing is deluded perception and lacks clarity; how can one forcibly assert right and wrong?

Deep and shallow, I shall probe with my staff; Suddenly, waves and billows rise from level ground. The torrential cascade overturns the mountains, startling heaven and earth;

The old woman said, "Go straight ahead. As soon as the monk had walked three or five paces, the old woman said, "What a fine monk, yet you go off like that!

The next day he went there and asked her the same thing. The old woman—

Three punches struck back; seven slaps across the cheeks. All the people in the great earth know not of their pain or itching.

"The Chan practitioners of the world speak of 'testing and breaking through,' but who knows that Zhaozhou has already fallen into a trap? He leads his descendants astray."
Now, everyone is clever enough to lie down on cold ground.

The Master answered the question. Quan said: "Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window.
Donglin’s verse says:
"What is seen habitually before the eyes is ordinary; it neither startles nor endures for long. It remains in the cold window of the night."
The Moon. The third watch shines as ever upon the thatched hall.

Measuring the body to cut the robe, gauging the water to drive the pestle—not a hair’s breadth of error, yet you still remain outside the gate.

Zhaozhou said to his attendant, "Tell him to leave. As soon as the attendant told him to go, the novice said, "I take my leave" (*zhēnzhòng*).
Zhaozhou said to a monk beside him, "The śrāmaṇera has entered the gate; the attendant is outside the gate.
The Donglin Verse says:
"Having entered the gate, he is outside the gate; He speaks to people, yet people do not understand. He raises his voice even higher: 'I am deaf.'"
